hubs.title: Cost of living
hubs.question: Why does it cost so much to live here?
hubs.intro: Housing, groceries, electricity and insurance take the largest share of most household budgets. A landlord, a grocer, a utility or an insurer sets each of those prices, and public rules shape the market where they set it. Zoning decides how many homes can exist near jobs. A state utility commission rules on what a power company may charge, and in many states the insurance department reviews home insurance rates before they take effect. Interest rates, droughts, animal disease and storms push prices from outside any single office. Each pathway below follows one bill to the people who set it and to the offices that can change the rules behind it. It also reports what the evidence says about proposed responses.

hubs.title: Health and care
hubs.question: Why is care so hard to get and to pay for?
hubs.intro: Getting care depends on whether a plan or program will pay and whether a clinician, a child care center or a home care aide is available to provide it. Employers, insurers, state Medicaid agencies and Congress settle most of the payment question. Licensing rules, training slots and wages settle much of the availability question, and state legislatures, state boards and the federal programs that pay for care set those. Prices add another layer: hospitals and insurers negotiate them privately, and pharmacy benefit managers stand between drug makers and pharmacies. The pathways here start with an appointment, a bill, a child care slot or care for an aging parent, and trace each one to the office that controls the decision.

hubs.title: Work and financial security
hubs.question: Why doesn't my paycheck go further?
hubs.intro: What a household keeps depends on what it earns and on what taxes and benefits add or subtract. Employers set pay inside a labor market shaped by how many employers compete for workers, by minimum wage laws and by the rules that govern unions. Congress and state legislatures then decide how much of that pay goes to taxes and which households qualify for credits, food assistance or health coverage. Social Security replaces part of a worker's earnings in retirement or after a disability, under a formula Congress wrote and can change. These pathways show where each decision is made and how proposed changes would reach different households over different periods.

hubs.title: Public services where you live
hubs.question: Who keeps the water, roads and schools working?
hubs.intro: Drinking water, streets, buses and public schools are run close to home, usually by a city, a county, a special district or an elected school board. Much of the money and many of the rules come from farther away. Federal law sets drinking water standards and states enforce them. Federal formulas and state budgets pay for a large part of road and transit work, and state aid formulas decide much of what each school district can spend. When a pipe fails or a repair stalls, the office that answers the phone may not be the one that controls the budget. Each pathway names both and shows how a resident can bring a problem to the body able to fix it.

hubs.title: Voice, power and information
hubs.question: How do my vote and my voice reach the people who decide?
hubs.intro: Every pathway in this Atlas ends at an office: a council, a commission, a legislature or an agency. This topic asks how residents reach those offices and how much that contact matters. In many districts a primary with low turnout settles who holds the seat, so the general election decides little. Who draws district lines and when local elections are held both change whose views officials need to weigh, and so does the way campaigns are paid for. Technology raises a newer question, since software now sets some prices, screens job applicants, ranks the news people see and decides eligibility for some public benefits. The two pathways here explain those mechanisms and connect them to the model of accountability at the center of the Atlas.

pathways.title: Housing costs
pathways.question: Why did my rent go up?
also_answers: Why is buying a home out of reach?
Who decides which homes can be built?
Did large investors or rent-pricing software raise my rent?
pathways.short_answer: Rent rises when more households compete for a limited number of homes where they need to live. City and town councils adopt zoning rules that set how many homes each lot may hold, and planning boards apply them project by project; in many high-demand regions those rules keep building below demand. Asking rents for professionally managed apartments were 29% higher in early 2026 than in 2020. For buyers, the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose from $1,240 at the end of 2020 to $2,420 in late 2025 as prices and mortgage rates climbed, and rates passed 7% in October 2026.
pathways.scope_note: Mortgage rates and federal housing programs are national, while zoning, property taxes, landlord-tenant law and building codes are set by states and localities, so the weight of each mechanism differs from one region to the next. A single household's rent increase can follow a change of owner or a tight local market, and one bill cannot show which applied.

mechanisms.title: Local zoning sets how many homes can be built
mechanisms.text: City and town councils adopt zoning ordinances, and planning and zoning boards apply them to each proposal. The ordinance sets minimum lot sizes, height limits, parking requirements and whether a lot may hold more than one home. Where the rules allow fewer homes than people seek near jobs, builders cannot add supply as demand grows, and prices and rents absorb the difference. Glaeser and Gyourko (2018) treat the gap between home prices and the cost of building as a regulatory tax, and their review suggests that this tax exceeds the harms of new construction in many areas. Published estimates of the national shortage range from 3.7 million to 5.5 million homes; the Congressional Research Service notes that methods differ and that some analysts dispute that a national shortage exists.

mechanisms.title: Nearby owners speak most at discretionary hearings
mechanisms.text: Many proposals need a special permit or variance, so the board holds a public hearing before deciding. Einstein, Glick and Palmer coded thousands of comments at planning and zoning meetings and matched speakers to a voter file. Speakers were disproportionately older, male, longtime residents and homeowners, and they opposed new housing far more than the general public. Where councils are chosen in local elections held apart from November, fewer residents vote: on-cycle elections generally double local turnout, and a study of California cities found on-cycle electorates more representative by age, race and partisanship. The model shows the feedback as loop R8 (Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building), running through L38 (scarcity raises owners' equity) and L39 (owners with equity at stake press to limit building).

mechanisms.title: Interest rates raise payments and keep owners in place
mechanisms.text: The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee sets a short-term interest rate, and expectations about that rate move the long-term rates that mortgage lenders charge. The 30-year fixed rate averaged 7.04% in January 2025 and 6.23% in late 2025; Freddie Mac's weekly survey showed 7.40% on October 15, 2026. Higher rates also hold back the supply of existing homes for sale. Half of outstanding mortgages carry rates below 4%, and owners give up that rate when they sell. An FHFA staff study estimated that this lock-in prevented 1.33 million sales from the second quarter of 2022 through 2023 and raised prices 5.7%, more than offsetting the 3.3% decline that higher rates caused directly.

mechanisms.title: Building costs and the apartment cycle
mechanisms.text: Developers build when expected rents or sale prices cover land, materials, labor, financing and fees. Prices for combined inputs to residential construction rose 40% from January 2020 to spring 2026, by Bureau of Labor Statistics data compiled by Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies (JCHS), with steel mill products up 84%. Apartments started during the low-rate years opened in 2024, when 608,000 multifamily units were completed, the most since 1986. That wave met cooling demand: asking rents slipped 0.5% in the year to early 2026, and the rental vacancy rate reached 7.3%. The consumer price index for rent, which tracks all tenants' rents including renewals, rose 2.8% in the year to September 2026. Completions fell 20% in 2025 while starts rose 17%.

mechanisms.title: Landlords set rents, some with shared pricing software
mechanisms.text: Landlords set rents at each new lease and renewal, and many large landlords use software that recommends prices. The Justice Department and several states sued RealPage, alleging that landlords pooled nonpublic rent data through its software. A final judgment entered May 19, 2026 bars RealPage from using competitors' nonpublic data in live pricing, limits model training to data at least 12 months old and lasts seven years; the government sought no financial penalty. On September 30, 2026 the federal court in North Carolina ruled that the states' claims could proceed. One working paper found that buildings using such software cut rents faster in downturns and estimated a coordination markup of about $25 a month per unit across 4.2 million units.

mechanisms.title: Property taxes and insurance raise the cost of staying
mechanisms.text: Local assessors value each home, and local governments set property tax rates within limits in state law. For owners, these bills come on top of any mortgage payment and continue after it is paid off. Property taxes rose 31% nationally from 2019 to 2025, and average monthly home insurance premiums rose 72% to $201 over the same years, by ICE Mortgage Monitor data reported by JCHS. The number of cost-burdened homeowners, those spending more than 30% of income on housing, reached 20.7 million in 2024, or 24% of owners, up 4.0 million since 2019. Insurance pricing has its own causes, traced in the insurance pathway (PW04).

pathways.household_effects: Renters feel these mechanisms at renewal and when they move. In 2024, 22.7 million renter households (49%) spent more than 30% of income on housing, and 12.1 million spent more than half. Owners who locked in fixed-rate mortgages before 2022 often pay far less each month than recent buyers of similar homes, which keeps their costs down and raises the cost of moving. A buyer needed about $120,800 a year in income to afford the median-priced home at the end of 2025, up from $68,700 five years earlier. Among homeowners, households headed by someone 65 or older had the highest cost-burden rate, 28%, as tax and insurance bills rose.

sub_issues.title: How big is the housing shortage?
sub_issues.text: Estimates published from 2020 to 2024 put the national shortfall at 3.7 million homes (Freddie Mac), 3.85 million (Up for Growth), 4.7 million (Zillow), 4.9 million (Brookings) or 5.5 million (National Association of Realtors). The Congressional Research Service traces the spread to different target vacancy rates, from 5% to 12%, and different base years. National totals say little about any one region, since shortages are uneven.

sub_issues.title: Do large investors drive up rents and prices?
sub_issues.text: The Government Accountability Office (GAO) reviewed 74 studies in 2024. It found that institutional investors may have contributed to higher prices and rents in some areas and helped stabilize neighborhoods after the 2008 crisis, with effects on homeownership unclear. In six metro areas GAO studied in 2026, investors owning at least 5,000 homes held 4% to 22% of single-family rentals and under 1% to 3% of all single-family homes. A federal law enacted July 11, 2026 bars investors that control 350 or more single-family homes from buying more, with exceptions such as homes built to rent.

sub_issues.title: Rent-pricing software rules in states and cities
sub_issues.text: New York made it unlawful in October 2025 to set rents on recommendations from software that coordinates competing landlords. California amended its antitrust law the same month to cover use of a common pricing algorithm in a conspiracy or to coerce others. San Francisco, Philadelphia, Minneapolis, Jersey City, Providence, San Diego, Hoboken and Seattle adopted local bans in 2024 and 2025, and Berkeley delayed its ban after RealPage sued. No evaluation yet measures how these laws change rents.

sub_issues.title: Help for renters with the lowest incomes
sub_issues.text: About one in four renter households earning no more than half the area median income receives a federal housing subsidy, and JCHS counts 13.8 million income-eligible households without one in 2023. Housing Choice Vouchers are run by local public housing agencies with funds Congress appropriates each year. The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) is allocated by states to developers who keep rents restricted. A 2025 tax law raised annual LIHTC allocations 12% from 2026 and eased a financing test for bond-funded projects.

sub_issues.title: Eviction and forced moves
sub_issues.text: When rent outpaces income, missed payments can lead to an eviction case in housing court. Using cases randomly assigned to judges of differing leniency in Cook County and New York City, Collinson and coauthors found that an eviction order increases homelessness and hospital visits and lowers earnings and access to credit over the following two years. Landlord-tenant law, including notice periods and any right to a lawyer, is set by state legislatures and, in some places, city councils.

sub_issues.title: Who owns a home, by age and race
sub_issues.text: In the second quarter of 2026, 35.2% of householders under 35 owned their homes, against 78.6% of those 65 and older. Ownership was 74.5% for non-Hispanic White householders, 45.4% for Black householders and 48.1% for Hispanic householders. JCHS reports that the Black-White gap of 28.7 percentage points in 2025 was wider than in 1995. The model traces how rising prices move owners' and renters' wealth apart in L38 (scarcity raises owners' equity) and LE25 (home equity is most owners' largest asset).

sub_issues.title: States that override local zoning
sub_issues.text: Oregon's 2019 law requires duplexes in cities over 10,000 people and other middle housing in cities over 25,000; Washington's 2023 law requires middle housing in areas once reserved for detached houses. Massachusetts requires multifamily zoning in communities served by the MBTA and listed 157 municipalities as compliant on August 27, 2026. Its Question 7, an initiative on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would allow single-family homes on lots of at least 5,000 square feet with public water and sewer. The 2026 federal housing law offers grants and nonbinding guidance and leaves zoning to states and localities.

decision_makers.who: City or town council (or county board where counties zone)
decision_makers.controls: Adopts and amends the zoning ordinance, including lot sizes, heights, parking rules and which housing types are allowed; sets the local property tax rate within state limits.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public comment at council meetings; agendas and minutes are posted by the city or town clerk. Find local officials through your city or county website or the USA.gov local government directory.

decision_makers.who: Planning board and zoning board of appeals
decision_makers.controls: Approves or denies site plans, special permits and variances under the existing ordinance, and recommends zoning changes to the council.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Speak or submit written comment at a public hearing; hearing notices are posted by the planning department and the city or town clerk.

decision_makers.who: Local assessor and board of assessment review
decision_makers.controls: Sets the assessed value of each property, to which the local tax rate is applied, and decides assessment appeals.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: File an abatement or assessment appeal with the assessor's office by the deadline printed on your tax bill or assessment notice.

decision_makers.controls: Write the zoning enabling law and can require localities to allow more homes; set property tax limits, landlord-tenant law and state antitrust rules on rent-pricing software.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your state senator and representative through your legislature's official website, and testify at committee hearings on housing bills.

decision_makers.who: State housing agency and housing finance agency
decision_makers.controls: Run state zoning-compliance programs where they exist and allocate federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits through a qualified allocation plan that sets which projects win credits.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Comment at the public hearing that federal tax law requires before a state adopts its qualified allocation plan; notices are posted on the agency's website.

decision_makers.who: Federal Open Market Committee of the Federal Reserve
decision_makers.controls: Sets the target for the federal funds rate, which influences mortgage rates through expectations about future short-term rates.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Statements and minutes are published at federalreserve.gov; members of Congress question the Fed Chair at semiannual monetary policy hearings.

decision_makers.controls: Sets the LIHTC through the tax code, appropriates voucher funding each year, and enacted the 2026 limit on large investors' purchases of single-family homes.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your U.S. representative and senators through the member directory at congress.gov/members.

decision_makers.controls: Writes the rules that carry out the 2026 limit on large investors' purchases of single-family homes, in consultation with HUD and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Comment on proposed rules at regulations.gov when they are published in the Federal Register.

decision_makers.who: HUD and local public housing agencies
decision_makers.controls: HUD sets voucher program rules and funds local public housing agencies, which issue vouchers and manage waiting lists.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Apply or join a waiting list through your local public housing agency, listed in HUD's public housing agency contact directory on hud.gov.

decision_makers.who: Justice Department Antitrust Division and state attorneys general
decision_makers.controls: Bring cases under federal and state antitrust law, including cases over shared rent data, and negotiate court-approved judgments.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Report suspected violations to the Antitrust Division's citizen complaint center on justice.gov or to your state attorney general's consumer protection office.

decision_makers.controls: Set rents at new leases and renewals within any local rent rules, and decide whether to use pricing software.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Ask for the terms of a renewal in writing; tenant complaints go to local housing offices where they exist or to the state attorney general.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: State legislatures hold the main authority over land use. Localities zone under state enabling laws, and a statute can require them to allow more homes, as Oregon (2019), Washington (2023) and Massachusetts, through its MBTA Communities law, have done. In states with citizen initiatives, voters can change those laws directly; Massachusetts voters decide Question 7 on November 3, 2026. City and town councils amend their own zoning ordinances and set property tax rates within state limits. Congress controls federal tax credits and voucher funding, and in Public Law 119-101 (July 11, 2026) it limited purchases by large single-family investors while leaving zoning to states and localities. The Federal Open Market Committee sets the short-term rate that shapes mortgage rates. The Justice Department and state attorneys general enforce antitrust law against shared rent data in court, and state legislatures and city councils have added their own bans.

responses.name: Allow more homes by right near jobs and transit
responses.what_it_does: A state law or local ordinance lets qualifying homes, such as duplexes, townhouses or apartments near transit, be approved when they meet published standards, without a separate discretionary hearing for each project. By-right approval means a building permit follows if the plans comply. Massachusetts's MBTA Communities law requires zoning for multifamily homes near transit, and Oregon and Washington require middle housing in many residential areas. Auckland, New Zealand upzoned about three-quarters of its residential land in 2016, a large test of the approach.
responses.requires: State legislatures can preempt local limits, and councils can amend their own ordinances. It works when the standards are clear, when the state checks that cities allow the homes in practice and not only on paper, when permit offices have enough staff, and when water, sewer and school systems can serve more residents. Direct public cost is small; infrastructure for added residents can be costly. Results arrive over several years as permits turn into completed homes.
responses.evidence: In Auckland, three-bedroom rents were 22% to 35% below a synthetic comparison six years after upzoning, though the pre-reform fit was weaker than for most comparison areas. A study of U.S. reforms from 2000 to 2019 found loosening associated with a 0.8% increase in housing supply within three to nine years, mostly in higher-rent units; a 2026 critique disputes how reforms were coded, and the authors' reply defends it. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis attributes much of that city's slow rent growth to a 2020 drop in demand.
responses.tradeoffs: Owners near new buildings give up some control over neighborhood change, and owners in high-demand places may see slower price growth. If infrastructure lags, localities face new costs. Homes allowed on paper may not be built when construction costs or financing stay high.

responses.name: Hold local elections on the November ballot
responses.what_it_does: A state law or city charter amendment moves council and other local elections to the same date as state and federal elections in November of even-numbered years. More residents vote in the contests that choose the officials who adopt zoning ordinances. The aim is a local electorate closer to the whole population by age and race at the point where housing rules are set, including more younger residents.
responses.requires: A state statute requiring consolidation, or a charter amendment where state home-rule law allows one. Election officials must print longer ballots, and sitting officials' terms shift during the transition. Voters must reach local contests near the end of a long ballot.
responses.evidence: On-cycle elections generally double local turnout compared with stand-alone local contests, and a study of California cities found the on-cycle electorate more representative by race, age and partisanship. Evidence linking the change to housing approvals or rents has not been established; the measured effect is on who chooses the council.
responses.tradeoffs: Local races sit at the bottom of a long ballot, and some voters skip them. Groups that do well in low-turnout elections lose influence, and local issues compete with national campaigns for attention.

responses.name: Limit shared private data in rent-pricing software
responses.what_it_does: Court judgments, state laws and city ordinances bar landlords and software vendors from feeding competitors' nonpublic rents and occupancy into live price recommendations. The RealPage judgment allows training only on data at least 12 months old, limits how narrowly models may group local markets and installs a government-selected monitor. New York and California laws reach rent-setting tools more broadly, and several cities have banned algorithmic rent setting outright.
responses.requires: Antitrust authority under the Sherman Act and state antitrust laws, enforced by the Justice Department, state attorneys general and private plaintiffs in court. State statutes need a legislature and governor; city bans depend on home-rule authority and can face lawsuits. Monitoring requires technical staff who can audit software and data flows. The RealPage judgment lasts seven years.
responses.evidence: No evaluation yet measures rent changes after these limits took effect. A working paper by Calder-Wang and Kim estimates a coordination markup of about $25 per unit per month, while also finding that pricing software helped buildings cut rents faster in downturns. RealPage made no admission in its settlement, and the states' case continues after a September 2026 ruling.
responses.tradeoffs: Landlords may lose some pricing accuracy, and buildings could fill more slowly in downturns. Coordination could shift to channels a judgment does not cover, and the RealPage judgment expires after seven years.

responses.name: Expand rental assistance and income-restricted homes
responses.what_it_does: Congress could fund more Housing Choice Vouchers, which pay part of the rent for eligible households in privately owned homes, and states could steer more tax-credit housing to the lowest-income renters. A voucher reaches a household within existing housing, while LIHTC adds new or rehabilitated units with restricted rents. This response targets the renters whom new market-rate building reaches last.
responses.requires: Congress appropriates voucher funding each year in the HUD budget, and the tax-writing committees set LIHTC allocations. Local public housing agencies need landlords willing to accept vouchers, and state housing finance agencies set priorities in their allocation plans. Costs grow with each added household; the 2025 increase in LIHTC allocations is permanent.
responses.evidence: JCHS projects that the expanded LIHTC could support about 1.2 million new units by 2035. In HUD's randomized Family Options Study of 2,282 homeless families in 12 communities, 88% of families offered priority access to a voucher used a permanent subsidy, against 38% under usual care, so offers turned into use. Supply limits the effect: vouchers depend on landlords who accept them, and tax-credit units take years to build.
responses.tradeoffs: Taxpayers bear a cost that grows with each household served. In markets with few vacancies, more voucher holders compete for the same homes, and tax-credit projects need long-term monitoring of rents and building condition.

responses.name: Limit purchases of single-family homes by large investors
responses.what_it_does: Public Law 119-101, enacted July 11, 2026, bars a for-profit entity or fund that controls 350 or more single-family homes from buying more, with exceptions that include newly built homes held for sale, build-to-rent communities, substantial renovations and foreclosure-related acquisitions. Investors are not required to sell homes they already own. Executive Order 14376 separately directs federal housing agencies, including the regulator of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, to stop arranging sales of federally held or backed homes to large investors.
responses.requires: The Treasury Department, consulting HUD and the Securities and Exchange Commission, writes implementing rules, and civil penalties apply per violation. Enforcement needs ownership data that can trace homes held through affiliated companies, which GAO found hard to define and measure. Agencies must also issue guidance under the executive order.
responses.evidence: No evaluation exists yet. GAO's 2024 review found that investor purchases may have contributed to price and rent increases in some areas while effects on homeownership were unclear. Its 2026 study of six metro areas found the largest investors held under 1% to 3% of all single-family homes, a share that limits how much the law can change prices outside neighborhoods where purchases concentrated.
responses.tradeoffs: Large investors own some of the rental houses in suburbs with few apartments, so fewer purchases could mean fewer rentals there. Exceptions for build-to-rent and renovation can shift purchases into those forms, and investors below the threshold are unaffected.

distribution.difference: Householders under 35 had a 35.2% ownership rate in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 78.6% for those 65 and older. Buying the median-priced home required about $120,800 a year in income at the end of 2025, up from $68,700 five years earlier, so younger households carry more of the cost of scarcity and high rates.

Older owners face rising property taxes, up 31% from 2019 to 2025, and insurance premiums, up 72%, whether or not they carry a mortgage. Among homeowners, households headed by someone 65 or older had the highest cost-burden rate, 28%, and many live on fixed retirement incomes.

Ownership in the second quarter of 2026 was 45.4% for Black householders and 48.1% for Hispanic householders, against 74.5% for non-Hispanic White householders. Rising prices add equity for owners, so the same price increase widens wealth gaps between groups with different ownership rates; JCHS reports the Black-White ownership gap was wider in 2025 than in 1995.

distribution.group: Renters earning up to half the area median income
distribution.difference: About three in four renter households in this income group receive no federal housing subsidy, and 12.1 million renter households spent more than half their income on housing in 2024. For these households a modest rent increase can exceed what remains after other necessities, and an eviction order raises the risk of homelessness.

how_to_judge.measure: Share of renter households paying more than 30% of income for housing
how_to_judge.where: Census American Community Survey, table B25070 (available for counties and cities)
how_to_judge.direction: Lower is better

how_to_judge.measure: New homes permitted per 1,000 residents in your city or county
how_to_judge.where: Census Building Permits Survey (annual, by permit-issuing place)
how_to_judge.direction: Higher where rents are rising shows that local rules let supply respond

how_to_judge.measure: Rental vacancy rate
how_to_judge.where: Census Housing Vacancies and Homeownership survey (quarterly, national and for the 75 largest metro areas)
how_to_judge.direction: A higher rate gives renters more choice and slows rent growth

how_to_judge.measure: Homeownership rate for householders under 35
how_to_judge.where: Census Housing Vacancies and Homeownership survey (quarterly)
how_to_judge.direction: Higher is better

check.prompt: A city's rents rise after its planning board turns down most apartment proposals near a new transit station. Which office adopted the rules the board was applying?
options: The city or town council, through its zoning ordinance
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
check.explanation: Planning boards apply the zoning ordinance adopted by the local council, unless a state law overrides it. The Federal Reserve influences mortgage rates and HUD funds rental assistance, and neither body votes on how many homes a local lot may hold.

pathways.title: Grocery prices
pathways.question: Why is my grocery bill higher?
also_answers: How do competition and supply conditions reach the prices I pay?
Who pays for a tariff on imported food?
What can the Federal Reserve do about food prices?
How do SNAP and WIC benefits keep up with prices?
pathways.short_answer: Grocery prices are still rising slowly: the Consumer Price Index for food at home, the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure of grocery prices, rose 1.8% in the year to September 2026. Farms receive about 12 cents of each food dollar, so wages, fuel, transport and store costs set most of the price. Particular foods jump when supply shrinks, as eggs did during bird flu outbreaks and beef has as cattle numbers fell. Tariffs add a cost that U.S. importers mostly pay first. Whether large meatpackers and grocers use market power to widen margins is disputed; the Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the competition laws.
pathways.scope_note: Price indexes, tariffs, antitrust law and SNAP benefit formulas are national, while store competition, SNAP administration and state antitrust enforcement vary by state and region. One household's bill depends on what it buys: in 2026 frequent beef buyers face larger increases than the national average shows, while egg prices are falling.

mechanisms.title: Wages, fuel and services after the farm make up most of the price
mechanisms.text: Farms received 11.8 cents of each dollar Americans spent on food in 2024, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Economic Research Service (ERS). The rest pays for processing, packaging, trucking, wholesale, stores and restaurants. Pay and benefits for workers along that chain took 54.1 cents. Property income, the ERS category for returns to the owners of businesses and their equipment, took 32.7 cents. When diesel, electricity or labor costs rise, those costs move into shelf prices with a lag. In September 2026 diesel averaged $6.29 a gallon while Middle East oil shipments stayed constrained, which raises the cost of moving food. The ERS figures run through 2024, so they cannot yet show how much of the 2026 fuel increase has reached grocery prices.

mechanisms.title: Disease and herd cycles cut the supply of particular foods
mechanisms.text: Some price jumps start with fewer animals. Highly pathogenic avian influenza, a bird flu strain circulating in U.S. flocks since 2022, cut the number of egg-laying hens and pushed the average price of a dozen Grade A large eggs to $6.23 in March 2025, by Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) count. As flocks rebuilt, the price fell to $2.27 in September 2026, and ERS forecasts egg prices 29.4% lower for 2026 as a whole. Beef runs on a slower cycle because ranchers need years to rebuild herds. The national cattle inventory stood at 86.2 million head on January 1, 2026, with beef cows down 1% from a year earlier, and beef output has stayed below year-earlier levels. ERS expects beef and veal prices to rise 9.4% in 2026, against 2.4% for groceries overall.

mechanisms.title: Presidents set most tariffs under laws Congress passed
mechanisms.text: A tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the U.S. company that brings goods into the country. The Constitution gives Congress the power to tax, and over decades Congress delegated tariff authority to the President through trade statutes. On February 20, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Learning Resources v. Trump that one of those laws, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, does not authorize tariffs. The administration replaced those tariffs with a temporary 10% charge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. From July 24, 2026, tariffs of 10% or 12.5% apply to goods from 60 economies under Section 301 of the same act, with exemptions for products that cannot be grown or produced in sufficient quantities in the United States. Imports supplied 59% of fresh fruit and 35% of fresh vegetables available in 2023.

mechanisms.title: U.S. buyers pay most tariff costs, and shelf prices follow over months
mechanisms.text: Who bears a tariff depends on whether foreign sellers cut their prices to keep customers. For the 2025 tariffs, a Federal Reserve Bank of New York study found U.S. importers bore 94% of the cost from January to August and 86% in November. A Peterson Institute for International Economics review found several 2026 studies placing about 90% of the burden on U.S. buyers. An importer can absorb the cost, pass it on to stores, or switch suppliers. Studies disagree on speed: one found full pass-through to consumer prices about seven months after a tariff took effect, and another found incomplete pass-through after six. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs in force in August 2026 cost the average household about $1,100 a year across all goods, a model estimate that does not break out food.

mechanisms.title: A few large firms buy most cattle and sell much of the food
mechanisms.text: Four meatpacking firms buy about 85% of the steers and heifers raised for beef, ERS reports. Their choices about plant capacity, bids for cattle and wholesale prices set the gap between what ranchers receive and what stores pay. Evidence on whether that concentration raises consumer prices is contested. Studies reviewed by ERS found that bigger plants cut processing costs enough to lower consumer prices in earlier decades. Since 2015, the spread between cattle prices and wholesale beef prices has grown to two or three times its earlier average, and higher plant costs explain only a small part of the rise. That spread contains both costs and profit, so it cannot isolate margins. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) staff reported that grocery retailers' revenues ran 7% above total costs in early 2023, above a 2015 peak of 5.6%.

mechanisms.title: Food benefits are reset once a year by formula
mechanisms.text: The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) gives eligible households a monthly benefit for groceries. The Agriculture Department prices the Thrifty Food Plan, a low-cost market basket, each June and sets maximum benefits from it each October 1. For October 2026 through September 2027, the maximum for a family of four in the 48 contiguous states and Washington, D.C. is $1,023 a month. Price increases between adjustments come out of the household's own cash. The 2025 budget law (Public Law 119-21) limits future increases in the food plan to inflation, applies work requirements to adults up to age 64, and from fiscal 2028 makes states with higher payment error rates pay part of benefit costs. WIC, a separate program for pregnant women, infants and young children, provides specific foods.

pathways.household_effects: The grocery bill rises unevenly, so two households can live through different inflation. Over the year to September 2026, the BLS index for meats, poultry, fish and eggs rose 0.3%, fruits and vegetables rose 3.7%, and meals away from home rose 3.5%. A household that buys beef often will feel more than the averages show, since ERS expects beef prices to climb about 9% in 2026 while eggs get cheaper. Food insecurity, meaning limited or uncertain access to enough food, reached 18.4% of households with children in 2024, compared with 13.7% of all households. SNAP households receive one benefit adjustment a year. Mid-year increases come out of their own cash until the next October.

sub_issues.title: Eggs: bird flu, recovery and a price-benchmark case
sub_issues.text: Bird flu losses explain much of the 2025 egg spike. How egg prices are set matters too. Many sales are priced off daily quotations from Urner Barry, a market reporting company. On June 30, 2026, the Justice Department and 17 state attorneys general filed a complaint alleging that Cal-Maine Foods, Hickman's Egg Ranch and Versova coordinated bids to inflate those quotations. The companies agreed to settle without admitting wrongdoing. The settlements need court approval under the Tunney Act, the law that requires public comment and a judge's review of antitrust settlements.

sub_issues.title: Beef: a smaller herd and a closer look at packers
sub_issues.text: Beef prices combine a slow supply cycle with an open question about market power. News reports in September 2026 said the Justice Department's Antitrust Division had asked eight grocery chains to explain their beef pricing and margins, widening an inquiry that began with the four largest packers. An inquiry asks for information; it makes no finding of wrongdoing. Research summarized by ERS found scale savings for consumers in earlier decades and spreads that widened faster than plant costs after 2015.

sub_issues.title: Who pays a tariff on imported food
sub_issues.text: The importer pays the duty when goods enter the country. What happens next depends on competition and on alternatives: an importer can raise prices, accept a smaller margin, or buy from a country with a lower rate. Fresh produce depends heavily on imports, so the product exemptions in the July 2026 tariff notice matter for what shoppers pay. Research on the 2025 tariffs finds most of the cost stayed with U.S. buyers.

sub_issues.title: Did grocery chains raise prices faster than costs?
sub_issues.text: FTC staff found grocery retailers' revenues exceeded total costs by more than 6% in 2021 and by 7% in the first three quarters of 2023, and reported that some retailers used rising costs as an opportunity to raise prices further. Economy-wide studies disagree on how much markups, the gap between price and cost, drove inflation: a Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco analysis found aggregate markups roughly flat from 2020 to 2023 while prices rose more than 10%. In December 2024, a federal court in Oregon and a Washington state court blocked the proposed $24.6 billion Kroger and Albertsons merger.

sub_issues.title: What the Federal Reserve can do about food prices
sub_issues.text: Congress assigned the Federal Reserve two goals, maximum employment and stable prices, and the Fed defines stable prices as 2% inflation over the longer run. Its Federal Open Market Committee uses tools that move the federal funds rate, the overnight rate banks charge each other, which shapes borrowing costs across the economy. Higher rates slow spending on everything at once. A bird flu outbreak or a short cattle supply sits outside the reach of interest rates, so the Fed's tools act on food prices through overall spending.

sub_issues.title: How SNAP and WIC keep up with prices
sub_issues.text: SNAP served an average of 42.1 million people a month in fiscal 2025, with benefits averaging $189 per person. Preliminary data for June 2026 show 36.4 million participants. The 2025 law narrowed eligibility for some noncitizens and extended work requirements, and the monthly counts alone cannot separate those changes from other causes. WIC served 6.9 million people in fiscal 2025. Its average food cost per participant rose from $61.07 to $64.89 a month, so higher grocery prices show up in the program's budget.

decision_makers.controls: Holds the constitutional power to set tariffs and decides how much of it to delegate; writes SNAP and WIC law and funds WIC; writes the Sherman and Clayton antitrust acts.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your U.S. representative and senators through the official directories at house.gov and senate.gov; trade bills go to the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees.

decision_makers.who: President and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative
decision_makers.controls: Imposes, changes and exempts tariffs under authority Congress delegated, including Sections 122 and 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Submit comments in Section 301 proceedings at regulations.gov during the comment periods announced in the Federal Register.

decision_makers.who: Justice Department Antitrust Division and the Federal Trade Commission
decision_makers.controls: Investigate and sue over mergers and agreements among competitors; negotiate settlements that a federal judge must approve.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Report suspected anticompetitive conduct through the complaint pages at justice.gov/atr and ftc.gov; comment on proposed settlements during the 60-day Tunney Act period published in the Federal Register.

decision_makers.controls: Enforce state antitrust and consumer protection laws and can join or bring federal antitrust cases, as 17 states did in the 2026 egg case.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: File a complaint with the consumer protection or antitrust division listed on your state attorney general's website.

decision_makers.who: U.S. Department of Agriculture (Food and Nutrition Service; Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service)
decision_makers.controls: Prices the Thrifty Food Plan and sets SNAP maximum benefits within the limits in statute; runs disease response for poultry and livestock, including indemnity payments to farmers.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Comment on proposed USDA rules at regulations.gov; program contacts are listed at usda.gov.

decision_makers.controls: Decide eligibility, renewals and work-requirement exemptions for individual households; run the payment accuracy reviews that will set each state's share of SNAP costs from fiscal 2028.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your state or county SNAP office; every household can request a fair hearing to contest a denial or reduction.

decision_makers.who: Federal Reserve Board and Federal Open Market Committee
decision_makers.controls: Sets monetary policy, which moves interest rates across the economy; has no authority over the price of any single food.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Statements and minutes are posted at federalreserve.gov; the Fed chair testifies to the House and Senate banking committees twice a year.

decision_makers.who: Meatpacking companies, egg producers and grocery chains
decision_makers.controls: Set wholesale and retail prices, bids for livestock, plant capacity and store locations.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public companies file annual and quarterly reports at sec.gov (EDGAR) and hold annual shareholder meetings.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress holds the tariff power under Article I of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held in February 2026 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs, while other delegations remain in force: Sections 122 and 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 and Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. Congress can narrow them by statute. Congress also writes SNAP rules in the Food and Nutrition Act, most recently amended by Public Law 119-21, and funds WIC through annual appropriations. Antitrust rules come from the Sherman and Clayton acts; the Justice Department and the FTC enforce them, and federal judges decide cases and approve settlements. State legislatures can pass state antitrust and price-gouging laws, which attorneys general enforce. The Federal Reserve sets monetary policy under the mandate Congress wrote.

responses.name: Require a vote in Congress for lasting tariffs
responses.what_it_does: A bill such as the Trade Review Act of 2025 (S. 1272) would require the President to notify Congress within 48 hours of a new or higher tariff and to assess its likely effects on U.S. businesses and consumers. The tariff would expire after 60 days unless Congress passed a joint resolution approving it, and Congress could end it sooner with a resolution of disapproval. Antidumping and countervailing duties, which answer unfair pricing by specific foreign firms, would stay outside the bill.
responses.requires: A statute passed by both chambers and signed by the President, or a two-thirds vote in each chamber to override a veto. The Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees would act first. A congressional bill tracker showed S. 1272 still at referral to the Senate Finance Committee on October 15, 2026, with its last action on April 3, 2025.
responses.evidence: No U.S. evaluation exists of a time limit on tariffs. The 2026 Supreme Court ruling showed that courts will hold one statute to its text. After the ruling, the administration imposed tariffs under Section 122 and then Section 301 within months, which shows that limits on one law can move tariffs to another.
responses.tradeoffs: Slower responses in trade disputes and less bargaining room for negotiators. Producers protected by a tariff could lose it if Congress does not vote, while importers and households gain predictability.

responses.name: Challenge mergers and coordination in food markets
responses.what_it_does: The Justice Department, the FTC and state attorneys general can sue to block mergers that would reduce competition and to stop agreements among competitors about prices or bids. Recent food cases include the blocked Kroger and Albertsons merger and the 2026 egg settlements, which would bar three producers from discussing bids with competitors and require compliance officers and monitoring. Remedies can also require a buyer to sell stores or plants to a new competitor.
responses.requires: Clayton Act and Sherman Act authority, litigation teams and economists, and a judge's approval of any settlement under the Tunney Act. State cases rely on state law and state budgets. Results depend on courts accepting the agencies' definition of the market.
responses.evidence: No study yet measures whether shoppers paid less because of these two food cases: Kroger and Albertsons remain separate competitors, and the egg settlements are too new to evaluate. ERS research on meatpacking shows that larger plants lowered costs in earlier decades, so blocking a combination can also forgo savings.
responses.tradeoffs: Litigation is slow and costly for agencies and firms. Conduct settlements depend on monitoring, and coordination can move to channels a decree does not cover.

responses.name: Prevent and contain animal disease outbreaks
responses.what_it_does: In February 2025 the Agriculture Department announced up to $1 billion for poultry biosecurity, payments to help farmers restock, and vaccine and treatment research, along with temporary egg imports. Biosecurity audits and cost sharing aim to keep the virus out of barns. Faster restocking shortens the supply gap after an outbreak. Indemnity payments to farmers whose flocks must be destroyed continued alongside the new money.
responses.requires: Appropriations from Congress for the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which runs the response; changes in barn practices by producers, with federal cost sharing; work with the Food and Drug Administration on egg supply rules; and coordination with trading partners before vaccinating flocks, since vaccination can affect poultry exports.
responses.evidence: Egg prices fell from $6.23 a dozen in March 2025 to $2.27 in September 2026, and ERS reports fewer new bird flu detections in early 2026 than a year earlier. Those changes do not show how much the plan contributed, because flocks also rebuild after outbreaks for reasons unrelated to the plan.
responses.tradeoffs: Public spending on indemnity and biosecurity, compliance costs that farms carry, and export risks for poultry producers if vaccination begins before trading partners agree.

responses.name: Keep SNAP benefits in step with grocery prices
responses.what_it_does: Benefits could be adjusted more than once a year, or the Thrifty Food Plan could be revised against current diets and prices without the 2025 cap that ties increases to inflation. Either change would shorten the stretch in which a price increase comes out of a household's own budget. Another option is a mid-year increase triggered when the food-at-home price index rises faster than a set threshold.
responses.requires: An act of Congress amending the Food and Nutrition Act; appropriations to cover the higher benefits; USDA guidance on the new formula; and changes to state eligibility and payment systems so that mid-year adjustments reach households' electronic benefit cards on time.
responses.evidence: The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the 2025 cap on food plan revisions will lower average monthly benefits by $14 by 2034, a measure of the gap this response would close. No evaluation exists of more frequent adjustment itself. In the year to September 2026, food-at-home prices rose 1.8%, so the gap between annual adjustments was smaller than in years of fast food inflation.
responses.tradeoffs: Higher federal spending, and more administrative work for state agencies, which now pay 75% of SNAP administrative costs, starting in fiscal 2027.

distribution.difference: Maximum benefits are fixed for 12 months at a time, so price increases between October resets come out of cash. The 2025 law applies work requirements to adults up to 64 and to parents whose youngest child is 14 or older; CBO estimated those changes would lower participation by about 2.4 million people in an average month.
In 2024, 18.4% of households with children were food insecure, compared with 13.7% of all households, by ERS count. A price increase on staples lands harder where the budget already falls short.

distribution.group: Shoppers who buy a lot of fresh produce
distribution.difference: Imports supplied 59% of fresh fruit and 35% of fresh vegetables in 2023, so tariff rates and product exemptions reach these bills more directly. The BLS fruit and vegetable index rose 3.7% in the year to September 2026, faster than groceries overall.

how_to_judge.measure: 12-month change in the Consumer Price Index for food at home
how_to_judge.where: Bureau of Labor Statistics monthly CPI news release (bls.gov/cpi)
how_to_judge.direction: Lower is better, and increases below wage growth mean groceries take a smaller share of pay

how_to_judge.measure: Spread between fed cattle prices and wholesale beef prices
how_to_judge.where: USDA Economic Research Service meat price spreads data
how_to_judge.direction: A spread that tracks processing costs points to competition; one that widens faster than costs calls for scrutiny

how_to_judge.measure: Shares of the food dollar going to farms, wages and property income
how_to_judge.where: USDA Economic Research Service Food Dollar Series
how_to_judge.direction: Property income rising faster than wages and input costs would support the market-power explanation

how_to_judge.measure: Share of households that are food insecure
how_to_judge.where: USDA Economic Research Service, Household Food Security in the United States (latest data year 2024)
how_to_judge.direction: Lower is better

how_to_judge.measure: SNAP maximum benefit compared with the monthly cost of the Thrifty Food Plan
how_to_judge.where: USDA Food and Nutrition Service cost-of-living adjustment notices and monthly food plan cost reports
how_to_judge.direction: A smaller gap means benefits are keeping pace

pathways.title: Electric and utility bills
pathways.question: Why is my electric bill going up?
also_answers: Who decides what I pay for electricity?
Who pays for new power lines and for the power data centers use?
What help exists if I cannot pay my utility bill?
pathways.short_answer: Your rate is approved by a regulator or a board. For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission sets rates in a rate case; for public power and cooperatives, a city council, utility board or co-op board does. Rates recover the cost of power plants, fuel, transmission lines and local wires, and investor-owned utilities also earn a regulated return on what they invest. Recent increases trace mainly to grid spending, natural gas prices and disaster recovery. In the 13-state PJM grid region, a capacity auction overseen by federal regulators has added costs, and its market monitor attributes $23.1 billion over three auctions to data center demand.
pathways.scope_note: Wholesale markets and interstate transmission fall under federal regulators, while retail rates are set state by state or by local boards, so the mechanism and the office to contact depend on where you live and who owns your utility; capacity auction effects apply only in PJM states. One household's bill also depends on its usage, weather and rate plan, so a single bill cannot show which cause dominates.

mechanisms.title: State commissions and local boards approve what utilities charge
mechanisms.text: About two-thirds of U.S. electricity customers buy from investor-owned utilities, private companies whose retail rates a state public utility commission approves. In a rate case, the utility files its costs and a proposed rate; the commission reviews them in a public proceeding and sets rates that cover operating costs and give the utility an opportunity to earn a fixed rate of return on its capital investments. About 15% of customers are served by public power utilities, most governed by a city council or an independent utility board, and about 13% by member-owned cooperatives. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) regulates wholesale power sales and interstate transmission. Retail rates are set by states and local boards.

mechanisms.title: Grid spending, gas prices and disaster repairs drive most increases
mechanisms.text: U.S. homes paid an average of 17.30 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2025, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) reports, and household prices rose another 4.4% in the year to September 2026. Generating the power is the largest part of the price. Natural gas fueled about 41% of U.S. generation in 2025, so gas prices pass into bills; EIA forecasts the Henry Hub benchmark at $3.48 per million British thermal units for 2026. Utilities also build and repair transmission lines and local distribution wires, including after storms, and recover that spending through rates. An analysis by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, summarized by the Congressional Research Service, found the main drivers of price increases from 2019 to 2025 were utility grid investments, natural gas prices, disaster recovery and state policies.

mechanisms.title: Regional grid operators buy future capacity through auctions
mechanisms.text: Across much of the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, PJM Interconnection runs the high-voltage grid for about 67 million people in 13 states and Washington, D.C. It holds auctions that pay power plants to be available years ahead, under rules FERC approves. The auction for June 2026 through May 2027 cleared at $329.17 per megawatt-day, the cap FERC had approved, up from $269.92 the year before in most of the region. PJM estimated bill increases of 1.5% to 5% for some customers, depending on how utilities and states pass the cost through. EIA expects wholesale power prices in PJM to average 41% more in 2026 than in 2025.

mechanisms.title: New data centers add demand that someone has to pay for
mechanisms.text: Technology companies decide where to build data centers, buildings full of servers that draw power around the clock. They used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023, and some projections show that use doubling or tripling by 2028. PJM's independent market monitor reran its latest auction without forecast data center load and found that load raised capacity costs for other customers by $23.1 billion across three auctions. That counterfactual holds all other offers fixed, so it measures pressure in one market. Nationally, the Berkeley Lab analysis found that states with the largest growth in data center demand generally saw electricity prices fall from 2019 to 2025; added sales can spread existing grid costs over more use.

mechanisms.title: Commissions decide how costs are split among customers
mechanisms.text: After approving total costs, a commission divides them among customer classes such as residential, commercial and industrial. The guiding principle, cost causation, says each class should pay the costs it causes, and applying it involves judgment. A 2025 Harvard Law School Electricity Law Initiative review of nearly 50 proceedings, including 40 before state commissions, found that state commissions often approved confidential special contracts with data centers in brief orders. FERC sets transmission revenue requirements, and each commission uses its own formula to divide those costs among classes, which can shift costs onto households. Some utilities have proposed large-load tariffs, separate rate schedules for the largest users; AEP Ohio's proposal would require a data center to pay for 90% of its maximum demand for ten years.

mechanisms.title: Bill help depends on yearly federal decisions
mechanisms.text: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) sends federal grants to states, tribes and territories, which help eligible low-income households pay home energy bills. Congress decides its funding in annual appropriations. The President's budget for fiscal 2026 proposed eliminating LIHEAP, and the association of state program directors reported that federal program staff were fired in April 2025. For fiscal 2027, Congress passed a stopgap funding law on September 2, 2026 that runs through December 11, 2026. The 2025 budget law also changed how SNAP food benefits count energy assistance, a provision CBO scored at $5.9 billion in reduced federal spending over ten years.

pathways.household_effects: Household electricity prices rose 4.4% in the year to September 2026 and piped gas service 5.0%, far below the 34% jump in gasoline. The size of the increase depends on place. Customers in PJM states carry capacity auction costs, while others see changes driven by local grid spending, gas prices or storm recovery. Customers of public power and co-ops answer to a local board, so their path to a rate decision runs through a council or co-op board meeting. Low-income, Black, Hispanic, Native American and older households spend a larger share of income on energy, an energy-efficiency research group found, so the same rate increase takes a larger bite from their budgets.

sub_issues.title: What happens in a rate case
sub_issues.text: An investor-owned utility asks the state commission for new rates by filing a case with its costs, investments and proposed charges for each customer class. The commission opens a docket, a public case file, takes testimony and holds hearings, then issues an order. Approved rates cover operating costs and allow a set return on capital investments, which gives the utility a reason to invest. Members of the public can file comments in the docket or speak at public hearings.

sub_issues.title: Who pays for power lines
sub_issues.text: Federal law gives FERC exclusive authority to set utilities' transmission revenue requirements. State commissions then choose how to divide those costs among residential, commercial and industrial customers, and their formulas can shift costs from large users to households. Distribution wires, the local lines to homes, are priced through state or local rate decisions. Utilities recover storm repairs through the same process.

sub_issues.title: Data centers and the PJM auction
sub_issues.text: PJM's market monitor estimates that forecast data center load added $9.3 billion to capacity costs for other customers in the 2025/2026 auction, $7.3 billion in 2026/2027 and $6.5 billion in 2027/2028. It recommends that new data center load bring its own new generation. The estimate rests on forecast load, and the monitor warns that uncertain forecasts put costs on other customers. Where existing lines and plants can absorb added load, average rates can fall, so the household effect depends on whether new investment is needed and how a commission allocates it.

sub_issues.title: Public power and co-ops
sub_issues.text: About 2,000 public power utilities and about 830 distribution cooperatives serve most of the customers that investor-owned utilities do not. Public power utilities are community-owned, and most are governed by a city council or an independent utility board. Cooperatives are owned by the consumers they serve. For these customers, rate decisions are made by local boards, so the place to speak up is a council or board meeting or a co-op membership meeting.

sub_issues.title: Gas and water bills
sub_issues.text: A natural gas bill has two main parts, the commodity cost of the gas and the cost of moving it by pipeline, plus taxes and fees. FERC regulates interstate pipelines; state commissions regulate retail gas sales by investor-owned gas utilities. Some state commissions also set rates for investor-owned water companies: California's commission, for example, processes water utility rate change requests. City-owned water systems set rates locally, a subject covered in the clean drinking water pathway.

sub_issues.title: When utility money reaches lawmakers
sub_issues.text: Utility rates depend on laws as well as commission orders. In Ohio, a federal jury convicted former House Speaker Larry Householder in a $60 million bribery scheme secretly funded by FirstEnergy, aimed at passing a $1 billion bailout of two nuclear plants owned by a FirstEnergy affiliate. He was sentenced to 20 years in 2023. FirstEnergy agreed in 2021 to a deferred prosecution agreement with a $230 million penalty.

sub_issues.title: Energy use and emissions are separate measures
sub_issues.text: Data center load raises electricity demand. Whether it raises greenhouse gas emissions, and by how much, depends on which plants supply the added power: in 2025 natural gas produced about 41% of U.S. utility-scale generation, nuclear about 18%, coal about 17% and renewables about 24%. Bills and emissions also follow different paths, since a commission's cost allocation decides who pays, while the generation mix decides what is emitted.

decision_makers.who: State public utility commission (called a public service commission in some states)
decision_makers.controls: Approves retail rates and capital spending recovery for investor-owned electric and gas utilities, divides costs among customer classes, approves special contracts and large-load tariffs; in some states also sets investor-owned water rates.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: File a public comment or speak at a public hearing in the rate case docket; open dockets and hearing schedules are posted on the commission's website, which your state government's official site links.

decision_makers.controls: Writes the laws that define the commission's powers, can require protections for existing customers when large loads connect, and can fund state bill assistance.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your state senator and representative through the legislature's official website; testify at committee hearings on energy bills.

decision_makers.who: City council or municipal utility board
decision_makers.controls: Sets rates and spending for public power and city-owned water utilities.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public comment at council or utility board meetings; agendas are posted by the city clerk or utility.

decision_makers.controls: Sets rates and investment plans for a member-owned cooperative.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Attend the co-op's annual membership meeting and board meetings; bylaws and board election notices come from the co-op.

decision_makers.controls: Approves wholesale market rules, including PJM's capacity auction design and price limits, and sets transmission revenue requirements.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Submit comments in the relevant docket through eComment on ferc.gov.

decision_makers.who: PJM Interconnection and other regional grid operators
decision_makers.controls: Forecast demand, run capacity auctions and plan transmission; rule changes must be filed with and approved by FERC.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Auction results, load forecasts and committee meeting materials are posted at pjm.com; formal rule changes can be commented on in FERC dockets.

decision_makers.who: Congress and the Department of Health and Human Services
decision_makers.controls: Congress appropriates LIHEAP funds and amends the Federal Power Act; HHS distributes LIHEAP grants to states, tribes and territories.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your U.S. representative and senators through house.gov and senate.gov; appropriations for LIHEAP go through the Labor-HHS subcommittees.

decision_makers.controls: Proposes rates, capital plans and contracts with large customers, and decides when to file a rate case.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Customer service for billing disputes; the utility's filings are public in the commission docket.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: State legislatures write the statutes that set each commission's authority, and commissions change rates and cost allocation through orders in rate cases and tariff proceedings, which state courts can review. FERC changes wholesale market rules and transmission pricing under the Federal Power Act, usually after a grid operator such as PJM files a proposal; federal appeals courts review FERC orders. Congress can amend the Federal Power Act and decides LIHEAP funding in annual appropriations. Public power rates change by vote of a city council or utility board, and cooperative rates by the co-op's board. Large-load protections can come from any of these: a state statute, a commission tariff, or a FERC-approved market rule.

responses.name: Make the largest new users pay the grid costs they cause
responses.what_it_does: A commission or legislature would place large new users such as data centers in their own rate class, with minimum demand charges and long contract terms so the utility recovers the plants and lines built for them even if the facility uses less power or leaves. AEP Ohio proposed requiring payment for 90% of maximum demand over ten years; Indiana Michigan Power proposed similar terms for customers of 150 megawatts or more over twenty years.
responses.requires: A commission order approving the tariff, or a state statute directing one; load forecasting and cost studies; enforcement through billing and contract terms. Existing special contracts may need to be reopened or allowed to expire. Commissions also need staff able to review the utility's load forecasts and the cost studies that assign new plants and lines to the large customer.
responses.evidence: No evaluation of household bill effects exists yet. The Harvard Electricity Law Initiative review documents how special contracts and allocation formulas can shift costs, which is evidence about the problem. The Berkeley Lab finding that high-growth states saw prices fall shows that the cost depends on whether new plants and lines are needed.
responses.tradeoffs: Data center developers may build in states with looser terms, moving the investment elsewhere, and long contract commitments raise developers' costs.

responses.name: Require new data centers to bring their own generation
responses.what_it_does: Grid operators would require new large loads to add new generating capacity, directly or by contract, before or as they connect. Capacity auctions would then clear without bidding up prices for existing customers to cover the new demand. The new supply could come from plants built on site or from contracts with new plants elsewhere in the region. The rule would apply to load not yet counted in forecasts.
responses.requires: A rule change filed by PJM or another grid operator and approved by FERC, or state commission conditions on interconnection; verification that the added generation is new; coordination with transmission planning. It also needs a definition of which loads count as large, since the rule would leave out data centers already included in forecasts.
responses.evidence: PJM's independent market monitor recommends this approach and states it would limit or eliminate the effect of uncertain data center forecasts on other customers. The claim rests on the monitor's counterfactual modeling; no market has tested the rule at scale.
responses.tradeoffs: Slower connection for new facilities and higher costs for developers; the effect of load already counted in forecasts would remain unless addressed separately.

responses.name: Open special contracts and cost studies to public review
responses.what_it_does: Commissions would stop approving confidential discounted contracts for single large customers and move those customers onto published tariffs that anyone can read. Utilities would disclose the load forecasts behind proposals for new plants and lines, and cost allocation studies would be reviewed in open dockets where consumer representatives and other parties can file testimony. Commissions could publish summaries of each contract's prices and terms where full disclosure would reveal trade secrets.
responses.requires: Commission rules or a state statute on confidentiality and special contracts; commission staff able to audit cost studies; filing deadlines that give outside parties time to participate; and a process for redacting trade secrets while keeping prices and terms public.
responses.evidence: The Harvard review of nearly 50 proceedings, including 40 before state commissions, found approvals often came in brief orders with little opposing evidence, which supports the case for closer review. No study measures whether disclosure changes outcomes for households. The same review reports that utilities often ask commissions for confidential treatment of data center contracts, which limits outside scrutiny.
responses.tradeoffs: Companies may resist sharing commercially sensitive terms and may favor states that allow more confidentiality; longer proceedings delay decisions for utilities and customers.

responses.name: Fund bill assistance and weatherization
responses.what_it_does: Congress would fund LIHEAP at a level set before each heating season, so states know how much help they can offer when cold weather arrives. The grants would keep flowing through states, tribes and territories, which set eligibility within federal income limits. States would pair bill payments with weatherization, such as insulation and sealing air leaks, which lowers energy use in low-income homes for years after the work is done.
responses.requires: Annual appropriations from Congress passed before winter, HHS staff to calculate and release grants on time, state and tribal agencies to take applications and pay utilities, trained weatherization crews and contractors, and money for administration at each of those levels.
responses.evidence: An energy-efficiency research group documents higher energy burdens for low-income and several racial and ethnic groups and names weatherization as a long-term way to lower them; the group advocates for efficiency programs. The state directors' association estimates LIHEAP reaches about 6 million households. Neither source measures the program's effect on shutoffs or unpaid bills, so the grade rests on the mechanism: aid paid toward a bill lowers what the household owes.
responses.tradeoffs: Federal cost, and assistance can be absorbed by higher bills without lowering the underlying rate. Funding gaps between appropriations leave households uncertain before winter.

distribution.group: Low-income, Black, Hispanic, Native American and older households
distribution.difference: These households spend a higher share of income on energy than the average household, nationally, by region and in every metro area studied, according to a 2020 analysis by the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy, an efficiency research and advocacy group.

Capacity auction prices set for the whole region reach their bills through utility rates. PJM estimated increases of 1.5% to 5% for some customers from the 2026/2027 auction, and the market monitor attributes $23.1 billion in costs across three auctions to data center load.

distribution.group: Customers of public power utilities and cooperatives
distribution.difference: About 15% of customers are served by public power and 13% by cooperatives, whose rates are set by a city council, utility board or co-op board. Their route to a rate decision runs through local board meetings.

distribution.group: Customers in states with fast data center growth
distribution.difference: The Berkeley Lab analysis found that states with the largest data center demand growth generally saw price decreases from 2019 to 2025, a pattern consistent with more sales spreading existing costs. Where new plants and lines must be built, the result depends on how the commission allocates them.

how_to_judge.where: EIA Electric Power Monthly, Table 5.6.A
how_to_judge.direction: Growth slower than household income is better

how_to_judge.where: PJM auction reports (pjm.com) and Monitoring Analytics reports (monitoringanalytics.com)
how_to_judge.direction: Lower prices and a smaller shifted amount are better

how_to_judge.where: U.S. Department of Energy Low-Income Energy Affordability Data (LEAD) Tool

how_to_judge.where: Cost allocation studies filed in the rate case docket at your state commission
how_to_judge.direction: A residential share that matches the costs residential customers cause
