pathways.title: Home and auto insurance
pathways.question: Why did my home insurance premium go up?
also_answers: Why did my insurer drop my policy?
Why did my auto insurance bill jump?
Who decides what insurers can charge?
Do I need separate flood insurance?
pathways.short_answer: Home insurance costs more because each claim costs more to pay and more homes stand where storms and wildfires strike. Reinsurance, the coverage insurers buy for themselves, also became more expensive. Average monthly premiums rose 72% from 2019 to 2025, to $201. Insurers propose rates, and each state's insurance commissioner or department reviews them under rules the state legislature writes, including which costs may count. Where approved rates fall below expected losses, some insurers stop renewing policies and households turn to state-created insurers of last resort. Flood damage needs a separate policy, mostly from a federal program that Congress has extended through December 11, 2026.
pathways.scope_note: Homeowners and auto insurance are regulated by each state, so rate review and insurers of last resort differ from state to state, and national averages blend calm regions with risky ones; Treasury found premiums 82% higher in the riskiest fifth of ZIP codes than in the least risky fifth. Flood insurance runs mainly through a federal program, and any one premium also depends on the home and its claims history, so a single bill cannot show which cause drove an increase.

mechanisms.title: Costly disasters strike more insured property
mechanisms.text: Climate Central counted 23 weather and climate disasters with at least $1 billion in damage in the United States in 2025, about $115 billion in total and the third-highest count since 1980. These totals grow both because hazards change and because more and costlier buildings stand in exposed places. Treasury's Federal Insurance Office, citing the Fifth National Climate Assessment, reports that changes in the frequency, severity or distribution of perils covered by homeowners policies have been attributed to climate change. Insurers price expected losses into each policy. Federal Reserve economists found that insurers raise rates in states with less restrictive rate rules after losses elsewhere, so a disaster in one region can show up in premiums in another.

mechanisms.title: Rebuilding costs push up each claim
mechanisms.text: A homeowners policy pays to repair or rebuild, so construction prices pass straight into claim costs. Treasury reports that replacement costs for property and casualty losses rose an average of 45% from 2020 to 2023, and its 2018 to 2022 data show average claims of about $24,000 in the riskiest ZIP codes against about $19,000 in the least risky. Prices for residential construction inputs rose 40% from January 2020 to spring 2026, and average homeowners premiums per policy grew 8.7% faster than inflation from 2018 to 2022. When State Farm General stopped accepting new property insurance applications in California in May 2023, the company cited construction costs rising faster than inflation, along with growing catastrophe exposure and a difficult reinsurance market.

mechanisms.title: Reinsurers charge more to carry catastrophe risk
mechanisms.text: Insurers buy reinsurance, coverage that pays part of their losses after a large event, so one disaster does not exhaust their capital. Treasury describes a hard reinsurance market in which reinsurers raised rates, tightened terms and required insurers to keep more risk themselves. Keys and Mulder studied 74 million premiums inferred from mortgage escrow payments from 2014 to 2024. They found that the pass-through from disaster risk to premiums doubled, with the largest increases in places facing rising climate risk, and they link the steeper slope to a repricing of catastrophe risk in global capital markets.

mechanisms.title: State regulators decide which rates and costs are allowed
mechanisms.text: Each state's insurance commissioner or department reviews homeowners and auto rate filings under the state's insurance code. Some states require approval before a new rate takes effect; others let insurers begin using a rate while regulators review it, and the rate must be withdrawn if rejected. States also decide which inputs count, such as catastrophe models or reinsurance costs. In the states with the most restrictive rules, Federal Reserve economists found that rates did not keep pace with rising losses, and insurers raised rates in less restrictive states, so households there carried part of the cost. Treasury reports that insurers raise premiums faster where approval rules are less restrictive.

mechanisms.title: Insurers pull back and state plans fill the gap
mechanisms.text: An insurer that expects losses above its approved rates can decline to renew policies or stop selling new ones in a state. Treasury found that nonrenewal rates in the riskiest fifth of ZIP codes rose from 1.10% in 2018 to 2.37% in 2022. Households that cannot find private coverage turn to insurers created by state law. California's FAIR Plan held 696,562 dwelling and commercial policies in June 2026, 157% more than in September 2022. Florida's Citizens Property Insurance peaked at 1,407,805 policies in September 2023 and held 254,413 on October 9, 2026, after the legislature changed claim and litigation rules in December 2022; the count alone does not separate that law's effect from other causes.

mechanisms.title: Flood coverage depends on a federal program
mechanisms.text: Standard homeowners policies typically exclude flood, so most flood coverage comes from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), which FEMA runs under authority that Congress must renew. Owners in mapped high-risk flood zones generally must buy it to get a federally backed mortgage. FEMA's Risk Rating 2.0, applied to new policies from October 2021 and to renewals from April 2022, ties each premium to the property's own flood risk; by statute, yearly increases for an individual property are generally capped at 18%. The program had nearly 4.5 million policies on August 31, 2026 and owed $22.525 billion to the Treasury. Its authority runs through December 11, 2026, and it lapsed from October 1 to November 12, 2025.

pathways.household_effects: Most owners see the change in a renewal notice or a higher mortgage escrow payment. From 2018 to 2022, homeowners in the riskiest fifth of ZIP codes paid an average of $2,321 a year, 82% more than in the least risky fifth, and average premiums grew 8.7% faster than inflation. A nonrenewal forces a search for another insurer or a move to a state plan of last resort. Rising premiums also lower home values; Keys and Mulder estimate more than $40,000 less price growth in the most exposed ZIP codes. Drivers saw auto insurance prices rise 18.9% in the year to September 2023 and 16.3% the next year before easing.

sub_issues.title: Why auto insurance jumped, then eased
sub_issues.text: Auto insurance rates are also filed with each state's insurance regulator. The consumer price index for motor vehicle insurance rose 18.9% in the year to September 2023, when vehicle repair and maintenance prices rose 10.2%, and 16.3% in the year to September 2024. By September 2026 the index was 5.0% below its level a year earlier, while repair prices were still rising 5.8%. The index tracks the price of a fixed set of coverage, so a driver's own premium also depends on the car and the driver's record.

sub_issues.title: Insurers of last resort
sub_issues.text: California and Florida created plans that sell property coverage when private insurers decline. California's FAIR Plan grew to 696,562 policies by June 2026, up 157% since September 2022, and to $768 billion in exposure, up 250%. Florida's Citizens shrank from 1.4 million policies in 2023 to about 254,000 in October 2026. California's insurance department describes its 2024 reforms as an effort to move households from the FAIR Plan back to regular insurers.

sub_issues.title: California's rate rule changes
sub_issues.text: California's Insurance Commissioner announced a Sustainable Insurance Strategy in September 2023 and issued regulations through December 2024. Insurers may use forward-looking catastrophe models that credit wildfire safety work, and the strategy counts the net cost of reinsurance for California risks in rates. In exchange, insurers using the new tools must write at least 85% of their statewide market share in wildfire-distressed areas. Whether this brings private coverage back has not been measured, and premiums can rise as more costs enter rates.

sub_issues.title: The flood insurance deadline
sub_issues.text: The NFIP's authority to issue new policies expires unless Congress extends it. The program lapsed from October 1 to November 12, 2025 and from February 1 to 3, 2026, and the current law runs to December 11, 2026. Owners required to carry flood insurance do not always keep it: one study found compliance in the mandatory-purchase areas it examined rose from 61% in 2012 to 73% in 2016.

sub_issues.title: How premiums affect home values
sub_issues.text: Insurance is part of the monthly cost of owning, so buyers pay less for homes that carry higher premiums. Keys and Mulder estimate that premium increases reduced home price growth by more than $40,000 in the most exposed ZIP codes, with larger effects where climate risk is rising. The model records this as LE23 (Climate risk weighs on home equity), graded plausible.

sub_issues.title: Building codes and home hardening
sub_issues.text: Fewer than half of U.S. jurisdictions had hazard-resistant building codes in FEMA's 2020 count, though about 80% of new construction occurs in communities with modern codes. Codes are adopted by states, and in many states also by cities and counties, and enforced by local building departments. Homes built before current codes stay exposed until owners retrofit them.

decision_makers.who: State insurance commissioner or department of insurance
decision_makers.controls: Reviews homeowners and auto rate filings and approves or rejects them where state law requires, licenses insurers, enforces rules on nonrenewal notices and claims handling, and adopts regulations such as which catastrophe models may be used.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact the department's consumer services division to ask questions or file a complaint; find your state's department in the NAIC directory of state insurance departments (content.naic.org/state-insurance-departments). Many states post rate filings through SERFF Filing Access.

decision_makers.controls: Write the insurance code: the rate review system, which costs may count in rates, the structure of FAIR plans or state insurers, claim and litigation rules, and statewide building codes.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your state legislators through your legislature's official website, and testify at insurance committee hearings.

decision_makers.who: FAIR plan or state-created insurer of last resort
decision_makers.controls: Sells basic property coverage to households that private insurers decline, under rules set by state law and the insurance regulator.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Apply through a licensed agent or broker; complaints go to the state insurance department.

decision_makers.controls: Propose rates, set underwriting rules, and decide where to sell and whether to renew, within state law.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Ask the insurer in writing for the reason for a nonrenewal or increase; state law sets notice requirements.

decision_makers.who: Reinsurers and other investors in catastrophe risk
decision_makers.controls: Set the price and terms of the coverage insurers buy for large events.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: No direct consumer process; state regulators review how reinsurance costs enter rates where state law allows.

decision_makers.controls: Authorizes the NFIP, sets its borrowing limit and statutory caps on premium increases, and funds FEMA mitigation programs.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your U.S. representative and senators through the member directory at congress.gov/members.

decision_makers.controls: Runs the NFIP, sets flood premiums through Risk Rating 2.0 within statutory caps, and publishes flood maps.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Check your property's flood zone at the FEMA Flood Map Service Center (msc.fema.gov) and request a map change through FEMA's Letter of Map Amendment process; your community's floodplain administrator can help.

decision_makers.who: Local building department and city or county council
decision_makers.controls: Adopt the building code where state law allows local adoption, issue permits and inspect construction.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Ask the building department which code edition it enforces; comment when the council considers code updates.

decision_makers.controls: Monitors the insurance industry and publishes analyses such as its homeowners insurance market study; it does not approve rates.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Reports are posted at home.treasury.gov.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: State legislatures write the insurance code, so they decide whether rates need approval before use, which costs may count, how FAIR plans or state insurers operate, and which building codes apply; Florida's legislature changed claim and litigation rules in Chapter 2022-271. State insurance commissioners adopt regulations within that code, as California's did in 2024 when it allowed catastrophe models in exchange for coverage commitments. Voters can change insurance law by initiative in states that allow it. Congress controls the NFIP's authorization, borrowing limit and premium caps, and the current authority ends December 11, 2026. FEMA sets flood rating methods and maps within the statute. Cities and counties adopt and enforce building codes where state law gives them that power.

responses.name: Adopt and enforce stronger building codes
responses.what_it_does: States and localities adopt current hazard-resistant building codes, such as stronger roof attachment in hurricane areas and ignition-resistant materials in wildfire zones, and building departments inspect new construction for compliance. Retrofit programs can extend some protections to existing homes. Fewer damaged homes after an event means smaller claims, which is the cost that premiums must cover. Codes apply to buildings built or substantially rebuilt after adoption, so the benefit grows as the housing stock turns over.
responses.requires: Authority sits with state legislatures and, in many states, city and county councils. Enforcement needs trained inspectors and permit fees or budgets to pay them. FEMA and Congress fund some mitigation grants. New construction costs more up front, and benefits arrive when a hazard strikes.
responses.evidence: California homes built after the state's 2008 wildfire building standards were about 40% less likely to be destroyed in a wildfire, and the codes also protected neighboring homes, by Baylis and Boomhower's analysis. FEMA's 2020 modeling estimates $132 billion in losses avoided by 2040 from modern codes adopted since 2000, a figure from a loss model. How much these savings lower premiums depends on state rate rules.
responses.tradeoffs: Builders and buyers pay more for new homes, which works against efforts to add housing at lower cost, such as R-30 (Allow more homes under clear rules near jobs and transit). Codes adopted without inspection staff deliver little, and older homes remain exposed.

responses.name: Allow forward-looking risk pricing tied to coverage commitments
responses.what_it_does: A state lets insurers base rates on catastrophe models that look ahead and on the cost of reinsurance, and in return requires them to write more policies in high-risk areas. California adopted this approach through regulations issued in 2024, requiring insurers that use the new tools to write at least 85% of their statewide market share in wildfire-distressed areas. Models can also credit home hardening and community wildfire work with lower rates.
responses.requires: A state insurance commissioner acting under existing law, or a legislature changing the insurance code. Regulators need staff who can review catastrophe models and track each insurer's coverage commitments, and they must enforce against insurers that fall short. Public reporting of each insurer's new policies in distressed areas lets households see whether coverage returns.
responses.evidence: Federal Reserve economists found that where rate rules were most restrictive, premiums lagged losses and insurers shifted costs to households in other states; Treasury reports faster premium increases where approval rules are less restrictive. No evaluation yet shows whether California's changes have brought insurers back. FAIR Plan policies grew 8% from September 2025 to June 2026.
responses.tradeoffs: Premiums rise for many households as more costs enter rates, and modeled risk is hard for consumers to check. If insurers do not meet their commitments, households pay more without gaining access.

responses.name: Pass a multi-year NFIP reauthorization
responses.what_it_does: Congress extends the NFIP's authority for several years at once, ending repeated lapses in the power to issue flood policies. Home sales in mapped flood zones that rely on a federally backed mortgage need a policy in place at closing. A long-term bill can also settle how the program handles its $22.525 billion debt to the Treasury, the statutory caps on yearly premium increases and help for policyholders who cannot afford risk-based rates.
responses.requires: A law passed by both chambers of Congress and signed by the President, starting in the House Financial Services Committee and the Senate Banking Committee. Debt cancellation or premium assistance requires appropriations or offsets. FEMA must then carry out any changes to rating, mapping and assistance.
responses.evidence: The program lapsed from October 1 to November 12, 2025 and briefly in February 2026, and during a lapse the NFIP cannot issue new contracts. A multi-year authorization removes that risk by design. How changes to pricing, debt or assistance would affect the number of insured homes has not been evaluated.
responses.tradeoffs: Canceling debt shifts costs to taxpayers, and holding premiums below risk keeps building attractive in flood-prone places. Raising premiums toward risk can lead some owners without a mortgage requirement to drop coverage.

responses.name: Change claim-litigation and last-resort insurer rules
responses.what_it_does: A state legislature changes the rules for insurance disputes and for its state-created insurer so that private insurers return and the state plan shrinks. Florida's December 2022 law created a state reinsurance assistance program, barred policyholders from assigning post-loss benefits to contractors under newer policies and amended the attorney-fee statutes for insurance lawsuits. Florida's Citizens later reduced its policy count from 1.4 million to about 254,000.
responses.requires: A state statute, a regulator able to review new insurers and rates, and state funds for any reinsurance assistance program. Insurers taking policies from the state plan need approved rates and enough reinsurance to cover a severe season. Courts apply new litigation rules to claims and policies covered by each provision's effective date.
responses.evidence: Citizens' policy count fell by more than 80% from its September 2023 peak, a documented change in who carries Florida's property risk. The count alone cannot separate the 2022 law from other changes in the market, and no evaluation of its effect on premiums or claim payments is available.
responses.tradeoffs: Policyholders who dispute a claim may find it harder to pay for a lawyer once the insurer no longer covers their fees. If private insurers leave again after a major storm, the state plan must take policies back.

distribution.group: Homeowners in the highest-risk ZIP codes
distribution.difference: From 2018 to 2022 they paid an average of $2,321 a year, 82% more than owners in the least risky fifth of ZIP codes, and faced nonrenewal rates about 80% higher. In the Southeast, where hurricanes drive losses, nonrenewals in the highest-risk group averaged 2.32%, the highest of any region.

distribution.group: Homeowners 65 and older on fixed incomes
distribution.difference: Insurance premiums rose 72% and property taxes 31% from 2019 to 2025, and both bills continue after a mortgage is paid off. Among homeowners, households headed by someone 65 or older had the highest cost-burden rate in 2024, 28%.

distribution.group: Households in states with less restrictive rate rules
distribution.difference: Federal Reserve economists found that insurers raised rates in states with less restrictive rules to offset losses where rules held rates down, so these households carry part of other states' risk. In their estimates, about $2.4 billion of an added $8 billion in premiums over ten years came from such spillovers.

JCHS reports that insurance costs are higher in disaster-prone markets such as Texas and Florida. Florida's state-created insurer held 1.4 million policies in 2023 and about 254,000 in October 2026, so many Florida households moved out of the state plan within three years.

how_to_judge.where: Treasury Federal Insurance Office homeowners insurance data (2018 to 2022) and your state insurance department's market reports
how_to_judge.direction: A smaller gap with stable or falling nonrenewals is better

how_to_judge.where: Plan statistics pages, such as the California FAIR Plan's key statistics and Citizens Property Insurance's policies-in-force report
how_to_judge.direction: Falling counts are better when private insurers are taking the policies; check the plan's eligibility rules as well

how_to_judge.where: FEMA NFIP data and Congressional Research Service report R44593
how_to_judge.direction: More insured properties in flood zones and a multi-year authorization are better

how_to_judge.direction: Higher is better

pathways.title: Health coverage and access
pathways.question: Why is it hard to find an appointment?
also_answers: What happens to my coverage when my job changes?
Who decides whether I qualify for Medicaid or a subsidized marketplace plan?
Who decides which doctors are in my plan's network?
pathways.short_answer: An appointment depends on coverage and on whether a clinician near you has time. Whether you have coverage turns on your employer's plan, on marketplace subsidies that Congress sets, and on your state Medicaid agency, which checks eligibility at each renewal. Insurers then choose which clinicians join a plan's network. The number of clinicians nearby depends on Medicare funding for residency training, state licensing laws and what each payer pays. As of December 2025, 92.3 million people lived in federal primary care shortage areas. A 2025 survey of offices in 15 large metro areas, run by a staffing company, found an average wait of 31 days for a new patient.
pathways.scope_note: Federal law sets COBRA, marketplace subsidies, the Medicaid work requirement and Medicare's residency funding. States run Medicaid, license clinicians and regulate insurance sold in the state, so rules and waits differ by state and by region. One person's long wait or lost coverage cannot show which of these decisions caused it.

mechanisms.title: Employers choose the plan, and coverage ends with the job
mechanisms.text: About 53.5% of people had coverage through an employer at some point in 2025, according to the Census Bureau. The employer decides whether to offer a plan, how much of the premium workers pay and which insurer or administrator runs it. In 2025 the average family premium reached $26,993, with workers paying $6,850 of it. When a job ends, coverage usually ends too. Employers with 20 or more workers must offer COBRA, which keeps the same plan for up to 18 months at up to 102% of its full cost. Many people instead use a 60-day special enrollment window to buy a marketplace plan.

mechanisms.title: Congress sets the tax credit that lowers marketplace premiums
mechanisms.text: People without job-based coverage can buy a plan on HealthCare.gov or a state marketplace. A federal premium tax credit, set by Congress, lowers the monthly premium according to income. Larger credits enacted in 2021 expired at the end of 2025, and Congress had not extended them as of October 2026. KFF, an independent health policy research organization, reported that people who kept the same plan saw premium payments rise 114% on average. Enrollment fell from 22.1 million in 2025 to 19.2 million in February 2026. Open enrollment for 2027 coverage on HealthCare.gov runs from November 1, 2026 to January 15, 2027.

mechanisms.title: State Medicaid agencies decide eligibility at every renewal
mechanisms.text: Each state runs Medicaid under federal rules. The state agency decides who qualifies and checks again at renewal, either from data it already holds or by asking the enrollee for paperwork. When pandemic-era continuous coverage ended, more than 25 million people were disenrolled, 69% for procedural reasons such as an unreturned form. Ten states have not expanded Medicaid to low-income adults. The 2025 federal budget law, Public Law 119-21, adds a work or community engagement requirement for expansion adults aged 19 to 64, starting no later than January 1, 2027, plus renewals every six months for that group.

mechanisms.title: Insurers build networks under state and federal standards
mechanisms.text: A plan pays in-network rates only to clinicians who sign its contract. The insurer decides whom to invite and what to pay, and it publishes a directory. State insurance departments set network adequacy rules for the plans they regulate, and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) sets them for plans sold on HealthCare.gov. Since 2025, those federal marketplace plans must offer routine primary care within 15 business days and behavioral health care within 10, at least 90% of the time. Directories can overstate access: in a 2023 test by Senate Finance Committee staff, callers secured appointments with 18% of listed mental health providers.

mechanisms.title: Residency funding, licensing laws and payment rates limit clinician supply
mechanisms.text: Medicare pays most residency training costs, about $22 billion in 2023, and federal law has capped the residents each hospital can count since 1997. Congress added 1,000 positions in 2021, phased in over five years. State legislatures decide what nurse practitioners may do without a physician. Payment rates also shape who gets seen: in 2024, Medicaid paid physicians about 75% of Medicare rates, and a 2025 survey found that 53% of offices in large metro areas accepted Medicaid patients.

mechanisms.title: Rural hospital closures move care farther away
mechanisms.text: A hospital's owner closes it or ends inpatient care when revenue no longer covers costs. Researchers at the University of North Carolina count 197 rural hospital closures and conversions since 2005. The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the auditing agency for Congress, found that after closures between 2013 and 2017, the median distance to inpatient care rose from 3.4 miles to 23.9 miles, and physicians per 100,000 residents fell in those counties. Congress created a $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program for 2026 to 2030 and required CMS to decide state applications by December 31, 2025; CMS released state-by-state funding announcements in October 2026.

pathways.household_effects: A worker who changes jobs can face a gap between plans, a COBRA bill for the whole premium, or a 60-day deadline to pick a marketplace plan. Marketplace enrollees who lost the larger credits in 2026 paid more each month or moved to plans whose deductibles were 37% higher on average. Medicaid enrollees can lose coverage over a missed form while they still qualify. In the Federal Reserve's 2025 survey, 26% of adults said they skipped medical expenses because of cost. Rural residents and Medicaid enrollees have fewer nearby clinicians who will take a new patient.

sub_issues.title: Changing or losing a job
sub_issues.text: When employment ends, job-based coverage usually ends with it. COBRA keeps the same plan for up to 18 months at employers with 20 or more workers, and the person pays up to 102% of the full premium. The deadline to elect it is 60 days after coverage ends or after the notice arrives, whichever is later. Losing job-based coverage also opens a 60-day marketplace window. Dropping COBRA early outside open enrollment generally does not open a new one.

sub_issues.title: Marketplace costs after the larger credits ended
sub_issues.text: Premium tax credits enlarged in 2021 expired at the end of 2025. Insurers sought a median premium increase of about 15% for 2027, by KFF's count. The 2025 budget law also requires enrollees who underestimated their income to repay all excess credits starting with tax year 2026, and it bars many lawfully present immigrants from the credit starting in 2027. New Mexico used state money to replace the lost federal help and was the only state where enrollment did not fall.

sub_issues.title: Medicaid renewals and the work requirement
sub_issues.text: Under the 2025 law, adults aged 19 to 64 covered through Medicaid expansion must show 80 hours a month of work, school, job training or community service, or earnings of at least $580 a month in 2026. Parents of children 13 and under, pregnant and postpartum people, people who are medically frail and several other groups are exempt. CMS issued the implementing rule on June 1, 2026. Nebraska and Montana started early. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated the requirement would leave 5.3 million more people uninsured in 2034.

sub_issues.title: Who regulates your plan
sub_issues.text: ERISA, the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, governs private employer plans. When an employer pays claims itself, called a self-funded plan, state insurance law does not apply and the U.S. Department of Labor oversees the plan. In 2025, 67% of covered workers were in self-funded plans. Policies that employers buy from insurers fall under the state insurance department. Either way, a denied claim can go to an internal appeal and then to an independent external reviewer whose decision the plan must accept.

sub_issues.title: Directories that list unavailable clinicians
sub_issues.text: A provider directory can list clinicians who have left, do not take new patients or cannot be reached, sometimes called a ghost network. Senate Finance Committee majority staff called 120 listed mental health providers in 12 Medicare Advantage plans across six states in 2023 and secured appointments with 18%. Federal rules now require HealthCare.gov plans and state Medicaid programs to run secret shopper surveys, in which callers pose as new patients, to test wait times.

sub_issues.title: Too few clinicians where people live
sub_issues.text: As of December 31, 2025, 92.3 million people lived in primary care shortage areas designated by the Health Resources and Services Administration, where available physicians met about 48% of estimated need. Congress added 1,000 Medicare-funded residency positions in 2021. GAO found that by September 2025 CMS had allocated 600 of them, nearly all to hospitals in urban areas.

sub_issues.title: Rural hospitals and travel time
sub_issues.text: When a rural hospital closes, residents travel farther for inpatient care and addiction treatment. GAO found the median distance to alcohol or drug treatment rose from 5.5 miles to 44.6 miles in the areas it studied. Some hospitals convert to Rural Emergency Hospitals, which end inpatient care; the University of North Carolina count of 197 closures leaves those conversions out. States are now receiving Rural Health Transformation awards that can pay for recruitment and telehealth.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress sets the core federal rules by statute: premium tax credit amounts, the Medicaid work requirement and six-month renewals in Public Law 119-21, COBRA and ERISA, and the cap on Medicare-funded residency positions. CMS writes regulations under those laws, including its June 2026 interim final rule on Medicaid work requirements and network standards for HealthCare.gov plans, and federal courts can set aside a rule that exceeds the statute. Each state legislature decides whether to expand Medicaid, whether to fund state premium subsidies, what clinicians may do under their licenses and what network adequacy law applies to state-regulated insurance. State insurance departments write and enforce regulations under that law. Employers decide plan design within ERISA, and insurers decide network contracts within state and federal standards.

responses.name: Renew coverage automatically from records agencies already hold
responses.what_it_does: State Medicaid agencies would renew eligibility by checking wage, tax and benefit records before asking an enrollee for paperwork, and would use the same records to confirm work hours or exemptions under the new requirement. Marketplaces would send deadline reminders and enroll eligible people by default where law allows. Children already keep Medicaid or CHIP for 12 months at a time under a 2023 law, which limits checks on them between renewals.
responses.requires: Eligibility systems that can match records, staff to correct errors and CMS review of state verification plans; CMS's June 2026 rule asks states to use available data where possible. Default enrollment in marketplace plans needs federal or state authority. The 2025 law's pre-enrollment verification, starting in 2028, limits automatic renewal of marketplace subsidies.
responses.evidence: During the Medicaid unwinding, automatic renewal rates ranged from 11% or less in Pennsylvania and Texas to 90% or more in Arizona, North Carolina and Rhode Island. In a randomized experiment in California, reminder letters raised marketplace enrollment by 16%. A study of a subsidized exchange found that removing automatic enrollment cut enrollment by 33%. None of these studies tested verification of Medicaid work hours, which has no evaluation yet.
responses.tradeoffs: Record matches can be wrong or out of date and may renew people whose circumstances changed. States pay to build and run the systems. Federal rules that require proof before subsidies flow limit how far automation can go.

responses.name: Set the size of marketplace premium help
responses.what_it_does: Congress would decide the premium tax credit schedule for 2027 and later years, choosing among restoring the larger credits, extending a modified version or keeping current law. States can add their own subsidies on top of the federal credit, as New Mexico did in 2026. A larger credit lowers the monthly premium an enrollee pays, with the federal or state budget covering the difference.
responses.requires: A federal statute passed by both chambers and signed, with a cost estimate from CBO. For a state subsidy, a state appropriation and a marketplace able to apply it at enrollment. Changes enacted after open enrollment closes on January 15, 2027 would mainly affect later plan years.
responses.evidence: After the larger credits expired, marketplace enrollment fell about 13% between 2025 and February 2026, and New Mexico, which replaced the lost credits with state funds, was the only state without a decline, according to KFF. CBO had estimated that expiration would add 4.2 million uninsured people by 2034. The 2026 drop comes from a before-and-after comparison, and other rule changes took effect at the same time.
responses.tradeoffs: Federal or state budgets bear the cost for as long as the credits continue. Letting them lapse shifts that cost to enrollees, and people who drop coverage may face medical bills without insurance.

responses.name: Verify work hours and exemptions before ending coverage
responses.what_it_does: State Medicaid agencies would confirm compliance or exemptions from payroll, SNAP, disability and medical claims records, send notices in more than one format and allow time to respond before ending coverage. A state that cannot build these systems in time may seek a federal good-faith exemption lasting no later than December 31, 2028. These choices sit inside Public Law 119-21 and CMS's June 2026 rule.
responses.requires: State agency staff, data-sharing agreements with labor and benefit agencies, outreach notices three months before the first lookback month, and CMS approval of any exemption request. Changing the requirement itself would take an act of Congress amending Public Law 119-21.
responses.evidence: When Arkansas required monthly online reporting in 2018, the uninsured rate among adults aged 30 to 49 rose from 10.5% to 14.6% with no measurable change in employment, according to a peer-reviewed survey study comparing Arkansas with three other states. Verification built on data matching under the new federal law has no evaluation yet.
responses.tradeoffs: Data systems cost money and can miss informal or irregular work. Exemptions delay the work incentive Congress intended. Enrollees who lose coverage over paperwork face medical debt and delayed care, as Arkansas residents did.

responses.name: Audit networks with secret shoppers and correct inaccurate directories
responses.what_it_does: Regulators would test whether listed clinicians answer, take the plan and offer an appointment within the standard, then require corrections or impose penalties when a plan falls short. CMS already requires these tests for HealthCare.gov plans, and Medicaid managed care programs must run annual surveys through an independent firm. State insurance departments can adopt similar tests for the plans they regulate and publish the results.
responses.requires: State statute or regulation for state-regulated plans; CMS enforcement for federal marketplace and Medicaid plans; budgets for survey firms; public reporting of results so enrollees can compare plans. Self-funded employer plans fall under the Department of Labor, so state network rules do not reach them.
responses.evidence: The 2023 Senate Finance staff test found appointments with 18% of listed mental health providers, from a small sample of 120 calls. Federal wait-time standards began in 2025, and no published evaluation yet shows whether audits shorten waits or improve directory accuracy.
responses.tradeoffs: Surveys cost plans and regulators money. Penalties may lead insurers to remove listings, which makes directories accurate without adding any clinicians.

responses.name: Train and license more clinicians where shortages are worst
responses.what_it_does: Congress would fund more Medicare residency positions aimed at shortage areas, and state legislatures would decide whether nurse practitioners can practice and prescribe without physician oversight. States could also raise Medicaid payment rates, which affects whether offices accept Medicaid patients. New residency positions add physicians only after residents finish several years of training, and a scope-of-practice law changes who can see patients once it takes effect.
responses.requires: A federal statute for new residency positions, which CMS then distributes to teaching hospitals, followed by several years before new residents finish training. State statutes or licensing board rules for scope of practice. State appropriations, matched by federal Medicaid funds, for higher payment rates.
responses.evidence: In one quasi-experimental study, state laws granting nurse practitioners independence were followed by more routine checkups and fewer emergency visits for conditions primary care can manage. A study in Veterans Health Administration emergency departments found nurse practitioners used more resources and had higher preventable hospitalization rates than physicians. GAO found nearly all new residency positions went to urban hospitals.
responses.tradeoffs: Medicare already spends about $22 billion a year on residency training. Wider scope shifts some care to clinicians with shorter training, and results differ by setting. Higher Medicaid rates cost state and federal budgets.

responses.name: Fund rural hospitals to keep essential services open
responses.what_it_does: The Rural Health Transformation Program sends $10 billion a year to states from fiscal year 2026 through 2030. States choose at least three of ten approved uses, such as paying providers, telehealth, and recruiting clinicians who commit to five years of rural service. CMS approves each state's plan, and state agencies then distribute the money to hospitals, clinics and other providers in rural areas.
responses.requires: Federal funding already enacted in Public Law 119-21; CMS approval of each state plan; state agencies with enough staff to award grants, track spending and report results to CMS. Support after fiscal year 2030 would need new legislation from Congress.
responses.evidence: The program began paying states in fiscal 2026, so no evaluation of results exists. GAO documented that closures between 2013 and 2017 lengthened travel to inpatient care, which is evidence about the problem; it does not show that grants prevent closures.
responses.tradeoffs: Funds can sustain hospitals with few patients at a high cost per visit. Money spread across many uses may not stop specific closures, and the program ends in 2030 unless Congress renews it.

distribution.group: Low-income adults in the 10 states without Medicaid expansion
distribution.difference: About 1.2 million adults earn too much for their state's Medicaid program and too little for marketplace subsidies, which begin at the federal poverty line, according to KFF. Most are adults without dependent children. Georgia and Wisconsin have no gap because their waivers cover adults up to the poverty line.

This group faces the work requirement and six-month renewals. Exempt groups include parents of children 13 and under, pregnant and postpartum people and people who are medically frail. CBO estimated 5.3 million more uninsured people in 2034 from the requirement (an average of 4.5 million a year over 2027 to 2034) and 700,000 from more frequent renewals, before accounting for overlap.

Starting October 1, 2026, Medicaid and CHIP eligibility is limited mainly to lawful permanent residents, certain Cuban and Haitian entrants and migrants from Compact of Free Association nations. From 2027, the same narrower groups can receive marketplace tax credits. The Atlas does not ask for or record anyone's immigration status.

After rural hospitals closed between 2013 and 2017, the median distance to inpatient care rose from 3.4 miles to 23.9 miles, GAO found, and physicians per 100,000 residents in those counties fell from 71.2 to 59.7.

distribution.group: Medicaid enrollees looking for a new doctor
distribution.difference: Medicaid paid physicians about 75% of Medicare rates in 2024 and 66% for primary care, with states ranging from 52% in Rhode Island to 132% in Montana. In a 2025 survey of offices in 15 metro areas, 53% accepted Medicaid patients and 82% accepted Medicare.

check.prompt: Your employer pays workers' medical claims itself through a self-funded plan. Which office oversees that plan under federal law?
options: The U.S. Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration
check.explanation: ERISA governs private employer plans. Self-funded plans are exempt from state insurance regulation, so the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration enforces the federal rules. A state insurance department regulates a policy that an employer buys from an insurer.

pathways.title: Medical bills and drug prices
pathways.question: Why can the same care produce different bills?
also_answers: What shapes the price of a medicine?
Who decides what a hospital charges my insurer?
What happens if I cannot pay a medical bill?
pathways.short_answer: Most of a medical bill's price comes from a private contract. Each insurer or employer plan negotiates its own rates with each hospital and clinician, so a scan can cost widely different amounts within one city. Hospitals with few nearby rivals win higher rates, and Medicare pays more for some services in hospital outpatient departments than in doctors' offices. RAND, a nonprofit research organization, found private plans paid hospitals 254% of Medicare rates in 2022. For medicines, the manufacturer sets a list price protected by patents, and pharmacy benefit managers negotiate rebates off that price, so a patient's coinsurance can still be based on the full list price.
pathways.scope_note: Contracts between insurers and hospitals are private and differ by market. Federal law sets Medicare prices, surprise billing protections, price posting rules, drug patents and Medicare drug negotiation; states regulate debt collection, credit reporting and much of insurance. One bill shows one contract and one plan design, so it cannot show what other patients pay.

mechanisms.title: Insurers and hospitals negotiate private prices
mechanisms.text: Medicare sets its payment rates by regulation. Private insurers and self-funded employers pay whatever each contract says, and those contracts are negotiated hospital by hospital. In insurer claims covering 28% of people with employer coverage, about half the difference in spending per person across regions came from prices, and prices also varied among hospitals in the same area. RAND found private payers paid hospitals 254% of Medicare rates on average in 2022, with state averages from under 170% in Arkansas to above 300% in states including California, Florida, New York and Wisconsin.

mechanisms.title: Fewer competing hospitals means higher negotiated prices
mechanisms.text: An insurer needs local hospitals in its network to sell plans. When a hospital has no nearby rival, the insurer has little room to walk away from its terms. In the same claims study, monopoly hospitals' prices were 12% higher than in markets with four or more hospitals. Among 366 mergers from 2007 to 2011, prices rose by more than 6% when the merging hospitals were within five miles of each other. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), the Justice Department and state attorneys general review mergers under federal antitrust law and can sue to block them.

mechanisms.title: Where care happens changes the payment
mechanisms.text: Medicare pays more for many services billed by a hospital outpatient department than for the same service in an independent office, and a patient's coinsurance rises with the payment. For an echocardiogram in 2023, Medicare paid 194% more in the hospital setting, according to the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC), which advises Congress. MedPAC found the difference gives hospitals a reason to buy physician practices. The share of physicians in hospital-owned practices or employed by hospitals rose from 29.0% in 2012 to 39.8% in 2020.

mechanisms.title: Manufacturers set list prices that patents protect
mechanisms.text: A drug company sets the list price of a brand-name medicine. Patents granted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office and exclusivity periods from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) keep generic or biosimilar copies off the market for a time. In FDA records from 2005 to 2015, 78% of drugs tied to new patents were existing drugs, a practice that can lengthen protection. Prices fall once copies arrive: the FDA reports about 30% lower prices with one generic competitor and nearly 85% with five. Since 2026, Medicare negotiates prices for some high-spending drugs that still lack competition.

mechanisms.title: Pharmacy benefit managers negotiate rebates and set coverage
mechanisms.text: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) run drug benefits for insurers and employers. They decide which drugs a plan covers, which pharmacies are in network and what rebates manufacturers pay. The three largest processed nearly 80% of about 6.6 billion prescriptions in 2023, according to the FTC, and each is tied to a major insurer and its own pharmacies. The FTC's 2024 complaint alleges that rebates tied to list prices led these PBMs to favor higher-priced insulins; no tribunal has found them liable. A patient whose coinsurance is based on the list price pays more when that price rises.

mechanisms.title: Collection and charity care rules govern unpaid bills
mechanisms.text: An unpaid bill can go to a collection agency, a credit report or a lawsuit. Nonprofit hospitals receive tax exemptions, and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) rules require them to accept financial assistance applications for 240 days and wait at least 120 days after the first bill before reporting debt to a credit bureau or suing. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) finalized a rule in January 2025 to keep medical bills off credit reports used by lenders; a federal court vacated it in July 2025. Some states, including Colorado, ban medical debt on credit reports by statute.

pathways.household_effects: A single hospital visit can produce separate bills from the hospital and each clinician, and the amount owed depends on the contract price and the plan's deductible. In KFF's 2022 survey, 41% of adults had debt from medical or dental bills, and 64% of them said someone in the household put off needed care because of cost. About 14 million adults owed more than $1,000, with shares from 17.7% of adults in South Dakota to 2.3% in Hawaii. Medicare enrollees pay at most $35 a month for each covered insulin and up to $2,100 in 2026 for covered Part D drugs; people with job-based or marketplace plans follow their plan's terms.

sub_issues.title: Same scan, different price
sub_issues.text: Each insurer's contract with each hospital sets a separate price, so patients in different plans can pay different amounts for the same service at the same hospital. Since January 2021, hospitals must post these rates in a machine-readable file, and since 2022 most insurers and group plans must post theirs. CMS enforces hospital posting through audits and complaints; its public list shows 29 civil monetary penalty notices to 28 hospitals as of mid-2026.

sub_issues.title: Hospital mergers and local prices
sub_issues.text: A merger between nearby hospitals can raise prices because the insurer loses the option of leaving one of them out of its network. In the studied deals, mergers of hospitals within five miles raised prices more than 6%, while mergers of hospitals more than 25 miles apart did not. Antitrust agencies decide whether to challenge a merger in court. The price evidence comes from deals made between 2007 and 2011.

sub_issues.title: Facility fees
sub_issues.text: When a hospital owns a clinic, services there can be billed as hospital outpatient care, with a facility payment added to the clinician's fee. MedPAC recommended in 2023 that Congress align Medicare payment across settings for selected services. For 66 payment groups, that would have cut Medicare spending by $6.0 billion and beneficiary cost sharing by $1.5 billion in 2021, before offsets that current budget-neutrality law requires.

sub_issues.title: Surprise bills and the dispute process
sub_issues.text: The federal No Surprises Act bars surprise out-of-network bills for emergency care, for many services at in-network hospitals and surgery centers, and for air ambulances. When a provider and plan disagree on payment, either side can start independent dispute resolution, a federal arbitration process. Parties started 712,561 disputes in June and July 2026 alone. Uninsured patients can request a good faith estimate and dispute a final bill that is $400 or more above it.

sub_issues.title: Medical debt and credit reports
sub_issues.text: At least 14 million adults owe more than $1,000 in medical debt. The federal rule that would have removed medical bills from credit reports was vacated in July 2025 after the CFPB and the plaintiffs jointly asked the court to do so, leaving state laws and the credit bureaus' own policies in place. Colorado has barred medical debt on credit reports since August 2023. Randomized experiments that paid off old medical debt found no average improvement in mental health or financial well-being.

sub_issues.title: Charity care at nonprofit hospitals
sub_issues.text: Nonprofit hospitals pay little or no income and property tax. KFF, an independent health policy research organization, estimated the exemption was worth about $28 billion in 2020, while these hospitals' charity care cost about $16 billion. Federal law does not define how much community benefit is enough, and GAO found the IRS could not show it reviewed each hospital's community benefit at least every three years.

sub_issues.title: Insulin, rebates and drug middlemen
sub_issues.text: The FTC sued the three largest PBMs in September 2024 over insulin rebates. Express Scripts reached a proposed settlement in February 2026 and Caremark in July. Optum Rx's case was withdrawn from adjudication on June 12, 2026 while the Commission considers a settlement that has not been published. As of October 15, 2026, none of the three had a final order. A 2026 federal law requires PBMs to pass manufacturer rebates through to Medicare drug plans from January 2028 and to employer plans for plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028 (January 2029 for most calendar-year plans).

sub_issues.title: Medicare drug price negotiation
sub_issues.text: Since January 1, 2026, Medicare pays negotiated prices for 10 drugs; CMS estimated a 22% net saving had those prices applied in 2023. Prices for 15 more, including Ozempic and Wegovy, take effect in 2027. Another 15, the first to include drugs given in doctors' offices under Part B, take effect in 2028. The 2025 budget law exempted more drugs that treat rare diseases, which CBO estimated will cost $8.8 billion over ten years.

decision_makers.controls: Whether medical debt can appear on credit reports, debt collection rules, and rules for state-regulated insurers and PBMs
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Testimony at legislative committee hearings; your state legislators' offices

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress sets Medicare payment law, including whether hospital outpatient departments are paid more than offices, the scope of Medicare drug price negotiation, the No Surprises Act, patent terms and the PBM rules in Public Law 119-75. CMS writes payment and price posting regulations each year, and the FTC and Justice Department enforce antitrust law in court or through consent orders. State legislatures decide whether medical debt can appear on credit reports, how debt collectors operate and many rules for state-regulated insurers and PBMs. Courts decide challenges to these rules, as a federal court in Texas did when it vacated the CFPB's medical debt rule in 2025. Private contracts among insurers, employers, hospitals and PBMs set most prices within these limits.

responses.name: Challenge mergers that reduce hospital competition
responses.what_it_does: The FTC, the Justice Department and state attorneys general would review hospital and physician practice acquisitions, sue to block those likely to raise prices, and require conditions or divestitures where a deal goes ahead. Later studies of mergers that were allowed would test whether prices rose afterward, so reviewers can adjust which deals they challenge. State laws can require advance notice of smaller deals.
responses.requires: Existing authority under the Clayton Act; budgets for staff economists and litigators; a court ruling when the merging parties contest a challenge. Smaller acquisitions can fall below federal premerger reporting thresholds, so states would need their own notice laws to see them.
responses.evidence: Studied mergers of hospitals within five miles of each other raised prices by more than 6%, which is evidence about the harm enforcement targets. Evidence that blocking particular deals lowers prices over time is thinner, because a blocked merger leaves no outcome to observe.
responses.tradeoffs: Some struggling rural hospitals seek a merger to stay open, and blocking the deal can remove that option. Litigation is costly, and agencies lose some cases in court.

responses.name: Pay the same Medicare rate across sites for routine services
responses.what_it_does: Congress would direct Medicare to pay hospital outpatient departments the same rate as independent offices or surgery centers for selected services that are safe in any of these settings. Beneficiaries' coinsurance would fall along with the payment. Private insurers could set similar limits on facility fees in their contracts, and state legislatures could set them in state law for plans they regulate.
responses.requires: A federal statute from Congress; CMS rulemaking to set and update the service list; protections for hospitals that keep services open in rural or underserved areas. Current law requires Medicare outpatient changes to be budget neutral, so program savings need a change in statute.
responses.evidence: MedPAC estimated that aligning payment for 66 service groups would have reduced Medicare spending by $6.0 billion and beneficiary cost sharing by $1.5 billion in 2021. These are estimates from payment data; no national rollout has been evaluated for effects on access or hospital finances.
responses.tradeoffs: Hospitals lose revenue that helps pay for emergency and standby services, so rural and safety-net hospitals may need separate support. Savings shrink if services move to other high-paying settings.

responses.name: Remove rebate incentives from drug benefits
responses.what_it_does: Rules would stop PBM pay from rising with a drug's list price and require rebates to reach plans and patients. Public Law 119-75 requires rebate pass-through to Medicare drug plans from January 2028 and full payment of rebates and fees to employer plans about 30 months after its February 2026 enactment. The FTC's proposed orders would add standard options in which patients pay based on the net price.
responses.requires: CMS and Department of Labor rules to implement the 2026 law; audits of the reports PBMs must give plan sponsors; final FTC orders and the monitors they appoint; state laws for plans states regulate. Self-funded employer plans follow the federal rules under ERISA.
responses.evidence: The FTC documented that the three largest PBMs process nearly 80% of prescriptions and that their pharmacies took in $7.3 billion above estimated acquisition cost on 51 specialty generic drugs from 2017 to 2022. These findings describe the problem. The 2026 law takes effect in 2028, and no national evaluation of pass-through or delinking exists yet.
responses.tradeoffs: If rebates stop offsetting premiums, some premiums could rise while patients who use rebated drugs pay less at the counter. PBMs can shift income into new fees, which audits must catch.

responses.name: Expand Medicare drug price negotiation
responses.what_it_does: Medicare negotiates a maximum price for selected high-spending drugs that have been sold for years without generic or biosimilar competition. Under current law, up to 20 drugs a year will be selected starting in 2027. Congress could change which drugs qualify, how many are chosen each year, or whether people with private coverage also receive the negotiated price at the pharmacy.
responses.requires: A federal statute from Congress to change eligibility, the annual number of drugs or who receives the price. CMS needs staff and contractors to negotiate each cycle, publish the prices and monitor that pharmacies and patients receive the negotiated price.
responses.evidence: CMS estimated net savings of 22% for the first 10 drugs and 44% for the next 15, measured against prior net prices, and beneficiaries were estimated to save about $1.5 billion in 2026. These are estimates made before full claims data; the sources do not measure effects on future drug development.
responses.tradeoffs: Manufacturers receive less revenue from selected drugs, which can affect which drugs they develop and how they set launch prices. Savings stay within Medicare unless Congress extends them to other payers.

responses.name: Bring generic and biosimilar competitors to market sooner
responses.what_it_does: The FDA would review copies of brand-name drugs faster, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office would examine patents on minor changes to existing drugs more closely, and the FTC would challenge settlements in which a brand company pays a generic maker to delay entry. Earlier competition lowers prices for every payer at once, including Medicare, Medicaid, employers and people paying cash.
responses.requires: FDA review staff and published guidance for drug makers; patent examination resources at the Patent and Trademark Office and, for changes to patent terms, an act of Congress; FTC enforcement under the antitrust laws, which can take years in court.
responses.evidence: The FDA reports prices about 30% lower with one generic competitor and nearly 85% lower with five. An analysis of FDA records found 78% of drugs tied to new patents from 2005 to 2015 were existing drugs. Neither source evaluates a specific patent reform.
responses.tradeoffs: Shorter protection lowers the expected return on new drugs, which could reduce investment in some research. Faster reviews require more FDA staff.

responses.name: Limit medical debt collection and credit reporting
responses.what_it_does: State laws would keep medical debt off credit reports, limit lawsuits and interest on medical bills, and require hospitals to screen every patient for financial assistance before sending a bill to a collection agency or court. The IRS would enforce existing limits on nonprofit hospitals' collection actions, and state attorneys general would enforce state debt collection rules against hospitals and collectors.
responses.requires: State statutes and attorney general enforcement; IRS examination staff for section 501(r) reviews; hospital billing systems that screen patients for assistance before collection begins. A federal credit reporting ban would need new authority from Congress after the 2025 court decision.
responses.evidence: Colorado's 2023 law is in effect, and the state must report on its effects by January 1, 2028, so no evaluation exists yet. In a related test, randomized experiments that paid off $169 million in old medical debt for 83,401 people found no average improvement in mental health or financial well-being, and credit access improved only modestly where the debt was still reported.
responses.tradeoffs: Lenders lose information about unpaid bills, which may change how they price credit. Hospitals collect less, and these limits do not lower the underlying price of care.

distribution.group: Patients who pay deductibles or coinsurance
distribution.difference: These patients pay a share of whatever price the contract sets, so price differences reach them directly. Caremark's proposed FTC order would offer a standard option in which members pay the contracted rate minus rebates instead of the list price, and an insulin program capping costs at $25 for up to a 34-day supply unless the plan sponsor opts out.

Medicare caps insulin at $35 a month for each covered product and out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs at $2,100 in 2026 and $2,400 in 2027. Negotiated drug prices apply only in Medicare. People in private plans follow their own plan's cost sharing.

distribution.group: Residents of states with more medical debt
distribution.difference: In 2021 survey data, 17.7% of adults in South Dakota and 15.2% in Mississippi had medical debt, compared with 2.3% in Hawaii, according to KFF. The shares come from a federal survey and do not by themselves show why states differ.

distribution.group: Patients at hospitals with no nearby rival
distribution.difference: Monopoly hospitals' prices were 12% higher than prices in markets with four or more hospitals in the claims study. Patients in high-deductible plans at those hospitals pay a larger part of that difference themselves until they reach their deductible.

People without insurance who schedule care at least three business days ahead can request a good faith estimate and dispute a final bill $400 or more above it. Nonprofit hospitals must accept their financial assistance applications for at least 240 days after the first bill.
