pathways.title: Childcare and family care
pathways.question: Why does childcare cost so much, and why can't I find an opening?
also_answers: Who sets the rules that childcare programs must follow?
Who helps pay for childcare besides parents?
What changed in federal childcare tax credits for 2026?
Who covers the time parents take off to care for a new baby?
pathways.short_answer: Childcare costs a lot because young children need many adults per child, and staff pay makes up most of a program's budget. State licensing agencies set those staff-to-child ratios. Pay stays low anyway: childcare workers earned a median $16.82 an hour in May 2025, and programs struggle to hire and keep staff. Parents cover most of the bill, an average of $13,184 a year in 2025 by the count of Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group. Subsidies reached 16 percent of children eligible under federal rules in 2022, and each state legislature decides how much more to add.
pathways.scope_note: Federal law sets block grant rules, Head Start standards and tax credits. Each state sets its own licensing rules, subsidy eligibility, copayments and provider payment rates, and some states and cities add their own money. Prices and waits differ by state, neighborhood and a child's age, so one family's bill shows local conditions and cannot stand in for the national picture.

mechanisms.title: State licensing rules decide how many adults each group needs
mechanisms.text: Each state's child care licensing agency writes the rules a program must meet to operate, including the maximum number of children per staff member and the size of each group. Infants and toddlers require the most adults. The U.S. Treasury reported in 2021 that wages make up at least 50 to 60 percent of a typical program's expenses, with a larger share in infant rooms, and that costs vary with each state's ratio rules. A 2011 study in the American Economic Review linked stricter state regulations to fewer centers, especially in lower-income markets, and to higher quality, mainly in higher-income areas.

mechanisms.title: Low pay limits how many programs can open and stay staffed
mechanisms.text: Providers pay staff out of what families and public programs pay them. Treasury found that many for-profit providers earn margins under 1 percent and that 26 to 40 percent of the workforce leaves each year. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) counts about 1.0 million childcare workers, with a median wage of $16.82 an hour in May 2025, and projects about 150,300 openings a year through 2035, all from replacing people who leave. A program that raises wages to hire faster has to raise fees or find public money. Without either, it hires fewer staff and enrolls fewer children.

mechanisms.title: Parents pay most of the price when they can least afford it
mechanisms.text: Most families pay for care themselves, at a stage Treasury described as the point when they can least afford it, and they cannot borrow against future earnings to spread the cost. Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group that compiles state price data, reports an average price of $13,184 a year in 2025. That equals about 10 percent of median income for a two-parent household and 33 percent for a single parent, and center care for two children cost more than median rent in every state with data. High prices keep some parents out of paid work: a 2017 research review estimated that a 10 percent price cut raises mothers' employment by roughly 0.5 to 2.5 percent.

mechanisms.title: Congress funds subsidies and Head Start for a minority of eligible children
mechanisms.text: Congress funds the Child Care and Development Block Grant, which states use to pay part of the cost of care for low-income working families, and Head Start, which pays local agencies to run early learning programs for children in families below the poverty line. States set income limits within the federal maximum, and many set them lower. In fiscal 2022, 11.8 million children were eligible under federal rules and 9.1 million under state rules, and about 1.8 million received a subsidy in an average month. Head Start funded 715,873 places for children and pregnant women in fiscal 2024. For fiscal 2026, Congress provided $8.831 billion for the block grant and about $12.36 billion for Head Start.

mechanisms.title: Pandemic relief paid for staff for a time, then ran out
mechanisms.text: The American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 sent states $23.975 billion for stabilization grants to providers, usable for wages, rent and other operating costs, plus $14.99 billion in extra block grant money that had to be obligated by the end of fiscal 2023. Providers taking stabilization grants had to certify they would keep paying employees full compensation. The Center for the Study of Child Care Employment (CSCCE) at UC Berkeley, a research center that advocates for higher educator pay, found that most states used relief funds to raise wages and wrote that the money was never intended to sustain the system. It points to Vermont's payroll tax and New Mexico's early childhood fund as examples of states that found ongoing revenue.

mechanisms.title: Federal rules on copayments and provider payments changed in 2026
mechanisms.text: The Administration for Children and Families (ACF) in the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) writes the regulations for the block grant. A 2024 rule required states to cap family copayments at 7 percent of income and to pay providers based on enrollment, so that a child's absences did not cut a program's payment; every state asked for temporary waivers of some provisions. A final rule published May 12, 2026 and effective July 13, 2026 rescinded those requirements, along with mandates to pay in advance and to fund some places through grants or contracts. States may keep any of these practices. Those paying after care is delivered must pay within 21 days of a complete invoice, and occasional absences still cannot reduce payments.

pathways.household_effects: For a family, these steps arrive as a monthly bill that can exceed rent, or as no opening nearby at all. Single parents face the steepest burden, about a third of median income by the Child Care Aware count. Families who qualify for a subsidy often still owe a copayment, which states may again set above 7 percent of income. The time cost lands unevenly: in 2025, women in households with children under 6 spent 2.8 hours a day on primary childcare, compared with 1.7 hours for men. Parents who cannot find or afford care cut hours or stop working, which lowers household income during the years when costs are highest.

sub_issues.title: What the child and dependent care credit pays from 2026
sub_issues.text: The federal child and dependent care tax credit returns part of what a family pays for care so parents can work. Starting with tax year 2026, the rate begins at 50 percent of up to $3,000 in costs for one child or $6,000 for two or more. It falls to 35 percent as income rises above $15,000, then steps down toward 20 percent above $75,000, or $150,000 for joint filers. The credit is nonrefundable, meaning it can only reduce income tax owed, so a family that owes no income tax gets nothing from it.

sub_issues.title: Workplace accounts and the employer credit
sub_issues.text: Employers can let workers set aside pre-tax pay for care through a dependent care assistance program, and the 2025 tax law raised that annual limit to $7,500 starting in 2026. The same law enlarged the federal credit for employers that provide or pay for childcare to 40 percent of qualified costs, or 50 percent for small businesses, up to $500,000 a year, or $600,000 for small businesses. The earlier credit was 25 percent with a $150,000 cap. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) estimated that only 169 to 278 corporate tax returns claimed it in 2016.

sub_issues.title: The child tax credit
sub_issues.text: The child tax credit goes to parents whether or not they pay for care. The 2025 law set it at $2,200 per child, removed its end date and indexed it to inflation after 2025. Families with low earnings receive only part of it as a refund, up to $1,700 per child for 2025 and 2026, a $1,400 statutory base indexed for inflation. Reform profile R-25: Pay the full child credit to families with little earned income describes proposals to remove that cap.

sub_issues.title: Head Start and a proposed change to staff pay rules
sub_issues.text: Head Start grants go straight from HHS to local agencies, bypassing state government. Funded preschool places have fallen about 15 percent since fiscal 2012, while Early Head Start places for infants and toddlers grew about 49 percent. Rules adopted in 2024 required programs to raise staff pay toward parity with public preschool teachers. In May 2026, ACF proposed rescinding the pay parity, minimum wage, wage comparability and staff benefits requirements, with comments closing June 11, 2026. A proposed rule does not change the requirements until ACF publishes a final rule.

sub_issues.title: New Mexico's no-cost childcare
sub_issues.text: New Mexico's Early Childhood Education and Care Department began offering no-cost childcare on November 1, 2025 to families working or in school, regardless of income. The state pays licensed and registered providers directly from its Early Childhood Trust Fund, Land Grant Permanent Fund distributions, state general funds and federal block grant and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) money. Providers on the higher payment rate must pay entry-level staff at least $16 an hour. Senate Bill 241, signed March 10, 2026, wrote the program into state law. Its effects on supply, prices and parents' work are not yet known.

sub_issues.title: State-funded preschool
sub_issues.text: States also pay for preschool, mostly for 4-year-olds and some 3-year-olds. The National Institute for Early Education Research (NIEER), a Rutgers University research institute, counted nearly 1.8 million children in state-funded preschool in the 2024-2025 school year. State spending reached nearly $14.4 billion, or $8,124 per child. Both figures set records, though growth slowed. Georgia became the first state with universal pre-K to meet all 10 of NIEER's quality benchmarks.

sub_issues.title: Paid leave after a birth or adoption
sub_issues.text: Paid family leave insurance replaces part of a worker's wages while caring for a new child or a seriously ill relative. As of October 8, 2026, 14 states and the District of Columbia had enacted mandatory programs, with Maryland's and Virginia's not yet active, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. California's program more than doubled the leave new mothers took, from about three weeks to six or seven. A later study using tax records found no long-run gain in mothers' employment or earnings and lower employment and earnings for first-time mothers about a decade after giving birth.

decision_makers.controls: Funding and statutory rules for the Child Care and Development Block Grant and Head Start, and the tax code provisions for the child and dependent care credit, dependent care accounts, the employer childcare credit and the child tax credit
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your U.S. representative and senators through the directories at house.gov and senate.gov. Yearly funding moves through the Labor, Health and Human Services subcommittees of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees.

decision_makers.who: HHS Administration for Children and Families (Office of Child Care and Office of Head Start)
decision_makers.controls: Block grant regulations at 45 CFR Part 98, approval of state block grant plans, the Head Start Program Performance Standards and grants to local Head Start agencies
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Comment on proposed rules during the comment period announced in the Federal Register, through regulations.gov.

decision_makers.who: State child care lead agency (the agency that runs the block grant in each state)
decision_makers.controls: Subsidy income limits within the federal maximum, waitlist policy, family copayments, provider payment rates and payment practices under the state's plan
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Find your state's agency through childcare.gov and ask how it takes public input on its block grant plan.

decision_makers.controls: Staff-to-child ratios, group sizes, staff qualifications, health and safety standards and inspections for licensed programs
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Submit comments when the agency proposes rule changes; proposed state rules appear in the state's administrative register.

decision_makers.controls: State appropriations for childcare and pre-K, dedicated early childhood funds, state tax credits and state paid family leave programs
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your state legislators and testify at appropriations or human services committee hearings.

decision_makers.who: Local Head Start and Early Head Start grant recipients
decision_makers.controls: Which eligible families are enrolled, program hours and locations, and staff pay within federal standards and the grant amount
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact the local program; each Head Start program has a policy council that includes parents of enrolled children.

decision_makers.who: Childcare centers and family child care homes
decision_makers.controls: Fees for private-pay families, staff wages, hours and which ages they serve, within licensing rules and subsidy payment terms
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Ask the program directly; report health and safety concerns to the state licensing agency.

decision_makers.controls: Local childcare or pre-K funding where state law allows, and local zoning and permits for childcare facilities
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public comment at city council or county board budget hearings, announced by the city or county clerk.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress can change the block grant's eligibility ceiling, funding level and federal requirements by statute, and changes the childcare tax credits through the Internal Revenue Code; annual appropriations set funding for the block grant and Head Start. ACF can rewrite the block grant regulations at 45 CFR Part 98 and the Head Start standards through notice-and-comment rulemaking, as it did in 2024 and again in 2026. State legislatures set state funding, create programs such as New Mexico's and can enact paid family leave insurance. State agencies set licensing rules and subsidy policy by regulation within federal law. A state constitutional amendment approved by voters is another route, the one New Mexico used to direct more Land Grant Permanent Fund money to early childhood. Cities and counties can add local funding where state law permits.

responses.name: Lower what families pay through public funding of care
responses.what_it_does: A state or Congress pays a larger share of the cost of each childcare place, either by widening subsidy eligibility and capping copayments or by offering care at no charge, as New Mexico does for families working or in school. Payments go to licensed providers at rates based on a cost model. Families pay less out of pocket, and providers receive a predictable rate for each enrolled child. Added demand has to be met with added staff and rooms.
responses.requires: A state statute or federal law with recurring appropriations, a cost model for setting rates, licensing and monitoring capacity, and a plan to add supply because lower prices raise demand. New Mexico combines a trust fund, permanent fund distributions, state general funds and federal block grant money. Costs grow with the number of children served.
responses.evidence: A 2017 review found lower childcare prices raise mothers' employment, most likely by 0.5 to 2.5 percent for a 10 percent price cut. Quebec's $5-a-day program raised mothers' work, and the same study measured worse child behavior and health outcomes and more strained parenting; how far that applies to U.S. programs with different quality rules is contested. New Mexico's program has not yet been evaluated.
responses.tradeoffs: Taxpayers carry large recurring costs. If demand grows faster than staff and space, waits lengthen and prices for families outside the program can rise. Rapid expansion under weak quality standards risks worse outcomes for children.

responses.name: Tie public payments to higher wages for care staff
responses.what_it_does: Public funders require programs that receive higher rates to pay staff a set minimum or follow a wage scale. New Mexico pays an enhanced rate to providers that pay entry-level staff at least $16 an hour and stay open at least 10 hours a day, five days a week. Head Start's 2024 standards required pay to move toward parity with public preschool teachers. The aim is to recruit and keep staff so rooms can open and children keep the same caregivers.
responses.requires: A dedicated, recurring funding source, because wages are the largest cost; a payment formula tied to compliance; and verification, such as New Mexico's provider attestations and survey visits. Head Start's requirement rests on federal regulation and appropriations, and the May 2026 proposal would remove it.
responses.evidence: Evaluations of U.S. wage requirements in childcare cover few places and programs. CSCCE documented that most states used pandemic relief for wage increases, without estimating the effect on supply once the money ended. New Mexico's wage floor is too new to evaluate, and the Head Start requirement had not reached full effect before the proposal to rescind it.
responses.tradeoffs: Higher wages raise the cost of each place, so the public share must grow or fewer children are served. Providers that cannot meet the floor may stay on lower rates or leave the program, and families paying privately can face higher fees.

responses.name: Paid family and medical leave insurance
responses.what_it_does: Workers, and in some states employers, pay a payroll premium into a state fund that replaces part of a worker's wages during leave to care for a new child or a seriously ill family member. It lowers the need for infant care in the first months after a birth and protects household income during that time. Fourteen states and the District of Columbia have enacted mandatory programs; Congress has not created a national one.
responses.requires: A state statute setting contribution rates and benefit rules, a state agency or insurer to process claims, job protection rules, and time between the start of contributions and the first benefits. A national program would require an act of Congress and a financing source.
responses.evidence: California's program more than doubled the leave new mothers took, and the authors found suggestive evidence of 6 to 9 percent more weekly work hours for employed mothers of toddlers. A later study using tax records and a regression discontinuity design, which compares similar groups on either side of a cutoff date, found no long-run employment or earnings gain and lower employment for first-time mothers a decade later.
responses.tradeoffs: Workers, and in some states employers, pay premiums, and small employers must cover absences. Low-wage workers may take less leave when wage replacement is low. Long-run career effects for mothers remain uncertain.

responses.name: Revisit state ratio and staffing rules
responses.what_it_does: A state licensing agency changes how many children each adult may supervise, maximum group sizes or staff credential requirements. Allowing more children per adult lowers the staff a program needs and can cut costs or open places. Requiring fewer children per adult or more staff training can raise quality and safety at a higher cost per place, and the same rule applies to every licensed program in the state.
responses.requires: State rulemaking under existing licensing statutes with public notice and comment, and in some states legislative review. Enforcement runs through licensing inspections. A change applies to every licensed program in the state, so the agency needs data on staffing, safety incidents and supply by neighborhood before acting.
responses.evidence: A 2011 study in the American Economic Review linked stricter state regulations to fewer centers, especially in lower-income markets, and to higher quality, mainly in higher-income areas. That finding suggests a supply and quality tradeoff that differs by community. It covers regulation in general and does not isolate the effect of any single ratio change.
responses.tradeoffs: More children per adult can lower prices while reducing attention to each child and raising safety risk. Stricter rules shrink supply most in lower-income areas, according to the 2011 study, and raise prices for families who pay privately.

responses.name: Use the expanded employer childcare credit
responses.what_it_does: Employers that build, operate or contract for childcare for their workers can claim a federal credit for 40 percent of qualified costs, or 50 percent for small businesses, up to $500,000 or $600,000 a year, for costs paid after 2025. Employers can also offer dependent care accounts that shield up to $7,500 of pay from tax. Both tools can add places or lower costs for employees of participating firms.
responses.requires: No further legislation; the Treasury Department and the IRS administer the credit. Each employer has to decide to invest, often with a provider as a partner, and the care must meet state licensing rules. Use depends on employer awareness and on whether the credit covers enough of the cost.
responses.evidence: Under the earlier, smaller credit, GAO estimated that 169 to 278 corporate returns claimed it in 2016, totaling $15.7 million to $18.8 million. Employers cited cost, complexity and low awareness. Whether the larger credit available from 2026 changes employer behavior has not been measured.
responses.tradeoffs: Benefits reach only workers at participating employers and, GAO noted, may miss shift workers. Federal revenue falls by the amount claimed.

distribution.difference: Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group, puts the average 2025 price at about 33 percent of median income for single-parent households, compared with 10 percent for two-parent households. Whether a single parent can get help depends on the income limit their state sets, which is often below the federal maximum.

Infant rooms need more adults per child, so labor makes up a larger share of their cost, according to Treasury. Federally funded places are also scarcer at these ages: Early Head Start funded 185,991 places in fiscal 2024, compared with 505,422 Head Start preschool places.

Stricter state regulations were linked to the largest drops in center supply in lower-income markets, while quality gains were largest in higher-income areas. A statewide rule change therefore reaches neighborhoods unequally even though it applies everywhere in the state.

In 2025, women in households with children under 6 spent 2.8 hours a day on primary childcare, compared with 1.7 hours for men, according to the American Time Use Survey. Childcare prices and leave policies therefore affect mothers' paid work most, and estimates of paid leave's long-run career effects conflict.

pathways.title: Long-term care and disability
pathways.question: Why is it so hard to get help at home as I age or live with a disability?
also_answers: Who pays for long-term care?
Why are there waiting lists for Medicaid home care?
Why are home care aides hard to find and keep?
Does Medicare pay for a home aide or a long nursing home stay?
pathways.short_answer: Most paid long-term care runs through Medicaid, which paid 61 percent of the $415 billion spent in 2022 on long-term services, meaning help with daily tasks such as bathing and dressing. Federal Medicaid law requires states to cover nursing home care but leaves most home and community services optional, so states cap enrollment: more than 710,000 people were on waiting or interest lists in 2024. Medicare does not cover ongoing personal care. Home care depends on aides paid a median $17.21 an hour in May 2025, and family members fill the gaps. Each state's Medicaid agency decides who gets services and what providers are paid.
pathways.scope_note: Federal Medicaid law, regulations from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and a 1999 Supreme Court ruling set the framework. Each state chooses which home and community services to cover, how many people to enroll and what to pay providers, so waits and services differ sharply from state to state. One person's wait or denial shows that state's choices and that person's eligibility, which turns on income, assets and level of need.

mechanisms.title: Medicaid pays most of the bill, for people with low income and few assets
mechanisms.text: Long-term services and supports (LTSS) means ongoing help with daily activities such as bathing, dressing and eating, at home, in the community or in a facility. KFF, a health policy research organization, reports that the U.S. spent $415 billion on LTSS in 2022: Medicaid paid 61 percent, people paid 17 percent out of pocket and other payers covered the rest. Medicaid eligibility for LTSS depends on each state's rules on income, assets and functional need. People who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), a federal cash benefit for people with low income who are older, blind or disabled, must keep countable savings under $2,000, or $3,000 for a couple, limits set in 1989.

mechanisms.title: Federal law requires nursing home coverage and leaves home care optional
mechanisms.text: Under federal Medicaid law, nursing facility care is a mandatory benefit, while most home and community-based services (HCBS) are optional for states. KFF calls this Medicaid's institutional bias. States have shifted spending anyway: HCBS rose from 10 percent of Medicaid LTSS spending in 1988 to 62 percent in 2020, and in 2021, 75 percent of Medicaid LTSS users received only home and community services. In Olmstead v. L.C. (1999), the Supreme Court held that unjustified isolation of people with disabilities is discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). States must offer community placement when their professionals find it appropriate, the person does not object, and it can be reasonably accommodated given state resources.

mechanisms.title: States limit waiver slots, and waiting lists form
mechanisms.text: Most HCBS reaches people through waivers under section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act, created in 1983, which let a state offer home services to people who would otherwise qualify for institutional care. Forty-seven states and the District of Columbia run at least one. Each state decides how many people a waiver serves and funds that number. In 2024 KFF counted more than 710,000 people on waiting or interest lists in 40 states, with an average wait of 40 months in the 32 states that reported it. About 73 percent of people on waiver waiting lists had intellectual or developmental disabilities. KFF calls these lists an incomplete measure of unmet need.

mechanisms.title: State payment rates bound what home care aides earn
mechanisms.text: State Medicaid agencies set the rates they pay home care agencies and individual providers, and those rates limit what agencies can pay aides. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) counted 4.68 million home health and personal care aides in 2025, with a median wage of $17.21 an hour in May 2025. It projects 18 percent job growth from 2025 to 2035 and about 760,500 openings a year. Every state reported shortages of HCBS workers to KFF, and most states that pay hourly personal care rates pay agencies under $20 an hour, out of which the agency covers wages and its own costs. KFF notes that waiting list sizes also depend on worker availability.

mechanisms.title: Medicare and private insurance cover little ongoing care
mechanisms.text: Medicare, the federal health program for people 65 and older and some younger people with disabilities, does not pay for custodial care, the ongoing help with daily tasks most people need. It covers up to 100 days in a skilled nursing facility after a qualifying hospital stay and part-time home health care. Private long-term care insurance fills little of the gap: about 7.1 million people paid premiums in 2021, averaging $1,860, and about 80,000 filed claims. Economists Jeffrey Brown and Amy Finkelstein argue that Medicaid's coverage itself holds down demand for private policies. KFF cites an estimate that an average 65-year-old will face $120,900 in future LTSS costs, with families paying over a third.

mechanisms.title: Families supply most of the help, without pay
mechanisms.text: When paid help is unavailable or unaffordable, relatives provide it. AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, both advocates for caregivers and older adults, counted 63 million family caregivers in 2025, nearly 50 percent more than in 2015, and 94 percent care for adults. Seven in ten are employed. Half report a negative financial effect, about one in five cannot afford basic needs such as food, and about a quarter are taking on debt. AARP valued unpaid care at about $600 billion in 2021, based on 38 million caregivers giving an average of 18 hours a week.

pathways.household_effects: A person who needs help may wait months or years for a waiver slot, then wait again for an aide to be available. Families cover the gap with unpaid time, fewer work hours and their own savings. People with disabilities who rely on SSI must keep savings under $2,000, which leaves little cushion for a car repair or a security deposit; ABLE accounts, tax-advantaged savings accounts for people with disabilities, can hold up to $100,000 without counting against SSI. Paid work is far less common: in 2025, 22.8 percent of people with a disability were employed, compared with 65.2 percent of people without one.

sub_issues.title: The 80 percent rule for home care pay
sub_issues.text: A 2024 CMS rule on access to Medicaid services requires states to ensure that providers spend at least 80 percent of Medicaid payments for homemaker, home health aide and personal care services on compensation for the workers who deliver them. States may set a different percentage for small providers and exempt providers facing hardship. Compliance begins six years after the rule took effect on July 9, 2024, which is July 9, 2030. The federal regulations current on October 8, 2026 still contain the requirement.

sub_issues.title: What the 2025 budget law changed for long-term care
sub_issues.text: The July 2025 budget law caps the home equity a person can hold and still qualify for Medicaid long-term care at $1,000,000 from 2028. From July 2028 it lets states create 1915(c) waivers for people whose needs fall below nursing home level, if waits for people at that level do not grow. It bars implementing the 2024 nursing home minimum staffing standards until October 1, 2034, after a court in Texas struck them down in April 2025. It also limits retroactive coverage from 2027 and restricts new provider taxes, with nursing facilities excluded from the new limit.

sub_issues.title: Who owns the nursing home
sub_issues.text: Ownership can change the care inside a nursing home. A study of Medicare data found that private equity acquisitions raised mortality among short-stay patients by about 11 percent, with declines in nurse staffing among the explanations. Federal minimum staffing standards finalized in 2024 cannot be enforced before October 2034 under the 2025 law, so staffing levels turn on state rules and on Medicaid and Medicare payment.

sub_issues.title: Savings limits for people on SSI
sub_issues.text: SSI pays a monthly benefit to people with low income and few assets who are 65 or older, blind or disabled. In 2027 the federal payment is $1,029 a month for an individual and $1,544 for a couple. The asset limit of $2,000, or $3,000 for a couple, has stayed the same since January 1989, while the payment rises each year with the cost-of-living adjustment. A home, one vehicle and up to $100,000 in an ABLE account do not count toward the limit.

sub_issues.title: Work and disability
sub_issues.text: In 2025, BLS found 22.8 percent of people with a disability employed, compared with 65.2 percent of people without one. Unemployment was 8.3 percent compared with 4.1 percent, and about 30 percent of workers with a disability usually worked part time, against 17 percent of other workers. These figures cannot separate the roles of health, workplace barriers and benefit rules. The 2025 figures exclude October, when the survey was not collected during the federal shutdown.

sub_issues.title: Finding local help
sub_issues.text: Area Agencies on Aging plan and arrange local services for older adults, such as meals and caregiver support, and can point families to Medicaid and other programs. The Eldercare Locator, a public service of the federal Administration for Community Living, connects callers to their local agency at 1-800-677-1116 or online at eldercare.acl.gov. Services and waits differ from one area to the next.

sub_issues.title: Washington's public long-term care insurance
sub_issues.text: Washington State created the WA Cares Fund, a public long-term care insurance program financed by contributions from workers' paychecks. Its site reports that benefits are now available statewide. Covered services include paid family caregiving, in-home care, home modifications, respite care, transportation, home-delivered meals and assistive devices. Its effects on family finances, care use and Medicaid spending have not yet been measured.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress can change the Medicaid statute, including whether home and community services are mandatory, the federal share of costs and the SSI asset limit, and can change what Medicare covers; it last made major changes in Public Law 119-21 in July 2025. CMS writes Medicaid regulations through notice-and-comment rulemaking and approves or denies each state's waivers and plan amendments, so it could also amend the 80 percent requirement before 2030. State legislatures appropriate the state share of Medicaid and decide whether to fund more waiver slots or higher rates. State Medicaid agencies carry out those choices through waiver and plan amendments that CMS must approve. Federal courts enforce the Olmstead community integration rule under Title II of the ADA. States can also create programs by statute, as Washington did with WA Cares and Minnesota did with its nursing home standards board.

responses.name: Fund more home and community waiver slots
responses.what_it_does: A state legislature pays for more 1915(c) waiver slots or adds home and community services to its regular Medicaid plan, so people on waiting lists start services sooner. From July 2028, the 2025 law also lets states create waivers for people whose needs fall below nursing home level, which can reach people earlier in a decline, provided waits for those at nursing home level do not grow.
responses.requires: State appropriations for the state share of costs, matched by federal Medicaid funds; a new waiver or amendment approved by CMS; and enough aides to deliver the added hours. The 2025 law provides $50 million in fiscal 2026 and $100 million in fiscal 2027 tied to the new waiver option.
responses.evidence: KFF documents the shift in spending toward home care, from 10 percent of Medicaid LTSS spending in 1988 to 62 percent in 2020, alongside persistent waiting lists. Studies linking HCBS expansion to less nursing home use are mostly observational, so effects on total Medicaid spending remain uncertain. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates the new waiver option will raise federal Medicaid spending by $7 billion over ten years.
responses.tradeoffs: State and federal Medicaid spending rise as enrollment grows, competing with other budget needs. Without enough aides, new slots can go unfilled and approved hours undelivered.

responses.name: Require most home care payments to go to worker pay
responses.what_it_does: Under the 2024 CMS rule, states must ensure that at least 80 percent of Medicaid payments for homemaker, home health aide and personal care services go to direct care workers' compensation, starting July 9, 2030. States show compliance each year through reports to CMS. The aim is to move rate increases into wages so agencies can hire and keep aides.
responses.requires: The requirement already sits in federal regulation at 42 CFR 441.302(k). States must collect provider cost data, set any small-provider percentage and hardship exemptions through public notice and comment, and enforce compliance. CMS could change or delay the requirement through new rulemaking before 2030.
responses.evidence: The requirement has not taken effect, so its effects on wages, agency finances and access are unknown, and no evaluation has tested whether a fixed wage share raises pay or leads some agencies to exit. Evidence on the problem itself is documented: every state reported HCBS worker shortages, and aides earned a median $17.21 an hour in May 2025.
responses.tradeoffs: Agencies with high training, travel or administrative costs could find the threshold hard to meet and may narrow service areas or close if rates do not rise. Workers gain only if total payments are adequate, because the rule fixes the wage share and leaves the payment rate to the state.

responses.name: Set wage floors through a state workforce standards board
responses.what_it_does: A state board with worker and employer members sets minimum wages and standards for a whole long-term care sector, so competitors face the same floor. Minnesota's Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board, created in 2023, set minimums that took effect September 10, 2026 after CMS approved the related Medicaid plan amendment: $19.00 an hour for general nursing home workers, $22.50 for certified nursing assistants, $23.50 for trained medication aides and $27.00 for licensed practical nurses.
responses.requires: A state statute creating the board and its authority, staff and wage data, rulemaking, and enforcement by the state labor agency. Where Medicaid pays most of the cost, the state also needs a plan amendment so payment rates cover the new wages. Federal labor law limits how far such boards can reach into collective bargaining.
responses.evidence: Minnesota's standards took effect in September 2026, so no outcome data exist yet. Evidence from sector-wide wage boards in the United States is limited and contested: the main other case, California's fast food council, has produced studies that disagree on employment and price effects.
responses.tradeoffs: Higher wage floors raise costs for nursing homes and, through Medicaid rates, for the state. If rates do not cover the floor, facilities may cut hours or beds.

responses.name: Create public long-term care insurance
responses.what_it_does: A state collects contributions from workers' paychecks and pays benefits toward care when a contributor later needs help with daily activities. Washington's WA Cares Fund pays for services such as in-home care, paid family caregiving, home modifications and respite care, and reports that benefits are now available statewide. The program spreads the risk across all workers and gives families a benefit to draw on before they would qualify for Medicaid.
responses.requires: A state statute, a dedicated trust fund, a system to collect contributions from paychecks, rules on who qualifies and for how much, and periodic actuarial review so that contributions and benefits stay in balance over time. The legislature sets the contribution rate and benefit level, and a state agency processes claims and pays approved care providers.
responses.evidence: Washington's program has only begun paying benefits, and no evaluation of its effects on family finances, care use or Medicaid spending is available. The problem it targets is documented separately: about 7.1 million people paid private long-term care premiums in 2021, and Medicaid pays most LTSS costs.
responses.tradeoffs: Workers contribute whether or not they ever need care. If benefits are modest relative to costs, they cover only part of a long need, and the program must keep contributions and promised benefits aligned as costs rise.

responses.name: Paid leave for family caregivers
responses.what_it_does: State paid family and medical leave insurance replaces part of a worker's wages while caring for a seriously ill family member, including an aging parent or a relative with a disability. A working caregiver can take time during a crisis, such as a hospital discharge, without losing all income, and return to the same job where the law protects it.
responses.requires: A state statute and payroll-funded insurance program run by a state agency or insurer, with job protection rules. Fourteen states and the District of Columbia have mandatory programs. A national program would require an act of Congress and a financing source.
responses.evidence: Most evaluations study new parents; California's program more than doubled the leave new mothers took. Use of paid leave to care for older or disabled relatives has been studied less. Leave lasts weeks, while many long-term care needs last years.
responses.tradeoffs: Workers, and in some states employers, pay premiums, and employers must cover absences. Leave covers a short period, so it adds to paid care for a limited time.

responses.name: Raise and index the SSI asset limit
responses.what_it_does: Congress raises the $2,000 SSI asset limit and adjusts it for inflation each year, so older adults and people with disabilities on SSI can keep more savings for emergencies, a car repair or a security deposit without losing benefits. ABLE accounts already allow up to $100,000 in savings for eligible people with disabilities, and a higher limit would extend room to save to all SSI recipients.
responses.requires: An amendment to Title XVI of the Social Security Act by Congress, with a CBO cost estimate of the added federal benefit payments. SSA would update its resource rules, notices and computer systems, and states that set their own Medicaid asset tests for long-term care would decide separately whether to follow.
responses.evidence: The limit itself is documented: $2,000 since January 1989 and unchanged for 2027, while the SSI payment rises yearly. No national trial has measured how a higher limit changes saving, work or program cost. ABLE accounts offer the closest existing comparison.
responses.tradeoffs: Federal SSI spending rises as more people keep eligibility. The change helps people near the asset limit and leaves the income test unchanged.

distribution.group: People with intellectual or developmental disabilities
distribution.difference: They made up about 73 percent of people on Medicaid waiver waiting lists in 2024, and 89 percent in states that do not screen people for eligibility before listing them. KFF notes that some families sign up children early in anticipation of future need, which lengthens lists.

Seven in ten family caregivers are employed, and half report a negative financial effect from caregiving, according to the AARP and National Alliance for Caregiving survey. About a quarter report taking on debt, and about one in five cannot afford basic needs such as food.

Medicaid pays only after income and assets fall within state limits, and Medicare does not cover custodial care, so people with modest savings pay first. KFF cites an estimate that families pay more than a third of an average 65-year-old's $120,900 in future LTSS costs.

Home health and personal care aides earned a median $17.21 an hour in May 2025, and most states that set hourly personal care rates pay agencies under $20 an hour. Because Medicaid pays most LTSS costs, state rate decisions shape these workers' pay more than any single family's budget.

distribution.difference: Where a person lives decides which home services exist and how long the wait is. Among the 32 states that reported in 2024, the average wait was 40 months, and eight states, including Texas and Illinois, list people without screening them, so their counts are not comparable.

pathways.title: Pay and working conditions
pathways.question: Why isn't my pay keeping up with what my work produces?
also_answers: Who receives the gains when workers produce more per hour?
What affects my ability to negotiate pay, hours and schedules?
Who can make an employer pay wages that are owed?
pathways.short_answer: Pay rises when workers produce more, though by less than the full gain, and bargaining power decides the split. In the U.S. nonfarm business sector, output per hour has grown about 2.1% a year since 1947. Workers' share of business income fell to 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest on record. Your bargaining power depends on how easily you can leave for a better offer, how many employers compete to hire you, whether you can bargain as a group, and the legal wage floor. Congress, the National Labor Relations Board, state legislatures and state labor departments set or enforce most of those rules.
pathways.scope_note: Productivity and labor-share figures cover the national nonfarm business sector, while minimum wages, noncompete limits, sick-leave mandates and scheduling rules differ by state and city. One worker's raise or pay cut depends on occupation, industry, employer and local job market, so it cannot confirm or refute the national pattern.

mechanisms.title: Higher output per hour raises what employers can pay
mechanisms.text: Labor productivity is the value of output produced in an hour of work. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that nonfarm business productivity grew at a 2.1% annual rate from late 2019 to mid-2026, the same as its long-run pace since 1947. Higher productivity gives an employer room to raise pay. How much reaches workers shows up in the labor share, the part of business income paid as wages, benefits and employer payroll taxes. BLS put it at 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, down from 65.5% in early 1947. Over the four quarters to mid-2026, productivity rose 2.2% while real hourly compensation, which adjusts pay for consumer prices, fell 0.1%.

mechanisms.title: Job openings and quits give workers outside offers
mechanisms.text: One source of bargaining power is a better offer somewhere else. When many employers are hiring, more people quit for new jobs, and employers raise pay to keep staff. The quits rate, quits as a share of all jobs, reached a series high of 3.0% in November 2021 in the BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey. Autor, Dube and McGrew found that the tight market of 2021 to 2023 raised pay fastest at the bottom, offsetting about a third of four decades of growth in wage inequality, with gains concentrated among people who changed employers. By August 2026 the quits rate was 1.9%. In September 2026 the Atlanta Fed measured median pay growth of 4.7% for job switchers and 3.4% for people who stayed.

mechanisms.title: Few employers and contract limits shrink those offers
mechanisms.text: Where a few employers do most of the hiring, each can pay less without losing many workers. Economists call that power monopsony. Across more than 8,000 local job markets in online postings, Azar, Marinescu and Steinbaum found that moving from a less concentrated market to a more concentrated one (the 25th to the 75th percentile) went with 17% lower posted wages. Hospital mergers that sharply raised local concentration slowed wage growth for workers whose skills fit mainly hospitals, in research by Prager and Schmitt. Employers can also limit exits by contract. The Treasury Department reported in 2022 that about one in five workers was bound by a noncompete agreement, a clause barring work for a competitor, and that about one in ten negotiated over it.

mechanisms.title: Federal labor law sets the terms for bargaining as a group
mechanisms.text: The National Labor Relations Act gives most private-sector employees the right to form a union and bargain together; it excludes agricultural laborers, domestic workers, supervisors and independent contractors. The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) runs union elections and decides unfair labor practice cases. For an illegal firing, the Board can order reinstatement and back pay, and the statute provides no civil fines. A study by the Economic Policy Institute (EPI), a labor-aligned research group, counted charges against employers in 41.5% of the 2016 and 2017 election campaigns; a charge is an allegation. After a union wins, a first contract took 461 days on average across 553 contracts from 2005 to 2025, by Bloomberg Law's count. Union membership stood at 10.0% of wage and salary workers in 2025, and 5.9% in the private sector.

mechanisms.title: Wage floors and enforcement set the bottom of the pay scale
mechanisms.text: Congress sets the federal minimum wage under the Fair Labor Standards Act. It has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, and it stays there until Congress acts. States and some cities set higher floors. As of July 1, 2026, the Department of Labor listed 30 states and the District of Columbia above $7.25. On January 1, 2026, 13 states raised their floors through automatic inflation formulas, by EPI's count. Enforcement agencies collect unpaid wages after the fact. The department's Wage and Hour Division recovered more than $259 million in back wages for 176,957 workers in fiscal year 2025. EPI estimated in 2017 that minimum-wage violations alone cost workers about $8 billion a year in the 10 most populous states.

pathways.household_effects: Most workers feel these rules in four places: the size of a yearly raise, whether switching jobs pays, the hours they can count on, and whether a sick day costs a day's pay. In 2025, full-time union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, against $1,174 for nonunion workers, a gap that also comes from differences in jobs and places. Among private-sector workers in the bottom quarter of wages, 58% could take paid sick leave in March 2025, compared with 94% in the top quarter. Women working full time, year-round earned 83.9% of what men earned in 2025.

sub_issues.title: Has pay fallen behind productivity?
sub_issues.text: EPI tracks a large gap: from 1979 to mid-2026, net productivity (output per hour after the wear on equipment) rose 93.7%, while pay for production and nonsupervisory workers rose 32.7%. How the gap is measured changes its size. EPI's own 2015 analysis attributed about 30% of the 1973 to 2014 gap to differences between consumer and producer prices. A 2017 BLS study of 183 industries found price differences and a falling labor share contributed about equally. Stansbury and Summers found pay still rises with productivity, though less than one for one.

sub_issues.title: Noncompete agreements after the federal rule
sub_issues.text: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) issued a nationwide ban on most noncompetes in May 2024. A federal district court stopped enforcement in August 2024, and in September 2025 the FTC dropped its appeals and turned to case-by-case enforcement and warning letters. State law now sets most limits. California, Minnesota, North Dakota and Oklahoma bar most employee noncompetes, Wyoming added a ban in July 2025, and Washington's ban for all workers takes effect June 30, 2027. Florida went the other direction in 2025 and made noncompetes easier to enforce.

sub_issues.title: Why a union vote does not settle a contract
sub_issues.text: Federal law sets no deadline for reaching a first contract. Workers at Amazon's JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island voted for a union in 2022; in October 2026 the NLRB's refusal-to-bargain case, filed in January 2023, was still open before a federal appeals court. The Board lacked a quorum, the minimum number of members needed to decide cases, from January 2025 to January 7, 2026. After the Supreme Court's June 2026 ruling in Trump v. Slaughter, a Texas federal court held that the President may remove NLRB members at will.

sub_issues.title: How high can a minimum wage go before jobs are lost?
sub_issues.text: Research disagrees at the margin. A study of 138 state increases from 1979 to 2016 by Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer found the number of low-wage jobs essentially unchanged five years later. Reviewing the wider literature, Neumark and Shirley reported a clear preponderance of negative estimates, strongest for teens, young adults and less-educated workers. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated in 2019 that a $15 federal floor by 2025 would lift 1.3 million people out of poverty, with a median job loss of 1.3 million and a likely range from about zero to 3.7 million.

sub_issues.title: Outsourcing and who counts as the employer
sub_issues.text: Many companies hire cleaning, security, delivery or warehouse work through contractors, staffing agencies or franchises, an arrangement the economist David Weil calls the fissured workplace. Studies summarized by the Treasury Department in 2022 found that pay drops when work moves out of the lead company: outsourced janitors and guards earned 4% to 24% less in the United States, and outsourced workers in Germany 10% to 15% less.

sub_issues.title: Sick days and predictable schedules
sub_issues.text: Apart from federal contractors, no federal law requires private employers to give paid sick days. In 2026, 17 states and the District of Columbia require it, according to the Congressional Research Service. Access follows pay: in March 2025, 58% of private-sector workers in the bottom quarter of wages could take paid sick leave, against 94% in the top quarter. Scheduling laws are rarer. Oregon requires large retail, hospitality and food-service employers to post schedules 14 days ahead and to pay extra for late changes.

sub_issues.title: Collecting unpaid wages
sub_issues.text: Wage theft means not paying wages owed, through pay below the minimum, unpaid overtime or work off the clock. Enforcement depends partly on workers coming forward. In a 2008 survey of 4,387 low-wage workers in Chicago, Los Angeles and New York, 26% had been paid below the minimum wage in the previous week. Of those who complained or tried to organize, 43% faced illegal retaliation, including threats to call immigration authorities. Federal recoveries are small next to survey-based estimates of losses.

decision_makers.who: Congress (House Committee on Education and Workforce; Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions)
decision_makers.controls: Writes the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act, including the federal minimum wage, who is covered, and which remedies the NLRB can order
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your U.S. representative and senators through the official House and Senate directories; committee websites post hearings and bill text

decision_makers.who: National Labor Relations Board and its General Counsel
decision_makers.controls: Runs union elections, decides unfair labor practice cases and sets Board doctrine on bargaining and remedies within the statute; the General Counsel prosecutes cases through regional offices
decision_makers.how_to_reach: File a charge or election petition at an NLRB regional office; offices are listed on nlrb.gov

decision_makers.who: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
decision_makers.controls: Enforces federal minimum wage, overtime and child labor law, investigates complaints, recovers back wages and issues regulations interpreting the statute
decision_makers.how_to_reach: File a complaint with a Wage and Hour Division district office; offices and contact details are on dol.gov

decision_makers.who: Federal Trade Commission and the Justice Department's Antitrust Division
decision_makers.controls: Bring cases against unlawful noncompete and no-poach agreements and review mergers, including effects on workers, under existing antitrust law
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Submit a report through the FTC's online complaint system or the Antitrust Division's complaint page on justice.gov

decision_makers.controls: Set state minimum wages and indexing, paid sick leave, scheduling rules, noncompete limits and industry standards boards
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Testify or submit written comments at labor committee hearings; legislature websites list bills and hearing schedules

decision_makers.who: State labor departments and state attorneys general
decision_makers.controls: Investigate wage claims under state law, order or sue for back pay and penalties, and enforce state noncompete laws where authorized
decision_makers.how_to_reach: File a wage claim with your state labor department; the attorney general's office takes complaints about unlawful employment practices

decision_makers.controls: Adopt local minimum wage, sick-leave and scheduling ordinances where state law allows
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public comment at council meetings; the city or county clerk posts agendas

decision_makers.who: Employers and unions at the bargaining table
decision_makers.controls: Agree on wages, schedules, grievance procedures and contract length for a represented workplace
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Workers can contact a union about representation or petition the NLRB for an election

decision_makers.controls: Review agency rules and decisions and rule on agency structure, as in the 2024 order that stopped the FTC noncompete rule and the 2026 rulings on removal of agency members
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Court dockets are public through PACER; parties and outside groups can file briefs

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress holds the main federal levers. It can amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise or index the $7.25 minimum wage, and amend the National Labor Relations Act to add penalties, cover excluded workers or set first-contract deadlines. The House passed a first-contract deadline bill, H.R. 5408, on June 9, 2026; the Senate had taken no recorded action by mid-October 2026. The NLRB changes doctrine through case decisions, which federal appeals courts review. The FTC and the Justice Department act through enforcement cases under existing antitrust law. State legislatures, and voters in states with ballot initiatives, can set higher minimum wages, sick-leave mandates, noncompete limits and industry wage boards, though the National Labor Relations Act limits state rules on private-sector union bargaining. City councils act where state law permits local wage and scheduling ordinances.

responses.name: Index the minimum wage to prices or wages
responses.what_it_does: A legislature sets a wage floor and a formula that raises it each year with a published price or wage index. Pay at the bottom then keeps pace with living costs without a new vote each time, and employers can plan for small yearly steps. Congress could do this for the federal floor, unchanged at $7.25 since 2009. States act on their own; 13 states raised their floors through such formulas on January 1, 2026. Many proposals first phase in a higher level, then index it.
responses.requires: Federal action needs an act of Congress signed by the President. States act by statute, or by ballot measure where their constitutions allow initiatives. Labor departments need investigators to enforce the floor. Setting the level relative to local median wages, and phasing it in, limits employment risk.
responses.evidence: CBO estimated that a $15 federal floor would raise pay for 17 million workers. Effects on jobs are contested. Cengiz and coauthors found no detectable loss of low-wage jobs after 138 state increases through 2016. Neumark and Shirley found that most studies report some job loss for teens and less-educated workers. CBO's own 2019 estimate for $15 ranged from about zero to 3.7 million jobs.
responses.tradeoffs: Owners of low-margin businesses, such as small restaurants, bear higher labor costs, and some pass them to customers through prices. A floor set high relative to local wages raises the risk of fewer hours or jobs for less experienced workers.

responses.name: Faster remedies and first-contract deadlines
responses.what_it_does: Congress would add civil penalties for illegal firings during organizing, speed reinstatement, and set a path to a first contract. Under H.R. 5408, the Faster Labor Contracts Act, an employer would have to start bargaining within 10 days of a request. After 90 days without agreement either side could call in federal mediators, and after 30 more days a three-member panel would issue a binding two-year contract. The House passed the bill on June 9, 2026.
responses.requires: An act of Congress, since the National Labor Relations Act governs private-sector bargaining nationwide. The Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service would need mediators and arbitrators for a larger caseload, and the NLRB would need a quorum and staff to process charges quickly. Courts would review any new penalties.
responses.evidence: Several Canadian provinces offer first-contract arbitration. Johnson's 2010 study found it cut first-agreement strikes by at least half, while arbitrators rarely imposed contracts, which suggests the threat pushed both sides to settle. In New York, arbitration for police and firefighters produced no strikes from 1974 to 2007, with arbitrated raises similar to negotiated ones. No test covers U.S. private employers.
responses.tradeoffs: Employers would lose some control over terms and share the cost of mediation and arbitration, which can run thousands of dollars a day. An imposed contract can set terms neither side would choose, and arbitrators unfamiliar with an industry can misjudge what a firm can pay.

responses.name: Industry wage boards
responses.what_it_does: A state creates a board of worker, employer and public members to set minimum pay and standards for one industry, so a company cannot undercut competitors by paying less. California's AB 1228 set a $20 minimum for large fast-food chains in April 2024 and created a council that can raise it. Minnesota's nursing home board set floors of $19 an hour for most workers and $22.50 for certified nursing assistants from September 10, 2026, rising in January 2027.
responses.requires: A state statute that defines the industry, the board's members and its authority, plus staff and data on industry pay. Federal labor law limits state rules on private bargaining, so boards set minimum standards. Seats must be filled for a board to act: California's council had no chair and did not meet in 2025.
responses.evidence: The California evidence conflicts. Reich, at a UC Berkeley labor research center, found pay up 8% to 9%, no employment loss, and prices up about 1.5%. Clemens, Edwards and Meer found California fast-food employment fell 2.7% to 3.2% relative to the rest of the country, about 18,000 jobs. Minnesota's nursing home standards are too new to evaluate.
responses.tradeoffs: Franchise owners with thin margins bear higher costs and may raise prices or cut hours. A board can stall when seats go unfilled, and industry boundaries can be hard to draw, which invites litigation.

responses.name: State limits on noncompete agreements
responses.what_it_does: A state law voids noncompete clauses for some or all workers, so an employee can take a job with a competitor or start a business. Laws vary. Some ban all employee noncompetes; others cover only hourly workers or those below a pay level, and most keep separate protection for trade secrets and the sale of a business. Washington's 2026 law adds $5,000 in statutory damages for workers and lets the attorney general sue.
responses.requires: A state statute, enforced by courts in private suits or by the attorney general. Workers need notice that a clause is void; Washington requires employers to notify affected workers by October 1, 2027. A national standard would need an act of Congress after the courts stopped the FTC rule.
responses.evidence: The problem side is documented: about one in five workers was bound by a noncompete and few negotiated over it, according to the Treasury Department's 2022 review, which also cites research linking noncompetes to lower job mobility. That review calls the net effect on wages theoretically ambiguous. Results from the newest state bans are not yet available.
responses.tradeoffs: Employers lose a tool to protect client lists and training investments and rely instead on trade-secret and nonsolicitation clauses. Different state rules raise compliance costs for multistate firms, and laws that void existing contracts can face constitutional challenge.

responses.name: Antitrust enforcement in job markets
responses.what_it_does: The FTC and the Justice Department can sue over agreements among employers not to hire each other's workers, challenge noncompetes as unfair competition, and block mergers that would leave workers with fewer employers to choose from. In September 2025 the FTC proposed an order requiring Gateway, a pet memorial services company, to stop enforcing one-year noncompetes covering about 1,800 workers, and it sent warning letters to other employers.
responses.requires: Existing law, mainly the Sherman, Clayton and FTC Acts, so no new statute is needed. Agencies need economists and litigators, and each case turns on facts about a specific local job market and who else hires there. Federal merger guidelines are non-binding, and courts decide contested cases.
responses.evidence: Harm is documented in some settings. Prager and Schmitt found slower wage growth after hospital mergers that sharply raised concentration, mainly for workers with hospital-specific skills, with smaller effects where unions were strong. Evidence that enforcement raises wages is thin, because few labor-market merger challenges exist to study. By one Census Bureau measure, local concentration declined from 1976 to 2015.
responses.tradeoffs: Defining a job market is hard and cases take years. Some mergers bring efficiencies that help customers. Enforcement priorities shift with agency leadership, and after Trump v. Slaughter the President can remove FTC commissioners at will.

responses.name: More wage investigators and protection from retaliation
responses.what_it_does: Congress and state legislatures would fund more wage investigators, require electronic pay records, and raise penalties for repeat violators and for retaliation against workers who complain. Agencies could then open investigations in industries where surveys find frequent violations, without waiting for a complaint. Electronic records would let investigators check hours and pay without relying on workers' memories, and community groups could reach workers who fear speaking up.
responses.requires: Appropriations for the Wage and Hour Division and state labor departments, and statutes for higher penalties. Anti-retaliation protection must act quickly, since a fired worker cannot wait months for a ruling. Whether labor complaints are kept separate from immigration enforcement affects whether undocumented workers come forward.
responses.evidence: The gap is documented. In fiscal year 2025 the Wage and Hour Division recovered $259 million for 176,957 workers, while EPI, a labor-aligned group, estimated minimum-wage violations at about $8 billion a year in the 10 most populous states alone. Strong evaluations of how added investigators change compliance with wage law are lacking.
responses.tradeoffs: Audits and record rules add paperwork for small employers, and penalties need appeal rights to avoid punishing honest errors. Funding competes with other priorities and can be cut in later budgets.

distribution.difference: In March 2025, 58% of private-sector workers in the bottom quarter of wages could take paid sick leave, compared with 94% in the top quarter, and 56% of part-time workers had access. Minimum-wage violations fall on low earners by definition. Pay gains during the tight job market of 2021 to 2023 went disproportionately to young workers without college degrees who changed employers.

distribution.group: Workers in states that use the $7.25 federal floor
distribution.difference: As of July 1, 2026, 13 states set their minimum at $7.25 and five had no state minimum wage law, so the federal floor applies to covered workers there. That floor loses purchasing power whenever prices rise. Workers in states whose floors rise by formula, including the 13 that adjusted on January 1, 2026, receive automatic yearly increases.

Full-time union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404 in 2025, against $1,174 for nonunion workers. Part of that gap comes from differences in industries, jobs and places. Farber and coauthors estimate a household union premium of 10 to 20 log points, roughly 10% to 22%, that held steady across most of the 20th century.

Women working full time, year-round earned 83.9% of men's median earnings in 2025, up from 80.6% in 2024, by the Census Bureau's measure. The ratio compares medians across all such workers, so by itself it does not measure pay differences within the same job.

distribution.group: Workers who fear retaliation, including immigrants
distribution.difference: In a 2008 survey of low-wage workers in Chicago, Los Angeles and New York, 43% of those who complained or tried to organize faced illegal retaliation, including threats to call immigration authorities. The same survey found many workers never complained, often out of fear, which leaves violations out of agency records.

check.prompt: A company's output per hour rises 10%. What decides how much of that gain reaches its workers' pay?
options: Nothing; pay rises by the same 10% automatically
Workers' bargaining power, shaped by outside job offers, union contracts and legal wage floors
The Federal Reserve sets each company's pay rate
Pay does not respond to productivity at all
check.explanation: Productivity raises what an employer can pay. Studies find pay rises with productivity, though by less than the full gain. The split depends on bargaining power: competing job offers, collective bargaining, and wage floors set by Congress, states and cities.
