pathways.title: Taxes, benefits and financial security
pathways.question: How do taxes and benefit rules change what my household keeps?
also_answers: Why can a raise leave my family barely better off?
Who qualifies for the refundable part of the Child Tax Credit?
What changed in SNAP and Medicaid under the 2025 federal law?
Could my household cover a $400 emergency?
pathways.short_answer: What a household keeps depends on rules Congress writes and agencies carry out. Workers pay 7.65% of wages in payroll taxes for Social Security and Medicare from the first dollar. Federal income tax applies above the standard deduction, and refundable credits, which pay out even when no tax is owed, add money back for low earners with children. Benefits such as SNAP food aid and Medicaid shrink or end as earnings rise, so a raise can leave a family little better off. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the 2025 federal law, Public Law 119-21, lowers resources for the lowest-income tenth of households and raises them for the top tenth.
pathways.scope_note: Federal tax and benefit rules apply nationwide, while state income and sales taxes, state credits, Medicaid expansion and SNAP administration differ by state. One household's refund or benefit depends on its income, family size, immigration status and state, and nothing here is tax advice.

mechanisms.title: Payroll and income taxes take a share of earnings
mechanisms.text: Congress sets both taxes in the Internal Revenue Code. Payroll taxes apply from the first dollar: employees pay 6.2% for Social Security on wages up to $184,500 in 2026 and 1.45% for Medicare on all wages, and employers pay matching amounts. Federal income tax applies only above the standard deduction, $16,100 for a single filer and $32,200 for a married couple in 2026, at rates that rise with income. For the lowest fifth of households, refundable credits outweigh income tax. CBO found their average federal income tax rate was negative 10% in 2022, against 17% for the top fifth. The average rate for all federal taxes combined was 20.6%.

mechanisms.title: Refundable credits pay more to working families with children
mechanisms.text: A refundable credit pays the household even when it owes no income tax. The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) is worth up to $8,231 in 2026 for a family with three or more children, and the IRS estimates that 80.8% of eligible taxpayers received it for tax year 2022. Public Law 119-21 set the Child Tax Credit at $2,200 per child, indexed to inflation after 2025. Only part is refundable: up to $1,700 per child, phased in at 15 cents per dollar earned above $2,500. A parent needs earnings of about $13,800 to receive the full refundable amount for one child, and a family with no earnings receives none.

mechanisms.title: Benefits shrink as earnings rise
mechanisms.text: Means-tested programs, which limit help to people below an income line, reduce benefits as pay goes up. SNAP food benefits phase down with income. In the 41 states, counting the District of Columbia, that expanded Medicaid, adults qualify up to 138% of the federal poverty level, $21,597 for one person in 2025, and coverage ends above that line. Together with taxes, these reductions produce an effective marginal tax rate: the share of an extra dollar of earnings lost to taxes and lower benefits. CBO estimated it averaged 31% in 2016 for workers with income below 450% of the poverty level, with wide variation between families.

mechanisms.title: The 2025 federal law moves net support between income groups
mechanisms.text: Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025, lowered taxes and reduced federal spending on Medicaid and SNAP. CBO estimates that, averaged over 2026 to 2034, households in the lowest tenth of income lose about $1,200 a year, 3.1% of income, mainly through smaller Medicaid and SNAP benefits. The top tenth gains about $13,600 a year, 2.7% of income, mostly from lower taxes, while the fifth and sixth tenths gain $800 to $1,200. These estimates are static: they leave out effects on the wider economy and the cost of added federal debt. The SNAP and Medicaid changes take effect in stages from November 2025 to October 2028, later for some states' SNAP cost shares.

mechanisms.title: State and local taxes add a second layer
mechanisms.text: States and cities collect income, sales and property taxes, and the mix decides who pays most relative to income. Sales taxes take a larger share from a low-income family because it spends most of what it earns. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), a research group that favors progressive taxation, estimates that under tax law in effect in January 2024 the lowest-income fifth paid 11.4% of income in state and local taxes, against 7.2% for the top 1%. Sales and excise taxes alone took 7.0% and 1.0%. In 2024, 31 states and the District of Columbia had their own EITC and 14 states had a child credit.

mechanisms.title: Agency capacity decides whether people receive what the law provides
mechanisms.text: Rules reach households through the IRS, state revenue departments, state SNAP offices and state Medicaid agencies. When those agencies have fewer staff or older systems, eligible people wait or drop out. The National Taxpayer Advocate reported that in the 2026 filing season the IRS had fewer employees, live phone assistors answered 20% fewer calls than a year earlier, and 42 walk-in centers were fully staffed, down from 102. The IRS did not offer Direct File, its free online filing tool, in 2026, after 296,531 returns used it in 2025. Paperwork also costs coverage: of more than 25 million people removed from Medicaid during the 2023 to 2024 renewal process, 69% lost it for procedural reasons such as missing forms.

pathways.household_effects: Households meet these rules when they file taxes, apply for SNAP, renew Medicaid or take a raise. A low-wage parent can receive a refund larger than any tax withheld, while a raise can cost SNAP dollars or Medicaid eligibility. Starting no later than January 1, 2027 under CMS's rule (the statute names December 31, 2026), adults covered through Medicaid expansion face renewals every six months and, unless exempt, must show 80 hours a month of work, school, training or service. Many households have little room for a delayed refund or a lost benefit: in October 2025, 63% of adults said they would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent, unchanged from the three years before.

sub_issues.title: Who is left out of the refundable child credit
sub_issues.text: Families can receive less than the full $2,200 per child for two reasons. Low earnings limit the refundable part, which phases in above $2,500 of earnings, so a parent earning $10,000 with no income tax owed can receive at most $1,125 for one child. Identification rules exclude others: each child needs a Social Security number valid for work, and so does the filer, or at least one spouse on a joint return. A citizen child with a valid number receives nothing if the parent filing has no qualifying number.

sub_issues.title: Child poverty and work after the 2021 credit
sub_issues.text: The Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) counts taxes, credits and benefits as income. In 2021, with a larger, fully refundable credit paid monthly and with stimulus payments, Census first reported SPM child poverty at 5.2%, down from 9.7% in 2020. For 2024, after the expansion ended, it first reported 13.4%, and in August 2026 it revised 2019 to 2024 rates after a threshold correction. Ananat and coauthors found no measurable short-run drop in parents' employment in 2021. A simulation by Corinth and coauthors projects that 1.5 million parents would stop working under a permanent version.

sub_issues.title: New SNAP work rules and state costs
sub_issues.text: Public Law 119-21 extended SNAP's time limit for adults who do not meet a work requirement to ages 18 to 64 and to parents whose youngest child is 14 or older. It removed exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness and former foster youth, and USDA required states to apply the rules by November 2, 2025. States pay 75% of administrative costs, up from 50%, starting in fiscal year 2027. From fiscal year 2028, states with payment error rates of 6% or more pay 5% to 15% of benefit costs.

sub_issues.title: Medicaid work requirements and six-month renewals
sub_issues.text: Starting no later than January 1, 2027 under CMS's rule (the statute names December 31, 2026), adults ages 19 to 64 covered through Medicaid expansion must show 80 hours a month of work, a work program, community service or half-time school unless exempt, for example as a parent of a child under 14 or as a medically frail person. States may request good-faith extensions to no later than the end of 2028. Renewals for this group move to every six months. CBO estimated the work rule would leave an average of 4.5 million more people uninsured each year from 2027 to 2034, and 5.3 million more in 2034.

sub_issues.title: When a raise leaves a family no better off
sub_issues.text: A benefit cliff happens when one more dollar of earnings ends eligibility for a whole benefit, such as Medicaid above 138% of the poverty level in expansion states. Combined with taxes and phase-outs, a raise can then leave a family with the same or fewer resources. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta publishes a database and dashboard showing, by location and family type, where this happens across SNAP, Medicaid, housing vouchers, child care subsidies and tax credits.

sub_issues.title: Tax breaks that flow mostly to higher incomes
sub_issues.text: Tax expenditures are deductions, exclusions and credits that lower taxes for particular activities. For fiscal 2026, the Joint Committee on Taxation estimates that lower rates on dividends and long-term capital gains cost $252.3 billion, the exclusion of employer health insurance $240.4 billion, and the Child Tax Credit $128.4 billion. CBO found that in 2019 the top fifth of households received about half the benefit of major income tax expenditures and the bottom fifth 9%. The top fifth received 95% of the capital gains and dividend preference.

sub_issues.title: How much cushion households have
sub_issues.text: The Federal Reserve's household survey asks whether adults could cover an unexpected $400 expense with cash or its equivalent. In October 2025, 63% said they could, the same share as in each of the three years before, and 23% of renters had fallen behind on rent in the past year. Tax and benefit timing matters for the rest: refundable credits arrive once a year at tax time, while SNAP and Medicaid cover costs month to month, so a delayed refund or a lapsed benefit leaves little room.

sub_issues.title: IRS service, enforcement and free filing
sub_issues.text: The IRS answers taxpayers, processes refunds and audits returns with the staff Congress funds. Audit rates fell from 0.9% to 0.25% of individual returns between tax years 2010 and 2019, with the largest drops above $200,000 of income, while EITC claimants were audited at above-average rates. Boning and coauthors estimate that $1 more spent auditing the top tenth of earners returns more than $12, counting deterrence. Two of the 11 critical legacy computer systems GAO reviewed in 2025, at 59 and 51 years old, belong to the Treasury Department.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress controls the core rules through the Internal Revenue Code, the Food and Nutrition Act and the Medicaid title of the Social Security Act. By statute it can change credit amounts and refundability, SNAP time limits and state cost shares, and Medicaid work requirements. It often does so through budget reconciliation, which needs only a simple majority in the Senate; Public Law 119-21 passed that way. Congress also sets IRS funding in annual appropriations. Treasury, the IRS, USDA and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services write regulations and guidance within those laws and decide how services are delivered. State legislatures set state taxes and credits, choose whether to expand Medicaid, and decide how to pay the new SNAP costs, and voters in initiative states can act on some of these directly. Federal courts review whether agency rules follow the statutes.

responses.name: Pay the full Child Tax Credit to families with little or no earnings
responses.what_it_does: Congress would remove the earnings phase-in so every eligible child receives the full credit, as in 2021. Families with the lowest earnings, who now receive part of the credit or none, would gain the most. The IRS could pay it monthly, as it did from July to December 2021, so money arrives monthly as rent, food and utility bills come due.
responses.requires: An act of Congress amending 26 U.S.C. 24, with decisions on cost and on Social Security number rules for parents. The IRS needs systems and outreach to reach families that do not usually file taxes, and staff to handle monthly payments. A permanent law would avoid a repeat of the 2021 expiration.
responses.evidence: Child poverty fell sharply in 2021 while the expansion and other pandemic aid were in place, and refundable credits moved 9.6 million people out of SPM poverty that year. Ananat and coauthors found small, statistically insignificant short-run employment effects. A simulation by Corinth and coauthors projects that a permanent version would lead 1.5 million parents to stop working, cutting its poverty effect.
responses.tradeoffs: The cost is large and recurring, paid by taxpayers or added to federal debt. If some parents work less, earnings and payroll taxes fall. Removing the phase-in also ends the credit's link to work, a link that supporters of work-based aid want to keep.

responses.name: Automatic aid that turns on in a recession
responses.what_it_does: Congress would write triggers into law so that unemployment benefits, SNAP or direct payments expand when a published measure, such as the unemployment rate, crosses a set line, and shrink when it recovers. Households would receive help without waiting for a new bill. Unemployment insurance already has a smaller version: the Extended Benefits program adds up to 13 weeks of benefits when a state has high unemployment.
responses.requires: A statute setting the triggers, benefit amounts and duration, passed by Congress and signed by the President. State unemployment and SNAP systems must be able to scale quickly and verify identity, which takes upgraded computer systems and staff. CBO would count costs that arise only in downturns.
responses.evidence: Cash delivered during the 2021 downturn lowered measured poverty: refundable credits and stimulus payments moved 9.6 million and 8.9 million people out of SPM poverty. Those payments were enacted one law at a time and expired on fixed dates. Delivery is the weak point. The Labor Department estimated improper unemployment payments rose from 9.2% in fiscal 2020 to 18.9% in fiscal 2021, with identity theft a main cause.
responses.tradeoffs: A trigger set too low could add spending when the economy is already recovering, and one set too high would miss regional slumps. Fast payment systems attract fraud unless identity checks keep pace.

responses.name: Smooth benefit phase-outs across programs
responses.what_it_does: Congress and states would replace sudden eligibility cutoffs with gradual phase-outs and align income limits across SNAP, Medicaid, child care and housing aid, so each extra dollar of earnings leaves the family better off. A parent offered more hours could then accept without losing a whole benefit at once. Agencies would publish, for common family types, the combined share of a raise lost to taxes and lower benefits.
responses.requires: Changes to several federal statutes and state rules, since each program has its own income test. Smoother phase-outs either cost more, because some families keep benefits longer, or reduce benefits for others. States need eligibility systems that share income data across programs with consent.
responses.evidence: The size of the problem is measured. CBO estimated an average effective marginal tax rate of 31% for low- and moderate-income workers in 2016, with wide variation, and the Atlanta Fed's database shows where cliffs occur by state and family type. No published evaluation of a coordinated phase-out across programs exists.
responses.tradeoffs: Longer phase-outs spread higher marginal rates over more households, so some families with moderate incomes face new reductions. Added cost competes with other spending.

responses.name: Rebuild IRS staff for service and high-income audits
responses.what_it_does: Congress would provide multi-year funding for IRS phone and walk-in service and for skilled auditors who examine complex, high-income returns. Taxpayers would get answers, corrected notices and refunds faster, including identity theft victims whose cases took an average of 600 days to close in fiscal 2026. People who underreport income would be more likely to be caught, which raises revenue without new tax rates.
responses.requires: Appropriations that stay stable for several years, since auditors take years to train, and oversight from the Taxpayer Advocate and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration to protect taxpayer rights. Enforcement funding added in 2022 was partly rescinded later, so durability depends on Congress.
responses.evidence: Boning, Hendren, Sprung-Keyser and Stuart, using IRS data, estimate that $1 more spent auditing taxpayers above the 90th income percentile returns more than $12, counting deterrence, and $5 for audits below the median. Audit rates for incomes above $200,000 fell the most from 2010 to 2019 as IRS staffing declined. The returns depend on hiring and training skilled examiners.
responses.tradeoffs: Audits impose costs on taxpayers who owe nothing, and EITC claimants have been audited at above-average rates. Enforcement funding competes with other spending and can be rescinded in later budgets.

responses.name: Free government filing and simpler claiming of credits
responses.what_it_does: The IRS would run a free online system that lets people file directly with the government, prefilled with wage and benefit data it already holds, and states would link their own returns to it. Families that do not usually file, including many eligible for the EITC or Child Tax Credit, would face fewer steps to claim what the law provides.
responses.requires: A Treasury decision to restart and fund the program, or a statute requiring it; staff with software skills; and data-sharing agreements with states. Direct File depended on executive decisions and ended for 2026, so a statute would make it more durable.
responses.evidence: Direct File grew from 140,803 returns in 12 states in 2024 to 296,531 in 25 states in 2025, a small share of all returns. About 19% of eligible taxpayers did not receive the EITC for tax year 2022. Evidence on whether free direct filing raises credit take-up is not yet available.
responses.tradeoffs: Commercial tax-preparation firms lose customers and have opposed government filing. The IRS must build and secure software, and a program run by executive decision can be closed by the next administration.

responses.name: State earned income and child credits
responses.what_it_does: A state adds its own refundable credit, often set as a percentage of the federal EITC, or a child credit paid through the state income tax return. The credit offsets part of the sales and other taxes that take a larger share of low incomes. A state can also extend it to families the federal rules leave out, such as parents with earnings below $2,500 or without a qualifying Social Security number.
responses.requires: A state statute and the revenue to pay for it, passed by the legislature and signed by the governor. States without an income tax need another way to deliver payments. State revenue departments need outreach to families that do not usually file, often through free tax help sites.
responses.evidence: ITEP, which favors progressive taxation, reports that all 10 of the least regressive state tax systems have a refundable EITC and nine have a child credit, while only three of the 10 most regressive have an EITC. That pattern is an association across states and does not measure how much each credit changes household resources or work.
responses.tradeoffs: Credits reduce state revenue, which must come from other taxes or spending cuts. States facing new SNAP administrative and benefit costs under the 2025 law may have less room in their budgets.

distribution.group: Families with children and low or no earnings
distribution.difference: A parent with no earnings receives no Child Tax Credit, and one earning $10,000 receives at most $1,125 for one child, against $2,200 for a family with moderate income. The lowest tenth of households also lose the most in CBO's estimate of the 2025 law, about $1,200 a year, mainly in Medicaid and SNAP.

Children of filers without a Social Security number valid for work receive no Child Tax Credit, even when the children are citizens. The 2025 law limited SNAP to lawful permanent residents and a few other groups, ending eligibility for refugees and asylees, and narrowed Medicaid eligibility for some qualified immigrants on October 1, 2026.

distribution.group: SNAP recipients ages 55 to 64 and parents of teenagers
distribution.difference: SNAP's time limit now reaches adults up to age 64 and parents whose youngest child is 14 or older, groups that were exempt before the 2025 law. Unless they meet the work requirement or qualify for an exemption, their benefits become time-limited. CBO projected the changes would cut average monthly participation by about 2.4 million people.

CBO estimates the top tenth gains about $13,600 a year from the 2025 law, mainly through lower taxes. In 2019 the top fifth received about half the benefit of major income tax expenditures, and the top 1% received about 75% of the preference for capital gains and dividends.

distribution.group: Low-income residents of states that rely on sales taxes
distribution.difference: In ITEP's estimates, sales and excise taxes took 7.0% of income from the lowest-income fifth of families under 2024 law, against 1.0% for the top 1%. Residents of states that rely heavily on these taxes and offer no refundable credit pay more relative to income.

check.prompt: A parent with one child earned $2,000 last year and owes no income tax. Under the federal Child Tax Credit rules for 2025 and 2026, how much of the credit can the family receive?
options: Nothing, because the refundable part starts only above $2,500 of earnings
check.explanation: The refundable part of the credit phases in at 15% of earnings above $2,500. A family that earned $2,000 is below that line, so it receives nothing, while a family with moderate income receives $2,200 per child.

pathways.title: Social Security and retirement
pathways.question: What will I get from Social Security, and could the rules change before I retire?
also_answers: How is my Social Security benefit calculated?
What happens when the trust fund runs low?
Who would pay under the main proposals to close Social Security's shortfall?
How long do people wait for help from Social Security?
How do people save for retirement beyond Social Security?
pathways.short_answer: Your benefit depends on your earnings record, the formula in the Social Security Act and the age you claim. The formula averages your highest 35 years of wage-indexed earnings and replaces a larger share of lower earnings. Benefits rise each year with inflation; the increase for 2027 is 3.6 percent. The 2026 Trustees Report projects that the retirement trust fund's reserves run out in late 2032, after which incoming taxes would cover 78 percent of scheduled benefits. Congress decides how to close that gap, and each option falls on different earners and birth years.
pathways.scope_note: Social Security's rules are national and set by federal statute; the Social Security Administration (SSA) applies them through field offices, a national phone line and state disability agencies. Savings outside Social Security depend on employers and, in some states, state-run automatic retirement accounts. An individual estimate depends on that person's own earnings record, and nothing here is financial or legal advice.

mechanisms.title: Covered work builds credits and an earnings record
mechanisms.text: Workers and employers each pay half of a combined 12.4 percent Social Security tax on wages, up to an annual limit called the taxable maximum. In 2026 that limit is $184,500; in 2027 it rises to $192,300. Each $1,890 of covered earnings in 2026 earns one work credit, up to four a year, and retirement benefits require 40 credits. SSA records each year's taxed earnings, and that record later sets the benefit. Pay above the taxable maximum is untaxed for Social Security and does not raise benefits.

mechanisms.title: A progressive formula turns the record into a monthly benefit
mechanisms.text: SSA adjusts each past year's earnings for growth in the national average wage, then averages the highest 35 years to get average indexed monthly earnings (AIME). The primary insurance amount (PIA), the benefit at full retirement age, equals 90 percent of AIME up to a first threshold, called a bend point, plus 32 percent up to a second and 15 percent above it. For workers first eligible in 2027, the bend points are $1,340 and $8,077 a month. Because the first slice is replaced at the highest rate, lower earners get back a larger share of past pay. The Census Bureau estimates Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025.

mechanisms.title: Claiming age and yearly inflation adjustments change the check
mechanisms.text: Full retirement age is 67 for people born in 1960 or later. Claiming at 62 cuts the monthly benefit by 30 percent for life, and each year of delay past full retirement age adds 8 percent until age 70. After claiming, the benefit rises each year by a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). On October 14, 2026, SSA announced a 3.6 percent COLA for 2027, which raises the estimated average retired worker's check from $2,095 to $2,170 a month starting in January.

mechanisms.title: Scheduled benefits outrun the money coming in
mechanisms.text: Social Security pays benefits from payroll taxes, income taxes on some benefits and trust fund reserves built in earlier years. The 2026 Trustees Report projects that reserves for retirement and survivor benefits run out in the fourth quarter of 2032; incoming revenue would then pay 78 percent of scheduled benefits, falling to 62 percent by 2100. Merging it with the disability fund, which would take a change in law, stretches reserves to 2034. The 75-year shortfall grew to 4.42 percent of taxable payroll, mostly because the trustees now assume fewer births and less immigration and because the 2025 tax law reduced income tax collected on benefits. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects the retirement fund is exhausted in fiscal 2032.

mechanisms.title: The wage cap leaves a growing share of earnings untaxed
mechanisms.text: The taxable maximum rises each year with average wages. When the highest salaries grow faster than average pay, more earnings land above the cap. The Congressional Research Service (CRS) reported that the share of covered earnings subject to the tax fell from about 90 percent in 1982 to about 83 percent, mainly because top salaries grew faster than other pay, and that about 6 percent of workers earned above the cap in 2019. With less of total earnings taxed, payroll tax revenue grows more slowly than total pay.

mechanisms.title: SSA's staffing and service capacity set how fast people get answers
mechanisms.text: Congress sets SSA's administrative budget each year, and SSA decides where to put staff. Office of Personnel Management data compiled by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (CBPP), an advocacy research group, show SSA's workforce fell from 57,384 in January 2025 to 49,880 in January 2026, the fewest since 1967. SSA reports national phone answers in about half a minute in August 2026. The SSA inspector general found that the agency's phone measure counts callers who accept a callback as waiting zero minutes, while in fiscal 2025 those callers waited about 109 minutes for the return call. A study of past field office closures found disability recipients in surrounding areas fell 16 percent.

pathways.household_effects: For most retirees the result is a monthly check, an estimated average of $2,170 for retired workers in January 2027. Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of poverty under the Census Bureau's Supplemental Poverty Measure in 2025. Women received less on average, $14,204 a year at 65 and older in 2021 compared with $18,108 for men, and live about three years longer after 65, so their benefits must stretch further. People applying for disability benefits wait months: SSA reported 188 days on average for an initial decision and 276 days for a hearing in August 2026.

sub_issues.title: Disability Insurance and SSI
sub_issues.text: Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) pays workers with enough recent credits, usually 20 earned in the 10 years before disability for those 31 and older, whose condition prevents substantial work for at least 12 months or is expected to result in death. Payments begin after a five-month waiting period. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is a separate, means-tested program for people with low income and few assets who are 65 or older, blind or disabled. In 2027 the federal SSI payment is $1,029 a month for an individual, and the asset limit stays at $2,000.

sub_issues.title: The Social Security Fairness Act
sub_issues.text: Signed January 5, 2025, the Social Security Fairness Act repealed the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset, two rules that reduced Social Security for people with pensions from jobs that did not pay Social Security tax, such as some teachers, police officers and federal workers under the Civil Service Retirement System. The repeal applies to benefits payable for January 2024 and later. SSA says it affects over 2.8 million people and had sent more than 3.1 million retroactive payments totaling $17 billion by July 7, 2025.

sub_issues.title: How the yearly adjustment is measured
sub_issues.text: The COLA follows the CPI-W. Some proposals would switch to a chained index, which accounts for shoppers substituting cheaper goods and which SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary (OCACT) assumes would run about 0.3 percentage point lower each year. Others would use an index weighted to older households' spending (CPI-E), assumed about 0.15 point higher. Because each year's raise builds on the last, a 0.3-point gap leaves a benefit roughly 3 percent lower after 10 years of receipt and 6 percent lower after 20, by simple calculation.

sub_issues.title: Retirement plans at work
sub_issues.text: Most savings beyond Social Security come through employers. In March 2026, 72 percent of private industry workers had access to a workplace retirement plan and 52 percent took part. Access is unequal by pay: in March 2025, 48 percent of civilian workers in the lowest-paid quarter could join a defined contribution plan such as a 401(k), compared with 77 percent in the highest-paid quarter, and participation was 22 percent compared with 64 percent.

sub_issues.title: State automatic IRA programs
sub_issues.text: Several states require employers without a retirement plan to enroll workers automatically in a state-run individual retirement account (IRA) that workers can leave. As of August 31, 2026, 15 state programs reported more than $3.4 billion in assets across more than 1.4 million funded accounts. In OregonSaves, 49.8 percent of eligible workers opted out within 12 months, and contributions averaged 1.3 percent of pay across all eligible workers. The researchers concluded the program meaningfully raised saving.

sub_issues.title: The federal Saver's Match
sub_issues.text: Starting in 2027, the Saver's Match largely replaces the nonrefundable Saver's Credit. The federal government will deposit a 50 percent match on up to $2,000 a year of retirement contributions, up to $1,000, into the saver's retirement account. The full match goes to savers with modified adjusted gross income below $20,500, or $41,000 for joint filers, and phases out over the next $15,000, or $30,000 for joint filers.

sub_issues.title: Workers left out at the start
sub_issues.text: The 1935 Social Security Act excluded agricultural and domestic workers. About 65 percent of Black workers held those jobs, compared with 27 percent of white workers, though 74 percent of the roughly 15.5 million excluded workers were white. Amendments in 1950 and 1954 brought these workers in. A 2010 article in SSA's Social Security Bulletin argues the exclusion followed tax collection concerns, an interpretation of motive that other historians dispute.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Only Congress can change Social Security benefits, the full retirement age, the COLA index or the payroll tax, by amending the Social Security Act and the Internal Revenue Code. Bills go through the House Ways and Means Committee and the Senate Finance Committee, and most legislation needs 60 votes to advance in the Senate while the filibuster stands. Congress also sets SSA's administrative budget through yearly appropriations, which shapes staffing and service. SSA can change its own procedures, including how it measures and reports phone waits, without new law. State legislatures can create or change automatic IRA programs, and employers decide their own plan design within federal pension and tax law. CBO and SSA's actuaries estimate the effects of proposals but cannot change the rules.

responses.name: Raise or remove the cap on taxed earnings
responses.what_it_does: Congress applies the payroll tax to more of the earnings of people above the taxable maximum, $192,300 in 2027. One version taxes all earnings from 2027 without raising those workers' benefits. Another taxes all earnings and gives benefit credit for the added earnings. Other versions apply the tax only above a threshold such as $250,000 or $400,000, or raise the cap until 90 percent of earnings are taxed.
responses.requires: An act of Congress amending the Internal Revenue Code and, for benefit credit, the Social Security Act. Employers would withhold on all wages, the IRS would collect the added tax and SSA would record the added earnings. Revenue begins in the first year the change takes effect.
responses.evidence: SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary estimates, under 2026 Trustees Report assumptions, that taxing all earnings with no added benefit credit would close 58 percent of the 75-year shortfall, and 45 percent with credit. These are projections that assume little shifting of pay into untaxed forms; actual revenue depends on how high earners and employers respond.
responses.tradeoffs: Workers earning above the cap, about 6 percent of workers in 2019, and their employers pay more. Without benefit credit the program becomes more redistributive; with credit, part of the revenue returns later as larger benefits for high earners.

responses.name: Raise the full retirement age
responses.what_it_does: Congress raises the age for a full benefit above 67 for people turning 62 from 2027, reaching 68 by 2032 in one version or 69 by 2038 in another, with later increases tied to longevity. Monthly benefits at every claiming age would fall for affected cohorts, because the reduction for claiming before full retirement age grows. People already 62 or older when the change starts keep current rules.
responses.requires: An act of Congress amending the Social Security Act, with a phase-in schedule by birth year announced years ahead so workers can plan. SSA would update its claiming tables and notices. OCACT and CBO would score the schedule before a vote, and savings would build slowly as each new cohort reaches 62.
responses.evidence: OCACT estimates raising the age to 68 would close 13 percent of the 75-year shortfall, and raising it to 69 with later longevity indexing would close 32 percent. CBO found that a full retirement age of 70 would mean a 45 percent cut for those claiming at 62. CRS, drawing on National Academies estimates, concluded such increases would affect low earners disproportionately because their life expectancy has barely risen.
responses.tradeoffs: Younger cohorts bear the cut. Workers who cannot keep working into their late 60s take a larger reduction when they claim early, and low earners lose a larger share of lifetime benefits.

responses.name: Change the cost-of-living index
responses.what_it_does: Congress switches the yearly COLA from the CPI-W to another index. A chained CPI-W would give smaller raises; the CPI-E, weighted to the spending of older households, would give larger ones. The change reaches everyone already receiving benefits as well as future retirees, starting with the first adjustment after the law takes effect. SSI payments, which rise by the same yearly percentage, would change too.
responses.requires: An act of Congress amending the Social Security Act's COLA provision and naming a published index for SSA to apply. SSA would use the new index when it announces each year's adjustment in October. Effects begin with the next adjustment and grow every year a person collects.
responses.evidence: OCACT estimates a chained CPI-W, assumed about 0.3 point lower a year, would close 15 percent of the 75-year shortfall; using the CPI-E, assumed 0.15 point higher, would widen it by 7 percent. CBO found the chained index grew about 0.25 point a year slower than the standard index since 2001. Which index best tracks older people's costs is debated.
responses.tradeoffs: A chained index lowers benefits most for people who collect longest, including the oldest beneficiaries, about 63 percent of whom are women. The CPI-E raises costs and deepens the shortfall unless paired with new revenue.

responses.name: Change the benefit formula
responses.what_it_does: Congress changes the 90, 32 and 15 percent factors or how the bend points grow. Gradually lowering the upper factors reduces benefits mainly for middle and higher earners. Progressive price indexing slows benefit growth for higher earners while lower earners keep the current path. A basic minimum benefit would raise payments for long-career low earners. Most proposals apply only to people newly eligible after a set year.
responses.requires: An act of Congress amending the benefit formula in the Social Security Act, and SSA changes to its benefit computation systems. Proposals usually start with a later eligibility year to protect people near retirement; the versions OCACT scored begin between 2027 and 2068. Changes for newly eligible workers take decades to reach their full effect.
responses.evidence: OCACT estimates that cutting the 32 and 15 percent factors to 10 and 5 percent by 2066 would close 25 percent of the shortfall, progressive price indexing at the 30th earnings percentile 38 percent, and a basic minimum benefit would widen it by 5 percent. CBO notes its comparable estimates count direct effects and leave out changes in claiming or work.
responses.tradeoffs: Future retirees bear the cuts, sized by lifetime earnings. Lower upper factors shrink Social Security's role for middle earners, and a minimum benefit costs money unless paired with revenue.

responses.name: Expand automatic retirement saving
responses.what_it_does: States require employers without a plan to enroll workers automatically in a state-run IRA, and the federal Saver's Match will add up to $1,000 a year to low and moderate earners' accounts from 2027. Both aim to raise savings beyond Social Security for workers whose jobs offer no plan, using defaults that keep people saving unless they choose to stop.
responses.requires: A state statute and a state board to run each program, with enforcement of employer participation. The Saver's Match is already law and depends on Treasury and IRS systems to deliver deposits. Neither changes Social Security's own finances or the trust fund shortfall.
responses.evidence: Danish administrative data show automatic contributions raise saving far more than tax subsidies, which mostly shift assets between accounts. In OregonSaves, about half of eligible workers opted out within a year and average contributions across eligible workers were 1.3 percent of pay, though researchers found the program meaningfully raised saving. The average balance was $754 in April 2020.
responses.tradeoffs: Low earners who cannot spare income opt out, and employers take on some administrative work. Account balances carry market risk and lack the inflation-adjusted lifetime income that Social Security pays.

responses.name: Fund and measure SSA service capacity
responses.what_it_does: Congress funds SSA's administrative budget at a level that supports hiring for field offices, the phone line and disability hearings, and SSA publishes full service measures, including callback waits, appointment waits and pending workloads. It would also restore the monthly reports on callback waits, appointment waits and backlogs that, according to CBPP, SSA stopped publishing in mid-2025. The aim is shorter waits for claims and appeals and public data that show what callers and visitors experience.
responses.requires: Annual appropriations from Congress for SSA's administrative budget, time to hire and train new staff, and SSA decisions on which measures to publish and how to count callbacks. The SSA inspector general can audit the measures, as it did for fiscal 2025 phone data.
responses.evidence: Evidence on access comes from the reverse case: field office closures cut disability receipt by 16 percent in surrounding areas, most among applicants with less education. SSA credits a new phone platform and staff reassignments for faster answers in 2026. No study has measured how much added staff would shorten waits under SSA's current service model.
responses.tradeoffs: Higher administrative spending competes with other appropriations. Publishing more measures can show worse performance on some services even as headline numbers improve.

distribution.difference: The formula replaces 90 percent of the first $1,340 of average monthly earnings in 2027, returning a larger share of pay to lower earners. Their life expectancy has barely risen: for men, the gap at 50 between the top and bottom earnings fifths grew from 5.1 years for those born in 1930 to 12.7 years for those born in 1960, so a higher retirement age cuts their lifetime benefits proportionally more.

Women made up 55.2 percent of beneficiaries 60 and older and received less on average in 2021, $14,204 a year compared with $18,108 for men 65 and older. At 65 they can expect 21.1 more years compared with 18.0 for men, so COLA changes, which compound with each year of receipt, affect them more.

distribution.group: Younger workers and later birth years
distribution.difference: People turning 62 in 2027 or later would face a retirement age increase under the versions OCACT scored, and people becoming eligible decades from now would bear most formula changes. If Congress does nothing, everyone collecting retirement or survivor benefits after late 2032 would face a cut to 78 percent of scheduled benefits, falling to 62 percent by 2100.

About 6 percent of workers earned above the taxable maximum in 2019. Removing the cap would raise their payroll taxes and their employers'; whether they receive larger benefits in return depends on the version Congress chooses, and OCACT scores the two versions differently.

distribution.group: Public employees with pensions from jobs outside Social Security
distribution.difference: Before 2025, the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset reduced Social Security for many teachers, police officers and federal retirees whose jobs did not pay Social Security tax. Their repeal raised benefits for over 2.8 million people, starting with benefits for January 2024.

pathways.title: Clean drinking water
pathways.question: Who makes sure my tap water is safe?
also_answers: Who tests and treats the water?
Who pays to replace aging pipes?
How does a household get a water problem addressed?
What is happening to the federal lead and PFAS rules?
pathways.short_answer: Your water utility tests and treats the water. It follows national limits set by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and in most states a state drinking water program enforces them. The utility can be a city department, a regional authority or a private company. Customers' bills pay for most pipes and treatment: in 2017, state and local sources covered 96% of public spending on water utilities. A city council or utility board sets rates for most publicly owned systems, and a state utility commission regulates many private ones. For a problem, start with the utility. If it is not resolved, contact the state drinking water program.
pathways.scope_note: Federal standards apply to every public water system. Enforcement, rate rules and funding programs vary by state, and about 15% of people use private wells that the Safe Drinking Water Act does not cover. One household's test result or bill describes that home and cannot show how a whole system performs.

mechanisms.title: Thousands of separate utilities run the water you drink
mechanisms.text: About 49,500 community water systems serve people where they live, and each runs its own treatment, testing and pipes. Most are small. According to the Congressional Research Service, 81% serve 3,300 people or fewer and together reach 7% of customers, while fewer than 10% of systems serve 84%. An owner can be a city, a regional authority or a private company. A small system spreads the fixed cost of operators, laboratory tests and new equipment across few customers, so a new standard or a failed main costs each household more. That cost pressure shapes how fast a small system can meet each new federal rule.

mechanisms.title: EPA sets limits and state programs enforce them
mechanisms.text: Under the Safe Drinking Water Act, EPA sets maximum contaminant levels (enforceable limits on a substance in tap water) and treatment requirements. A state agency with primacy, meaning authority EPA has delegated to it, inspects systems, reviews test results and takes enforcement action. On most tribal lands, EPA's regional offices do that work directly. Each community system must send customers a Consumer Confidence Report, a yearly summary of detected contaminants and violations, by July 1. Rule revisions from 2024 require systems serving more than 10,000 people to send it twice a year, under a schedule that starts in late 2027.

mechanisms.title: New lead and PFAS rules set the next round of work
mechanisms.text: Two national rules drive much of the planned work. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, finalized in October 2024, require most systems to replace lead service lines (the pipe from the main to a building) within 10 years after a November 1, 2027 compliance date. EPA estimates about 4 million lead lines remain. A 2024 rule limits PFOA and PFOS, two long-lasting industrial chemicals, to 4 parts per trillion. In May 2026 EPA proposed allowing extensions to 2031 for those two and rescinding limits on four other PFAS. Federal appeals against both rules were argued in September 2026 and await decision.

mechanisms.title: Customers pay most costs, with loans from state revolving funds
mechanisms.text: Water bills pay for most pipes and plants. In 2017 the federal government supplied 4% of public spending on water utilities, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The main federal channel is the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund: EPA grants money to each state, the state adds a 20% match, and the state program lends to water systems and relends the repayments. The 2021 infrastructure law added $15 billion for lead line replacement over five years. For fiscal 2026, Congress directed 64% of the regular drinking water fund appropriation to named local projects, which left less for state loan programs to allocate.

mechanisms.title: Rate decisions turn those costs into household bills
mechanisms.text: Whoever sets rates decides how costs reach each bill. A publicly owned system usually adopts rates through its own council or board after a rate study and a hearing. In many states a public utility commission sets rates for some systems, including investor-owned utilities; California's commission regulates more than 100 investor-owned water and sewer utilities serving about 16% of residents. A 2025 Congressional Research Service report summarizes research finding that household payments for water and sewer rose about twice as fast as consumer prices from 1998 to 2024, with estimates of 12.1 million to 19.2 million households lacking affordable service.

pathways.household_effects: Households meet this system through the bill, the yearly water quality report and any notice about a violation or a lead line. An owner of an older home can learn the service line is lead and need to give the utility access to replace the part on private property; whether the owner shares the cost depends on the local program. Customers of small systems can pay more each for the same treatment upgrade. Rising bills weigh most on low-income households, and research summarized by CRS puts 11% to 20% of customers in arrears. People on private wells get no utility testing: the owner is responsible for testing and treatment.

sub_issues.title: Lead pipes and the replacement deadline
sub_issues.text: Utilities had to publish service line inventories in October 2024 and must post replacement plans. Replacement runs about 10% of lines a year after November 2027, and the full job is due about 10 years later. EPA's estimate of remaining lead lines changed from up to 9 million in 2024 materials to about 4 million on its updated survey page, which rests mostly on counts reported by systems. The utility association's challenge to the rule awaits a D.C. Circuit decision after September 2026 argument, and the rule stays in effect meanwhile.

sub_issues.title: PFAS chemicals and changing federal limits
sub_issues.text: PFAS are a family of industrial chemicals that persist in water and the body. The 2024 rule requires first monitoring by 2027 and treatment by 2029 where levels exceed the limits. EPA's May 2026 proposals would keep the PFOA and PFOS limits, let systems request two more years, and drop the other four limits. The D.C. Circuit refused in January 2026 to vacate those four limits before full review. Until a final rule or court decision, the 2024 requirements remain in place.

sub_issues.title: Small systems with few customers
sub_issues.text: Four in five community systems serve 3,300 people or fewer. With few customers, a small system has little revenue to pay for certified operators, testing and new treatment. EPA encourages partnerships, from shared equipment and contract operators to joint agencies and full consolidation. State revolving funds may set aside 2% of each grant for small-system technical help, and USDA lends to rural systems. EPA's partnership page lists expected benefits without measured results.

sub_issues.title: Private wells
sub_issues.text: About 43 million people drink from private wells, which no federal drinking water standard covers. The owner decides whether and how often to test, which contaminants to test for, and pays for any treatment. A well owner who finds contamination has no utility to call; the response depends on the owner's resources and any state or local assistance program.

sub_issues.title: Paying the bill
sub_issues.text: Bills rose faster than inflation for more than two decades. A federal assistance program created during the pandemic helped 1.7 million households with water bills through mid-2024 and was temporary; Congress has not funded the follow-on pilot. Help now depends on whether the local utility offers a discount or payment plan and whether state law allows it. Rate hearings are where councils and boards decide those programs.

sub_issues.title: When a system fails: Flint and Jackson
sub_issues.text: Two regional cases show where accountability can break down. In Flint, emergency managers appointed by Michigan's governor changed the water source in 2014 without corrosion control, and EPA's Inspector General found lapses at the city, state and federal levels; EPA lifted its emergency order in 2025. In Jackson, Mississippi, a federal judge placed the system under an interim third-party manager in November 2022. Neither case measures how often such failures occur nationally.

decision_makers.who: Your water utility (city water department, regional water authority or private water company)
decision_makers.controls: Runs treatment and testing, decides the order of main and lead line replacements in its plan, issues notices, and corrects violations under state oversight
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Customer service number on the water bill; the utility's contact listed in its Consumer Confidence Report; public meetings of its board where one exists

decision_makers.who: City council, town meeting or water utility board
decision_makers.controls: Approves water rates, the capital plan, borrowing and any customer assistance program for a publicly owned system
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public comment at the rate hearing or budget hearing; agendas are posted by the city or town clerk or the utility board secretary

decision_makers.who: State drinking water program (the state's primacy agency)
decision_makers.controls: Enforces federal drinking water standards in the state, reviews test results, issues violations and orders, and runs the state revolving loan fund
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Drinking water program within the state environmental or health department; complaints and records requests go to that program

decision_makers.controls: Sets rates and service standards for the water systems state law places under its authority, mostly investor-owned utilities
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Written comments or testimony in the utility's rate case docket; public hearings announced by the commission

decision_makers.who: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Office of Water
decision_makers.controls: Sets national drinking water standards, including the lead and PFAS rules, and allocates revolving fund grants to states
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Comments on proposed rules through regulations.gov dockets, such as EPA-HQ-OW-2025-1742 for the PFAS extension proposal

decision_makers.controls: Amends the Safe Drinking Water Act and decides annual revolving fund appropriations and earmarked projects
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Your U.S. representative and senators; House and Senate appropriations subcommittees on Interior and Environment

decision_makers.who: Private well owner, with the local or state health department
decision_makers.controls: The owner decides testing and treatment; health departments provide guidance and certified laboratory lists
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Local board of health or state health department environmental health office

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress can amend the Safe Drinking Water Act and decides each year how much goes to the revolving funds and how much is earmarked. EPA changes national standards through notice-and-comment rulemaking; its 2026 PFAS proposals and any revision of the lead rule follow that route. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit reviews petitions against national drinking water rules and can uphold or vacate them, as the pending lead and PFAS cases show. State legislatures and agencies set state standards, primacy procedures, affordability rules and the reach of the utility commission. City councils, utility boards and, for regulated private systems, state utility commissions set rates and capital plans through rate hearings and rate cases.

responses.name: Replace lead service lines on a fixed schedule
responses.what_it_does: Under the 2024 lead rule, each system keeps a public inventory and replaces lead and galvanized lines that need replacement, both the utility side and the private side, within 10 years after November 2027. Replacement must average about 10% a year. Systems also lower the action level that triggers treatment changes to 10 micrograms per liter. Revolving fund money, including $15 billion from the 2021 law, helps pay for replacements, with half of that amount set aside as grants or forgiven loans for disadvantaged communities.
responses.requires: The rule must survive review in the D.C. Circuit. Utilities need access agreements with property owners, contractors and crews, and rate or loan financing. EPA estimated costs at $1.5 billion to $2 billion a year; the challenging utility association argues total costs exceed $100 billion. State programs track progress and enforce deadlines.
responses.evidence: EPA estimated annual benefits of $13 billion to $25 billion, mostly from avoided harm to children and adults from lead. These are agency model estimates, and the rule has no completed national track record yet. The court case turns partly on whether the 10-year deadline and private-side access are workable, so feasibility is the main open question.
responses.tradeoffs: Ratepayers carry costs not covered by grants, and owners can face disruption or cost-sharing on private property. Small systems with few staff can struggle to keep pace.

responses.name: Treat water for PFAS under national limits
responses.what_it_does: Systems sample for regulated PFAS by 2027 and install treatment where results exceed the limits, then keep monitoring to show compliance. EPA's 2026 proposals would keep the 4 parts per trillion limits for PFOA and PFOS, allow systems to request extra time to 2031, and remove limits on four other PFAS. Federal infrastructure money, including revolving fund grants aimed at emerging contaminants, offsets part of the cost.
responses.requires: EPA must finalize or withdraw its proposals, and the D.C. Circuit must decide the pending challenge. Systems need money for design, construction and ongoing operation, and state programs must review any exemption requests and track monitoring results from each system.
responses.evidence: EPA estimated that the 2024 rule would prevent PFAS exposure for about 100 million people over time. Challengers argue EPA lacked adequate national occurrence data, and EPA itself conceded a procedural error in how it regulated four of the chemicals. Evidence on health effects of the specific limits and on national costs therefore remains disputed in court.
responses.tradeoffs: Treatment raises bills, most in small systems with high PFAS levels. Extended deadlines lower near-term cost while prolonging exposure where levels exceed the limits.

responses.name: Pool small systems through partnerships or consolidation
responses.what_it_does: Neighboring systems share operators, laboratories and purchasing, contract for management, form a joint agency, or merge into a larger system. A merged system spreads fixed costs, such as a certified operator and laboratory contracts, over more customers and can borrow on better terms. States can steer revolving fund set-asides and technical assistance toward systems that partner, and USDA rural loans can finance the physical connections.
responses.requires: State drinking water programs must identify candidates and offer incentives. Mergers need willing owners and local governments, or state authority to require them where systems keep failing, plus capital for interconnecting pipes and rate agreements that settle who pays for past deferred maintenance.
responses.evidence: EPA describes expected gains in economies of scale, compliance and service and publishes case studies of lessons learned. Its program page reports no measured outcomes, and the sources cited include no evaluation of effects on violations or bills. Issue record I165 rates shared services as a hypothesis.
responses.tradeoffs: Residents of a small system can lose local control over rates and decisions. Customers of the larger system can absorb upgrade costs for the system it takes in.

responses.name: Keep federal water money flowing through state loan programs
responses.what_it_does: Congress funds revolving fund capitalization grants, which states lend according to project priority lists ranked by public health need, and limits how much of each account it earmarks for named projects. States can then plan multi-year lending and subsidize disadvantaged communities from a predictable base. Repayments from loans return to the fund, so each grant dollar finances more than one project over time.
responses.requires: The House and Senate appropriations committees decide the split each year. States must supply staff to run priority lists and the 20% match. Each dollar left out of earmarks moves project selection from members of Congress to state programs that rank projects with needs data.
responses.evidence: CRS documents that earmarks took 64% of the fiscal 2026 drinking water fund appropriation, and EPA told states this reduced their allotments. No evaluation in the sources compares water quality or cost results of earmarked projects with state-selected loans, so the effect on outcomes is untested.
responses.tradeoffs: Earmarks let members fund local projects quickly, sometimes as grants. Formula lending favors systems able to repay loans unless states add subsidies.

responses.name: Help low-income households pay water bills
responses.what_it_does: A federal or state program pays part of water and sewer bills for eligible households, or a utility offers income-based discounts, payment plans and limits on shutoffs. The temporary federal program run during the pandemic followed this model, sending money through state agencies that already handled home energy assistance and paying utilities directly on a household's behalf. Local discount programs work through the utility's own billing system.
responses.requires: Funding comes from appropriations by Congress or a state legislature, or from rate-funded discounts where state law permits them. An agency must verify income and share data with utilities. A utility discount needs approval by its council, board or utility commission.
responses.evidence: CRS reports the pandemic program reached 1.7 million households through mid-2024. The sources document reach only and give no measure of effects on arrears or shutoffs. Congress has not funded the related pilot, so there is no current national program to evaluate.
responses.tradeoffs: Rate-funded discounts shift costs to other customers. Tax-funded aid competes with other budget needs and can lapse when temporary money ends.

distribution.difference: Systems serving 3,300 people or fewer make up 81% of community systems but serve 7% of customers. Each new requirement, such as PFAS treatment, is spread over a small customer base, so the cost per household is higher than in a large system making the same upgrade.
About 43 million people rely on private wells outside the Safe Drinking Water Act. They receive no required testing or public notice, and the owner pays for any test and treatment.

Water and sewer payments rose about twice as fast as consumer prices from 1998 to 2024. Estimates put 12.1 million to 19.2 million households without affordable service, and the federal assistance program created in the pandemic has ended.

distribution.group: Residents of homes with lead service lines
distribution.difference: EPA estimates about 4 million lead lines remain in service. These residents depend on the replacement schedule in their utility's plan, on local rules for private-side costs, and on the outcome of the pending court case.
On most tribal lands, an EPA regional office acts as the enforcing agency because the Navajo Nation is the only tribe holding primacy. Tribal systems receive revolving fund money directly from EPA.

The customers who receive the Consumer Confidence Report

pathways.title: Roads, bridges and transit
pathways.question: Why is the repair on my street taking so long?
also_answers: Who controls funding, maintenance and service decisions?
Why do transit projects cost so much?
Who decides whether my bus or train keeps running?
pathways.short_answer: It depends first on who owns the road. Counties, cities and towns own about three-quarters of public road miles, and state transportation departments own most of the rest. A pothole waits for the local public works budget and crew schedule. Larger work that uses federal aid must be listed in a multi-year program adopted by the regional planning organization and approved by the governor, so it waits for money and its place in line. Federal money is under strain: CBO projects the highway account of the Highway Trust Fund will run out in 2028, and the 2021 infrastructure law covered fiscal years through 2026.
pathways.scope_note: Federal rules govern how federal aid is planned and spent. Each state, county and city sets its own repair priorities and budgets, and regional or local boards decide transit service. One delayed repair can come from a crew schedule, a contract dispute or a funding gap, so a single case cannot show how the whole system performs.

mechanisms.title: The owner of a road or bridge decides when it gets fixed
mechanisms.text: Ownership decides who must make a repair. In 2022, counties owned 43% of the 4.2 million miles of public roads and towns and cities 33%, while state highway agencies owned 19% and federal agencies about 4%, according to the Federal Highway Administration. A pothole on a city street goes to the city's public works department. Damage on a state route goes to the state transportation department's district office. Bridges follow the same pattern; the 2026 National Bridge Inventory rated 41,148 of 624,939 bridges, or 6.6%, in poor condition. Each owner sets its own repair queue within the money it has.

mechanisms.title: Federal aid arrives by formula from a trust fund that runs short
mechanisms.text: Federal money covers a minority of the cost: in 2017 it paid 26% of public highway spending and 23% of transit and rail spending, the Congressional Budget Office reports. Most federal aid flows by formula from the Highway Trust Fund, which fuel taxes support. Those receipts no longer cover payments. CBO's June 2026 baseline shows the highway account collecting $41.6 billion in 2026 while paying out $62.2 billion, with the transit account exhausted in 2027 and the highway account in 2028 unless Congress adds money. The 2021 infrastructure law authorized these programs through fiscal 2026, which ended September 30, 2026; carrying them past that date takes a new authorization or a short-term extension.

mechanisms.title: Federally funded projects wait in a multi-year program
mechanisms.text: A project that uses federal highway or transit money must be listed in the Transportation Improvement Program (TIP), a schedule of funded projects covering at least four years. A metropolitan planning organization (MPO), the regional body federal law requires for every urbanized area of more than 50,000 people, adopts the TIP. The governor approves it before it joins the statewide program. The MPO must give the public a reasonable chance to comment. A repair left out of one cycle waits for an amendment or the next update, and it competes with new projects for the same formula money.

mechanisms.title: Committed money takes years to reach construction
mechanisms.text: Money is obligated, meaning legally committed to a project, long before contractors are paid. By July 31, 2026, the Department of Transportation had obligated 75.7% of the $545.7 billion it administers under the 2021 law and paid out 46.6%. Design, environmental review, land purchases, utility relocation and bidding all sit between the commitment and the work. Meanwhile, state and local governments carry the daily repair load: they put 62% of their 2023 transportation and water infrastructure spending into operation and maintenance, CBO reports.

mechanisms.title: Project choices and contracts drive construction costs
mechanisms.text: What a project costs depends on decisions by the public agency and its contractors. The Transit Costs Project at New York University compared rail projects in 59 countries and ranked the United States sixth most expensive. In its New York case study, the researchers attribute higher costs to oversized stations, staffing levels, procurement that pushed risk onto contractors, and heavy reliance on consultants. A higher cost per mile means a fixed budget buys less repair and less new service. The study's estimates come from a small number of detailed cases.

mechanisms.title: Transit service depends on operating money that pandemic aid propped up
mechanisms.text: Transit boards set routes and frequency, and their budgets depend on fares, state and local taxes and federal aid. During the pandemic, Congress sent transit agencies $25 billion through the CARES Act in 2020 and $30.5 billion through the American Rescue Plan in 2021, with part of it aimed at day-to-day operating costs. As that money is spent, boards must replace it with other revenue or cut service. The federal transit account, which pays for capital grants, faces its own projected shortfall in 2027.

pathways.household_effects: People feel these decisions as rough pavement, detours that last for seasons, bridges posted for lighter loads and buses that come less often. Rural residents depend heavily on county roads and bridges, while many city residents depend on transit schedules. Reporting a problem through a city's 311 system creates a record and, in many cities, a tracking number; the work order then joins the department's queue. Larger repairs can take years because they move through budgets, regional programs and contracts before crews arrive, and a household has no single office to call for all of it.

sub_issues.title: Bridges rated poor
sub_issues.text: About 1 in 15 highway bridges was rated poor in 2026. A poor rating means a major part, such as the deck or supports, needs repair. Owners can post lower weight limits or close a bridge after inspection. Replacing one bridge can take years of design and funding. The American Society of Civil Engineers, whose members design and build infrastructure, graded the nation's bridges C and its roads D+ in 2025.

sub_issues.title: The federal funding deadline
sub_issues.text: The 2021 law authorized highway and transit programs for fiscal years 2022 to 2026. In May 2026 the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee approved H.R. 8870, the BUILD America 250 Act, a five-year bill that adds a new revenue source for the trust fund. The committee vote came before the September 30, 2026 deadline, and the sources cited here do not show later action by the full House or the Senate. States plan their construction seasons around whatever authority is in force.

sub_issues.title: Why construction costs are high
sub_issues.text: Comparisons of rail projects across countries point to choices U.S. agencies control: station size, design standards, staffing, how contracts assign risk, and how much design work goes to consultants. The Transit Costs Project recommends building in-house engineering staff, standardizing station designs and keeping more risk in the public sector. These are lessons from case studies, and no controlled test shows how much each change saves.

sub_issues.title: Transit budgets after pandemic aid
sub_issues.text: Pandemic relief helped transit agencies keep running through 2020 and 2021, and some of it paid day-to-day operating costs. Agencies that used relief for operations now need state or local money, fare changes or service cuts to balance budgets. The decision sits with each transit board and the state legislature or local governments that fund it. The federal transit account cannot fill the gap because it mainly pays for capital projects and faces its own shortfall.

sub_issues.title: Reporting a repair through 311
sub_issues.text: Many cities run a 311 line, app or website for non-emergency problems such as potholes and dark streetlights. In Boston, each online request gets a tracking number and is routed to the responsible team. Towns without 311 take reports through the public works or highway department. Routine repairs come from the local operating budget, while larger reconstruction goes into the capital plan.
