pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress writes the surface transportation law, including the funding formulas, the federal fuel taxes and any new trust fund revenue; the BUILD America 250 Act is the House committee's current vehicle. The U.S. Department of Transportation writes the planning and program regulations that MPOs and states follow. State legislatures set state fuel taxes, transportation budgets and transit funding, and in some states authorize regional transit taxes. MPO boards decide which projects enter the regional program. City councils, town meetings and county boards adopt local maintenance budgets and capital plans. Transit boards change service and fares after public hearings.

responses.name: Pass multi-year federal funding with new trust fund revenue
responses.what_it_does: Congress enacts a five-year surface transportation law that sets formula amounts for each year and adds revenue to the Highway Trust Fund, so states and transit agencies know what they can commit to. The House committee's BUILD America 250 Act follows this approach. Options CBO lists for revenue include raising existing fuel taxes and transferring general revenue; new fees on vehicles that use little or no fuel are another route.
responses.requires: The bill needs passage by both chambers and the president's signature. Congress must choose revenue that covers projected shortfalls of $11.9 billion in 2028, rising to $221.4 billion by 2036. USDOT then issues guidance and apportionments so states can obligate funds before construction seasons.
responses.evidence: CBO documents the shortfall. Reform profile R-36: Sustain public research and infrastructure investment records evidence that sustained public investment raises productivity over time, and records delivery and durability as less established. No study in the sources separates the effect of multi-year certainty from the effect of the dollar amount on how fast individual repairs happen.
responses.tradeoffs: Higher fuel taxes or fees raise costs for drivers, most for those who drive long distances. General fund transfers add to federal deficits and weaken the link between road users and road costs.

responses.name: Put repair ahead of expansion in state and regional programs
responses.what_it_does: State transportation departments and MPOs reserve a larger share of formula money for keeping existing pavement and bridges in good condition before funding new capacity. Projects are ranked using inspection data such as the National Bridge Inventory and pavement ratings, and the TIP shows how much goes to repair. Local governments can adopt the same rule in their capital plans.
responses.requires: The MPO board and the state transportation department must adopt the priority in their programs, or the legislature can set it in state law. Agencies need current condition data, asset management staff and a yearly public report on how funds are divided between repair and expansion.
responses.evidence: Evidence on the problem: 6.6% of bridges were rated poor in 2026. The sources cited include no outcome evaluation of repair-first rules; Issue record I142 notes that maintenance-first plans have engineering support and few outcome studies.
responses.tradeoffs: Growing regions can face more congestion if new capacity waits. Rural and urban areas compete over which repairs rank first.

responses.name: Build in-house engineering and change how contracts share risk
responses.what_it_does: Transit and highway agencies hire permanent engineers and project managers to design and oversee work, and rely less on consultants. They standardize station and bridge designs, use itemized contracts with public cost data, give technical merit at least half the weight in contract awards, and keep more construction risk in public hands so bidders add smaller contingencies to their prices.
responses.requires: Agencies need budget authority to hire and pay technical staff at competitive salaries, which governors, legislatures and transit boards control. States that require lowest-bid awards must change procurement law. Leadership has to stay long enough to build the team, often across several election cycles.
responses.evidence: The Transit Costs Project's case studies attribute large cost differences to these practices, comparing U.S. projects with lower-cost projects in Italy, Sweden and Turkey. The evidence is comparative and case-based, with no controlled test, and Issue record I061 rates the procurement problem plausible with no evaluated remedy.
responses.tradeoffs: Agencies take on more risk and staff costs, and a poorly managed in-house team can raise costs. Consulting and construction firms lose work.

responses.name: Give transit agencies stable operating revenue
responses.what_it_does: A state or regional government dedicates a tax or fee to transit operations, or the state budget commits multi-year operating support, so service does not depend on temporary federal aid. Transit boards can then plan schedules, hiring and maintenance for several years at a time. Riders get advance notice of service levels, and the agency avoids repeated rounds of proposed cuts and reversals.
responses.requires: The revenue needs a state law or, where state law allows, a regional ballot measure or local ordinance. Lawmakers usually attach accountability terms such as published service targets. The transit board must then show it can deliver the promised service with the money.
responses.evidence: FTA's records show Congress sent $55.5 billion through two pandemic laws, part of it to cover operating costs at agencies in 18 states. That documents the dependence on temporary aid. These records do not show whether dedicated operating revenue improves ridership or reliability.
responses.tradeoffs: New taxes fall on residents who may rarely ride transit. Guaranteed money can reduce pressure on agencies to control costs.

responses.name: Publish the repair queue and project status
responses.what_it_does: Cities publish 311 requests with open dates, closing dates and the department responsible, and states and MPOs post the status of each TIP project, including obligated and spent amounts. Residents can then see where their request stands and which stage is holding up a larger project. Councils and MPO boards can use the same data to question departments at budget time.
responses.requires: Public works departments need data systems and staff time to keep records current and to close requests promptly. A city ordinance or state policy has to require publication, and departments must agree on consistent definitions of when a request or project counts as complete.
responses.evidence: Boston's 311 system already issues tracking numbers, and USDOT publishes obligation and outlay totals for 2021 law funds. Issue record I148 rates publishing decision calendars and explanations as a hypothesis with no causal evaluation, so effects on repair speed are untested.
responses.tradeoffs: Publishing costs staff time. If crews follow the complaint queue, neighborhoods where residents report more often can receive faster service than places with equal need.

distribution.difference: Counties own 43% of public road miles, including many rural roads and bridges. A county highway department's budget and crew size therefore decide how quickly much of the rural network is repaired, and federal aid reaches those roads only through state and regional programs.

distribution.group: People who rely on buses and trains
distribution.difference: Riders without another way to travel depend on operating budgets that pandemic aid propped up. When that aid ends, transit boards cut service or raise fares unless states or localities replace the money.

Towns, townships and municipalities own a third of public road miles. A town without engineering staff has a harder time preparing a project for federal aid, the gap described in I165: Small local governments lack professional capacity, so more repairs fall to the local budget.

pathways.title: Public schools
pathways.question: Why does my child's school have less than schools in other districts?
also_answers: Which decisions belong to the school board, the state or the federal government?
Does more school funding improve results?
What do vouchers, savings accounts and tax-credit scholarships change?
When is the school board elected, and does the timing matter?
pathways.short_answer: Most school money comes from local property taxes and state aid. In 2020-21, local sources supplied 44% of public school revenue and states 46%, and 83% of the local share came from property taxes. A district with more taxable property can raise more per student at the same tax rate. The state aid formula, written by the legislature, decides how much of that gap is closed, and state courts have ordered changes when formulas fall short of state constitutions. Studies comparing students before and after state finance reforms estimate that sustained increases raised schooling and adult earnings, most for children from low-income families.
pathways.scope_note: Each state writes its own funding formula, standards and choice programs, so national figures hide large differences between states and between districts in one state. Federal law sets testing and civil rights requirements and adds money for specific groups of students. One school's budget or test scores cannot show whether a funding rule works across a state.

mechanisms.title: Local property wealth sets the starting point
mechanisms.text: School districts raise their local share mainly through property taxes, which supplied 36% of all public school revenue nationally in 2020-21, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. A district with valuable homes and businesses collects more per student at a given tax rate than a district with modest property. District boundaries, drawn under state law, decide which tax base pays for which students. The result shows up in budgets: total spending per student ranged from $11,686 in Idaho to $37,835 in the District of Columbia that year, and gaps between districts within a state can be large too.

mechanisms.title: State aid formulas decide how much of the gap closes
mechanisms.text: State legislatures write the aid formula that supplies 46% of school revenue. A formula can send more per student to districts with less property wealth or more students in poverty, learning English or with disabilities. When residents sue, state courts decide whether funding meets the state constitution's education clause, and some rulings have forced legislatures to rewrite formulas. A study of reforms after 1990 estimated immediate spending increases in low-income districts and test score gains that grew over the following years. A meta-analysis of such studies estimated that $1,000 more per student for four years raised graduation rates by about 2 percentage points.

mechanisms.title: Federal law adds targeted money and testing rules
mechanisms.text: The federal government supplied 11% of school revenue in 2020-21, mostly tied to specific purposes such as schools with many low-income students and special education. In return, federal law requires each state to set academic standards and test reading and math every year in grades 3 to 8 and once in high school. The Department of Education administers these programs. A March 2025 executive order directed the Secretary to take steps toward closing the Department as far as the law permits, and the Department announced cutting its staff from 4,133 to about 2,183. The Supreme Court let the layoffs proceed in July 2025 while litigation continued.

mechanisms.title: Staff pay and vacancies shape what money buys
mechanisms.text: School money turns mostly into teachers and aides, so the local supply of teachers shapes what added money can buy. The average base salary for full-time public school teachers was $61,600 in 2020-21, not measurably different from 2011-12 after inflation. In October 2022, 44% of public schools reported at least one vacant teaching position. A district that cannot fill a position covers it with substitutes, larger classes or fewer course offerings. School boards negotiate pay with teachers' unions where state law allows collective bargaining, within the budget their revenue supports.

mechanisms.title: Falling enrollment and slow learning recovery strain budgets
mechanisms.text: The pandemic cut public school enrollment by about 1.4 million students, from 50.8 million in fall 2019 to 49.4 million in fall 2020, and federal projections show a further 5% decline by 2031. Formulas that pay per student shrink revenue as enrollment drops, while buildings and many staff costs stay fixed. Learning has recovered unevenly: in 2024, fourth-grade reading was 5 points below 2019, and fourth-grade math gains went to middle and higher performers while the lowest performers showed no gain over 2022.

mechanisms.title: Public money is opening private school options
mechanisms.text: Legislatures in several states now fund education savings accounts, which let money that would follow a student in public school pay for private tuition or other approved costs. Arizona's program enrolled 108,416 students in October 2026. A 2025 federal law adds a tax credit of up to $1,700 for donations to scholarship organizations starting in 2027, in states that opt in; 30 states had done so by September 2026. Studies disagree on effects. A lottery study found Louisiana voucher users lost ground in math, and a Florida study found an association between a scholarship program's growth and gains for nearby public school students.

pathways.household_effects: Families see these decisions as class sizes, course offerings, support staff for students with disabilities, the condition of buildings and how long a teaching job stays vacant. A district with little property wealth leans on state aid, so a change in the state formula reaches its classrooms quickly. Families in districts losing students can face consolidated classes or closed buildings as the district adjusts. Homeowners pay for schools through property tax bills, renters indirectly through rent. In states with savings accounts or scholarships, some families gain a private option, and the public district plans around the students and funding that leave.

sub_issues.title: Does more money improve results?
sub_issues.text: Several quasi-experimental studies estimate that sustained increases in per-pupil spending raised test scores, graduation and adult earnings, with the largest effects for children from low-income families. A meta-analysis estimated improvements in more than 90% of simulated cases, with capital spending effects about half as large and slower to appear. A review by other economists argues the link is inconsistent and that how districts spend the money matters most.

sub_issues.title: Who elects the school board, and when
sub_issues.text: In most districts an elected board adopts the budget and hires the superintendent; in some cities a mayor or other officials appoint the board. Where board elections fall in spring or odd years, they take place apart from the November contests most voters attend. Research on California cities found on-cycle elections associated with roughly double the turnout and a more representative electorate. Issue record X03: Off-cycle elections draw fewer and different voters links off-cycle timing to the influence of organized groups; for school policy that link is less established than the turnout effect.

sub_issues.title: Changes at the federal Department of Education
sub_issues.text: Since March 2025 the Department has operated under an executive order to move toward its closure as far as law allows, and it announced cutting staff by about half. Congress created the Department and the main grant programs by statute, so funding formulas for Title I and special education continue unless Congress changes them. Court challenges to the layoffs continued after the Supreme Court's July 2025 stay.

sub_issues.title: Teacher pay and vacancies
sub_issues.text: Teacher base pay was flat after inflation for about a decade through 2020-21, and in fall 2022 more than two in five public schools had at least one teaching vacancy. Pay is set in district budgets and, in many states, through bargaining with teachers' unions. State licensing rules decide who can fill a vacancy. A review of the research finds direct tests of salary incentives have not clearly shown gains in the United States.

sub_issues.title: Learning recovery after the pandemic
sub_issues.text: National tests in 2024 showed fourth-grade reading still below 2022 and 2019 levels at most points in the score range. Fourth-grade math improved over 2022 for average and higher performers, but students at the 10th and 25th percentiles showed no significant gain. Recovery plans, such as tutoring or extended learning time, are chosen by districts and states, and NAEP cannot show which local choices worked.

sub_issues.title: Vouchers, savings accounts and tax-credit scholarships
sub_issues.text: These programs use public money or tax credits to pay for private schooling. Education savings accounts deposit funds a family can spend on approved costs; vouchers pay tuition directly; tax-credit scholarships are funded by donors who receive a credit. Evidence is contested: a Louisiana lottery study found math losses for users, and a Florida study found an association between program growth and gains for nearby public school students. Costs and effects depend on program design and which private schools take part.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: State legislatures hold most of the authority: they write the aid formula, property tax limits, choice programs and the dates of school board elections, through statute. State courts can order changes when funding violates a state constitution. State boards of education set standards and accountability rules by regulation. Congress amends federal education law, sets appropriations, decides whether the Department of Education is restructured, and wrote the 2025 scholarship tax credit; each state chooses whether to take part. The Department writes federal regulations and approves state plans. Local school boards, and voters where levies or budgets go to the ballot, decide local tax requests and budgets. City charters set board election dates in some places.

responses.name: Weight state aid toward students and districts with greater need
responses.what_it_does: The legislature rewrites the aid formula to give each district a base amount per student plus extra weight for students in poverty, learning English or with disabilities, and to offset differences in local property wealth. Districts with less taxable property receive more state aid per student. The formula is phased in over several years and paired with public reporting of how districts spend the added money.
responses.requires: The change needs a state statute and sustained appropriations, sometimes prompted by a court ruling. The state education agency must collect accurate student counts and audit spending. Districts need plans for hiring and programs that put the money into instruction and support.
responses.evidence: Quasi-experimental studies of earlier finance reforms estimate gains in test scores, graduation and adult earnings, largest for low-income children, and a meta-analysis estimated positive effects in over 90% of simulated cases. A review by Handel and Hanushek finds the relationship inconsistent and stresses how money is used. Issue record I137 rates weighted formulas as well-supported.
responses.tradeoffs: Higher state taxes or reduced aid to wealthier districts. Gains depend on districts spending well, and formula disputes can last years in the legislature and courts.

responses.name: Hold school board elections on the November ballot
responses.what_it_does: A state law or local charter moves school board elections from spring or odd-year dates to the November general election in even years. More voters see the board races on a ballot they already use. Studies of city elections suggest the electorate becomes larger and closer to the community's makeup in age, race and partisanship, including residents who rarely attend board meetings. Election offices also run fewer separate elections.
responses.requires: A state statute or local charter amendment, a transition plan that lengthens or shortens one set of terms, and ballot design that keeps local races visible. Election officials must update calendars and candidate filing deadlines. R-06: Hold local elections alongside major November elections describes the same change for all local offices.
responses.evidence: In California cities, on-cycle elections were associated with roughly double the turnout and an electorate more representative by race, age and partisanship. X03: Off-cycle elections draw fewer and different voters also links off-cycle timing to policy outcomes, which is less firmly established for schools. Voters can skip races at the bottom of a long ballot, so the turnout gain for board races can be smaller.
responses.tradeoffs: School races compete with national and state contests for attention, and partisan cues can enter nonpartisan board races. Groups that do well in low-turnout elections lose influence.

responses.name: Raise teacher pay and widen hiring pipelines
responses.what_it_does: Districts and states raise base salaries, add pay for hard-to-staff subjects and schools, and open more routes into teaching, such as paid residencies and alternative certification. The aim is to fill vacancies with qualified teachers and keep experienced ones in the classroom. States can fund raises through the aid formula so low-wealth districts can match the salaries offered by wealthier neighbors.
responses.requires: Raises need appropriations by the legislature or local tax increases, and bargaining agreements where state law provides for them. New hiring routes need licensing rule changes by the state board or legislature. Districts must track vacancies and retention to see whether the changes work.
responses.evidence: Evidence on the problem: base pay was flat after inflation through 2020-21, and 44% of schools had a vacancy in fall 2022. Evidence on remedies is mixed: the Handel and Hanushek review reports that direct tests of teacher salary incentives have not clearly shown gains in U.S. schools, and the sources cited include no evaluation of new hiring routes.
responses.tradeoffs: Raises compete with class size and programs for the same budget. Faster licensing routes can admit less-prepared teachers if training and support are weak.

responses.name: Expand private school choice with savings accounts and tax-credit scholarships
responses.what_it_does: States fund education savings accounts or vouchers that families can spend on private tuition and other approved costs, or opt into the federal scholarship tax credit so donors who fund scholarship organizations receive up to $1,700 in credits from 2027. Families gain options outside their assigned school. Public districts lose the students who leave and, in many formulas, the state aid attached to them.
responses.requires: A state statute and appropriation for savings accounts or vouchers; for the federal credit, a state election to participate and a list of qualifying scholarship organizations. An agency must manage accounts, approve expenses and audit spending. Treasury regulations for the federal credit were still pending as of October 15, 2026.
responses.evidence: Findings conflict. A lottery study of Louisiana's voucher program found math scores fell by 0.4 standard deviations for users in the first year. A Florida study found an association between that state's scholarship program growth and gains for public school students near more private options. Evidence on universal savings accounts, the newest model, is thin, and Arizona's program page reports enrollment without results.
responses.tradeoffs: Costs fall on state budgets or federal revenue, and spending on families already paying private tuition raises costs without moving students. Each state decides what testing and reporting to require of participating private schools, which limits how much the public can learn about results.

responses.name: Settle the federal education role in statute
responses.what_it_does: Congress passes a law that either transfers named Department of Education programs to other agencies or confirms where they stay, with staffing and funding to run them. States and districts would then know which agency handles Title I, special education grants and civil rights complaints, and on what schedule, without depending on executive actions that courts can later reverse or uphold.
responses.requires: The bill must move through the House Education and Workforce Committee and the Senate HELP Committee, pass both chambers and receive the president's signature. Appropriations must follow each program, and a transition plan must keep grant payments to states and districts on time.
responses.evidence: The current changes rest on an executive order, a reduction in force and a Supreme Court stay pending appeal, so the legal footing can shift. No evaluation exists of how a statutory restructuring would affect grant delivery or student outcomes.
responses.tradeoffs: Any transfer can disrupt payments and expertise during the move. Keeping the current structure preserves established offices but leaves the dispute over its scope unresolved.

distribution.difference: Studies of finance reforms estimated the largest gains in schooling and adult earnings for children from low-income families when spending rose. Formulas that add weight for poverty send more of any new state money to the districts they attend.

distribution.group: Students in districts with little taxable property
distribution.difference: Property taxes supply 36% of school revenue nationally, so districts with modest property raise less per student at the same tax rate. Their resources depend on how much the state formula makes up.

In 2024, fourth graders at the 10th and 25th percentiles showed no significant math gain over 2022, while middle and higher performers improved. Reading fell at every reported percentile except the 90th.

distribution.group: Families in states with savings accounts or the federal credit
distribution.difference: In Arizona, 108,416 students used savings accounts in October 2026, and 30 states opted into the federal credit for 2027. Families in other states have no access to these programs, and effects on users and on public schools are contested.

check.explanation: Property taxes supplied 83% of local school revenue in 2020-21, according to NCES. That is why districts with more taxable property can raise more per student, and why state aid formulas matter.

pathways.title: Voting and public influence
pathways.question: Which election decides who represents me, and how can I influence the people who decide?
also_answers: Which election decides the office?
How can voters influence the people making these decisions?
Who draws my district lines?
What do the election-rule measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot do?
pathways.short_answer: The election that decides an office is the one whose outcome is still in doubt. In a district one party wins reliably, that is the party primary, a nominating election often held months before November with far fewer voters. Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026. Unite America, an advocacy group, counts 383 as effectively decided in primaries, by 9.4% of eligible voters. State legislatures, or commissions in some states, draw the districts that make seats safe. Between elections, randomized experiments in two state legislatures found that constituent calls and emails about a specific bill changed legislators' votes.
pathways.scope_note: Primary rules, district maps and local election dates are set state by state, so the national counts here describe a pattern and each state's rules decide your own ballot. Counts of seats decided in primaries depend on how the source defines a safe seat. One district's turnout shows who chose a representative; it cannot show how that person responds to you.

mechanisms.title: State legislatures and commissions draw the district lines
mechanisms.text: Each state redraws its U.S. House and legislative districts after every census, and some redraw in between. In most states the legislature draws the congressional map; ten states give a commission primary responsibility. In 2019 the U.S. Supreme Court held in Rucho v. Common Cause that federal courts cannot decide claims of partisan map-drawing, which leaves those disputes to state courts, state law and Congress. No federal law bars a mid-decade redraw. In 2025 and 2026, new congressional maps came from the legislatures of Texas, North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana, from Ohio's commission, from California voters and from a Utah court. Where one party's voters are concentrated in cities, lines can produce lopsided seats even without that aim.

mechanisms.title: In a safe seat, the dominant party's primary picks the winner
mechanisms.text: A safe seat is one where a single party wins by a wide margin election after election. There the November result is predictable, and the primary, where each party chooses its nominee, becomes the deciding contest (link L08, from variable C1 to variable C2). How many seats fit depends on the definition. Unite America, an advocacy group, began with Cook Political Report ratings, which rated 398 of 435 House seats safe in 2026. It then removed seats with a same-party November contest (nine in California) and Louisiana's six all-candidate House races. Its count is 383 seats (88%), decided by 22.7 million primary voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. In 147 of those districts the winner had no opponent in the dominant party's primary.

mechanisms.title: Fewer and different voters choose in primaries and city elections
mechanisms.text: Turnout falls when an election is limited to one party's voters or held apart from a November general election. Ballots cast in the 2022 midterm primaries equaled 21.3% of eligible voters, by the Bipartisan Policy Center's count. In that November's House elections, 45.1% of eligible voters took part, according to a Pew Research Center tally of official returns. City elections held on their own dates, called off-cycle elections, often draw fewer still: a 2016 Portland State University study found mayoral turnout under 20% of eligible citizens in 15 of the 30 largest cities. A study of California cities found that moving local elections onto the November ballot makes the electorate considerably more representative by race, age and party.

mechanisms.title: A small deciding electorate weakens the threat of losing in November
mechanisms.text: Electoral pressure means the credible chance that an officeholder could lose (variable C3). The sanction is the defeat or forced retirement itself (variable C5). Loop B4, the ballot-box loop, runs from poor performance through both steps to better performance, and either step can fail. General-election voters apply pressure where seats are competitive. A study of close U.S. House primaries from 1980 to 2010 found that nominating the more extreme candidate cut the party's November vote share by about 9 to 13 percentage points. In safe districts that penalty largely disappeared. Where the primary decides the seat, an incumbent's main electoral risk comes from the small group who vote in it (link L25).

mechanisms.title: Constituent contact changes some votes on specific bills
mechanisms.text: Between elections, officeholders hear from residents through calls, emails, letters, meetings, public comment and testimony. Two randomized field experiments in state legislatures found that this contact can change votes. In New Hampshire, a grassroots email campaign had a substantial influence on House members' votes on tobacco-control legislation. In Michigan, constituent phone calls raised legislators' support for an anti-bullying bill by about 12 percentage points. Both tested a single issue with an organized campaign behind the contact. The people who show up also differ from the public: speakers at local planning and zoning meetings were older, more often homeowners and far more opposed to new housing than residents generally. Federal agencies must consider the relevant matter in rule comments and respond to significant ones.

mechanisms.title: Officeholders and courts set the rules for the next election
mechanisms.text: Legislators elected under today's rules write the next ones: district maps, primary types, local election dates and limits on local voting methods. Nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting, a method where voters rank candidates, in some or all elections; Indiana and Ohio added bans in 2026. Courts set the outer limits. In Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is violated only when evidence supports a strong inference that a state intentionally drew districts to give minority voters less opportunity. Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana enacted new congressional maps the next month. Voters can act directly where the state constitution provides an initiative, a petition that places a proposed law or amendment on the ballot; NCSL counts 24 such states, including Mississippi, whose process was found void.

pathways.household_effects: Readers see this mechanism on their own ballot. Many November ballots list one candidate for a legislative seat, and for those seats the deciding vote came in a primary months earlier or never happened. Access to the deciding contest also differs. In 2022, about 14% of voters with disabilities reported difficulty voting, compared with about 4% of other voters. In 2024, 82.5% of citizens with an advanced degree voted, against 52.5% of high school graduates. Residents of counties without a local news source have fewer ways to learn what their officials did.

sub_issues.title: Find the election that decides each office
sub_issues.text: Start with your sample ballot, then check certified results from the last two elections for each office. If the November winner ran unopposed or won by a wide margin, the primary decided the seat; in Massachusetts in 2026, 60% of state House and Senate races have one name on the November ballot. Nine states hold a primary runoff when no candidate reaches a set share, usually a majority. Many city and school elections fall on separate dates, and California bars that practice where it sharply cuts turnout.

sub_issues.title: Closed, open and all-party primaries
sub_issues.text: Each state decides who may vote in a party primary. The National Conference of State Legislatures counts 8 states with closed primaries limited to party members, 9 where each party decides whether to admit unaffiliated voters, and 28 with some form of open or unaffiliated access. California and Washington send the top two finishers of one all-candidate primary to November. In Alaska, the four leading finishers advance and November ballots are ranked. Massachusetts lets unenrolled voters (those not registered in a party) choose a party ballot and bars party members from crossing over.

sub_issues.title: Who draws districts, and the 2025 to 2026 redraws
sub_issues.text: By late September 2026, eight states had new congressional maps in force for November: maps passed by the legislatures of Texas, North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana, Ohio's commission map, California's voter-approved map and a Utah court's map. Missouri's 2025 map is suspended until voters decide Proposition A, and Virginia's supreme court struck down the constitutional amendment its new map depended on. Alabama returned to its 2023 map after a U.S. Supreme Court stay. Most of these maps face pending lawsuits.

sub_issues.title: Massachusetts Question 3 (November 3, 2026)
sub_issues.text: Question 3, a law proposed by initiative petition, would replace party primaries for statewide, congressional, legislative and county offices with one primary open to all voters and candidates. The top two finishers would advance to November regardless of party. Presidential and city elections would not change. It would take effect January 1, 2028. The Coalition for Healthy Democracy sponsors it, with support from State Auditor Diana DiZoglio. Voter Rights MA leads the opposition, joined by the state Democratic and Republican parties and several unions. The Atlas takes no position on Question 3. Disclosure: Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead.

sub_issues.title: Alaska Ballot Measure 2 (November 3, 2026)
sub_issues.text: Ballot Measure 2 would repeal the top-four open primary and ranked-choice general election that Alaska voters adopted in 2020, restoring party primaries and single-choice general elections. It would also repeal campaign finance limits and disclosure rules from the 2020 law, including disclosure of the true source of donations. Repeal Now, the sponsoring campaign, backs it. Opposition is organized as No on 2, registered as Protect Alaska's Elections. A similar repeal failed in 2024 by 743 votes out of 321,203 after a December 2024 recount. The Alaska Supreme Court upheld the ballot summary with one added sentence. The Atlas takes no position on Ballot Measure 2.

sub_issues.title: Missouri Proposition A (November 3, 2026)
sub_issues.text: Proposition A is a referendum, a statewide vote on a law the legislature already passed: here, the congressional map the General Assembly adopted in a 2025 special session. Voting yes approves that map. If the no side wins, the districts enacted in 2022 stay in place. The 2025 map divides Kansas City among three districts. Governor Mike Kehoe, a Republican, supports the map. People Not Politicians, which gathered the referendum signatures, opposes it. Under a September 25, 2026 U.S. Supreme Court order, Missouri's 2026 House elections use the 2022 map.

sub_issues.title: Reaching the people who decide
sub_issues.text: Find your U.S. representative by ZIP code at house.gov and your senators at senate.gov; the Capitol switchboard is (202) 224-3121. USA.gov links every state legislature's website, where state legislators are listed, and directories for mayors and county executives. City councils and county commissions post agendas through the clerk's office. The experiments that found effects on votes involved constituents writing or calling about a named bill before the vote.

sub_issues.title: Local news and accountability
sub_issues.text: Local reporting is how many voters learn what officials did. Where newspaper markets matched congressional districts poorly, coverage fell, fewer voters could recall their representative, and those members testified at fewer hearings and their areas received less federal spending, in a study that used redistricting to compare otherwise similar places. As newspapers cut staff, their coverage of city halls, school boards and county commissions shrank. Medill's 2025 State of Local News report counted 213 counties with no local news source and about 50 million people with limited or no access to local news.

decision_makers.controls: Enacts the statutes that set primary type, election calendars, registration rules and local election dates; draws congressional and legislative maps in most states; decides whether cities may use methods such as ranked-choice voting; refers constitutional amendments to voters.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your own state representative and state senator through the legislature's website (USA.gov links every state legislature); testify or submit written comment at the elections committee hearing on a bill.

decision_makers.who: Redistricting commission (in states that have one)
decision_makers.controls: Adopts congressional maps in the ten states where a commission has primary responsibility (Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Virginia, Washington); advises the legislature or acts as a backup in several others.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public hearings and written comment periods the commission holds on draft maps during redistricting.

decision_makers.controls: Approve or reject citizen initiatives in the 23 states with a working initiative process and the District of Columbia, popular referenda on new laws in 23 states, and constitutional amendments the legislature refers to them in every state.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Read the official voter guide from the secretary of state or state election office; petitions circulate for signatures before a measure qualifies.

decision_makers.controls: Can set rules for U.S. House and Senate elections under the Constitution's Elections Clause, including district requirements; has not enacted limits on mid-decade redistricting.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Your representative through the ZIP code lookup at house.gov; your two senators through senate.gov or the Capitol switchboard, (202) 224-3121.

decision_makers.who: Federal courts, including the U.S. Supreme Court
decision_makers.controls: Decide whether maps and election rules meet the U.S. Constitution and the Voting Rights Act; since Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) they do not review partisan map-drawing, and since Louisiana v. Callais (2026) Section 2 districting claims require evidence supporting a strong inference of intentional discrimination.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Through lawsuits filed by voters or organizations with legal counsel; opinions and orders are public at supremecourt.gov and on lower-court websites.

decision_makers.controls: Apply state constitutions to district maps, ballot measure language and election procedures, as the Missouri, Virginia and Alaska supreme courts did in 2026.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Through lawsuits filed by voters or organizations with legal counsel; opinions are public on the state judiciary's website.

decision_makers.who: Secretary of state or state election office
decision_makers.controls: Certifies candidates and ballot measures, publishes official measure summaries and voter guides in many states, and certifies statewide results. It administers rules the legislature and voters set.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: The state election office linked from vote.gov or the U.S. Election Assistance Commission's state directory.

decision_makers.who: County or municipal election office, or city or town clerk
decision_makers.controls: Runs voter registration, polling places and mail ballots for local residents, posts sample ballots and reports local results.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: The local election office listed in the U.S. Election Assistance Commission's state-by-state directory, or the city or town clerk.

decision_makers.controls: In the nine partially closed primary states, each party decides whether unaffiliated voters may vote in its primary.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: The state party committee's published meeting schedule and rules.

decision_makers.controls: Passes local ordinances and budgets; where state law and the local charter allow, proposes charter changes to local election dates or voting methods.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public comment at a regular meeting; agendas are posted by the city, town or county clerk; members are listed on the local government's website.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: State legislatures hold most of this authority. By statute they set primary types, election calendars and registration rules and, in most states, draw district maps; by referral they place constitutional amendments before voters. In the 23 states with a working initiative process, and in the District of Columbia, residents can bypass the legislature, the route that put Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska Ballot Measure 2 on the ballot. In 23 states a popular referendum lets voters approve or reject a new law, as Missouri voters will do with Proposition A. Congress can regulate U.S. House and Senate elections under the Elections Clause. Federal courts enforce the Constitution and the Voting Rights Act but have not reviewed partisan map-drawing since Rucho v. Common Cause (2019); state courts apply state constitutions. Cities and counties can change their own election dates or methods only where state law allows, and 19 states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections.

responses.name: One primary open to all voters and candidates
responses.what_it_does: All candidates for an office run in a single primary, and every registered voter may take part regardless of party. California, Washington and the Massachusetts proposal advance the top two finishers to November; Alaska advances four and uses a ranked-choice general election. The design aims to make the November election, with its larger electorate, the deciding contest for more seats, so incumbents in one-party districts answer to voters beyond their own party's primary electorate.
responses.requires: A state statute or constitutional change, passed by the legislature or by initiative where the state allows it. Election officials need new ballot layouts, candidate filing rules and voter education; a ranked general election also needs certified counting software. Massachusetts would have about two years to prepare, since Question 3 takes effect January 1, 2028.
responses.evidence: Effects on participation and on legislators' positions point in different directions. The Bipartisan Policy Center estimated that states switching to top-two or top-four primaries saw primary turnout rise about 3 percentage points. A study of California and Washington found an inconsistent moderating effect after top-two primaries: part of California's change appeared to come from new commission-drawn districts and term-limit changes, and Washington showed little effect.
responses.tradeoffs: Parties lose control over who carries their label in November. Some voters face a general election with two candidates from one party and none from their own. The official argument against Massachusetts Question 3 contends that third-party and independent candidates would be shut out of the general election.

responses.name: Independent redistricting commissions
responses.what_it_does: A commission whose members are not sitting legislators draws congressional and legislative districts under written criteria, after public hearings on draft maps. Ten states give a commission primary responsibility for congressional maps, and several more use advisory or backup commissions. The design separates the people who draw a district from the people who run in it, which reduces maps drawn to protect one party's seats.
responses.requires: A state constitutional amendment, by legislative referral or initiative, setting how members are chosen, the map criteria, deadlines and court review. The commission needs staff, mapping data and money to defend its maps in court. Without constitutional protection, a later ballot measure or legislature can set its maps aside, as California's Proposition 50 did for 2026.
responses.evidence: In the 2021 to 2022 redistricting cycle, nonpartisan commissions produced maps that were less biased toward either party and more competitive than maps drawn by party-controlled legislatures, according to a study of that cycle's maps. The study is descriptive and covers one cycle. It also found that Democratic voters' concentration in cities still gave Republicans an advantage in converting votes to seats, which a commission does not remove.
responses.tradeoffs: A state that adopts a commission alone gives up a map-drawing tool that legislatures in other states still use, which matters for the national House balance. Commissions can produce maps the legislative majority dislikes, which invites override attempts.

responses.name: Hold local elections on the November ballot
responses.what_it_does: City council, mayoral and school board elections take place on the same date as state and federal November elections. People who already come out to vote for governor or president then also choose the council and board members who decide zoning, local budgets and school policy. Local officials then answer to a larger electorate that more closely matches the community by age and race.
responses.requires: A state statute or a city charter amendment, depending on home-rule law. California's 2015 law, SB 415, bars a city from holding off-cycle elections when its turnout falls at least 25% below its average in the previous four statewide general elections. Officeholders' terms may need a one-time extension or reduction during the switch.
responses.evidence: Earlier research found that holding local elections in November roughly doubles turnout, and a study of California cities found that it makes local electorates considerably more representative by race, age and party, with the largest change in presidential years. Evidence that the switch changes local policy decisions is thinner than the evidence on who votes.
responses.tradeoffs: Longer ballots, and local races compete with national campaigns for attention, so some voters leave local contests blank. Groups that organize well in low-turnout elections lose an advantage.

responses.name: Automatic voter registration
responses.what_it_does: When an eligible person deals with a state agency, usually the motor vehicle office, the state registers that person to vote or updates the address on file unless the person opts out. More eligible residents are on the rolls before a primary or local election, which removes one step between a resident and the deciding contest. People still choose whether to vote, and those who opt out stay off the rolls.
responses.requires: A state statute, data links between agencies and election offices, checks of eligibility and identity, and a way for people to correct errors. Twenty-four states and the District of Columbia use it, by the National Conference of State Legislatures' count. Congress could set a national floor for federal elections.
responses.evidence: A Brennan Center for Justice analysis that matched early-adopting jurisdictions with similar ones that had not adopted estimated registration gains ranging from 9% to 94%. The study measured registration. A larger voter roll does not by itself raise turnout in a primary or a city election.
responses.tradeoffs: Errors in agency records can add wrong addresses or ineligible names unless verification works. Some residents object to data sharing between agencies.

responses.name: Fund independent local reporting
responses.what_it_does: A public or philanthropic fund, governed apart from elected officials, pays for reporters who cover city councils, school boards, county commissions and local courts. Grants are made by formula or competition under rules that bar funders from editing coverage. The aim is to restore the information voters use to judge local officials at election time, including in the counties that now have no local news source.
responses.requires: A state appropriation or committed donors, an independent board whose members elected officials cannot remove at will, editorial safeguards written into law or grant terms, and public records of who receives money. Funding has to last several years for newsrooms to hire and keep reporters.
responses.evidence: Evidence about the problem is strong: where districts and newspaper markets matched poorly, voters knew less about their representatives and those members did less for their districts. Evidence about funds as a remedy is missing. Reform profile R-32 records no causal evaluation showing that public local-news funds improve accountability.
responses.tradeoffs: Public money raises concerns about government influence over the press. Funds can go to outlets that do little coverage of government.

distribution.group: Voters not enrolled in a party
distribution.difference: In the 8 closed-primary states, unaffiliated voters cannot vote in any party's primary, and in 9 others each party decides whether to admit them. Where the primary decides the seat, they have no vote in the deciding contest. Massachusetts lets unenrolled voters choose a party ballot.

distribution.group: Younger residents and renters in local decisions
distribution.difference: California city electorates in off-cycle elections were less representative by age and race than on-cycle electorates. Speakers at local planning and zoning meetings were older and more often homeowners than residents generally, and far more opposed to new housing.

In 2022, about 14% of voters with disabilities reported difficulty voting, compared with about 4% of voters without disabilities, in a national survey for the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. Turnout among people with disabilities was 3.6 percentage points lower.

In November 2024, 82.5% of citizens with an advanced degree reported voting, compared with 52.5% of high school graduates, in the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey. The survey covers November general elections only.

distribution.group: Residents of places with little local news
distribution.difference: Where local coverage of a House member was thin, residents were less able to recall or rate that member, in a study of newspaper and district overlap. Medill counted 213 counties with no local news source in 2025.

options: The county's official canvass of votes
check.explanation: When the November result is predictable, the dominant party's primary chooses the eventual winner (link L08, from variable C1 to variable C2). Turnout in that primary is usually far below November turnout, so a small share of residents makes the choice.

pathways.title: Algorithms in daily life
pathways.question: How do algorithms affect the prices I pay, my job, what I see online and the services I get?
also_answers: Can software help landlords or stores charge more?
Do social media feeds change what I believe?
Is AI taking jobs?
Why was my benefit cut off by a computer system?
pathways.short_answer: Companies and public agencies use software to set prices, screen job applicants, rank what you see online and decide benefit renewals, and the effects depend on the data fed in and the rules around it. Rent-pricing software that pooled competitors' private data led to a Justice Department case against RealPage. Large experiments found that changing a feed shifts what people see, with small measured effects on how they feel about the other party. Evidence on AI and jobs is early: one payroll study finds fewer jobs for workers aged 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, while others find no broad effect. Federal agencies, state legislatures and courts set the limits.
pathways.scope_note: Antitrust and consumer protection law is national, but most rules written for algorithms are state or city laws, such as those in New York and Colorado, so protections differ by where you live. Feed experiments and AI job studies cover particular platforms, periods and countries, and one person's experience with an app, a hiring decision or a benefit renewal cannot by itself show a general effect.

mechanisms.title: Pricing software can let competitors pool private data
mechanisms.text: Landlords and retailers use software that recommends prices. Competition law treats software that draws on a seller's own data or public prices differently from software that pools competitors' nonpublic data, since pooling can work like an agreement not to compete. The Justice Department alleged that RealPage's rent software worked this way. A final judgment entered May 19, 2026 bars RealPage from using competing properties' nonpublic data in live recommendations, requires training data at least 12 months old, lets landlords override suggested rents and installs a monitor for three years; the judgment runs seven years, and RealPage admitted no liability. The states' separate claims continue after a September 30, 2026 ruling. New York made it unlawful in October 2025 for software providers to help landlords coordinate rents.

mechanisms.title: Personal data can shape the price one shopper sees
mechanisms.text: Surveillance pricing uses data about a person, such as location, browsing and purchase history, to set or target the price that person sees. In 2024 the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) ordered eight firms that sell pricing and data tools to describe their products and customers. Preliminary findings released in January 2025 reported that these intermediaries worked with at least 250 clients, including grocery stores, and could track signals as fine as cursor movements. The FTC's examples were hypothetical, and two commissioners dissented from releasing the findings. New York requires a seller that uses personal data in algorithmic pricing to show the notice "THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA." The FTC findings did not measure how often shoppers paid different prices.

mechanisms.title: Employers screen and monitor workers with software
mechanisms.text: Employers use software to rank applicants, schedule shifts and track productivity. A 2021 University of California, Berkeley Labor Center review found that U.S. workers generally had no legal right to know what data employers collect about them or to challenge automated decisions. New York City's Local Law 144 requires an annual bias audit of automated hiring tools, a posted summary of the results and notice to candidates. A December 2025 audit by the New York State Comptroller found that the city's enforcement agency received two complaints in two years and found one violation among 32 companies it reviewed. The comptroller's auditors examined the same companies and identified at least 17 potential violations.

mechanisms.title: Employers adopt AI for some tasks, with early and mixed job effects
mechanisms.text: Employers decide which tasks to hand to generative AI. Evidence on what that does to jobs is early and points in different directions. Using records from the largest U.S. payroll software provider, Stanford researchers found a 13% relative decline in employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations after generative AI spread, while older workers in the same occupations held steady. The authors call the pattern consistent with an AI effect, and the data cannot rule out other causes. In Denmark, a study of 11 exposed occupations ruled out effects on earnings or hours larger than 1% through 2024. The Yale Budget Lab found the U.S. mix of occupations changing about 1 percentage point faster than during the internet's spread, with no link between AI exposure and unemployment.

mechanisms.title: Feed ranking changes exposure; measured effects on hostility are small
mechanisms.text: Platforms rank posts with algorithms tuned to goals such as engagement. During the 2020 election, researchers working with Meta switched consenting Facebook and Instagram users to a chronological feed for three months. Those users saw more political posts and more posts from untrustworthy sources, saw less uncivil content on Facebook, and spent less time on the apps; their polarization and political knowledge did not change measurably. A companion experiment with 23,377 users cut exposure to like-minded sources by about one-third and ruled out effects of 0.12 standard deviations or more on eight attitudes. On X in 2023, switching users to the algorithmic feed shifted some policy opinions in a conservative direction, again with no measured change in hostility toward the other party.

mechanisms.title: Government software decides who keeps benefits
mechanisms.text: State agencies run eligibility systems that decide who keeps Medicaid, SNAP and other benefits. Renewal that uses data the state already holds, called ex parte renewal, spares people from returning forms. After the pandemic, states disenrolled more than 25 million people from Medicaid by mid-2024, and 69% of them lost coverage for paperwork or other procedural reasons. Automatic renewal rates ranged from 90% or more in Arizona, North Carolina and Rhode Island to 11% or less in Pennsylvania and Texas. Much of this software sits on old foundations: GAO found the 11 most critical federal legacy systems were 23 to 60 years old. From fiscal 2028, states with SNAP payment error rates of 6% or more must pay part of benefit costs, which raises the stakes of how their systems verify eligibility.

pathways.household_effects: A renter may pay rent shaped by software that also prices competing buildings nearby. An online shopper may see prices or rankings tailored to personal data, and New York requires a disclosure when that happens. A job applicant may be screened by software before anyone reads the application; in New York City the employer must say so in advance. A family renewing Medicaid can lose coverage over a missed form, and the odds depend on how often its state renews automatically. Among workers, the clearest employment change so far appears for people aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations.

sub_issues.title: Rent-pricing software and the RealPage case
sub_issues.text: The Justice Department case against RealPage sits in the federal court for the Middle District of North Carolina and also named property management companies; Greystar and Cortland have final judgments, and LivCor a proposed one. The RealPage judgment, entered May 19, 2026, bars nonpublic competitor data from live pricing and bars training its main models on any geographic unit smaller than a state. New York's 2025 law treats a landlord that sets rents from a coordinating tool's recommendations as party to an unlawful agreement.

sub_issues.title: Surveillance pricing
sub_issues.text: The FTC's early findings drew on documents from six of the eight companies it ordered: Mastercard, Accenture, PROS, Bloomreach, Revionics and McKinsey. Its illustrations included a cosmetics company targeting promotions by skin type and a shopper profiled as a new parent seeing higher-priced baby thermometers first, both presented as hypothetical. The FTC described the study as ongoing in January 2025. New York's disclosure law is enforced by the attorney general, with civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.

sub_issues.title: Automated hiring and workplace monitoring
sub_issues.text: Colorado's 2024 law on high-risk AI systems never took effect. After xAI sued in April 2026 and the Justice Department filed a companion complaint, the state agreed to pause enforcement, and in May 2026 the legislature replaced the law with SB 26-189, effective January 1, 2027. The new law requires notice when automated decision technology is used in consequential decisions, a plain-language explanation after an adverse outcome, and human review, enforced by the attorney general after a 60-day period to cure violations.

sub_issues.title: AI and jobs: what the early evidence shows
sub_issues.text: Most studies measure exposure, an estimate of which tasks AI could do, which differs from what employers have adopted. The Yale Budget Lab notes that exposure scores rest on theory and that the usage data available come from one company's chatbot users. Findings through 2025 fit modest early effects concentrated among young workers, with no broad rise in unemployment, and later years could look different.

sub_issues.title: Do feeds drive polarization?
sub_issues.text: A 2024 field experiment on X used a language model to rerank posts expressing partisan animosity for 1,256 users over ten days and moved feelings toward the other party by about 2 points on a 100-point scale, in either direction. The pattern across studies suggests targeted changes to hostile content move attitudes slightly, while wholesale changes to ranking move exposure. Courts limit what government can require: in Moody v. NetChoice (2024), the Supreme Court held that a platform's choices about what to include and rank in its main feed are protected editorial activity.

sub_issues.title: Benefits decided by software
sub_issues.text: System failures at scale show up in payment errors. Improper payments in unemployment insurance rose from 9.2% in fiscal 2020 to 18.9%, or $78.1 billion, in fiscal 2021, and GAO, the Labor Department and its inspector general have reported a need to modernize state systems. The 2025 SNAP cost-sharing rule gives states a financial reason to lower error rates, and the design of their verification decides whether that happens through better data matching or more paperwork.

sub_issues.title: Who builds public digital services
sub_issues.text: Federal agencies spend about 80% of their technology budgets running existing systems, GAO reports. In-house teams can be closed by the next executive decision: the General Services Administration shut its 18F digital team in March 2025, and the IRS did not offer its free Direct File service for 2026 after accepting 296,531 returns in 25 states in 2025.

decision_makers.controls: Sues over agreements among competitors, including pooled pricing data, and negotiates settlements that a federal judge must approve.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Report suspected conduct through justice.gov/atr; comment on proposed final judgments during the Tunney Act period published in the Federal Register.

decision_makers.controls: Investigates unfair or deceptive practices and unfair methods of competition, runs industry studies under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act, and can issue rules under its statutes.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Report practices at reportfraud.ftc.gov; comment on studies and proposed rules at regulations.gov.

decision_makers.controls: Pass laws on algorithmic pricing disclosure, rent-setting software and automated decisions in hiring, lending and housing.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your state legislators through the legislature's official website; testify at committee hearings on technology or consumer protection bills.

decision_makers.controls: Enforce state laws such as New York's pricing disclosure law and Colorado's automated decision law, and write implementing rules where a statute directs.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: File a complaint with the consumer protection division on your attorney general's website.

decision_makers.who: City councils and city consumer protection agencies
decision_makers.controls: Pass local rules such as New York City's Local Law 144 on automated hiring tools and enforce them through agencies such as the city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Public comment at council hearings; complaints to the city agency named in the law.

decision_makers.controls: Build and run eligibility systems, decide how often renewals happen automatically, and decide individual cases, subject to fair hearings.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your state or county benefits office; request a fair hearing within the deadline on any termination notice.

decision_makers.controls: Writes antitrust, consumer protection and benefit program laws, could set national rules for automated decisions, and funds federal technology work.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Contact your U.S. representative and senators through house.gov and senate.gov.

decision_makers.controls: Choose ranking objectives, offer or withhold feed options, and decide what data independent researchers can access.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Feed settings within each app; company transparency reports and policies posted on each platform's website.

decision_makers.controls: Enter or reject antitrust judgments and decide whether laws regulating feeds or requiring AI disclosures are constitutional.
decision_makers.how_to_reach: Case records are public through PACER and supremecourt.gov; Tunney Act comments reach the court through the Justice Department's filings.

pathways.who_can_change_the_rules: Congress can amend the Sherman Act and the FTC Act, set national rules for automated decisions or personal data, and decide whether federal law overrides state laws on AI. The FTC can write rules within its statutes, and the Justice Department and FTC shape practice through cases and settlements that federal judges approve. State legislatures have acted first: New York passed a pricing disclosure law and a ban on algorithmic rent coordination, and Colorado replaced its AI law in 2026. City councils can regulate hiring tools within state home-rule limits. Any rule on how platforms rank content must respect the First Amendment, which the Supreme Court in Moody v. NetChoice applied to feed curation. Benefit eligibility systems follow program laws written by Congress and state legislatures and the agency rules that implement them.

responses.name: Bar competitors' private data from live pricing tools
responses.what_it_does: Court judgments or state statutes would stop pricing software from using competitors' nonpublic data in current price recommendations, limit models to older or aggregated data, and require that users can override recommendations. The RealPage judgment and New York's 2025 rent law follow this approach. Monitors would review model code and data inputs, and landlords would keep the final say over the rents they charge.
responses.requires: Sherman Act cases by the Justice Department or state attorneys general, or state statutes like New York's; a technical monitor able to audit software code and data feeds; courts to enforce decrees; and statutes or renewed decrees once a time-limited judgment expires.
responses.evidence: No evaluation of rent or price effects exists yet; the RealPage judgment was entered only on May 19, 2026. The main risk is that coordination moves to channels a decree does not cover, such as older shared data.
responses.tradeoffs: Some pricing accuracy may be lost; vendors and landlords bear compliance costs; and state statutes can face legal challenges from software vendors, which can delay enforcement.

responses.name: Require notice, explanation and human review of automated decisions
responses.what_it_does: People would be told when software helps decide whether they get a job, apartment, loan or service, receive a plain-language explanation after an adverse decision, and be able to ask a person to review it. Workers with unions could bargain over how tools are used. Independent bias audits, like those New York City requires for hiring tools, would test whether a tool's outcomes differ across demographic groups.
responses.requires: State or local statutes such as Colorado SB 26-189 or New York City's Local Law 144; an enforcing agency with auditors; complaint channels that reach that agency; rulemaking to define covered decisions. Complaints filed with other city offices also need a route to the enforcing agency, a gap the New York audit identified.
responses.evidence: The New York State Comptroller found enforcement of Local Law 144 weak, with two complaints and one violation found where auditors saw at least 17 potential violations. Colorado's law takes effect in 2027, so no outcome data exist. No study has measured whether notice or audits change hiring outcomes.
responses.tradeoffs: Compliance costs for employers and vendors, possible delays in adopting useful tools, and narrow definitions that let some systems escape coverage.

responses.name: Give users feed choices and researchers usable data
responses.what_it_does: Large platforms would let users pick how their feed is ranked, including a chronological option, and give vetted independent researchers access to data under privacy safeguards so that the effects of ranking can be measured. Platforms would report how many users pick each option, so the effect of offering a choice can be tracked. Rules would govern the choices offered and leave the content of each feed to the platform.
responses.requires: A federal or state statute enforced by the FTC or another agency; privacy protections for shared data; drafting that avoids dictating what content platforms rank, given Moody v. NetChoice. Researchers would work in secure environments where approved teams can analyze data without copying it.
responses.evidence: Randomized experiments show ranking changes move exposure substantially, and the 2020 experiments relied on the platform's cooperation and data. Effects on partisan hostility were absent in large ranking changes and about 2 points on a 100-point scale in a targeted reranking test.
responses.tradeoffs: Privacy risks from data access; platforms bear costs; benefits depend on users choosing other feeds, and changes to exposure may leave attitudes unchanged.

responses.name: Build automatic renewal and public digital teams into benefit delivery
responses.what_it_does: Agencies would renew benefits automatically from data they already hold wherever rules allow, and keep in-house technology teams able to build and fix systems such as eligibility portals and free tax filing. Teams would include engineers and designers employed by the agency, able to fix a failing system without waiting for a new contract, and could run free public services such as Direct File.
responses.requires: Federal and state funding for staff and modern systems; civil service hiring that can recruit technologists; data-sharing agreements; statutory charters so teams survive changes of administration. Congress or legislatures would also set performance measures, such as processing time and error rates, that agencies report publicly.
responses.evidence: Automatic renewal rates varied from about 11% to over 90% across states during Medicaid unwinding, when 69% of disenrollments were procedural. Direct File accepted 296,531 returns in 2025 before it was discontinued. These are descriptive comparisons and case results, with no causal evaluation of team models.
responses.tradeoffs: Up-front public cost; government builds software it could buy; automated data matches can also produce errors that need appeal routes.

responses.name: Disclose when personal data sets a price
responses.what_it_does: Sellers that set individual prices with personal data would have to say so at the point of sale, as New York requires, so shoppers can compare offers and regulators can see where the practice is common. The notice would appear next to the price itself. Regulators would also gain a record of where personalized pricing is used, which would help them decide whether further limits are needed.
responses.requires: State statutes like New York's or an FTC rule; attorney general or FTC enforcement with staff who can test websites and apps; and definitions of personalized pricing broad enough to reach the data brokers and pricing firms that supply sellers.
responses.evidence: No evaluation of disclosure effects on prices or shopping exists. The FTC's preliminary findings show the tools are offered to at least 250 clients, which describes the practice without measuring its effects. The FTC's January 2025 findings relied on hypothetical examples because company data were confidential, so even the extent of the practice remains uncertain.
responses.tradeoffs: Notices may become routine and ignored; sellers may shift to methods outside the statute's definitions; compliance costs fall on small online sellers as well as large ones.

distribution.group: Workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations
distribution.difference: Payroll data show a 13% relative employment decline for this group after generative AI spread, while older workers in the same occupations held steady. The pattern fits an AI effect without proving one.

distribution.group: Renters whose landlords use shared-data pricing software
distribution.difference: The RealPage case alleged that pooled nonpublic data let competing landlords align rents. The final judgment entered May 19, 2026 limits that use for RealPage customers going forward, and New York renters have an added state ban.

distribution.group: People renewing Medicaid in states with low automatic renewal rates
distribution.difference: Automatic renewal ran at 11% or less in Pennsylvania and Texas and 90% or more in Arizona, North Carolina and Rhode Island during unwinding, so the paperwork burden on families differed sharply by state.

distribution.group: Job applicants inside and outside places with hiring-tool laws
distribution.difference: Applicants in New York City are entitled to notice and published bias audits, and Colorado residents gain notice and review rights from 2027; a 2021 review found workers elsewhere generally lacked such rights, and even in New York City enforcement has been weak.

how_to_judge.measure: Monitor reports on RealPage's compliance with the final judgment
how_to_judge.where: Filings in United States v. RealPage, No. 1:24-cv-00710 (M.D.N.C.), available through PACER
how_to_judge.direction: Findings of compliance and no new shared-data features

how_to_judge.measure: Share of Medicaid renewals completed automatically (ex parte), by state
how_to_judge.where: State-reported renewal data published by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
how_to_judge.direction: Higher is better, with low procedural termination rates

how_to_judge.measure: Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations relative to older workers
how_to_judge.where: Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey and updates of payroll-based studies
how_to_judge.direction: No widening gap

how_to_judge.measure: Complaints filed and resolved under automated hiring and decision laws
how_to_judge.where: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection reports; Colorado Attorney General enforcement reports from 2027
how_to_judge.direction: Complaints routed to the agency and resolved, with audits that match independent reviews

reader_actions.action: Report suspected price coordination or unfair use of personal data in pricing
reader_actions.office: Federal Trade Commission (reportfraud.ftc.gov) or your state attorney general's consumer protection division
reader_actions.decision: Whether to investigate under the FTC Act or state consumer protection and antitrust law

reader_actions.action: Testify or comment on bills about automated decisions
reader_actions.office: Your state legislature's committee on technology, labor or consumer protection
reader_actions.decision: Whether to require notice, explanation and human review when software helps make decisions about people

reader_actions.action: Ask for automatic renewal or a fair hearing when benefits are cut
reader_actions.office: Your state Medicaid or SNAP agency
reader_actions.decision: Renewal and termination of your benefits; a fair hearing officer can reverse a termination

reader_actions.action: File a complaint about an automated hiring tool
reader_actions.office: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (in New York City) or the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission for discrimination anywhere
reader_actions.decision: Whether an employer's use of a hiring tool violated local law or federal anti-discrimination law

check.prompt: Which feature of rent-pricing software led to the Justice Department's case against RealPage?
options: Using a landlord's own past rents to suggest a price
Pooling competing landlords' nonpublic data into live rent recommendations
Posting advertised rents on public websites
