check.explanation: The case alleged that pooled nonpublic data from competitors let landlords align rents. The final judgment bars that data from live recommendations and requires training data at least 12 months old, while software built on a landlord's own data raises different questions.

cross_links.why: Rent-setting software is one influence on rents, alongside housing supply
AI adoption and workplace monitoring change working conditions and bargaining power
Feed ranking shapes the political information people see before they vote
Eligibility systems decide who receives benefits and tax refunds
Data centers built for AI add electricity demand that someone pays for

CL1400.claim: Staff wages are the largest cost in childcare, and infant care costs more because state rules require more adults per child.
CL1400.supports: Treasury reported that wages are at least 50 to 60 percent of child care program expenses on U.S. averages. Labor is a larger share for younger children because they need more oversight and more adults per child, and costs vary with state regulations on the required number of providers per child.
CL1400.period: Report published September 2021, using pre-2021 cost data
CL1400.limitation: The labor share comes from a Center for American Progress cost estimate reproduced by Treasury; actual shares vary by program size, setting and state.

CL1401.claim: Stricter state childcare regulations are linked to fewer centers in lower-income markets and higher quality mainly in higher-income areas.
CL1401.supports: Hotz and Xiao report that state child care regulations reduce the number of center-based establishments, with the largest reductions in lower-income markets, while improving the quality of services, with the largest gains in higher-income areas. They conclude regulation creates winners and losers.
CL1401.limitation: One major study of regulations in general; it does not isolate any single rule such as a ratio change, and markets have changed since its data period.

CL1402.claim: Childcare workers earned a median $16.82 an hour in May 2025.
CL1402.supports: BLS reports a median hourly wage of $16.82 ($34,980 a year) for childcare workers in May 2025, about 1,010,300 jobs in 2025, a projected 2 percent employment decline from 2025 to 2035, and about 150,300 openings a year, all from replacing workers who leave the occupation.
CL1402.limitation: Excludes self-employed home-based providers from wage estimates and covers one occupation; preschool teachers and center directors are counted separately.

CL1403.claim: Childcare jobs pay near the bottom of all occupations, turnover is high, and many providers run on thin margins.
CL1403.supports: Treasury reported average annual pay of $24,230, placing child care workers in the second percentile of all occupations, estimated that 26 to 40 percent of the workforce leaves their job each year, and noted that many for-profit providers have profit margins usually under 1 percent.
CL1403.limitation: Turnover is a range of national estimates; pay figures predate the wage changes during and after the pandemic.

CL1404.claim: The average price of childcare was $13,184 in 2025, a third of median income for single parents.
CL1404.supports: Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group, reports a national average annual price of $13,184 in 2025, equal to 10 percent of median income for two-parent households and 33 percent for single-parent households. Center care for two children exceeded median rent in every state with data. Licensed centers fell 1 percent from 2024 to 2025 while family child care homes rose 1.4 percent.
CL1404.jurisdiction: United States, state data compiled nationally
CL1404.limitation: Advocacy compilation of state market-rate and referral data whose methods differ by state; averages mix ages and settings and are not a price any one family pays.

CL1405.claim: Lower childcare prices raise mothers' employment, with most estimates showing modest effects.
CL1405.supports: Morrissey's review finds U.S. elasticity estimates clustering around 0.05 to 0.25, implying that a 10 percent price reduction raises maternal employment by about 0.5 to 2.5 percent, within a wider range of 0.25 to 11 percent. Lower out-of-pocket costs and expanded public care are associated with more maternal work.
CL1405.limitation: Estimates vary widely by method and period; newer and non-U.S. studies tend to find smaller effects than 1990s U.S. data.

CL1406.claim: About 16 percent of children eligible for childcare subsidies under federal rules received them in 2022.
CL1406.supports: ASPE estimates that in an average month of fiscal 2022, 11.8 million children were eligible under federal rules and 9.1 million under state rules, while 1.8 million received subsidies: 16 percent of federally eligible and 20 percent of state-eligible children.
CL1406.population: Children ages 0 to 12 in low-income working families
CL1406.limitation: Eligibility is simulated from survey data; not every eligible family wants paid care, so the gap overstates unmet demand for subsidies.

CL1407.claim: Head Start funded 715,873 places in fiscal 2024.
CL1407.supports: The Office of Head Start reports funded enrollment of 715,873 children and pregnant women in fiscal 2024, including 505,422 Head Start preschool and 185,991 Early Head Start places in non-migrant programs plus tribal and migrant programs, with 805,919 served over the program year and about $12.27 billion in total funding.
CL1407.population: Children in low-income families and pregnant women
CL1407.limitation: Funded slots count capacity; cumulative enrollment is higher because children leave and are replaced during the year.

CL1408.claim: Congress provided $8.831 billion for the childcare block grant and about $12.36 billion for Head Start in fiscal 2026.
CL1408.supports: The First Five Years Fund, an advocacy group, reports that the FY2026 appropriations law signed February 3, 2026 provided $8.831 billion for the Child Care and Development Block Grant and $12.357 billion for Head Start, each $85 million above FY2025. The Bipartisan Policy Center reports $12.36 billion for Head Start.
CL1408.limitation: Appropriations figures exclude mandatory child care entitlement funds that also flow through CCDF; the advocacy tracker was cross-checked against one other source.

CL1409.claim: The American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 provided $23.975 billion in childcare stabilization grants and $14.99 billion in extra block grant funds.
CL1409.supports: Section 2202 of Public Law 117-2 appropriated $23,975,000,000 for subgrants to child care providers for personnel costs, rent, utilities and other operating costs, with providers certifying they would keep paying employees full compensation. Section 2201 appropriated $14,990,000,000 for the block grant, to be obligated in fiscal 2021 or the two following fiscal years.
CL1409.population: Child care providers and state lead agencies
CL1409.limitation: The statute excerpt read did not show the stabilization subgrant obligation deadline; the 2201 funds had to be obligated by the end of fiscal 2023.

CL1410.claim: Most states used pandemic relief money for childcare wage increases, funding that was temporary.
CL1410.supports: The Center for the Study of Child Care Employment reports that the majority of states used pandemic relief funds for workforce initiatives that increased wages, that relief funding was never sufficient nor intended to sustain the system, and that the national median wage for child care workers was $14.60 in 2023.
CL1410.limitation: Descriptive policy review by a center that advocates for higher pay; it does not estimate the effect of the funds ending on supply or prices.

CL1411.claim: A 2026 federal rule rescinded the 2024 requirements to cap copayments at 7 percent of income and to pay providers by enrollment.
CL1411.supports: The final rule published May 12, 2026, effective July 13, 2026, rescinds requirements to limit family copayments to 7 percent of income, provide some services through grants or contracts, pay providers prospectively and pay based on enrollment. States may keep these practices, must delink payments from occasional absences, and must pay within 21 days of a complete invoice if paying after care. HHS reports CCDF funding rose from $8.1 billion in FFY2019 to $12.4 billion in FFY2026.
CL1411.population: State CCDF lead agencies, providers and subsidized families
CL1411.period: Rule published May 12, 2026; status checked October 15, 2026
CL1411.limitation: The rule removes federal mandates without requiring states to change; how many states keep a 7 percent cap or enrollment-based payment is not yet reported.

CL1412.claim: In May 2026 ACF proposed rescinding Head Start's 2024 staff pay requirements; preschool slots have fallen about 15 percent since 2012.
CL1412.supports: The Bipartisan Policy Center reports that ACF proposed rescinding the 2024 Head Start rule's pay parity, minimum wage, wage comparability and staff benefits requirements, with comments closing June 11, 2026. Funded Head Start preschool slots declined about 15 percent since FY2012 while Early Head Start slots grew about 49 percent. Grants go directly to local providers, bypassing states.
CL1412.period: Proposal issued May 2026; slot trend FY2012 to FY2026
CL1412.limitation: A proposed rule does not change the requirements until ACF publishes a final rule.

CL1413.claim: In 2025, women in households with young children spent more time on primary childcare than men.
CL1413.supports: The American Time Use Survey reports that among adults in households with children under 6, women spent an average of 2.8 hours a day on primary childcare and men 1.7 hours in 2025.
CL1413.population: Adults in households with children under age 6
CL1413.limitation: Survey operations were suspended October 1 to November 12, 2025; fourth-quarter estimates were reweighted, and the shutdown's effect cannot be quantified.

CL1414.claim: From tax year 2026 the child and dependent care credit rate starts at 50 percent and steps down with income.
CL1414.supports: Section 21 as amended by Public Law 119-21 sets the applicable percentage at 50 percent, reduced 1 point per $2,000 of adjusted gross income above $15,000 but not below 35 percent, then further reduced to no less than 20 percent above $75,000 ($150,000 joint). Creditable expenses remain capped at $3,000 for one qualifying individual and $6,000 for two or more.
CL1414.population: Taxpayers paying for care so they can work
CL1414.limitation: Statutory parameters only; actual benefit depends on tax liability, expenses and any employer-provided dependent care benefits that reduce the expense cap.

CL1415.claim: The dependent care credit is nonrefundable, and the dependent care account limit rose to $7,500 for 2026.
CL1415.supports: Section 21 sits in the Internal Revenue Code subpart titled Nonrefundable Personal Credits, so it can only reduce income tax owed. Section 129 as amended sets the exclusion for employer dependent care assistance at $7,500 ($3,750 for married filing separately) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
CL1415.limitation: Distribution of benefits by income was not estimated here; families must owe income tax or have employer accounts to benefit.

CL1416.claim: The 2025 tax law raised the employer childcare credit to 40 percent of costs, 50 percent for small businesses.
CL1416.supports: Section 45F as amended by Public Law 119-21 provides a credit of 40 percent of qualified child care expenditures, or 50 percent for an eligible small business, capped at $500,000 a year ($600,000 for small businesses), replacing the earlier 25 percent rate and $150,000 cap, for amounts paid after December 31, 2025, indexed after 2026.
CL1416.population: Employers providing or contracting for child care
CL1416.period: Amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2025
CL1416.limitation: Statutory design only; IRS data on how many employers claim the credit under the new rates and caps are not yet available.

CL1417.claim: Few employers claimed the earlier employer childcare credit.
CL1417.supports: GAO estimated that 169 to 278 corporate income tax returns claimed the employer-provided child care credit in 2016, totaling $15.7 million to $18.8 million, and reported that employers cited lack of awareness, high cost and complexity of providing care, and a credit too small to motivate them.
CL1417.limitation: Covers corporate returns; pass-through businesses were harder to measure, and the credit has since been enlarged.

CL1418.claim: The child tax credit is $2,200 per child, refundable up to $1,700 per child for 2025 and 2026 (a $1,400 statutory base indexed for inflation).
CL1418.supports: Section 24 as amended by Public Law 119-21 sets the credit at $2,200 per qualifying child, with no end date in subsection (h), and indexes it after 2025. The refundable amount per child is capped at $1,400, adjusted for inflation from a 2017 base, with increases rounded down to $100. The IRS lists the refundable maximum as $1,700.
CL1418.limitation: The statute sets the $1,400 base, and the IRS sets the inflation-adjusted refundable amount each year.

CL1419.claim: New Mexico began no-cost childcare for families working or in school regardless of income on November 1, 2025.
CL1419.supports: New Mexico's Early Childhood Education and Care Department reports no-cost care since November 1, 2025 for families working or in school regardless of income, funded by the Early Childhood Trust Fund, Land Grant Permanent Fund distributions, general funds and federal CCDF and TANF money. Providers on the enhanced rate must pay entry-level staff at least $16 an hour. SB 241, signed March 10, 2026, waives copayments at or below 600 percent of the poverty level.
CL1419.population: New Mexico families with children in care and participating providers
CL1419.limitation: Agency descriptions; no independent evaluation of effects on supply, prices or parental work is available yet.

CL1420.claim: Nearly 1.8 million children attended state-funded preschool in 2024-2025.
CL1420.supports: NIEER reports nearly 1.8 million children enrolled in state-funded preschool in the 2024-2025 school year, with state spending of nearly $14.4 billion, an average of $8,124 per child, record highs in both, and substantially slower growth.
CL1420.population: Children in state-funded preschool, mostly ages 3 and 4
CL1420.limitation: Program hours and quality standards vary widely by state; enrollment counts do not show how many families still need care outside preschool hours.

CL1421.claim: Fourteen states and the District of Columbia have enacted mandatory paid family leave programs.
CL1421.supports: The Bipartisan Policy Center lists mandatory programs in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Washington and the District of Columbia, with Maryland (2027/2028) and Virginia (2028/2029) not yet active.
CL1421.population: Private-sector workers in states with programs
CL1421.limitation: A tracker by a policy organization; benefit start dates for the newest programs were inferred from listed effective years.

CL1422.claim: California's paid family leave more than doubled the leave new mothers took.
CL1422.supports: Rossin-Slater, Ruhm and Waldfogel found that California's program raised typical new mothers' leave from about three weeks to six or seven, with large gains for less advantaged groups, and suggestive evidence of 6 to 9 percent higher usual weekly hours for employed mothers of 1- to 3-year-olds.
CL1422.limitation: Difference-in-differences with Current Population Survey data; the work-hours finding is labeled suggestive by the authors.

CL1423.claim: A long-run study found California's paid leave did not raise mothers' employment or earnings and lowered them for first-time mothers a decade later.
CL1423.supports: Bailey, Byker, Patel and Ramnath, using tax records and a regression discontinuity design, found no evidence the program increased employment, earnings or childbearing, and found reduced employment and earnings for first-time mothers about ten years after birth.
CL1423.period: Births around 2004 followed for about a decade; published 2025
CL1423.limitation: Conflicts with shorter-run evidence of higher work hours; the design compares births close to the program start and may not capture later program changes.

CL1424.claim: Quebec's low-fee universal childcare raised mothers' work, with measured costs to some child and family outcomes.
CL1424.supports: Baker, Gruber and Milligan found that Quebec's $5-a-day program shifted families into new care use, raised maternal labor supply with an elasticity of 0.236, and was associated with worse child behavior and health measures, more hostile parenting and lower-quality parental relationships.
CL1424.jurisdiction: Quebec, Canada, compared with other provinces
CL1424.limitation: Effects on child outcomes are contested; results depend on program quality during a rapid expansion and may not transfer to U.S. states.

CL1425.claim: Parents must pay for childcare when they can least afford it, and government already supplies close to half of providers' revenue.
CL1425.supports: Treasury wrote that parents are asked to pay for child care when they can least afford it and are unlikely to be able to borrow against future earnings. It cited Census estimates that 47 percent of the $48 billion in 2019 child care operating revenue came from federal and state government spending.
CL1425.population: Families with young children; child care industry
CL1425.limitation: Revenue shares predate pandemic relief funds and the later funding changes; the borrowing constraint is an economic argument with limited direct measurement.

CL1426.claim: Every state requested waivers to delay parts of the 2024 childcare rule.
CL1426.supports: GAO reports that a CCDF rule effective April 2024 capped family copayments at 7 percent of income and required paying providers in advance, and that every state and the District of Columbia requested temporary waivers to delay certain provisions for up to two years.
CL1426.limitation: Waiver requests show implementation difficulty but not the provisions' effects; the 2024 requirements were later rescinded in 2026.

CL1600.claim: Most community water systems are small, while a small share of large systems serves most customers.
CL1600.supports: CRS reports nearly 49,500 community water systems serving more than 324 million people. Of these, 81% serve 3,300 or fewer people and together serve 7% of the community water system population, while fewer than 10% serve 10,000 or more and serve 84% of customers.
CL1600.population: Community water systems regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act
CL1600.limitation: Counts come from EPA's compliance database, which depends on state reporting. Size alone does not measure a system's finances or compliance.

CL1601.claim: More than 148,000 public water systems operate in the United States, and they can be publicly or privately owned.
CL1601.supports: EPA's program page states that there are over 148,000 public water systems and that a public water system may be publicly or privately owned. The figure includes systems that serve schools, workplaces and campgrounds as well as residential systems.
CL1601.limitation: EPA gives no split between public and private ownership on this page, and the total differs slightly from CRS's figure of nearly 144,000.

CL1602.claim: A state agency with primacy enforces federal drinking water rules, and EPA regional offices usually do so on tribal lands.
CL1602.supports: EPA delegates primary enforcement responsibility to states that meet requirements such as authority to inspect, require records and assess penalties. Where EPA keeps that role, it directly implements and enforces the rules. EPA regional offices generally act as the primacy agency in Indian Country; the Navajo Nation is the only tribe with primacy.
CL1602.jurisdiction: United States, states and tribal lands
CL1602.period: Status shown on EPA page, checked October 2026
CL1602.limitation: The page does not list which states hold primacy, so state-by-state arrangements need separate checking.

CL1603.claim: Community water systems must send customers an annual water quality report by July 1, and larger systems will send it twice a year.
CL1603.supports: Federal regulations require each community water system to deliver its Consumer Confidence Report by July 1 each year. Rule revisions announced in May 2024 require systems serving more than 10,000 people to distribute reports twice per year, with the codified compliance schedule beginning November 1, 2027.
CL1603.limitation: The report summarizes the prior year's monitoring, so it can lag a new problem by many months.

CL1604.claim: The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements require most systems to replace lead service lines within 10 years after a November 2027 compliance date.
CL1604.supports: The final rule, published October 30, 2024 and effective December 30, 2024, requires water systems to complete replacements within 10 years of the rule's compliance date of November 1, 2027. It lowers the lead action level from 15 to 10 micrograms per liter and requires public inventories and replacement plans.
CL1604.population: Community and non-transient non-community water systems
CL1604.period: Rule text as published; status checked October 15, 2026
CL1604.limitation: A limited number of systems can receive more time. The rule's survival depends on a pending court challenge.

CL1605.claim: EPA estimates that about 4 million lead service lines remain in use.
CL1605.supports: EPA's needs survey page, updated in May 2026, states that the 7th survey estimates about four million lead service lines, roughly 75% reported by systems and 25% predicted. The same survey estimates $625 billion in drinking water needs over 20 years, $422.9 billion of it for transmission and distribution pipes.
CL1605.population: Public water systems responding to EPA's needs survey
CL1605.limitation: EPA's 2024 rule fact sheet cited up to 9 million lead lines, so the estimate has changed as inventories improved. A quarter of the current count is modeled.

CL1606.claim: The water utility association's court challenge to the lead rule was argued on September 30, 2026 and awaits decision, with EPA defending the rule.
CL1606.supports: The American Water Works Association petitioned the D.C. Circuit (No. 24-1376), arguing that costs, private-property access and the 10-year deadline are unworkable. EPA's brief states the rule is lawful and should be upheld. Oral argument took place September 30, 2026; the intervenor's docket page reports no decision. The rule remains in effect during review.
CL1606.jurisdiction: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
CL1606.limitation: Status summaries come from an intervenor and an engineering firm. A ruling could arrive at any time and change deadlines.

CL1607.claim: EPA's 2024 PFAS rule set limits of 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS, with monitoring due by 2027 and compliance by 2029.
CL1607.supports: EPA's April 10, 2024 rule set enforceable limits of 4.0 ppt for PFOA and PFOS, 10 ppt for PFHxS, PFNA and HFPO-DA, and a hazard index for mixtures. Systems must complete initial monitoring by 2027 and meet the limits by 2029. EPA estimated the rule would prevent PFAS exposure for about 100 million people and announced $1 billion from the 2021 infrastructure law for PFAS testing and treatment.
CL1607.period: Rule of April 2024; page updated May 18, 2026
CL1607.limitation: The 100 million figure is EPA's own estimate. Challengers dispute the national occurrence data behind it.

CL1608.claim: In 2026 EPA proposed keeping the PFOA and PFOS limits with a possible extension to 2031 and rescinding the other four PFAS limits; a court challenge awaits decision.
CL1608.supports: On May 18, 2026 EPA proposed letting systems seek up to two more years, to April 2031, for PFOA and PFOS without changing the limits, and proposed rescinding limits for PFHxS, PFNA, HFPO-DA and the mixture index. Comments closed July 20, 2026. On January 21, 2026 the D.C. Circuit denied EPA's motion to vacate four limits; argument was held September 18, 2026.
CL1608.limitation: No final rule had been reported as of the check date. Litigation summaries come from law firms and legal press.

CL1609.claim: State and local governments paid 96% of public spending on water utilities in 2017, with the federal government paying 4%.
CL1609.supports: CBO's compilation of public infrastructure spending shows that in 2017 the federal share of spending on water supply and wastewater treatment was 4% and the state and local share 96%. State and local figures are net of federal grants and loan subsidies, so they show money raised by states, localities and their utilities.
CL1609.population: Public spending on water supply and wastewater utilities
CL1609.limitation: The figures predate the 2021 infrastructure law, which raised federal water funding for fiscal years 2022 to 2026.

CL1610.claim: The Drinking Water State Revolving Fund combines federal grants with a 20% state match and lends the money to systems, recycling repayments.
CL1610.supports: EPA describes the fund, created by the 1996 Safe Drinking Water Act amendments: EPA awards capitalization grants to states based on the needs survey; states add 20%; states may set aside about 31% for program work, including 2% for small-system technical assistance; the rest funds loans of up to 30 years at zero to market interest, and repayments return to the fund. Some aid can be principal forgiveness or grants.
CL1610.limitation: Program rules describe design, and the page gives no data on which systems apply or receive loans.

CL1611.claim: The 2021 infrastructure law provided $15 billion for lead service line replacement over five years.
CL1611.supports: EPA's lead rule fact sheet states that the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law includes $15 billion for lead service line replacement, and that half of this funding goes to disadvantaged communities as grants or principal forgiveness loans.
CL1611.population: State revolving fund programs and water systems
CL1611.limitation: EPA has not published, in the sources reviewed here, how many lines this money has replaced.

CL1612.claim: For fiscal 2026, Congress directed 64% of the drinking water revolving fund appropriation to named local projects, reducing money available to state loan programs.
CL1612.supports: CRS reports that P.L. 119-74 provided $410.7 million in drinking water fund capitalization grants and $715.4 million for congressionally directed projects (64% of the account), and $746.1 million and $892.8 million (54%) for the clean water fund. EPA's allotment memo states that these earmarks reduced SRF funding available to states.
CL1612.population: Federal appropriations to EPA water infrastructure accounts
CL1612.limitation: Earmarked projects still receive federal water money; the figures show who chooses projects, and they do not measure project quality.

CL1613.claim: Water systems with rate-setting authority adopt rates through their governing board, while state commissions regulate rates for some systems.
CL1613.supports: A technical assistance guide for small systems describes systems that set their own rates subject to board approval. It notes that most states have a public utility or public service commission and that some, but not all, water and wastewater systems fall under commission regulation, in which case the commission's ratemaking process applies.
CL1613.limitation: Which systems a commission regulates differs by state; a few states also regulate some publicly owned systems.

CL1614.claim: California's utility commission regulates more than 100 investor-owned water and sewer utilities serving about 16% of residents.
CL1614.supports: The California Public Utilities Commission's Water Division states that it regulates over 100 investor-owned water and sewer utilities that provide water service to about 16% of California residents, and that about 95% of those customers are served by nine large utilities.
CL1614.limitation: This is one state's arrangement. Other states draw the line between commission-regulated and locally governed systems differently.

CL1615.claim: Water and sewer payments rose about twice as fast as consumer prices from 1998 to 2024, and estimates suggest 12 million to 19 million households lack affordable access.
CL1615.supports: CRS summarizes research finding that household payments for water and sewer increased at roughly twice the rate of the consumer price index between 1998 and 2024. It reports estimates that 12.1 million to 19.2 million households (9.2% to 14.6%) lack affordable water services and that 11% to 20% of customers are in arrears.
CL1615.population: U.S. households served by water and sewer utilities
CL1615.limitation: Affordability counts depend on the income threshold chosen, such as 3% or 4.5% of household income, and on incomplete billing data.

CL1616.claim: Private wells serve about 43 million people and are not regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act.
CL1616.supports: EPA states that private well water is not regulated by the federal government under the Safe Drinking Water Act and that most states do not regulate it either. About 15% of the population, over 43 million people, rely on private wells, and owners are responsible for the safety of their water.
CL1616.limitation: Some states and counties require testing at property sale or new construction, which this national figure does not show.

CL1617.claim: EPA promotes partnerships among water systems, from shared equipment to full consolidation, but its program page reports no measured outcomes.
CL1617.supports: EPA defines four partnership types: informal cooperation, contractual assistance, joint power agencies and ownership transfer, including consolidation. It says partnerships can improve economies of scale, compliance and service. The page offers case studies and handbooks and contains no outcome statistics.
CL1617.limitation: Benefits listed by EPA are expected benefits; the page reports no measured effect on compliance or bills.

CL1618.claim: A temporary federal water bill assistance program reached 1.7 million households, and Congress has not funded the follow-on pilot.
CL1618.supports: CRS reports that the Low Income Household Water Assistance Program, created during the COVID-19 pandemic, had assisted 1.7 million households through the second quarter of 2024, and that Congress has not provided an appropriation for a related low-income water assistance pilot.
CL1618.population: Low-income households with water and wastewater bills
CL1618.limitation: Counts show how many households were reached. The sources do not measure effects on shutoffs or arrears.

CL1619.claim: In Flint, state-appointed emergency managers switched the water source in 2014 without corrosion control, and the state did not require it.
CL1619.supports: EPA's Inspector General found that Flint switched to Flint River water in April 2014 under governor-appointed emergency managers as a cost-saving step, that treatment lacked corrosion control, and that the state environmental agency did not require it or take formal enforcement until August 2015. It found oversight lapses at EPA, the state and the city.
CL1619.population: Flint residents served by the city system
CL1619.limitation: This is one city's case; it shows how oversight failed and does not estimate how common such failures are.

CL1620.claim: EPA lifted its 2016 emergency order for Flint in May 2025 after the city completed its requirements.
CL1620.supports: EPA announced on May 19, 2025 that the City of Flint had completed all requirements of the Safe Drinking Water Act emergency order issued in January 2016, and it lifted the order that had governed the city's system.
CL1620.limitation: Completion of the order's requirements does not by itself measure residents' past exposure or health outcomes.

CL1621.claim: A federal judge placed Jackson's water system under an interim third-party manager in November 2022.
CL1621.supports: JXN Water states that a federal court order of November 29, 2022 by U.S. District Judge Henry Wingate authorized an interim third-party manager to reestablish Jackson's water system, and reports repairing nearly 2,000 leaks and opening 3,300 closed valves since February 2023.
CL1621.population: Customers of the Jackson water system
CL1621.limitation: Repair counts are reported by the managing utility itself and are not independently audited in this source.

CL1622.claim: EPA estimated the lead rule's annual benefits at $13 billion to $25 billion against annual costs of $1.5 billion to $2 billion.
CL1622.supports: EPA's fact sheet reports estimated benefits of $13 billion to $25 billion per year and costs of $1.5 billion to $2 billion per year, including avoided low birthweight, ADHD cases, heart-disease deaths and lost IQ points in children.
CL1622.population: U.S. population served by systems with lead service lines
CL1622.limitation: These are EPA model estimates. The utility association challenging the rule argues total costs exceed $100 billion.

CL1623.claim: Rural communities can also borrow for water systems through USDA programs, and EPA funds tribal systems directly.
CL1623.supports: CRS lists USDA Water and Waste Disposal loans and grants for eligible rural communities, USDA emergency community water grants, and the Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act loans with minimum project costs of $20 million, or $5 million for communities of 25,000 or fewer. EPA funds territories, the District of Columbia and tribes directly.
CL1623.population: Rural, small and tribal water systems
CL1623.limitation: The brief lists programs and does not report how much each program lends or to whom.

CL1234.claim: Investor-owned utilities serve about two-thirds of U.S. electricity customers, public power about 15% and cooperatives about 13%; most public power utilities are governed by a city council or utility board.
CL1234.supports: EIA reports investor-owned utilities served 72% of customers in 2017, with 1,958 publicly owned utilities averaging 12,100 customers and 812 cooperatives averaging 24,500. The American Public Power Association reports shares of 66%, 15% and 13% and says most public power utilities are governed by a city council or an independent utility board. NRECA counts 830 distribution and 60 generation and transmission cooperatives serving 42 million people.
CL1234.limitation: The association figures come from industry groups representing public power and cooperatives; the EIA count is older. Customer counts differ from shares of electricity sold.

CL1235.claim: FERC regulates interstate transmission and wholesale electricity sales, while state commissions regulate retail sales to consumers.
CL1235.supports: FERC's description of its duties states that it regulates the transmission and wholesale sale of electricity in interstate commerce and does not regulate retail electricity and natural gas sales to consumers or approve construction of generation, which fall to state public utility commissions. The Harvard review adds that federal law gives FERC exclusive authority over transmission revenue requirements.
CL1235.limitation: Texas's main grid operates largely outside FERC wholesale jurisdiction; public power and many cooperatives are outside state commission rate authority in many states.

CL1236.claim: Commission-approved rates cover operating costs and give investor-owned utilities an opportunity to earn a fixed rate of return on capital investments, with costs divided among customer classes by cost causation.
CL1236.supports: The Harvard Electricity Law Initiative report explains that rates provide utilities an opportunity to earn a fixed rate of return on capital investments, that the cost causation principle aligns prices with the costs a utility incurs to serve each class, and that utilities divide revenue requirements among residential, commercial and industrial classes based on usage patterns.
CL1236.population: Investor-owned utilities under state rate regulation
CL1236.limitation: Describes the standard framework; each state's statutes and commission practice differ in details such as formula rates and riders.

CL1237.claim: The average U.S. residential electricity price was 17.30 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2025, and generation is the largest cost component.
CL1237.supports: EIA's guide to electricity prices reports the 2025 residential average of 17.30 cents per kilowatt-hour, states that generation is the largest component of the price, and lists fuel costs, power plant costs, transmission and distribution (including storm damage repair), weather and regulation as factors; in some states commissions fully regulate prices.
CL1237.limitation: A national average; state averages vary widely, and the page does not give current shares for each component.

CL1238.claim: Natural gas produced about 41% of U.S. utility-scale electricity in 2025, and EIA forecasts the Henry Hub price at $3.48 per million Btu for 2026.
CL1238.supports: EIA reports 2025 utility-scale generation shares of about 41% natural gas, 18% nuclear, 17% coal and 24% renewables. EIA's October 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook forecasts Henry Hub spot prices of $3.48 in 2026 and $3.16 in 2027, citing above-average inventories.
CL1238.limitation: Regional generation mixes differ sharply, so national shares do not show how much gas prices affect any one utility's bills.

CL1239.claim: A Berkeley Lab analysis found that the main drivers of electricity price increases from 2019 to 2025 were grid investments, natural gas prices, disaster recovery and state policies, and that states with the largest data center growth generally saw prices fall.
CL1239.supports: CRS Report R48646 (updated May 12, 2026) summarizes the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory finding that states with the largest data center demand growth generally saw electricity price decreases between 2019 and 2025, with utility grid investments, natural gas prices, disaster recovery and state policies as main drivers of increases. CRS notes that added sales can lower rates when existing infrastructure absorbs new load, and that new infrastructure can raise them.
CL1239.limitation: An observational state-level comparison read through a CRS summary; it does not isolate the effect of data centers in places where large new plants and lines are being built, and it predates most new data center capacity charges.

CL1240.claim: PJM's capacity auction for June 2026 to May 2027 cleared at the FERC-approved cap of $329.17 per megawatt-day, and PJM estimated bill increases of 1.5% to 5% for some customers.
CL1240.supports: PJM's July 22, 2025 release reports the 2026/2027 clearing price of $329.17 per MW-day across the footprint, equal to the FERC-approved cap, compared with $269.92 for 2025/2026 outside the BGE and Dominion zones. PJM said forecast peak load rose by more than 5,400 MW, driven largely by data center expansion, electrification and economic growth, and that it serves about 67 million people in 13 states and D.C.
CL1240.limitation: Bill effects depend on how each state and utility passes costs through; PJM's 1.5% to 5% range applies to some customers only, and two zones saw lower prices.

CL1241.claim: EIA forecasts U.S. wholesale electricity prices averaging $52 per megawatt-hour in 2026, 11% above 2025, with PJM up 41%.
CL1241.supports: EIA's October 6, 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook forecasts wholesale prices of $52 per MWh in 2026, 11% above 2025, with PJM up 41% and the Northwest Mid-Columbia hub down 23%.
CL1241.limitation: Wholesale prices are one input to retail bills and reach households with a lag that depends on utility purchasing and rate design.

CL1242.claim: Data centers used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023, and some projections show that use doubling or tripling by 2028.
CL1242.supports: CRS Report R48646 cites a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimate of about 176 terawatt-hours, about 4.4% of U.S. consumption in 2023, excluding cryptocurrency, and an EPRI estimate of about 4%. It states that some projections show data center consumption could double or triple by 2028.
CL1242.limitation: Projections vary widely and depend on chip efficiency, investment plans and whether announced facilities are built; the 2023 figure is an estimate.

CL1243.claim: PJM's independent market monitor estimates that forecast data center load raised capacity costs for other customers by $23.1 billion across three auctions, and recommends that new data center load bring its own generation.
CL1243.supports: Monitoring Analytics' January 5, 2026 analysis of the 2027/2028 auction reruns the auctions with the same offers and rules but without data center load in the forecast. It reports cost increases to other customers of $9.33 billion (2025/2026), $7.27 billion (2026/2027) and $6.50 billion (2027/2028), totaling $23.1 billion, and total 2027/2028 capacity revenues of $16.4 billion. It recommends that new data center load bring its own new generation.
CL1243.limitation: A counterfactual model holding all other offers fixed; it does not show how capacity costs pass into each state's retail bills, and suppliers might have offered differently with lower demand.

CL1244.claim: A 2025 review found state commissions often approved confidential data center special contracts in brief orders, and that commission formulas for dividing FERC-approved transmission costs can shift costs onto households.
CL1244.supports: Martin and Peskoe of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative reviewed nearly 50 regulatory proceedings, including 40 state commission proceedings on data center special contracts, and found approvals often came in brief orders with confidential treatment. They report that FERC sets transmission revenue requirements, that commissions choose their own allocation methods, and that those methods can shift data center costs onto residential bills.
CL1244.population: State utility commission proceedings on data center rates
CL1244.limitation: A legal review of selected proceedings; it does not quantify the cost shifted to households, and the authors argue for policy changes.

CL1245.claim: AEP Ohio proposed requiring data centers to pay for 90% of their maximum demand for ten years, and Indiana Michigan Power proposed similar terms over twenty years for customers of 150 megawatts or more.
CL1245.supports: The Harvard Electricity Law Initiative report describes AEP Ohio's proposed tariff requiring a data center to pay 90% of costs associated with its maximum demand over ten years, and Indiana Michigan Power's proposal covering customers of at least 150 MW with a 90% capacity payment and a twenty-year term.
CL1245.limitation: These are proposals as described in March 2025; the cited report does not give final commission decisions or later terms.

CL1246.claim: The President's fiscal 2026 budget proposed eliminating LIHEAP, and state program directors reported that federal LIHEAP staff were fired in April 2025.
CL1246.supports: The HHS Fiscal Year 2026 Budget in Brief states that the budget eliminates funding for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program. The National Energy Assistance Directors Association reports that since April 1, 2025 it has sought reinstatement of fired HHS LIHEAP staff and release of remaining fiscal 2025 funds, and estimates the proposed cut would remove $4 billion in assistance to about 6 million households.
CL1246.limitation: The budget is a proposal; the cited sources do not report the enacted fiscal 2026 LIHEAP level or fiscal 2027 funding under the stopgap law. NEADA represents state program directors and advocates for the program.

CL1247.claim: Public Law 119-21 changed how SNAP treats energy assistance, a provision CBO estimated would reduce federal spending by $5.9 billion over ten years.
CL1247.supports: CRS Report R48552 lists the energy assistance provision among the SNAP changes in Public Law 119-21 with a CBO estimate of $5.9 billion in reduced budget authority over fiscal 2025 to 2034.
CL1247.limitation: The cited summary gives the provision's cost estimate without its full mechanics; CBO figures are projections made in 2025 before implementation.

CL1248.claim: Residential natural gas prices combine the commodity cost with the cost of moving gas by pipeline, and retail gas sales are regulated by states.
CL1248.supports: EIA explains that the consumer price of natural gas has two main components, the commodity cost and the cost of moving gas by pipeline, plus taxes and fees, and that state regulations are among the factors behind price differences; it refers consumers to the state public utility or service commission. FERC states that it does not regulate retail natural gas sales to consumers.
CL1248.limitation: Shares of each component vary with market conditions; municipal gas utilities may be outside state commission rate authority.

CL1249.claim: California's Public Utilities Commission processes rate change requests from the water utilities it regulates.
CL1249.supports: The California Public Utilities Commission's water page states that its Water Division investigates water and sewer system service quality issues, analyzes and processes utility rate change requests, and works with utility management to track and certify compliance with commission requirements.
CL1249.limitation: One state example; whether commissions in other states regulate investor-owned water utilities is outside this claim.

CL1250.claim: Former Ohio House Speaker Larry Householder was sentenced to 20 years for a $60 million bribery scheme funded by FirstEnergy to pass a $1 billion nuclear plant bailout, and FirstEnergy paid a $230 million penalty.
CL1250.supports: PBS NewsHour reported on June 29, 2023 that a federal judge sentenced Householder to 20 years after jurors found he orchestrated a $60 million bribery scheme secretly funded by FirstEnergy to pass a $1 billion bailout of two nuclear plants owned by a FirstEnergy affiliate. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Ohio announced on July 22, 2021 a deferred prosecution agreement with a $230 million penalty.
CL1250.jurisdiction: Ohio; federal court (Southern District of Ohio)
CL1250.limitation: A single state case; it documents one scheme and does not measure how often utility spending shapes energy laws elsewhere.

CL1251.claim: Low-income, Black, Hispanic, Native American and older adult households have higher energy burdens than the average household.
CL1251.supports: The American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy's 2020 report (Drehobl, Ross and Ayala) finds these groups face higher energy burdens, the share of income spent on energy bills, nationally, regionally and in all 25 metro areas studied, and names weatherization as a long-term way to reduce them.
CL1251.population: U.S. households in national data and 25 metro areas
CL1251.period: Published September 2020, using earlier survey data
CL1251.limitation: The report page states the direction of differences without burden percentages; the data predate recent price increases, and the organization advocates for efficiency programs.

CL1252.claim: In the 12 months to September 2026, the CPI for electricity rose 4.4%, utility gas service 5.0% and gasoline 34.2%.
CL1252.supports: The BLS Consumer Price Index release for September 2026 (October 14, 2026) reports the electricity index up 4.4%, the natural gas index up 5.0%, gasoline up 34.2% and energy overall up 20.4% over 12 months.
CL1252.limitation: National averages for urban consumers; regional electricity price changes differ widely, and one month's 12-month change can move with weather.

CL1253.claim: Congress passed a stopgap law on September 2, 2026 funding federal agencies through December 11, 2026.
CL1253.supports: The White House statement on H.R. 6500, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027, says the President signed it on September 2, 2026 and that it provides short-term fiscal 2027 funding to federal agencies through December 11, 2026, along with extensions of surface transportation and veterans programs.
CL1253.limitation: The statement does not name LIHEAP or say how the stopgap law treats LIHEAP funding during the stopgap period.

CL1200.claim: In 2024 farms received 11.8 cents of each U.S. food dollar, while salaries and benefits took 54.1 cents and property income 32.7 cents.
CL1200.supports: The ERS Food Dollar Series, updated March 10, 2026, reports a farm share of 11.8 cents in 2024, down from 12.1 cents in 2023. In the primary factor accounts, salaries and benefits rose to 54.1 cents from 52.0, property income fell to 32.7 cents from 34.5, and output taxes were 7.2 cents. Food services accounted for 38.6 cents.
CL1200.population: All U.S. food spending, at home and away from home
CL1200.limitation: Annual data with a lag; the series cannot show 2025 or 2026 cost changes. Property income combines profits with interest, rent and depreciation, so it does not measure profit margins alone.

CL1201.claim: In the 12 months to September 2026, the CPI for food at home rose 1.8%, food away from home 3.5%, fruits and vegetables 3.7%, and meats, poultry, fish and eggs 0.3%.
CL1201.supports: The BLS Consumer Price Index news release for September 2026, published October 14, 2026, reports all items up 3.7%, food up 2.5%, food at home up 1.8% and food away from home up 3.5% over 12 months, before seasonal adjustment, with the subindex changes listed.
CL1201.limitation: National averages; regional and store-level prices differ, and the index tracks a fixed national basket, which differs from any one household's purchases.

CL1202.claim: ERS reports food-at-home prices rose 2.3% in 2025 and forecasts a 2.4% rise in 2026.
CL1202.supports: The ERS Food Price Outlook of September 25, 2026 reports 2025 increases of 2.9% for all food, 2.3% for food at home and 3.8% for food away from home, and forecasts 2026 increases of 2.9%, 2.4% (prediction interval 1.8 to 3.0) and 3.5%.
CL1202.population: All U.S. food purchases tracked in the CPI
CL1202.limitation: The 2026 figures are statistical forecasts with prediction intervals and change monthly as new CPI data arrive.

CL1203.claim: Bird flu reduced egg-laying flocks, egg prices peaked at $6.23 a dozen in March 2025, and they averaged $2.27 in September 2026.
CL1203.supports: ERS states that the avian influenza outbreak that began in 2022 raised egg prices by reducing egg-layer flocks and production, that 2026 had fewer early detections than 2025, and forecasts egg prices 29.4% lower in 2026 after a 21.9% rise in 2025. BLS average price data show Grade A large eggs at $6.227 in March 2025 and $2.272 in September 2026.
CL1203.population: U.S. retail egg buyers; commercial layer flocks
CL1203.limitation: Average prices hide regional differences; BLS published no October 2025 value. The ERS statement links bird flu to prices without estimating how much of the price change it explains.

CL1204.claim: The U.S. cattle herd stood at 86.2 million head on January 1, 2026, beef output remains below year-earlier levels, and ERS forecasts beef and veal prices up 9.4% in 2026.
CL1204.supports: The NASS Cattle report of January 30, 2026 counts 86.2 million cattle and calves, with beef cows at 27.6 million, down 1%. ERS reports federally inspected beef production about 2% below a year earlier, expected to stay lower through 2026, and forecasts beef and veal prices up 9.4% (interval 7.4 to 11.6).
CL1204.population: U.S. cattle inventory; retail beef buyers
CL1204.period: January 2026 inventory; 2026 forecast as of September 2026
CL1204.limitation: Supply data do not by themselves show how much of the price rise comes from fewer cattle versus processor or retailer margins.

CL1205.claim: In 2026 constrained Middle East oil flows raised fuel prices: diesel averaged $6.29 a gallon in September 2026 and the gasoline CPI was up 34.2% from a year earlier.
CL1205.supports: EIA's Short-Term Energy Outlook of October 6, 2026 assumes Middle East oil flows stay constrained through the fourth quarter, with convoys through the Strait of Hormuz, and reports September averages of $4.35 for gasoline and $6.29 for diesel. The BLS September 2026 CPI release reports gasoline up 34.2% and energy up 20.4% over 12 months.
CL1205.limitation: Neither source measures how much higher diesel costs have passed into food prices; the food dollar data that would show it run only through 2024.

CL1206.claim: USDA announced up to $1 billion in February 2025 for poultry biosecurity, farmer relief and restocking, and vaccine research to address bird flu and egg prices.
CL1206.supports: The USDA release of February 26, 2025 lists up to $500 million for biosecurity with up to 75% cost sharing, up to $400 million for farmer relief and repopulation, up to $100 million for vaccines and therapeutics, and steps to expand temporary egg imports, alongside continued indemnity payments.
CL1206.limitation: The release states amounts as ceilings; it does not report how much was spent or evaluate effects on outbreaks or prices.

CL1207.claim: The Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize the President to impose tariffs.
CL1207.supports: The syllabus of Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, No. 24-1287, consolidated with Trump v. V.O.S. Selections, states that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. A law firm summary reports a 6-3 vote and that the Court treated tariffs as a taxing power belonging to Congress.
CL1207.limitation: The ruling addresses one statute; tariffs under Sections 122, 232 and 301 rest on other laws and were not decided in this case.

CL1208.claim: After the ruling, the administration imposed a temporary Section 122 tariff and, from July 24, 2026, Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on 60 economies, with exemptions that include products not producible in sufficient quantity in the United States.
CL1208.supports: A law firm analysis reports a 10% Section 122 tariff as a bridge, capped by statute at 15% for 150 days. USTR announced on July 23, 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies at 10% (17 economies, including Canada and Mexico) or 12.5%. The Federal Register notice sets the effective time as 12:01 a.m. on July 24, 2026 and lists exemption categories; a second law firm analysis reports 471 product exclusions including certain food and agricultural products.
CL1208.population: U.S. imports from the 60 investigated economies
CL1208.limitation: Product-level exemption lists sit in annexes to the notice, so the treatment of specific foods such as coffee or beef is not shown in the cited text. Section 301 actions can be challenged in court.

CL1209.claim: Imports supplied 59% of fresh fruit and 35% of fresh vegetables available in the United States in 2023.
CL1209.supports: An ERS Chart of Note (January 16, 2025) reports that the import share of fresh fruit availability grew from 50% in 2007 to 59% in 2023, and of fresh vegetables (excluding potatoes, sweet potatoes and mushrooms) from 20% to 35%.
CL1209.population: U.S. fresh fruit and vegetable supply
CL1209.limitation: Shares cover fresh produce only; processed foods and other categories have different import shares, and the data end in 2023.

CL1210.claim: Studies of the 2025 tariffs find that U.S. buyers bore about 90% of the cost, and they disagree on how quickly it reached consumer prices.
CL1210.supports: A Federal Reserve Bank of New York analysis of monthly product-level import data found U.S. importers bore 94% of tariff incidence in January to August 2025, 92% in September and October, and 86% in November. A Peterson Institute review found several 2026 studies implying about 90% borne by U.S. buyers; one study found complete consumer pass-through after about seven months, another incomplete pass-through after six months.
CL1210.limitation: The New York Fed estimate splits the burden between importers and foreign exporters and does not measure pass-through to consumers; it uses unit values as a proxy for prices, and the late-2025 shift rests on one month.

CL1211.claim: The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs in force in August 2026 cost the average household about $1,100 a year.
CL1211.supports: The Yale Budget Lab's State of U.S. Tariffs (August 24, 2026) reports an average statutory tariff rate of 11.0%, scheduled to reach 11.8% by year end, household costs of about $1,100 a year under current law, and an ultimate price level effect of about 0.7%. It notes Section 122 tariffs expired July 24 and were replaced under Section 301.
CL1211.limitation: A model estimate covering all goods; it does not report a food-specific figure, and results depend on assumptions about pass-through and substitution.

CL1212.claim: The four largest meatpacking firms buy about 85% of U.S. steers and heifers sold for slaughter.
CL1212.supports: An ERS Amber Waves article by James MacDonald (January 25, 2024) reports that the four largest firms handled 85% of steer and heifer purchases, up from 36% in 1980 and 81% in 1995.
CL1212.limitation: The article does not give the exact year of the 85% figure; national shares do not show competition in each regional cattle market.

CL1213.claim: Whether meatpacker concentration raises consumer beef prices is contested: scale savings lowered prices in earlier decades, while price spreads widened well beyond plant costs after 2015.
CL1213.supports: ERS summarizes 1990s and 2000s studies finding some packer market power that was more than offset by lower processing costs from larger plants, which lowered consumer prices. It reports that the spread between cattle and wholesale beef prices rose after 2016 to two or three times its earlier average, with only a small part explained by rising plant costs, and links this to high concentration and limited plant capacity.
CL1213.limitation: The spread includes both processing costs and profits, so it cannot isolate margins; the link to lost spare capacity is an interpretation, and planned new plants could add about 13% of 2022 capacity.

CL1214.claim: FTC staff reported that grocery retailers' revenues exceeded total costs by more than 6% in 2021 and 7% in early 2023, above the 2015 peak of 5.6%.
CL1214.supports: The FTC's March 21, 2024 release on its grocery supply chain report states that food and beverage retailer revenues rose to more than 6% over total costs in 2021 and 7% in the first three quarters of 2023, above the 2015 peak of 5.6%, and that some retailers used rising costs as an opportunity to raise prices further. The Commission voted 3-0 to issue it.
CL1214.limitation: Revenue over cost is an industry aggregate drawn from orders to eight companies and public data; it does not show which retailers or regions drove the change.

CL1215.claim: Research disagrees on how much higher markups drove recent inflation.
CL1215.supports: A Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Letter (May 13, 2024) found aggregate markups stayed essentially flat from 2020 to 2023 while core PCE prices rose more than 10%, though markups rose over 10% in some industries. Basu (2019) concludes that existing methods cannot determine whether markups have been stable or risen modestly.
CL1215.limitation: Economy-wide studies are not food-specific; the San Francisco Fed method assumes a stable share of costs going to inputs.

CL1216.claim: On June 30, 2026, the Justice Department and 17 states sued three egg producers, alleging coordinated bids to inflate a price benchmark, and filed proposed settlements that still require court approval.
CL1216.supports: The Justice Department release names Cal-Maine Foods, Hickman's Egg Ranch and Versova in a complaint in the Northern District of Iowa alleging coordination to inflate Urner Barry egg quotations, and says quotations fell sharply after the companies learned of the investigation in March 2025. Cal-Maine's quarterly report for the period ended August 29, 2026 says the settlement is proceeding through the Tunney Act, that it denied wrongdoing, and that it will pay $1.5 million to settling states.
CL1216.jurisdiction: United States (federal court, Northern District of Iowa)
CL1216.limitation: The complaint states allegations; no court has found a violation. Washington State did not join the settlement, which takes effect only when the court enters it.

CL1217.claim: News reports in September 2026 said the Justice Department asked eight grocery chains about beef pricing, extending an inquiry into the four largest meatpackers.
CL1217.supports: A Gray News report of September 3, 2026, citing Forbes, Reuters and a Justice Department post, says the Antitrust Division asked Ahold Delhaize USA, Albertsons, Aldi, Amazon, Costco, Kroger, Publix and Walmart to explain beef pricing, margins, costs and wholesale arrangements, after an inquiry announced in May into Cargill, Tyson Foods, JBS and National Beef.
CL1217.population: Large U.S. meatpackers and grocery chains
CL1217.limitation: Based on news reports without a department filing. An inquiry is a request for information and does not establish any violation.

CL1218.claim: Courts blocked the $24.6 billion Kroger and Albertsons merger in December 2024, and Albertsons ended the deal.
CL1218.supports: The FTC states that the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon granted a preliminary injunction on December 10, 2024 in a case the FTC brought over grocery prices and union workers' wages. A trade press report says a Washington state judge also blocked the merger that day and that Albertsons terminated the agreement on December 11 and sued Kroger for breach of contract.
CL1218.population: Kroger and Albertsons stores and workers
CL1218.jurisdiction: United States (federal court in Oregon; Washington state court)
CL1218.limitation: A preliminary injunction rests on likely harm; no study has measured prices in the markets where the companies would have combined.

CL1219.claim: SNAP maximum benefits are calculated each June from the cost of the Thrifty Food Plan and reset on October 1; the fiscal 2027 maximum for four people is $1,023.
CL1219.supports: The Food and Nutrition Service cost-of-living page states that maximum allotments are calculated from the Thrifty Food Plan cost every June and adjusted at the start of each fiscal year on October 1, and lists $1,023 for a household of four in the 48 states and D.C. from October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027. The August 21, 2026 USDA memo confirms the amount.
CL1219.population: SNAP households in the 48 contiguous states and D.C.
CL1219.limitation: Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the Virgin Islands have different amounts; most households receive less than the maximum because benefits fall as net income rises.

CL1220.claim: Public Law 119-21 caps Thrifty Food Plan revisions at inflation, extends SNAP work requirements to age 64, shifts costs to states, and was estimated to cut federal nutrition spending by about $187 billion over 10 years.
CL1220.supports: CRS Report R48552 describes state benefit cost shares from fiscal 2028 of 5% to 15% for payment error rates of 6% or more; federal reimbursement of administrative costs falling from 50% to 25% from fiscal 2027; time limits for adults 18 to 64 and parents of children 14 and older; and food plan revisions capped at inflation. CBO estimated ten-year savings of $186.65 billion, 2.4 million fewer participants from the work rules, and a $14 lower average benefit by 2034.
CL1220.limitation: CBO figures are projections made in 2025. CRS notes an internal inconsistency on the start year of administrative cost sharing; the enacted section says fiscal 2027.

CL1221.claim: SNAP averaged 42.1 million participants a month in fiscal 2025; preliminary data show 36.4 million in June 2026.
CL1221.supports: The FNS SNAP National View Summary, updated September 18, 2026, reports an FY2025 average of 42,145,499 persons with an average benefit of $189.36 per person, and preliminary June 2026 figures of 36,352,716 persons and $186.53.
CL1221.limitation: Fiscal 2026 data are preliminary and subject to revision; the counts do not identify whether rule changes, the economy or administrative factors caused the decline.

CL1222.claim: WIC served about 6.9 million people in fiscal 2025, at an average food cost of $64.89 per person per month, up from $61.07 in fiscal 2024.
CL1222.supports: The FNS WIC annual national summary reports participation of 6,704,000 in FY2024 and 6,867,000 in FY2025 (preliminary), average monthly food cost per person of $61.07 and $64.89, and total program cost of $7,793.6 million in FY2025.
CL1222.limitation: Fiscal 2025 figures are preliminary; food cost per person also changes with the mix of participants and food packages.

CL1223.claim: In 2024, 13.7% of U.S. households and 18.4% of households with children were food insecure.
CL1223.supports: ERS key statistics for Household Food Security in the United States in 2024 report that 13.7% of households (18.3 million) were food insecure at some time during 2024, and 18.4% of households with children (6.7 million).
CL1223.limitation: Annual survey measure from the Current Population Survey supplement; 2024 is the latest year reported.

CL1224.claim: Congress assigned the Federal Reserve goals of maximum employment and stable prices, and its tools work by moving the federal funds rate.
CL1224.supports: The Federal Reserve's FAQ states that Congress assigned it the goals of maximum employment and stable prices and that it judges 2% inflation over the longer run, measured by the PCE price index, most consistent with price stability. Its FOMC page says the Committee is responsible for open market operations and that the Fed's tools alter the federal funds rate, the overnight lending rate between banks.
CL1224.limitation: The sources describe goals and tools; how quickly rate changes affect food prices is outside what they report.

CL1225.claim: The Trade Review Act of 2025 (S. 1272) would end new tariffs after 60 days unless Congress approves them; it remained in the Senate Finance Committee as of October 15, 2026.
CL1225.supports: The bill text adds Section 155 to the Trade Act of 1974, requiring notice to Congress within 48 hours of imposing or increasing a duty, a 60-day limit absent a joint resolution of approval, and expedited disapproval resolutions, excluding antidumping and countervailing duties. It was introduced April 3, 2025 by Sen. Cantwell with Sens. Grassley, Moran, Klobuchar, Murkowski, Warner, McConnell and Bennet. A legislative tracker lists referral to the Finance Committee on April 3, 2025 as the latest action.
CL1225.period: Introduced April 3, 2025; status as of October 15, 2026
CL1225.limitation: Status comes from a private tracker summarizing congressional actions; companion House bills and other legislative approaches are outside this claim.

CL1300.claim: In 2025, 7.9% of people in the United States, 26.7 million, were uninsured for the whole year, and 53.5% had job-based coverage at some point.
CL1300.supports: The Census Bureau's 2025 report finds 26.7 million people (7.9%) uninsured for the entire year, not statistically different from 2024. Employment-based coverage covered 53.5% of people for some or all of the year, Medicaid 17.1% (down 0.5 points) and Medicare 20.1%.
CL1300.limitation: Full-year uninsured counts miss people who lacked coverage for part of the year, and 2025 data predate the 2026 marketplace enrollment drop.

CL1301.claim: Job-based family coverage averaged $26,993 a year in 2025, workers paid $6,850 of it, and 67% of covered workers were in self-funded plans.
CL1301.supports: KFF's 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey reports average family premiums of $26,993, up 6% from 2024, with an average worker contribution of $6,850; single premiums averaged $9,325. Sixty-seven percent of covered workers were in self-funded plans, including 80% at larger firms and 27% at firms with 10 to 199 workers.
CL1301.population: Covered workers at firms with 10 or more employees
CL1301.limitation: Survey of employers. The 2026 survey is scheduled for release on October 22, 2026.

CL1302.claim: Self-funded employer plans are exempt from state insurance regulation under ERISA, while states regulate insurance policies that employers buy.
CL1302.supports: The NAIC explains that ERISA preempts most state laws relating to employee benefit plans, that the deemer clause stops states from treating self-funded plans as insurers, and that the savings clause lets states regulate insurance, so insured plans face indirect state regulation. The Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration enforces Title I.
CL1302.limitation: Summary by an association of state regulators; specific state laws can still reach self-funded plans in narrow areas decided by courts.

CL1303.claim: COBRA lets workers at employers with 20 or more employees keep their plan, usually for up to 18 months, at up to 102% of its cost.
CL1303.supports: CMS guidance states that employers with 20 or more employees generally must offer COBRA, that coverage after job loss or reduced hours generally lasts up to 18 months (36 in some cases), that premiums cannot exceed 102% of plan cost, and that people have 60 days after losing coverage or receiving the notice, whichever is later, to elect it.
CL1303.population: Workers and dependents in group health plans of employers with 20 or more employees
CL1303.period: Federal law in force; guidance dated 2022 and 2025
CL1303.limitation: Some states require continuation coverage for smaller employers; those state laws are not summarized here.

CL1304.claim: Losing job-based coverage opens a 60-day window to enroll in a marketplace plan, and ending COBRA early outside open enrollment generally does not.
CL1304.supports: CMS guidance says people have 60 days before or after losing job-based coverage to enroll in a marketplace plan, and that voluntarily dropping coverage does not qualify for a special enrollment period. A CMS presentation adds that ending COBRA early outside open enrollment does not allow a switch unless another special enrollment period applies.
CL1304.limitation: State-run marketplaces can set some of their own enrollment procedures, so deadlines and documentation rules may differ outside HealthCare.gov.

CL1305.claim: After the larger premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, marketplace enrollment fell about 13% and enrollees' premium payments rose sharply.
CL1305.supports: KFF reported that the enhanced credits expired at the end of 2025 with no extension enacted as of October 6, 2026. Enrollment fell from 22.1 million in 2025 to 19.2 million in February 2026. Keeping the same plan raised premium payments 114% on average; after switching, net payments rose 58% and deductibles 37%. Insurers sought a median increase of about 15% for 2027. Only New Mexico, which used state subsidies, avoided a decline.
CL1305.period: 2025 to February 2026 enrollment; status checked October 15, 2026
CL1305.limitation: Before-and-after comparison; other rule changes took effect in 2026. KFF's October brief gives 21.8 million for 2025, a different enrollment measure.

CL1306.claim: Open enrollment for 2027 coverage on HealthCare.gov runs from November 1, 2026 to January 15, 2027.
CL1306.supports: HealthCare.gov lists November 1 as the first day to enroll for 2027 coverage, December 15 as the last day for coverage starting January 1, and January 15 as the end of open enrollment, with coverage from February 1 for plans chosen December 16 through January 15.
CL1306.limitation: State-run marketplaces publish their own open enrollment dates, which can start or end on different days than HealthCare.gov.

CL1307.claim: The 2025 budget law requires full repayment of excess premium credits from tax year 2026 and narrows immigrant eligibility for Medicaid in October 2026 and for marketplace credits in 2027.
CL1307.supports: KFF's summary of Public Law 119-21 lists: full repayment of excess advance credits for tax years after 2025; no credits for enrollees using an income-based special enrollment period from plan year 2026; Medicaid and CHIP eligibility limited mainly to lawful permanent residents, certain Cuban and Haitian entrants and COFA migrants from October 1, 2026; the same limit on marketplace credits from January 1, 2027; and pre-enrollment verification from 2028.
CL1307.period: Statute enacted July 4, 2025; effective dates 2026 to 2028
CL1307.limitation: Some related administrative rules are on hold in litigation, according to KFF's October 2026 brief.

CL1308.claim: More than 25 million people were disenrolled from Medicaid when pandemic continuous coverage ended, 69% for procedural reasons, and automatic renewal rates varied widely by state.
CL1308.supports: KFF's tracker counts at least 25,198,000 disenrollments as of September 12, 2024, with 69% terminated for procedural reasons such as incomplete paperwork. A separate KFF analysis found the share of renewals completed automatically from existing data (ex parte) ranged from 90% or more in Arizona, North Carolina and Rhode Island to 11% or less in Pennsylvania and Texas.
CL1308.limitation: State-reported data with differing time periods; some people disenrolled for procedural reasons were later found ineligible or re-enrolled.

CL1309.claim: Starting no later than January 1, 2027, Medicaid expansion adults aged 19 to 64 must show 80 hours a month of work or other qualifying activity unless exempt.
CL1309.supports: CMS's June 1, 2026 interim final rule requires 80 hours a month of qualifying activity, or income of at least 80 times the federal minimum wage ($580 a month in 2026), for adults in the expansion group or similar waivers in 43 states and D.C. Exemptions include pregnant or postpartum people, the medically frail and parents of children 13 and under. CRS reports states may start earlier and can receive good-faith exemptions lasting no later than December 31, 2028.
CL1309.limitation: The statute says the requirement applies beginning December 31, 2026, while CMS's rule states January 1, 2027; implementation details vary by state.

CL1310.claim: The 2025 law requires Medicaid renewals every six months for expansion adults starting with renewals on or after December 31, 2026.
CL1310.supports: KFF's section summary of Public Law 119-21 lists six-month redeterminations for expansion adults (section 71107) for renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026, shorter retroactive coverage from January 1, 2027, and new cost sharing for some expansion adults from October 1, 2028.
CL1310.limitation: This is KFF's summary of the statute. CMS guidance on how states must conduct six-month renewals is not summarized here.

CL1311.claim: Nebraska and Montana began work requirements early, and most states had to send outreach notices in September 2026.
CL1311.supports: KFF reports that Nebraska and Montana had already implemented work requirements and sent notices before the federal rule was published. The law requires notices three months before the first lookback month, so most states that look back one month at application had to send notices in September 2026, and states with three-month lookbacks such as Idaho and Indiana in July.
CL1311.limitation: Based on state announcements compiled by KFF; state start dates and lookback choices can change before the federal deadline.

CL1312.claim: CBO estimated the 2025 budget law would increase the uninsured population by 10 million in 2034, including 5.3 million from the Medicaid work requirement.
CL1312.supports: The Congressional Budget Office's August 11, 2025 estimates, summarized by Georgetown University's Center for Children and Families, project 10 million more uninsured people in 2034 from the law. Before interactions, the work requirement accounts for 5.3 million and more frequent redeterminations for 700,000. Earlier CBO estimates found expiration of the enhanced credits would add 4.2 million uninsured by 2034.
CL1312.limitation: CBO projections depend on assumptions about state implementation and enrollee behavior; the summary comes from a policy center that supports Medicaid coverage.

CL1313.claim: When Arkansas required monthly work reporting in 2018, coverage fell and uninsurance rose among adults aged 30 to 49 without a measurable gain in employment.
CL1313.supports: A peer-reviewed survey study compared Arkansas with three other states. Medicaid or marketplace coverage among Arkansans aged 30 to 49 fell from 70.5% in 2016 to 63.7% in 2018, and the uninsured rate rose from 10.5% to 14.6%. Work and hours did not change significantly. Coverage partly recovered after a court blocked the policy in 2019; 49.8% of those who lost coverage reported serious problems paying medical debt.
CL1313.jurisdiction: Arkansas compared with Kentucky, Louisiana and Texas
CL1313.limitation: Survey data from one state; Arkansas required online reporting, and the 2025 federal law allows more data matching.

CL1314.claim: In a randomized experiment, reminder letters raised marketplace enrollment by 16%, and the added enrollees were healthier on average.
CL1314.supports: Researchers randomly varied letters to about 87,000 households in Covered California. Deadline reminders raised enrollment by 1.3 percentage points, a 16% increase, and lowered average spending risk by 5.1%, with the largest effects among low-income households.
CL1314.population: Uninsured households eligible for Covered California
CL1314.period: Field experiment, 2015 to 2016 enrollment period (paper issued 2019)
CL1314.limitation: One state marketplace; letters tested were inexpensive nudges and do not measure the effect of full automatic enrollment.

CL1315.claim: Removing automatic enrollment from a subsidized insurance program reduced enrollment by 33%, mostly among young, healthy and lower-income people.
CL1315.supports: Shepard and Wagner study the end of automatic enrollment in a subsidized exchange and find that adding the extra step reduced enrollment by 33%, with losses concentrated among young, healthy and economically disadvantaged people.
CL1315.population: Low-income people eligible for subsidized coverage
CL1315.period: Working paper issued December 2022, revised August 2024
CL1315.limitation: Quasi-experimental working paper from one subsidized program; effects of automatic processes in Medicaid renewals were not tested.

CL1316.claim: Since plan year 2025, HealthCare.gov plans must offer routine primary care within 15 business days and behavioral health care within 10 business days at least 90% of the time.
CL1316.supports: CMS technical guidance sets appointment wait-time standards for qualified health plans sold through HealthCare.gov starting January 1, 2025: 10 business days for behavioral health, 15 for routine primary care and 30 for non-urgent specialty care, met at least 90% of the time. Issuers must hire an independent firm to run secret shopper surveys.
CL1316.limitation: State-regulated and self-funded plans follow different standards; no published results show how many plans meet them.

CL1317.claim: A 2024 federal rule set appointment wait-time standards for Medicaid managed care, with annual secret shopper surveys.
