CL1317.supports: CMS's April 2024 final rule sets maximum waits of 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use services and 15 business days for routine primary care and for obstetric and gynecological care, and requires states to use an independent entity for annual secret shopper surveys of compliance and directory accuracy.
CL1317.period: Final rule issued April 22, 2024; standards phased in over later years
CL1317.limitation: Exact compliance dates follow a separate CMS applicability chart, which is not summarized here.

CL1318.claim: In a 2023 Senate Finance Committee staff test, callers got appointments with 18% of listed mental health providers in Medicare Advantage plans.
CL1318.supports: Majority staff called 120 listed providers, 10 from each of 12 Medicare Advantage plans in six states. They secured appointments in 22 calls (18%), or 13% after excluding six calls routed to a matching service; 33% of listings had wrong or non-working numbers or unreturned calls. The report counts more than 80% of listings as inaccurate or unavailable.
CL1318.population: Listed behavioral health providers in 12 Medicare Advantage plans
CL1318.limitation: Small sample prepared by committee majority staff; it is not a representative survey of all plans.

CL1319.claim: A 2025 survey of doctors' offices in 15 large metro areas found an average wait of 31 days for a new-patient appointment and 53% acceptance of Medicaid.
CL1319.supports: AMN Healthcare's survey reached 1,391 offices in six specialties across 15 metro areas from January to February 2025. The average wait was 31 days, up from 26 days in 2022 and 21 days in 2004. Fifty-three percent of offices accepted Medicaid and 82% accepted Medicare.
CL1319.limitation: Run by a health care staffing company; offices were found through online listings, and only 1,391 of 3,656 contacted were reached.

CL1320.claim: Medicaid paid physicians about 75% of Medicare rates in 2024, and 66% for primary care.
CL1320.supports: The Urban Institute's survey of state Medicaid fee schedules, published by KFF, shows a national Medicaid-to-Medicare fee index of 0.75 for all services and 0.66 for primary care in 2024. States ranged from 0.52 in Rhode Island to 1.32 in Montana.
CL1320.limitation: Covers fee-for-service rates; most Medicaid enrollees are in managed care plans, which can pay different rates.

CL1321.claim: As of December 31, 2025, 92.3 million people lived in primary care shortage areas where available physicians met about 48% of need.
CL1321.supports: HRSA's quarterly summary, published by KFF, lists 8,467 primary care Health Professional Shortage Area designations covering 92,285,375 people, with 48% of need met and 15,604 practitioners needed to remove the designations.
CL1321.population: People in designated primary care shortage areas
CL1321.limitation: Designations can overlap, so some people may be counted more than once; the ratio method (3,500 people per physician) is a federal convention.

CL1322.claim: Medicare-funded residency positions were capped in 1997; Congress added 1,000 in 2021, and by September 2025 CMS had allocated 600, nearly all to urban hospitals.
CL1322.supports: A medical education journal notes resident caps set by the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 and that the 2021 law added the first new positions since then. GAO reports CMS is distributing 1,000 positions over five years, had allocated 600 by September 2025, mostly to hospitals in urban areas, and that Medicare paid about $22 billion for residency training at over 1,400 hospitals in 2023.
CL1322.limitation: Residency counts do not show where graduates practice; GAO did not assess effects on access.

CL1323.claim: State laws letting nurse practitioners practice independently were followed by more routine checkups and fewer avoidable emergency visits.
CL1323.supports: Traczynski and Udalova use differences in when states passed these laws and find that independence increased routine checkups and reduced emergency room use for conditions that good primary care can manage, which they attribute to lower administrative and access costs.
CL1323.population: Patients in states that changed nurse practitioner rules
CL1323.period: Laws passed over several decades; published 2018
CL1323.limitation: One quasi-experimental study; it measures use of care more than clinical outcomes, and other settings show different results.

CL1324.claim: In Veterans Health Administration emergency departments, nurse practitioners used more resources and had higher preventable hospitalization rates than physicians on average.
CL1324.supports: Chan and Chen use quasi-experimental assignment of patients in VA emergency departments and find nurse practitioners use more resources and have a higher 30-day preventable hospitalization rate on average, though nurse practitioners outperform physicians in 38% of random pairs.
CL1324.limitation: Emergency care in one health system; results may not apply to primary care offices where most scope-of-practice debates focus.

CL1325.claim: Researchers at the University of North Carolina count 197 rural hospital closures and conversions since 2005.
CL1325.supports: The Sheps Center lists 197 rural hospitals since January 2005: 109 complete closures and 88 converted closures that stopped inpatient care but kept some services. Conversions to Rural Emergency Hospitals are not counted as closures.
CL1325.limitation: Counts exclude Rural Emergency Hospital conversions, which also end inpatient care, so the total understates lost inpatient capacity.

CL1326.claim: After rural hospitals closed between 2013 and 2017, the median distance to inpatient care rose from 3.4 miles to 23.9 miles.
CL1326.supports: GAO analyzed 64 rural hospitals that closed from 2013 to 2017. Median travel distance for general inpatient care rose from 3.4 miles in 2012 to 23.9 miles in 2018, and for alcohol or drug treatment from 5.5 to 44.6 miles. Physicians per 100,000 residents in closure counties fell from 71.2 to 59.7.
CL1326.population: Residents of areas served by closed rural hospitals
CL1326.limitation: Closure counties already had fewer clinicians before closing, so GAO's comparison does not isolate the closure's effect.

CL1327.claim: The Rural Health Transformation Program provides $50 billion to states over fiscal years 2026 to 2030, and the statute required CMS to decide state applications by December 31, 2025.
CL1327.supports: CMS states the program allocates $10 billion a year from fiscal year 2026 through 2030, half split equally among approved states and half by CMS formula. States must use funds for at least three of ten uses, including clinician recruitment with five-year rural service commitments. State-by-state announcements from October 7 to 14, 2026 include about $209 million for Iowa and $177 million for Nebraska.
CL1327.limitation: The program is new and has not been evaluated. The October 2026 announcements cover individual states and give no national total.

CL1328.claim: Ten states have not expanded Medicaid, leaving about 1.2 million adults with incomes too high for Medicaid and too low for marketplace subsidies.
CL1328.supports: KFF counts 41 states, including D.C., that have adopted the expansion and 10 that have not. It estimates 1.2 million adults in the coverage gap in those states, using 2024 American Community Survey data and 2025 eligibility levels. Georgia and Wisconsin have no gap because waivers cover adults up to the poverty line.
CL1328.period: Status as of October 1, 2026; estimate from 2024 data
CL1328.limitation: The coverage gap figure is a model-based estimate of eligibility from survey data, not a count of enrollees.

CL1329.claim: In 2025, 26% of adults said they skipped medical expenses because of cost.
CL1329.supports: The Federal Reserve's survey, fielded in October 2025, reports that 26% of adults skipped medical expenses in the prior year because of cost, down from 28% in 2024. About 21% had a major unexpected medical expense in the prior 12 months.
CL1329.limitation: Self-reported; the measure combines several kinds of medical expense and does not separate insured from uninsured adults in this summary.

CL1330.claim: A denied claim can go to external review by an independent reviewer, and the insurer must accept the decision.
CL1330.supports: HealthCare.gov states that external review is run through a state process meeting federal standards or an HHS-administered process, that requests must be filed within 4 months of a final denial, that insurers must accept the reviewer's decision, and that expedited reviews are decided within 72 hours and standard reviews within 45 days.
CL1330.population: People in non-grandfathered private health plans
CL1330.period: Federal standards in force, checked October 15, 2026
CL1330.limitation: Medicaid, Medicare and some grandfathered plans follow separate appeal processes with different deadlines and reviewers.

CL1331.claim: Since January 1, 2024, Medicaid and CHIP must provide 12 months of continuous eligibility for children under 19.
CL1331.supports: CMS's State Health Official letter #23-004 explains that section 5112 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 requires states to provide 12 months of continuous eligibility for children under 19 in both Medicaid and CHIP, effective January 1, 2024.
CL1331.limitation: The letter describes the rule and its exceptions; it does not measure effects on coverage.

CL1100.claim: Home prices exceed construction costs in many U.S. areas by more than the harms of new building would justify, a gap economists attribute to regulation.
CL1100.supports: Glaeser and Gyourko compare market prices with the cost of producing housing and treat the gap as an implicit regulatory tax. Their review concludes that the available evidence suggests this tax is higher in many areas than any reasonable estimate of the negative effects of new construction.
CL1100.limitation: The authors say the evidence suggests this result without definitively proving it, and the size of the gap varies by area.

CL1101.claim: Published estimates of the U.S. housing shortage range from 3.7 million to 5.5 million homes.
CL1101.supports: A Congressional Research Service Insight dated December 15, 2025 compares estimates from Freddie Mac (3.7 million, third quarter of 2024), Up for Growth (3.85 million, 2022), Zillow (4.7 million, 2023), Brookings (4.9 million, fourth quarter of 2023) and the National Association of Realtors (5.5 million, 2020).
CL1101.limitation: Methods differ, including target vacancy rates from 5% to 12%. CRS notes there is no universal agreement that a national shortage exists, and national totals do not show where shortages are.

CL1102.claim: People who speak at local planning and zoning meetings are disproportionately older, male, longtime residents and homeowners, and they oppose new housing more than the public does.
CL1102.supports: Einstein, Glick and Palmer coded thousands of instances of residents speaking at planning and zoning board meetings about housing development and matched speakers to a voter file. Speakers were disproportionately older, male, longtime residents, local voters and homeowners, and they overwhelmingly opposed new housing, to a much greater degree than the general public.
CL1102.population: Speakers at planning and zoning meetings in the municipalities studied
CL1102.limitation: The sample covers the municipalities whose meeting minutes were coded, and speaking at a meeting is one of several ways residents influence decisions.

CL1103.claim: Holding local elections on the November ballot generally doubles local turnout and makes the electorate more representative by race, age and partisanship.
CL1103.supports: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian summarize prior research showing that on-cycle November elections generally double local turnout compared with stand-alone local contests. Using California election timing and voter microtargeting data, they find on-cycle electorates considerably more representative in race, age and partisanship, most of all when local contests coincide with a presidential election.
CL1103.population: Local electorates; composition analysis of California cities
CL1103.jurisdiction: United States; California for the composition analysis
CL1103.limitation: The study measures who votes. It does not measure whether zoning decisions or rents change after elections move on-cycle.

CL1104.claim: The Federal Open Market Committee sets the short-term policy rate, and expectations about that rate affect longer-term rates, including mortgage rates.
CL1104.supports: The Federal Reserve Board explains that monetary policy decisions are made at Federal Open Market Committee meetings, that revisions to expected short-term rates can affect longer-term interest rates, and that easier policy brings lower mortgage rates, which make buying a house more affordable and encourage refinancing.
CL1104.limitation: The explainer describes the channel in general terms and does not estimate how much of any change in mortgage rates comes from Fed policy.

CL1105.claim: The monthly payment on a median-priced home nearly doubled from the end of 2020 to late 2025, and the average 30-year mortgage rate exceeded 7% in October 2026.
CL1105.supports: JCHS reports a payment of $2,420 on the median-priced home in the fourth quarter of 2025 against $1,240 at the end of 2020, with the 30-year fixed rate at 7.04% in January 2025 and 6.23% in the fourth quarter. Freddie Mac's weekly survey showed a 7.40% average on October 15, 2026, against 6.27% a year earlier.
CL1105.population: Buyers of a median-priced U.S. home with a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage
CL1105.limitation: The payment estimate assumes a standard loan and down payment; actual payments vary with price, down payment, taxes and insurance. The weekly rate is a survey average.

CL1106.claim: Mortgage rate lock-in reduced home sales and raised prices; an FHFA staff estimate puts the effect at 1.33 million fewer sales from mid-2022 through 2023 and 5.7% higher prices.
CL1106.supports: An FHFA staff working paper finds that each percentage point by which market rates exceed a borrower's original rate lowers the probability of sale by 18.1%. It estimates that lock-in prevented 1.33 million sales from the second quarter of 2022 to the fourth quarter of 2023 and raised prices 5.7%, outweighing a 3.3% direct price decline from higher rates.
CL1106.period: Second quarter of 2022 to fourth quarter of 2023
CL1106.limitation: The magnitudes come from one staff working paper, which states the authors' views. Existing-home sales near 30-year lows in 2024 and 2025 are consistent with the finding.

CL1107.claim: Half of outstanding U.S. mortgages carried interest rates below 4% in late 2025.
CL1107.supports: JCHS, citing the National Mortgage Database, reports that half of all outstanding mortgages had an interest rate below 4 percent in late 2025, when the average rate on new 30-year fixed loans was 6.23%. JCHS also reports existing-home sales of 4.1 million in 2025, two-thirds of the 6.1 million sold in 2021.
CL1107.limitation: The share falls over time as owners sell or refinance, and it does not show how many owners would sell at lower rates.

CL1108.claim: Prices of inputs to residential construction rose 40% from January 2020 to spring 2026.
CL1108.supports: JCHS reports, from Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price data, that the price of combined inputs to residential construction rose 40 percent since January 2020, with gypsum up 47 percent and steel mill products up 84 percent through April 2026.
CL1108.population: Inputs used in U.S. residential construction
CL1108.limitation: Input price indexes leave out land and financing costs, which also shape whether projects proceed, and costs vary by region.

CL1109.claim: A record wave of apartment completions in 2024 coincided with flat to falling asking rents and a 7.3% rental vacancy rate by 2026.
CL1109.supports: JCHS reports 608,000 multifamily completions in 2024, the most since 1986, and a 20% decline to 483,700 in 2025, with starts up 17% to 416,100. Asking rents for professionally managed apartments fell 0.5% year over year in the first quarter of 2026 while remaining 29% above 2020. Census put rental vacancy at 7.3% in the second quarter of 2026.
CL1109.population: U.S. rental market; professionally managed apartments for asking rents
CL1109.limitation: Asking-rent data come from RealPage and cover professionally managed buildings. The timing shows an association; changes in demand also affected rents.

CL1110.claim: A federal court entered a final judgment on May 19, 2026 barring RealPage from using competitors' nonpublic data in live rent pricing, and on September 30, 2026 allowed the states' claims against RealPage and several landlords to proceed.
CL1110.supports: The Justice Department's response to public comments describes the terms: no competitors' nonpublic data in runtime pricing, training only on data at least 12 months old, limits on geographic detail, a monitor, and no financial penalty sought. The court's September 30 opinion says the judgment lasts seven years, does not bind the states and leaves their plausibly pleaded Sherman Act claims alive.
CL1110.jurisdiction: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina
CL1110.limitation: A ruling that claims are plausibly alleged is not a finding of liability. The judgment contains no admission and does not show how much rents changed.

CL1111.claim: Algorithmic rent pricing made adopting buildings more responsive to market conditions and, by one estimate, added about $25 per unit per month through coordination.
CL1111.supports: Calder-Wang and Kim find that buildings using pricing software lowered rents faster than non-adopters in downturns, while in recoveries markets with more adoption had higher rents and lower occupancy. Their structural tests favor joint profit maximization among adopters of the same software, with an estimated markup of about $25 per unit per month across about 4.2 million units.
CL1111.limitation: An unpublished working paper; the markup comes from a structural model, and the same data show efficiency gains. Estimates of the rent effect of shared pricing software vary.

CL1112.claim: GAO's review of 74 studies found that institutional investors may have contributed to higher home prices and rents in some areas, with unclear effects on homeownership and tenants.
CL1112.supports: GAO reports that studies found institutional investors may have contributed to increasing home prices and rents and helped stabilize neighborhoods after the financial crisis. Effects on homeownership opportunities and on tenants, such as eviction rates, were unclear. Data are limited, and there is no consistent definition of an institutional investor.
CL1112.population: Single-family rental markets in the studies reviewed
CL1112.jurisdiction: United States, concentrated in Sunbelt metro areas
CL1112.limitation: GAO summarized existing studies and did not estimate effects itself; findings vary by metro area and by how investors are defined.

CL1113.claim: In six metro areas, investors owning at least 5,000 single-family homes held 4% to 22% of single-family rentals and at most 3% of all single-family homes in 2024.
CL1113.supports: GAO's March 2026 study of Cincinnati, Dallas, Jacksonville, Nashville, Phoenix and Seattle found investor holdings rose from 2018 to 2024, with the largest gains in 2021 to 2023. Investors owned 4% (Seattle) to 22% (Jacksonville) of single-family rentals and under 1% (Cincinnati and Seattle) to 3% of all single-family homes.
CL1113.jurisdiction: Cincinnati, Dallas, Jacksonville, Nashville, Phoenix and Seattle metro areas
CL1113.limitation: GAO calls the sample nongeneralizable, and its definition counts only investors with 5,000 or more homes in at least five metro areas.

CL1114.claim: Public Law 119-101, enacted July 11, 2026, bars entities controlling 350 or more single-family homes from buying more, with exceptions and no requirement to sell homes already owned.
CL1114.supports: The enacted 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act includes Section 1001 on large institutional investors. Law firm summaries report a 350-home threshold, exceptions for build-to-rent, renovation, homes held for sale and foreclosure-related acquisitions, no divestiture requirement, Treasury rules in consultation with HUD and the SEC, and civil penalties per violation.
CL1114.population: For-profit entities and funds controlling single-family homes
CL1114.limitation: Details of Section 1001 come from law firm summaries, which differ on when the ban takes effect; Treasury rules will set implementation.

CL1115.claim: Executive Order 14376 directs federal housing agencies and the mortgage enterprises to stop arranging sales of single-family homes to large institutional investors.
CL1115.supports: The order, signed January 20, 2026 and published at 91 FR 3023, directs Treasury to define a large institutional investor within 30 days and directs Agriculture, HUD, Veterans Affairs, GSA and FHFA to issue guidance within 60 days limiting sales and transfers of federally held or backed single-family homes to such investors, with build-to-rent exceptions. It also asks DOJ and the FTC to review large acquisitions.
CL1115.limitation: The order does not bar private purchases and creates no enforceable private rights; its effect depends on agency guidance.

CL1116.claim: New York and California enacted laws in October 2025 restricting rent-setting through coordinating algorithms, and at least eight cities adopted local bans in 2024 and 2025.
CL1116.supports: New York's S7882, signed as Chapter 437 on October 16, 2025, makes it unlawful to help competing landlords coordinate through software or to set rents on such recommendations. California's AB 325, signed October 6, 2025, amends the Cartwright Act on common pricing algorithms. A law firm review lists ordinances in San Francisco, Philadelphia, Minneapolis, Jersey City, Providence, San Diego, Hoboken and Seattle.
CL1116.population: Residential landlords and pricing software vendors
CL1116.jurisdiction: New York, California and eight cities
CL1116.limitation: Enactment is documented; effects on rents are not yet measured, and Berkeley delayed its ban after RealPage sued.

CL1117.claim: About one in four renter households with incomes at or below half the area median receives a federal housing subsidy, leaving 13.8 million income-eligible households unassisted in 2023.
CL1117.supports: JCHS reports that only about one in four renter households in HUD's lowest income category, at or below half the area median, receive a housing subsidy and that 13.8 million income-eligible households were unassisted as of 2023. It also reports that voucher funding rose 7 percent in 2026 appropriations, while public housing is not expanding.
CL1117.population: U.S. renter households with incomes at or below half the area median
CL1117.limitation: Eligibility counts depend on HUD income limits, and the figures do not show how many households applied or wait on lists.

CL1118.claim: A 2025 federal tax law permanently raised annual 9% LIHTC allocations by 12% starting in 2026 and lowered the bond-financing test for 4% credit projects from 50% to 25%.
CL1118.supports: Moss Adams describes the One Big Beautiful Bill Act changes: a permanent 12% increase in 9% allocation authority beginning in 2026 and a reduction of the bond test from 50% to 25% of aggregate basis for bonds issued in 2026 or later. JCHS reports the expansion could support about 1.2 million new units by 2035.
CL1118.limitation: The 1.2 million figure is a projection. Moss Adams expects the 9% increase alone to shift production little, with most added output depending on the bond-test change.

CL1119.claim: An eviction order increases homelessness and hospital visits and lowers earnings and access to credit.
CL1119.supports: Collinson and coauthors use eviction cases randomly assigned to judges of varying leniency in Cook County and New York City. They find that an eviction order increases homelessness and hospital visits and reduces earnings, durable goods consumption and access to credit in the first two years, with longer-run increases in debt and lower credit scores.
CL1119.jurisdiction: Cook County, Illinois, and New York City
CL1119.limitation: Results come from two large urban court systems and may differ where eviction procedures or housing markets differ.

CL1120.claim: In the second quarter of 2026, 35.2% of householders under 35 owned their homes, against 78.6% of those 65 and older, and ownership was 45.4% for Black, 48.1% for Hispanic and 74.5% for non-Hispanic White householders.
CL1120.supports: Census Housing Vacancies and Homeownership data for the second quarter of 2026, released July 28, 2026, report a national homeownership rate of 65.0% with these rates by age and race. JCHS reports that the Black-White ownership gap was 28.7 percentage points in 2025, wider than the 28.0-point gap in 1995.
CL1120.period: Second quarter of 2026; 1995 and 2025 for the gap
CL1120.limitation: Quarterly survey estimates carry sampling error, and JCHS annual figures differ slightly from quarterly ones.

CL1121.claim: Massachusetts listed 157 municipalities as compliant with its MBTA Communities multifamily zoning law as of August 27, 2026.
CL1121.supports: The Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities' list of district approval letters, dated August 27, 2026, places 157 municipalities under compliant municipalities, and several determination letters set conditions for continued compliance.
CL1121.population: Massachusetts municipalities subject to the MBTA Communities law
CL1121.limitation: Compliance means zoning that allows multifamily housing; it does not show how many homes have been permitted or built.

CL1122.claim: Massachusetts Question 7, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would allow single-family homes on residential lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of frontage and public water and sewer.
CL1122.supports: The Secretary of the Commonwealth's voter information describes Question 7 as a law proposed by initiative petition. It would allow single-family homes on such lots, while cities and towns could still reasonably regulate height, setbacks, open space, parking and short-term rentals, and the state housing office could issue guidance or regulations.
CL1122.limitation: The voter information describes the measure's text; it does not estimate how many homes would be built.

CL1123.claim: Oregon (2019) and Washington (2023) passed laws requiring cities to allow duplexes or other middle housing in areas zoned for detached homes.
CL1123.supports: Oregon's HB 2001 (Chapter 639, 2019) requires cities over 10,000 people or within Metro to allow duplexes, and cities over 25,000 and Metro jurisdictions to permit middle housing within urban growth boundaries. Washington's HB 1110, signed May 8, 2023 as Chapter 332, increases middle housing in areas traditionally dedicated to single-family detached housing.
CL1123.limitation: The bill records document enactment; they do not show how many homes have been built under these laws.

CL1124.claim: The 2026 federal housing law offers grants and nonbinding zoning guidelines and bars HUD from preempting local zoning.
CL1124.supports: Public Law 119-101 directs HUD to publish nonbinding Housing Supply Frameworks and bars adverse action against localities that decline them (Section 107). It creates an Innovation Fund for places that have increased housing supply while barring HUD from mandating, superseding or preempting local zoning or land use policy (Section 208).
CL1124.limitation: Section 1202 authorizes no additional funds, so grant amounts depend on appropriations; effects on local zoning choices are not yet known.

CL1125.claim: Six years after Auckland's 2016 upzoning, three-bedroom rents were 22% to 35% below a synthetic comparison.
CL1125.supports: Greenaway-McGrevy compares Auckland with a weighted mix of 51 other New Zealand urban areas. Three-bedroom rents were 22 to 35 percent below the comparison six years after the reform, significant at the 5% level, and two-bedroom effects of about 14 to 22 percent were weaker. Consents for new dwellings rose sharply from 2016, all in upzoned areas.
CL1125.limitation: The pre-reform fit was weaker than for many comparison areas, effect sizes vary by specification, and most comparison areas are small towns. New Zealand's planning system differs from U.S. local zoning.

CL1126.claim: U.S. reforms that loosened land-use rules from 2000 to 2019 were associated with a 0.8% increase in housing supply within three to nine years, mostly in higher-rent units; the estimate is disputed.
CL1126.supports: Stacy and coauthors built a panel of local land-use reforms from news reports and found loosening associated with a 0.8% supply increase and no significant evidence of more lower-cost units; tightening was associated with higher median rents. A 2026 critique argues most reforms were misclassified, and the authors' reply defends the coding and notes that both analyses find supply increases.
CL1126.limitation: Reforms were identified from news articles. Three of the four critics are affiliated with the American Enterprise Institute; they cite case studies of by-right reforms showing supply growth of 1% to 2.5% a year.

CL1127.claim: Minneapolis's slower rent growth after its 2040 Plan owes much to a 2020 drop in demand, by the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis's analysis.
CL1127.supports: The Minneapolis Fed finds median rent in Minneapolis rose 25.7% from 2019 to 2023, 3.2 percentage points less than in comparison cities, with the gap opening in mid-2020 as vacancies peaked at 9.5%. Small two- to four-unit buildings added 225 units from 2020 to 2024, against 11,503 units in larger buildings.
CL1127.limitation: The authors state that their findings do not show whether the 2040 Plan has succeeded, and earlier city policies are not separated from the plan.

CL1128.claim: In 2024, 22.7 million U.S. renter households (49%) spent more than 30% of income on housing, and 12.1 million spent more than half.
CL1128.supports: JCHS reports, from American Community Survey data, a record 22.7 million cost-burdened renter households in 2024, 49 percent of renters, including 12.1 million (26 percent) with severe burdens above half of income. The number of burdened renters rose by 2.3 million since 2019.
CL1128.limitation: Cost burden uses a fixed 30% threshold that does not adjust for income level or household size.

CL1129.claim: From 2019 to 2025, U.S. property taxes rose 31% and average monthly home insurance premiums rose 72% to $201.
CL1129.supports: JCHS reports these increases from ICE Mortgage Monitor data (March 2026) and identifies property taxes and insurance as the main drivers of rising costs for older owners, many of whom are retirees on fixed incomes.
CL1129.limitation: The figures are national averages from a private data provider and hide large state and local differences.

CL1130.claim: A buyer needed about $120,800 in annual income to afford the median-priced home at the end of 2025, up from $68,700 five years earlier.
CL1130.supports: JCHS calculates the income required to afford monthly payments on the median-priced home, which rose to $120,800 at the end of 2025 from $68,700 at the end of 2020, as the median price reached $409,000 in the fourth quarter of 2025.
CL1130.limitation: The estimate assumes a standard loan, down payment and payment-to-income ratio; required income varies widely by metro area.

CL1131.claim: The consumer price index for rent of primary residence rose 2.8% in the year to September 2026.
CL1131.supports: Table 2 of the September 2026 Consumer Price Index, released October 14, 2026, shows unadjusted 12-month increases of 2.8% for rent of primary residence, 3.3% for owners' equivalent rent and 3.2% for shelter, against 3.7% for all items.
CL1131.limitation: The CPI rent index covers all leases, including renewals, so it changes more slowly than asking rents on new leases.

CL1132.claim: In 2024, 20.7 million homeowner households (24%) were cost-burdened, and households headed by someone 65 or older had the highest owner burden rate, 28%.
CL1132.supports: JCHS reports that cost-burdened homeowners rose by 4.0 million since 2019 to 20.7 million in 2024 and that households headed by someone age 65 and over have the highest cost-burden rates, at 28 percent, with property taxes and insurance as the main drivers.
CL1132.limitation: Burden rates for older owners combine those with and without mortgages, and fixed retirement incomes make the 30% threshold a rough measure.

CL1133.claim: In HUD's randomized Family Options Study, 88% of homeless families offered priority access to a housing subsidy used a permanent subsidy, against 38% of families in usual care.
CL1133.supports: The study randomly assigned 2,282 homeless families in 12 communities to interventions that included priority access to long-term rent subsidies, usually Housing Choice Vouchers. By the 37-month survey, 83% of the subsidy group had used the offered subsidy and 88% had used any permanent subsidy, compared with 38% of the usual-care group.
CL1133.population: Homeless families enrolled in the study
CL1133.limitation: These figures show that offers led to use. The study's estimates of effects on homelessness and family stability are reported separately in the full report.

CL1150.claim: Climate Central counted 23 U.S. weather and climate disasters with at least $1 billion in damage in 2025, totaling about $115 billion.
CL1150.supports: Climate Central's 2025 report lists 23 billion-dollar weather and climate disasters, about $115.0 billion in direct costs and 276 deaths, adjusted to 2025 dollars. The count was the third highest since 1980, after 2023 (28) and 2024 (27). The report examines exposure, vulnerability and climate change as influences on the trend.
CL1150.population: U.S. disasters with at least $1 billion in damage
CL1150.limitation: Billion-dollar counts rise with more and costlier exposed property as well as with changes in hazards, so the count alone does not separate the two.

CL1151.claim: Treasury's Federal Insurance Office reports that changes in the frequency, severity or distribution of perils covered by homeowners insurance have been attributed to climate change.
CL1151.supports: In its January 2025 analysis of homeowners insurance markets, the Federal Insurance Office states that homes are increasingly vulnerable to natural catastrophes, that annual major disaster declarations for climate-related events were almost double the 1960 to 2010 average, and, citing the Fifth National Climate Assessment, that changes in homeowners insurance perils have been attributed to climate change.
CL1151.limitation: Disaster declarations depend on federal decisions as well as events, attribution differs by peril and region, and the report notes the difficulty of attributing premium changes to specific causes.

CL1152.claim: Replacement costs for property and casualty losses rose an average of 45% from 2020 to 2023, and average claims were about $24,000 in the riskiest ZIP codes against $19,000 in the least risky.
CL1152.supports: The Federal Insurance Office reports the 45% replacement-cost increase for 2020 to 2023. From data on more than 246 million policies from over 330 insurers for 2018 to 2022, it reports average claim severity of about $24,000 in the highest-risk fifth of ZIP codes and about $19,000 in the lowest, with more frequent claims in riskier areas.
CL1152.limitation: The policy data exclude residual-market plans, surplus lines insurers and flood coverage, and end in 2022.

CL1153.claim: Prices of inputs to residential construction rose 40% from January 2020 to spring 2026.
CL1153.supports: The Joint Center for Housing Studies reports, from Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price data, that the price of combined inputs to residential construction rose 40 percent since January 2020, with gypsum up 47 percent and steel mill products up 84 percent through April 2026.
CL1153.population: Inputs used in U.S. residential construction
CL1153.limitation: Input prices are one part of rebuilding costs; labor and local demand after a disaster also move repair prices.

CL1154.claim: State Farm General stopped accepting new property insurance applications in California on May 27, 2023, citing construction costs, catastrophe exposure and the reinsurance market.
CL1154.supports: State Farm's May 26, 2023 announcement said its California company would stop accepting new applications for business and personal property and casualty lines, excluding personal auto, citing historic increases in construction costs outpacing inflation, rapidly growing catastrophe exposure and a challenging reinsurance market.
CL1154.limitation: These are the company's stated reasons in its own announcement; the announcement gives no independent measure of its rates or losses.

CL1155.claim: Reinsurers raised rates, tightened terms and required insurers to retain more risk in the market Treasury described.
CL1155.supports: The Federal Insurance Office describes a hard reinsurance market, with reinsurers tightening terms and conditions, raising rates and requiring ceding insurers to retain more risk, as one factor in homeowners insurance costs alongside replacement costs and catastrophe losses.
CL1155.population: Reinsurance purchased by U.S. homeowners insurers
CL1155.period: Market conditions described in a January 2025 report
CL1155.limitation: The report does not quantify how much reinsurance costs added to homeowners premiums, and reinsurance prices change at each renewal season.

CL1156.claim: The pass-through from disaster risk to homeowners premiums doubled over 2014 to 2024, and higher premiums reduced home price growth by more than $40,000 in the most exposed ZIP codes.
CL1156.supports: Keys and Mulder use more than 74 million premiums inferred from mortgage escrow payments, 2014 to 2024. They document rapidly rising premiums and a doubling of the pass-through from disaster risk, which they link partly to a repricing of catastrophic risk in global capital markets, and they find premiums capitalized into home values, most in areas facing rising climate risk.
CL1156.population: U.S. homes with mortgage escrow accounts
CL1156.limitation: Escrow data cover mortgaged homes only. The paper is a working paper revised in November 2025, and the capital-markets explanation is the authors' interpretation of the timing.

CL1157.claim: In states with the most restrictive insurance rate rules, homeowners rates did not keep pace with rising losses, and insurers raised rates in less restrictive states to compensate.
CL1157.supports: Oh, Sen and Tenekedjieva classify states by regulatory friction. Rates tracked risk least closely in high-friction states, where they grew about 4 percentage points slower, while insurers raised rates in low-friction states by about 0.94% a year after out-of-state losses. About $2.4 billion of an added $8 billion over ten years came from these spillovers. Treasury reports a similar pattern.
CL1157.population: U.S. homeowners insurance markets by state
CL1157.limitation: The paper predates recent reforms, and the friction classification is the authors' own. Regulators can hold rates down for stated reasons such as affordability.

CL1158.claim: Treasury found that insurers raise premiums faster in states with less restrictive rate approval processes.
CL1158.supports: The Federal Insurance Office notes that rate regulation can affect premium changes: insurers generally are able to increase premiums at a faster pace in states with relatively less restrictive approval processes, and states using open rating, use-and-file or file-and-use systems rely mainly on market competition to keep rates from being excessive.
CL1158.limitation: This is an observed pattern; it does not show whether slower increases kept insurers in a state or pushed them out.

CL1159.claim: Nonrenewal rates in the riskiest fifth of ZIP codes rose from 1.10% in 2018 to 2.37% in 2022 and averaged about 80% above the least risky fifth.
CL1159.supports: The Federal Insurance Office reports average nonrenewal rates of 1.61% in the highest-risk ZIP code group against 0.90% in the lowest over 2018 to 2022. The highest-risk rate more than doubled over the period, and the Southeast's highest-risk group reached 2.32%, the highest of seven regions.
CL1159.limitation: Nonrenewals here are insurer-initiated and exclude residual-market plans; the data end in 2022, before State Farm's 2023 California pause.

CL1160.claim: California's FAIR Plan had 696,562 dwelling and commercial policies and $768 billion in exposure in June 2026, up 157% and 250% since September 2022.
CL1160.supports: The California FAIR Plan's key statistics report 696,562 policies in force as of June 2026, an 8% increase since September 2025 and 157% since September 2022, and total exposure of $768 billion, up 11% and 250% over the same periods.
CL1160.limitation: The totals combine dwelling and commercial policies and do not show why each policyholder joined the plan.

CL1161.claim: Florida's Citizens Property Insurance peaked at 1,407,805 policies in September 2023 and held 254,413 on October 9, 2026, after a December 2022 law changed claim and litigation rules.
CL1161.supports: Citizens' policies-in-force series shows the September 30, 2023 peak and 254,413 policies on October 9, 2026 (266,231 on August 31). Florida's SB 2-A, approved December 16, 2022 as Chapter 2022-271, created an optional reinsurance assistance program, barred assignment of post-loss benefits under newer policies and amended the attorney-fee statutes for insurance cases.
CL1161.limitation: The counts and the law are documented; the decline in Citizens policies has several possible causes, and no evaluation separates the law's effect.

CL1162.claim: The NFIP is authorized through December 11, 2026 under a short-term extension, had nearly 4.5 million policies on August 31, 2026, and owes $22.525 billion to the Treasury.
CL1162.supports: CRS report R44593, updated October 5, 2026, states that NFIP authorization runs to December 11, 2026 under P.L. 119-103, after lapses from October 1 to November 12, 2025 and February 1 to 3, 2026. It reports nearly 4.5 million policies with over $1.3 trillion in coverage and $7.9 billion of borrowing authority left. The continuing resolution signed September 2, 2026 runs to the same date.
CL1162.limitation: Authorization can change with any new law before or after December 11, 2026, and the policy count does not show how many flood-exposed homes lack coverage.

CL1163.claim: Standard homeowners insurance policies typically exclude flood damage.
CL1163.supports: Treasury's announcement of its homeowners insurance analysis explains that the study covers nine climate-related perils and excludes flooding, which is typically not covered by homeowners policies, along with non-climate perils such as earthquakes. The analysis covered more than 246 million policies from over 330 insurers.
CL1163.limitation: Policy terms vary by insurer and state, and separate flood coverage can be bought from the NFIP or private insurers.

CL1164.claim: The consumer price index for motor vehicle insurance rose 18.9% in the year to September 2023 and 16.3% in the year to September 2024, then fell 5.0% in the year to September 2026.
CL1164.supports: BLS releases for the September 2023 and September 2024 Consumer Price Index report 12-month increases of 18.9% and 16.3% for motor vehicle insurance. Table 2 of the September 2026 release, published October 14, 2026, shows an unadjusted 12-month change of minus 5.0%.
CL1164.limitation: The index tracks the price of a fixed set of coverage; individual premiums depend on driver, vehicle, location and insurer. The year to September 2025 is not among these readings.

CL1165.claim: Vehicle maintenance and repair prices rose 10.2% in the year to September 2023 and 5.8% in the year to September 2026.
CL1165.supports: BLS Table 2 shows unadjusted 12-month changes for motor vehicle maintenance and repair of 10.2% in September 2023 and 5.8% in September 2026, while used car and truck prices fell 8.0% and 1.5% over the same 12-month periods.
CL1165.limitation: Repair prices are one input to claim costs; the CPI does not show how much of any premium change they explain.

CL1166.claim: California's Sustainable Insurance Strategy lets insurers use forward-looking catastrophe models in rates and requires those that do to write at least 85% of their statewide market share in wildfire-distressed areas.
CL1166.supports: The California Department of Insurance describes the strategy, announced September 21, 2023 with regulations issued through December 2024: catastrophe models that credit wildfire safety measures, counting California-only net reinsurance costs in rates, a commitment to write no less than 85% of statewide market share in underserved areas, and FAIR Plan modernization to move people back to the regular market.
CL1166.population: Insurers writing homeowners coverage in California
CL1166.limitation: The department's page describes the rules; effects on availability and premiums have not been evaluated.

CL1167.claim: Owners in FEMA's mapped high-risk flood areas generally must buy flood insurance to get a federally backed mortgage, though compliance has been incomplete.
CL1167.supports: CRS report R44593 explains the mandatory purchase requirement for properties in Special Flood Hazard Areas with loans from federal agency lenders, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or federally regulated banks. It cites a post-Sandy finding that about 65% of required New York City properties were insured and a study reporting compliance rising from 61% in 2012 to 73% in 2016.
CL1167.population: Mortgaged properties in Special Flood Hazard Areas
CL1167.period: 2012 to 2016 compliance data; report updated October 5, 2026
CL1167.limitation: Compliance figures come from specific studies and places, and the requirement does not reach homes outside mapped zones or homes without such loans.

CL1168.claim: Average monthly home insurance premiums rose 72% from 2019 to 2025, to $201, with higher costs in disaster-prone markets such as Texas and Florida.
CL1168.supports: The Joint Center for Housing Studies reports, from ICE Mortgage Monitor data published in March 2026, that average monthly insurance premiums increased 72 percent to $201 between 2019 and 2025 and that insurance costs are even higher in markets susceptible to natural disasters, such as Texas and Florida. Property taxes rose 31 percent over the same years.
CL1168.jurisdiction: United States; Texas and Florida as examples
CL1168.limitation: National averages from a private data provider; the report does not give figures for every state.

CL1169.claim: FEMA's modeling estimates that modern building codes adopted since 2000 will avoid $132 billion in losses by 2040, while fewer than half of jurisdictions have hazard-resistant codes.
CL1169.supports: FEMA's Building Codes Save study (November 2020) modeled about 18.1 million buildings built after 2000 with its Hazus loss model, estimating $1.6 billion a year in losses avoided in 2020 dollars for flood, hurricane wind and earthquake. It notes that fewer than half of jurisdictions have hazard-resistant codes, while nearly 80% of construction occurs in communities with them.
CL1169.limitation: Savings come from Hazus loss modeling and exclude wildfire; results depend on assumptions about future hazards and construction.

CL1170.claim: California homes built after the state's 2008 wildfire building code were about 40% less likely to be destroyed in a wildfire, and the codes also protected neighboring homes.
CL1170.supports: Baylis and Boomhower analyze structure losses in California wildfires and report large resilience effects from building codes adopted after the 1991 Oakland Firestorm. The NBER summary reports that homes built after 2008 under statewide wildfire codes were 40 percent less likely to be destroyed, and the abstract states that codes also benefit neighbors.
CL1170.limitation: A working paper focused on California wildfire; it does not estimate effects for other hazards or states, or on premiums.

CL1171.claim: From 2018 to 2022, homeowners in the riskiest fifth of ZIP codes paid an average of $2,321 a year, 82% more than in the least risky fifth.
CL1171.supports: Treasury's Federal Insurance Office, using data on over 246 million policies from more than 330 insurers, reports the $2,321 average premium in the highest-risk fifth of ZIP codes by expected climate-related losses, 82% above the lowest-risk fifth, with nonrenewal rates about 80% higher.
CL1171.limitation: Data exclude flood, residual-market plans and surplus lines insurers. Premiums are per policy, so they also depend on how much coverage each home carries.

CL1172.claim: In 2024, households headed by someone 65 or older had the highest cost-burden rate among U.S. homeowners, 28%.
CL1172.supports: The Joint Center for Housing Studies reports that households headed by someone age 65 and over have the highest cost-burden rates, at 28 percent, and identifies property taxes and insurance as the main drivers for older owners, many of whom are retirees on fixed incomes.
CL1172.population: U.S. homeowner households headed by someone 65 or older
CL1172.limitation: The rate combines owners with and without mortgages, and the 30% threshold is a rough measure for fixed retirement incomes.

CL1173.claim: Average homeowners premiums per policy grew 8.7% faster than inflation from 2018 to 2022.
CL1173.supports: Treasury's January 16, 2025 announcement reports that average premiums per policy nationwide increased 8.7 percent faster than inflation over 2018 to 2022, with some consumers seeing increases well above the national average, based on data from more than 330 insurers.
CL1173.limitation: These years precede the largest recent increases; a different data source shows a 72% rise in average monthly premiums from 2019 to 2025.

CL1433.claim: Medicaid paid 61 percent of the $415 billion spent on long-term services and supports in 2022.
CL1433.supports: KFF reports U.S. spending of $415 billion on long-term services and supports in 2022, $284 billion for home and community-based services and $131 billion for institutional care. Medicaid paid 61 percent, individuals paid 17 percent out of pocket, and other public and private payers covered 21 percent.
CL1433.limitation: KFF calculation from national health spending data; excludes the value of unpaid family care, which is far larger in hours.

CL1434.claim: SSI's asset limit has been $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple since 1989.
CL1434.supports: SSA lists countable resource limits of $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple, excluding a home, one vehicle used for transportation and up to $100,000 in an ABLE account. The regulation set these amounts beginning January 1, 1989, and SSA's 2027 fact sheet keeps them unchanged.
CL1434.limitation: Medicaid asset rules for long-term care are set by each state and can differ from SSI's limits.

CL1435.claim: Federal Medicaid law requires nursing facility coverage while most home and community services are optional, yet home care now takes most Medicaid LTSS spending.
CL1435.supports: KFF reports that states must cover nursing facility LTSS while HCBS coverage is largely optional, a pattern it calls institutional bias. HCBS rose from 10 percent of Medicaid LTSS spending in 1988 to 62 percent in 2020, and in 2021, 75 percent of Medicaid LTSS users received only HCBS.
CL1435.limitation: National shares hide large differences between states and between populations, such as older adults and people with developmental disabilities.

CL1436.claim: The Supreme Court held in 1999 that unjustified isolation of people with disabilities is discrimination under the ADA.
CL1436.supports: In Olmstead v. L.C., the Court held that unjustified isolation is discrimination based on disability under Title II of the ADA, requiring community-based treatment when state professionals find it appropriate, the person does not oppose it, and it can be reasonably accommodated considering state resources and the needs of others with disabilities.
CL1436.population: People with disabilities served by state programs
CL1436.limitation: The reasonable-accommodation limit lets states cite resources, so enforcement depends on later litigation and Justice Department action.

CL1437.claim: Section 1915(c) waivers, created in 1983, are the main route for Medicaid home and community services, and 47 states plus DC run at least one.
CL1437.supports: Medicaid.gov states that Congress created section 1915(c) in 1983 to let states waive Medicaid rules governing institutional care and offer HCBS, that 47 states and the District of Columbia operate at least one such waiver, and that HCBS became a formal state plan option in 2005.
CL1437.limitation: The page does not describe enrollment caps; waiting list practices come from KFF's state survey.

CL1438.claim: More than 710,000 people were on Medicaid HCBS waiting or interest lists in 2024.
CL1438.supports: KFF counted 354,299 people on waiting lists and 356,440 on interest lists in 40 states in 2024, an average wait of 40 months in the 32 states that reported, and 73 percent of waiver waiting list members with intellectual or developmental disabilities (89 percent in states that do not screen). Over 80 percent are eligible for state plan services while they wait.
CL1438.limitation: KFF calls lists an incomplete measure of unmet need; states screen and prioritize differently, so totals are not comparable across states or years.

CL1439.claim: Home health and personal care aides earned a median $17.21 an hour in May 2025.
CL1439.supports: BLS reports a median wage of $17.21 an hour ($35,800 a year) for home health and personal care aides in May 2025, 4,677,100 jobs in 2025, projected employment growth of 18 percent from 2025 to 2035, and about 760,500 openings a year on average.
CL1439.population: Home health and personal care aides
CL1439.limitation: Survey wage data exclude many independent providers paid through self-directed programs and family members paid as aides.

CL1440.claim: Every state reported shortages of home and community care workers, and most hourly personal care rates were under $20.
CL1440.supports: KFF reports that all states reported HCBS worker shortages, most often direct support professionals, personal care attendants, nursing staff and home health aides; that most states with time-based personal care rates pay under $20 an hour; and that LTSS employment remained 4 percent below pre-pandemic levels in January 2024.
CL1440.population: LTSS workforce and state Medicaid programs
CL1440.period: State survey responses and January 2024 employment
CL1440.limitation: State-reported shortages are not a uniform measure, and rates paid to agencies cover more than wages.

CL1441.claim: Medicare does not pay for ongoing custodial care.
CL1441.supports: Medicare.gov states that Medicare does not provide long-term care or custodial care unless medical care is needed, and points people to Medicaid or private insurance. KFF notes Medicare covers up to 100 days of skilled nursing after a qualifying hospital stay and part-time or intermittent home health care.
CL1441.limitation: Medicare Advantage plans may offer limited extra in-home supports that this general description does not cover.

CL1442.claim: Few people hold private long-term care insurance, and a typical 65-year-old faces large future care costs.
CL1442.supports: KFF reports that about 7.1 million people paid long-term care insurance premiums in 2021, averaging $1,860 a year, and about 80,000 filed claims. It cites an estimate that an average 65-year-old faces $120,900 in future LTSS costs, with families paying more than a third out of pocket.
CL1442.population: Adults 65 and older; private insurance holders
CL1442.limitation: The lifetime cost figure is a projection averaged over people who need little or no care and those who need years of it.

CL1443.claim: Medicaid's coverage of long-term care is a main reason the private insurance market stays small.
CL1443.supports: Brown and Finkelstein describe long-term care costs as one of the largest uninsured financial risks for older Americans, review evidence on why the private market is small, including market imperfections and limited demand, and argue that Medicaid's public coverage is an important factor suppressing private demand.
CL1443.limitation: A review drawing on earlier work; premium increases and insurer exits since 2011 have also shaped the market.

CL1444.claim: About 63 million Americans were family caregivers in 2025, most of them employed.
CL1444.supports: AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving report 63 million family caregivers in 2025, nearly 50 percent more than in 2015; 94 percent care for adults. Seven in ten are employed, half report a negative financial impact, about one in five cannot afford basic needs such as food, and about a quarter are taking on debt.
CL1444.limitation: Survey by advocacy organizations; caregiver counts depend on how caregiving is defined, and changes in definition affect growth since 2015.

CL1445.claim: AARP valued unpaid family care at about $600 billion in 2021.
CL1445.supports: AARP estimates the value of unpaid family care at $600 billion in 2021, based on about 38 million caregivers providing an average of 18 hours of care a week, a total of 36 billion hours valued at $16.59 an hour.
CL1445.limitation: An estimate built from average hours and an assumed hourly value; it does not measure lost earnings or caregivers' own costs.

CL1446.claim: In 2025, 22.8 percent of people with a disability were employed, compared with 65.2 percent of people without one.
CL1446.supports: BLS reports 2025 employment-population ratios of 22.8 percent for people with a disability and 65.2 percent for those without, unemployment rates of 8.3 and 4.1 percent, and part-time work for about 30 percent of workers with a disability versus 17 percent without.
CL1446.limitation: October 2025 data were not collected because of the shutdown, so 2025 uses 11-month averages; disability is self-reported.

CL1447.claim: A 2024 CMS rule requires that 80 percent of Medicaid home care payments go to direct care workers' compensation starting in 2030.
CL1447.supports: The Ensuring Access to Medicaid Services rule, effective July 9, 2024, added 42 CFR 441.302(k). States must ensure each provider spends 80 percent of payments for homemaker, home health aide and personal care services on direct care worker compensation, with state-set percentages for small providers, hardship exemptions, annual reporting and compliance beginning six years after July 9, 2024.
CL1447.population: Medicaid HCBS providers and direct care workers
CL1447.period: Rule effective July 9, 2024; compliance from July 9, 2030
CL1447.limitation: The rule has not reached its compliance date, so no data exist on its effects on wages or provider supply.

CL1448.claim: As of October 2026 the 80 percent requirement remained in the federal regulations.
CL1448.supports: The eCFR text of 42 CFR 441.302, up to date as of October 8, 2026, contains paragraph (k) on HCBS payment adequacy, including the 80 percent minimum and the applicability date six years after July 9, 2024, with no later amendment listed in the section's source note.
CL1448.limitation: The eCFR shows rules in force; proposed changes appear only in the Federal Register.

CL1449.claim: The 2025 budget law capped home equity for Medicaid long-term care, added a new waiver option and delayed nursing home staffing standards to 2034.
CL1449.supports: KFF summarizes Public Law 119-21: a $1,000,000 home equity limit from January 1, 2028; a 1915(c) option from July 1, 2028 for people below institutional level of care if average waits for that level do not rise; a bar on implementing nursing home minimum staffing standards until October 1, 2034, after a Texas court overturned them April 7, 2025; retroactive coverage limits from January 1, 2027; and new provider tax limits that exclude nursing facilities.
CL1449.population: Medicaid enrollees, states and nursing facilities
CL1449.period: Enacted July 4, 2025; KFF page modified July 23, 2026
CL1449.limitation: Secondary summary of statute with CBO estimates; effects on state HCBS spending from broader Medicaid cuts have not yet been documented.

CL1450.claim: Private equity acquisitions of nursing homes raised patient mortality by about 11 percent.
CL1450.supports: Gupta, Howell, Yannelis and Gupta, using Medicare data and an instrumental variables design, estimate that private equity ownership raised mortality among nursing home patients by about 11 percent, shifted admissions toward lower-risk patients and was accompanied by declines in nurse staffing that help explain the result.
CL1450.population: Short-stay Medicare patients in nursing homes
CL1450.period: Acquisitions in the 2000s and 2010s; working paper revised 2023, published 2024
CL1450.limitation: One quasi-experimental study of short-stay Medicare patients; effects for long-stay Medicaid residents and for other ownership types were not estimated.

CL1451.claim: SSI's federal payment rises to $1,029 a month for an individual in 2027.
CL1451.supports: SSA's 2027 fact sheet sets the monthly SSI federal payment standard at $1,029 for an individual and $1,544 for a couple, up from $994 and $1,491 in 2026 with the 3.6 percent COLA, while the resource limits remain $2,000 and $3,000.
CL1451.limitation: Many states add a supplement, and countable income reduces the federal payment, so actual payments vary.

CL1452.claim: The federal Eldercare Locator connects callers to their local Area Agency on Aging.
CL1452.supports: The Eldercare Locator is a public service of the Administration for Community Living within HHS. It can be reached at 1-800-677-1116 or online, and it connects people to Area Agencies on Aging and community services that help older adults live independently at home.
CL1452.limitation: The page does not describe which services each Area Agency on Aging offers; services and waits vary locally.

CL1453.claim: Washington's public long-term care insurance program reports that benefits are available statewide.
CL1453.supports: The WA Cares Fund site states that benefits are now available statewide, that workers contribute a small amount from each paycheck, and that benefits can pay for services including paid family caregiving, in-home care, home modifications, respite care, transportation, home-delivered meals and assistive devices.
CL1453.population: Washington workers who qualify for WA Cares
CL1453.limitation: The home page does not give the benefit amount, contribution rate or qualifying rules, and no evaluation of the program's effects exists yet.

CL1454.claim: Minnesota's nursing home workforce standards board set minimum wages that took effect September 10, 2026.
CL1454.supports: The Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry reports that the board, created in 2023 law, adopted minimum wages of $19.00 for general nursing home workers, $22.50 for certified nursing assistants, $23.50 for trained medication aides and $27.00 for licensed practical nurses, effective September 10, 2026, 30 days after CMS approved the state plan amendment on August 11, 2026.
CL1454.limitation: The standards are new, so effects on staffing, facility finances and resident care are not yet measured.

CL1455.claim: Fourteen states and DC have mandatory paid family leave programs, and California's raised leave-taking among new mothers.
CL1455.supports: The Bipartisan Policy Center lists 14 states and the District of Columbia with mandatory paid family leave programs as of October 8, 2026, with Maryland and Virginia not yet active. Rossin-Slater, Ruhm and Waldfogel found California's program more than doubled the leave new mothers took.
CL1455.population: Workers in states with programs; new mothers in California
CL1455.limitation: The leave-taking evidence covers new parents; use of paid leave to care for older or disabled relatives is less studied.

CL1340.claim: In 2022, employers and private insurers paid hospitals 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same services, with wide differences by state.
CL1340.supports: RAND's round 5.1 study of 2020 to 2022 claims finds private payers paid 254% of Medicare rates on average in 2022; the state median was 253%. Only Arkansas was below 170%, while California, Florida, New York and Wisconsin were among states above 300%. Ambulatory surgery centers averaged 171% of Medicare.
CL1340.population: Privately insured patients in participating employer and insurer data
CL1340.limitation: Claims come from participating employers and insurers, not a random sample of all private plans.

CL1341.claim: Hospital prices vary widely, monopoly hospitals charge about 12% more, and mergers of nearby hospitals raised prices by more than 6%.
CL1341.supports: Cooper, Craig, Gaynor and Van Reenen use insurer claims covering 28% of people with employer coverage. Spending per privately insured person varies threefold across areas, about half from price. Monopoly hospitals' prices were 12% higher than in markets with four or more rivals. Among 366 mergers from 2007 to 2011, prices rose over 6% when hospitals were within five miles of each other and did not rise beyond 25 miles.
CL1341.limitation: Data from three large insurers; merger effects come from deals before 2012, and quality effects are not measured in this study.

CL1342.claim: Medicare pays much more for some services in hospital outpatient departments than in independent offices, which gives hospitals a reason to buy physician practices.
CL1342.supports: MedPAC reports that in 2023 Medicare paid 194% more for a transthoracic echocardiogram in a hospital outpatient department than in a freestanding office. It finds the payment difference gives hospitals an incentive to acquire practices and bill under the higher outpatient system, and that physicians in hospital-owned practices or employed by hospitals rose from 29.0% in 2012 to 39.8% in 2020.
CL1342.limitation: Medicare rates only; commercial contracts set their own facility payments, and the rise in hospital ownership has several causes.

CL1343.claim: MedPAC estimated that aligning Medicare payment across settings for 66 service groups would have cut Medicare spending by $6.0 billion and beneficiary cost sharing by $1.5 billion in 2021.
CL1343.supports: MedPAC recommended in June 2023 that Congress more closely align payment rates across ambulatory settings for services safe in all settings. Aligning 66 ambulatory payment classifications, 57 to physician fee schedule rates and 9 to surgery center rates, would have reduced 2021 outlays by $6.0 billion and cost sharing by $1.5 billion, though current budget-neutrality rules would offset the outlay savings.
CL1343.population: Medicare beneficiaries and hospital outpatient departments
CL1343.limitation: A static estimate; it does not model changes in where services move or effects on hospital access.

CL1344.claim: Since January 1, 2021, hospitals must post their prices online, and CMS began enforcing updated requirements on April 1, 2026.
CL1344.supports: CMS states that each U.S. hospital must post a comprehensive machine-readable file of standard charges and a consumer-friendly display of shoppable services. Enforcement of updated requirements from the calendar year 2026 outpatient payment rule began April 1, 2026, and CMS sought comment through August 31, 2026 on standardizing files and displays.
CL1344.limitation: Posting rules do not set prices; the CMS page does not report overall compliance rates.

CL1345.claim: CMS's public list shows 29 civil monetary penalty notices issued to 28 hospitals for price transparency violations.
CL1345.supports: The CMS enforcement page lists 29 civil monetary penalty notices covering 28 hospitals, including two notices to one hospital dated February and June 2026. The page does not list warning letters or corrective action plans.
CL1345.limitation: Penalty counts do not measure compliance; most enforcement steps short of penalties are not on this list.

CL1346.claim: Insurers and most group health plans must post negotiated rates and offer online cost estimates under the Transparency in Coverage rule.
CL1346.supports: The 2020 final rule requires most non-grandfathered group plans and insurers to post machine-readable files of in-network rates, out-of-network payments and drug prices for plan years beginning in 2022, and to offer a personalized cost-estimate tool for 500 services from 2023 and all services from 2024.
CL1346.population: Non-grandfathered group health plans and health insurers
CL1346.limitation: The fact sheet dates from 2020 and predates later amendments or enforcement changes.

CL1347.claim: Federal law protects insured patients from surprise out-of-network bills for emergency care, many services at in-network facilities and air ambulances, and lets uninsured patients dispute bills $400 or more above a good faith estimate.
CL1347.supports: CMS states the No Surprises Act protects people from unexpected out-of-network bills for emergency room visits, non-emergency care related to a visit to an in-network hospital, outpatient department or surgery center, and air ambulance services. Uninsured or self-pay patients scheduling care at least three business days ahead get a good faith estimate and may dispute a bill at least $400 above it. The help line is 1-800-985-3059.
CL1347.population: Insured patients and uninsured or self-pay patients
CL1347.limitation: Ground ambulance bills and some other services fall outside these federal protections, and state laws can add further protections.

CL1348.claim: Insurers and providers started 712,561 federal payment disputes in June and July 2026 alone.
CL1348.supports: CMS's bi-monthly report as of July 31, 2026 counts 712,561 independent dispute resolution cases initiated in June and July 2026, with 394,140 in July, and 671,465 closed, including 561,572 payment determinations and 98,398 found ineligible.
CL1348.population: Out-of-network payment disputes between providers and plans
CL1348.limitation: Counts do not show who prevailed or payment amounts; those appear in separate public use files.

CL1349.claim: At least $220 billion is owed in medical debt, and about 14 million adults owe more than $1,000.
CL1349.supports: KFF's analysis of the Census Bureau's 2021 Survey of Income and Program Participation finds at least $220 billion in medical debt, with about 14 million adults (6%) owing more than $1,000 and 3 million (1%) owing more than $10,000. Shares were highest in South Dakota (17.7%) and Mississippi (15.2%) and lowest in Hawaii (2.3%).
CL1349.limitation: Survey-based and self-reported; data predate the 2023 credit bureau changes and the 2025 end of the enhanced marketplace credits.

CL1350.claim: In a 2022 KFF survey, 41% of adults had debt from medical or dental bills, and most of them had cut back on basic needs.
CL1350.supports: KFF's survey of 2,375 adults in February and March 2022 found 41% with current debt from medical or dental bills. Among them, 63% said someone in the household cut back on food, clothing or basic items, and 64% said someone put off needed care because of cost in the past year, compared with 28% of adults without debt.
CL1350.limitation: Broad definition includes bills on credit cards and payment plans; associations do not show the debt caused delayed care.

CL1351.claim: A federal court vacated the CFPB's 2025 rule that would have kept medical bills off credit reports.
CL1351.supports: The CFPB finalized a rule on January 7, 2025 banning medical bills from credit reports used by lenders. On July 11, 2025, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas vacated it in Cornerstone Credit Union League v. CFPB at the joint request of the Bureau and the plaintiffs, finding the rule exceeded the Bureau's authority under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
CL1351.limitation: Credit bureaus' own reporting policies and state laws still limit some medical debt reporting, and bureau policies can change.

CL1352.claim: Colorado bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt in credit reports.
CL1352.supports: Colorado's HB23-1126, signed June 5, 2023 and effective August 7, 2023, bars consumer reporting agencies from including adverse information they know or should know concerns medical debt, with an exception for loans above the national conforming loan limit, and requires the Department of Revenue to report on effects by January 1, 2028.
CL1352.limitation: Colorado is one state example, and other states' medical debt laws differ.

CL1353.claim: Randomized experiments that paid off old medical debt found no average improvement in mental health or financial well-being.
CL1353.supports: Kluender, Mahoney, Wong and Yin relieved $169 million of medical debt held by collectors for 83,401 people in two randomized experiments. Relief modestly improved credit access only where the debt was still reported, reduced payment of existing medical bills, and had no effect on survey measures of mental or physical health, health care use or financial well-being.
CL1353.population: People with medical debt sold to collectors
CL1353.limitation: Covers older debt already in collections; preventing new debt or relieving it earlier may have different effects.

CL1354.claim: Tax-exempt hospitals must wait at least 120 days after the first bill, and give 30 days' notice, before extraordinary collection actions such as credit reporting or lawsuits.
CL1354.supports: The IRS explains that under section 501(r)(6), extraordinary collection actions include selling debt, reporting to credit bureaus, denying care for unpaid bills and legal actions such as liens, lawsuits and wage garnishment. Hospitals must refrain for at least 120 days from the first post-discharge bill, accept financial assistance applications for 240 days, and give at least 30 days' written notice.
CL1354.limitation: Applies only to hospitals with tax-exempt status under section 501(c)(3); for-profit hospitals follow state law.

CL1355.claim: KFF estimated nonprofit hospitals' tax exemption was worth about $28 billion in 2020, compared with about $16 billion in charity care costs.
CL1355.supports: KFF, an independent health policy research organization, estimated the federal, state and local tax exemption for nonprofit hospitals at about $28.1 billion in 2020, roughly 44% of their net income, against total charity care costs of about $16 billion. Charity care is one part of reported community benefit.
CL1355.limitation: Property tax values are estimated, and 2020 net income was inflated by pandemic relief; community benefit also counts unreimbursed Medicaid costs and training.

CL1356.claim: Federal law does not define how much community benefit a nonprofit hospital must provide, and GAO found the IRS could not show it reviewed each hospital as required.
CL1356.supports: GAO reported in 2023 that federal law does not define community benefit, leaving hospitals wide latitude, that the IRS could not show it reviews hospitals' community benefit activities at least every three years, and that 30 hospitals reported no community benefit spending in 2016. GAO had recommended that Congress specify qualifying services.
CL1356.limitation: GAO's findings date to April 2023 and predate later IRS form or process changes.

CL1357.claim: The three largest pharmacy benefit managers processed nearly 80% of U.S. prescriptions in 2023 and are tied to major insurers and pharmacies.
CL1357.supports: The FTC's July 2024 interim staff report finds the top three PBMs processed nearly 80% of about 6.6 billion prescriptions dispensed in 2023 and the top six more than 90%. The largest PBMs are vertically integrated with major insurers and specialty and retail pharmacies; their affiliated pharmacies account for nearly 70% of specialty drug revenue.
CL1357.limitation: These are interim staff findings, not a Commission ruling, and PBM market shares vary by market segment.

CL1358.claim: Pharmacies affiliated with the three largest PBMs took in more than $7.3 billion above estimated acquisition cost on 51 specialty generic drugs from 2017 to 2022.
CL1358.supports: The FTC's January 2025 second interim staff report finds affiliated pharmacies of the three largest PBMs generated over $7.3 billion of dispensing revenue above estimated acquisition cost, measured against NADAC, on 51 specialty generic drugs for commercial and Medicare Part D members, with markups of hundreds or thousands of percent on some drugs.
CL1358.population: Commercial and Medicare Part D plan members
CL1358.limitation: Revenue above drug acquisition cost, not profit; other pharmacy costs are not subtracted, and it is not a judicial finding.

CL1359.claim: The FTC's 2024 complaint alleges the three largest PBMs used rebates that favored high-list-price insulins.
CL1359.supports: The FTC announced on September 20, 2024 an administrative complaint alleging that Caremark, Express Scripts and Optum Rx and their purchasing groups built a rebate system that favored high rebates and inflated insulin list prices and kept lower list-price insulins off formularies. The complaint cites Humalog's list price rising from $21 in 1999 to more than $274 by 2017.
CL1359.population: People using insulin with commercial coverage
CL1359.limitation: These are allegations; no court or administrative judge found the companies liable, and the case moved to settlements.

CL1360.claim: Two insulin cases have proposed settlements and the third was withdrawn from adjudication for a settlement that has not been published; no final FTC order existed for any of them as of October 15, 2026.
CL1360.supports: Express Scripts' proposed consent agreement was published in February 2026. The FTC accepted Caremark's proposed order for comment on July 14, 2026; comments closed September 4. That order would require a standard option where members pay the contracted rate minus rebates instead of the list price, and an insulin program capping costs at $25 for up to a 34-day supply. Optum Rx's case was withdrawn from adjudication on June 12, 2026 while the Commission considers a settlement that has not been published.
CL1360.limitation: Proposed orders can change before the Commission makes them final, and no data on outcomes for patients exist yet.

CL1361.claim: A 2026 federal law requires PBMs to pass manufacturer rebates through to Medicare drug plans from January 1, 2028, and to employer plans for plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028.
CL1361.supports: Sidley Austin's summary of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, signed February 3, 2026, reports Part D and Medicare Advantage drug plan reforms taking effect January 1, 2028, including full pass-through of manufacturer rebates to plan sponsors, and commercial provisions requiring PBMs to remit 100% of rebates and fees 30 months after enactment, which applies to plan years beginning on or after August 3, 2028, or January 1, 2029 for calendar-year plans.
CL1361.population: Medicare drug plans and employer group health plans
CL1361.limitation: Dates come from a law firm summary of Public Law 119-75, and implementing rules are pending.
