CL1362.claim: Medicare limits insulin costs to $35 for a one-month supply of each covered insulin, with no deductible.
CL1362.supports: Medicare.gov states that people pay no more than $35 for a one-month supply of each Part B or Part D covered insulin, up to about $105 for a three-month supply, that the deductible does not apply, and that the Part D limit applies to everyone, including people with Extra Help.
CL1362.limitation: Applies to Medicare only; private plans set their own insulin cost sharing unless a state law or settlement applies.

CL1363.claim: Out-of-pocket spending on covered Medicare Part D drugs is capped at $2,100 in 2026 and $2,400 in 2027.
CL1363.supports: Medicare.gov states the annual out-of-pocket cap on covered Part D drugs is $2,100 in 2026 and $2,400 in 2027, after which enrollees pay nothing for covered drugs for the rest of the year.
CL1363.limitation: The cap covers drugs on the plan's formulary only; monthly premiums and drugs outside the formulary are separate.

CL1364.claim: Medicare has paid negotiated prices for 10 drugs since January 1, 2026; CMS estimated 22% net savings.
CL1364.supports: KFF reports CMS estimated Medicare would have saved $6 billion, a 22% net saving, had the first 10 negotiated prices applied in 2023, and that beneficiaries would save about $1.5 billion in 2026. Starting in 2027, up to 20 Part B or Part D drugs a year will be selected.
CL1364.limitation: Savings are CMS estimates against prior net prices; the sources do not measure effects on drug development.

CL1365.claim: Negotiated prices for 15 more drugs take effect in 2027 and 15 more, including Part B drugs, in 2028.
CL1365.supports: CMS announced on November 25, 2025 negotiated prices for 15 drugs effective January 1, 2027, estimating 44% net savings, about $12 billion. KFF reports the group includes Ozempic and Wegovy, that 15 Part B and Part D drugs were selected in January 2026 for 2028, and that the 2025 budget law's wider orphan-drug exclusion will cost about $8.8 billion over ten years, per CBO.
CL1365.limitation: Savings are estimates measured against prior net prices, and third-cycle prices were not final as of October 15, 2026.

CL1366.claim: Most drugs that received new patents from 2005 to 2015 were existing drugs.
CL1366.supports: Feldman's analysis of FDA Orange Book records finds that 78% of the drugs associated with new patents in 2005 to 2015 were existing drugs, that extensions were especially common for best-selling drugs and that many companies added protections repeatedly.
CL1366.population: Small-molecule drugs listed in the FDA Orange Book
CL1366.limitation: A new patent listing does not always delay generic entry; the study counts listings and does not measure price effects.

CL1367.claim: Generic competition lowers drug prices, by about 30% with one competitor and nearly 85% with five, according to the FDA.
CL1367.supports: The FDA states that a single generic competitor can lead to price reductions of 30% and that five competitors are associated with price drops of nearly 85%. It cites an IMS Health estimate that generics saved the U.S. health system $2.2 trillion from 2009 to 2019.
CL1367.limitation: Agency summary of its own analyses; effects for biosimilars, which are copies of biologic drugs, are smaller and slower.

CL1500.claim: U.S. nonfarm business productivity grew at a 2.1% annual rate from late 2019 to mid-2026, while real hourly compensation fell 0.1% over the latest four quarters.
CL1500.supports: The BLS Productivity and Costs release for the second quarter of 2026 (revised, September 3, 2026) reports productivity up 2.2% over four quarters and a 2.1% annual rate since the fourth quarter of 2019, equal to the long-term rate since 1947. Real hourly compensation fell 0.1% over the same four quarters.
CL1500.limitation: Quarterly figures are revised. Real compensation uses consumer prices; productivity uses output prices, so the two series are not deflated the same way.

CL1501.claim: Faster productivity growth has gone with faster pay growth, though less than one for one, and less for production and nonsupervisory workers.
CL1501.supports: Stansbury and Summers (NBER Working Paper 24165, 2017) estimate that from 1973 to 2016 one percentage point of extra productivity growth was associated with 0.7 to 1.0 point of extra growth in average and median compensation, and 0.4 to 0.7 point for production and nonsupervisory workers.
CL1501.population: U.S. workers, average, median and nonsupervisory compensation
CL1501.limitation: A time-series association from observational data. EPI argues the level gap matters more than the co-movement, and estimates differ by period and pay measure.

CL1502.claim: EPI measures a wide gap between net productivity and typical workers' pay since 1979, and part of the gap depends on how prices are measured.
CL1502.supports: EPI's tracker (updated September 14, 2026) shows net productivity up 93.7% and compensation of production and nonsupervisory workers up 32.7% from 1979 to the second quarter of 2026. Bivens and Mishel's 2015 EPI decomposition attributed 29.6% of the 1973 to 2014 gap to the divergence of consumer and output prices, 58.9% to compensation inequality and 11.5% to a lower labor share.
CL1502.population: Production and nonsupervisory workers in the private sector
CL1502.limitation: EPI is a labor-aligned think tank. The share attributed to price measurement varies by period and method; the current tracker deflates both lines with consumer prices.

CL1503.claim: Workers' share of nonfarm business income was 52.8% in the second quarter of 2026, the lowest since the series began in 1947.
CL1503.supports: BLS (The Economics Daily, September 15, 2026) reports the nonfarm business labor share at 52.8% in 2026 Q2, down from 53.6% in Q1 2026 and 65.5% in Q1 1947. Labor share counts wages, salaries, benefits and employer payments for social insurance as a share of output.
CL1503.limitation: Measuring the income of self-employed people requires an allocation between labor and capital, and the method affects the level. A smaller labor share does not by itself show who owns capital.

CL1504.claim: The quits rate peaked at 3.0% in late 2021 and stood at 1.9% in August 2026.
CL1504.supports: The BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey reported quits at a series high of 4.5 million in November 2021, with a 3.0% rate matching the September 2021 high. The August 2026 release (September 29, 2026) reported 3.1 million quits, a 1.9% rate, and 7.1 million job openings.
CL1504.limitation: Monthly estimates are revised. Quits move with the business cycle and with workers' confidence, so a low rate does not isolate employer power.

CL1505.claim: The tight labor market after the pandemic raised pay fastest at the bottom and offset about a third of four decades of growth in wage inequality.
CL1505.supports: Autor, Dube and McGrew (NBER Working Paper 31010, 2023, revised 2024) find that post-pandemic tightness compressed U.S. wages, counteracting about one-third of the four-decade rise in 90/10 wage inequality, with gains concentrated among young workers without college degrees who changed employers. They interpret this as reduced employer market power.
CL1505.population: U.S. wage earners, especially young workers without a college degree
CL1505.limitation: Working paper. The compression is measured; the interpretation as reduced employer power rests on a job-ladder model, and later loosening of the labor market may reverse part of it.

CL1506.claim: In September 2026 median pay growth was 4.7% for job switchers and 3.4% for job stayers.
CL1506.supports: The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Wage Growth Tracker reports a three-month moving average of median wage growth of 3.9% overall in September 2026, 4.7% for job switchers and 3.4% for job stayers, each slightly lower than in August.
CL1506.population: Individuals observed in the Current Population Survey a year apart
CL1506.limitation: The tracker follows the same people across 12 months and excludes those without wages in both periods; switchers differ from stayers in age and occupation.

CL1507.claim: Local job markets where a few employers dominate hiring are associated with lower posted wages.
CL1507.supports: Azar, Marinescu and Steinbaum (NBER Working Paper 24147; Journal of Human Resources, 2022) use CareerBuilder postings across more than 8,000 local occupational markets. They find the average market highly concentrated under federal merger guidelines, and that moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of concentration is associated with 17% lower posted wages.
CL1507.population: Online job postings in U.S. commuting zones and occupations
CL1507.limitation: Online postings underrepresent some jobs. Rinz (Census Bureau, 2018) finds local concentration declined from 1976 to 2015, so concentration alone does not explain long-run wage trends.

CL1508.claim: Hospital mergers that sharply raised local employer concentration slowed wage growth for workers with hospital-specific skills.
CL1508.supports: Prager and Schmitt (American Economic Review, 2021) find reduced wage growth only where a merger caused a large increase in concentration and workers' skills were industry-specific. Effects were weaker in markets with strong unions, and wages did not slow after out-of-market mergers that left local concentration unchanged.
CL1508.population: Nurses, pharmacy workers and other hospital staff in merging markets
CL1508.limitation: Hospitals only; the authors fail to reject zero effects for other merger types and workers.

CL1510.claim: About one in five U.S. workers was bound by a noncompete agreement, and few negotiated over it.
CL1510.supports: The Treasury Department's March 2022 report on labor market competition cites research estimating that one in five workers was currently subject to a noncompete, about twice that share had been bound by one in the past, and only about 10% of employees negotiated over the agreement. The report cites research linking noncompetes to lower mobility and longer tenure.
CL1510.limitation: Prevalence comes from one large survey (Starr, Prescott and Bishara). Treasury calls the net effect on wages theoretically ambiguous.

CL1511.claim: Federal labor law lets the NLRB order reinstatement and back pay for unlawful firings, and provides no civil penalties.
CL1511.supports: Section 10(c) of the National Labor Relations Act (29 U.S.C. 160(c)) authorizes the Board to order a party to cease and desist and to take affirmative action, including reinstatement of employees with or without back pay. The text contains no civil penalty or punitive damages provision.
CL1511.population: Private-sector employers and employees covered by the NLRA
CL1511.limitation: Courts have rejected some NLRB efforts to expand compensatory remedies, so practical remedies depend on current appellate rulings.

CL1512.claim: Employers were charged with violating federal labor law in 41.5% of union election campaigns in 2016 and 2017.
CL1512.supports: EPI researchers matched NLRB elections filed or held in 2016 and 2017 to unfair labor practice charges. Employers were charged in 41.5% of campaigns; charges involving illegal firing appeared in 19.9% of elections under a narrow definition and 29.6% under a broad one.
CL1512.period: 2016 to 2017 elections; charges FY2015 to FY2018
CL1512.limitation: Charges are allegations that had not been adjudicated. EPI is a labor-aligned think tank; unreported violations would make the count low.

CL1513.claim: Reaching a first union contract took about 460 days on average.
CL1513.supports: Bloomberg Law analyses report an average of 461 days to ratify a first contract across 553 first contracts from 2005 to 2025, and a mean of 463 days in a June 15, 2026 update, close to the 465 days found in its 2022 analysis.
CL1513.population: Newly certified bargaining units that reached a first contract
CL1513.limitation: The sample includes only units that reached a contract, so units that never did are excluded. The 553-contract figure comes from a law firm summary of the study.

CL1514.claim: Union membership was 10.0% of U.S. wage and salary workers in 2025, and 5.9% in the private sector, with higher median weekly earnings for members.
CL1514.supports: The BLS Union Members 2025 release (February 18, 2026) reports 14.7 million members, a 10.0% rate, down from 20.1% in 1983; 5.9% in the private sector and 32.9% in the public sector. Median weekly earnings of full-time members were $1,404, against $1,174 for nonunion workers.
CL1514.limitation: 2025 annual figures average 11 months because the October 2025 survey was not collected during the shutdown. The earnings gap is not adjusted for job or location.

CL1515.claim: Union households have earned a premium of about 10 to 20 log points, and unions reduced inequality in the 20th century.
CL1515.supports: Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2021) use Gallup surveys back to 1936. The household union premium stayed between ten and twenty log points despite large swings in density, and instrumental-variable estimates indicate unions reduced inequality, explaining a significant share of its fall from the mid-1930s to the late 1940s.
CL1515.limitation: Survey-based; the premium is a household comparison and part of it can come from who joins unions.

CL1516.claim: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 since July 24, 2009, and 30 states plus the District of Columbia set higher floors as of July 1, 2026.
CL1516.supports: The Labor Department's history chart shows $7.25 effective July 24, 2009. Its state minimum wage page, updated July 1, 2026, lists 30 states and DC above $7.25, 13 states at $7.25, Georgia and Wyoming at $5.15, and five states with no minimum wage law, where the federal rate applies to covered employers.
CL1516.limitation: Some states have lower tiers for small employers, and city minimums can exceed state floors. Coverage under federal law depends on employer size and interstate commerce.

CL1517.claim: Thirteen states raised their minimum wages on January 1, 2026 through inflation formulas.
CL1517.supports: EPI's January 2026 chart lists 19 states raising minimum wages on January 1, 2026: 13 by inflation adjustment (Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Maine, Minnesota, Montana, New Jersey, Ohio, South Dakota, Vermont, Virginia and Washington), four by legislation and two by ballot measure.
CL1517.limitation: Counts only January 1 increases; some states index on other dates. EPI is a labor-aligned think tank.

CL1518.claim: The Wage and Hour Division recovered more than $259 million in back wages for 176,957 workers in fiscal year 2025.
CL1518.supports: The Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division data page states that the division recovered more than $259 million in back wages for 176,957 employees nationwide in fiscal year 2025, which ran from October 2024 through September 2025.
CL1518.population: Workers covered by federal wage law whose cases WHD resolved
CL1518.limitation: Recoveries count resolved cases only and exclude state agency recoveries and private lawsuits; they do not measure total violations.

CL1519.claim: Minimum-wage violations cost workers an estimated $8 billion a year in the 10 most populous states.
CL1519.supports: Cooper and Kroeger (EPI, May 10, 2017) used Current Population Survey data for 2013 to 2015 in the 10 most populous states. They estimate 2.4 million workers, 17.2% of eligible low-wage workers, lost about $8 billion a year, or about $3,300 per year-round worker, and extrapolate more than $15 billion nationally.
CL1519.limitation: Self-reported wages and hours; covers only minimum-wage violations. EPI is a labor-aligned think tank, and the national figure assumes similar rates elsewhere.

CL1520.claim: Outsourced service workers earn less than comparable in-house workers.
CL1520.supports: The Treasury Department's 2022 report summarizes Dube and Kaplan's estimate that outsourcing reduced wages of U.S. janitors and guards by 4% to 24%, and Goldschmidt and Schmieder's finding that wages fell 10% to 15% for outsourced workers in Germany. Weil's The Fissured Workplace describes the shift of work to subcontractors and franchises.
CL1520.population: Janitors, guards and other outsourced service workers
CL1520.limitation: Estimates vary widely by occupation and method; outsourced and in-house workers can differ in ways the studies do not observe.

CL1521.claim: A BLS study found consumer-versus-output price differences and a falling labor share contributed about equally to the productivity-pay gap in the median industry.
CL1521.supports: Brill and coauthors (BLS Beyond the Numbers, June 2017) examined 183 industries from 1987 to 2015. Productivity outpaced compensation in 83% of them. At the median, the gap between consumer and output price measures and the decline in labor share each contributed about 0.6 percentage point a year.
CL1521.limitation: Industry-level decomposition; it does not give a single economy-wide split, and its data end in 2015, before the recent fall in labor share.

CL1522.claim: The FTC's nationwide noncompete rule never took effect, and the FTC dropped its appeals in September 2025 in favor of case-by-case enforcement.
CL1522.supports: The FTC's rule page states the rule (May 7, 2024) is not in effect, that a district court stopped enforcement on August 20, 2024, and that on September 5, 2025 the FTC took steps to dismiss its appeal; a February 12, 2026 notice removed the rule. Debevoise reports the shift to Section 5 cases, warning letters, a request for information and a proposed order against Gateway covering about 1,800 workers.
CL1522.limitation: Case-by-case enforcement reaches only firms the FTC chooses to pursue; the law firm summary describes employer compliance risk.

CL1523.claim: State noncompete law diverged in 2025 and 2026, with new bans in Wyoming and Washington and easier enforcement in Florida.
CL1523.supports: Manatt (May 2025) lists California, Minnesota, North Dakota and Oklahoma as prohibiting noncompetes and Wyoming's ban effective July 1, 2025. Morgan Lewis reports Washington's HB 1155 bans noncompetes for all workers from June 30, 2027 with $5,000 statutory damages. The ABA Labor and Employment section reports Florida's 2025 CHOICE Act eased enforcement and governors in New York, Maine and Rhode Island vetoed bans.
CL1523.population: Employee noncompete agreements under state law
CL1523.limitation: Law firm and bar association summaries of the statutes; exceptions differ by state and Washington's retroactive voiding may be challenged.

CL1524.claim: The NLRB refusal-to-bargain case involving Amazon's JFK8 warehouse remained open before a federal appeals court in October 2026.
CL1524.supports: The NLRB docket for Amazon.com Services LLC, case 29-CA-310869 (filed January 25, 2023, Region 29), alleging refusal to recognize and bargain, shows the case open, with the General Counsel filing answering briefs to the court of appeals on October 9, 2026. Workers at the warehouse voted for a union in 2022.
CL1524.population: Workers at Amazon's JFK8 warehouse, Staten Island
CL1524.limitation: The docket page does not show every action or the Board's decision text; one case does not measure typical delays.

CL1525.claim: The NLRB regained a quorum on January 7, 2026, and 2026 court rulings removed job protection for agency members.
CL1525.supports: Hunton reports the Board lost its quorum in January 2025 and regained it January 7, 2026; the NLRB lists four members after James Macy's August 17, 2026 swearing-in. In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026, 6 to 3) the Supreme Court held FTC commissioners' removal protection unconstitutional. On July 27, 2026, the Eastern District of Texas severed removal protection for NLRB members in Aimbridge v. NLRB.
CL1525.limitation: Slaughter did not decide the NLRB directly; the Aimbridge ruling binds only that case. Effects on Board decisions depend on future appointments and removals.

CL1526.claim: A study of 138 state minimum wage increases found no detectable loss of low-wage jobs over five years.
CL1526.supports: Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer (NBER Working Paper 25434; Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2019) use a bunching estimator on 138 prominent state increases from 1979 to 2016 and find the overall number of low-wage jobs remained essentially unchanged over the five years after each increase.
CL1526.limitation: Covers the range of increases states adopted, mostly below about 60% of the local median wage; other methods find job losses for some groups.

CL1527.claim: A review of the newer minimum wage literature found a preponderance of negative employment estimates.
CL1527.supports: Neumark and Shirley (NBER Working Paper 28388; Industrial Relations, 2022) assemble estimates from U.S. studies and find a clear preponderance of negative estimates, strongest for teens, young adults and the less-educated and for directly affected workers, and less one-sided for low-wage industries.
CL1527.population: U.S. minimum wage studies, mainly teens and low-skill workers
CL1527.limitation: The authors select and classify studies; other researchers weigh designs differently and find smaller or zero effects.

CL1528.claim: CBO estimated that a $15 federal minimum by 2025 would lift 1.3 million people out of poverty with a median loss of 1.3 million jobs and wide uncertainty.
CL1528.supports: CBO's July 2019 report estimated, for 2025, 17.0 million directly affected workers with higher pay, 1.3 million people lifted out of poverty, and a median employment reduction of 1.3 million (0.8%), with a two-thirds chance the change lies between about zero and 3.7 million.
CL1528.limitation: A projection of a policy that was never enacted, built on CBO's reading of contested research and its own assumptions.

CL1529.claim: Seventeen states and DC require private employers to provide paid sick leave in 2026, and access is lowest for low-wage and part-time workers.
CL1529.supports: CRS report R48921 (April 28, 2026) counts 18 jurisdictions including DC with private-sector paid sick leave mandates in 2026 and notes no general federal requirement apart from contractors under Executive Order 13706. Citing BLS for March 2025, it reports 80% access overall, 58% in the bottom quarter of wages, 94% in the top quarter and 56% for part-time workers.
CL1529.limitation: Access measures plan availability only; use without penalty is unmeasured, and state laws differ in accrual and coverage.

CL1530.claim: Oregon requires large retail, hospitality and food-service employers to give 14 days' notice of schedules and to pay for late changes.
CL1530.supports: The Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries states that employers with at least 500 employees worldwide in these industries must post schedules 14 days ahead, pay an extra hour for added time or changed shifts, and pay time and a half for hours cut, under ORS 653.412 to 653.490.
CL1530.population: Covered hourly workers at large employers
CL1530.limitation: Statewide scheduling laws are rare, and this agency guidance does not measure how the law changed schedules or pay in Oregon.

CL1531.claim: In a 2008 survey of low-wage workers in three cities, 26% were paid below the minimum wage and 43% of those who complained faced retaliation.
CL1531.supports: Bernhardt and coauthors surveyed 4,387 workers in low-wage industries in Chicago, Los Angeles and New York City in 2008. In the prior week 26% were paid below the minimum, 76% of those working over 40 hours were not paid required overtime, and 43% of those who complained or tried to organize faced illegal retaliation.
CL1531.jurisdiction: Chicago, Los Angeles and New York City
CL1531.limitation: Three large cities in 2008; co-published by a worker advocacy group; findings may differ elsewhere and today.

CL1532.claim: Studies of California's $20 fast-food minimum wage disagree on employment effects.
CL1532.supports: Reich (UC Berkeley Institute for Research on Labor and Employment brief, February 23, 2025) reports pay up 8% to 9%, no negative employment effect and prices up about 1.5%. Clemens, Edwards and Meer (NBER Working Paper 34033, July 2025) find fast-food employment fell 2.7% relative to the rest of the U.S., 3.2% after trend adjustment, about 18,000 jobs.
CL1532.limitation: Both are early analyses without peer review, and they use different comparison groups, data sources and periods.

CL1533.claim: California's Fast Food Council had no chair and did not meet in 2025, so it took no vote on raising the $20 floor.
CL1533.supports: Restaurant Business reported that the council could not meet without a chair after its chair stepped down in May 2025, that the full council never met in 2025, and that a cost-of-living increase placed on a future agenda was never voted on.
CL1533.limitation: A trade press report from late 2025 with no exact date; whether the council met or voted in 2026 is unconfirmed.

CL1534.claim: Minnesota's Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board set minimum wages of $19 for most nursing home workers and $22.50 for nursing assistants from September 10, 2026.
CL1534.supports: The Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry lists adopted standards: $19.00 general, $22.50 certified nursing assistant, $23.50 trained medication aide and $27.00 licensed practical nurse from September 10, 2026, each rising $1.50 on January 1, 2027, plus holiday pay from January 1, 2025.
CL1534.limitation: The wage standards took effect on September 10, 2026, so no data on pay, staffing or employment outcomes exist yet.

CL1535.claim: Canadian first-contract arbitration cut first-agreement strikes by at least half, and interest arbitration in New York produced no strikes.
CL1535.supports: Johnson (ILR Review, 2010) finds that across Canadian jurisdictions adopting first-contract arbitration at different times, it reduced first-agreement work stoppages by at least 50%, while arbitration was rarely used. Kochan and coauthors (ILR Review, 2010) find no strikes under New York's police and firefighter arbitration from 1974 to 2007 and arbitrated raises similar to negotiated ones.
CL1535.population: Newly certified units (Canada); police and firefighters (New York)
CL1535.limitation: Canadian labor law and U.S. public-safety bargaining differ from U.S. private-sector law; no U.S. private-sector test exists.

CL1536.claim: The House passed the Faster Labor Contracts Act on June 9, 2026, setting deadlines and binding arbitration for first contracts.
CL1536.supports: Duane Morris reports H.R. 5408 reached the floor by discharge petition and passed June 9, 2026. It requires bargaining within 10 days of a request, mediation after 90 days, and a binding two-year arbitration award if mediation fails within 30 days. McDermott reports the same passage date. The Senate companion is S. 844; no Senate vote was recorded by mid-October 2026.
CL1536.population: Private-sector employers and newly certified unions
CL1536.limitation: Law firm summaries report different vote totals; the bill is not law and its terms could change.

CL1537.claim: The National Labor Relations Act excludes agricultural laborers, domestic workers, independent contractors and supervisors from its definition of employee.
CL1537.supports: 29 U.S.C. 152(3) states that the term employee shall not include any individual employed as an agricultural laborer, in the domestic service of any family or person at home, as an independent contractor, or as a supervisor, among other exclusions.
CL1537.limitation: Some states cover excluded workers under their own laws, such as California for farmworkers; coverage of other excluded groups varies.

CL1538.claim: Women working full time, year-round earned 83.9% of men's median earnings in 2025.
CL1538.supports: The Census Bureau's Income in the United States: 2025 (P60-289, September 15, 2026) reports the women's-to-men's earnings ratio rose to 83.9% from 80.6% in 2024, and real median household income of $87,460, up 2.6%.
CL1538.population: Full-time, year-round workers ages 15 and older
CL1538.limitation: A ratio of medians across all jobs; it does not compare pay for the same job, and the survey response rate was 61.3%.

CL1541.claim: Local labor market concentration declined from 1976 to 2015 by one Census Bureau measure.
CL1541.supports: Rinz (Census Bureau CARRA Working Paper 2018-10) finds local industrial concentration generally declined across its distribution from 1976 to 2015, while national concentration fell in the early 1980s and then rose. Higher local concentration is estimated to lower earnings.
CL1541.limitation: Industry-based market definitions differ from occupation-based ones used in posting studies, which find higher concentration.

CL1660.claim: Local sources supply 44% of public school revenue, mostly from property taxes, while states supply 46% and the federal government 11%.
CL1660.supports: NCES reports $954 billion in public elementary and secondary revenue in 2020-21 (in 2022-23 dollars): 46% state, 44% local and 11% federal. Property taxes made up 83% of local revenue, or 36% of all revenue nationally.
CL1660.limitation: One school year. Shares differ widely by state, and federal shares changed during the pandemic relief years.

CL1661.claim: Spending per student differs by more than three to one across states.
CL1661.supports: NCES reports national current expenditure of $16,280 per pupil in 2020-21 (2022-23 dollars). Total expenditure per pupil was lowest in Idaho ($11,686) and Utah ($12,301) and highest in the District of Columbia ($37,835) and New York ($32,184).
CL1661.limitation: State averages hide gaps between districts within a state, and costs of living and student needs differ across states.

CL1662.claim: A study of school finance reforms estimated that sustained increases in per-pupil spending raised completed schooling and adult earnings, most for children from low-income families.
CL1662.supports: Using variation from school finance reforms, Jackson, Johnson and Persico estimate in their working paper that a 10% increase in per-pupil spending for all 12 school years leads to 0.27 more completed years of education, 7.25% higher wages and a 3.67 percentage-point lower annual incidence of adult poverty, with effects much more pronounced for children from low-income families.
CL1662.population: Children exposed to school finance reforms, followed into adulthood
CL1662.period: Childhood school years affected by reforms; outcomes measured in adulthood
CL1662.limitation: Quasi-experimental design relying on the timing of reforms. Effects of older reforms may differ from today's spending.

CL1663.claim: Post-1990 state finance reforms raised spending and, gradually, test scores in low-income districts.
CL1663.supports: Lafortune, Rothstein and Schanzenbach use an event study of adequacy-era reforms after 1990. They find immediate and lasting spending increases in low-income districts and NAEP achievement gains that build over the years after each reform, implying a large effect of school resources on achievement.
CL1663.population: Public school students in states with finance reforms
CL1663.limitation: State-level NAEP samples limit precision for individual districts, and the reforms studied differed in design and size.

CL1664.claim: A meta-analysis found that a $1,000 increase in per-pupil spending sustained for four years raises test scores, graduation and college-going on average.
CL1664.supports: Jackson and Mackevicius pool quasi-experimental U.S. studies. A $1,000 per-pupil increase for four years raises test scores by 0.035 standard deviations, high school graduation by 1.92 points and college-going by 2.65 points, improving test scores or attainment over 90% of the time. Capital spending effects take about five years and are about half as large.
CL1664.population: U.S. public school students in the studies pooled
CL1664.limitation: Averages across studies hide variation in how districts used the money. The working-paper figures may differ slightly from the 2024 published version (Q361).

CL1665.claim: A review by other economists concludes that added spending does not reliably improve outcomes and that how money is used matters most.
CL1665.supports: Handel and Hanushek review older and newer studies and conclude that how resources are used is key to outcomes, finding little consistent relationship between spending and achievement. They report that direct tests of capital spending, class-size reduction and teacher salary incentives do not clearly support those policies in the United States.
CL1665.limitation: A literature review whose conclusions differ from the meta-analysis in CL1664; the disagreement turns partly on which studies are weighted and how.

CL1666.claim: Federal law requires states to set academic standards and test reading and math every year in grades 3 to 8 and once in high school.
CL1666.supports: The Elementary and Secondary Education Act, as amended by the Every Student Succeeds Act, requires each state to adopt challenging academic content standards and administer mathematics and reading or language arts assessments in each of grades 3 through 8 and at least once in grades 9 through 12.
CL1666.limitation: The statute sets minimum requirements; states choose the standards, tests and how results count in school ratings.

CL1667.claim: A March 2025 executive order directed the Education Secretary to take steps toward closing the Department to the extent permitted by law.
CL1667.supports: Executive Order 14242, signed March 20, 2025 and published at 90 FR 13679, directs the Secretary of Education, to the maximum extent appropriate and permitted by law, to take steps toward the closure of the Department while keeping services, programs and benefits running without interruption.
CL1667.limitation: The order cannot abolish the Department, which Congress created by statute; its effect depends on later actions and court rulings.

CL1668.claim: The Department of Education announced a reduction in force cutting its workforce from 4,133 to about 2,183.
CL1668.supports: The Department's March 2025 release says its workforce was 4,133 at the January 2025 inauguration and would total roughly 2,183 after the announced actions, including nearly 600 voluntary departures. It says it would continue formula funding, student loans, Pell Grants, funding for students with special needs and competitive grants.
CL1668.limitation: Staffing after later court rulings, rehiring or further transfers is not shown in this release.

CL1669.claim: The Supreme Court allowed the Department's layoffs to proceed while the legal challenge continued.
CL1669.supports: On July 14, 2025, the Supreme Court granted the government's application in McMahon v. New York and stayed a May 22, 2025 district court injunction pending appeal in the First Circuit and any petition for certiorari. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson dissented.
CL1669.limitation: A stay is an interim order and does not decide the merits. The docket entry covers the stay only, and later appeals court rulings are outside it.

CL1670.claim: Average teacher base pay was not measurably different in 2020-21 than in 2011-12 after inflation.
CL1670.supports: NCES reports an average base salary of $61,600 for regular full-time public school teachers in 2020-21 and states it was not measurably different in constant dollars from 2011-12. Traditional public schools employed 3.5 million teachers and public charter schools 251,000.
CL1670.limitation: Base salary excludes summer and supplemental pay and benefits, and averages vary widely across states and districts.

CL1671.claim: In October 2022, 44% of public schools reported at least one vacant teaching position.
CL1671.supports: The NCES School Pulse Panel reported that 44% of public schools had one or more vacant teaching positions in October 2022, and 53% reported in August 2022 feeling understaffed entering the 2022-23 school year.
CL1671.population: U.S. public schools in the panel
CL1671.limitation: Data are from one school year shortly after the pandemic, and a school-level vacancy count does not show how long positions stay open.

CL1672.claim: Public school enrollment fell about 3% in 2020 and is projected to fall another 5% by 2031.
CL1672.supports: NCES reports 50.8 million public preK-12 students in fall 2019, 49.4 million in fall 2020 and 49.6 million in fall 2022, the latest actual count, and projects 46.9 million in fall 2031.
CL1672.population: Public preK-12 students, traditional and charter
CL1672.limitation: Projections assume recent birth and migration trends continue, and changes vary widely by state and district.

CL1673.claim: Fourth-grade reading scores in 2024 were lower than in 2022 and 2019, with declines across most of the score range.
CL1673.supports: NAEP reports the 2024 national grade 4 reading average was 2 points lower than in 2022 and 5 points lower than in 2019. Scores at every reported percentile except the 90th were lower than in 2022, and 31% of students performed at or above NAEP Proficient.
CL1673.limitation: NAEP measures national achievement and cannot attribute changes to particular causes such as school closures.

CL1674.claim: Fourth-grade math recovered partly by 2024, with gains among higher performers and no gain for the lowest performers.
CL1674.supports: NAEP reports the 2024 national grade 4 math average was 2 points higher than in 2022 and 3 points lower than in 2019. Scores rose at the 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles but showed no significant change at the 10th and 25th, and 24% scored below NAEP Basic.
CL1674.limitation: National averages hide state and district differences, and the source does not explain why lower performers did not gain.

CL1675.claim: A 2025 federal law creates a tax credit of up to $1,700 for donations to scholarship organizations in states that opt in, starting in 2027.
CL1675.supports: The IRS describes Section 70411 of the 2025 tax law: from January 1, 2027, individuals can claim a nonrefundable credit for cash contributions of up to $1,700 to scholarship granting organizations, which fund qualified elementary and secondary education expenses. A state must elect to participate and provide a list of qualifying organizations.
CL1675.limitation: Proposed regulations were still pending in IRS materials, so eligibility and reporting details can change before 2027.

CL1676.claim: Thirty states had elected to participate in the federal scholarship tax credit for 2027 as of September 14, 2026.
CL1676.supports: The IRS list of participating states for 2027, dated September 14, 2026, names 30 states, from Alabama to Wyoming, including Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Virginia. The District of Columbia is not listed. In June 2026 the count was 27.
CL1676.limitation: Participation is voluntary, and states can join or leave the list before the credit takes effect.

CL1677.claim: Arizona's education savings account program enrolled 108,416 students as of October 13, 2026.
CL1677.supports: The Arizona Department of Education reports 108,416 participating students for 2026-27 as of October 13, 2026, and describes the program as letting money that would pay for a student's public school education follow the student to private school tuition or other approved options, including home education.
CL1677.population: Arizona students in the Empowerment Scholarship Account program
CL1677.limitation: The department notes the count is in flux until September stabilizes it, and the page does not report costs or results.

CL1678.claim: A lottery-based study found that Louisiana's voucher program lowered participants' math scores.
CL1678.supports: Abdulkadiroglu, Pathak and Walters use randomized admission lotteries in the Louisiana Scholarship Program for disadvantaged students. They find that participation lowered math scores by 0.4 standard deviations and reduced achievement in reading, science and social studies, and suggest low-quality private schools selected into the program.
CL1678.population: Low-income Louisiana students applying for vouchers
CL1678.period: First year of the statewide program, 2012-13
CL1678.limitation: Covers one program in its early years and measures test scores only; it does not measure attainment or programs in other states.

CL1679.claim: A Florida study found an association between a scholarship program's growth and gains for nearby public school students.
CL1679.supports: Figlio, Hart and Karbownik link Florida school and birth records and use a student fixed-effects design. As the state's tax-credit scholarship program matured, public school students with more nearby private options before the program had higher test scores and lower absenteeism and suspensions, with the largest benefits for lower-income students.
CL1679.period: Program years from 2002 through the late 2010s
CL1679.limitation: An observational design that measures competitive effects on public school students, separate from effects on scholarship users.

CL1680.claim: In California cities, on-cycle November elections are associated with about twice the turnout of stand-alone local contests and a more representative electorate.
CL1680.supports: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian find that on-cycle November elections generally double local voter turnout compared with stand-alone local contests, and that moving to on-cycle elections in California makes the electorate considerably more representative in race, age and partisanship, especially in presidential years.
CL1680.limitation: The study covers city elections in one state. Effects on school board elections and on school policy decisions are less established.

CL1466.claim: Retirement benefits require 40 work credits, and one credit in 2026 takes $1,890 of covered earnings.
CL1466.supports: SSA states that 40 credits are needed for retirement eligibility, that workers can earn up to four credits a year, and that one credit in 2026 requires $1,890 in covered earnings, so $7,560 earns the yearly maximum. The 2027 fact sheet raises the amount per credit to $1,970.
CL1466.limitation: Credits determine eligibility only; the benefit amount depends on lifetime earnings through the formula, and disability and survivor benefits use different credit tests.

CL1467.claim: The Social Security payroll tax applies to earnings up to $184,500 in 2026 and $192,300 in 2027.
CL1467.supports: SSA's fact sheet lists maximum taxable earnings for Social Security of $184,500 in 2026 and $192,300 in 2027, with no limit for Medicare's hospital insurance tax, and an employee tax rate of 7.65 percent including Medicare. OCACT describes the current combined Social Security payroll tax rate as 12.4 percent.
CL1467.limitation: The combined rate is split equally between worker and employer for employees; self-employed people pay both halves.

CL1468.claim: The benefit formula replaces 90 percent of the first part of average indexed earnings, then 32 and 15 percent.
CL1468.supports: SSA computes average indexed monthly earnings from up to 35 years with the highest wage-indexed earnings. For workers first eligible in 2027, the primary insurance amount is 90 percent of the first $1,340 of AIME, 32 percent up to $8,077 and 15 percent above; 2026 bend points were $1,286 and $7,749. The 2027 maximum at full retirement age is $4,188 a month.
CL1468.limitation: The formula sets the benefit at full retirement age; claiming age, family benefits and the earnings test change what a person receives.

CL1469.claim: Full retirement age is 67 for people born in 1960 or later; claiming at 62 cuts benefits 30 percent, and delay adds 8 percent a year to 70.
CL1469.supports: SSA's tables give a full retirement age of 67 for those born in 1960 and later and a 30 percent reduction for claiming at 62, so a $1,000 benefit becomes $700. Delayed retirement credits raise the benefit 8 percent a year for people born in 1943 or later, stopping at age 70.
CL1469.limitation: Reductions apply to monthly amounts; whether early or late claiming pays more over a lifetime depends on how long a person lives.

CL1470.claim: SSA announced a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment for 2027.
CL1470.supports: SSA announced on October 14, 2026 a 3.6 percent COLA for 2027. Increased benefits reach nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries in January 2027 and about 7.3 million SSI recipients on December 31, 2026. The estimated average retired worker benefit rises from $2,095 to $2,170 a month.
CL1470.population: Social Security beneficiaries and SSI recipients
CL1470.limitation: The press release quotes both 72 million and 76 million affected people without reconciling them; averages hide wide variation in individual benefits.

CL1471.claim: The 2026 Trustees Report projects the retirement trust fund's reserves run out in late 2032, when 78 percent of benefits would be payable.
CL1471.supports: SSA's June 9, 2026 release reports the trustees' projection that OASI reserves are depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032 with 78 percent of benefits then payable; combined OASI and DI reserves would last to 2034 with 83 percent payable; DI stays solvent for 75 years; and the 75-year deficit is 4.42 percent of taxable payroll, up from 3.82 percent.
CL1471.limitation: Projections under intermediate assumptions on fertility, immigration, wages and mortality; different assumptions move the dates.

CL1472.claim: The 75-year shortfall grew mainly because of lower fertility and immigration assumptions and the 2025 tax law.
CL1472.supports: Munnell reports the trustees' reconciliation: the deficit rose 0.60 point, with lower ultimate fertility (1.90 to 1.75) subtracting 0.35, immigration 0.18 and the 2025 law's reduced income tax revenue on benefits 0.16, partly offset by productivity and mortality assumptions. Closing the gap requires an immediate 4.42-point payroll tax increase or a 22 percent benefit cut rising to 38 percent by 2100; OASI payable benefits fall to 62 percent by 2100.
CL1472.limitation: Secondary analysis of official tables by a university research center; the size of each factor depends on the trustees' assumptions.

CL1473.claim: CBO projects the retirement trust fund is exhausted in fiscal 2032.
CL1473.supports: CBO's long-term projections released September 17, 2026 state that the balance of the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund is exhausted in fiscal year 2032 and that the gap between outlays and revenues generally widens over the next 75 years.
CL1473.limitation: CBO uses its own economic and demographic assumptions, so its dates and shortfall differ from the trustees' estimates.

CL1474.claim: The share of covered earnings subject to the payroll tax fell from 90 percent in 1982 to about 83 percent.
CL1474.supports: CRS reports that about 90 percent of covered earnings were taxable in 1982 and about 83 percent more recently, mainly because salaries for top earners grew faster than pay below the cap, which rises with average wages. About 6.2 percent of workers, 10.9 million, earned above the taxable maximum in 2019.
CL1474.limitation: Older report; the share fluctuates with the business cycle, and the report projected 82.5 percent by 2030 under 2021 assumptions.

CL1475.claim: SSA's workforce fell from about 57,400 in January 2025 to about 49,900 in January 2026.
CL1475.supports: CBPP, an advocacy research group, reports from Office of Personnel Management data that SSA headcount fell from 57,384 in January 2025 to 49,880 in January 2026, the fewest since 1967. It reports SSA stopped publishing monthly callback, appointment and backlog metrics in summer 2025. Federal News Network reports SSA cut about 7,000 employees in 2025, has about 50,000 staff and plans to hire 1,000.
CL1475.limitation: Headcount alone does not show workload or productivity; SSA attributes efficiency gains to automation and staff reassignment.

CL1476.claim: SSA reports faster phone answers and fewer pending initial disability claims, while pending hearings rose.
CL1476.supports: SSA's performance page reports, for August 2026, a national 800-number average speed of answer of 0.5 minutes and an answer rate near 99 percent; for fiscal 2026 through August, field office waits just under 21 minutes; about 900,000 pending initial disability claims averaging 188 days; and about 360,000 pending hearings, up from about 280,000 a year earlier, averaging 276 days.
CL1476.population: People contacting SSA and disability applicants
CL1476.limitation: Agency-reported metrics; the page's text and chart give different August 2025 phone figures, and callback waits are not reported.

CL1477.claim: The inspector general found SSA's phone metric counts callers who accept a callback as waiting zero minutes.
CL1477.supports: The SSA Office of the Inspector General found average speed of answer of about 15 minutes in fiscal 2025, falling to 7 minutes by September. Callers accepting a callback are counted as zero wait, though the average time until callback was about 109 minutes; about 23.8 million callers received callbacks and about 25 million calls ended without service. It found the data accurate.
CL1477.limitation: Covers fiscal 2025; later improvements reported by SSA in 2026 were outside the audit period.

CL1478.claim: Field office closures reduced the number of people receiving disability benefits in surrounding areas.
CL1478.supports: Deshpande and Li found that Social Security field office closures produced a persistent 16 percent decline in disability recipients in surrounding areas and about a 10 percent drop in applications, with the largest effects among people with moderately severe conditions and low education. Congestion at neighboring offices was the main channel.
CL1478.population: Disability applicants near closed field offices
CL1478.limitation: Measures closures, not staffing cuts at open offices or phone service changes; effects of current service models may differ.

CL1479.claim: Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of poverty in 2025 under the Supplemental Poverty Measure.
CL1479.supports: The Census Bureau reports that the Supplemental Poverty Measure (SPM) rate, which counts taxes, benefits and necessary expenses, was 13.1 percent in 2025 and that Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty that year.
CL1479.limitation: The estimate removes Social Security income without modeling how people would otherwise behave, so it overstates a counterfactual change.

CL1480.claim: Women receive lower average Social Security benefits and live longer after 65 than men.
CL1480.supports: SSA's 2023 fact sheet reports women were 55.2 percent of beneficiaries 60 and older and about 63 percent of those 85 and older; average annual Social Security income at 65 and older was $14,204 for women and $18,108 for men in 2021; and life expectancy at 65 in 2023 was 21.1 more years for women and 18.0 for men.
CL1480.limitation: Averages combine retired-worker, spousal and survivor benefits; differences among women by marital and work history are large.

CL1481.claim: Disability Insurance requires recent work credits, a five-month wait and a condition that blocks substantial work for at least a year.
CL1481.supports: SSA states that workers 31 or older generally need 40 credits, 20 earned in the 10 years before disability; that disability means inability to do substantial gainful activity for at least 12 months or a condition expected to result in death; and that payments generally begin after a five-month waiting period. The average disabled worker benefit rises from $1,642 to $1,701 in January 2027.
CL1481.limitation: Younger workers can qualify with fewer credits; approval rates and processing times vary by state disability agency.

CL1482.claim: In 2027 SSI pays up to $1,029 a month to an individual, and about 7.4 million people received SSI in January 2026.
CL1482.supports: SSA's fact sheet sets the 2027 federal SSI payment standard at $1,029 for an individual and $1,544 for a couple, with resource limits of $2,000 and $3,000. SSA's January 2026 snapshot counts 7.37 million SSI recipients, 2.51 million of them 65 or older, with an average payment of $737.
CL1482.limitation: Payments are reduced by countable income, and many states add supplements, so individual amounts vary.

CL1483.claim: The Social Security Fairness Act ended the WEP and GPO for benefits from January 2024.
CL1483.supports: SSA reports the act, signed January 5, 2025, ended the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset for benefits payable for January 2024 and later, affecting over 2.8 million people with pensions from work not covered by Social Security, and that by July 7, 2025 SSA had sent over 3.1 million retroactive payments totaling $17 billion.
CL1483.population: Beneficiaries with pensions from non-covered work
CL1483.limitation: Agency-reported implementation figures; disputes over retroactive pay for some new applicants were reported in 2026.

CL1484.claim: Removing the taxable maximum would close about half of the 75-year shortfall, by SSA's actuarial estimates.
CL1484.supports: OCACT estimates, under 2026 Trustees Report assumptions, that applying the 12.4 percent tax to all earnings from 2027 with no added benefit credit improves the long-range balance by 2.55 percent of payroll, eliminating 58 percent of the shortfall; with benefit credit for the added earnings, 1.98 percent, or 45 percent.
CL1484.population: Workers above the taxable maximum and their employers
CL1484.limitation: Projections assume limited shifts of pay into untaxed forms; behavioral responses by high earners and employers could lower revenue.

CL1485.claim: Raising the full retirement age to 68 or 69 would close 13 to 32 percent of the shortfall, by SSA's actuarial estimates.
CL1485.supports: OCACT estimates that raising the normal retirement age 2 months a year for those turning 62 from 2027 until it reaches 68 in 2032 would eliminate 13 percent of the 75-year shortfall, and continuing to 69 by 2038 with later longevity indexing would eliminate 32 percent.
CL1485.limitation: Estimates of program finances; they do not measure effects on disability claims, work or poverty among affected cohorts.

CL1486.claim: Switching the COLA to a chained index would close 15 percent of the shortfall; switching to an elderly index would widen it 7 percent.
CL1486.supports: OCACT estimates that using a chained CPI-W from December 2027, assumed about 0.3 percentage point lower a year, eliminates 15 percent of the 75-year shortfall; using the CPI-E from December 2028, assumed about 0.15 point higher, worsens it by 7 percent; and cutting the COLA by 1 point eliminates 46 percent.
CL1486.limitation: The size of the index gap is an assumption; the chained and elderly indexes have differed from the standard index by varying amounts over time.

CL1487.claim: Benefit formula changes and tax rate increases close different shares of the shortfall, by SSA's actuarial estimates.
CL1487.supports: OCACT estimates that gradually cutting the 32 and 15 percent factors to 10 and 5 percent by 2066 eliminates 25 percent of the shortfall; progressive price indexing at the 30th earnings percentile, 38 percent; a basic minimum benefit worsens it by 5 percent; and raising the payroll tax rate from 12.4 to 17.0 percent in 2027 eliminates 101 percent.
CL1487.limitation: Each estimate is for one provision alone; combined packages interact, and estimates exclude most behavioral responses.

CL1488.claim: A full retirement age of 70 would mean a 45 percent cut for those claiming at 62, and the chained index has grown about 0.25 point slower a year.
CL1488.supports: CBO reports that raising the full retirement age to 70 reduces lifetime benefits for every affected recipient, with claiming at 62 then cutting the monthly benefit by 45 percent. It notes the chained CPI grew about 0.25 percentage point more slowly per year than the standard index since 2001, and savings compound. Its estimates count primary effects, without changes in claiming or work.
CL1488.limitation: Older analysis with an outdated baseline; the reduction percentages follow from the formula and remain valid, while dollar effects have changed.

CL1489.claim: Life expectancy has risen much more for high earners, so raising the retirement age falls hardest on low earners.
CL1489.supports: CRS, citing National Academies estimates, reports that the gap in life expectancy at 50 between top and bottom earnings quintiles for men grew from 5.1 years (1930 cohort) to 12.7 years (1960 cohort), with no gain for the bottom quintile, and that proposals to raise the retirement age would affect low earners disproportionately.
CL1489.population: Men and women by lifetime earnings quintile
CL1489.period: Birth cohorts 1930 and 1960; report updated July 2021
CL1489.limitation: Projections for the 1960 cohort depend on modeled mortality; the gap for women grew from 3.9 to 13.6 years in the same estimates.

CL1490.claim: In March 2026, 72 percent of private industry workers had access to a workplace retirement plan and 52 percent took part, with access lower for the lowest paid.
CL1490.supports: BLS reports retirement benefits were available to 72 percent of private industry workers in March 2026 and 52 percent participated. Its March 2025 chart for civilian workers shows defined contribution plan access of 48 percent in the lowest wage quarter and 77 percent in the highest, with participation of 22 and 64 percent.
CL1490.limitation: Establishment survey of employer offerings; it does not measure balances or whether savings will be adequate.

CL1491.claim: State auto-IRA programs held more than $3.4 billion in over 1.4 million funded accounts by August 2026.
CL1491.supports: Georgetown University's Center for Retirement Initiatives reports that, as of August 31, 2026, 15 reporting state automatic IRA programs held more than $3.4 billion in assets across more than 1.4 million funded accounts, with CalSavers, OregonSaves and Illinois Secure Choice the largest.
CL1491.population: Workers enrolled in state auto-IRA programs
CL1491.limitation: Compiled from program reports by a center that supports these programs; funded accounts include small and inactive balances.

CL1492.claim: About half of eligible workers opted out of OregonSaves within a year, and average contributions were low.
CL1492.supports: Chalmers, Mitchell, Reuter and Zhong report that 49.8 percent of eligible OregonSaves employees opted out by month 12, about 40 percent had a positive balance within 12 months, and average contributions were 1.3 percent of pay across all eligible workers. Their earlier paper concludes the program meaningfully increased saving by reducing search costs; the average balance was $754 in April 2020.
CL1492.population: Eligible workers at Oregon employers without a plan
CL1492.limitation: Working papers on one state's early years; job turnover and later default increases may change results.

CL1493.claim: From 2027 the federal Saver's Match will deposit up to $1,000 a year into eligible savers' retirement accounts.
CL1493.supports: CRS reports that the Saver's Match, enacted in 2022 and starting in 2027, provides a 50 percent federal match on up to $2,000 of retirement contributions, a maximum of $1,000, deposited into a traditional retirement account, with the full match below $20,500 of modified adjusted gross income ($41,000 joint) and phasing out over the next $15,000 ($30,000 joint).
CL1493.limitation: Not yet operating; take-up depends on Treasury and IRS delivery systems and on savers making their own contributions.

CL1494.claim: The 1935 Social Security Act excluded agricultural and domestic workers, jobs held by most Black workers at the time.
CL1494.supports: DeWitt, writing in the Social Security Bulletin, reports that the original act excluded agricultural and domestic workers; about 65 percent of Black workers and 27 percent of white workers were in excluded jobs; 74 percent of the roughly 15.5 million excluded workers were white; and amendments in 1950 and 1954 extended coverage.
CL1494.limitation: The author argues the exclusion reflected tax-collection feasibility; that interpretation of motive is contested by other historians.

CL1495.claim: Automatic contributions raise retirement saving far more than tax subsidies do.
CL1495.supports: Chetty and coauthors, using 41 million observations from Denmark, found that each unit of government spending on retirement tax subsidies raised total saving by about 1 cent, mainly by shifting assets between accounts, while automatic contributions that people must opt out of substantially increased wealth. About 85 percent of people were passive savers who responded to defaults.
CL1495.limitation: Evidence from Denmark's pension institutions and tax rules; the size of effects in U.S. state programs and the federal Saver's Match may differ.

CL1550.claim: Employees pay 6.2% of wages for Social Security up to $184,500 in 2026 and 1.45% for Medicare, matched by employers.
CL1550.supports: The Social Security Administration lists the contribution and benefit base, the maximum earnings subject to the Social Security tax, as $176,100 for 2025 and $184,500 for 2026, with tax rates of 6.2% for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare paid by employees and employers each.
CL1550.population: Wage earners covered by Social Security
CL1550.limitation: Self-employed workers pay both halves, and an additional Medicare tax applies to wages above a high-income threshold.

CL1551.claim: In 2022 the lowest fifth of households had a negative average federal income tax rate, and the average rate for all federal taxes was 20.6%.
CL1551.supports: CBO's The Distribution of Household Income, 2022 (January 2026) reports average individual income tax rates ranging from negative 10% in the lowest quintile to 17% in the highest, because refundable credits exceed income tax at the bottom, and an average federal tax rate of 20.6% for all households.
CL1551.limitation: Rates rose in 2022 for lower quintiles as pandemic credits expired; CBO's income measure includes in-kind benefits and differs from Census measures.

CL1552.claim: The Child Tax Credit is $2,200 per child, but only up to $1,700 is refundable, phased in above $2,500 of earnings, and Social Security number rules exclude some families.
CL1552.supports: 26 U.S.C. 24 sets $2,200 per child, indexed after 2025, makes the credit refundable at 15% of earned income above $2,500 up to an inflation-adjusted $1,400 cap, and requires the child's and the taxpayer's Social Security numbers (one spouse on a joint return). The IRS lists the refundable maximum as $1,700 and requires numbers valid for employment.
CL1552.limitation: Families with three or more children can use an alternative refundability formula based on payroll taxes; amounts above are per child and phase out above $200,000 or $400,000 of income.

CL1553.claim: For 2026 the maximum EITC is $8,231 for families with three or more children, and the standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for married couples.
CL1553.supports: The IRS announced tax year 2026 inflation adjustments on October 9, 2025 (IR-2025-103, Revenue Procedure 2025-32), including a $16,100 standard deduction for single filers, $32,200 for married couples filing jointly, $24,150 for heads of household, and a maximum EITC of $8,231 for taxpayers with three or more qualifying children.
CL1553.limitation: Credit amounts for smaller families and the income ranges where the credit phases out differ and are set in Revenue Procedure 2025-32.

CL1554.claim: About 80.8% of eligible taxpayers received the EITC in tax year 2022.
CL1554.supports: IRS EITC Central reports a national participation rate of 80.8% for tax year 2022, defined as the percentage of eligible taxpayers who receive an EITC payment, using an eligibility model built on American Community Survey data and IRS records of payments.
CL1554.limitation: The eligible count comes from a model, so the rate carries estimation error; rates vary by state.

CL1555.claim: SPM child poverty fell to 5.2% in 2021 from 9.7% in 2020 and was first reported at 13.4% for 2024; refundable credits and stimulus payments moved millions out of poverty in 2021.
CL1555.supports: Census report P60-277 states the SPM child poverty rate fell 46%, from 9.7% in 2020 to 5.2% in 2021, and that refundable tax credits and stimulus payments moved 9.6 million and 8.9 million people out of SPM poverty. Census report P60-287 covers 2024, when the child SPM rate was first published as 13.4%.
CL1555.population: Children under 18; all people for program effects
CL1555.limitation: Several pandemic programs operated in 2021, so the drop is not a single-policy experiment. Census revised all 2019 to 2024 SPM rates in August 2026, and those revisions supersede the first-published child rates.

CL1556.claim: Census revised SPM rates for 2019 to 2024 after a BLS threshold correction, and the overall 2025 SPM rate was 13.1%.
CL1556.supports: Census P60-290 (September 15, 2026) reports an SPM rate of 13.1% for 2025, not statistically different from 2024, an official child poverty rate of 13.4%, a record low, and Social Security moving 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty. Census working paper SEHSD-WP2026-17 (August 19, 2026) revised 2019 to 2023 rates down 0.1 to 0.3 point and 2024 from 12.9% to 13.0%.
CL1556.limitation: The report's summary page gives no SPM rate for children; the official and SPM measures use different resources and thresholds, so their child rates differ.

CL1557.claim: Monthly expanded Child Tax Credit payments in 2021 had no measurable short-run effect on parents' employment.
CL1557.supports: Ananat, Glasner, Hamilton and Parolin (NBER Working Paper 29823, March 2022) use difference-in-differences with Current Population Survey and Census Pulse data from April to December 2021 and find small, inconsistently signed and statistically insignificant effects on employment and labor force participation among adults with children.
CL1557.limitation: Covers a temporary, nine-month policy during an unusual labor market; long-run responses to a permanent credit are not observed.

CL1558.claim: A simulation projected that a permanent child allowance would lead 1.5 million working parents to leave the labor force.
CL1558.supports: Corinth, Meyer, Stadnicki and Wu (NBER Working Paper 29366, revised March 2022) model replacing the Child Tax Credit with a child allowance like the 2021 design. They project 1.5 million workers, 2.6% of working parents, would exit the labor force, so child poverty would fall by at most 22%, compared with 34% before work responses.
CL1558.limitation: Results depend on assumed labor supply elasticities drawn from earlier welfare and EITC research; the 2021 payments did not show such exits in the short run.

CL1559.claim: Public Law 119-21 extended SNAP's time limit to adults up to age 64 and parents of children 14 and older, removed several exemptions and narrowed noncitizen eligibility.
CL1559.supports: CRS report R48552 states the law raised the time-limit age range from 18 to 54 to 18 to 64, applied it to parents whose youngest child is 14 or older, removed exemptions for veterans, homeless people and former foster youth, limited waivers to areas above 10% unemployment, and limited noncitizen eligibility to permanent residents, Cuban-Haitian entrants and COFA migrants. CRS R48755 reports USDA required implementation by November 2, 2025.
CL1559.limitation: CBO's participation estimate of about 2.4 million fewer people per month is a projection; Alaska and Hawaii may receive exemptions through 2028.

CL1560.claim: States now pay 75% of SNAP administrative costs and, from fiscal 2028, will pay up to 15% of benefits depending on error rates.
CL1560.supports: CRS report R48552 states that the federal share of SNAP administrative costs falls from 50% to 25% beginning in fiscal year 2027, and that from fiscal 2028 states with payment error rates of 6% to under 8% pay 5% of benefit costs, 8% to under 10% pay 10%, and 10% or more pay 15%, with delays for the highest-error states.
CL1560.limitation: CRS text gives fiscal 2026 in one place for the administrative change; the statute's provision table and most summaries give fiscal 2027.

CL1561.claim: Medicaid expansion adults face an 80-hour monthly work requirement starting no later than January 1, 2027, six-month renewals, and new immigrant eligibility limits.
CL1561.supports: CRS R48755 reports that nonpregnant, nondisabled expansion adults ages 19 to 64 must show 80 hours a month of work, a work program, community service or half-time education by December 31, 2026, with exemptions such as parents of children under 14, and CBO's estimate of 4.5 million more uninsured a year. KFF reports six-month renewals from December 31, 2026 and immigrant limits from October 1, 2026.
CL1561.population: Adults enrolled through the ACA Medicaid expansion; some qualified immigrants
CL1561.limitation: The statute names December 31, 2026 and CMS's rule January 1, 2027. States can seek good-faith exemptions to December 31, 2028, so start dates will vary; coverage losses are CBO projections.

CL1562.claim: Forty-one states including DC have expanded Medicaid to adults with incomes up to 138% of the federal poverty level.
CL1562.supports: KFF's status tracker (October 1, 2026) reports 41 states including the District of Columbia have adopted the ACA Medicaid expansion, covering adults with incomes up to 138% of the federal poverty level, $21,597 for an individual in 2025, and 10 states have not adopted it.
CL1562.limitation: Income limits for parents and others differ in non-expansion states.

CL1563.claim: Low- and moderate-income workers faced an average effective marginal tax rate of 31% in 2016, with wide variation.
CL1563.supports: CBO's November 2015 report estimates that workers with income below 450% of the federal poverty guidelines would face an average marginal rate of 31% in 2016, combining federal and state income taxes, payroll taxes, and the phaseout of SNAP and ACA cost-sharing subsidies, with wide variation among people with similar earnings.
CL1563.population: Workers below 450% of federal poverty guidelines
CL1563.limitation: The estimate predates the 2017 and 2025 tax laws and excludes some benefits such as housing aid and child care subsidies.

CL1564.claim: The Atlanta Fed publishes tools that show where wage gains leave families no better off because of benefit cliffs.
CL1564.supports: The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta's Policy Rules Database and dashboard standardize eligibility rules for SNAP, Medicaid and CHIP, housing vouchers, child care subsidies, TANF, WIC and other programs, together with federal and state taxes and credits, and can identify when wage gains make a family worse off or no better off.
CL1564.jurisdiction: United States, by state and locality
CL1564.limitation: A modeling tool that maps where cliffs exist under program rules; it does not count how many families face them or change their work.

CL1566.claim: State and local taxes take a larger share of income from the lowest-income families than from the top 1%, mainly through sales and excise taxes.
CL1566.supports: ITEP's Who Pays? (7th edition, tax law as of January 1, 2024, 2023 incomes) estimates state and local taxes at 11.4% of income for the lowest-income 20%, 10.5% for the middle 20% and 7.2% for the top 1%. Sales and excise taxes take 7.0%, 4.8% and 1.0%. In 2024, 31 states plus DC had EITCs and 14 states had child credits.
CL1566.limitation: ITEP favors progressive taxation and uses its own model and incidence assumptions; measuring taxes against annual income makes consumption taxes look more regressive than lifetime measures.

CL1567.claim: The largest individual tax expenditures in fiscal 2026 include preferential rates on capital gains and dividends and the exclusion for employer health insurance.
CL1567.supports: The Joint Committee on Taxation's Estimates of Federal Tax Expenditures for Fiscal Years 2025-2029 (JCX-45-25, December 3, 2025) lists fiscal 2026 costs of $252.3 billion for reduced rates on dividends and long-term capital gains, $240.4 billion for the employer health exclusion, $128.4 billion for the child tax credit, $76.4 billion for the business income deduction and $72.5 billion for gains at death.
CL1567.limitation: Tax expenditure estimates are not additive and do not show revenue that repeal would raise, because behavior and interactions change.

CL1568.claim: In 2019 the top fifth of households received about half the benefit of major income tax expenditures.
CL1568.supports: CBO's The Distribution of Major Tax Expenditures in 2019 (October 2021) found about half of the benefits of major income tax expenditures went to the highest quintile, 18% to the top 1% and 9% to the lowest quintile. Ninety-five percent of the benefit of preferential rates on capital gains and dividends went to the top quintile, and about 75% to the top 1%.
CL1568.limitation: Predates the 2025 law; refundable credits count as tax expenditures and favor lower quintiles, which the average combines with other items.

CL1569.claim: CBO estimates Public Law 119-21 lowers resources for the lowest tenth of households by about $1,200 a year and raises them for the top tenth by about $13,600.
CL1569.supports: CBO's August 11, 2025 letter estimates that over 2026 to 2034 resources fall about $1,200 a year (3.1% of income) for the lowest decile, mainly from reduced Medicaid and SNAP, and rise about $13,600 (2.7%) for the top decile, mainly from lower taxes. The fifth and sixth deciles gain $800 and $1,200.
CL1569.limitation: Static allocation that excludes macroeconomic effects and debt-service costs; later regulations and state responses can change the outcome.

CL1570.claim: The IRS did not offer Direct File for the 2026 filing season after it handled 296,531 returns in 2025.
CL1570.supports: CPA Practice Advisor (November 5, 2025) reports the IRS told the 25 partner states by email that Direct File would not be offered in 2026 and no future launch date was set. Direct File accepted 140,803 returns in 2024 in 12 states and 296,531 in 2025 in 25 states.
CL1570.limitation: Trade press report of an agency email, which does not say whether a replacement program will follow.

CL1571.claim: In the 2026 filing season live IRS assistors answered 20% fewer calls and 42 taxpayer assistance centers were fully staffed, down from 102.
CL1571.supports: The National Taxpayer Advocate's Fiscal Year 2027 Objectives Report (June 2026) filing season review states the IRS operated with fewer employees, live assistors answered 20% fewer calls than the prior season, 42 taxpayer assistance centers were fully staffed versus 102 in 2025, and identity theft victim cases averaged 600 days to close in fiscal 2026.
CL1571.limitation: The report gives no staffing count; the Taxpayer Advocate is an independent office inside the IRS with a mandate to report problems.

CL1572.claim: Two of the federal government's most critical legacy computer systems belong to the Treasury Department and are 59 and 51 years old.
CL1572.supports: GAO-25-107795 (July 17, 2025) reviewed 11 critical legacy systems. Two belong to the Department of the Treasury, labeled Systems 9 and 10, at 59 and 51 years old, and agencies typically spend about 80% of IT budgets on operations and maintenance of existing systems.
CL1572.limitation: GAO withheld system names for security reasons, so the report does not confirm which Treasury or IRS functions the systems run.

CL1573.claim: An additional dollar spent auditing taxpayers above the 90th income percentile returns more than $12 in revenue, counting deterrence.
CL1573.supports: Boning, Hendren, Sprung-Keyser and Stuart (NBER Working Paper 31376, June 2023) use IRS audit data. They estimate more than $12 in revenue per extra $1 spent auditing taxpayers above the 90th percentile, about $5 below the median, and find deterrence effects at least three times the revenue from the audit itself.
CL1573.period: Audits of returns from the 2000s and 2010s
CL1573.limitation: Returns at the margin can fall as audits expand, and the estimates assume examiners of similar skill can be hired and trained.

CL1574.claim: IRS audit rates fell from 0.9% to 0.25% between tax years 2010 and 2019, most for high incomes, while EITC claimants were audited above average.
CL1574.supports: GAO-22-104960 (May 17, 2022) found the average individual audit rate fell from 0.9% to 0.25% for tax years 2010 to 2019, with the largest declines for incomes of $200,000 and above, which IRS officials attributed mainly to reduced staffing. Lower-income EITC claimants were audited at higher-than-average rates.
CL1574.limitation: Audit rates for recent years are incomplete because returns can still be audited; the report predates 2022 funding and 2025 staff cuts.

CL1575.claim: In late 2025, 63% of adults said they would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent.
CL1575.supports: The Federal Reserve's Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025 (May 2026; survey fielded October 17 to 28, 2025) reports 63% would cover a hypothetical $400 expense with cash or its equivalent, unchanged from the prior three years, 73% doing at least okay financially, and 23% of renters behind on rent.
CL1575.limitation: A self-reported hypothetical; some adults who would not use cash have other ways to pay, such as a credit card paid off later.

CL1576.claim: During the Medicaid unwinding, over 25 million people were disenrolled and 69% lost coverage for procedural reasons.
CL1576.supports: KFF (September 18, 2024) reports that over 25 million people were disenrolled after continuous enrollment ended, 69% for paperwork or procedural reasons, and that automatic (ex parte) renewal rates ranged from 90% or more in Arizona, North Carolina and Rhode Island to 11% or less in Pennsylvania and Texas.
CL1576.limitation: State-reported data; some people disenrolled for procedural reasons were no longer eligible or later re-enrolled.

CL1578.claim: Unemployment insurance's Extended Benefits program adds up to 13 weeks of benefits when a state has high unemployment.
CL1578.supports: The Labor Department's Employment and Training Administration describes Extended Benefits as up to 13 additional weeks after regular benefits are exhausted when a state is experiencing high unemployment, with an optional additional 7 weeks in some states during extremely high unemployment.
CL1578.population: Unemployed workers who exhaust regular state benefits
CL1578.limitation: The program description omits trigger thresholds and financing; whether a state's program turns on depends on state law choices.

CL1579.claim: The Labor Department estimated improper unemployment payments rose from 9.2% in fiscal 2020 to 18.9% in fiscal 2021.
CL1579.supports: GAO's work on unemployment insurance (GAO-22-105162, updated September 2024) reports that the Labor Department's estimated improper payment rate rose from 9.2% of payments in fiscal 2020 to 18.9%, or $78.1 billion, in fiscal 2021, and that increased identity theft was a main cause during the pandemic.
CL1579.limitation: Total improper payments in pandemic programs are unknown because some were not estimated; improper payments include errors as well as fraud.

CL1267.claim: A final judgment entered May 19, 2026 bars RealPage from using competitors' nonpublic data in live rent recommendations; RealPage admitted no liability.
