CL1267.supports: The department's May 8, 2026 response to comments in United States v. RealPage, No. 1:24-cv-00710 (M.D.N.C.), describes the terms: no nonpublic competitor data in runtime pricing, training data at least 12 months old, no geographic variable narrower than a state in its main models, landlord override, and a three-year monitor. It notes no admission of liability, final judgments for Greystar and Cortland, and that the United States would move for entry. The court entered the judgment on May 19, 2026, and its September 30, 2026 opinion describes the judgment as lasting seven years.
CL1267.population: RealPage and landlords using its software
CL1267.jurisdiction: United States (federal court, Middle District of North Carolina)
CL1267.limitation: The complaint's allegations were not adjudicated, and the judgment does not show how much rents changed.

CL1268.claim: New York enacted a law in October 2025 making it unlawful to help landlords coordinate residential rents through software.
CL1268.supports: New York Senate bill S7882 adds General Business Law section 340-b, making it unlawful to knowingly or recklessly help bring about an agreement among rental property owners or managers not to compete, including by operating software that performs a coordinating function, and treating an owner who sets rents from such recommendations as party to the agreement. It was signed October 16, 2025 as Chapter 437, effective on the 60th day.
CL1268.population: Residential landlords and pricing software vendors in New York
CL1268.limitation: The statute page does not report legal challenges or enforcement actions under the law, and its effective date is computed from the signing date.

CL1269.claim: In July 2024 the FTC ordered eight companies to provide information on surveillance pricing products.
CL1269.supports: The FTC's July 23, 2024 release states that the Commission voted 5-0 to issue 6(b) orders to Mastercard, Revionics, Bloomreach, JPMorgan Chase, Task Software, PROS, Accenture and McKinsey, seeking information on products, data inputs, customers and effects on consumers and prices.
CL1269.limitation: The orders gather information for a study; they make no finding of wrongdoing by any of the eight companies.

CL1270.claim: Preliminary FTC findings in January 2025 reported that pricing intermediaries served at least 250 clients and could use location, demographics, browsing and even cursor movements to set prices.
CL1270.supports: The FTC's January 17, 2025 release reports initial staff findings from documents of six companies: data such as location, demographics, browsing and shopping history, and behaviors like cursor movements and abandoned carts can feed pricing; the intermediaries worked with at least 250 clients including grocery stores; examples were hypothetical. The vote to release was 3-2, with Commissioners Ferguson and Holyoak dissenting.
CL1270.population: Six pricing and data intermediaries and their clients
CL1270.limitation: Preliminary and based on aggregated documents; it does not measure how often consumers paid different prices, and the release does not report the study's later status.

CL1271.claim: New York requires sellers that use personalized algorithmic pricing to disclose that the price was set by an algorithm using the consumer's personal data.
CL1271.supports: New York General Business Law section 349-a requires the statement "THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA" when an entity sets and publishes a price to a New York consumer using that consumer's personal data, exempts certain insurers and financial institutions, and lets the attorney general seek civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation after a cease-and-desist letter.
CL1271.population: Sellers using personalized pricing with New York consumers
CL1271.limitation: Disclosure only; the law does not limit the practice, and the statute page does not state an effective date.

CL1272.claim: A 2021 Berkeley Labor Center review found that U.S. workers generally lacked rights to know what data employers collect or to challenge automated decisions.
CL1272.supports: Bernhardt, Kresge and Suleiman's policy review documents employer use of electronic monitoring and algorithms in hiring and management across many industries and reports that workers generally have no right to know, review or correct data or to challenge automated decisions, and that employers are generally not required to give notice of monitoring or algorithms.
CL1272.limitation: A policy review drawing on interviews and secondary research, not a legal census; several state and local laws have passed since 2021.

CL1273.claim: New York City's enforcement of its automated hiring law has been weak, with two complaints and one violation found where state auditors saw at least 17 potential violations.
CL1273.supports: The New York State Comptroller's December 2, 2025 audit covering July 2023 to June 2025 found the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection received two complaints, reviewed 32 companies and found one instance of non-compliance; auditors reviewing the same companies identified at least 17 potential instances. Local Law 144 requires annual bias audits, published summaries and candidate notice.
CL1273.population: Employers using automated hiring tools in New York City
CL1273.limitation: One city's enforcement over two years; potential violations identified by auditors are not adjudicated findings.

CL1274.claim: In a three-month randomized experiment during the 2020 election, switching Facebook and Instagram users to chronological feeds changed what they saw but did not measurably change polarization or political knowledge.
CL1274.supports: Guess et al. (Science, 2023) assigned consenting users to reverse-chronological feeds. Users spent less time on the platforms, saw more political and untrustworthy content, and on Facebook saw less uncivil content, with no significant change in issue polarization, affective polarization or political knowledge.
CL1274.population: Consenting adult U.S. Facebook and Instagram users
CL1274.limitation: Three months during one election on two platforms; effects of long-term exposure or spillovers between users were outside what the design could test.

CL1275.claim: Cutting Facebook users' exposure to like-minded sources by about one-third had no measurable effect on eight attitudes, ruling out effects of 0.12 standard deviations or more.
CL1275.supports: Nyhan et al. (Nature, 2023) ran a field experiment with 23,377 users from September 24 to December 23, 2020. The median user received 50.4% of content from like-minded sources; treatment lowered that to 36.2%, raised cross-cutting exposure and reduced uncivil language, with no measurable effects on eight preregistered attitudes including affective polarization.
CL1275.limitation: One platform during one campaign season; small effects below the detectable range cannot be excluded.

CL1276.claim: On X in 2023, switching users from a chronological to the algorithmic feed shifted some opinions toward conservative positions without changing affective polarization.
CL1276.supports: Gauthier, Hodler, Widmer and Zhuravskaya (Nature, 2026) randomly assigned active U.S. users to algorithmic or chronological feeds for seven weeks. Switching to the algorithm raised engagement and shifted opinion toward conservative positions, especially on policy priorities; neither switching on nor off significantly affected affective polarization, and switching off had no comparable effects.
CL1276.limitation: One platform's algorithm at one time; the asymmetry between switching on and off is not explained by the design.

CL1277.claim: Reranking posts with partisan animosity on X for ten days moved feelings toward the other party by about 2 points on a 100-point scale.
CL1277.supports: Piccardi et al. (Science, 2025) ran a preregistered ten-day field experiment with 1,256 X users during the 2024 campaign, using a language model to decrease or increase exposure to posts expressing antidemocratic attitudes and partisan animosity; out-party feelings shifted by about 2 points on a 100-point thermometer in the corresponding direction.
CL1277.limitation: Short duration and a volunteer sample using a browser extension; persistence beyond ten days was not tested.

CL1278.claim: The Supreme Court held in Moody v. NetChoice (2024) that platforms' choices about including and ranking posts in their main feeds are protected editorial activity.
CL1278.supports: The syllabus of Moody v. NetChoice, Nos. 22-277 and 22-555, decided July 1, 2024, states that platforms' decisions about which posts to include, rank or label in main feeds are an exercise of protected editorial control, and that Texas was unlikely to be able to enforce its law against that curation.
CL1278.limitation: The Court remanded facial challenges; how the ruling applies to data access or user-choice mandates was not decided.

CL1279.claim: During Medicaid unwinding, more than 25 million people were disenrolled, 69% for procedural reasons, and automatic renewal rates ranged from about 11% to over 90% by state.
CL1279.supports: KFF's analysis of state-reported data through June 2024 counts over 25 million disenrollments among about 56 million renewals; 69% of those disenrolled lost coverage for paperwork or procedural reasons. Ex parte renewal rates ran 90% or higher in Arizona, North Carolina and Rhode Island and 11% or lower in Pennsylvania and Texas.
CL1279.limitation: State-reported data with different time periods and pending cases; procedural disenrollment does not show how many people were still eligible.

CL1280.claim: Under Public Law 119-21, states with SNAP payment error rates of 6% or more will pay 5% to 15% of benefit costs from fiscal 2028.
CL1280.supports: CRS Report R48552 describes state benefit cost shares beginning in fiscal 2028 of 5% for error rates from 6% to under 8%, 10% for 8% to under 10%, and 15% for 10% or more, with delayed starts for states with the highest rates.
CL1280.limitation: How states will change verification in response is a projection; the law does not specify system design.

CL1281.claim: GAO found the 11 most critical federal legacy IT systems were 23 to 60 years old, and agencies spend about 80% of IT budgets operating existing systems.
CL1281.supports: GAO-25-107795 (July 17, 2025) identifies 11 critical legacy systems at 10 agencies including Health and Human Services and Treasury, aged 23 to 60 years, and reports that agencies typically spend about 80% of IT spending on operations and maintenance.
CL1281.limitation: Federal systems only; most benefit eligibility systems are run by states and were not part of this review.

CL1282.claim: Unemployment insurance improper payments rose from 9.2% in fiscal 2020 to 18.9% ($78.1 billion) in fiscal 2021, and GAO has reported a need to modernize state systems.
CL1282.supports: GAO's report on unemployment insurance (GAO-22-105162) cites Labor Department estimates of improper payment rates of 9.2% ($8.0 billion) in fiscal 2020 and 18.9% ($78.1 billion) in fiscal 2021, and states that GAO, the Labor Department and its inspector general have reported on the need to modernize state IT systems.
CL1282.limitation: Pandemic programs had unusual volume and new rules; improper payments include both overpayments and documentation errors, and IT is one factor among several.

CL1283.claim: GSA closed its 18F digital team in March 2025, and the IRS did not offer Direct File for 2026 after it accepted 296,531 returns in 2025.
CL1283.supports: Federal News Network reported that GSA's Federal Acquisition Service commissioner announced the shutdown of 18F by email in March 2025, affecting about 85 people, and that 18F built the IRS Direct File platform. CPA Practice Advisor reported the IRS told partner states Direct File would not be offered in 2026, after 140,803 accepted returns in 2024 and 296,531 in 2025 across 25 states.
CL1283.population: Federal digital service teams; Direct File users
CL1283.limitation: Both sources are trade press; neither evaluates the effect of the closures on service quality.

CL1284.claim: Payroll data show a 13% relative employment decline for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations after generative AI spread, while older workers held steady.
CL1284.supports: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (Stanford, August 2025) use administrative data from the largest U.S. payroll software provider. Early-career workers in the most exposed occupations saw a 13% relative decline in employment after controlling for firm-level shocks; less exposed and more experienced workers were stable or growing, and declines concentrated in occupations where AI tends to automate tasks.
CL1284.population: U.S. workers in firms using the payroll provider
CL1284.limitation: The authors describe the evidence as consistent with an AI effect; the design cannot exclude other causes that hit young workers in the same occupations.

CL1285.claim: In Denmark, AI chatbots had no significant effect on earnings or recorded hours in 11 exposed occupations, ruling out effects larger than 1%.
CL1285.supports: Humlum and Vestergaard (Becker Friedman Institute working paper 2025-56) link adoption surveys from late 2023 and 2024 to Danish employer-employee records and find no significant impact on earnings or hours in any occupation, with confidence intervals ruling out effects above 1%, and average time savings of about 3%.
CL1285.population: Workers in 11 AI-exposed occupations in Denmark
CL1285.limitation: An early period in a country with different labor institutions and social insurance from the United States.

CL1286.claim: The Yale Budget Lab found the U.S. occupational mix changing about 1 percentage point faster than in the internet era, with no link between AI exposure and unemployment through 2025.
CL1286.supports: Gimbel, Kinder, Kendall and Lee (Yale Budget Lab, October 1, 2025) report that the occupational mix has shifted only slightly faster since late 2022 than around 2000, that the shares of workers in low, medium and high exposure jobs stayed stable, and that exposure and usage measures show no relation to employment or unemployment changes, with a possible exception among recent graduates.
CL1286.limitation: Exposure measures are theoretical and the usage data come from one AI company's users; the authors plan regular updates.

CL1287.claim: Evidence on AI's effects on employment is early and mixed.
CL1287.supports: A U.S. payroll study finds a relative decline for young workers in exposed occupations, while a Danish study rules out earnings and hours effects above 1% and a Yale Budget Lab analysis finds no relation between exposure and unemployment. The studies differ in country, period, data and outcome.
CL1287.limitation: All three studies cover the first two to three years of adoption; later effects may differ in size or direction.

CL1288.claim: Colorado's 2024 AI law never took effect; after a federal lawsuit and a Justice Department complaint, the state replaced it with SB 26-189, effective January 1, 2027.
CL1288.supports: A McDermott Will & Emery analysis (May 2026) reports that SB 24-205 was delayed to June 30, 2026; xAI sued on April 9, 2026 and the Justice Department filed a companion complaint on April 24 in the U.S. District Court for Colorado; an April 27 stipulated order paused enforcement; and SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026, requires notice, explanation after adverse outcomes and human review, enforced by the attorney general with a 60-day cure period, from January 1, 2027.
CL1288.population: Developers and deployers of automated decision technology in Colorado
CL1288.limitation: Secondary legal analysis; the article does not list the decisions SB 26-189 covers, so coverage of employment decisions is unclear, and later litigation is outside the cited source.

CL1630.claim: Counties, towns and cities own about three-quarters of U.S. public road miles; state highway agencies own about a fifth.
CL1630.supports: FHWA's 2022 table counts 4,197,446 miles of public roads in the 50 states and DC. Counties own 1,801,179 miles (42.9%), towns, townships and municipalities 1,368,765 (32.6%), state highway agencies 783,674 (18.7%), federal agencies 153,108 (3.6%) and other jurisdictions 89,903 (2.1%).
CL1630.limitation: Mileage counts every road equally. State highways carry far more traffic per mile than most local roads, so ownership of travel differs from ownership of miles.

CL1631.claim: In 2026, 41,148 of the nation's 624,939 highway bridges, or 6.6%, were rated in poor condition.
CL1631.supports: FHWA's 2026 National Bridge Inventory table counts 624,939 bridges and rates 268,737 (43.0%) good, 315,054 (50.4%) fair and 41,148 (6.6%) poor. Bridges rated poor hold 4.8% of total bridge deck area.
CL1631.population: Public highway bridges longer than 20 feet
CL1631.limitation: A poor rating means a major element needs repair; it does not mean the bridge is unsafe to use. Inspectors restrict or close bridges separately.

CL1632.claim: The federal government paid about a quarter of public spending on highways and on transit in 2017.
CL1632.supports: CBO reports that in 2017 the federal government accounted for 26% of public spending on highways and 23% on mass transit and rail, with state and local governments paying the rest after counting federal grants as federal money.
CL1632.population: Public spending on highways and transit
CL1632.limitation: The figures predate the 2021 infrastructure law, which raised federal highway and transit funding from 2022 to 2026.

CL1633.claim: CBO projects the Highway Trust Fund's transit account will be exhausted in 2027 and its highway account in 2028.
CL1633.supports: CBO's June 2026 baseline shows the highway account receiving $41.6 billion in 2026 against $62.2 billion in outlays, with a cumulative shortfall of $11.9 billion in 2028 growing to $221.4 billion by 2036. The transit account shows a $2.9 billion shortfall in 2027.
CL1633.limitation: The projection assumes current spending patterns and that fuel taxes scheduled to expire in 2028 continue. A new law could change both.

CL1634.claim: The 2021 infrastructure law authorized highway and transit programs through fiscal 2026, and a five-year successor bill cleared the House committee in May 2026.
CL1634.supports: FTA states that the 2021 law reauthorized surface transportation programs for fiscal years 2022 through 2026. The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee approved H.R. 8870, the BUILD America 250 Act, on May 22, 2026 after a 14-hour markup; its release says current law expires September 30 and the bill adds a new trust fund revenue stream.
CL1634.limitation: The committee pages show no House floor vote or enactment, and they predate the September 30, 2026 expiration.

CL1635.claim: Federally funded projects must appear in a regional Transportation Improvement Program covering at least four years, with a public comment opportunity.
CL1635.supports: Federal regulations require a metropolitan planning organization for each urbanized area over 50,000 people. Its Transportation Improvement Program must cover at least four years, be updated at least every four years and be approved by the MPO and the governor. The MPO's participation plan must give a reasonable opportunity to comment on the plan and the program.
CL1635.population: Metropolitan areas receiving federal highway and transit funds
CL1635.limitation: The rule sets minimum process. How much influence public comments have on project selection varies by MPO.

CL1636.claim: By July 31, 2026, USDOT had obligated about 76% of its 2021 infrastructure law funds and paid out about 47%.
CL1636.supports: The Department of Transportation's funding status table shows $545.7 billion in enacted budget authority for DOT-administered funds under the 2021 law, with 75.65% obligated and 46.60% outlaid as of July 31, 2026.
CL1636.population: DOT-administered funds under the 2021 infrastructure law
CL1636.limitation: Outlays lag obligations by design for construction projects, so a low outlay share alone does not show waste or delay on a given project.

CL1637.claim: State and local governments spent 62% of their 2023 transportation and water infrastructure money on operation and maintenance.
CL1637.supports: CBO reports that state and local governments spent $494 billion on transportation and water infrastructure in 2023, of which $307 billion (62%) went to operation and maintenance and $187 billion (38%) to capital. The federal government spent $132 billion, 64% of it on capital.
CL1637.limitation: The totals combine highways, transit, water and other systems, so the split for roads alone differs.

CL1638.claim: A comparative study found U.S. rail transit among the most expensive to build, driven by station design, staffing, procurement and consultant costs.
CL1638.supports: The Transit Costs Project compared more than 900 projects in 59 countries and ranks the United States sixth most expensive. Its New York Second Avenue Subway case estimates oversized stations multiplied costs by about 2.06, procurement practices by 1.85, labor by about 1.5 and consultant-heavy soft costs by about 1.2; soft costs ran 21% versus 5% to 10% in comparison cases.
CL1638.jurisdiction: International comparison; New York and Boston case studies
CL1638.limitation: Case-study multipliers are the researchers' estimates from a few projects. They are not causal estimates and may differ for road repair or bus projects.

CL1639.claim: Federal pandemic laws sent transit agencies $25 billion in 2020 and $30.5 billion in 2021, including aid for operating costs.
CL1639.supports: FTA states that it allocated $25 billion from the CARES Act to formula recipients, and that the American Rescue Plan of March 2021 included $30.5 billion for public transportation at a 100% federal share, including additional assistance to 35 transit systems in 18 states to cover operating expenses.
CL1639.population: Public transit agencies receiving FTA formula funds
CL1639.limitation: The pages cited cover two of the three pandemic relief laws for transit; the December 2020 law is not counted here, and the pages do not report how quickly agencies spent the money or what happened after it ran out.

CL1640.claim: City 311 systems route non-emergency repair requests to the responsible team and issue a tracking number.
CL1640.supports: Boston's 311 page describes phone, app and web channels open every day, a Streets category covering potholes and street lights, routing of each request to the right team, and an email with a tracking number after an online submission.
CL1640.limitation: This is one city's system. Not every town has 311, and response times are not reported on this page.

CL1641.claim: The civil engineers' 2025 report card graded U.S. roads D+, bridges C and transit D.
CL1641.supports: The American Society of Civil Engineers' 2025 report card gives infrastructure overall a C, roads D+, bridges C and transit D, and estimates a $3.6 trillion investment gap over ten years.
CL1641.limitation: The grades come from a professional association whose members design and build infrastructure. They are expert judgments based on needs estimates and are not causal findings.

CL1642.claim: CBO lists raising fuel taxes and transferring general revenue among the ways to close the trust fund gap.
CL1642.supports: CBO's 2025 presentation on surface transportation lists options for addressing the trust fund's shortfall, including increasing existing fuel taxes and transferring money from the Treasury's general fund. The House committee's 2026 bill describes adding the fund's first new revenue stream in over three decades.
CL1642.limitation: The presentation lists options without recommending one, and the committee release does not name its revenue source.

CL1700.claim: By Unite America's count, 383 of 435 U.S. House seats (88%) were effectively decided in 2026 primaries by 22,680,444 voters, 9.4% of eligible voters nationwide.
CL1700.supports: Unite America's September 16, 2026 analysis starts from Cook Political Report ratings, subtracts seats with a same-party November contest and Louisiana's all-candidate races, and counts 383 House seats as decided in dominant-party primaries. It reports 22,680,444 voters in those primaries, 9.4% of eligible voters, and 26 Senate races (74% of those up) decided the same way.
CL1700.population: U.S. House seats and eligible voters
CL1700.limitation: Advocacy calculation by an organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. 'Effectively decided' is the group's own definition built on ratings, and its 2024 figure (87%) used voting-age population, so the years are not comparable.

CL1701.claim: Counts of primary-decided seats change with the definition: Cook rated 398 House seats safe in 2026, Unite America's adjusted count is 383, and 147 districts had no contest in the dominant party's primary.
CL1701.supports: Unite America reports that Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe; removing nine California same-party general elections and Louisiana's six all-candidate races left 383. It also identifies 147 districts where the candidate ran unopposed in the dominant party's primary for a safe seat, holding 85 million eligible voters.
CL1701.limitation: Ratings are forecasts, and variable C1 uses a different rule (a margin above ten points), so the same seat can be counted differently by each source.

CL1702.claim: NCSL classifies primaries as closed in 8 states, partially closed in 9, partially open in 5, open to unaffiliated voters in 8 (including Massachusetts), open in 15, top-two in 2, top-four in 1, and other systems in Nebraska and Louisiana.
CL1702.supports: The National Conference of State Legislatures' primary-type brief (updated May 19, 2026) lists closed primaries in Delaware, Florida, Kentucky, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Wyoming; partially closed primaries where each party decides on unaffiliated voters; top-two primaries in California and Washington; and Alaska's top-four primary. Massachusetts is open to unaffiliated voters, who may choose a party ballot while party members cannot cross over.
CL1702.population: Primary systems for state and congressional offices
CL1702.limitation: Categories simplify varied rules, and in partially closed states access can change when a party changes its rules. Louisiana uses different systems for different offices.

CL1703.claim: Nine states hold primary runoffs: seven require a majority, North Carolina allows a runoff on request below 30%, and South Dakota uses a 35% threshold for some offices; Georgia also holds general-election runoffs.
CL1703.supports: NCSL lists majority primary runoffs in Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Texas; a runoff in North Carolina when the leader has under 30% and the runner-up requests it; and in South Dakota a runoff for U.S. Senate, U.S. House and governor when no candidate reaches 35%. Georgia requires a general-election runoff when no candidate exceeds 50%.
CL1703.population: Primary and general election runoff rules
CL1703.limitation: The NCSL page is internally inconsistent about the total (it says seven in one place and ten in another while listing nine), so check your state's election code.

CL1704.claim: Ballots cast in the 2022 midterm primaries equaled 21.3% of eligible voters nationally, up from 19.9% in 2018 and 14.3% in 2014.
CL1704.supports: The Bipartisan Policy Center's 2022 primary turnout report (Thorning and Ferrer, March 2023) compiled primary returns from 49 states and the District of Columbia and reported total primary ballots cast as 21.3% of the eligible electorate in 2022, 19.9% in 2018, 14.3% in 2014 and 18.3% in 2010.
CL1704.limitation: A national total combines states with different primary types, dates and contested races; turnout in a single safe-seat primary can be much lower or higher.

CL1705.claim: Turnout in the 2022 U.S. House general elections was about 45.1% of the voting-eligible population, down from 48.1% in 2018.
CL1705.supports: Pew Research Center's analysis of final official returns counted nearly 107.7 million valid votes in 2022 House elections, about 45.1% of the estimated voting-eligible population, compared with 48.1% in 2018 and 34.4% in 2014.
CL1705.limitation: Uses estimated eligible population; uncontested races record few or no votes, which lowers House totals relative to top-of-ticket turnout.

CL1706.claim: Open primaries averaged higher turnout than closed primaries, and states that switched to open or top-two and top-four primaries saw turnout rise about 2 to 3 points.
CL1706.supports: Across four midterm cycles, the Bipartisan Policy Center reports average primary turnout of 21.9% in fully open states and 18.5% in closed states. Its within-state analysis estimated that switching from closed to open primaries raised turnout by nearly 2 percentage points, and switching to top-two or top-four by about 3 points.
CL1706.limitation: Observational comparison across a few switching states; other changes adopted at the same time could explain part of the difference. The sponsoring organization recommends opening primaries.

CL1707.claim: In 15 of the 30 largest U.S. cities, turnout in the most recent mayoral election studied was under 20% of eligible citizens.
CL1707.supports: Portland State University's 2016 'Who Votes for Mayor?' study (Jurjevich, Keisling and colleagues) examined mayoral elections in the 30 largest cities and reported turnout of eligible citizens below 20% in 15 of them.
CL1707.limitation: A decade-old snapshot of one office in large cities; some cities have since moved elections to November.

CL1708.claim: Moving city elections to the November ballot makes local electorates considerably more representative by race, age and partisanship, with the largest change in presidential years.
CL1708.supports: Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian (American Political Science Review, 2022) combined election timing with voter-level microtargeting data for California cities. They report that on-cycle timing makes the electorate considerably more representative by race, age and partisanship, and cite prior work finding that on-cycle November elections generally double local turnout.
CL1708.limitation: One state's cities; the turnout-doubling figure comes from earlier studies, and the paper addresses who votes more than what policies follow.

CL1709.claim: California's SB 415 bars a city or other political subdivision from holding elections off the statewide date when its turnout has fallen at least 25% below its average in the previous four statewide general elections, starting January 1, 2018.
CL1709.supports: The bill text on California's official legislative information site provides that, beginning January 1, 2018, a political subdivision may not hold an election other than on a statewide election date if a prior election produced turnout at least 25% less than its average over the previous four statewide general elections, and lets a voter sue in superior court.
CL1709.limitation: The law triggers on a turnout test, so some off-cycle elections remain; enforcement depends on lawsuits.

CL1710.claim: Ten states give a commission primary responsibility for congressional maps; in most other states the legislature draws them.
CL1710.supports: NCSL's congressional commissions page lists primary-responsibility commissions in Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Virginia and Washington, advisory commissions in states including Maine, New Mexico, New York and Utah, and backup commissions in Connecticut, Indiana and Ohio. It states that all other states draw congressional districts through state legislative authority; Iowa's legislature votes on maps drawn by nonpartisan staff.
CL1710.limitation: NCSL does not classify how independent each commission is, and the page's counts differ from its own tables by one state.

CL1711.claim: In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the U.S. Supreme Court held that partisan gerrymandering claims are political questions beyond the reach of federal courts, while noting that states and Congress can act.
CL1711.supports: The 5 to 4 opinion by Chief Justice Roberts, decided June 27, 2019, held that partisan gerrymandering claims present political questions beyond the reach of the federal courts. The syllabus notes that states are addressing the issue through constitutional amendments and legislation, including commissions, and that the Elections Clause gives Congress power to act.
CL1711.population: Federal court jurisdiction over districting claims
CL1711.limitation: Covers federal courts only; state courts can still review maps under state constitutions, and racial-discrimination claims follow other doctrine.

CL1712.claim: Mid-decade congressional redistricting is prohibited by neither the U.S. Constitution nor federal law; some states bar it under state law.
CL1712.supports: The Congressional Research Service's In Focus on mid-decade redistricting (IF13082, updated March 4, 2026) states that mid-decade redistricting is prohibited by neither the Constitution nor federal law, that states largely set their own timing, that some states restrict it, and that Congress has considered but not enacted limits. It names California, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Texas and Utah as states with new maps.
CL1712.limitation: Written before the spring 2026 redraws in Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana and the Callais decision.

CL1713.claim: Eight states had new congressional maps in force for November 2026, enacted by legislatures, a commission, voters or a court; Missouri's and Virginia's redraws did not take effect, and Alabama returned to its 2023 map.
CL1713.supports: A September 2026 tracker lists new maps in Texas (August 29, 2025), North Carolina (October 22, 2025), Ohio (commission, October 31, 2025), California (Proposition 50, November 4, 2025), Utah (court, November 10, 2025), Florida (May 4, 2026), Tennessee (May 7, 2026) and Louisiana (May 29, 2026, confirmed by Ballotpedia News). Missouri's map is blocked pending a referendum, Virginia's amendment was struck down May 8, 2026, and a June 2, 2026 U.S. Supreme Court stay restored Alabama's 2023 plan.
CL1713.limitation: Compiled by secondary trackers; each state's map has its own primary record, and several maps face lawsuits whose outcomes could change later elections.

CL1714.claim: In Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act imposes districting liability only when evidence supports a strong inference of intentional discrimination.
CL1714.supports: Justice Alito's opinion, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett, held that Louisiana's second majority-Black district was not required by Section 2 as properly construed and so failed strict scrutiny. Justice Kagan dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson. CRS reported that some legislatures were considering or had enacted maps eliminating majority-minority districts for 2026.
CL1714.population: Voting Rights Act Section 2 districting claims
CL1714.limitation: The ruling narrows Section 2 districting claims; it does not end all Section 2 protections, and effects on later maps depend on pending litigation.

CL1715.claim: In the 2021 to 2022 redistricting cycle, nonpartisan commissions produced less biased and more competitive maps than party-controlled processes, while both parties drew more extreme gerrymanders where they controlled the process.
CL1715.supports: Warshaw, McGhee and Migurski (Publius, 2022) report that both parties enacted increasingly extreme partisan gerrymanders when they controlled redistricting, that Republicans controlled more states and that Democrats' concentration in cities made their votes less efficient, and that nonpartisan commissions appear to offer a consistent means to produce less biased and more competitive maps.
CL1715.limitation: Descriptive comparison of one cycle; states that chose commissions may differ from those that did not, and the study predates the 2025 to 2026 mid-decade redraws.

CL1716.claim: When a party narrowly nominated the more extreme U.S. House candidate, its general-election vote share fell about 9 to 13 points and its chance of winning about 35 to 54 points; the penalty largely disappeared in safe districts.
CL1716.supports: Hall (American Political Science Review, 2015) used a regression discontinuity design on close House primaries from 1980 to 2010, measuring candidate ideology from donor patterns. Nominating the more extreme candidate lowered the party's general-election vote share and win probability and shifted the district's roll-call representation the other way, with effects lasting about four terms. In safe districts the penalty and the roll-call reversal largely disappeared.
CL1716.population: U.S. House primaries decided by narrow margins
CL1716.limitation: Close primaries are a minority of races, and the ideology measure comes from donors. The article body reports slightly smaller ranges (about 8 to 12 points) than its abstract.

CL1717.claim: Evidence that top-two primaries elect more moderate legislators is inconsistent: California's change appears partly due to commission-drawn districts and term-limit changes, and Washington shows little effect.
CL1717.supports: McGhee and Shor (Perspectives on Politics, 2017) found an inconsistent effect of top-two primaries on legislator ideology in California and Washington. Moderation was clearest among California Democrats, and part of it appeared to stem from district lines drawn by the state's new commission and possibly from term-limit changes; they found little or no effect for California Republicans or Washington legislators.
CL1717.limitation: Few cycles and two states; Alaska's top-four system is too new for comparable estimates; Issue record I026 cites an earlier multi-state study (McGhee and colleagues, 2014) with a similar null finding.

CL1718.claim: Randomized field experiments in two state legislatures found that constituent contact about a specific bill changed legislators' votes.
CL1718.supports: Bergan (American Politics Research, 2009) randomly assigned 143 New Hampshire House members to receive or not receive a grassroots email campaign on tobacco-control legislation and found a substantial influence on voting. Bergan and Cole (Political Behavior, 2015) randomly assigned Michigan legislators to receive constituent phone calls about anti-bullying bills and found support rose by about 12 percentage points.
CL1718.population: State legislators voting on specific bills
CL1718.limitation: Each test involved one issue with an organized campaign; effects on high-profile, party-line votes or on members of Congress were not tested.

CL1719.claim: Residents who speak at local planning and zoning meetings are older, more often men, longtime residents and homeowners, and far more opposed to new housing than the general public.
CL1719.supports: Einstein, Palmer and Glick (Perspectives on Politics, 2019) coded thousands of comments at planning and zoning board meetings on housing proposals and matched speakers to a voter file. Speakers were disproportionately older, male, longtime residents, local-election voters and homeowners, and opposed new housing to a much greater degree than the general public.
CL1719.population: Speakers at planning and zoning meetings
CL1719.limitation: Covers housing hearings in the sampled communities; meetings on other subjects may draw different speakers.

CL1720.claim: Federal agencies must consider the relevant matter in public comments on proposed rules and respond to significant comments; ACUS guidance does not treat mass comment campaigns as a problem in itself and leaves the weight of comment counts unaddressed.
CL1720.supports: The Administrative Conference of the United States' Recommendation 2021-1 cites 5 U.S.C. 553 and case law requiring agencies to consider and respond to significant comments, says widespread participation is not a problem in itself, and states that it does not address what weight particular types of comments should carry. Separate statements by senior fellows argue that comment counts are not a reliable measure of public views.
CL1720.limitation: Applies to federal agency rules; state agencies and local boards follow their own procedures, and how much any comment changes a rule is not measured here.

CL1721.claim: Where newspaper markets and congressional districts overlapped poorly, coverage of the House member fell, voters were less able to recall or rate the member, and members testified less and their areas received less federal spending.
CL1721.supports: Snyder and Strömberg (NBER Working Paper 13878, 2008; Journal of Political Economy, 2010) used changes in the fit between newspaper markets and districts caused by redistricting. Less coverage was associated with voters less able to recall their representative's name, members less likely to testify at hearings or vote against the party line, and lower federal spending in those areas.
CL1721.population: U.S. House districts and their residents
CL1721.limitation: Measures coverage by local newspapers before the steepest closures; online sources and television are not fully captured.

CL1722.claim: As local newspapers cut staff, their coverage of mayors, city halls, school boards and county commissions shrank, and fewer residents knew their local officials.
CL1722.supports: Hayes and Lawless (News Hole, Cambridge University Press, 2021) analyzed fifteen years of reporting from more than 200 local papers alongside surveys and election returns. They report sharply reduced coverage of local government and link it to lower knowledge of local officials and falling local turnout.
CL1722.limitation: Much of the engagement evidence is cross-sectional; the authors' causal claims are bounded by the data.

CL1723.claim: Medill's 2025 State of Local News report counted 213 U.S. counties with no local news source and about 50 million people with limited or no access to local news.
CL1723.supports: Northwestern University's Medill School announced on October 20, 2025 that its State of Local News report counted 213 counties with no local news source and about 50 million people with limited or no access to local news.
CL1723.limitation: Counts depend on Medill's definitions of a local news source, which can change between years.

CL1724.claim: Massachusetts Question 3 would replace separate party primaries with a single all-party primary in which the top two finishers advance, effective January 1, 2028.
CL1724.supports: The Secretary of the Commonwealth's Information for Voters page summarizes Question 3 as eliminating party primaries for state elections, listing all candidates on one ballot, advancing the two highest vote-getters, requiring joint governor and lieutenant governor candidacies, and granting party status at 3% of primary ballots. A yes vote eliminates separate party primaries; a no vote changes nothing. A majority of the Special Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions recommended no action on May 4, 2026.
CL1724.limitation: The measure's effects depend on implementation and on candidate behavior; the official summary is the authoritative description.

CL1725.claim: Question 3 would cover primaries for statewide, U.S. House and Senate, state legislative, Governor's Council and county or district offices, and would not change presidential or municipal elections.
CL1725.supports: WBUR's October 5, 2026 explainer lists the offices covered: statewide offices including governor, U.S. House and Senate, state legislature, the Governor's Council and county or district offices such as sheriff and district attorney. It states that presidential elections are excluded and municipal elections would not change. The official text applies to state primaries held under chapter 53, sections 41 to 53A.
CL1725.population: Offices elected at Massachusetts state primaries
CL1725.limitation: Office coverage is stated by a news organization; the official summary refers to state elections without listing each office.

CL1726.claim: Question 3 is sponsored by the Coalition for Healthy Democracy and opposed by Voter Rights MA, the Massachusetts Democratic and Republican parties and several unions.
CL1726.supports: The official argument for Question 3 is written by Danielle Allen of the Coalition for Healthy Democracy and the argument against by Vanessa A. Snow of Voter Rights MA. WBUR reported support from State Auditor Diana DiZoglio, former Governor Deval Patrick and former Lieutenant Governor Kerry Healey, and a No on 3 coalition including the AFL-CIO, several SEIU locals, the American Federation of Teachers and the state Democratic Party. Boston.com reported opposition from both state party chairs.
CL1726.limitation: Endorsement lists change during a campaign; positions are as reported by news organizations on the dates given, and campaign filings are the primary record.

CL1727.claim: In 2026, 60% of Massachusetts state House and Senate races have only one candidate on the November ballot.
CL1727.supports: WBUR's October 5, 2026 explainer on Question 3 reports that 60% of state House and Senate races this cycle have only one candidate on the November ballot, and that a Boston state Senate primary was won with about 11,000 votes in a district of about 180,000 people.
CL1727.limitation: A news organization's count; certified candidate lists from the Secretary of the Commonwealth are the primary record.

CL1728.claim: Alaska Ballot Measure 2 (petition 24ESEG) would end the open primary and ranked-choice general election, restore party primaries and single-choice general elections, and repeal campaign finance limits and disclosure rules adopted in 2020.
CL1728.supports: The lieutenant governor's December 31, 2025 letter found the petition properly filed with 42,837 verified signatures (34,098 required), scheduled it for the November 3, 2026 ballot, and summarized it as restoring party primaries, single-choice general elections, party petitions and special runoffs while removing various contribution limits and disclosure rules. The Division of Elections lists 24ESEG as properly filed.
CL1728.population: Alaska elections and campaign finance law
CL1728.limitation: The official ballot summary was amended by court order in August 2026; the final ballot language governs.

CL1729.claim: The Alaska Supreme Court upheld the Division of Elections' ballot summary for Ballot Measure 2 as true and impartial but ordered one addition about governor and lieutenant governor candidates running separately.
CL1729.supports: The Anchorage Daily News reported on August 28, 2026 that the court affirmed the lower court's finding and required the division to add language explaining that, if open primaries end, governor and lieutenant governor candidates would run separately in the primary, before the September 2 ballot-printing deadline.
CL1729.limitation: Reported by a newspaper; the court's fuller written opinion was to follow, and the final ballot wording is the Division of Elections' version.

CL1730.claim: Repeal Now sponsors Alaska Ballot Measure 2 and the No on 2 campaign, registered as Protect Alaska's Elections, opposes it; by late July 2026 the opposition had raised about $5.75 million and the sponsors about $1.1 million.
CL1730.supports: The Alaska Beacon reported on July 29, 2026 that Repeal Now's primary sponsors include Bernadette Wilson, Judy Eledge and Ken McCarty and that it had raised $1.1 million, including $846,000 from the Aurora Action Network. No on 2 had raised $5.75 million, including $4 million from Unite America PAC and $1.5 million from Voters for the American Center.
CL1730.limitation: Campaign totals were reported before the final pre-election filings; Alaska Public Offices Commission reports are the primary record.

CL1731.claim: A 2024 measure to repeal Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election failed by 743 votes out of 321,203 after a December 2024 recount.
CL1731.supports: The Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Alaska's recount results of December 11, 2024 show 160,973 votes against repeal and 160,230 for it. The Alaska Beacon's July 29, 2026 report describes the 2026 vote as the second statewide decision on the same system within two years.
CL1731.limitation: The margin is the official recount result; the 2026 measure differs from the 2024 one because it also repeals campaign disclosure rules.

CL1732.claim: On Missouri Proposition A, a yes vote approves the congressional map in House Bill 1 (2025) and a no vote leaves the 2022 districts in place.
CL1732.supports: The Missouri Secretary of State's 2026 ballot measures page gives the official ballot title asking whether voters approve House Bill No. 1 (2025 Second Extraordinary Session), which replaces the existing congressional plan with new boundaries that keep more counties intact; a yes vote approves the act and a no vote leaves the 2022 boundaries in place. The fiscal note estimates no costs or savings.
CL1732.limitation: The ballot title's description of the map (keeping more counties intact) is the state's own wording; the map's effects on each district are described in news reports.

CL1733.claim: A September 25, 2026 U.S. Supreme Court order requires Missouri to use its 2022 congressional map in the 2026 election.
CL1733.supports: In People Not Politicians v. Onder (No. 26A388), the Court stayed lower-court injunctions and stated that, as a matter of state law, Missouri must use its 2022 map in the 2026 congressional election, citing the principle against federal courts changing rules close to an election. No dissent is noted.
CL1733.limitation: Governs the 2026 election only; the map for later elections depends on Proposition A and further litigation.

CL1734.claim: Governor Mike Kehoe supports Missouri's 2025 map and People Not Politicians opposes it; the map divides Kansas City among three districts.
CL1734.supports: KCTV5 reported on September 21, 2026 that Governor Kehoe, a Republican, called the map compact and consistent with the state constitution, and that People Not Politicians, led by Richard von Glahn, opposes it; a Saint Louis University and YouGov poll found likely voters split roughly into thirds. KCUR reported on September 29, 2026 that the map divides Kansas City among the 4th, 5th and 6th districts.
CL1734.limitation: Campaign positions as reported by news organizations; poll field dates were not published in the report.

CL1735.claim: Twenty-four states, the District of Columbia and the U.S. Virgin Islands have a citizen initiative process (Mississippi's has been ruled void), 23 states have the popular referendum, and legislatures in all 50 states can refer measures to voters.
CL1735.supports: NCSL's initiative and referendum overview states that 24 states, DC and the U.S. Virgin Islands have an initiative process, notes that Mississippi's initiative law was found void, reports popular referendum in 23 states, DC and the Virgin Islands, and states that legislative referenda may appear on the ballot in all 50 states.
CL1735.limitation: Signature thresholds, subject limits and legislative override rules vary widely by state and change over time.

CL1736.claim: Nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections; Indiana and Ohio enacted bans in 2026.
CL1736.supports: Ballotpedia News reported on August 28, 2026, with data through August 14, that Indiana and Ohio, both with Republican trifectas, enacted legislation prohibiting ranked-choice voting in 2026, bringing the number of states with a ban to 19.
CL1736.limitation: Bans differ in scope (some cover only certain elections), and the count is a secondary compilation.

CL1737.claim: Official directories let residents find their U.S. representative by ZIP code, their senators' contact details, state legislature websites, local officials and state and local election offices.
CL1737.supports: House.gov's lookup matches a ZIP code to a congressional district; Senate.gov lists contact forms, offices and the Capitol switchboard, (202) 224-3121; USA.gov's elected-officials page links to state legislature websites, a mayors directory and a county executive search; vote.gov is the federal voter registration site; the Election Assistance Commission's state directory links state and local election offices.
CL1737.limitation: Directories for city council members and county commissioners are kept by each locality; ZIP codes can span two districts, so confirm with a street address.

CL1738.claim: In November 2024, 65.3% of the citizen voting-age population reported voting, with turnout of 82.5% among those with an advanced degree and 52.5% among high school graduates.
CL1738.supports: The Census Bureau's April 30, 2025 release of 2024 Current Population Survey voting tables reports that 65.3% (about 154 million people) of the citizen voting-age population voted and 73.6% were registered, with turnout of 82.5% for advanced-degree holders, 77.2% for bachelor's degree holders and 52.5% for high school graduates.
CL1738.limitation: Self-reported voting in a survey, which tends to overstate turnout; covers the November general election, not primaries.

CL1739.claim: In 2022, about 14% of voters with disabilities reported difficulty voting, compared with about 4% of voters without disabilities, and their turnout was 3.6 percentage points lower.
CL1739.supports: Schur, Kruse, Ameri and Adya's July 2023 report for the U.S. Election Assistance Commission found that about one in seven voters with disabilities encountered difficulties voting in 2022, over three times the rate for others, and a 3.6-point turnout gap in the survey (1.5 points in Census data; 10.0 points after adjusting for age).
CL1739.population: U.S. voters with and without disabilities
CL1739.limitation: Survey-based; disability is self-reported, and the size of the turnout gap depends on the data source and age adjustment.

CL1740.claim: Twenty-four states and the District of Columbia have automatic voter registration, under which eligible people are registered through agency transactions unless they opt out.
CL1740.supports: NCSL's automatic voter registration page, updated August 19, 2026, categorizes 24 states and Washington, D.C. as having automatic registration, under which eligible people are registered through a state agency transaction, and notes that registration is not compulsory because individuals may opt out.
CL1740.limitation: State programs differ in which agencies participate, when the program began and how opt-outs work, so counts can change as programs start.

CL1741.claim: In early-adopting jurisdictions, automatic voter registration was associated with registration increases of 9% to 94%.
CL1741.supports: Morris and Dunphy of the Brennan Center for Justice (April 11, 2019) matched jurisdictions that implemented automatic registration with demographically similar jurisdictions that had not and estimated increases in registrants ranging from 9% to 94% across the states studied.
CL1741.limitation: Matching study by an organization that advocates expanded voter access; it measures registration, and its estimates span a wide range across states.

domains.title: News, records and public information
domains.everyday_question: How can I find out what my local officials are doing, and whether what I read about them is true?
domains.overview: Voters depend on information they cannot gather themselves: what the council decided, whether a claim about an election holds up, what the unemployment rate was last month. This domain follows how that information is paid for, how it reaches people and who can distort it. Local newsrooms lost most of the advertising that once paid reporters, and a few large platforms now rank much of what people see. Congress, the Federal Trade Commission, the Federal Communications Commission, courts and state legislatures set the rules. Newsrooms, platforms, records offices and statistical agencies make daily choices within them. When reporting thins out, challengers enter fewer races and officials face less scrutiny, which weakens the electoral pressure traced under Elections and representation. Missing records and weaker watchdogs also make favoritism harder to detect, a link followed under Money, lobbying and influence.

domains.title: Elections and representation
domains.everyday_question: Does my vote change who represents me and what they do in office?
domains.overview: Elections are the main way residents reward or replace the people who govern them. This domain follows each step: registering, casting a ballot, drawing districts, choosing nominees, counting votes and certifying results. States write most of these rules, and the legislators who write them often have a stake in the outcome. Congress sets some floors for federal elections, and courts decide which rules stand. In most House districts one party is sure to win, so a low-turnout primary picks the officeholder and the November election carries little threat. Incumbents who face little risk of losing feel less pressure to perform, a path that leads to the quality of public services. Who votes also shapes whose interests policy serves, which connects elections to political money and to household finances.

domains.title: Money, lobbying and influence
domains.everyday_question: Who gets a meeting with my representative, and what does it cost them?
domains.overview: Between elections, officials hear most from the people and groups who can pay for campaigns, lobbyists and expert advice. This domain traces those channels: campaign contributions and outside spending, disclosure of who pays, lobbying and the move between public office and industry jobs, officials' personal financial stakes, public contracting, and the tax and regulatory favors that can follow. Congress, state legislatures and the Federal Election Commission write and enforce the rules, and Supreme Court rulings under the First Amendment set their outer limits. Evidence that donors get more access is strong. Evidence on how far that access changes policy is weaker and contested. The money comes disproportionately from the households with the most wealth, and the advantages it secures can protect that wealth. Weak enforcement by agencies and watchdogs lets the cycle run with fewer checks.

domains.title: Congress, agencies and public services
domains.everyday_question: Why does it take so long to get a benefit, a permit or a new law?
domains.overview: A law helps people only when Congress can write it well and an agency can carry it out. This domain covers both halves. On the legislative side it looks at Congress's own staff and research agencies, the floor rules that decide what gets a vote, budget deadlines that can shut the government down, and the power to demand information from the executive branch. On the delivery side it looks at hiring, civil-service protection, aging software, contracting, paperwork that keeps eligible people from benefits, and permitting. Congress funds and structures agencies, the President and agency heads run them, and courts police the limits. When Congress lacks its own experts it leans on industry for drafting. Service failures feed a proposed loop in which trust and funding fall together, which ties this domain to elections and to presidential power.

domains.title: Checks on power and equal justice
domains.everyday_question: What stops a president, a court or the police from overstepping, and can I get a fair hearing if they do?
domains.overview: Every office in this Atlas works within legal limits set by the Constitution, by statutes and by court rulings. This domain asks whether those limits hold. It covers emergency powers, executive orders, withheld funds, war powers, pardons and the removal of watchdogs and regulators. It looks at how judges are appointed, assigned and held to ethics rules. It also asks whether the law treats people equally when they deal with police, prosecutors, surveillance or discrimination. Congress can write limits and refuse funds, courts decide disputes, and inspectors general and independent commissions investigate. Since 2024 several Supreme Court rulings have widened presidential control over agencies, while rulings on tariffs and the National Guard have bounded it. When Congress cannot legislate, more policy moves into executive action. Court rulings on maps and political money feed back into elections and influence.

domains.title: Competition and market power
domains.everyday_question: Why do I have so few choices, and such high prices, for things like prescriptions, hospital care or concert tickets?
domains.overview: Competition is supposed to keep prices in check: if one seller charges too much, another can win the customer. This domain looks at what weakens that check. Mergers, including strings of small acquisitions, can leave a market with few sellers. A firm that controls a gateway, such as a search engine, a pharmacy benefit network or a regional hospital system, can favor itself or raise rivals' costs. Hidden fees, forced arbitration, patent tactics and licensing rules add other barriers. The Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general and the courts enforce antitrust law, and Congress sets their budgets and powers. Concentration among employers can also hold down wages, and platforms' share of advertising has drained money from local news. The 2025 and 2026 court record shows liability findings against some firms and losses for enforcers in other cases.

domains.title: Work, pay and bargaining power
domains.everyday_question: Why is it so hard to get a raise, a predictable schedule or a fair hearing at work?
domains.overview: Most households live on what they earn, so the rules that shape pay and working conditions reach almost everyone. This domain looks at workers' bargaining power: whether they can organize and win a contract, switch to a better job, recover unpaid wages, get predictable hours and paid leave, work safely and have a say when employers bring in new technology. Congress writes the core labor laws. The National Labor Relations Board and the Labor Department enforce them, and states and cities set many floors of their own. Union membership fell from 20.1% of wage and salary workers in 1983 to 10.0% in 2025. Where workers bargain from weakness, a smaller share of each dollar of output goes to wages, which feeds wealth concentration and, through political spending, influence over policy. Employer concentration ties this domain to competition policy.

domains.title: Taxes, wealth and economic security
domains.everyday_question: Why can some families build wealth while others cannot cover a $400 emergency?
domains.overview: Income is what a household receives over a year. Wealth is what it owns after debts. This domain follows the rules that decide how both are taxed, protected and passed on: tax rates on wages compared with investment gains, inheritance, audits, profits shifted abroad, tax breaks, cash support for families, Social Security, household debt, financial crises, recession support and the federal budget. Congress writes the tax code and benefit laws, and the IRS, the Treasury, the Federal Reserve and financial regulators carry them out. In 2025, 37% of adults could not cover a $400 expense with cash. Wealth at the top is held mostly in stocks, while middle-class wealth is mostly home equity, which ties this domain to housing. Concentrated wealth funds political spending, and rules shaped by that spending can protect it, the cycle shown as loop R1: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other.

domains.title: Housing, health care and getting ahead
domains.everyday_question: Why do rent, child care and medical bills take so much of my paycheck, and does where I grew up decide where I end up?
domains.overview: Households spend most of their income on housing, health care, child care, food, transportation and energy. This domain asks why those costs run high and why the chance of doing better than one's parents depends so much on place and family. Local zoning boards and state legislatures decide how many homes can be built. Congress, the states and insurers shape health coverage and prices. States and school districts fund schools. When homes are scarce, existing owners gain equity and often oppose new building, which keeps rents high (loop R8: Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building). High costs for essentials leave less for savings and add to household insecurity, and financial strain makes it harder to take part in public decisions. Absolute mobility, the chance of out-earning one's parents, fell from about 90% for children born in 1940 to about 50% for those born in the 1980s.

domains.title: Taking part, trust and shared norms
domains.everyday_question: Why does showing up feel pointless, and why do people across the party divide distrust each other so much?
domains.overview: Democracy depends on more than election rules. People need time, skills and a reason to believe that taking part matters, and enough shared ground to accept results they dislike. This domain looks at who takes part between elections, how civic organizations and everyday contact across groups have thinned, how hostility toward the other party has grown, and how threats, false fraud claims and party tolerance for misconduct strain democratic norms. Cities, schools, libraries, civic groups and parties shape these conditions more than Congress does. Hostility toward the other party gives voters a reason to excuse misconduct by their own side, which weakens the threat of losing office. Financial strain and weaker worker organizations reduce participation, so policy answers less to the households under the most pressure. A belief that nothing can change keeps people home and leaves decisions to the organized few.

I001.title: Local newsrooms close and fewer reporters watch local government
I001.summary: When a local paper or station closes, fewer reporters attend council meetings, read budgets or question officials. Residents lose a shared source of facts about local decisions, and local officials face less public scrutiny.
I001.mechanism: When local news outlets close, fewer reporters examine local government, and residents share less common knowledge about the decisions made in their name.
I001.evidence_note: Well supported. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 U.S. counties with no local news source (the report's landing page gives 213). A 2020 study by Gao, Lee and Murphy linked newspaper closures to higher borrowing costs for local governments. Hayes and Lawless (2021) found that shrinking local coverage goes with lower political engagement and knowledge; their panel and content data support associations, and the authors limit their causal claims.
I001.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Public funds for local news already operate, including New Jersey's Civic Information Consortium and Canada's Local Journalism Initiative. No published study has measured whether these funds improve accountability, such as closer scrutiny of officials.
I001.response: State legislatures and local philanthropies would create an independently governed local-news fund. It would pay formula grants, keep funders away from editorial decisions and publish data on every award.
I001.tradeoff: Public money can invite political control of coverage. The design keeps the people who appoint the fund's board separate from the people who make editorial decisions.
I001.success_measure: Counties with a local news source, reporters per resident, and the corrections that funded outlets publish.

aimed_reforms.why: Pays reporters to cover local government with an editorial firewall, which is the fund this record proposes.

I002.title: Chain owners cut local reporting
I002.summary: When one company buys many local papers or stations, it often cuts local staff and shares content across its outlets. The strongest study, of one TV station owner, found coverage moved toward national politics and viewers left.
I002.mechanism: Chains that buy local outlets often cut local reporting staff. One strong study found that one owner, Sinclair Broadcast Group, shifted its acquired stations toward national political coverage; whether common owners in general centralize the news agenda is untested.
I002.evidence_note: Plausible. Martin and McCrain (2019, American Political Science Review) found that local TV stations bought by Sinclair shifted toward national and right-leaning political coverage and lost viewers. The study covers one ownership group. Staff cuts at chain-owned outlets appear in industry counts such as the 2025 State of Local News report.
I002.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Merger review that weighs the number of independent news voices has not been tested for U.S. media. The Federal Communications Commission has loosened its ownership rules, and no evaluation has measured what those changes did to coverage.
I002.response: Congress, the Federal Communications Commission and the federal antitrust agencies would review local news mergers for their effect on competition and on the number of independent outlets. Owners would disclose who ultimately owns each outlet and how many newsroom staff it employs.
I002.tradeoff: Owning many outlets proves neither biased coverage nor illegal market power, so each deal needs its own evidence.
I002.success_measure: More distinct owners in each local market and more original local reporting.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds independent local reporters, which offsets the staff cuts that follow acquisitions; ownership itself stays unchanged.

I003.title: Platforms take the advertising that once paid for reporting
I003.summary: Most of the advertising money that used to support newspapers now goes to large online platforms. News organizations still pay the cost of reporting, so they cover fewer public decisions.
I003.mechanism: Large online platforms now collect most of the advertising money that once paid for news, while publishers still carry the cost of reporting.
I003.evidence_note: Well supported. Industry estimates compiled by the Pew Research Center show U.S. newspaper advertising revenue falling from about $49 billion in 2005 to under $10 billion in 2022. The 2025 State of Local News census counted 212 counties with no local news source.
I003.remedy_note: Hypothesis. No U.S. evaluation of reader vouchers or refundable subscription credits exists. Canada's digital news subscription tax credit has data on how many people claim it and no measure of its effect on reporting.
I003.response: A state legislature would pilot reader vouchers and refundable tax credits for local news subscriptions. Nonprofit and small independent outlets would qualify alongside established publishers.
I003.tradeoff: Subsidies can flow mostly to large, established publishers. Eligibility rules need to be neutral about viewpoint and simple enough for small outlets to use.
I003.success_measure: New subscribers, readers reached in places with little coverage, and public cost per reader.

aimed_reforms.why: Replaces part of the lost advertising money with public and philanthropic funding behind an editorial firewall.
Opens search and ad-tech markets so a smaller share of advertising money is captured by a few platforms.

I004.title: False claims outlast their corrections
I004.summary: People who hear a false claim several times tend to keep believing part of it after it is corrected. Researchers infer that this makes it harder for voters to judge officials, though that step has not been measured.
I004.mechanism: Repeating a false claim raises belief in it, and corrections reduce that belief only partly and fade over time. The further step, that this weakens voters' ability to hold officials to account, is inferred; no study listed for this record measures it.
I004.evidence_note: Well supported for the psychology of belief. A 2022 review in Nature Reviews Psychology (Ecker and colleagues) found that repetition raises belief and that corrections work partly and fade. A 2020 meta-analysis by Walter and Tukachinsky found that corrections reduce reliance on misinformation without removing it. These lab and field studies measure belief; none measures election outcomes. In US Dominion v. Fox (March 2023), a Delaware court ruled at summary judgment that specific broadcast claims about Dominion were false; the ruling covers those claims only.
I004.remedy_note: Well supported. A meta-analysis found that corrections and prominent retractions reduce belief in a false claim without erasing it. Defamation judgments punish a publisher, and audiences who already absorbed the claim keep part of their belief.
I004.response: Newsrooms, courts and funders would each act. Funders would pay for public-interest reporting that shows its sources. Courts would apply existing defamation law with due process, and newsrooms would run corrections as prominently as the original error.
I004.tradeoff: Opinion and honest mistakes need protection, and no government body should license what counts as true.
I004.success_measure: How many people see a correction compared with the original claim, and whether they later recall the accurate facts.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds source-transparent public-interest reporting, the funding half of this record's response.

I005.title: Readers cannot tell reporting from opinion or paid content
I005.summary: Many readers cannot tell whether a piece reports verified facts, gives an opinion or promotes a sponsor. Clear labels help a little, and their effect depends on how they are written and placed.
I005.mechanism: Many readers cannot reliably tell reported fact from opinion, or news from sponsored content.
I005.evidence_note: Well supported. In a 2018 Pew Research Center survey of 5,035 U.S. adults, 26% correctly classified all five factual statements and 35% all five opinion statements. Amazeen and Wojdynski (2020) found that fewer than one in ten readers recognized native ads, paid articles styled to look like news, as advertising.
I005.remedy_note: Plausible. Disclosure labels raise recognition of sponsored content modestly, and the gain depends on wording and placement. No study shows that labels change trust or the beliefs that bear on voting.
I005.response: The Federal Trade Commission, within its existing authority, and publishers would act. Paid content would carry clear labels, and publishers would post standards that separate reported facts from opinion.
I005.tradeoff: Labels have small effects on their own, and readers can skip them.
I005.success_measure: The share of people in user tests who correctly identify who sponsored a piece.

I006.title: Feeds built for attention reward attacks on the other side
I006.summary: Platforms rank posts to keep people scrolling, and posts attacking an opposing group draw more shares. Studies show ranking changes what people see far more clearly than it changes how they feel about the other party.
I006.mechanism: Feeds ranked to hold attention give more reach to posts that attack an out-group (people seen as the opposing side) and to misleading claims.
I006.evidence_note: Well supported for engagement and exposure. Rathje, Van Bavel and van der Linden (2021) examined 2.7 million posts and found an association: each word about the opposing political group went with about 67% more shares. On X in 2023, a seven-week randomized experiment with 4,965 U.S. users showed the ranked feed changed what people saw, though one platform, period and sample limit how far that generalizes. When researchers reranked hostile partisan posts for 1,256 users over ten days of the 2024 campaign, feelings toward the other party shifted.
I006.remedy_note: Plausible. In one experiment, reranking feeds to show fewer hostile partisan posts lowered hostility toward the other party over ten days. In a larger randomized experiment during the 2020 election, moving Facebook and Instagram users to a chronological feed for three months changed what they saw and how long they stayed, and researchers found no significant change in polarization or political knowledge. Rules giving users a choice of feed have mixed evidence, and Moody v. NetChoice (2024) limits how far government can direct a platform's editorial choices.
I006.response: Congress and the platforms would act. Users would choose how their feed is ranked, independent researchers would get platform data under privacy safeguards, and independent risk audits would be tied to remedies when they find problems.
I006.tradeoff: Effects differ from platform to platform, and auditor access can expose users' private information. Obligations have to fit the limits on regulating editorial discretion and compelled disclosure set out in Moody v. NetChoice.
I006.success_measure: Quality of the content users are shown, measured hostility toward the other party, and privacy incidents.

aimed_reforms.why: Gives users a choice of ranking and gives researchers data to measure what attention-based ranking does.

I007.title: People cannot see or challenge platform decisions
I007.summary: Platforms decide which posts people see and which they remove, often with little explanation or route to appeal. No one has measured how often those decisions are wrong, so the size of the problem remains a hypothesis.
I007.mechanism: Users of large platforms cannot see how content reaches them or contest moderation errors. The scale is unmeasured: no source counts moderation errors or appeal outcomes.
I007.evidence_note: Hypothesis. The only U.S. evidence concerns perception. In a 2020 Pew Research Center survey, 73% of U.S. adults said social media sites censor political viewpoints. That figure measures belief; it does not show how often platforms make mistakes.
I007.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The European Union's Digital Services Act requires explanations and appeal routes, and no evaluation of its effects has been found. Similar U.S. mandates face First Amendment limits.
I007.response: Congress would require large platforms to explain moderation decisions in terms a user can act on, offer appeal routes and publish aggregate enforcement data. The platforms would carry out these duties.
I007.tradeoff: Trade secrets limit full disclosure, and detailed rules can teach abusers how to evade enforcement. Obligations must fit the limits on regulating editorial discretion set out in Moody v. NetChoice.
I007.success_measure: How quickly appeals are resolved, how many errors are reversed, and whether platforms pass compliance audits.

aimed_reforms.why: Researcher access to platform data would let independent teams measure how content reaches users, the unmeasured part of this record.

I008.title: A few platforms control how news reaches people
I008.summary: About half of U.S. adults get news from social media at least sometimes, so a handful of companies decide how much of it they see. When one of them changes its rules, news outlets can lose much of their audience overnight.
I008.mechanism: News organizations lose reach when a few platforms change who gets access or how content is discovered.
I008.evidence_note: Plausible. In 2024 about half of U.S. adults got news from social media at least sometimes, according to the Pew Research Center, which shows how much distribution runs through a few platforms.
