When Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada in 2023, Canadian outlets lost reach.
I008.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Portable subscriptions and interoperability remedies (rules that let users and content move between services) have not been tested for news. Canada's 2023 news block showed outlets losing reach; it produced no evidence about which remedy would help.
I008.response: Congress and competition regulators would support subscriptions readers can carry between services, tools for publishers to reach readers directly, and public-interest ways to find news. Market-wide interoperability remedies would follow the response in I087: Exclusive data makes dominant platforms hard to challenge.
I008.tradeoff: Interoperability can let spam travel more easily between services and can weaken privacy.
I008.success_measure: The cost of switching services for readers and publishers, and the number of competing services in active use.

I009.title: Foreign sponsors disguise political messages as domestic speech
I009.summary: Foreign governments have run covert campaigns that hide who is paying, so their political messages look like ordinary American speech. The operations are documented; the strongest study of one campaign found no measurable change in attitudes or votes.
I009.mechanism: Foreign governments run covert operations that hide their sponsorship so strategic political messages look like ordinary U.S. speech. The operations are documented. Their effect on votes is unestablished, and the one strong study found no measurable effect.
I009.evidence_note: Documented. A declassified 2021 assessment by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence found that Russia and Iran ran covert influence operations during the 2020 federal elections and found no evidence that votes were altered. In September 2024 the Justice Department indicted two RT employees; the indictment states allegations of covert financing and direction. A 2023 study of the Russian Internet Research Agency's 2016 Twitter campaign (Eady and colleagues, Nature Communications) found exposure concentrated among a small group of strongly Republican users and no measurable relationship with attitudes or votes.
I009.remedy_note: Plausible. Enforcement of the Foreign Agents Registration Act and of campaign-finance law are established tools. Their effect on audiences is unproven, and the best study of 2016 Russian activity found no measurable attitude change.
I009.response: The Justice Department, the Federal Election Commission and election agencies would enforce foreign-agent and campaign-finance law, require disclosure of who pays for political messages and publish threat notices grounded in evidence.
I009.tradeoff: An indictment is an allegation. Enforcement must protect domestic dissent and legitimate foreign journalism.
I009.success_measure: Undisclosed networks disrupted, and how accurately operations are traced to their sponsors.

aimed_reforms.why: Disclosure of the original funders of political spending targets the hidden sponsorship at the center of this record.

I010.title: Fake audio and video can impersonate candidates
I010.summary: Cheap software can fake a candidate's voice or face and reach voters just before they decide. The harm depends on timing, reach and whether a verified correction reaches the same people.
I010.mechanism: Cheap fabricated audio and video can mislead voters at decisive moments, such as the days before an election.
I010.evidence_note: Plausible. In January 2024 an AI-generated robocall imitating President Biden's voice reached New Hampshire voters before the primary. The Federal Communications Commission imposed a $6 million forfeiture on the consultant behind it and reached a $1 million settlement with the carrier. The case shows the method in use; no study listed for this record measures its effect on votes.
I010.remedy_note: Hypothesis. More than 25 states have enacted election deepfake laws, according to a tracker kept by the advocacy group Public Citizen. The laws are new, a federal court blocked California's law on First Amendment grounds in X Corp. v. Bonta, and no study has measured whether any of them deter fakes.
I010.response: Congress and the states would ban fraudulent election impersonation under narrow definitions. Platforms would add provenance records showing where a file came from, and channels for fast, authenticated corrections.
I010.tradeoff: Satire, journalism and lawful anonymous speech need protection.
I010.success_measure: How fast fakes are verified and corrected, and how many lawful posts are removed by mistake.

I011.title: Targeted political ads escape public scrutiny
I011.summary: Campaigns and groups can send different political claims to different audiences, out of view of everyone else. A searchable record of every ad, its funder and its targeting would let the public examine them.
I011.mechanism: Microtargeted political ads let sponsors send different claims to different groups without the wider public seeing them.
I011.evidence_note: Plausible. Kim and colleagues (2018) collected 2016 Facebook ads from a volunteer panel and found that most divisive issue ads came from groups that could not be identified or looked suspicious. The study covers one election cycle and one volunteer panel. Meta's Ad Library shows spending ranges and audiences, though only for one company and only for ads that advertisers declare as political.
I011.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Ad archives exist voluntarily at Meta and Google and by law in the European Union. No study shows that an archive changes advertiser behavior or what voters know.
I011.response: Congress would require, and platforms would maintain, searchable archives of political ads, including issue ads. Each entry would show the sponsor, the spending, the targeting criteria and the ad itself.
I011.tradeoff: Archives must protect the privacy of the people targeted, and the law has to define an issue ad carefully.
I011.success_measure: How complete the archive is, and whether each ad can be traced to its sponsor.

I012.title: Threats drive reporters and researchers out of public debate
I012.summary: Threats and harassment lead some journalists, researchers and election officials to stop speaking or leave their work. Residents then have fewer people able to investigate and explain public problems.
I012.mechanism: Threats push journalists and researchers out of public debate, leaving fewer people to investigate and explain public problems.
I012.evidence_note: Well supported. In a 2021 global survey by the International Center for Journalists and UNESCO, 73% of 901 women journalists reported online violence and 30% said they censored themselves; respondents chose to take part. In the Brennan Center's survey of 858 U.S. local election officials (April to May 2025), 38% reported threats, harassment or abuse and 52% worried about their staff's safety.
I012.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Press-freedom groups recommend threat investigation and legal-defense support as standard practice. No study has measured whether that support keeps reporters in their jobs.
I012.response: The Justice Department, the states and news organizations would investigate threats, fund legal defense and help people whose home details are published to target them (doxxing), under narrowly drawn laws.
I012.tradeoff: The law has to separate threats from harsh criticism that is lawful.
I012.success_measure: Threat cases resolved, and reporters who stay in their jobs.

I013.title: Public records arrive too late to be useful
I013.summary: Federal agencies take weeks or months to answer requests for public records, and backlogs keep growing. Slow answers stall investigations by reporters and residents.
I013.mechanism: Slow responses to public-records requests obstruct investigations. The claim that delay favors people with inside access is an inference the sources do not test.
I013.evidence_note: Documented. The Justice Department reported 1.50 million federal Freedom of Information Act requests in fiscal year 2024, up 25%, with simple requests taking 44 days on average, the longest since 2011. A tabulation of FOIA.gov data by the Brechner Center counted a year-end backlog of 267,056 requests, up 33%, and a record-low 12% of requests granted in full.
I013.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Response deadlines already exist in law, and agencies miss them. More funding and rules requiring agencies to publish records before anyone asks are plausible fixes; neither has been evaluated for its effect on backlogs.
I013.response: Congress, federal agencies and the states would fund records officers, publish records openly in machine-readable form and enforce response deadlines with an appeal that works.
I013.tradeoff: Redactions still have to protect privacy and legitimate security interests.
I013.success_measure: Age of the request backlog, and how complete agencies' proactive publication is.

I014.title: Removals and cuts put public statistics at risk
I014.summary: Jobs, price and population figures depend on statistical agencies that work free of political pressure. The 2025 removal of the labor statistics chief and budget cuts raised that risk, though no measurement yet shows the numbers have worsened.
I014.mechanism: Removal of agency heads, budget cuts and interference can weaken the official statistics people rely on. The August 2025 removal at the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the cuts are documented; no measurement yet shows that data quality has declined.
I014.evidence_note: Plausible. On August 1, 2025, the President removed the commissioner of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a jobs report, the first such removal, as documented in Urban Institute commentary. The American Statistical Association's 2024 and 2025 reviews documented budget, staffing and independence pressures across federal statistical agencies. Effects on data quality have not been measured.
I014.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Laws protecting release schedules and methods have been proposed. The view that independent statistical agencies sustain trust in data rests on expert consensus and has not been measured.
I014.response: Congress would protect statistical agencies' methods, release schedules and career experts by law. The agencies would publish revision logs and submit to independent audits.
I014.tradeoff: Independent agencies still have to answer for their methods.
I014.success_measure: Releases published on schedule, and how openly revisions are explained.

aimed_reforms.why: Builds agency independence from public reasons for removal, protected records and budget protection, which would cover statistical agency heads.

I015.title: Public information is out of reach for some residents
I015.summary: Slow or missing internet service and websites that do not work with screen readers can keep people from public services and civic information. Residents need formats that fit their devices, languages and assistive tools.
I015.mechanism: Gaps in internet access and in accessible design keep some residents from public services and reliable civic information.
I015.evidence_note: Plausible. The Pew Research Center's 2024 survey put home broadband adoption at about 80% of U.S. adults, with gaps by income, age and rural residence. The survey measures access; it does not measure how many people fail to complete a public service.
I015.remedy_note: Plausible. A 2024 Justice Department rule under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act requires state and local government websites and apps to meet a set accessibility standard (WCAG 2.1 AA). Deadlines fall in 2026 and 2027, so compliance and outcome data do not exist yet.
I015.response: Federal and state agencies and libraries would make public records and civic information work with assistive technology, slow connections, plain language and several languages. Broadband construction belongs with the infrastructure response in I142: Poor transport and utility connections raise the cost of living.
I015.tradeoff: Construction grants for broadband need conditions on affordability and maintenance.
I015.success_measure: Affordable broadband coverage, and the share of people who complete a public service using accessible tools.

I016.title: People share claims before checking them
I016.summary: Material often spreads before anyone looks at where it came from or what supports it. Checking what other sources say about an unfamiliar claim is a skill that can be taught.
I016.mechanism: Many people share material without checking its origin or the evidence behind it.
I016.evidence_note: Well supported. A national study of 3,446 U.S. students (Breakstone and colleagues, 2021) found that large majorities failed basic checks of where online material came from.
I016.remedy_note: Well supported. A randomized study across one school district found that teaching lateral reading (checking what other sources say about a source) improved students' evaluation of online material. Prompts asking people to consider accuracy modestly improved the quality of what they shared in lab tests and a field experiment on Twitter (Pennycook and colleagues, 2021).
I016.response: Schools, libraries and civic groups would teach lateral reading with real comparisons between sources, and test whether the skill holds up on unfamiliar examples.
I016.tradeoff: Training individuals cannot change every incentive in the media market.
I016.success_measure: Whether verification skills carry over to new material, and the accuracy of what people share.

I017.title: Registration hurdles and roll errors keep eligible people from voting
I017.summary: Eligible people can miss an election because registering is hard or because their record was wrongly removed from the rolls. The burden falls hardest on people who move often.
I017.mechanism: Registration hurdles and flawed maintenance of voter rolls keep some eligible people from voting, and the burden falls unevenly.
I017.evidence_note: Well supported. The Brennan Center for Justice, a voting-rights research and advocacy organization, counted about 16 million voters removed from rolls nationwide between 2014 and 2016, with removal rates rising in places formerly covered by federal preclearance after Shelby County v. Holder (2013). These are removal rates. The count does not show how many removals were mistakes.
I017.remedy_note: Well supported for registration. Across seven early-adopting states, automatic voter registration raised registration by 9% to 94% after adjusting for trends, according to a Brennan Center analysis; effects on turnout are smaller and debated. As of November 2025, 24 states plus DC had automatic registration.
I017.response: States, and Congress for federal elections, would adopt automatic and same-day registration, keep rolls accurate with secure methods, and give voters notice and a chance to correct their record before any removal.
I017.tradeoff: Rules must protect eligibility checks and data security, and keep noncitizens from being enrolled by mistake.
I017.success_measure: Share of eligible people registered, wrongful removals, and provisional ballots accepted.

aimed_reforms.why: Registers eligible people through routine dealings with state agencies, removing the registration step that falls hardest on people who move.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, 24 states and the District of Columbia have enacted or put in place automatic voter registration (National Conference of State Legislatures, August 19, 2026).

I018.title: Long lines make voting cost more in some neighborhoods
I018.summary: In some places voters wait far longer to cast a ballot, often because their polling places get fewer machines and staff. Waiting costs the most for people who cannot leave work.
I018.mechanism: Long lines and limited hours cost more for workers and for voters in minority precincts, where polling places often get fewer resources.
I018.evidence_note: Well supported. Using smartphone location data from the 2016 election, Chen, Haggag, Pope and Rohla (2019) found that residents of Black neighborhoods waited 29% longer to vote than residents of white neighborhoods; the measurement is strong and covers one election. Pettigrew (2017), working from surveys and observational data, found that minority voters wait longer and traced the gap to how local officials allocate precinct resources. A 2014 Government Accountability Office review of the 2012 election reported that some voters waited over an hour.
I018.remedy_note: Plausible. The Presidential Commission on Election Administration recommended in 2014 that no voter wait more than 30 minutes and offered tools for allocating machines and staff; these are consensus best practice. No rigorous evaluation shows that such standards reduce disparities in waiting.
I018.response: States and local election offices would set service standards for polling-place access, early voting and mail voting, fund the staff needed to meet them and track the results.
I018.tradeoff: Costs and geography differ from place to place, and any expansion has to keep a secure chain of custody for ballots.
I018.success_measure: Wait times by precinct, and ballot rejection rates.

I019.title: Voters with disabilities and limited English face barriers to voting on their own
I019.summary: Some voters with disabilities cannot cast a private ballot without help, and some voters who need language assistance do not receive it. Each voting method needs testing with the people who use it.
I019.mechanism: Voters with disabilities cannot reliably vote independently, and required language assistance does not always reach the voters who need it.
I019.evidence_note: Documented. The U.S. Election Assistance Commission's survey series found that the turnout gap between voters with and without disabilities fell from 16.8 points in 2000 to 11.3 points in 2020, with difficulties persisting. In a sample of 178 polling places in 2016, the Government Accountability Office found that 60% had at least one impediment to access.
I019.remedy_note: Plausible. The Help America Vote Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act require accessibility, including audits. The narrowing turnout gap since 2000 is consistent with an effect; no study isolates the audits as its cause.
I019.response: Election administrators would audit every voting method for disability access and provide the language assistance the law requires, testing each with the voters who use it. The Justice Department would enforce these duties.
I019.tradeoff: Accessible voting technology needs security protections and a backup method.
I019.success_measure: Voters with disabilities who vote independently and successfully, and accessibility complaints.

I020.title: Conviction rules keep millions from voting
I020.summary: About 4 million Americans could not vote in 2024 because of a felony conviction, under rules that differ by state. Lifetime bans, confusing eligibility and payment conditions keep many excluded after release.
I020.mechanism: Lifetime or confusing voting exclusions after a criminal conviction keep people from rejoining political life.
I020.evidence_note: Documented. The Sentencing Project, an advocacy organization, estimated that about 4.0 million people were barred from voting by a felony conviction in 2024, including 4.5% of Black adults compared with 1.3% of other adults. The estimate comes from a model built on correctional data.
I020.remedy_note: Plausible. Laws restoring voting rights are documented. Evidence that people whose rights are restored then register and vote is weak; registration stayed low after Florida's Amendment 4. Automatic notification of eligibility is the untested part of the design.
I020.response: States, and Congress where it has authority, would restore voting rights on release from prison, notify eligible people automatically and remove payment conditions that make voting depend on wealth.
I020.tradeoff: Eligibility law varies by state, and constitutional litigation may be needed.
I020.success_measure: Registrations by people whose rights were restored, and eligibility errors.

I021.title: DC and territorial residents have no vote in Congress
I021.summary: About 700,000 people in Washington, DC, along with residents of the U.S. territories, have no voting member of the House or Senate. Changing that takes legislation or a constitutional amendment, and territorial residents' own choices about political status.
I021.mechanism: Residents of Washington, DC and the U.S. territories have no voting representation in Congress.
I021.evidence_note: Documented. The Census Bureau puts the District of Columbia's population at about 700,000, and the District has no voting member of the House or Senate.
I021.remedy_note: Hypothesis. DC statehood or a constitutional amendment would provide representation by definition, so the open question is the legal route, which is contested.
I021.response: Congress would pursue representation for DC and a political status for each territory chosen by its residents, through lawful legislation and, where needed, a constitutional amendment.
I021.tradeoff: Residents' consent, the constitutional structure and territorial self-determination all have to be respected.
I021.success_measure: Residents with full voting representation in Congress.

I022.title: Map-drawers lock in a party's seats
I022.summary: Officials who draw district lines can arrange them so their party keeps its seats even as voters change their minds. Federal courts do not hear these claims, so state rules and commissions decide how far it goes.
I022.mechanism: When the party in power draws district maps, it can entrench itself despite shifts in voters' preferences.
I022.evidence_note: Well supported. In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Supreme Court ruled that federal courts cannot hear partisan gerrymandering claims; state law and other federal voting protections still apply. Warshaw, McGhee and Migurski (2022) found that maps drawn by commissions and courts in the 2021 to 2022 cycle showed less partisan bias than maps drawn by legislatures, using descriptive measures from one cycle. The Congressional Research Service has documented the mid-decade redraws of 2025 and 2026.
I022.remedy_note: Plausible. Commission and court-drawn maps showed lower partisan bias in the 2021 to 2022 cycle. In 2025 and 2026, commissions were bypassed or overridden, including through California's Proposition 50 and mid-decade redraws in other states, so whether commissions last is unproven.
I022.response: States, and Congress for House elections, would give map-drawing to independent commissions, publish draft maps, set explicit neutral criteria and allow enforceable review in state courts.
I022.tradeoff: Geography limits how many districts can be competitive, and neutral criteria can conflict with protecting minority voters' ability to elect candidates.
I022.success_measure: Partisan bias measured across a range of possible vote outcomes, and districts where minority voters can elect their preferred candidates.

aimed_reforms.why: Moves map-drawing away from the majority whose seats the map would protect.
Proportional counting in multi-member districts makes seat shares follow vote shares, so district lines matter less.

status.text: About ten states use commissions to draw congressional districts. In 2025 and 2026 several states redrew their maps in the middle of the decade, among them Texas (signed August 29, 2025), Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana. California voters approved Proposition 50 on November 4, 2025 with 64% of the vote, replacing the citizen commission's map with one drawn by the legislature. Virginia voters approved a constitutional amendment allowing a mid-decade redraw on April 21, 2026, and the Supreme Court of Virginia struck it down on May 8, 2026.

I023.title: District lines and at-large elections can dilute minority votes
I023.summary: How districts are drawn, or electing a whole council at large, can keep a protected racial group from electing its preferred candidates. After the Supreme Court's 2026 Callais decision, the legal standard for a remedy is much harder to meet.
I023.mechanism: District lines and at-large election rules can reduce the effective voting strength of groups protected by the Voting Rights Act.
I023.evidence_note: Documented. In Allen v. Milligan (2023), the Supreme Court found that Alabama's congressional map likely diluted Black votes under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. Shelby County v. Holder (2013) struck down the formula that decided which places needed federal approval before changing voting rules, leaving the rest of the Act in place. Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026) revised how courts analyze Section 2 districting claims; it left Section 2 in force and did not bar every majority-minority district.
I023.remedy_note: Plausible. Enforcement of Section 2 has produced remedial districts, as after Milligan. After Callais the standard is far harder to meet, and Congress has passed no statutory response.
I023.response: Congress, the Justice Department, the states and the courts would enforce voting-rights protections and adopt district or proportional remedies that have held up in court, with input from affected communities.
I023.tradeoff: Each case and remedy has to be checked against current doctrine. Callais changes Section 2 districting standards substantially, so a current analysis of race and party voting patterns has to come before any remedy is designed.
I023.success_measure: Whether protected groups can elect their preferred candidates, and gaps in access to voting.

aimed_reforms.why: Proportional counting lets a cohesive group win seats in proportion to its votes without depending on single-district lines.

I024.title: Winner-take-all districts can leave large groups of voters with few seats
I024.summary: When the top vote-getter takes a district's only seat, a party with substantial support across a state can win few of that state's seats. Nationally the 2024 House result was close to each party's vote share; the gaps appear inside individual states and in uncontested seats.
I024.mechanism: Single-member districts decided by plurality can turn a party's statewide vote share into a much smaller or larger share of that state's seats. In 2024 the national House result was close to proportional; the distortion appears within states and in seats left uncontested.
I024.evidence_note: Documented. Federal law (2 U.S.C. 2c) requires single-member House districts, so each state's delegation is chosen one winner-take-all seat at a time. Nationally the 2024 split of House seats came close to the split of votes; the disproportion shows up in individual states and in seats without major-party competition.
I024.remedy_note: Plausible. Cross-national research by Carey and Hix (2011) found that proportional systems with three to eight seats per district improve proportionality without splintering governments. No U.S. congressional test exists, and the federal single-member district law would have to change first.
I024.response: Congress would authorize multi-member House districts elected by single transferable vote or another tested proportional method. State legislatures would draw them and keep protections for minority voters.
I024.tradeoff: Party competition and the way members serve constituents would change, and voters and officials would need education and tested ballots. The post-Callais legal framework has to be checked before adoption.
I024.success_measure: How closely each state's seat shares match its vote shares, and whether voters have meaningful choices.

aimed_reforms.why: Multi-member districts with proportional counting are the direct response to winner-take-all seat distortion.

I025.title: Similar candidates split the vote and push voters off their first choice
I025.summary: When two similar candidates run, they can divide their supporters and let a third candidate win with less than a majority. Voters who see this coming often abandon their favorite to avoid helping the candidate they like least.
I025.mechanism: Under plurality rules, similar candidates split their shared support, and voters abandon their first choice to avoid a worse outcome.
I025.evidence_note: Well supported. The spoiler effect follows from the counting rule: when only first choices count, supporters of two similar candidates divide their votes. The sources listed for this record study the ranked alternative and give no count of U.S. races decided by a spoiler.
I025.remedy_note: Plausible. Ranked-choice voting removes the spoiler effect mechanically. In four local elections studied by Burnett and Kogan (2015), 9.6% to 27.1% of ballots were exhausted, meaning they ranked no candidate still in the count, and winners often lacked a majority of all ballots cast. Results on turnout and on candidate moderation are mixed. Alaska voters decide on November 3, 2026 whether to repeal the state's top-four primary and ranked general election.
I025.response: States and cities would pilot single-winner ranked-choice voting or another majority method, with clear counting rules, full release of ballot data and audits.
I025.tradeoff: Ranked counting leaves some ballots exhausted and can produce nonmonotonic results, where ranking a candidate higher causes that candidate to lose. It elects one winner per seat, so it leaves proportional representation unchanged.
I025.success_measure: Ballot errors, exhausted ballots, and a published definition of the support a winner needs.

aimed_reforms.why: Ranked ballots transfer to a later choice, which removes the penalty for running or voting for a similar candidate.
Fusion voting lets two parties nominate the same candidate, so allied parties can combine support instead of splitting it.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting in statewide elections. FairVote, an advocacy group, counted 36 cities and 3 counties using it or scheduled to use it as of March 2026, including New York City for primaries. Nineteen states prohibit it in some or all elections, by the National Conference of State Legislatures' count; Missouri's prohibition is written into its state constitution. Alaska Ballot Measure 2, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would repeal the top-four primary, the ranked-choice general election and the campaign disclosure rules adopted in 2020, including the requirement to report the true source of donations.

I026.title: Closed primaries shut unaffiliated voters out of the deciding election
I026.summary: In a closed primary only voters enrolled in a party can help choose its nominee. Where the primary effectively decides the seat, unaffiliated voters have no say in the contest that settles it.
I026.mechanism: Party-membership rules restrict who can vote in nomination contests, and in safe seats those contests decide who takes office.
I026.evidence_note: Documented. Ballotpedia's 2026 state-by-state count classifies each state's primary as closed, semi-closed, open, top-two or top-four. California and Washington use top-two primaries, and Alaska uses a top-four primary with a ranked general election. Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would replace party primaries with a single primary in which the top two finishers advance, without ranked ballots.
I026.remedy_note: Plausible. Opening primaries has little consistent effect on how liberal or conservative state legislators vote, according to McGhee, Masket, Shor, Rogers and McCarty (2014), the main evidence against claims of moderation. Effects on who participates are better supported.
I026.response: States and parties would compare semi-open primaries, nonpartisan qualifying elections and party-run nominations, judged by who participates and what choices voters get.
I026.tradeoff: Parties have a constitutional right of association that limits how far states can open their nominations, and evidence that open primaries produce more moderate legislators is mixed.
I026.success_measure: Participation among eligible voters, the range of candidates, and how well voters understand the ballot.

aimed_reforms.why: An all-party primary lets every voter take part in the contest that narrows the field.

status.text: California and Washington use top-two primaries, in which all candidates run on one ballot and the two leaders advance. Alaska uses a top-four primary followed by a ranked-choice general election; Ballot Measure 2 on its November 3, 2026 ballot would repeal that system. Massachusetts Question 3, on the same ballot, would create a single all-candidate primary for state and congressional offices, with the top two advancing to a general election that keeps one-choice ballots. It would take effect January 1, 2028.

I027.title: Ballot-access rules make it harder for new candidates to run
I027.summary: States set signature counts, fees and filing deadlines for getting on the ballot, and these are often heavier for minor parties and independents. High hurdles can keep credible challengers out of a race.
I027.mechanism: Petition and filing requirements deter credible challengers, and the size of the barrier depends on each state's rules.
I027.evidence_note: Plausible. Ballotpedia's 2026 state-by-state tables document signature and fee requirements that are heavier for minor-party and independent candidates than for major-party nominees. The tables show the rules; no study listed for this record measures how many credible candidates they deter.
I027.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Thresholds set in proportion to the size of the electorate are a logical design. No evaluation of threshold changes on candidate quality or voter choice has been found.
I027.response: States would set signature thresholds in proportion to the size of the electorate and uniform filing deadlines. Debate sponsors would adopt neutral criteria for who gets on stage.
I027.tradeoff: Thresholds set too low lengthen ballots and add work for election offices.
I027.success_measure: Candidates who qualify, signatures rejected, and how many viewers debates reach.

I028.title: Equal Senate seats give small-state residents more weight
I028.summary: Every state has two senators whatever its population, so a resident of a small state has far more Senate representation per person than a resident of a large one. Article V of the Constitution bars changing a state's equal Senate vote without that state's consent.
I028.mechanism: Equal Senate seats for every state give residents of small states far more national influence per person.
I028.evidence_note: Documented. The 2020 Census counted California at about 39.5 million residents and Wyoming at about 577,000, roughly 68 to 1, and each state elects two senators.
I028.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Article V bars changing a state's equal Senate vote without its consent. No evidence bears on the remedy beyond that legal constraint.
I028.response: Congress and the states would analyze options for admitting states and for representation, and would pursue any constitutional change toward population equality with Article V's limits stated openly.
I028.tradeoff: Article V protects each state's equal Senate vote unless that state consents to a change.
I028.success_measure: Residents per senator across states, and the size of the representation gap.

aimed_reforms.why: Keeps Senate apportionment options under examination with Article V's constraints explicit.

I029.title: The Electoral College can elect the national vote's runner-up
I029.summary: Because most states give all their electoral votes to the statewide winner, a candidate can win the presidency with fewer votes nationwide. The alternatives, a constitutional amendment or an interstate compact, each carry legal questions.
I029.mechanism: Allocating electoral votes state by state can elect a president who lost the national popular vote.
I029.evidence_note: Documented. In the 2000 and 2016 presidential elections, the Electoral College winner received fewer popular votes nationwide than the runner-up.
I029.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Under the National Popular Vote compact, member states would award their electoral votes to the national winner once states holding 270 votes join. By its advocates' count it has 18 states plus DC with 222 electoral votes, 48 short, after Virginia joined on April 14, 2026. No court has tested whether it is valid under the Constitution's Compact Clause, and a constitutional amendment has no active momentum.
I029.response: Congress and the states would compare direct popular election by constitutional amendment with the interstate compact, planning for litigation and for how each would operate.
I029.tradeoff: The compact's validity and operation remain contested, and no simple federal statute can replace the Electoral College nationwide.
I029.success_measure: Whether the presidential winner matches the national popular-vote winner, and how widely campaigns spread their attention across states.

aimed_reforms.why: Covers both an Electoral College amendment and the National Popular Vote compact.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, 18 states and the District of Columbia, with 222 electoral votes, have enacted the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. It takes effect only when its members hold at least 270 electoral votes, 48 more than today. Virginia joined in April 2026. Because the compact has never taken effect, no court has ruled on whether it needs the consent of Congress under the Constitution's Compact Clause.

I030.title: Threats and pressure drive election officials out
I030.summary: Local election officials face threats and pressure over counting and certifying results, duties the law defines. Experienced staff leave, and the personal cost of serving rises.
I030.mechanism: Partisan pressure over counting and certification, along with threats, politicizes legal duties and drives experienced staff out of election work.
I030.evidence_note: Well supported. In the Brennan Center's survey of 858 local election officials (April to May 2025), 38% reported threats, harassment or abuse, 52% worried about their staff's safety and 60% worried about federal cuts to election security support.
I030.remedy_note: Plausible. Officials themselves ask for professional standards and funding for threat response, and 87% want state support. No study has evaluated the outcomes.
I030.response: States, Congress and the Justice Department would professionalize election administration, protect certification as a defined legal duty and fund threat response under public standards.
I030.tradeoff: Independent election offices still need accountable appointments and public audits.
I030.success_measure: Vacancies in election offices, threats reported, and certifications completed on time and as the law requires.

aimed_reforms.why: Protects election officials and makes certification a scheduled legal duty.

I031.title: Election offices run on irregular funding
I031.summary: U.S. elections cost about $2 billion a year, paid mostly by local governments on an irregular basis. Old equipment and staff turnover raise the risk of errors and security problems.
I031.mechanism: Aging equipment and staff turnover increase errors and security weaknesses in election administration.
I031.evidence_note: Plausible. The MIT Election Data and Science Lab's 2021 synthesis estimated that elections cost roughly $2 billion a year nationally, with funding that is local and irregular. In the Brennan Center's 2025 survey of 858 local election officials, 60% worried about federal cuts to security support. Neither source measures error rates.
I031.remedy_note: Plausible. Paper records and risk-limiting audits, statistical checks of paper ballots against reported results, are consensus security practice. Congress has never enacted recurring formula grants for election offices, so there is no evidence on their effect.
I031.response: Congress and the states would provide recurring formula grants for paper records, risk-limiting audits, cybersecurity and trained staff.
I031.tradeoff: Federal requirements should come with funding, and equipment contracts should avoid locking offices into one vendor.
I031.success_measure: Audits completed, age of voting equipment, and recovery exercises held.

aimed_reforms.why: Sets the floor of paper records and audits that recurring grants would pay for.

I032.title: Late rule changes and slow rulings shake confidence in results
I032.summary: When voting rules change close to an election, voters and poll workers struggle to keep up. If disputes then take too long to settle, access suffers and fewer people accept the result.
I032.mechanism: Rule changes late in an election cycle and slow resolution of disputes reduce access to voting and acceptance of results.
I032.evidence_note: Plausible. In Watson v. Republican National Committee (2026), the Supreme Court ruled that federal Election Day statutes do not bar counting mail ballots postmarked by Election Day, one example of rules litigated close to an election. No source listed for this record measures the effect of late changes on turnout or acceptance.
I032.remedy_note: Plausible. The Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022 clarified certification duties, created expedited court review and raised the threshold for objections in Congress. It worked as written in 2024, its only cycle of use.
I032.response: States, and Congress within its authority, would publish rules early and set up fast, neutral adjudication with clear certification deadlines and defined remedies.
I032.tradeoff: Emergencies still require limited exceptions, subject to court review.
I032.success_measure: Rule changes made late in the cycle, contests unresolved at deadlines, and compliance with certification dates.

aimed_reforms.why: Requires certification on a schedule, which narrows the window for late disputes.

I033.title: Donors get more of lawmakers' time
I033.summary: Candidates and their staff give more time to people who can fund campaigns. In a field experiment, congressional offices granted meetings with senior staff three to four times as often when the request came from donors.
I033.mechanism: Candidates and officeholders give time and access to people who can finance campaigns.
I033.evidence_note: Well supported. In a randomized field experiment across 191 congressional offices, Kalla and Broockman (2016) found that people identified as donors got meetings with senior staff three to four times as often as people identified only as constituents. Bonica, McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal (2013) documented that contributions scale with wealth and that the largest donors supply a growing share of itemized money. OpenSecrets tallies of Federal Election Commission data put outside spending on the 2024 elections at $4.5 billion. Gilens and Page (2014), studying 1,779 policy questions from 1981 to 2002, found that outcomes tracked the preferences of affluent citizens and business groups more closely than those of median voters; the association is conditional and leaves room for ordinary voters' influence.
I033.remedy_note: Plausible. New York City's matching program raised the share of money from small donors and widened the range of people who give. No evidence shows that matching changes policy outcomes or reduces outside spending.
I033.response: Congress, the states and cities would offer voluntary matching of small donations, with qualification thresholds, spending limits for participating candidates, audits and sanctions.
I033.tradeoff: Public funds require controls against fraud, and outside spending continues regardless.
I033.success_measure: Share of money from small donors who live in the district, and how many candidates take part.

aimed_reforms.why: Matching and vouchers make small donors worth a candidate's time, which changes whose calls get returned.

I034.title: Fundraising takes time away from legislating
I034.summary: Members of Congress spend part of their working day calling donors, time that could go to committee work. How many hours this takes has never been reliably measured.
I034.mechanism: Fundraising demands displace committee work and deliberation. No reliable measure of the hours involved exists.
I034.evidence_note: Plausible. A 2013 survey of members by the Congressional Management Foundation found that members describe fundraising as a significant use of their time; the answers are self-reported and dated. A leaked 2013 model schedule from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, reported by HuffPost, set aside four hours a day for donor calls. It is one party's planning document and records no actual behavior.
I034.remedy_note: Hypothesis. No intervention has been evaluated. The evidence base is one leaked party schedule and a dated member survey.
I034.response: Legislatures and parties would combine public financing with party rules that end fundraising dues tied to committee assignments, and publish aggregate time diaries that members complete voluntarily.
I034.tradeoff: No reliable estimate of hours exists, and compulsory caps on fundraising time would run into free-speech protections and evasion.
I034.success_measure: Time members spend on legislative work, time spent contacting donors, and how long members and staff stay.

aimed_reforms.why: Public matching is the financing half of this response; its effect on total call time is unmeasured.

I035.title: Outside groups run campaigns that no candidate answers for
I035.summary: Super PACs and other independent groups spent a record $4.5 billion on 2024 elections, much of it on messages no candidate has to own. Voters can find it hard to tell who paid and whom to hold responsible.
I035.mechanism: Outside groups shape campaigns through messages that no candidate owns, which makes it harder for voters to assign responsibility.
I035.evidence_note: Documented. OpenSecrets tallies of Federal Election Commission filings put outside spending on the 2024 elections at $4.5 billion, with more than $1 billion reaching super PACs from groups that do not disclose their donors. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) allowed unlimited independent spending by corporations and unions while upholding disclosure, and SpeechNow.org v. FEC (2010) allowed unlimited contributions to groups that spend independently.
I035.remedy_note: Hypothesis. NRSC v. FEC (June 30, 2026) struck down limits on party spending coordinated with candidates, which narrows the legal room for coordination rules, so this response needs redesign.
I035.response: Congress and the Federal Election Commission would tighten rules against coordination between campaigns and outside groups, require timely disclosure and enforce separation from campaigns.
I035.tradeoff: The Constitution protects independent political spending, and after NRSC v. FEC the room for coordination limits is narrower.
I035.success_measure: Findings of illegal coordination, and the time between spending and its disclosure.

aimed_reforms.why: Disclosure of original funders lets voters see who paid for outside messages.
Coordination and disclosure rules mean nothing without a commission able to enforce them.

I036.title: Intermediaries hide who funds political spending
I036.summary: Political money can pass through nonprofits and shell companies before it is spent, so the final report names a group and leaves out the people who supplied the money. In 2024 more than $1 billion reached super PACs from sources that do not disclose donors.
I036.mechanism: Nonprofits and shell entities pass political money through layers that hide where it came from.
I036.evidence_note: Documented. OpenSecrets, using Federal Election Commission data, counted more than $1 billion flowing to super PACs in 2024 from sources that do not disclose their donors. In the Ohio nuclear-bailout case, a federal court in the Southern District of Ohio sentenced former House Speaker Larry Householder in June 2023 for a racketeering scheme in which utility money passed through a nonprofit; FirstEnergy entered a deferred prosecution agreement.
I036.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Disclosure of original funders has to survive the exacting scrutiny the Supreme Court applied in Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta (2021). No study has evaluated disclosure's effects on spending or trust.
I036.response: Congress and the states would require election spenders to disclose their original funders above reasonable thresholds and to trace money passed between entities.
I036.tradeoff: Small donors who face credible threats of harassment need narrow exemptions.
I036.success_measure: Share of election spending traceable to its original source, and the length of chains of intermediaries.

aimed_reforms.why: Requires disclosure of the original funders, including money passed through intermediaries.

I037.title: Straw donors hide the real source of contributions
I037.summary: Someone who wants to give more than the law allows can route money through other people or shell companies whose names go on the report. Prosecutions show this happens, and no one has measured how often.
I037.mechanism: Contributions are reported in the name of a stand-in, which hides the real source and evades limits. Prosecutions show the practice exists; its scale is unknown.
I037.evidence_note: Plausible. Federal law prohibits contributions made in the name of another person, according to the Federal Election Commission, and the Justice Department has prosecuted such cases. No estimate of how common the practice is exists.
I037.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Certification of the beneficial owner, the person who ultimately supplies the money, is untested.
I037.response: Congress, the Federal Election Commission and the Justice Department would require donors to certify the beneficial owner of a contribution, keep audit trails for payments and impose meaningful penalties for knowing evasion.
I037.tradeoff: Privacy, access to banking and due process need protection.
I037.success_measure: Evasion cases resolved, and the share of contributions whose source is verified.

aimed_reforms.why: Tracing money to its actual source is the disclosure task this reform sets.
Straw-donor cases need a commission with a quorum to investigate and refer them.

I038.title: A campaign-finance agency without a quorum cannot enforce the law
I038.summary: The Federal Election Commission needs four votes to act, and since May 2025 it has not had four commissioners. With no quorum, complaints wait and no violation can be penalized.
I038.mechanism: A commission that cannot act leaves violations unresolved. The Federal Election Commission has lacked a quorum since May 2025, which halts enforcement entirely, a step beyond the deadlocks that came before.
I038.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Research Service reports that the commission needs four votes to act, that the current gap is the fourth loss of quorum in its history, and that it had two commissioners as of March 2026. The commission issued a notice of lack of quorum on April 6, 2026.
I038.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Restructuring the commission with an odd number of members is a design proposal with no test. The immediate problem is vacancy as well as deadlock.
I038.response: Congress would restructure the commission's voting and appointment rules, with due process, judicial review and a funded professional staff. The President would nominate and the Senate confirm enough commissioners to restore a quorum.
I038.tradeoff: Ending deadlock can open the door to control by one party unless appointments and procedures stay balanced.
I038.success_measure: Age of pending cases, decisions on the merits, and how often courts reverse them.

aimed_reforms.why: Restores a quorum and addresses deadlock so the commission can enforce the law.

I039.title: Lobbying disclosure misses advisers who direct influence campaigns
I039.summary: Federal rules require registration only when paid contacts with officials pass narrow thresholds, so advisers who plan influence campaigns can stay off the books. One estimate puts about half of active lobbyists outside the registration system.
I039.mechanism: Advisory and indirect influence work avoids narrow registration triggers, so public lobbying records are incomplete.
I039.evidence_note: Well supported. LaPira and Thomas (2017) estimate that roughly half of active lobbyists are unregistered 'shadow' lobbyists; the estimate depends on their method's assumptions. A 2026 Government Accountability Office audit found that 22% of reports omitted required disclosure of prior government jobs and counted 12,391 referrals for failure to file from 2016 to 2025. The audit covers registrants only.
I039.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Some states define lobbying more broadly, and no study has evaluated whether that makes disclosure more complete.
I039.response: Congress and ethics agencies would cover paid direction of lobbying strategy and publish clients, issues, meetings and spending in standard records.
I039.tradeoff: Ordinary petitioning of government needs protection, and small groups should not face heavy filing burdens.
I039.success_measure: Paid contacts left undisclosed, and how complete filings are.

aimed_reforms.why: Requires meaningful lobbying disclosure, which this record would extend to strategic advisers.

I040.title: The revolving door turns access into a paid asset
I040.summary: Former officials and staff can sell their relationships to lobbying clients, and officials hoping for such jobs may decide with future employers in mind. Research shows that lobbying firms pay for that access.
I040.mechanism: Officials' past relationships and prospects of future employment can distort the decisions they make in office.
I040.evidence_note: Well supported for the value of access. Blanes i Vidal, Draca and Fons-Rosen (2012) found that a former staffer's lobbying revenue fell 24% when the senator they had worked for left office, which shows that access carries a price. OpenSecrets keeps counts of former members and staff registered as lobbyists.
I040.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Cooling-off periods are common and have no rigorous evaluation. Executive-order bans have been adopted and rescinded repeatedly.
I040.response: Congress, agencies and states would set targeted cooling-off periods, require officials to recuse themselves while negotiating for jobs, and require disclosure for senior officials and industry contractors.
I040.tradeoff: Bans drawn too broadly can deter skilled recruits, so public pay for expertise has to be adequate.
I040.success_measure: Recusal compliance, and revolving-door violations found.

aimed_reforms.why: Revolving-door limits reduce the value of insider access that this record describes.

I041.title: Understaffed offices lean on industry for expertise
I041.summary: Congressional offices with few experienced staff rely on lobbyists and interest groups to explain technical issues and draft text. That reliance lets those groups shape which options lawmakers consider.
I041.mechanism: Understaffed offices rely on interested parties to draft and analyze rules.
I041.evidence_note: Well supported. Hertel-Fernandez, Mildenberger and Stokes (2019) surveyed senior congressional staff and found that they misjudge constituent opinion and lean on contacts from interest groups. OpenSecrets, using Lobbying Disclosure Act filings, reports federal lobbying above $4 billion a year since 2022, a figure that leaves out unregistered work.
I041.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The House Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress recommended expanding support agencies in 2022. No causal evidence links more capacity funding to less reliance on industry.
I041.response: Congress would expand nonpartisan bill drafting, the Congressional Research Service, the Congressional Budget Office and the Government Accountability Office, and publish material submissions received on legislation.
I041.tradeoff: Outside experts remain useful, and records need to identify whose interests they represent.
I041.success_measure: Use of independent analysis in legislation, and how long staff stay.

aimed_reforms.why: Gives Congress its own experts so members depend less on interested drafting.

I042.title: Fake public comments manufacture the look of public support
I042.summary: Organizers can flood an agency with comments under stolen or invented names, so manufactured support looks like independent public opinion. In the Federal Communications Commission's net neutrality proceeding, about 18 million of 22 million comments were fake.
I042.mechanism: Fabricated mass submissions to agencies conceal who organized them and can use stolen identities.
I042.evidence_note: Documented. The New York Attorney General's 2021 investigation found that about 18 million of the 22 million comments filed with the Federal Communications Commission on net neutrality were fake, and that firms funded by the broadband industry submitted comments using stolen identities.
I042.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Identity verification and sponsor disclosure are proposed. No study has evaluated their effect on the quality of rulemaking.
I042.response: Agencies, and Congress where legislation is needed, would verify organizational sponsors, detect identity theft and disclose coordinated campaigns, while still counting comments that share a view honestly.
I042.tradeoff: Anonymous public comment can be legitimate.
I042.success_measure: Fraudulent submissions detected, and sponsors identified.

I043.title: Lawmakers' stock holdings create conflicts of interest
I043.summary: Members of Congress and their families can own and trade stocks in industries their votes affect, which gives them an incentive to misuse what they learn and weakens public trust. The best study of returns found members' portfolios underperformed the market, so the documented harm concerns incentives and trust.
I043.mechanism: Officials' personal financial stakes in industries they regulate create incentives to misuse information or authority and erode public trust. Violations of disclosure rules are documented; the best study does not support systematic profit from trading.
I043.evidence_note: Plausible. A 2021 Business Insider investigation found that dozens of members of Congress had violated STOCK Act reporting rules. Eggers and Hainmueller (2013) found that members' portfolios underperformed the market, which counts against systematic insider gains. In a May 2023 University of Maryland survey of 2,625 registered voters, 86% favored a ban on stock trading by members, including 87% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats.
I043.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Trading bans are untested at the federal level, and portfolio studies show no systematic insider gains for a ban to remove. The House passed H.R. 7008 on July 22, 2026, by 232 to 198; it would ban new stock purchases by members and their families and also carries a voter-ID title. A Senate vote to end debate on taking up the bill failed 53 to 47 on September 30, 2026.
I043.response: Congress and ethics bodies would require covered officials, spouses and dependents to hold broad diversified funds or qualified blind trusts, with rules for the transition out of individual stocks.
I043.tradeoff: Assets and family coverage need careful definitions, and a trust that keeps the owner informed would be cosmetic.
I043.success_measure: Compliance, unexplained trades, and enforcement outcomes.

aimed_reforms.why: A congressional stock-trading ban removes the financial stake behind this conflict.

status.text: The House passed H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026: 218 Republicans, 13 Democrats and 1 independent voted yes, and 198 Democrats voted no. The bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children from buying new individual stocks, without requiring them to sell stocks they already own, and it carries a separate title requiring photo identification to vote in federal elections. On September 30, 2026 a Senate motion to end debate on taking up the bill failed 53 to 47, short of the 60 votes required. As of October 15, 2026 the Senate has not passed it.

I044.title: Gifts and paid travel can buy access to officials
I044.summary: Officials, including Supreme Court justices, can receive gifts and sponsored trips from people with interests before them. When those benefits go undisclosed, the public cannot see the conflict, even where no decision is shown to have changed.
I044.mechanism: Private benefits such as gifts and sponsored travel can influence official conduct or create the appearance of influence.
I044.evidence_note: Plausible. ProPublica reported in 2023 that Justice Clarence Thomas accepted luxury travel and gifts from a Republican donor over two decades without disclosing them; the reporting documents the benefits and shows no effect on his decisions. Fix the Court, an advocacy group, reported in 2025 that the Supreme Court's ethics code still lacks enforcement, that the Judicial Conference dropped a referral concerning Justice Thomas, and that the Supreme Court Ethics, Recusal and Transparency Act had not been enacted.
I044.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The Judicial Conference adopted stricter disclosure rules in 2023, and nothing enforces them for the justices. No study has measured the effect of gift rules.
I044.response: Legislatures, courts and executive agencies would set stricter gift rules, disclose travel sponsors in real time and create independent ethics review.
I044.tradeoff: Ordinary educational events need workable exceptions.
I044.success_measure: Benefits left undisclosed, and ethics reviews completed.

I045.title: Political connections can steer public contracts
I045.summary: Firms with political ties can gain an edge when governments award contracts. Open contracting records and independent review of bids make it possible to check whether the winner offered the public the best deal.
I045.mechanism: Donations and relationships give some bidders an advantage in public contracting.
I045.evidence_note: Plausible. Goldman, Rocholl and So (2013) found that firms with board members connected to the winning party gained more federal procurement contracts after elections, using data from 1994 to 2004. The Securities and Exchange Commission's 2010 pay-to-play rule for investment advisers documents the same problem in the management of public pension money.
I045.remedy_note: Plausible. The SEC's pay-to-play rule and state limits on contributions from contractors exist. Evaluations cover compliance and leave contract outcomes unmeasured.
I045.response: Congress, the states and procurement offices would publish open contracting data, require independent bid review and conflict disclosure, and adopt legally tailored limits on contributions from contractors.
I045.tradeoff: Compliance costs should not shut out small vendors.
I045.success_measure: Competitive bids received, single-source awards, and outcomes of bid protests.

I046.title: Narrow tax and regulatory favors are hard to see
I046.summary: A small exception in the tax code or a regulation can deliver a large benefit to a few while spreading the cost across everyone else. Federal tax breaks cost about $2.3 trillion a year in lost revenue, and most are never evaluated.
I046.mechanism: Narrow exceptions in tax law and regulation give concentrated gains to a few and spread the costs thinly across many.
I046.evidence_note: Well supported. The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates federal tax expenditures, the revenue lost to special deductions, exclusions and credits, at about $2.3 trillion in fiscal year 2026. The largest items are the exclusions for retirement saving and employer health coverage and the lower rates on capital gains; the total covers broad provisions and narrow ones alike. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2012 that most tax expenditures are never evaluated.
I046.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The Government Accountability Office has published a framework for evaluating tax expenditures. Systematic review with expiry dates has never been enacted, so there is no evidence on its effect.
I046.response: Congress and agencies would publish estimates of who benefits from major tax expenditures and regulatory exemptions, and schedule unjustified preferences for review and expiry.
I046.tradeoff: Some targeted provisions correct real failures in a market.
I046.success_measure: Cost of preferences, and the share of renewals that follow an evaluation.

aimed_reforms.why: Narrows two large preferences, untaxed gains at death and lower rates on capital income.

I047.title: Residents with less time and money have less say between elections
I047.summary: People with more time, money and organizational backing take part far more often in hearings, public comments and meetings. Officials making detailed decisions hear mostly from them.
I047.mechanism: Advantages in time and money skew who takes part in public decisions between elections.
I047.evidence_note: Well supported. Schlozman, Verba and Brady (2012), drawing on surveys and a census of organizations, found that participation and organized interests tilt heavily toward affluent people and business. In Massachusetts planning and zoning meeting minutes, Einstein, Glick and Palmer (2019) found that participants were older, whiter and more likely to own homes than other residents, and mostly opposed new housing.
I047.remedy_note: Plausible. Citizen panels chosen by lottery produce more representative participants by design, according to an OECD review. Evidence that their proposals change policy comes from individual cases.
I047.response: Legislatures and foundations would fund accessible public hearings, paid citizen panels and legal help for underrepresented groups.
I047.tradeoff: Whoever selects panel members and sets the agenda can tilt the results toward the sponsor.
I047.success_measure: How representative participants are, and how many of their proposals receive an official answer.

I048.title: Court rulings limit what campaign-finance laws can do
I048.summary: Supreme Court rulings under the First Amendment have struck down many limits on political spending and contributions. Disclosure and public financing remain legal options, while broader limits would need a constitutional amendment.
I048.mechanism: Current First Amendment doctrine blocks many proposed limits on political money.
I048.evidence_note: Documented. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) allowed unlimited independent spending by corporations and unions and upheld disclosure. McCutcheon v. FEC (2014) struck down aggregate contribution limits and held that only quid pro quo corruption or its appearance justifies limits. NRSC v. FEC (June 30, 2026) struck down limits on party spending coordinated with candidates.
I048.remedy_note: Hypothesis. A constitutional amendment would be legally sufficient and has no realistic path to ratification. Disclosure and public financing remain the feasible tools.
I048.response: Congress and the states would pursue disclosure and public financing now, and separately draft a constitutional amendment authorizing reasonable limits on political money with safeguards for speech.
I048.tradeoff: Amendments are hard to pass, and vague language could give officials power to censor.
I048.success_measure: A route to enactment, review for effects on rights, and durable compliance.

aimed_reforms.why: Public financing is one of the tools current doctrine allows.
Disclosure survived Citizens United and is the other tool current doctrine allows.

I049.title: Low pay and turnover drain Congress's staff expertise
I049.summary: Committee staff have fallen by roughly a third since the 1980s, and low pay drives experienced aides out. With less knowledge in house, Congress has a harder time judging competing claims on its own.
I049.mechanism: Low pay and turnover reduce Congress's institutional knowledge and its independence when weighing claims from outside interests.
I049.evidence_note: Well supported. The Brookings Institution's Vital Statistics on Congress, compiled from official counts, shows committee staff down roughly a third since the 1980s. Hertel-Fernandez, Mildenberger and Stokes (2019) surveyed senior staff and found that they misjudge constituent opinion and rely on contacts from interest groups.
I049.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The House raised staff pay floors and caps in 2022, and no study of the effect on retention has been published.
I049.response: Congress, through its appropriations and the administration of each chamber, would raise pay and build career paths for specialist staff, expand committee capacity and publish data on retention and workload.
I049.tradeoff: More staff alone does not raise quality, so professional standards have to stay in place.
I049.success_measure: Staff tenure, and the share of legislation that receives technical review.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds congressional staff and support agencies directly, which is this record's response.

I050.title: Congress's research agencies cannot keep up with technical questions
I050.summary: Questions about new technology and the federal budget can outrun the capacity of Congress's nonpartisan research agencies. Members then decide with less neutral analysis in hand.
I050.mechanism: Technology and budget questions outrun the neutral expertise available to Congress.
I050.evidence_note: Well supported. Brookings' series on congressional support-agency staffing documents the long decline in Congress's in-house capacity. The Government Accountability Office created a technology assessment team in 2019, a partial answer to the gap left when Congress closed its Office of Technology Assessment in 1995.
I050.remedy_note: Hypothesis. GAO's technology assessment team rebuilt part of the lost capacity, and its output has been measured only by counts of requests.
I050.response: Congress would expand the Congressional Research Service, the Congressional Budget Office and the Government Accountability Office, and establish a modern technology-assessment function with public methods.
I050.tradeoff: The agencies have to stay nonpartisan, and new units should avoid duplicating existing offices.
I050.success_measure: Requests completed, turnaround time, and external peer review of the work.

aimed_reforms.why: Expands support-agency capacity, including technical analysis.

I051.title: A few leaders decide which bills get debated
I051.summary: House and Senate leaders control floor time and which amendments get a vote, which limits committee work and open debate. Most enacted laws still pass with support from both parties.
I051.mechanism: A few leaders control access to the floor and to amendments.
I051.evidence_note: Well supported. The Bipartisan Policy Center's Healthy Congress Index tracks open and closed rules, committee activity and days in session, and finds that closed rules, which bar or limit floor amendments, dominate recent Congresses. Curry and Lee (2020) found that most enacted laws remain bipartisan, so leadership control has not produced purely partisan output.
I051.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Restoring open rules and committee markups is a choice each chamber can make. Evidence that it improves outcomes is contested, since bipartisan lawmaking persists under current practice.
I051.response: The House and Senate would change their rules to restore regular committee consideration, reasonable access to amendments and published exceptions for real emergencies.
I051.tradeoff: Unlimited amendments can become obstruction, and time limits have to be applied fairly.
I051.success_measure: Committee markups held, amendment access, and time to read bills before votes.

I052.title: The Senate filibuster lets a minority block ordinary bills
I052.summary: Most Senate bills need 60 votes to end debate, so a minority can stop measures a majority supports. Voters then have a harder time telling who could have acted and who blocked action.
I052.mechanism: Minority vetoes through the Senate's cloture rule block ordinary legislation and blur who is responsible for the result.
I052.evidence_note: Well supported. Senate records show cloture motions, votes to end debate that usually need 60 senators, rising from single digits per Congress before 1970 to 200 to 300 in recent Congresses.
I052.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The Senate changed its rules for nominations by simple majority in 2013 and 2017, which shows that rule change is feasible. The effects of a talking filibuster or a declining vote threshold are untested.
I052.response: The Senate would reform cloture with a threshold that declines over time or a majority vote on final passage, keeping protected debate and amendments for the minority.
I052.tradeoff: Protection of rights should not depend entirely on temporary majorities.
I052.success_measure: Debates completed, votes held on substance, and outcomes for rights.

aimed_reforms.why: Lets a Senate majority reach a final vote on ordinary legislation.

I053.title: Deadline bills bundle unrelated choices with little scrutiny
I053.summary: Congress often passes sprawling spending bills right before a deadline, combining unrelated policies in one vote. Members and the public get little time to read individual provisions.
I053.mechanism: Bills passed at crisis deadlines bundle unrelated provisions and limit scrutiny.
I053.evidence_note: Plausible. The Congressional Research Service documents the frequency and size of omnibus and consolidated appropriations acts since the 1980s. It records the practice; no source listed for this record measures how many provisions escape review.
I053.remedy_note: Hypothesis. The House has a rule requiring bill text 72 hours before a vote and often waives it. Change logs and separate votes on unrelated provisions have not been evaluated.
I053.response: Congress would set earlier committee calendars, publish readable bill texts and change logs, and hold separate recorded votes on major unrelated provisions.
I053.tradeoff: Some packages are needed to reach a bargain, so rules should avoid forcing every provision into its own bill.
I053.success_measure: Time bill text is public before votes, and riders passed without review.

aimed_reforms.why: Automatic continuing funding removes the shutdown deadline that drives last-minute bundling.

I054.title: Shutdown threats interrupt government services
I054.summary: When Congress misses a funding deadline, agencies close or slow down, federal workers go without pay and planning stalls. The threat of a shutdown also becomes a bargaining tool.
I054.mechanism: Lapses in appropriations damage planning, services and workers, and the threat of a lapse becomes a tool in budget negotiations.
I054.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the 43-day lapse in 2025, the longest on record, cut fourth-quarter growth by 1.0 to 2.0 percentage points and permanently lost $7 billion to $14 billion of output; the estimate is a scenario. The Congressional Research Service summarized the lapse's effects on services. CBO estimated that the 35-day shutdown ending in January 2019 permanently cost $3 billion of GDP.
I054.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Automatic continuing resolutions have been proposed repeatedly and never enacted. The concern that they weaken the incentive to pass budgets is theoretical.
I054.response: Congress would adopt automatic temporary funding, with rules that keep old priorities from being frozen in place, and require timely votes on budgets.
I054.tradeoff: Automatic funding can reduce the pressure to finish full-year appropriations.
I054.success_measure: Shutdown days, and full-year appropriations passed on time.

aimed_reforms.why: Continues funding at the prior level if appropriations lapse, so services do not stop.

I055.title: Debt-limit standoffs create a risk of default
I055.summary: Congress passes spending and tax laws, then votes separately on whether the Treasury may borrow to pay for them. Standoffs over that second vote raise borrowing costs and the risk of missed payments.
I055.mechanism: Separating borrowing authority from fiscal decisions Congress has already enacted creates default risk and extra cost.
I055.evidence_note: Documented. The Government Accountability Office estimated that the 2011 debt-limit delay raised Treasury borrowing costs by about $1.3 billion in fiscal year 2011. Fitch Ratings cited repeated debt-limit standoffs as a governance factor when it downgraded the United States to AA+ in 2023.
I055.remedy_note: Plausible. From 1979 to 1995 a House rule, known as the Gephardt rule, automatically linked borrowing authority to the budget Congress adopted. No formal evaluation of it exists.
I055.response: Congress would tie borrowing authority automatically to the spending and tax laws it enacts, and publish debt projections.
I055.tradeoff: The change leaves the underlying gap between spending and revenue untouched.
I055.success_measure: Events that raise the risk of default, and disruptions to Treasury financing.

I056.title: Congress's demands for information can expire unanswered
I056.summary: When the executive branch resists a congressional subpoena, the court case can outlast the two-year Congress that issued it. Delay weakens oversight even when Congress has a valid claim to the information.
I056.mechanism: Slow litigation over subpoenas weakens congressional checks within a two-year Congress.
I056.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Research Service explains why civil enforcement of subpoenas against the executive branch routinely outlasts a Congress. In Trump v. Mazars USA (2020), the Supreme Court set a new balancing test for subpoenas of a President's records, and the records reached Congress years after the request.
I056.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Expedited civil enforcement has been proposed. Constitutional limits on standing and executive privilege remain unresolved.
I056.response: Congress, with the courts, would create expedited civil enforcement and clear standing where the Constitution allows, with procedures for privilege claims and sanctions after review.
I056.tradeoff: Disputes over executive privilege require fair adjudication.
I056.success_measure: Time to final compliance, and requests resolved.

aimed_reforms.why: Provides timely subpoena enforcement and records access when oversight is obstructed.

I057.title: Programs continue without evidence of results
I057.summary: Many federal programs and tax breaks run for years without a credible check on whether they work. A 2018 law created evaluation officers, and agencies still rarely use findings when deciding renewals.
I057.mechanism: Spending and rulemaking continue without anyone learning what works.
I057.evidence_note: Documented. The Government Accountability Office reported in 2012 that most tax expenditures are never evaluated. Its 2025 High Risk List names 38 areas where government effectiveness depends on leadership, capacity, monitoring and demonstrated progress. The Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018 requires evaluation officers and learning agendas, and GAO finds implementation uneven.
I057.remedy_note: Plausible. The 2018 Evidence Act created evaluation officers and learning agendas. GAO finds uneven implementation and little use of evaluations when programs come up for renewal.
I057.response: Congress and agencies would require evaluation plans in proportion to a program's size, open administrative data to evaluators and base renewal decisions on published findings.
I057.tradeoff: Poor metrics can push aside long-term public value that is hard to measure.
