I109.summary: In 2024, 5,070 U.S. workers died from injuries on the job, and hot days raise workplace injuries. A federal heat standard has been proposed and not finalized.
I109.mechanism: Weak safety and heat protections impose injuries and health costs on workers.
I109.evidence_note: Well supported. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counted 5,070 fatal work injuries in 2024, a rate of 3.3 per 100,000 full-time-equivalent workers. Park, Pankratz and Behrer (2021) found from California workers' compensation claims that hot days raise workplace injuries by 5% to 15%. OSHA proposed a heat standard in August 2024 and had no final rule as of September 2026.
I109.remedy_note: Well supported. California workplaces picked at random for government safety inspections had 9.4% fewer injuries and 26% lower injury costs than 409 matched workplaces, with no detectable loss of jobs, sales or firm survival. The result is strong causal evidence that inspection capacity prevents injuries.
I109.response: OSHA, the states and Congress would strengthen inspection capacity, heat and injury prevention, injury reporting and protection from retaliation.
I109.tradeoff: Rules need to fit how each sector works.
I109.success_measure: Injuries and illnesses, inspections, and compliance.

I110.title: Workers have little say over new technology and restructuring
I110.summary: Employers can introduce monitoring software or reorganize jobs without consulting the people affected. Federal law requires advance notice only for mass layoffs, 60 days ahead.
I110.mechanism: Workplace technology and restructuring proceed without worker input, which can intensify surveillance and displacement.
I110.evidence_note: Plausible. A 2021 UC Berkeley Labor Center report documents algorithmic management and workplace surveillance. The OECD's 2023 Employment Outlook synthesizes survey evidence on AI adoption and on consulting workers. The federal WARN Act requires 60 days' notice for mass layoffs and nothing for other changes.
I110.remedy_note: Plausible. A study of a 1994 German reform found that worker seats on company boards had no effect on wages and came with more capital invested per worker. Its estimates for productivity were positive but too imprecise to rule out no effect. U.S. consultation mandates have no evaluation.
I110.response: Congress, the states and firms would require notice and consultation before major workplace technology changes and layoffs, and support worker representation on relevant boards.
I110.tradeoff: Consultation has to be meaningful without blocking every innovation.
I110.success_measure: Worker input given, outcomes for displaced workers, and privacy complaints.

aimed_reforms.why: Gives workers notice, a way to contest decisions and a bargaining role when employers deploy AI.

I111.title: Training often fails to lead to better jobs
I111.summary: A credential can cost time and money without opening the door to a good job. Programs tied to employer demand, such as sectoral training and apprenticeships, show large earnings gains in rigorous studies.
I111.mechanism: Credentials often cost time and money without improving opportunity.
I111.evidence_note: Well supported. Using administrative data, a 2019 study in the Journal of Human Resources found that for-profit certificate students earned no more, and often less, after enrolling. In a resume experiment, Deming and colleagues (2016) found employers responded less to for-profit credentials. A randomized evaluation of adult training under the Workforce Investment Act found no earnings gain at 30 months (Labor Department, 2017).
I111.remedy_note: Well supported. Randomized evaluations of sector-focused training programs for low-wage workers found earnings gains of 11% to 40% that lasted after training ended. A Department of Labor study comparing registered apprentices in 10 states with nonparticipants found an association with substantially higher earnings.
I111.response: Congress, the states and colleges would fund paid apprenticeships and evaluated community-college pathways tied to portable credentials and real employer demand.
I111.tradeoff: Forecasts of employer demand can be wrong, so completion and wage outcomes should be published.
I111.success_measure: Completion, earnings gains, and student debt.

I112.title: Losing a job can do lasting financial damage
I112.summary: Workers displaced in a mass layoff lose about 20% of their earnings for 15 to 20 years, more in a recession. Unemployment insurance reaches only a quarter to a third of unemployed people.
I112.mechanism: Weak unemployment insurance and reemployment support turn job loss into lasting insecurity.
I112.evidence_note: Well supported. Using administrative data, Davis and von Wachter (2011) found that displaced workers lose about 20% of earnings for 15 to 20 years, more when the layoff comes in a recession, building on Jacobson, LaLonde and Sullivan (1993). The Labor Department's recipiency series shows unemployment insurance reaching roughly a quarter to a third of unemployed people.
I112.remedy_note: Plausible. The Government Accountability Office documented failures in unemployment insurance systems in 2020 and 2021. Evidence on wage insurance from Trade Adjustment Assistance is limited, and automatic extension triggers have been modeled without being tested.
I112.response: Congress and the states would modernize unemployment insurance, add automatic extensions in recessions, pilot wage insurance and support rapid job placement.
I112.tradeoff: Wage insurance can subsidize low-paying employers, so it needs a separate evaluation.
I112.success_measure: Share of lost income replaced, quality of new jobs, and take-up.

I113.title: Investment gains are taxed more lightly than wages
I113.summary: Long-term capital gains and dividends face a top federal rate of 20%, against 37% on wages, and gains can be deferred until sale or go untaxed if held until death. Over time the lighter treatment helps existing owners build further advantages.
I113.mechanism: Capital income and asset appreciation are taxed more lightly than labor income, so owners accumulate advantages over time.
I113.evidence_note: Documented. Federal law sets a 20% top rate on long-term capital gains and qualified dividends against 37% on ordinary income, and deferral until sale plus the reset of an asset's tax basis at death widen the gap. The White House Council of Economic Advisers and Office of Management and Budget estimated in 2021 that the 400 wealthiest families paid about 8.2% in federal individual income tax from 2010 to 2018 when unrealized gains count as income; the result depends on that definition. Auten and Splinter (2024) find much smaller top-income shares than other leading estimates, so the size of the gap among the highest earners is contested.
I113.remedy_note: Plausible. Proposals to tax gains as they accrue or to set a minimum tax on the wealthiest have Treasury and Joint Committee on Taxation cost estimates and no enacted U.S. test. In Denmark, Jakobsen and colleagues (2020) found that wealth taxes reduced measured wealth accumulation at the top through avoidance and behavior, and a review by Scheuer and Slemrod (2021) sets out problems of valuation, liquidity and avoidance.
I113.response: Congress and the Treasury would tax comparable returns to work and capital more alike, close avoidable loopholes and publish estimates of who pays.
I113.tradeoff: Changes in when people sell assets, effects on investment and legal limits all affect how much revenue is raised.
I113.success_measure: Effective tax rates by income group under stated definitions of income, and net revenue.

aimed_reforms.why: Taxes capital income more like wages and taxes gains at death, narrowing the gap this record describes.

I114.title: Large inheritances carry advantages across generations
I114.summary: Inheritances and gifts make up a substantial share of top wealth, and only about 0.1% to 0.2% of estates pay federal estate tax. From 2026 the exemption is $15 million per person.
I114.mechanism: Large wealth transfers compound advantages across generations.
I114.evidence_note: Well supported. A 2018 Federal Reserve analysis of the Survey of Consumer Finances estimated that inheritances and gifts account for a substantial share of top wealth and reinforce concentration; it is a simulation from survey data. The Tax Policy Center estimates that only about 0.1% to 0.2% of estates pay estate tax under current exemptions. Public Law 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025, set the exemption at $15 million per person from 2026.
I114.remedy_note: Plausible. Avoidance of the estate tax and understated valuations are documented. Ending the reset of basis at death, with options to defer payment, has cost estimates and no U.S. evaluation.
I114.response: Congress and the IRS would reform estate and gift taxation and the trusts used to avoid it, and end the reset of an asset's tax basis at death, with deferral for family businesses that cannot easily be sold.
I114.tradeoff: Valuing assets, and paying the tax without forced sales, are hard problems that need safeguards.
I114.success_measure: Taxable transfers, measured avoidance, and wealth concentration.

aimed_reforms.why: Taxes inherited gains, which slows the compounding of large fortunes across generations.

I115.title: Complex finances and thin audits let top earners underreport
I115.summary: The IRS projects a gross tax gap of $696 billion for 2022, about 15% of what was owed. Audit rates for people with incomes over $5 million fell from 16% to about 2% between 2010 and 2019.
I115.mechanism: Filers with complex finances hide income while compliant taxpayers carry the burden.
I115.evidence_note: Documented. The IRS projects a gross tax gap of $696 billion for tax year 2022, about 15% of true liability, in a model-based estimate. The Government Accountability Office found that audit rates for taxpayers with incomes over $5 million fell from 16% to about 2% between 2010 and 2019. Drawing on random audits and offshore data, Guyton and colleagues (2021) estimate that the top 1% underreport about a fifth of their income; the methods are contested.
I115.remedy_note: Well supported. Boning, Hendren, Sprung-Keyser and Stuart estimate that IRS audits of taxpayers in the top tenth of incomes return about $12 for every $1 spent once later deterrence is counted. Enforcement funding from the Inflation Reduction Act was partly rescinded from 2023 to 2025, which limits the test.
I115.response: Congress and the IRS would fund skilled audits of high-end returns, information reporting and taxpayer service, with independent oversight of taxpayer rights.
I115.tradeoff: Audit yields vary, and intrusive enforcement can harm filers who did nothing wrong.
I115.success_measure: Net collections, audit errors, and time to get service.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds skilled audits of high-income returns, the response this record proposes.

I116.title: Multinational firms book profits in low-tax countries
I116.summary: By one estimate, about 36% of multinational profits worldwide are shifted to tax havens. A January 2026 international arrangement exempts U.S.-based groups from the global minimum tax, which limits coordination.
I116.mechanism: Multinational companies shift taxable profit to low-tax jurisdictions without matching real activity there.
I116.evidence_note: Well supported. Torslov, Wier and Zucman (2023) estimate from macro accounts that about 36% of multinational profits are shifted to tax havens globally. Clausing (2020) found from tax returns that U.S. profit shifting persisted after the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
I116.remedy_note: Plausible. Minimum taxes, including the U.S. tax on global intangible low-taxed income and the OECD's Pillar Two, are in force abroad and partly at home, and early evidence on how shifting responds is not conclusive. The January 2026 side-by-side arrangement exempts U.S.-parented groups from Pillar Two, which limits coordination.
I116.response: Congress, the Treasury and treaty partners would coordinate minimum taxation and reporting, strengthen enforcement of transfer pricing (the prices firms charge their own subsidiaries) and evaluate anti-avoidance rules.
I116.tradeoff: Measures one country takes alone can invite arbitrage and retaliation.
I116.success_measure: Profits shifted, effective tax rates, and investment.

I117.title: Tax breaks give the largest benefits to higher-income households
I117.summary: The top fifth of households received about half the benefit of major tax breaks in 2019. Deductions are worth more to people in higher tax brackets, and some subsidies barely change behavior.
I117.mechanism: Deductions and exclusions deliver larger benefits to higher-income taxpayers.
I117.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Budget Office found that the top fifth of households received about half the benefits of major tax expenditures in 2019. Using Danish administrative data, Chetty and colleagues (2014) found that tax subsidies for retirement saving barely raised total saving, while automatic enrollment did.
I117.remedy_note: Plausible. Converting deductions to credits has revenue estimates and no U.S. evaluation. The Saver's Match, created by the SECURE 2.0 Act and starting in 2027, will be the first federal test of a refundable saving credit.
I117.response: Congress would convert selected deductions into capped refundable credits and evaluate housing and retirement subsidies by who receives them.
I117.tradeoff: Removing subsidies can disrupt prices, such as home values, and plans people made around them.
I117.success_measure: Benefits by income group, and cost per dollar of added saving.

I118.title: Children from families without wealth start far behind
I118.summary: Families with little wealth have less to fall back on in a crisis or to invest in a child's future. In 2022, median family wealth differed widely by race and by whether a family owned its home.
I118.mechanism: Children in families without assets lack financial buffers and investment options, so they start adult life far behind.
I118.evidence_note: Documented. The Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances shows median family wealth differing substantially by race and by whether families own or rent their homes, with separate figures for medians and means and for income and net worth.
I118.remedy_note: Plausible. A simulation using national panel data estimated that universal baby bonds would shrink the median wealth gap between young white and Black adults from about 16 to 1 to about 1.4 to 1, assuming no change in behavior. The only randomized trial, SEED for Oklahoma Kids, found that child accounts modestly improved early social-emotional scores, and long-run outcomes are unknown. The federal account enacted in July 2025 gives the same $1,000 to every eligible child born from 2025 to 2028, without extra support for children from families with less wealth.
I118.response: Congress and the states would create publicly funded child trust accounts weighted toward children from families with little wealth, with low-cost investment and protected rules for access.
I118.tradeoff: Benefits arrive only when children reach adulthood, and measuring family assets and limiting uses both need evaluation.
I118.success_measure: Account values at 18 by family wealth, wealth gaps, and use for education or starting a business.

status.text: Federal Trump accounts, enacted July 4, 2025 in Public Law 119-21, receive a one-time $1,000 Treasury deposit for each U.S. citizen child born from January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2028; accounts could first receive money on July 4, 2026. Connecticut operates a state-funded baby bonds program with more than 33,000 eligible children as of July 2025.

I119.title: Most workers own little of the stock market's gains
I119.summary: The top 10% of households hold roughly 87% to 93% of corporate stock and mutual fund shares. When asset prices rise, most of the gain goes to people who already own them.
I119.mechanism: Gains from rising asset values go to existing equity owners because most workers hold little diversified ownership.
I119.evidence_note: Documented. The Federal Reserve's Distributional Financial Accounts show the top 10% of households holding roughly 87% to 93% of corporate equities and mutual fund shares. The 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances shows wide differences in family wealth by race and homeownership.
I119.remedy_note: Plausible. Broad-based employee ownership plans are associated with job retention and stability, mostly in observational studies. Concentrating a worker's savings in the employer's own stock adds risk.
I119.response: Congress, the states and firms would expand broad-based profit sharing, cooperative finance and diversified retirement saving with fiduciary protection.
I119.tradeoff: Holding the employer's stock can concentrate a worker's risk in one firm.
I119.success_measure: Diversified assets held by workers, plan coverage, and fees.

I120.title: Temporary or partial cash support leaves families exposed
I120.summary: The expanded 2021 child tax credit cut child poverty to a record low and expired after one year. Child poverty under the supplemental measure rose from 5.2% in 2021 to 13.4% in 2024.
I120.mechanism: Income shocks and child poverty harm children's development and later participation, and cash support is incomplete or temporary.
I120.evidence_note: Well supported. The National Academies' 2019 report A Roadmap to Reducing Child Poverty concluded that income support improves child outcomes. The Census Bureau's 2024 poverty report puts child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts taxes and benefits, at 13.4% in 2024, compared with 5.2% in 2021 when the expanded credit was in effect.
I120.remedy_note: Well supported. The 2021 expansion of the child tax credit cut child poverty. Monthly survey data for April to December 2021 showed small, statistically insignificant effects on employment among adults in households with children. Longer-run effects on work are modeled and have not been observed. The expansion expired, and the 2025 law set the credit at $2,200 with partial refundability.
I120.response: Congress and the states would establish a fully refundable child benefit and strengthen earned-income support, with automatic delivery and stable funding.
I120.tradeoff: Phasing benefits out as income rises can create high effective tax rates on extra earnings.
I120.success_measure: Poverty under the supplemental measure, take-up, and changes in work.

aimed_reforms.why: A fully refundable child credit pays families with little or no earnings and cuts child poverty directly.

status.text: The 2021 expansion, which made the child tax credit fully refundable for that year only, has expired. The July 2025 tax law (Public Law 119-21) set the credit at up to $2,200 per child, with at most $1,700 refundable and an earnings floor of $2,500 for the refundable part.

I121.title: A raise can cost a family more in lost benefits
I121.summary: When benefits end abruptly at an income line, a household can end up worse off after earning more. Some low-income workers face effective tax rates above 50% on added earnings once lost benefits are counted.
I121.mechanism: Abrupt benefit phase-outs make additional earnings financially unattractive.
I121.evidence_note: Documented. Congressional Budget Office simulations show effective marginal tax rates, counting lost benefits, above 50% for some low-income workers. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta's benefit-cliff tools document cliffs household by household.
I121.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Studies find that people respond to cliffs less than the rates alone would predict. No evaluation of coordinated phase-outs across programs exists.
I121.response: Congress and the states would coordinate phase-outs across programs and publish effective marginal rates for typical households.
I121.tradeoff: Smoother phase-outs either cost more or change benefit levels.
I121.success_measure: Size of cliffs, and net income gained from added earnings.

I122.title: Delay on Social Security financing pushes costs onto later retirees
I122.summary: The 2026 Trustees project that the retirement trust fund runs out in late 2032, after which incoming taxes would cover 78% of scheduled benefits. Each year Congress waits narrows the options and shifts more of the adjustment onto later cohorts.
I122.mechanism: Delayed action on Social Security financing concentrates adjustment costs on later cohorts.
I122.evidence_note: Documented. The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report projects that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund reserves run out in late 2032, after which 78% of benefits would be payable, with a 75-year deficit of 4.42% of taxable payroll. The Congressional Budget Office publishes options and projections for closing the gap.
I122.remedy_note: Documented. The Social Security actuaries can score any package of revenue and benefit changes, and distributional evidence exists for each option. The choice among them is political.
I122.response: Congress would adopt a gradual package combining revenue and progressive benefit changes, protecting low earners and people with disabilities.
I122.tradeoff: Every package spreads costs across generations and income groups.
I122.success_measure: Long-run actuarial balance, and poverty among older people.

I123.title: High-cost loans drain households with little cushion
I123.summary: In 2025, 37% of U.S. adults could not cover a $400 expense with cash or its equivalent. Four in five payday loans are rolled over or renewed within 14 days, so a short loan can become a long, expensive one.
I123.mechanism: High-cost credit and collection practices drain fragile household finances.
I123.evidence_note: Well supported. The Federal Reserve's survey of household economics found that 37% of adults could not cover a $400 expense with cash or its equivalent in 2025. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau reported in 2014 that four in five payday loans are rolled over or renewed within 14 days. Melzer (2011) found that access to payday loans increased difficulty paying bills and delayed medical care, a quasi-experimental result that later studies contest.
I123.remedy_note: Plausible. The CFPB's 2017 ability-to-repay rule was rescinded in 2020. State caps at 36% annual interest reduce high-cost lending, with contested effects on access to credit. Small-dollar loan programs at banks are unevaluated.
I123.response: Congress, consumer regulators and the states would enforce ability-to-repay and fair collection rules, expand low-cost small loans through banks and keep bankruptcy accessible on fair terms.
I123.tradeoff: Credit restrictions can reduce access, so the alternatives people turn to need tracking.
I123.success_measure: Strain from debt payments, defaults, and availability of affordable credit.

I124.title: Borrowed money and flighty funding turn bank losses into public crises
I124.summary: When banks and other lenders rely on heavy borrowing and deposits that can leave overnight, a loss can set off a run. The 2008 crisis and the 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank left the public bearing rescue costs and job losses.
I124.mechanism: Heavy borrowing and funding that can be withdrawn quickly in private finance produce public rescue costs and unemployment.
I124.evidence_note: Documented. The Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission concluded in 2011 that the 2008 crisis was avoidable and was driven by heavy borrowing and regulatory failures; minority members dissented. The Federal Reserve's 2023 review of Silicon Valley Bank found failures of supervision and management, and the 2023 runs were driven by uninsured deposits.
I124.remedy_note: Well supported. Across 14 countries and 140 years, Jordà, Schularick and Taylor (2013) found that credit booms predict deeper recessions, evidence cited in support of capital and liquidity safeguards. The U.S. capital proposal known as the Basel III endgame was withdrawn and reproposed, so the current package is unsettled.
I124.response: Congress and financial regulators would maintain capital and liquidity safeguards, stress tests, resolution plans and oversight of risk outside the banking system.
I124.tradeoff: Rules can push risk into less regulated institutions.
I124.success_measure: Resilience in stress tests, and the amount of uninsured funding that could run.

I125.title: Recessions hit young, low-wage and minority workers hardest
I125.summary: Job losses in downturns fall disproportionately on young, less-educated, Black and Hispanic workers. A layoff during a recession can cut earnings for 15 to 20 years.
I125.mechanism: Recessions hit low-wage, young and minority workers hardest, weakening their bargaining power and delaying their progress.
I125.evidence_note: Well supported. Using Current Population Survey data, Hoynes, Miller and Schaller (2012) found that recession job losses fall disproportionately on men, Black and Hispanic workers, young workers and less-educated workers. Davis and von Wachter (2011) found that displaced workers lose about 20% of earnings for 15 to 20 years, more in recessions.
I125.remedy_note: Plausible. Proposals for automatic stabilizers include direct payments triggered by a rise in unemployment (the Sahm rule, a recession signal) and revised unemployment insurance triggers, and some have been simulated. Congress passed direct payments and wider unemployment benefits in 2020 as one-time laws. No automatic trigger of this kind has been enacted and tested in the United States.
I125.response: Congress would build automatic fiscal stabilizers into law, and the Federal Reserve would continue evidence-led monetary policy with accountable independence.
I125.tradeoff: Stimulus during supply shortages can worsen inflation.
I125.success_measure: Employment gaps, inflation, and time to recovery.

aimed_reforms.why: Benefits that expand automatically when unemployment rises reach the workers hit first.

I126.title: Rising interest costs shrink room for future public spending
I126.summary: The Congressional Budget Office projects federal debt rising from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036, with net interest at 3.3% of GDP. Rising interest and fixed commitments leave less room for services and investment.
I126.mechanism: Rising interest costs and rigid commitments reduce the government's future capacity.
I126.evidence_note: Documented. The Congressional Budget Office's February 2026 outlook projects debt held by the public at 101% of GDP in 2026 rising to 120% in 2036, with net interest at 3.3% of GDP. The Government Accountability Office's 2025 High Risk List ties government effectiveness to capacity and demonstrated progress.
I126.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Fiscal rules have a mixed record internationally, and program review has no U.S. causal evidence. The CBO baseline documents the need and tests no remedy.
I126.response: Congress and the Treasury would publish long-term budgets, raise adequate progressive revenue and review programs periodically while protecting productive investment.
I126.tradeoff: Spending cuts during a downturn can worsen both debt and hardship.
I126.success_measure: Debt service as a share of the budget, fiscal room, and service outcomes.

I127.title: National growth figures hide who gains
I127.summary: GDP can rise while many households see little income growth or struggle with the cost of essentials. The Bureau of Economic Analysis now publishes prototype statistics on how income is distributed.
I127.mechanism: Aggregate measures such as GDP hide unequal gains and the burden of essential costs. The further claim, that this weakens accountability, has no supporting evidence.
I127.evidence_note: Well supported for the measurement point. Piketty, Saez and Zucman (2018) built distributional national accounts showing stagnant income for the bottom half since 1980, a result other researchers, including Auten and Splinter, contest. The Bureau of Economic Analysis now publishes prototype statistics on the distribution of personal income.
I127.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Publication is already feasible, as the BEA prototypes show. No evidence shows that better measures change how officials are held to account.
I127.response: The Bureau of Economic Analysis and the Census Bureau, with support from Congress, would track distributional national accounts, median disposable resources, productivity and essential costs alongside GDP.
I127.tradeoff: Different definitions of income answer different questions.
I127.success_measure: Median household resources, distribution of income, and productivity.

I128.title: Broad access to asset ownership (retired record)
I128.summary: This record is retired, because its subject is covered by loop R1, in which wealth and political influence reinforce each other. It had no source of its own and adds no separate finding.
I128.mechanism: Retired. The claim that households without diversified assets cannot share in capital gains or absorb risk, and so hold fewer political resources, is covered by loop R1: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other.
I128.evidence_note: Retired. The record had no source of its own.
I128.remedy_note: Retired. No remedy evidence is recorded.
I128.response: Retired. The proposed mix of child trust accounts, automatic diversified saving, employee profit sharing and fair access to business finance is covered by the reforms linked to the wealth-and-influence loop (R1) and is not counted again here.
I128.tradeoff: Retired. No single lever establishes the size of the full feedback effect.
I128.success_measure: Retired. Wealth shares, donor concentration and policy responsiveness are tracked under the wealth-and-influence loop (R1).

status.text: Retired record, merged into loop R1: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other. Kept for reference only.

I129.title: Zoning limits on new homes push up rents near good jobs
I129.summary: Rules that restrict apartments and smaller homes near jobs keep housing scarce and rents high. The shortage also keeps workers from moving to places with better-paying work.
I129.mechanism: Restrictive land-use rules create housing scarcity near productive jobs, which raises rents and keeps people from moving to opportunity.
I129.evidence_note: Well supported. Glaeser and Gyourko (2018) linked land-use regulation to the gap between home prices and construction costs in coastal metro areas. Ganong and Shoag (2017) found, using a causal design, that rising housing costs ended the long convergence of incomes across U.S. regions for workers without college degrees.
I129.remedy_note: Well supported. Upzoning in Auckland, New Zealand roughly doubled building permits in upzoned areas (Greenaway-McGrevy and Phillips, 2023), and three-bedroom rents there were 22% to 35% below a comparison estimate six years later. Rents grew more slowly in Minneapolis after its zoning reform, according to the Pew Charitable Trusts. State housing-supply laws in California, Oregon, Washington, Montana and Massachusetts are too new for full evaluation.
I129.response: States and cities would allow apartment buildings and accessory dwellings by right near jobs and transit, without a separate discretionary approval for each project, alongside investment in infrastructure and protection against displacement.
I129.tradeoff: New supply takes years to arrive, and infrastructure and displacement need attention.
I129.success_measure: Permits, completed homes, rent burden, and moves to higher-opportunity areas.

aimed_reforms.why: Allows homes by right where demand is high, which is this record's response.
On-cycle local elections bring renters and younger voters into the electorate that sets zoning.

status.text: State laws now allow more homes by right in places zoned for single-family houses: California's SB 9 (2021) allows two homes per lot and lot splits with ministerial approval; Oregon's HB 2001 (2019) requires larger cities to allow duplexes and other middle housing; Washington's HB 1110 (2023) requires middle housing in areas zoned for detached houses; Montana passed similar laws in 2023; and Massachusetts's MBTA Communities Act requires multifamily zoning near transit, with 157 communities found compliant as of August 27, 2026.

I130.title: New market-rate homes alone do not reach the lowest-income renters
I130.summary: In 2021, 8.53 million very-low-income renter households, those at or below half the local median income, had worst-case housing needs, and the poorest renters face a shortage of about 7.1 million affordable homes. Rental assistance and permanently affordable housing serve a need that market-rate building leaves unmet.
I130.mechanism: Market housing supply alone does not reach very-low-income renters.
I130.evidence_note: Documented. The Department of Housing and Urban Development reported that 8.53 million very-low-income renter households had worst-case housing needs in 2021. Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies found record rates of rent burden in 2024 data. The National Low Income Housing Coalition, an advocacy group, estimates a shortage of 7.1 million affordable and available rental homes for extremely low-income renters.
I130.remedy_note: Well supported. In a randomized trial with 2,282 homeless families, priority access to a long-term housing voucher cut later episodes of homelessness by more than half over three years; a drop in child separations seen at 20 months was no longer detected at 37 months. Making vouchers more generous across a metro area raised the rents landlords received with little gain in housing or neighborhood quality, which supports pairing vouchers with new supply.
I130.response: Congress, the states and housing authorities would expand rental assistance and social or nonprofit housing, with long-term maintenance and homes spread across different neighborhoods.
I130.tradeoff: Subsidies in tight markets can raise rents, so they need to be paired with new supply.
I130.success_measure: Severe rent burden, homelessness, and housing quality.

I131.title: Homebuying subsidies can end up in higher prices
I131.summary: When housing supply is tight, tax breaks and credits for buyers tend to raise home prices. Existing owners gain, and first-time buyers still struggle to get in.
I131.mechanism: Homeownership subsidies are absorbed into home prices, rewarding existing owners over first-time buyers.
I131.evidence_note: Well supported. Sommer and Sullivan (2018), using a model fitted to data, found that eliminating the mortgage interest deduction would lower house prices and raise homeownership. Berger, Turner and Zwick (2020) found that the 2009 first-time buyer credit mostly shifted when people bought. The Congressional Budget Office found that the top fifth of households received about half the benefits of major tax expenditures in 2019.
I131.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Shared-equity and first-generation buyer programs have only descriptive evaluations. The risk that subsidies raise prices is the better-evidenced part.
I131.response: Congress and the states would target help to first-generation buyers only alongside more housing supply and fair lending, and expand shared-equity housing.
I131.tradeoff: Subsidies for buyers can be absorbed into prices.
I131.success_measure: New owners, effects on prices, and equity that lasts.

I132.title: Eviction disrupts work, schooling and health
I132.summary: U.S. courts saw about 3.6 million eviction filings a year from 2000 to 2018. Eviction causes more homelessness and hospital use and lowers earnings.
I132.mechanism: Forced moves disrupt schooling, work and health.
I132.evidence_note: Well supported. The Eviction Lab (Gromis and colleagues, 2022) estimated about 3.6 million eviction filings a year from 2000 to 2018. Using the random assignment of cases to judges in Chicago and New York, Collinson and colleagues (2024) found that eviction causes higher homelessness and hospital use and lower earnings.
I132.remedy_note: Well supported. Using the rollout of New York City's universal access program and housing court records from 2016 to 2019, Cassidy and Currie found that tenants who gained lawyers were less likely to receive possession judgments or to be evicted. Emergency rental assistance in 2021 and 2022 lacks a rigorous evaluation.
I132.response: States, cities and courts would fund eviction prevention, legal counsel and emergency assistance, with fair procedures and a way to settle what landlords are owed.
I132.tradeoff: Persistent unpaid rent needs lasting affordability solutions.
I132.success_measure: Evictions, repeat displacement, and unpaid rent.

I133.title: Coverage gaps and renewal paperwork interrupt health care
I133.summary: In 2024, 8.0% of people in the United States had no health insurance, and more than 25 million people lost Medicaid when pandemic rules ended, most for procedural reasons. People who qualify for coverage can still lose it or put off care.
I133.mechanism: People lose coverage or delay care despite being eligible, because of gaps in coverage and paperwork at enrollment and renewal.
I133.evidence_note: Documented. The Census Bureau reported that 8.0% of people were uninsured in 2024. KFF's tracker found that more than 25 million people were disenrolled from Medicaid as pandemic continuous coverage ended, 69% for procedural reasons. KFF has also tracked marketplace enrollment after enhanced premium credits expired in 2026.
I133.remedy_note: Plausible. In a randomized trial with about 87,000 California marketplace households, mailed reminders of the enrollment deadline raised enrollment by 1.3 percentage points, or 16%. Continuous eligibility for children reduces churn in coverage. A public insurance option has no completed U.S. evaluation.
I133.response: Congress and the states would simplify enrollment and renewal, expand affordable coverage and compare a public option with other routes to universal coverage.
I133.tradeoff: Financing and provider payment affect access, and no single insurance model removes shortages of care.
I133.success_measure: Uninsured rate, delayed care, and continuity of coverage.

I134.title: High prices and confusing bills leave families with medical debt
I134.summary: The United States spends more on health care than other rich countries mainly because its prices are higher. In 2022, 41% of adults carried debt from health care.
I134.mechanism: Complex pricing and providers' bargaining power create avoidable financial exposure for households.
I134.evidence_note: Well supported. Anderson and colleagues (2019) found that the U.S. spending gap with other countries is driven by prices more than by how much care people use. A 2022 KFF survey found that 41% of adults carry health-care debt. Mergers of nearby hospitals raised prices by more than 6%, according to Cooper and colleagues (2019).
I134.remedy_note: Well supported. The Congressional Budget Office scored Medicare drug price negotiation, and the first negotiated prices took effect in 2026. Site-neutral payment has cost estimates from the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission and CBO. Protection from surprise bills took effect in 2022, with early evidence of lower out-of-network bills.
I134.response: Congress, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and the states would expand price negotiation by public purchasers, adopt site-neutral payment where appropriate, protect patients from surprise bills and require clear total prices.
I134.tradeoff: Payment cuts can threaten providers in underserved areas unless targeted support comes with them.
I134.success_measure: Out-of-pocket burden, access to care, and health outcomes.

I135.title: Child care costs too much for parents and pays too little to staff it
I135.summary: High child-care fees keep some parents out of paid work, while low pay for care workers limits how many places exist. The market falls short for families and providers at the same time.
I135.mechanism: High child-care costs reduce parents' employment, while low pay limits how many providers can operate.
I135.evidence_note: Well supported. The Treasury Department's 2021 report found median pay for child-care workers near the bottom of the wage distribution and a market that fails both families and providers. Morrissey's 2017 review found that a 10% drop in child-care costs raises mothers' employment by 0.25% to 11%, a wide range. Quebec's universal child-care program raised mothers' employment and had some negative effects on child behavior, a contested tradeoff on quality (Baker, Gruber and Milligan, 2008).
I135.remedy_note: Plausible. Funding the supply of child care has evidence from Quebec and from the District of Columbia's pay equity fund for early educators. Subsidies paid to parents without added supply raise prices.
I135.response: Congress and the states would finance affordable child care through stable operating support, better pay for the workforce and quality standards.
I135.tradeoff: Subsidies paid to parents quickly, without more workers, raise prices.
I135.success_measure: Child-care places, costs to families, staff retention, and quality.

aimed_reforms.why: Funds child-care supply with decent workforce pay, which lowers prices and keeps centers open.

I136.title: Long-term care drains family earnings and savings
I136.summary: Unpaid family caregiving was valued at $600 billion in 2021, and more than 710,000 people were on waiting lists for Medicaid home care in 2024. Caregiving reduces women's employment and wages.
I136.mechanism: Unpaid care and fragmented coverage deplete families' earnings and assets.
I136.evidence_note: Well supported. AARP's Public Policy Institute, part of an advocacy organization, valued unpaid family caregiving at $600 billion in 2021. KFF counted more than 710,000 people on waiting lists for Medicaid home and community-based services in 2024, an incomplete measure of unmet need. Using panel data, Van Houtven, Coe and Skira (2013) found that caregiving reduces women's employment and wages.
I136.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Expanding home and community-based services reduces use of institutions in observational studies. Washington's public long-term care insurance begins paying benefits in 2026 and has no evaluation yet.
I136.response: Congress and the states would expand home and community services, support family caregivers and put long-term care financing on a sustainable footing.
I136.tradeoff: Limits on the care workforce and on budgets require phasing in.
I136.success_measure: Unmet care needs, caregivers' earnings, and moves into institutions.

aimed_reforms.why: Paid leave insurance lets family caregivers take time without losing their jobs.

I137.title: School resources follow neighborhood wealth
I137.summary: Where school funding depends on local property wealth and neighborhoods are separated by income and race, children get unequal preparation. More spending per pupil raises completed schooling and adult earnings.
I137.mechanism: Unequal school funding and segregation reproduce unequal preparation for children.
I137.evidence_note: Well supported. Jackson, Johnson and Persico (2016) found that 10% more spending per pupil over 12 years raised completed education and adult earnings, using court-ordered finance reforms. A 2024 meta-analysis of U.S. evaluations found that spending increases improve outcomes on average.
I137.remedy_note: Well supported. School finance reforms that sent more money to low-income districts raised achievement there (Lafortune, Rothstein and Schanzenbach, 2018), and court-ordered increases raised adult earnings. Tools for integrating schools rest on older desegregation evidence with fewer recent tests.
I137.response: States, school districts and Congress would use weighted state funding formulas, equitable facilities, effective early learning and integration tools with local participation.
I137.tradeoff: Money has to turn into better teaching and supportive conditions to make a difference.
I137.success_measure: Resource gaps between districts, learning, and completion.

I138.title: Students borrow without finishing a credential that pays
I138.summary: Six-year completion rates at four-year colleges sit around 60% to 65%, and loan defaults concentrate among students who did not finish or attended for-profit schools. Support to finish, and accountability for schools, address the risk before repayment begins.
I138.mechanism: Students take on debt without earning credentials that raise their earnings.
I138.evidence_note: Well supported. Using administrative data, Looney and Yannelis (2015) found that student-loan defaults concentrate among borrowers who did not complete and those who attended for-profit schools. The National Center for Education Statistics reports six-year completion around 60% to 65% at four-year institutions. A 2019 study found that for-profit certificate students earned no more, and often less, after enrolling.
I138.remedy_note: Well supported. In a randomized trial, CUNY's ASAP program raised three-year graduation rates by 18 percentage points and six-year rates by 10 points. An early guarantee of free tuition at a flagship university, tested by random assignment, raised enrollment among high-achieving low-income students from 12% to 27%. Federal accountability rules for colleges were adopted and then revised, with no stable evaluation.
I138.response: Congress, the states and colleges would increase need-based aid, completion support and accountability for institutions, simplify repayment and evaluate targeted relief.
I138.tradeoff: Debt relief alone leaves future pricing and low-value programs unchanged.
I138.success_measure: Completion, debt burden, earnings, and repayment.

I139.title: The neighborhood where a child grows up shapes later earnings
I139.summary: Children whose families moved to lower-poverty neighborhoods before age 13 earned about 31% more as adults. Help finding homes in high-opportunity areas, and investment in existing neighborhoods, offer two routes to better outcomes.
I139.mechanism: Neighborhood conditions in childhood shape later earnings and access to opportunity.
I139.evidence_note: Well supported. In the Moving to Opportunity randomized trial, Chetty, Hendren and Katz (2016) found that children who moved to lower-poverty areas before age 13 earned about 31% more as adults. Chetty and colleagues (2020) document large gaps in mobility by race and place using tax data.
I139.remedy_note: Well supported. In a randomized trial in Seattle, mobility counseling raised the share of voucher families moving to high-opportunity areas from 15% to 53%.
I139.response: The Department of Housing and Urban Development, the states and cities would combine affordable housing in high-opportunity areas with mobility counseling and investment in existing communities.
I139.tradeoff: Moving can break community ties, and families need a real choice.
I139.success_measure: Children's time in high-opportunity areas, later outcomes, and residents who stay.

aimed_reforms.why: Allowing more homes by right in high-demand areas opens high-opportunity neighborhoods to more families.

I140.title: Past exclusion and present barriers sustain racial wealth gaps
I140.summary: White households hold about six times the wealth of Black households, and the gap stopped narrowing around 1980. Redlining maps drawn in the 1930s still show up in lower homeownership and home values decades later.
I140.mechanism: Historic exclusion and current barriers compound unequal assets across racial groups.
I140.evidence_note: Well supported. Derenoncourt and colleagues (2024), using data back to 1860, found the white-to-Black wealth ratio at about 6 to 1, with convergence stalled since 1980. Comparing areas on either side of map boundaries, Aaronson, Hartley and Mazumder (2021) found that the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's 1930s redlining maps reduced homeownership and home values for decades. The Federal Reserve's 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances shows median family wealth differing widely by race.
I140.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Fair-lending enforcement has case evidence. Asset-building programs have simulations and one randomized trial, Oklahoma's SEED child accounts, with modest early effects. Targeted repair programs are small and unevaluated.
I140.response: Congress, the states and the courts would enforce fair lending, widen access to asset building and evaluate targeted repair for documented public harms.
I140.tradeoff: Legal design and accurate attribution of harm matter.
I140.success_measure: Wealth gaps, access to credit, and whether remedies work.

I141.title: Rural and former industrial regions lose jobs and people
I141.summary: Regions hit by import competition from China had not recovered their lost employment by 2019. Weak services and people moving away can make the decline harder to reverse.
I141.mechanism: Trade and technology shocks, weak services and outmigration reinforce local decline.
I141.evidence_note: Well supported. Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2021) found that regions exposed to the China trade shock had not recovered employment by 2019. Austin, Glaeser and Summers (2018) argue for targeted place-based policy in an analytical paper.
I141.remedy_note: Plausible. The Tennessee Valley Authority raised long-run regional incomes, while many enterprise zones did not, according to Bartik's 2020 review of place-based policy. Design matters, and whether subsidized jobs would have appeared anyway is hard to verify.
I141.response: Congress, the states and regional bodies would invest in broadband, transport and health access, and use place-based grants that show they add jobs, with support for workers changing jobs.
I141.tradeoff: Subsidies can chase firms without helping residents.
I141.success_measure: Residents' earnings, access to services, and jobs that would not otherwise exist.

I142.title: Poor transport and utility connections raise the cost of living
I142.summary: U.S. infrastructure earns a C grade from civil engineers, and drinking-water systems need $625 billion over 20 years. Unreliable connections make it harder to reach work or care and raise household costs.
I142.mechanism: Poor transport and utility connections restrict access to jobs, school and care and raise household costs.
I142.evidence_note: Well supported. In the Moving to Opportunity study, access to a car predicted employment gains (Blumenberg and Pierce, 2014). The Environmental Protection Agency's 2023 survey estimates $625 billion in drinking-water infrastructure needs over 20 years. The American Society of Civil Engineers gave U.S. infrastructure an overall C in 2025, a needs assessment by a professional association.
I142.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Evaluations find modest employment effects from transit investment. Plans that put maintenance first have engineering support and few outcome studies.
I142.response: Congress, the states and local utilities would put maintenance first and fund reliable transit, safe streets, water and affordable energy through accountable capital plans.
I142.tradeoff: Projects need funding for their whole life and credible cost estimates.
I142.success_measure: Travel time to jobs and services, reliability, and household costs.

I143.title: Pollution and disaster losses fall hardest on low-income communities
I143.summary: Fine-particle pollution falls disproportionately on people of color, and climate damage hits poorer counties hardest. In the riskiest ZIP codes, home insurance premiums ran 82% higher and nonrenewals about 80% higher from 2018 to 2022.
I143.mechanism: Low-income communities face more pollution, larger disaster losses and insurers pulling back from coverage.
I143.evidence_note: Documented. A Treasury Department report of January 2025 found that from 2018 to 2022 homeowners insurance premiums were 82% higher, and nonrenewal rates about 80% higher, in the riskiest ZIP codes. Using modeled exposure, Tessum and colleagues (2021) found that fine-particle pollution falls disproportionately on people of color across income levels. Hsiang and colleagues (2017) project that climate damages fall hardest on poorer counties in the South.
I143.remedy_note: Well supported. The benefits of the Clean Air Act exceed its costs by about 30 to 1, and the law narrowed racial gaps in exposure. Managed relocation away from high-risk areas has no U.S. evaluation.
I143.response: Congress, the Environmental Protection Agency, the states and cities would reduce emissions and local pollution, fund resilience and fair relocation, and reform how risk is priced, with targeted help on affordability.
I143.tradeoff: Pricing risk without alternatives can hit low-income households hardest, and relocation must guard against forced displacement.
I143.success_measure: Pollution exposure, losses avoided, and access to insurance.

aimed_reforms.why: Building codes and mitigation cut disaster losses, which keeps insurance available and protects owners' equity.

I144.title: National averages hide barriers to getting ahead
I144.summary: About 90% of children born in 1940 grew up to earn more than their parents, compared with about 50% of those born in the 1980s. Results differ sharply by race and place, so a single national figure hides where pathways are blocked.
I144.mechanism: Absolute mobility, relative mobility and mobility by group move differently, so averages hide blocked pathways.
I144.evidence_note: Well supported. Chetty and colleagues (2017) found that absolute mobility, the chance of earning more than one's parents at age 30 after inflation, was about 90% for children born in 1940 and about 50% for those born in the 1980s. Using tax data, Chetty and colleagues (2020) showed large gaps by race and place in relative mobility, the chance of moving up the income ranking.
I144.remedy_note: Documented. The Opportunity Atlas, built with the Census Bureau, already publishes mobility measures for small areas, so the proposal is feasible.
I144.response: The Census Bureau, research institutions and agencies would publish mobility measures by birth cohort, race, gender, disability and place, with privacy protection and consistent definitions.
I144.tradeoff: Estimates for small areas carry uncertainty and arrive years after the fact.
I144.success_measure: Mobility by birth cohort, data quality, and groups missing from the data.

I145.title: Work and care leave some people little time for civic life
I145.summary: People holding several jobs or caring for family can struggle to attend meetings and stay involved. Money and civic skills predict participation more strongly than free time, so time pressure is one barrier among several.
I145.mechanism: Multiple jobs and care duties can reduce civic participation outside elections, though money and civic skills predict participation more strongly than free time does.
I145.evidence_note: Plausible. In their civic voluntarism model, Verba, Schlozman and Brady (1995) found that money and civic skills predict participation more strongly than free time. AmeriCorps and the Census Bureau report that 28.3% of people volunteered through an organization in 2023.
I145.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Paying participants in intensive deliberative panels is standard practice, according to the OECD's 2020 review of close to 300 such processes. There is no causal evidence on how payment changes participation by income.
I145.response: Local governments, employers and civic groups would offer evening and hybrid meetings, child care and interpretation, and pay participants in intensive civic panels.
I145.success_measure: Participation by income, and people who come back to take part again.

I146.title: Public meetings hear mostly from organized insiders
I146.summary: People who speak at local public meetings are older, more often male, more likely to own homes and more opposed to new housing than the voters around them. Officials can come away with a distorted picture of what residents want.
I146.mechanism: Self-selection into public meetings distorts whose preferences officials hear.
I146.evidence_note: Well supported. Matching meeting minutes to voter files, Einstein, Palmer and Glick (2019) found that commenters were older, more often male, more likely to own homes and more opposed to housing than voters overall. Using a regression discontinuity, Yoder (2020) found that owning property causally raises participation in local politics.
I146.remedy_note: Plausible. Assemblies selected by lottery produce bodies that match the population, according to the OECD's 2020 review. Evidence that governments act on their recommendations comes from individual cases.
I146.response: Legislatures and cities would combine open public comment with civic lotteries stratified to match the population, and publish their responses to panel recommendations.
I146.tradeoff: A randomly selected panel cannot replace the accountability of elected officials.
I146.success_measure: How representative participants are, public responses, and policy follow-up.

aimed_reforms.why: Lottery-selected assemblies with a duty to respond bring in residents who would not self-select.
Allowing homes by right moves housing decisions out of the meetings that owners dominate.

I147.title: Civic associations are losing members and support
I147.summary: Membership in local associations and congregations has fallen for decades, and church membership dropped below half of U.S. adults in 2020. Fewer places for recurring shared work mean fewer chances to build local trust.
I147.mechanism: Civic associations struggle to sustain shared work and local trust.
I147.evidence_note: Well supported. Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) documents a long decline in membership associations, though some of its measures are contested. Skocpol (2003) traces a shift from membership federations to professionally managed advocacy groups. Gallup found that church membership fell to 47% of U.S. adults in 2020, the first time below half.
I147.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Neutral grants for libraries and associations have no evaluation of their effect on civic trust.
I147.response: States, cities and philanthropies would support libraries, community spaces and independent associations through neutral grants and affordable access.
I147.tradeoff: Funding has to avoid favoring any party.
I147.success_measure: Active associations, and the diversity of people taking part.

aimed_reforms.why: Builds membership organizations where people of different parties do shared work.

I148.title: Residents cannot see how to influence a decision
I148.summary: When people cannot tell when a decision will be made or who makes it, taking part feels futile and insiders gain. Belief that government responds to people like oneself is at or near record lows.
I148.mechanism: Opaque processes produce a sense of futility and dependence on insiders.
I148.evidence_note: Plausible. The American National Election Studies series shows external political efficacy, the belief that government responds to people like oneself, at or near record lows. Michener (2018) found that experiences with Medicaid administration shape later political participation, and Soss (1999) found that the design of welfare programs teaches recipients lessons about government.
I148.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Publishing decision calendars and explanations has no causal evaluation, and transparency experiments show mixed effects on trust.
I148.response: Governments at every level would publish decision calendars, the officials responsible, the ways to take part and plain-language explanations of final choices.
I148.tradeoff: Information without real influence can deepen cynicism.
I148.success_measure: Understanding of the process, official responses, and participation.

aimed_reforms.why: Requires officials to answer recommendations in public, showing residents what their input changed.
Gives residents a defined budget decision they can see and affect.

I149.title: Hostility toward the other party leads voters to excuse their own side
I149.summary: When partisans dislike or fear the other party, many will still vote for their own candidate after that candidate breaks democratic rules. That weakens the electoral cost of misconduct, though researchers dispute how much.
I149.mechanism: Hostility toward the other party leads partisans to excuse misconduct by their own side.
I149.evidence_note: Well supported. In Graham and Svolik's 2020 experiments, only about 3.5% of voters were willing to defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups, although the average penalty in vote share was 11.7 points. Iyengar and colleagues (2019) review the causes and consequences of affective polarization, the dislike of the other party's supporters. Broockman, Kalla and Westwood (2023) found that affective polarization does not clearly reduce accountability, so the link is contested.
I149.remedy_note: Plausible. A megastudy testing 25 interventions reduced partisan animosity, and several also reduced support for undemocratic practices or partisan violence. Durability was measured over about two weeks, and effects on conduct outside the study are untested.
I149.response: Civic groups, parties and local institutions would organize structured cross-party work on concrete shared problems and apply equal standards to political conduct.
I149.tradeoff: Contact reduces hostility only under certain conditions, and surface civility cannot settle conflicts over rights.
I149.success_measure: Attitudes toward the other party, joint work across parties, and consistent application of conduct standards.

aimed_reforms.why: Cross-partisan membership and service is the structured contact this record proposes.

I150.title: Scapegoating divides people who could work together
I150.summary: Blaming racial or identity groups for hardship can pull attention away from the institutions that cause it. It also denies people equal standing and splits potential coalitions.
I150.mechanism: Scapegoating diverts grievances from institutional causes and denies equal standing.
I150.evidence_note: Plausible. Sides, Tesler and Vavreck's Identity Crisis (2018) found from surveys that identity attitudes predicted vote shifts in 2016 more than economic distress did. In a field experiment, Enos (2014) found that brief exposure to members of an outgroup increased exclusionary attitudes.
I150.remedy_note: Plausible. A review of 27 randomized studies that measured outcomes at least a day after contact between groups found that contact typically reduces prejudice. Effects were weaker for racial and ethnic prejudice, no study addressed adults' racial or ethnic prejudice, and long-term studies are scarce.
I150.response: Schools, civic groups and parties would protect equal participation and create local forums that connect material problems to evidence without blaming whole groups.
I150.tradeoff: Dialogue requires safety and equal status for those taking part.
I150.success_measure: Gaps in participation, and discriminatory incidents.

aimed_reforms.why: Repeated shared work across groups is the kind of contact this record's response relies on.

I151.title: Living apart reduces everyday contact across groups
I151.summary: Americans increasingly live in neighborhoods separated by income and, to a degree, by party. Fewer shared places mean less ordinary contact across groups, though the effect on cooperation has not been measured.
I151.mechanism: Residential and institutional separation narrows shared experience across groups. Its consequences for cooperation are plausible and unmeasured.
I151.evidence_note: Plausible. Brown and Enos (2021) measured partisan residential sorting for 180 million voters. Mummolo and Nall (2017) found that partisans rarely choose neighborhoods by politics, which limits how much of the sorting is deliberate. Income segregation rose along with income inequality, according to Reardon and Bischoff (2011).
I151.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Inclusive public spaces and service across communities have no causal evaluation of their effect on belonging.
I151.response: Cities, schools and civic organizations would expand inclusive public spaces, service projects across communities and access to housing, with evaluation.
I151.tradeoff: Forced contact or displacement can backfire.
I151.success_measure: Sustained contact across groups, and a sense of belonging.

aimed_reforms.why: Cross-community civic service creates the shared experience that separation removes.

I152.title: Loneliness and distrust may make cooperation harder
I152.summary: Americans spend more time alone than they did two decades ago, and loneliness carries well-documented health risks. Whether it weakens communities' ability to solve problems together has not been measured.
I152.mechanism: Weak relationships and low trust make collective problem-solving harder. The health effects of loneliness are well supported; the step to weaker collective problem-solving is asserted without measurement.
I152.evidence_note: Plausible. The U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory synthesizes evidence on loneliness and health. Using the American Time Use Survey, a 2023 study found that time alone rose and social engagement fell from 2003 to 2020. Neither source measures collective problem-solving.
I152.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Investment in community institutions has no evaluation of its effect on cooperation.
I152.response: States, cities and nonprofits would invest in accessible community institutions and repeated shared activities, in partnership with public health agencies.

aimed_reforms.why: Repeated shared work in membership organizations builds the relationships this record finds missing.

I153.title: Parties tolerate conduct that weakens democratic rules
I153.summary: When voters rarely punish their own side, parties pay little price for nominating or protecting members who deny election results or intimidate opponents. Party rules and discipline are one place this can be checked.
I153.mechanism: Electoral incentives reward parties that tolerate election denial, intimidation or abuse by their members.
I153.evidence_note: Well supported. Graham and Svolik (2020) found that only about 3.5% of voters would defect from their party's candidate over an undemocratic position in realistic matchups. Levitsky and Ziblatt's How Democracies Die (2018) argues from comparative history that party gatekeeping is a central safeguard. Bright Line Watch surveys of experts and the public track the erosion of democratic norms through 2026.
I153.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Party conduct standards have comparative examples abroad and no U.S. test.
I153.response: Political parties and civic organizations would adopt enforceable standards for nominations and conduct, with transparent disciplinary procedures.
I153.tradeoff: Gatekeeping needs internal democracy and due process.
I153.success_measure: Compliance with party rules, and consistent sanctions.

I154.title: Threats and violence raise the cost of public life
I154.summary: The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat cases in 2025, the third straight annual rise, and 43% of state legislators surveyed reported threats. When serving in office or speaking up invites danger, fewer people take part.
I154.mechanism: Threats raise the personal cost of public service and of public disagreement.
I154.evidence_note: Documented. The U.S. Capitol Police opened 14,938 threat-assessment cases in 2025, the third straight annual increase. In a 2024 Brennan Center survey, 43% of state legislators reported threats.
I154.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Funding for threat prevention has no outcome evaluation; the case for it rests on official counts and surveys.
I154.response: The Justice Department, the states and local law enforcement would fund lawful threat prevention, protect people who are targeted and prosecute violence under viewpoint-neutral standards.
I154.tradeoff: Broad labels of extremism can chill lawful protest.
I154.success_measure: Threat cases resolved, safety of victims, and public participation.

I155.title: Unsupported fraud claims weaken acceptance of defeat
I155.summary: After the 2020 election, claims of fraud large enough to change the outcome failed in court, and a review by conservative lawyers found no supporting evidence in any of 64 cases. Such claims still threaten the peaceful transfer of power when officials act on them.
I155.mechanism: Unsupported claims of election fraud weaken the peaceful transfer of power.
I155.evidence_note: Documented. The House Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol issued its final report in 2022 on the effort to overturn the 2020 result. Lost, Not Stolen (2022), an independent review by conservative lawyers and former officials, found no evidence of outcome-changing fraud in any of 64 court cases.
I155.remedy_note: Plausible. Experiments show mixed effects of audit evidence on belief. The Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022 clarified certification duties.
I155.response: Election offices, parties and courts would publish audit evidence people can understand, require officials to follow lawful certification and treat concession after a resolved contest as the norm.
I155.tradeoff: Legitimate challenges to results must remain available.
I155.success_measure: Public understanding of audit evidence, and lawful transfers of power.

I156.title: A sense that nothing works keeps people from taking part
I156.summary: Trust in the federal government stood at 17% in September 2025, near historic lows. People who believe every institution is beyond repair may stop trying to influence decisions, leaving more room for organized insiders.
I156.mechanism: A belief that institutions cannot be repaired reduces participation and leaves more room for capture by organized interests.
I156.evidence_note: Plausible. A long-running survey series on trust in the federal government put it at 17% in September 2025, near historic lows; question wording, poll source and smoothing affect the series. Hetherington (2005) found from panel data that low trust reduces support for redistributive policy. The Pew Research Center found in 2023 that majorities describe politics as exhausting.
I156.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Pairing candor about failure with visible repair has no evaluation, and some transparency experiments backfire.
I156.response: Governments, civic educators and newsrooms would pair honest accounts of failure with visible institutional repair and verified local results.
I156.tradeoff: Claims of success that read as propaganda damage credibility.
I156.success_measure: Knowledge of outcomes, participation, and trust that matches performance.

aimed_reforms.why: Reliable delivery of benefits, refunds and permits is the visible repair most people would notice.

I157.title: Civics classes teach facts more than practice
I157.summary: Eighth graders' national civics scores fell for the first time in 2022. Students learn the branches of government and get little practice taking part in a real public decision.
I157.mechanism: Civics instruction emphasizes recall over the skills of participation.
I157.evidence_note: Documented. The National Assessment of Educational Progress recorded its first decline in eighth-grade civics scores in 2022, leaving the average no different from 1998. Campbell's 2019 review found that an open classroom climate and applied practice predict later participation.
I157.remedy_note: Plausible. Campbell's 2019 review found that an open classroom climate and applied practice predict later participation. Those findings are associations from observational studies, and action civics programs have little rigorous evaluation.
I157.response: States, schools and libraries would teach budgeting, evaluating sources, rights and deliberation through nonpartisan local projects.
I157.tradeoff: Curriculum has to avoid party indoctrination and protect open discussion.
I157.success_measure: Civic skills applied in practice, and sustained engagement.

I158.title: Selling reforms as cure-alls invites disappointment
I158.summary: Presenting a complicated reform as a complete fix sets expectations it cannot meet. Whether that disappointment turns into resistance is a hypothesis that has not been tested in reform campaigns.
I158.mechanism: Overpromising what a reform will do produces later disappointment and resistance. The claim is a hypothesis.
I158.evidence_note: Hypothesis. No study listed for this record measures disappointment or resistance after an overpromised reform. Ballotpedia records the 2026 initiative to repeal Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election, one case of a reform facing reversal; the record does not show why voters sought it.
I158.remedy_note: Hypothesis. In experiments, Fernbach and colleagues (2013) found that asking people to explain how a policy works reduced the extremity of their positions. Framing research from the FrameWorks Institute informs layered explanation. Neither has been evaluated in a reform campaign.
I158.response: Educators and reform organizations would explain one mechanism, one concrete policy and its tradeoff at a time, in layered materials with accessible sources.
I158.tradeoff: Simplifying can erase real uncertainty about causes.
I158.success_measure: Comprehension, the rate of misconceptions, and accurate recall.

I159.title: Public feedback rarely turns into better services
I159.summary: Congressional offices and agencies receive large volumes of messages and have little capacity to connect them to recurring service failures. A visible response process would show residents whether their experience led to a change.
I159.mechanism: Constituent messages arrive in high volume and are poorly connected to service improvement.
I159.evidence_note: Plausible. The Congressional Management Foundation's 2017 survey of offices found rising volumes of constituent contact and limited staff capacity. Bergan (2009) found in a field experiment that a constituent email campaign shifted state legislators' votes, which shows that some feedback registers.
I159.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Public issue tracking with required responses has no evaluation.
I159.response: Legislatures and agencies would create accessible feedback systems with public issue tracking and required responses, while protecting personal records.
I159.tradeoff: Automated summaries of feedback need audits and a human route for appeal.
I159.success_measure: Quality of responses, issues resolved, and privacy protection.

aimed_reforms.why: A public duty to respond is the element this record's feedback systems would require.

I160.title: Future generations have little voice in current decisions
I160.summary: Voters reward disaster relief after the fact and give little credit for spending to prepare beforehand. People who will bear later costs, including today's children, have little organized voice in current decisions.
I160.mechanism: Short political horizons neglect prevention and future burdens.
I160.evidence_note: Well supported. Healy and Malhotra (2009) found that voters reward disaster relief spending and give no electoral credit for preparedness spending, a causal result. Jacobs (2011) gives a comparative account of when democracies invest for the long term. The Congressional Budget Office projects federal debt rising from 101% of GDP in 2026 to 120% in 2036.
I160.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Wales's Well-being of Future Generations Act is the main institutional example and has no rigorous evaluation.
I160.response: Congress, the states and audit institutions would require long-term impact statements, youth participation and independent review of future risks for major decisions.
I160.tradeoff: Forecasts are uncertain, and the authority of unelected reviewers needs limits.
I160.success_measure: Long-term risks addressed, and how costs and benefits are spread across generations.

I161.title: Presidential direction of prosecutions threatens equal enforcement
I161.summary: In 2025 the President publicly urged prosecutions of named critics, and a newly appointed prosecutor brought them days later. A judge dismissed those cases because the prosecutor was unlawfully appointed, and no court has found the prosecutions selective.
I161.mechanism: Political direction of law enforcement can be used to punish opponents or protect allies. The documented case shows public presidential direction followed by indictments; no court has found selective prosecution.
I161.evidence_note: Documented. On November 24, 2025, a federal judge dismissed without prejudice the indictments of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James, finding that the interim U.S. Attorney who brought them had been unlawfully appointed; NPR reported that the President had publicly urged the prosecutions days before her appointment. The Congressional Research Service has analyzed the appointment ruling. The dismissal rested on the appointment defect, and no court has made a finding about motive.
I161.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Policies governing contacts between the White House and the Justice Department, and recusal rules, have been proposed. The 2025 dismissals rested on appointment defects, with no finding of selective prosecution.
I161.response: Congress, the Justice Department and the courts would publish enforcement criteria and policies for White House contacts with the Justice Department, keep records of those contacts, require recusal for conflicts and provide oversight and court remedies where the law allows.
I161.tradeoff: Prosecutors keep discretion and presidents keep lawful supervision of the executive branch, so full independence cannot be assumed.
I161.success_measure: Consistent treatment of comparable cases, documented contacts, and conflicts resolved.

I162.title: Pardons can remove consequences for conduct that served those in power
I162.summary: On January 20, 2025, the President granted about 1,500 pardons and commutations for offenses connected to the events at the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. A statute can require disclosure; narrowing the pardon power itself would take a constitutional amendment.
I162.mechanism: Pardons reduce accountability for conduct that benefited powerful officials.
I162.evidence_note: Documented. A White House proclamation of January 20, 2025 granted about 1,500 pardons and commutations for offenses related to the events at or near the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021.
I162.remedy_note: Hypothesis. Disclosure of reasons and contacts are statutory proposals. The pardon power itself cannot be narrowed by statute.
I162.response: The President would give prompt reasons for each grant and lawful disclosure of contacts, and Congress would require that disclosure and independent review of conflicts by law. Congress and the states would use a constitutional amendment for any restriction beyond what a statute can reach.
I162.tradeoff: Ordinary legislation cannot narrow the constitutional pardon power in any comprehensive way.
I162.success_measure: Timeliness of disclosure, and conflict reviews completed.

I163.title: At-will removal of regulators narrows agency independence
I163.summary: In June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that the President can remove FTC commissioners at will, and the same day left protection for Federal Reserve governors in place. Whether the change has altered enforcement priorities has not yet been measured.
