C4.indicator_note: Three counts: the share of congressional and legislative maps drawn by the party they favor, the number of access restrictions passed by states where one party holds the governorship and both chambers, and the number of state laws preempting local election choices. Each rises with the variable. No values or periods are listed, and the counts use different units, so they are read side by side and are not added together.

D1.title: Congress's ability to write and check policy
D1.description: The staff and independent expertise Congress needs to investigate problems, draft laws and oversee how agencies carry them out. Committee staffing and the budgets of its support agencies help track that ability.
D1.increase_means: A higher value means Congress has more staff and expertise to draft laws and oversee agencies.
D1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D1.indicator: Committee staff FTE; CRS, GAO, CBO budgets; substantive bills enacted per Congress
D1.indicator_note: Committee staff in full-time equivalents, the budgets of the Congressional Research Service, GAO and CBO, and the number of substantive bills enacted per two-year Congress. Each rises with the variable. Bills enacted measure output, which also depends on partisan division, while staff and budgets measure capacity. No values are listed.

D2.title: Presidential action without new legislation
D2.description: How far the executive sets policy through orders, emergency powers or other action without a new law. Different actions carry different legal limits.
D2.increase_means: A higher value means more policy is set by presidential order or emergency power without a new law.
D2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D2.indicator: National emergencies in force; executive orders per year; impoundments; removals of protected officials
D2.indicator_note: National emergencies in force (a count at a point in time), executive orders per year (a count per period), impoundments and removals of officials protected by statute. Each rises with the variable. The measures mix stocks and flows, and a count of orders says nothing about each order's scope. No values are listed.

D3.title: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition
D3.description: Rulings on political money, election rules and executive power that benefit the coalition that appointed the judges. It is a proposed pattern read across decisions, with exceptions recorded in the evidence.
D3.increase_means: A higher value means more of the body of rulings favors the coalition responsible for the appointments.
D3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D3.indicator: Index of rulings on money, maps, access and removal (Buckley to Callais)
D3.indicator_note: A proposed index of rulings on money, maps, voting access and removal of officials, from Buckley v. Valeo (1976) to Louisiana v. Callais (2026). A ruling favoring the appointing coalition moves it up. No scoring formula or coding scheme is supplied, so the index cannot be reproduced; read the variable through the named decisions and the counterexamples, such as Trump v. Cook, Trump v. Illinois and Learning Resources (2025 to 2026).

D4.title: Ability to investigate and enforce the rules
D4.description: Whether watchdogs can obtain records, investigate wrongdoing and secure a response. Vacancies, quorums and enforcement of subpoenas decide whether that authority works in practice.
D4.increase_means: A higher value means watchdogs can get records, investigate and make findings stick.
D4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D4.indicator: IG vacancies; FEC and NLRB quorum status; GAO recommendations implemented; subpoena enforcement outcomes
D4.indicator_note: Inspector general vacancies run opposite to the variable. Quorum status at the Federal Election Commission and the National Labor Relations Board is a yes-or-no state, and having a quorum moves the variable up: the FEC has lacked one since May 1, 2025, and the NLRB has had one since January 7, 2026. GAO recommendations implemented and subpoena enforcement outcomes move with the variable. The measures use different units and are read side by side.

D5.title: Quality of public services
D5.description: How reliably government delivers the services people use. Waiting times, error rates and the time needed to finish a task make performance visible.
D5.increase_means: A higher value means services are delivered faster and with fewer errors.
D5.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D5.indicator: IRS answer rate; SSA wait times; permitting durations; federal civilian workforce down about 256,000 (over 11%) at CFO Act agencies, Dec 2024 to Jan 2026, after about 378,000 separations in 2025 (GAO-26-108583, W010)
D5.indicator_note: The IRS phone answer rate moves with the variable; Social Security wait times and permitting durations move opposite, since longer waits mean lower quality. The listed workforce figure, a net decline of about 256,000 employees (over 11%) at 24 CFO Act agencies from December 2024 to January 2026 (GAO), measures staffing, an input to service quality and a different quantity from it. No current values are listed for the service measures.

D6.title: State and local testing of reforms
D6.description: The ability of states and local governments to try a policy and learn from its results. Adoption, spread to other places and state limits on local choice help track it.
D6.increase_means: A higher value means states and localities try more new policies and pass on what they learn.
D6.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). The listed indicators count adoptions per year, which is a flow; the stock would be the number of reforms in force or the legal room states and localities have to act.
D6.indicator: Reforms adopted per year by initiative or statute; diffusion count; preemption count
D6.indicator_note: Reforms adopted per year by initiative or statute, and later adoptions of the same reform elsewhere, move with the variable. The count of state preemption laws moves opposite, since each one narrows the room for local tests. No values are listed. Adoption counts measure activity only.

E1.title: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests
E1.description: How far rules favor wealthy people or well-organized groups over less organized residents. Tax benefits and research on whose preferences receive a response give partial measures.
E1.increase_means: A higher value means rules deliver more of their benefits to wealthy people and organized groups.
E1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
E1.indicator: Share of tax expenditures to top decile (CBO); responsiveness gap (Gilens data, with caveats)
E1.indicator_note: The share of tax expenditures going to the top tenth of households (CBO) and a responsiveness gap built from data assembled by Gilens both move with the variable. The cited CBO report gives shares by fifths and for the top 1%: in 2019 the top fifth received about half of income-tax expenditure benefits. Tax expenditures cover one policy area, and the responsiveness measure is contested (Bashir 2015; Enns 2015), so each is a partial measure.

E2.title: Trust earned through performance
E2.description: Confidence in institutions that rests on evidence of how competently and honestly they act. Survey trust is an imperfect measure because performance is one of several influences on what people believe.
E2.increase_means: A higher value means more of the public's confidence rests on evidence that institutions perform.
E2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
E2.indicator: Pew trust in federal government (17%, Sept 2025, the latest Pew reading); Gallup confidence in Congress (9%, June 2026; W020); Gallup trust in mass media (33%, Sept 2026; W018); Gallup trust in the judicial branch (46%, Sept 2026; W019)
E2.indicator_note: Four surveys of U.S. adults, each a percentage: Pew trust in the federal government (17%, September 2025), Gallup confidence in Congress (9%, June 2026), Gallup trust in mass media (33%, September 2026) and Gallup trust in the judicial branch (46%, September 2026). Higher readings move the variable up. They ask about different institutions and cannot be combined without a stated method, and survey trust also moves with partisanship, so they measure trust in general, a different quantity from trust earned by performance.

X1.title: What new technology can do
X1.description: Technical advances that change which tasks can be automated and how much workers can produce. Their effects on pay and jobs depend on how employers use them.
X1.increase_means: A higher value means machines and software can do more tasks.
X1.indicator: Labor share; automation exposure; productivity growth
X1.indicator_note: The listed measures are the labor share, exposure to automation and productivity growth. They measure technology's effects on work, which differ from capability itself; a benchmark of what systems can do would measure the variable directly. Exposure and productivity growth rise with it, and the labor share tends to move opposite. No values are listed.

X2.title: Population patterns and residential sorting
X2.description: Where people live and how communities differ by age, education or party. These patterns can make districts politically lopsided before any map is drawn.
X2.increase_means: A higher value means communities are more sorted by party, age or education.
X2.indicator: Urban-rural partisan gap; age structure; education realignment
X2.indicator_note: The urban-rural partisan gap (the difference in party vote share between urban and rural areas), age structure and the realignment of voters by education. A wider urban-rural gap moves the variable up. Age structure describes the population and has no single direction for this variable. No values are listed.

X3.title: Trade and the movement of capital
X3.description: The movement of goods, investment and wealth across borders. Import competition and offshore assets connect this wider setting to local jobs and bargaining power.
X3.increase_means: A higher value means more import competition and more capital moving across borders.
X3.indicator: Import penetration by commuting zone; offshore wealth share. Chinese import competition explains about a quarter of the 1990-2007 manufacturing job decline (W067), with effects persisting through 2019 (W068)
X3.indicator_note: Import penetration by commuting zone (imports relative to the local economy) and the share of wealth held offshore both rise with the variable. The listed finding, that Chinese import competition explains about a quarter of the 1990 to 2007 decline in U.S. manufacturing jobs, with effects lasting through 2019 (Autor, Dorn and Hanson), is an effect estimate and a different quantity from trade exposure itself.

X4.title: Foreign interference
X4.description: Documented efforts by foreign actors to influence U.S. political information or processes. Showing that an operation happened takes different evidence from showing that it changed votes.
X4.increase_means: A higher value means more foreign efforts to influence U.S. political information or processes.
X4.indicator: Documented operations (ODNI); measured exposure (Eady et al. 2023)
X4.indicator_note: Documented operations (reports by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence) and measured exposure (Eady and coauthors 2023, U.S. Twitter users during the 2016 election). Both rise with the variable. A count of operations measures effort and exposure measures reach; neither measures effects on voters, which that study did not find.

X5.title: Major external shocks
X5.description: Events such as wars, pandemics and climate disasters that strain households and public institutions. The model treats them as outside pressures and does not explain how each begins.
X5.increase_means: A higher value means more frequent or more severe wars, pandemics and disasters.
X5.indicator: Disaster losses; insurance availability; emergency declarations
X5.indicator_note: Disaster losses in dollars, insurance availability and emergency declarations. Losses and declarations rise with the variable; insurance availability moves opposite. Losses also grow with the amount of property in harm's way, and declarations depend on official decisions, so each measure tracks more than the shocks themselves. No values are listed.

A6.title: Homeowners' equity
A6.description: The value owners hold in their homes after mortgage debt. The housing loop follows this stake and the wealth gap between owners and renters, which is a separate measure from the top 1% share of wealth.
A6.increase_means: A higher value means owners hold more value in their homes, relative to their mortgages and to renters' wealth.
A6.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
A6.indicator: Owner-renter net worth gap (Fed SCF, 1989 to 2022); owner home equity share of household net worth
A6.indicator_note: The owner-renter net worth gap comes from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances, taken every three years from 1989 to 2022 (median net worth $396,200 for owners and $10,400 for renters in 2022). Owner home equity as a share of household net worth is the second measure. Both rise with the variable. The gap also moves with renters' wealth, so it measures relative position, which differs from owners' equity in dollars ($35.8 trillion in 2026 Q2, Federal Reserve Z.1).

C5.title: Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement
C5.description: Officeholders who lose an election or retire under threat of defeat. This consequence is measured separately from the pressure they face while still in office.
C5.increase_means: A higher value means more incumbents lose or retire under threat of defeat in an election cycle.
C5.indicator: Incumbents defeated or retiring under threat, by cycle (House and Senate); state legislative incumbent defeats
C5.indicator_note: Incumbents defeated or retiring under threat in each election cycle for the House and Senate, plus state legislative incumbent defeats. More of either moves the variable up. Counting a retirement as 'under threat' requires a judgment about motive, so that part of the count depends on a stated coding rule. No values are listed.

D7.title: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions
D7.description: Lasting control of a legislature or another body that sets election rules or confirms judges. The model tracks how safe seats help a majority keep this control and use it again.
D7.increase_means: A higher value means the same majority holds rule-setting bodies longer and is harder to unseat.
D7.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
D7.indicator: Years the same party has held a state legislature or trifecta; seat share needed to flip a chamber versus vote share needed (seats-votes curve); share of rule-setting bodies (legislatures that draw maps, the Senate that confirms judges) held by a majority insulated by safe seats
D7.indicator_note: Years the same party has held a state legislature or trifecta (the governorship and both chambers), a seats-votes comparison of the seat share needed to flip a chamber against the vote share needed, and the share of rule-setting bodies held by a majority insulated by safe seats. Each rises with the variable. Years of control count duration, which also grows when a majority keeps winning competitive races; the seats-votes measure comes closer to insulation. No values are listed.

EC1.title: Output produced per hour of work
EC1.description: How much workers produce in an hour. Higher productivity can support higher living standards, and the rules governing pay decide who receives the gains.
EC1.increase_means: A higher value means workers produce more per hour.
EC1.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). Output per hour is a ratio of two flows; the model treats its level as the result of accumulated capital, skills and know-how.
EC1.indicator: Nonfarm business output per hour (BLS): +2.1% a year 2019 Q4 to 2026 Q2 (W007)
EC1.indicator_note: BLS nonfarm business output per hour worked, published quarterly, grew 2.1% a year on average from 2019 Q4 to 2026 Q2. Faster growth moves the variable up. The listed figure is a growth rate, so it measures change in the variable, and the nonfarm business sector leaves out government and farm work.

EC2.title: Public investment in research and infrastructure
EC2.description: Government funding for research and for the systems that support economic activity. Money committed to a project and money spent on it can differ for years.
EC2.increase_means: A higher value means more public money going to research and infrastructure each year.
EC2.indicator: Federally funded R&D share of GDP: 1.86% (1964) to 0.63% (2022) (W053); IIJA DOT funds 75.7% obligated, 46.6% spent by July 2026 (W054)
EC2.indicator_note: Federally funded R&D as a share of GDP (National Science Foundation: 1.86% in 1964, 0.63% in 2022) rises with the variable. The infrastructure law's transportation funds, 75.7% obligated and 46.6% spent as of July 31, 2026 (Department of Transportation), measure how fast committed money is spent, a different quantity from the amount invested.

EC3.title: Workers' share of income
EC3.description: The portion of business income paid to workers as compensation. It describes how income is divided as it is earned, which is separate from how accumulated wealth is distributed.
EC3.increase_means: A higher value means workers receive a larger share of the income businesses produce.
EC3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). The share is a ratio of income flows in each period, so it behaves like a condition (auxiliary); the model treats it as a stock because it changes slowly.
EC3.indicator: Nonfarm business labor share 52.8% (2026 Q2), lowest since 1947 (W008); corporate profits 13.0% of gross domestic income in 2025 (W016, W052)
EC3.indicator_note: The BLS nonfarm business labor share, quarterly, was 52.8% in 2026 Q2, the lowest since the series began in 1947. A higher share moves the variable up. Corporate profits as a share of gross domestic income (13.0% in 2025, BEA) generally move opposite, though the two use different income totals and do not sum to 100%.

EC4.title: Concentration of stock ownership
EC4.description: How much of households' corporate stock and mutual fund holdings belongs to the wealthiest groups. This decides who receives much of the gain when those assets rise in value.
EC4.increase_means: A higher value means the wealthiest households hold a larger share of household stocks and mutual funds.
EC4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
EC4.indicator: Top 1% hold 50.9% and the next 9% hold 37.2% of household corporate equities and mutual fund shares (2026 Q2, W112)
EC4.indicator_note: Federal Reserve Distributional Financial Accounts, quarterly, U.S. households: the top 1% held 50.9% and the next 9% held 37.2% of household corporate equities and mutual fund shares in 2026 Q2. A higher top share moves the variable up. The shares are modeled from national accounts and survey data, and price changes in assets held by different groups move them alongside purchases and sales.

EC5.title: Where newly created credit goes
EC5.description: Banks create deposits when they lend, so lending directs new purchasing power toward homes, businesses and other uses. The model tracks where credit goes and the risks that grow with it.
EC5.increase_means: A higher value means more new credit flowing to the use being discussed, such as mortgages or loans to nonbank lenders.
EC5.indicator: Bank loans $14.09T: real estate 41.4%, business 21.0%, consumer 13.7%, loans to nonbank lenders 14.6% (H.8, Oct 2026, W060); private credit about $1.4T (W062); banks create deposits when they lend, and reserve requirements have been zero since March 2020 (W058, W059)
EC5.indicator_note: The listed figures are amounts outstanding at a point in time: commercial bank loans of $14.09 trillion (Federal Reserve H.8, October 2026), of which 41.4% real estate, 21.0% business, 13.7% consumer and 14.6% loans to nonbank lenders, plus about $1.4 trillion of private credit. Outstanding loans are a stock, so new credit per period is the change in these amounts. A larger share going to a use moves the variable up for that use.

EC6.title: Net support from taxes and public benefits
EC6.description: Taxes collect resources and public benefits return income or services to households. In this model a higher value means more net support or redistribution toward the households being discussed, and who pays and who receives decide the effect.
EC6.increase_means: A higher value means taxes and benefits leave the households being discussed with more net support.
EC6.indicator: Top 1% income share 18% before and 14% after taxes and transfers (CBO, 2022, W063); Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty in 2025 (W001)
EC6.indicator_note: CBO estimates the top 1% share of U.S. household income at 18% before and 14% after taxes and transfers (2022); a larger drop from before to after moves the variable up for households below the top. Census reported that Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty in 2025, a measure that rises with the variable for retirees. Both measure effects of the system, and raising a tax and raising a benefit reach different households.

EC7.title: Household income
EC7.description: Money a household receives over a period, including earnings and other income. It pays current expenses and can add to savings; wealth records what the household has kept after debts.
EC7.increase_means: A higher value means households receive more money over the year.
EC7.indicator: Real median household income $87,460 (2025), +2.6% (W002); consumer spending was 67.6% of GDP in 2025 (W016)
EC7.indicator_note: Census real median household income was $87,460 in 2025, up 2.6% from 2024 in 2025 dollars, measured annually. A higher median moves the variable up. The median describes the middle household and shows nothing about the top or bottom. Consumer spending's share of GDP (67.6% in 2025) measures how income is used across the economy, a different quantity.

EC8.title: Household assets and debts
EC8.description: What households own and what they owe. Savings, home equity and debt shape their ability to withstand a lost paycheck or an unexpected bill.
EC8.increase_means: A higher value means households hold more assets relative to their debts.
EC8.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
EC8.indicator: Median net worth: homeowners $396,200, renters $10,400 (SCF 2022, W072); household debt $18.77T (Q2 2026, W012); 63% could cover a $400 expense with cash (W074)
EC8.indicator_note: Median net worth from the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances ($396,200 for homeowners, $10,400 for renters) moves with the variable. Total household debt ($18.77 trillion in 2026 Q2, New York Fed) moves opposite, though a debt total says nothing about the assets behind it. The share of adults who could cover a $400 expense with cash (63% in 2025, Federal Reserve) measures liquid savings, one part of the balance sheet.

EC9.title: Cost of essentials
EC9.description: What households pay for necessities such as housing, care and insurance. Costs measured against income show pressure that national growth figures can miss.
EC9.increase_means: A higher value means necessities take more of a household's income.
EC9.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time). Costs are paid each period, so the measures behave like flows or conditions; the model treats the level of prices as persistent.
EC9.indicator: 49% of renter households cost-burdened (W013); child care $13,184 a year (W015); family health premium $26,993 (W014); home insurance premiums +72% 2019-2025 (W013)
EC9.indicator_note: Four measures, each rising with the variable: 49% of renter households cost-burdened (Harvard JCHS, 2024 data), an average child care price of $13,184 in 2025 (Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy compilation), an average family health premium of $26,993 (KFF, 2025 survey) and home insurance premiums up 72% from 2019 to 2025. They use different units and populations, so they are read side by side.

EC10.title: Costs of tariffs and trade rules
EC10.description: Import taxes and related trade rules can raise costs for U.S. buyers. The burden depends on prices, purchasing choices and which households or businesses use the affected goods.
EC10.increase_means: A higher value means tariffs add more to what U.S. buyers pay.
EC10.indicator: Average statutory tariff rate about 11.0% (Aug 2026); about $1,100 per household a year (W069); 86-94% of the cost borne by U.S. buyers (W070)
EC10.indicator_note: The average statutory tariff rate (about 11.0% in August 2026) and an estimated cost of about $1,100 per household a year (Yale Budget Lab) rise with the variable. The share of tariff cost borne by U.S. buyers (86% to 94%, New York Fed, 2025) describes who pays. The rate measures the policy and the household cost estimates its burden, so they are related quantities that can move apart.

EC11.title: Climate hazards and insurance costs
EC11.description: The financial risk from climate-related damage and the cost or availability of insurance against it. Exposure varies by location and by a household's ability to adapt or move.
EC11.increase_means: A higher value means greater risk of climate damage and higher costs to insure against it.
EC11.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
EC11.indicator: Highest-risk fifth of ZIP codes paid 82% more for home insurance (W076); 23 billion-dollar disasters in 2025 (W080)
EC11.indicator_note: The highest-risk fifth of ZIP codes paid 82% more for homeowners insurance than the lowest-risk fifth (Treasury Federal Insurance Office, 2018 to 2022 data, disputed by the industry), and 23 billion-dollar disasters occurred in 2025 (Climate Central). Both rise with the variable. The premium gap compares places at one time, and disaster counts mix hazard with growth in exposed property.

EC12.title: Energy demand and emissions
EC12.description: The energy the economy uses and the greenhouse gases released in producing and using it. These are separate quantities: electricity demand affects the grid, and its emissions depend on the sources that supply it.
EC12.increase_means: A higher value means more energy use or more emissions; the two can move apart when cleaner sources meet new demand.
EC12.indicator: Electricity use forecast +1% (2026) and +3% (2027) (W079); emissions +2.4% in 2025, preliminary (W078)
EC12.indicator_note: The Energy Information Administration forecasts U.S. electricity use rising 1% in 2026 and 3% in 2027, and a preliminary Rhodium Group estimate puts 2025 U.S. emissions up 2.4%. Both rise with the variable. They measure different quantities, so each connection names the half it uses: data-center load raises the demand half, and climate hazard responds to the emissions half.

TC1.title: How platforms rank feeds and seek attention
TC1.description: The choices platforms make about which posts and recommendations people see. Ranking can change exposure a great deal even when measured changes in political attitudes are small or absent.
TC1.increase_means: A higher value means more of what people see is chosen by ranking built to hold attention, compared with a time-ordered feed.
TC1.indicator: Share of time in algorithmically ranked feeds; ranking objectives disclosed by platforms
TC1.indicator_note: The share of time spent in algorithmically ranked feeds rises with the variable; disclosed ranking objectives describe what a ranking optimizes and have no single direction. No values are listed. Time in ranked feeds measures reliance on ranking, and the direction of its effect on content depends on the platform and the rule used.

TC2.title: Concentration of platforms and digital advertising
TC2.description: The share of digital advertising and distribution held by a few platforms. It affects publishers' revenue and the choices open to advertisers and users.
TC2.increase_means: A higher value means a few platforms take a larger share of digital advertising and distribution.
TC2.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC2.indicator: Worldwide digital ad share 2026: Meta 26.8%, Google 26.4%, Amazon 9.0% (eMarketer forecast, W099)
TC2.indicator_note: eMarketer forecasts 2026 worldwide digital ad revenue shares of 26.8% for Meta, 26.4% for Google and 9.0% for Amazon. Larger shares for the leading firms move the variable up. This is a vendor forecast for the world market, a different population from U.S. local advertising, which is the market that pays for local news.

TC3.title: Use of AI at work
TC3.description: How workers and employers adopt generative AI for their tasks. Measured time savings in particular settings leave the wider effects on jobs and pay to be assessed separately.
TC3.increase_means: A higher value means more workers and employers use generative AI in their tasks.
TC3.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC3.indicator: Share of workers and firms using generative AI at work; task-time savings (W105, W107)
TC3.indicator_note: The share of workers and firms using generative AI at work rises with the variable; no U.S. value is listed. Task-time savings (about 2.8% of work hours in a Danish study by Humlum and Vestergaard, 2025) measure an effect of use, a different quantity from use itself.

TC4.title: Concentration of AI funding and computing power
TC4.description: How much of the capital and computing infrastructure used to build advanced AI sits with a few firms. The amount built is a separate variable, TC8: Computing capacity built for AI.
TC4.increase_means: A higher value means a few firms hold more of the capital and computing power used for advanced AI.
TC4.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC4.indicator: Nearly 90% of notable 2024 models from industry (W113)
TC4.indicator_note: Nearly 90% of notable 2024 AI models came from industry, by the Stanford AI Index. That share shows where model building happens. No current value exists for the share of computing held by the largest firms.

TC5.title: Government's ability to build and run digital services
TC5.description: The public teams and skills needed to deliver services through reliable software. Aging systems and dependence on outside contractors affect how quickly agencies can improve a service.
TC5.increase_means: A higher value means agencies can build, run and fix their own digital services.
TC5.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC5.indicator: Eleven most critical legacy systems 23-60 years old; about 80% of IT spending on operations (W116); 18F closed March 2025 (W119); Direct File not offered for 2026 (W120)
TC5.indicator_note: GAO reported in 2025 that the eleven most critical federal legacy systems are 23 to 60 years old and that about 80% of IT spending goes to operations and maintenance; both run opposite to the variable. The closure of 18F in March 2025 and the end of Direct File for 2026 are events that lowered it. These describe systems and spending, inputs to capacity, and no count of in-house digital staff is listed.

TC6.title: Data centers' demand on the electricity grid
TC6.description: The power and grid capacity data centers need. Large new loads can raise system costs, and the effect on households depends on how regulators assign those costs.
TC6.increase_means: A higher value means data centers draw more power and need more grid capacity.
TC6.indicator: Data centers 4.4% of U.S. electricity (2023), 6.7-12% projected by 2028 (W081); PJM monitor: $23.1B added by data-center load across three auctions (W126)
TC6.indicator_note: Data centers used 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023 and are projected at 6.7 to 12% by 2028 (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory for the Department of Energy); a higher share moves the variable up. The PJM market monitor's figure, $23.1 billion added by data-center load across three capacity auctions, measures cost, an effect of the load and a different quantity.

TC7.title: Use of pricing algorithms
TC7.description: Software that sellers or landlords use to set prices. Software fed with competitors' private information raises different competition questions from software that uses public data or a firm's own data.
TC7.increase_means: A higher value means more sellers and landlords set prices with software, especially software fed with competitors' nonpublic data.
TC7.indicator: Landlords and sellers using shared nonpublic data in pricing software; state and local bans (W127, W128, W129)
TC7.indicator_note: The number of landlords and sellers using shared nonpublic data in pricing software rises with the variable; state and local bans move opposite, since each ban limits that use. No counts are listed.

TC8.title: Computing capacity built for AI
TC8.description: How much computing infrastructure, mostly data centers filled with specialized chips, has been built to train and run AI systems. TC4 measures how few firms hold that capacity, a separate quantity.
TC8.increase_means: A higher value means more computing capacity has been built for AI.
TC8.kind_plain: Stock (an amount built up over time)
TC8.indicator: 2025 capex Amazon $134.7B, Microsoft $118B, Alphabet $91.5B, Meta $72.2B (secondary compilation, W111)
TC8.indicator_note: Capital spending in 2025 was $134.7 billion at Amazon, $118 billion at Microsoft, $91.5 billion at Alphabet and $72.2 billion at Meta, by a secondary compilation whose definitions vary by company. Spending is a yearly flow that adds to the stock and covers more than AI, so it shows the pace of building.

L01.name: Concentrated wealth funds more political spending
L01.plain: People with more wealth can give more to campaigns, outside groups and lobbyists, so wealth concentrated at the top raises the money spent to influence politics.
L01.sign_meaning: When wealth becomes more concentrated at the top, spending to influence politics tends to rise.
L01.mechanism: Contributions and lobbying scale with wealth; top 0.01% of donors give about 40% of itemized money
L01.citation: Bonica, McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal 2013, J. Econ. Perspectives

L02.name: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors
L02.plain: Donors gain meetings with officeholders and a say in which issues reach the agenda and how bills are drafted, which can shift rules toward their interests.
L02.sign_meaning: When more money is spent to influence politics, policy tends to favor wealthy and organized interests more.
L02.qualification: A 2016 field experiment (Kalla and Broockman) found congressional offices granted meetings more often to people identified as donors; affluent and middle-income Americans want the same policy about 90% of the time, so any tilt shows on the issues where they differ.
L02.mechanism: Access, agenda and drafting; donors get meetings; affluent and median preferences agree about 90% of the time so the tilt shows at the margin
L02.citation: Kalla and Broockman 2016, AJPS (field experiment); Gilens and Page 2014 with Bashir 2015 and Enns 2015 critiques

L03.name: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top
L03.plain: Tax breaks for investment income and rules that protect existing profits deliver most of their value to the top tenth of households, which adds to their wealth.
L03.sign_meaning: When policy favors wealthy and organized interests more, wealth tends to become more concentrated at the top.
L03.qualification: CBO estimated that about 75% of the benefit of lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends went to the top 1% of households in 2019; asset prices also move the top share, so policy is one cause among several.
L03.mechanism: Tax expenditures, capital-income preferences and rent-protecting rules accrue to the top decile
L03.citation: CBO, The Distribution of Major Tax Expenditures

L04.name: Political money helps shape judicial confirmations
L04.plain: Outside groups pay for campaigns for and against judicial nominees and bring test cases, which can affect who reaches the bench and which questions courts decide.
L04.sign_meaning: When more money is spent on politics, court rulings favoring the appointing coalition tend to increase.
L04.qualification: The evidence is a history of organized legal movements (Teles 2008); it does not show that any donation caused a particular confirmation or ruling.
L04.mechanism: Funding of confirmation campaigns and litigation; influence on Senate outcomes
L04.citation: Teles 2008, The Rise of the Conservative Legal Movement

L05.name: Court rulings widen permitted political spending
L05.plain: Supreme Court decisions from Buckley v. Valeo (1976) through NRSC v. FEC (2026) struck limits on political spending and opened new channels for money.
L05.sign_meaning: As rulings of this kind accumulate, more money tends to flow into politics.
L05.qualification: The rulings are on the record, but the variable they come from has no published scoring rule, so read it through the named decisions: Buckley (1976), Citizens United (2010), McCutcheon (2014) and NRSC v. FEC (2026).
L05.citation: Buckley 1976; Citizens United 2010; McCutcheon 2014; NRSC v. FEC 2026

L06.name: Court rulings expand incumbents' control of election rules
L06.plain: Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) closed federal courts to partisan-map claims, and Shelby County (2013) and Louisiana v. Callais (2026) removed federal checks on changes to voting rules.
L06.sign_meaning: When rulings of this kind accumulate, officeholders tend to gain more control over maps and voting rules.
L06.qualification: Each ruling removed one federal check; state courts and state constitutions still limit maps in some states, so the effect differs from state to state.
L06.mechanism: Rucho removes federal review of partisan maps; Shelby and Callais remove preclearance and most Section 2 constraints on access rules
L06.citation: Rucho v. Common Cause 2019; Shelby County 2013; Louisiana v. Callais 2026

L08.name: Safe seats make the primary decisive
L08.plain: When one party is sure to win the general election, the real choice happens in that party's primary.
L08.sign_meaning: More safe seats go with more seats effectively decided in the primary.
L08.qualification: Unite America, a reform advocacy group, counted 88% of House seats (383 of 435) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries using Cook Political Report ratings; the count depends on the group's own definition of a decided seat.
L08.mechanism: When the general election is settled, the primary decides
L08.citation: Unite America Institute, The Primary Problem, 2024 cycle

L09.name: Decisive primaries may deepen partisan hostility
L09.plain: Nominees chosen by a party's most engaged voters may campaign to the base and send hostile signals about the other party to their supporters.
L09.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: when more seats are decided in primaries, hostility toward the other party tends to rise.
L09.qualification: Contested. The strongest tests (McGhee and coauthors 2014) found that opening primaries did not measurably change legislators' voting records, and they measured legislators; this link concerns voters' feelings toward the other party. A study of one Alaska election cycle found some moderation (Reilly, Wright and Lublin 2025).
L09.mechanism: Base-oriented nominees and party leaders' cues; the best tests of primary openness on legislator extremism are null
L09.citation: McGhee, Masket, Shor, Rogers and McCarty 2014, AJPS; Hirano et al. 2010; Reilly, Wright and Lublin 2025 (Alaska, one cycle, moderation)

L10.name: Partisan hostility weakens Congress's capacity
L10.plain: Polarized chambers pass fewer major laws and move decisions to party leaders, which leaves committees and their staff with less work and less say.
L10.sign_meaning: When hostility toward the other party rises, Congress's ability to write and check policy tends to fall.
L10.qualification: The studies (Binder 2003; Lee 2016) measure polarization among members of Congress and the number of laws passed; they did not measure public hostility or committee staff capacity directly.
L10.mechanism: Polarized chambers legislate less and centralize in leadership

L11.name: A weaker Congress invites presidential action
L11.plain: When Congress does not legislate, presidents fill the gap with executive orders, emergency declarations, tariffs and spending freezes.
L11.sign_meaning: When Congress's capacity falls, presidential action without new legislation tends to rise.
L11.mechanism: Legislative abdication is filled by orders, emergencies, tariffs and impoundment

L12.name: Presidential action erodes Congress's will to legislate
L12.plain: When the executive settles questions alone, members of Congress have less reason to build the staff and skills needed to write laws.
L12.sign_meaning: When presidents act more without new laws, Congress's capacity tends to fall further.
L12.qualification: This return effect rests on legal and historical analysis (Chafetz 2017) and has no quantitative test.
L12.mechanism: Atrophy of the incentive and capacity to legislate

L13.name: Recent rulings, on balance, expand presidential power
L13.plain: Rulings on presidential immunity and the removal of officials widened what a president can do alone, while rulings on tariffs, the National Guard and the Federal Reserve set limits.
L13.sign_meaning: On the 2024 to 2026 record, more rulings of this kind go with more presidential action without new legislation.
L13.qualification: The positive sign is a net reading of 2024 to 2026 decisions: Trump v. United States and Trump v. Slaughter widened presidential power, and Learning Resources, Trump v. Illinois and Trump v. Cook limited it. A different set of rulings could reverse the sign.
L13.mechanism: Immunity and removal rulings expand unilateral power; tariff, Guard and Fed rulings bound it. Net positive 2024 to 2026
L13.citation: Trump v. United States 2024; Trump v. Slaughter 2026; Learning Resources 2026; Trump v. Illinois 2025; Trump v. Cook 2026

L14.name: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies
L14.plain: Firing inspectors general and commissioners, leaving boards without a quorum and cutting staff all reduce what watchdogs can investigate and enforce.
L14.sign_meaning: When presidential action without new legislation rises, the ability to investigate and enforce the rules tends to fall.
L14.mechanism: Removal of inspectors general and commissioners; quorum losses; reductions in force
L14.citation: 17 IGs removed Jan 24, 2025; ruled unlawful Sept 24, 2025; FEC without quorum since May 1, 2025

L15.name: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action
L15.plain: Audits, lawsuits and enforcement raise the cost of acting without a law, provided the enforcer does not answer to the official being checked.
L15.sign_meaning: When oversight grows stronger, presidential action without new legislation tends to fall.
L15.qualification: GAO found several 2025 impoundments unlawful, and its findings carry no penalty of their own; the restraint depends on courts and Congress acting on them.
L15.mechanism: Audits, litigation and enforcement restrain unilateral action when the enforcer is independent
L15.citation: GAO impoundment findings 2025 (official); Vladeck 2023 on the shadow docket

L16.name: Watchdogs reduce favoritism and waste in policy
L16.plain: Investigators who find an agency captured by the industry it regulates, or money wasted, can force corrections that remove some advantages built into rules and contracts.
L16.sign_meaning: When oversight grows stronger, policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests tend to shrink.
L16.qualification: GAO credits its High Risk List work with about $84 billion in financial benefits since 2023 by its own accounting; most of that is waste and payment errors, a broader category than favoritism toward organized interests.
L16.mechanism: Detection and remedy of capture and waste
L16.citation: GAO High Risk List, about $84B saved since 2023 (official)

L17.name: Visible favoritism can prompt investigations
L17.plain: When a scandal or obvious harm comes to light, prosecutors, auditors and legislators open inquiries into it.
L17.sign_meaning: When policy favoritism grows and becomes visible, investigation and enforcement tend to increase in response.
L17.qualification: Investigations follow only some scandals, such as the federal case over Ohio House Bill 6 that ended in convictions in 2023; a response needs a watchdog with the staff and legal power to act.
L17.mechanism: Visible harm and scandal trigger scrutiny and investigations

L18.name: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence
L18.plain: Committees with their own experts rely less on bill text and analysis supplied by interested groups.
L18.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more congressional capacity goes with fewer policy advantages for insiders.
L18.qualification: Hypothesis. The cited research shows reliance on lobbyists' expertise (Drutman 2015) and on model bills in state legislatures (Hertel-Fernandez 2019); no study tests what added congressional staff would change.
L18.mechanism: Own expertise reduces dependence on interested drafting

L19.name: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise
L19.plain: Rules shaped by outside interests can reduce the demand for independent analysis inside Congress, which makes staff cuts easier to pass.
L19.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more policy advantages for insiders go with less congressional capacity.
L19.qualification: Hypothesis. The cited evidence is one event, the 1995 House staff cuts and the closing of the Office of Technology Assessment, and it does not show that insider influence caused them.
L19.mechanism: Insider-tilted policy weakens support for public expertise

L20.name: Better public services build earned trust
L20.plain: People who receive a service that works on time have a reason to trust the agency that delivered it.
L20.sign_meaning: When public services improve, trust based on performance tends to rise.
L20.qualification: Survey trust also moves with which party holds office (Hetherington 2005), so the share of trust that comes from performance is uncertain.
L20.mechanism: Experienced competence; trust also tracks partisanship of the incumbent, so the causal share is uncertain

L21.name: Earned trust supports compliance and service funding
L21.plain: People who trust an agency are more likely to pay taxes and follow its rules, which gives it the revenue and cooperation to keep services working.
L21.sign_meaning: When earned trust rises, the quality of public services tends to rise.
L21.qualification: Studies of tax morale (Luttmer and Singhal 2014) and COVID-19 rules (Bargain and Aminjonov 2020) support the compliance channel; the claim that trust raises political support for funding is a hypothesis.
L21.mechanism: Compliance and revenue channel (well-supported); support-for-funding channel (hypothesis)
L21.citation: Luttmer and Singhal 2014, JEP (tax morale); Bargain and Aminjonov 2020 (COVID compliance)

L22.name: Insider-tilted policy cuts public service capacity
L22.plain: Tax cuts and budget austerity often fall on the staff who run programs, so agencies answer fewer calls and process claims more slowly.
L22.sign_meaning: When policy favors insiders more, the quality of public services tends to fall.
L22.qualification: Staff losses are documented in agency data, including TIGTA and OPM figures for the IRS in 2025; the step from favoritism in tax law to a specific agency's cuts passes through budget decisions with several causes.
L22.mechanism: Austerity and tax cuts fall on administrative capacity; IRS lost about a quarter of staff in 2025

L23.name: Poor service raises incumbents' risk of losing
L23.plain: Voters judge officeholders on results, so visible failures make a challenger more credible and an incumbent easier to replace.
L23.sign_meaning: When public services get worse, the risk of losing office tends to rise; better service lowers it.
L23.qualification: Retrospective voting is well documented (Healy and Malhotra 2013), and voters also punish officials for events outside their control, such as natural disasters, so the pressure does not track performance alone.
L23.mechanism: Poor performance raises pressure to replace officials (retrospective voting)
L23.citation: Healy and Malhotra 2013, Annual Review of Political Science

L24.name: Electoral pressure leads to actual defeats
L24.plain: Where seats are competitive, a credible threat turns into an incumbent's defeat or a retirement taken to avoid one.
L24.sign_meaning: When the risk of losing office rises, more incumbents tend to be defeated or pushed to retire.
L24.qualification: Pressure can change an official's behavior before any defeat occurs, so testing the whole chain needs evidence on both the threat and the defeats over several election cycles.
L24.mechanism: Credible pressure becomes an actual removal or a forced retirement where seats are competitive
L24.citation: Fiorina 1981; Jacobson and Carson, incumbent defeat series

L25.name: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure
L25.plain: When the primary decides the seat, the November election poses little threat, and incumbents answer mainly to the smaller group that votes in primaries.
L25.sign_meaning: When more seats are decided in primaries, the risk of losing office in November tends to fall.
L25.qualification: Incumbents can still lose primaries; this link measures the loss of general-election pressure, and total pressure depends on how often primaries are contested.
L25.mechanism: A decisive low-turnout primary removes the general-election sanction; incumbents answer to the few
L25.citation: Unite America 2024; Hill 2015, Journal of Politics (primary electorates)

L26.name: Local reporting raises pressure on incumbents
L26.plain: Coverage of local officials draws more challengers and more voters, which narrows the advantage incumbents hold.
L26.sign_meaning: When local reporting becomes more available, the risk of losing office tends to rise.
L26.qualification: The electoral evidence comes from U.S. mayoral elections (Rubado and Jennings 2020). The finding that newspaper closures raise municipal borrowing costs (Gao, Lee and Murphy 2020) concerns a separate outcome.
L26.mechanism: Local coverage raises challenger entry and turnout, lowers incumbent advantage and borrowing costs
L26.citation: Rubado and Jennings 2020, Urban Affairs Review; Gao, Lee and Murphy 2020, JFE

L27.name: Local reporting can temper partisan hostility
L27.plain: When a local paper closes, residents follow national politics more and vote a straight party ticket more often.
L27.sign_meaning: When local reporting shrinks, hostility toward the other party tends to rise.
L27.qualification: The study (Darr, Hitt and Dunaway 2018) measured split-ticket voting after newspaper closures, which stands in for partisan hostility and is a different quantity from it.
L27.mechanism: When local news dies, voting nationalizes (less split-ticket voting)
L27.citation: Darr, Hitt and Dunaway 2018, Journal of Communication

L28.name: Market concentration shrinks local reporting
L28.plain: Large platforms took much of the advertising that paid for local news, and chain owners merged or cut newsrooms.
L28.sign_meaning: When markets become more concentrated, local reporting tends to shrink.
L28.qualification: The evidence covers concentration in advertising and in newspaper ownership, the two markets that pay for local news; it does not extend to concentration in other industries.
L28.mechanism: Platform capture of advertising; chain consolidation
L28.citation: Pew State of the News Media; Medill 2025

L29.name: Employer concentration lowers workers' bargaining power
L29.plain: Where few employers hire for a type of job, workers have fewer places to go, and wages are lower.
L29.sign_meaning: When markets grow more concentrated, workers' bargaining power tends to fall.
L29.qualification: The study (Azar, Marinescu and Steinbaum 2022) measured concentration among employers posting jobs in local labor markets, which differs from concentration among sellers in product markets.
L29.citation: Azar, Marinescu and Steinbaum 2022, Journal of Human Resources

L30.name: Worker bargaining power limits top wealth concentration
L30.plain: Unions raise and compress pay, so stronger bargaining keeps more income with workers and less with the owners of capital.
L30.sign_meaning: When workers' bargaining power rises, wealth tends to become less concentrated at the top.
L30.qualification: The main study (Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu 2021) linked union membership to income inequality from 1936 onward; the step from income to accumulated wealth adds savings and asset prices, which it did not measure.
L30.mechanism: Union wage premium and compression; labor share
L30.citation: Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu 2021, QJE

L31.name: Insider-tilted labor rules weaken worker bargaining
L31.plain: Labor laws that make organizing harder, and enforcement that lapses, leave workers less able to bargain.
L31.sign_meaning: When policy favors insiders more, workers' bargaining power tends to fall.
L31.qualification: The evidence is a sequence of legal events: the Taft-Hartley Act (1947), Janus v. AFSCME (2018) and the National Labor Relations Board's period without a quorum in 2025, which ended January 7, 2026. Their combined effect on bargaining has not been estimated.

L32.name: Strong unions build cross-group civic ties
L32.plain: Unions bring together members of different parties, incomes and backgrounds who work side by side and meet regularly.
L32.sign_meaning: When workers' bargaining power rises, civic ties across groups tend to grow.
L32.qualification: The review (Ahlquist 2017) describes unions as organizations that cut across class and party; the size of their effect on ties outside the workplace is not measured.
L32.citation: Ahlquist 2017, Annual Review of Political Science

L33.name: Cross-group ties reduce partisan hostility
L33.plain: People who know and work with supporters of the other party tend to judge that party's voters less harshly.
L33.sign_meaning: When civic ties across groups grow, hostility toward the other party tends to fall.
L33.qualification: Contact research (Pettigrew and Tropp 2006) pools studies of many kinds of groups; direct tests with partisan groups are fewer.
L33.mechanism: Cross-cutting contact and shared identity reduce out-party hostility

L34.name: Civic ties make turnout more equal
L34.plain: Members of organizations are asked to vote, learn how, and gain confidence that taking part matters, which lifts turnout among groups that vote less.
L34.sign_meaning: When civic ties grow, turnout tends to become more equal across income groups.

L35.name: Financial security makes turnout more equal
L35.plain: Households with steady income and some savings have more time and attention for voting, so security narrows the turnout gap between income groups.
L35.sign_meaning: When household financial security rises, turnout tends to become more equal across income groups.
L35.qualification: The income gap in turnout is well documented (Schlozman, Verba and Brady 2012); civic skills and being asked to vote explain part of it, so security is one cause among several.
L35.mechanism: Participation costs fall with security; the income gradient in turnout
L35.citation: Schlozman, Verba and Brady 2012, The Unheavenly Chorus

L36.name: More equal turnout reduces policy favoritism
L36.plain: Officeholders respond to the people who vote, so a broader electorate pulls policy toward groups that were underrepresented.
L36.sign_meaning: When turnout becomes more equal, policy advantages for insiders tend to shrink.
L36.qualification: The main evidence is Australia's adoption of compulsory voting in the early 20th century (Fowler 2013), which raised turnout sharply and shifted policy; the effect of smaller U.S. turnout changes has not been estimated.

L37.name: Insider-tilted benefit rules reduce household security
L37.plain: How benefits are designed, and when they are allowed to expire, decides how much support reaches households with little cushion.
L37.sign_meaning: When policy favors insiders more, household financial security tends to fall.
L37.qualification: Census figures as first published show SPM child poverty at 5.2% in 2021 under the expanded child tax credit and 13.4% in 2024 after it lapsed; Census revised the 2019 to 2024 rates in 2026, and the credit's expiry alone does not show favoritism toward wealthy interests.
L37.mechanism: Benefit design and expiry; SPM child poverty 5.2% (2021) to 13.4% (2024), as originally published as originally published (W200 records the 2026 release and revision question)

L38.name: Scarcity raises existing home values
L38.plain: When homes are scarce, the homes that already exist sell for more, so owners' equity grows relative to renters' wealth.
L38.sign_meaning: When housing scarcity rises, existing home values and owners' equity tend to rise.
L38.mechanism: Scarcity raises the price of the existing stock, so owner equity rises relative to renters
L38.citation: Fischel 2001; Fed SCF owner-renter wealth gap 1989-2022; Glaeser and Gyourko 2018

L39.name: Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing
L39.plain: Owners whose wealth sits in their home attend zoning hearings and object to new construction nearby, which keeps supply short.
L39.sign_meaning: When owners' equity rises, housing scarcity tends to increase.
L39.qualification: Einstein, Glick and Palmer (2019) found that people commenting at Massachusetts planning and zoning meetings were disproportionately older homeowners opposed to new housing; the study does not separate equity from other motives, such as traffic or school crowding.
L39.mechanism: Owners with equity at stake organize to block supply (homevoter politics); the zoning room is filled by owners
L39.citation: Fischel 2001; Einstein, Glick and Palmer 2019, Neighborhood Defenders

L40.name: Housing scarcity weakens household financial security
L40.plain: Scarce housing pushes rents up, and higher rent each month leaves less for savings and emergencies.
L40.sign_meaning: When housing scarcity rises, household financial security tends to fall.
L40.citation: JCHS State of the Nation's Housing

L41.name: Partisan hostility lowers trust in government
L41.plain: People who dislike the other party see its time in power as illegitimate, so their trust falls whenever it governs.
L41.sign_meaning: When hostility toward the other party rises, trust in government tends to fall.
L41.qualification: The evidence (Hetherington and Rudolph 2015) concerns survey trust, which falls among supporters of the party out of power regardless of performance; that is a different quantity from trust earned by performance.
L41.citation: Hetherington and Rudolph 2015, Why Washington Won't Work

L42.name: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats
L42.plain: Officeholders who draw district lines can pack or split voters to make their seats safer, and redrawing between censuses repeats the effect sooner.
L42.sign_meaning: When officeholders control more of the rules, safe seats tend to increase.
L42.qualification: Residential sorting also produces safe seats without any map drawing (Chen and Rodden 2013), so the count of safe seats has more than one cause.
L42.mechanism: Incumbent-drawn maps produce safe seats; mid-decade redraws removed the decennial delay
L42.citation: CRS IF13082 (2025-26 redistricting); Texas Aug 2025; California Prop 50

L44.name: Restrictive access rules widen turnout gaps
L44.plain: Rules that make registering or voting harder lower turnout most among the groups that face the highest costs.
L44.sign_meaning: When incumbents' control over election rules grows, turnout tends to become less equal.
L44.qualification: Effects differ by rule: Cantoni and Pons (2021) found voter ID laws had effects near zero, while registration barriers had larger ones.
L44.mechanism: Access restrictions lower turnout among affected groups; effects of ID laws near zero, registration barriers larger
L44.citation: Cantoni and Pons 2021, QJE; McGhee and Romero (AVR)

L45.name: Broad turnout makes entrenchment harder
L45.plain: A wider, more representative electorate is harder to draw maps or set rules against, especially in closely divided states.
L45.sign_meaning: When turnout becomes more equal, officeholders' control over election rules tends to weaken.
L45.qualification: The evidence (Grumbach 2022) comes from comparisons across states; which party gains from broader turnout varies by state and year.
L45.mechanism: A broader electorate is harder to entrench against; composition effects matter in close states

L46.name: Hostility increases demand for hostile content
L46.plain: Hostile partisans click on and share attacks on the other side, and outlets supply more of what holds that audience.
L46.sign_meaning: When hostility toward the other party rises, exposure to hostile content tends to rise.
L46.qualification: The supply-side evidence is one case: internal messages released in Dominion v. Fox (2023) showed coverage choices made to keep an audience. The demand side has no separate estimate in this model.
L46.mechanism: Hostility raises demand for and supply of hostile content (Dominion discovery shows the supply-side choice)

L47.name: Hostile content may raise partisan hostility slightly
L47.plain: Repeated exposure to posts that attack the other party can make people feel colder toward its supporters, though measured effects are small.
L47.sign_meaning: When exposure to hostile content rises, hostility toward the other party tends to rise slightly.
L47.qualification: Large randomized feed experiments in 2020 and 2023 changed exposure a great deal and found precisely estimated null effects on partisan hostility. A 10-day 2024 reranking test on X moved out-party warmth about 2 points on a 0 to 100 scale, and four weeks off Facebook in 2018 cut a polarization index by 0.16 standard deviations.
L47.mechanism: Exposure to hostile content raises hostility. Large randomized feed changes moved exposure a lot and affective polarization little or not at all (precisely estimated nulls in 2020 and 2023 experiments); a 2024 reranking test moved out-party warmth about 2 points on a 0-100 scale; four weeks off Facebook in 2018 cut a polarization index by 0.16 SD. The effect exists at the margin and is small.
L47.citation: Guess et al. 2023 (W090); Nyhan et al. 2023 (W091); Allcott et al. 2024 (W093); Gauthier et al. 2026 (W095); Piccardi et al. 2025 (W096); Allcott et al. 2020 (W094); Budak et al. 2024 on concentrated exposure (W098)

L48.name: Visible policy problems prompt state experiments
L48.plain: When a problem becomes visible, states and cities try their own fixes, often through ballot initiatives.
L48.sign_meaning: When policy favoritism grows, state and local testing of reforms tends to increase.
L48.qualification: The diffusion research (Walker 1969; Boehmke and Skinner 2012) shows how policies spread among states; the trigger from favoritism to new experiments has no direct test.
L48.mechanism: Visible problems drive state and local experiments, often by initiative

L49.name: Proven state reforms can reduce policy favoritism
L49.plain: Reforms that work in one state spread to others and sometimes become federal law, which can undo advantages built into older rules.
L49.sign_meaning: When state and local testing increases, policy advantages for insiders tend to shrink.
L49.qualification: Spread is documented: automatic voter registration went from Oregon in 2016 to 24 states plus DC by 2026. Adoption elsewhere does not by itself show a reform worked, and state preemption can stop the spread.
L49.mechanism: Proven reforms spread and are sometimes adopted federally; preemption cuts the link
L49.citation: AVR diffusion Oregon 2016 to 24 states (documented); Grumbach 2022 on preemption

L50.name: Partisan loyalty shields incumbents from voter punishment
L50.plain: Strong partisans rarely vote against their own party's candidate, even one who breaks democratic norms, so the threat of losing shrinks.
L50.sign_meaning: When hostility toward the other party rises, the risk of losing office tends to fall.
L50.qualification: Graham and Svolik (2020) found in survey experiments with 1,691 U.S. respondents that about 3.5% of respondents defected from their own party's candidate in realistic matchups, and the average penalty across all matchups was 11.7 points.
L50.mechanism: Few partisans abandon a co-partisan who violates democratic norms

L51.name: Electoral pressure restrains unilateral presidential action
L51.plain: Presidents who face voters, or whose party does, hold back from unpopular actions taken without Congress.
L51.sign_meaning: When electoral pressure rises, presidential action without new legislation tends to fall.
L51.qualification: The restraint works through public opinion and the reaction in Congress (Christenson and Kriner 2020), so it weakens when partisans do not punish their own side.
L51.citation: Howell 2003; Christenson and Kriner 2020, The Myth of the Imperial Presidency

L52.name: Unilateral action deepens partisan hostility
L52.plain: When a president acts alone on major questions, supporters of the other party feel threatened, which can deepen their hostility.
L52.sign_meaning: When presidential action without new legislation rises, hostility toward the other party tends to rise.
L52.qualification: This rests on social identity research (Mason 2018); no direct test of unilateral action's effect on partisan hostility is cited.
L52.mechanism: Unilateral escalation raises identity threat on the other side

L53.name: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves
L53.plain: Officeholders who face little risk of losing can redraw maps and change election rules to protect their position.
L53.sign_meaning: When the risk of losing office falls, officeholders' control over election rules tends to grow.
L53.qualification: The evidence is events, chiefly the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control, and legal analysis (Hasen 2020); no study measures this link directly.
L53.mechanism: Officials who cannot be removed write rules for themselves
L53.citation: Mid-decade redistricting 2025 in safe trifectas (event); Hasen 2020

LX1.name: Automation weakens workers' bargaining power
LX1.plain: Machines and software that take over routine tasks reduce demand for some workers and lower the share of income paid as wages.
LX1.sign_meaning: When technical capability expands, workers' bargaining power tends to fall.
LX1.qualification: The evidence (Acemoglu and Restrepo 2020) covers industrial robots and measures employment and wages; any effect of generative AI runs through AI use at work and is contested.
LX1.mechanism: Automation of routine tasks lowers the labor share (well-supported). Generative AI's effect runs through adoption (TC3) and is contested; see the technology layer.

LX2.name: Residential sorting creates safe seats
LX2.plain: When one party's voters cluster in cities, districts become lopsided even when no one draws them to be.
LX2.sign_meaning: When residential sorting increases, safe seats tend to increase.
LX2.mechanism: Urban concentration of one party produces safe seats without intent

LX3.name: Trade shocks lower local household security
LX3.plain: Import competition closed factories in exposed areas, and lower employment and earnings there persisted for a decade or more.
LX3.sign_meaning: When trade exposure rises, household financial security in exposed places tends to fall.
LX3.qualification: The study (Autor, Dorn and Hanson 2013) covers Chinese import competition from 1990 to 2007 in local labor markets; it is a regional effect, and national gains from trade are measured separately.
LX3.mechanism: Trade shocks lower local employment and earnings for a decade or more

LX4.name: Foreign operations add hostile political content
LX4.plain: Foreign influence campaigns post material meant to inflame divisions between the parties.
LX4.sign_meaning: When foreign interference increases, exposure to hostile content tends to increase.
LX4.qualification: A study of Russian accounts on Twitter in 2016 (Eady and coauthors 2023) found 1% of users accounted for 70% of exposures, and domestic sources supplied far more political content.
LX4.mechanism: Foreign operations add hostile content; measured exposure was concentrated (1% of users, 70% of exposures) and dwarfed by domestic sources

LX5.name: Emergencies expand presidential power
LX5.plain: Wars, pandemics and disasters lead presidents to declare emergencies, and the powers those declarations unlock are rarely given back in full.
LX5.sign_meaning: When major shocks occur, presidential action without new legislation tends to rise.
LX5.mechanism: Emergencies expand unilateral power and rarely fully retract
LX5.citation: Brennan Center emergency powers tracker; 2001, 2020, 2025 declarations

T01.name: Competitive politics may sustain demand for local news
T01.plain: Where officials can lose, residents and advertisers may have more reason to pay for coverage of local races and local government.
T01.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more electoral pressure goes with more local reporting, and weak pressure with less demand for it.
T01.qualification: Hypothesis with no cited study. It is the only step that closes loop R16, so that whole loop stays unconfirmed until this step is tested.
T01.mechanism: Accountable local politics sustains demand for local news

T02.name: Concentrated platforms may amplify hostile content
T02.plain: Platforms built to maximize engagement may rank emotional and hostile posts higher because those posts draw more reactions.
T02.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more market concentration goes with more exposure to hostile content.
T02.qualification: Hypothesis. The cited study (Brady and coauthors 2017) found an association between moral and emotional words and sharing on Twitter; it did not test market concentration.

T03.name: Oversight corrects failing public services
T03.plain: Audits and investigations identify what is failing in a program, and agencies that act on the findings deliver services more reliably.
T03.sign_meaning: When oversight grows stronger, the quality of public services tends to rise.
T03.qualification: The evidence is GAO's count of recommendations that agencies implemented; it shows corrections were made, and the resulting change in service quality is not measured.

T04.name: Partisan hostility makes lean seats safe
T04.plain: When voters stick with one party in every race, districts that lean slightly toward a party become hard to flip.
T04.sign_meaning: When hostility toward the other party rises, safe seats tend to increase.
T04.qualification: Martin and Webster (2020) found that residential sorting explains little of the trend in safe seats, so this link runs through straight-ticket voting, whose size here is not measured directly.
T04.mechanism: Straight-ticket voting makes lean seats safe; the residential-sorting channel is contradicted
T04.citation: Martin and Webster 2020, PSRM (contradicts sorting channel)

T05.name: State control limits local reform experiments
T05.plain: State legislatures can ban local choices, such as ranked-choice voting, and make citizen initiatives harder to pass.
T05.sign_meaning: When officeholders control more of the rules, state and local testing of reforms tends to fall.
T05.qualification: By a 2026 count from the National Conference of State Legislatures, 19 states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections. Ohio's August 2023 Issue 1, which would have raised the vote needed to amend the state constitution to 60%, was rejected by voters.
T05.mechanism: Preemption of local electoral choice; initiative-threshold increases

T06.name: Data and computing scale favor large firms
T06.plain: Firms with more data and computing power can serve more customers at lower cost, which helps the largest firms grow their share.
T06.sign_meaning: When technical capability expands, market concentration tends to rise.
T06.qualification: The cited source (Philippon 2019) attributes most of the rise in U.S. concentration to weaker competition and regulation; scale economies from data and computing apply mainly in digital markets.

T07.name: Synthetic media cuts the cost of hostile content
T07.plain: Tools that generate text, images and video make it cheaper to produce large amounts of political content that attacks the other side.
T07.sign_meaning: When technical capability expands, exposure to hostile content tends to rise.
T07.qualification: Lower production cost is the supported part; whether more content produced means more content seen depends on platform ranking and has not been measured.
T07.mechanism: Synthetic media lowers the cost of hostile content

T08.name: Trade shocks deepen partisan polarization
T08.plain: Districts hit hard by import competition replaced moderate members of Congress with more partisan ones.
T08.sign_meaning: When trade exposure rises, hostility toward the other party tends to rise.
T08.qualification: Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Majlesi (2020) measured the ideology of elected members and party vote shares from 2002 to 2010, which differs from voters' feelings toward the other party.
T08.mechanism: Trade-exposed districts removed moderates and polarized
T08.citation: Autor, Dorn, Hanson and Majlesi 2020, AER

T09.name: Capital mobility shields top wealth from taxes
T09.plain: Wealth that can move abroad or into offshore accounts is harder to tax, so more of it stays and grows at the top.
T09.sign_meaning: When capital becomes more mobile, wealth tends to become more concentrated at the top.
T09.qualification: Zucman (2015) estimated hidden offshore wealth worldwide; how much this moves the U.S. top wealth share is not estimated in this model.
T09.mechanism: Capital mobility limits taxation of wealth

T10.name: Foreign interference can lower trust in elections
T10.plain: A lasting effect of foreign influence campaigns can be doubt about whether elections are legitimate.
T10.sign_meaning: When foreign interference increases, trust tends to fall.
T10.qualification: This rests on the discussion section of one study (Eady and coauthors 2023), which found no relationship between exposure and attitudes or voting; the effect on trust was not tested.
T10.mechanism: Doubt about election legitimacy as the main secondary effect

T11.name: Disasters reduce household financial security
T11.plain: Disaster losses, and insurers leaving high-risk areas, raise costs and destroy savings for the households affected.
T11.sign_meaning: When major shocks increase, household financial security tends to fall.
T11.citation: Treasury FIO 2025 report on climate and insurance

L54.name: Removing incumbents improves performance of those remaining
L54.plain: When officials see colleagues lose office, those who remain have reason to perform better, and replacements can bring better performance.
L54.sign_meaning: When more incumbents are defeated or pushed to retire, the quality of public services tends to rise.
L54.qualification: The main study (Ferraz and Finan 2011) found that Brazilian mayors who could run again misused less federal money than mayors facing term limits; U.S. service quality was not studied.
L54.mechanism: Replacement, and the demonstration that it happens, improves performance among those who remain
L54.citation: Ferraz and Finan 2011 (audits and reelection incentives); Besley 2006

T12.name: Rising home equity lowers the top wealth share
T12.plain: Homes are the main asset of middle-class households, so when house prices rise faster than stocks, the top 1%'s share of wealth tends to fall.
T12.sign_meaning: When owners' equity rises, all else equal, wealth tends to become less concentrated at the top.
T12.qualification: Kuhn, Schularick and Steins (2020) found this pattern in U.S. data from 1949 to 2016. In 2026 Q2 stock gains outran real estate gains about ten to one, and the top 1% share reached a record 32.5%.
T12.mechanism: Owner equity is the main asset of middle-class households, while the top 1% hold mostly equities and business assets. When house prices rise faster than stocks, the top 1% share of wealth falls, all else equal; when stocks lead, it rises. In 2026 Q2 equities added about ten times as much as real estate and the top 1% share reached a record 32.5%.
T12.citation: Kuhn, Schularick and Steins 2020, JPE (W073); Fed Z.1 and DFA 2026 Q2 (W003, W006)

L55.name: Safe seats keep majorities in power
L55.plain: When most seats are safe, a swing in the popular vote flips few seats, so the same party keeps control of the chamber.
L55.sign_meaning: When safe seats increase, majority control tends to become more entrenched.
L55.qualification: Seat safety is documented (Unite America's 2026 count, an advocacy source); the effect on how long majorities last relies on seats-votes analysis with no single estimate in this model.
L55.mechanism: When most seats are safe, the majority rarely flips: the seats-votes curve flattens and control persists through swings in the popular vote.
L55.citation: Unite America 2026 (W017) for seat safety; seats-votes analysis in the redistricting literature

L56.name: Durable majorities control maps and voting rules
L56.plain: A party that holds the legislature for years can redraw districts and change access rules, as Texas, Missouri, North Carolina and Ohio did in 2025 and 2026.
L56.sign_meaning: When majority control becomes more entrenched, officeholders' control over election rules tends to grow.
L56.qualification: Courts and voters can block the step: Missouri's 2025 map was set aside for 2026 by court order pending a November 3, 2026 referendum, and California voters approved Proposition 50 in November 2025 at the legislature's request.
L56.mechanism: A durable majority uses its hold on the legislature to draw maps and set access rules. The 2025-26 mid-decade redraws were passed by unified state governments in Texas, Missouri, North Carolina and Ohio, and answered by California voters at a legislature's request.
L56.citation: Map record in loop R4a case (); People Not Politicians v. Onder order (W043); Allen v. Milligan stay order (W045)

L57.name: Durable Senate majorities shape court appointments
L57.plain: A Senate majority working with a president of the same party decides which judges are confirmed, so over decades the courts take on the outlook of the coalitions that held the Senate.
L57.sign_meaning: When majority control is more entrenched, court rulings favoring the appointing coalition tend to increase.
L57.qualification: Confirmations are documented; whether later rulings favor the appointing coalition is a pattern read across decisions, and some 2025 to 2026 rulings went against it. Each state's two Senate seats, regardless of population, are a fixed feature of this step.
L57.mechanism: A durable Senate majority, with the presidency, decides which judges are confirmed; over decades the bench takes on the outlook of the coalitions that held the Senate. Senate malapportionment is a fixed parameter on this link.

LE01.name: Public research investment raises productivity
LE01.plain: Government-funded research and infrastructure raise what private businesses can produce per hour, with effects that take a decade or more to appear.
