LE01.sign_meaning: When public investment rises, labor productivity tends to rise.
LE01.qualification: Fieldhouse and Mertens (a 2024 working paper) estimate returns of 140 to 210% on nondefense research spending with wide confidence bands, and Gross and Sampat (2023) studied one wartime program, so the size of the effect is uncertain.
LE01.mechanism: Public research and infrastructure raise private productivity with long lags.
LE01.citation: Fieldhouse and Mertens (W056): returns of 140-210% on nondefense R&D; Gross and Sampat (W057): WWII research seeded lasting clusters
LE01.counterevidence: One identification strategy each; wide confidence bands; a wartime shock may not generalize.

LE02.name: Congress decides public investment levels
LE02.plain: Congress writes the laws that set how much the government invests in research and infrastructure, and on what terms.
LE02.sign_meaning: This line shows who has the power to decide. It does not say which way they will decide.
LE02.qualification: Money appropriated and money spent can differ for years: as of July 31, 2026, 75.7% of the infrastructure law's transportation funds were obligated and 46.6% spent (Department of Transportation).
LE02.mechanism: Congress appropriates public investment and sets its terms.

LE03.name: The executive administers appropriated public investment
LE03.plain: Agencies under the president decide when to award, delay or cancel funds Congress has appropriated, within limits set by the Impoundment Control Act.
LE03.sign_meaning: This line shows who has the power to decide. It does not say which way they will decide.
LE03.qualification: GAO documented in 2026 that $7.8 billion of $11 billion in CHIPS research awards had been canceled; whether a given withholding is lawful is decided case by case.
LE03.mechanism: The executive can withhold, cancel or redirect appropriated investment. In 2025-26, $7.8 billion of $11 billion in CHIPS research awards was canceled.

LE04.name: Productivity growth partly raises household income
LE04.plain: When workers produce more per hour, pay tends to rise as well, though by less than the productivity gain for many workers.
LE04.sign_meaning: When productivity grows faster, household income tends to grow faster, by a smaller amount.
LE04.qualification: Contested. Stansbury and Summers estimate 0.7 to 1.0 point of average pay growth per point of productivity growth (0.4 to 0.7 for nonsupervisory workers); the Economic Policy Institute, an advocacy group, reports a wider gap, much of it from the choice of price index and the exclusion of benefits.
LE04.mechanism: Faster productivity growth goes with faster pay growth, though not one for one.
LE04.citation: Stansbury and Summers (W089): 0.7-1.0 point of pay per point of productivity on average, 0.4-0.7 for nonsupervisory workers
LE04.counterevidence: EPI (W088) shows productivity +93.7% against typical compensation +32.7% since 1979; much of that gap is the choice of price index and the exclusion of benefits.

LE05.name: Bargaining power raises workers' share of income
LE05.plain: Where workers can bargain or quit easily, employers pay out more of each dollar of output as wages.
LE05.sign_meaning: When bargaining power rises, workers' share of income tends to rise.
LE05.qualification: Yeh, Macaluso and Hershbein (2022) estimate that U.S. manufacturing plants pay about 65 cents per marginal dollar of product; the estimate rests on assumptions about how plants produce output.
LE05.mechanism: Where workers can bargain or quit easily, more of each dollar of output is paid as wages.
LE05.citation: Yeh, Macaluso and Hershbein (W087): plants pay about 65 cents per marginal dollar of product
LE05.counterevidence: Markdown estimates rest on production-function assumptions.

LE06.name: Market concentration lowers workers' income share
LE06.plain: As sales shift to large firms that pay out a smaller share of revenue as wages and charge higher markups, the economy-wide labor share falls.
LE06.sign_meaning: When markets become more concentrated, workers' share of income tends to fall.
LE06.qualification: Contested. Basu (2019) found current methods cannot tell stable markups from modestly rising ones, and Rossi-Hansberg and coauthors found local concentration fell from 1990 to 2014 while national concentration rose.
LE06.mechanism: Sales shift to large, low-labor-share firms, and markups rise, so the economy-wide labor share falls.
LE06.citation: Autor et al. (W085); De Loecker, Eeckhout and Unger (W083)
LE06.counterevidence: Basu (W084): current methods cannot tell stable from modestly rising markups; Rossi-Hansberg et al. (W086): local concentration fell while national rose.

LE07.name: Workers' income share feeds household income
LE07.plain: The labor share is the part of income paid to workers, so when it falls, households that live on wages receive less of what the economy produces.
LE07.sign_meaning: When workers' share of income rises, household income tends to rise.
LE07.qualification: Household income also includes transfers and investment income, and total output can grow, so a falling labor share does not by itself mean falling household income.
LE07.mechanism: The labor share is the part of income paid as compensation; households that live on wages get less of output when it falls.

LE08.name: A falling labor share may concentrate stock ownership
LE08.plain: A smaller labor share leaves a larger share of income for capital, which raises the value of stocks held mostly by the wealthiest households.
LE08.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: when workers' share of income falls, stock ownership tends to become more concentrated.
LE08.qualification: A larger capital share raises income to stockholders and does not by itself make ownership more concentrated; that depends on who holds the shares, including pension funds and middle-income retirement accounts.
LE08.mechanism: A smaller labor share is a larger capital share, which accrues to the owners of equity and raises what that equity is worth.
LE08.citation: BLS labor share (W008); DFA equity holdings (W112)
LE08.counterevidence: Capital income also flows to pension funds and retirement accounts held by the middle.

LE09.name: Concentrated stock ownership raises top wealth share
LE09.plain: Stocks are the main asset of the top 1%, so with ownership concentrated, rising stock prices push their share of all wealth up.
LE09.sign_meaning: When stock ownership becomes more concentrated, wealth tends to become more concentrated at the top.
LE09.qualification: The documented quarter shows a price effect: household equities rose $10.7 trillion in 2026 Q2 and the top 1% share reached 32.5% (Federal Reserve). Changes in who owns stock move more slowly.
LE09.mechanism: Equities are the top 1%'s main asset, so stock gains raise the top share of wealth. In 2026 Q2 household equities rose $10.7 trillion and the top 1% share reached a record 32.5%.
LE09.citation: Fed Z.1 (W006); DFA (W003, W112); Kuhn, Schularick and Steins (W073)

LE10.name: Mortgage credit bids up home equity
LE10.plain: More mortgage lending lets buyers bid more for a fixed number of homes, which raises prices and the equity of current owners.
LE10.sign_meaning: When more credit flows to mortgages, homeowners' equity tends to rise.
LE10.qualification: Favara and Imbs (2015) studied bank branching deregulation in the 1990s and found the price effect where housing supply could not expand; where builders can add homes, more of the credit goes into construction.
LE10.mechanism: More mortgage credit, with supply fixed, bids up house prices and owner equity.
LE10.citation: Favara and Imbs 2015 (W202); Bank of England on money creation (W058)
LE10.counterevidence: Estimated on 1990s branching deregulation; effects depend on how elastic supply is.

LE11.name: Private credit may concentrate business ownership
LE11.plain: Bank loans to private credit funds and other nonbank lenders pay for debt-financed purchases of businesses, which can place ownership in fewer hands.
LE11.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more credit to nonbank lenders goes with more concentrated ownership.
LE11.qualification: Hypothesis. The growth of this lending is documented (FDIC: about 22% a year from 2010 to 2024); its effect on who owns businesses or stocks has not been measured.
LE11.mechanism: Lending to nonbank lenders and private credit funds finances leveraged purchases of businesses, concentrating ownership.
LE11.citation: FDIC on nonbank lending growth (W061); Fed Financial Stability Report (W062)
LE11.counterevidence: Growth is documented; the effect on ownership concentration is not measured.

LE12.name: Insider-tilted tax law reduces net household support
LE12.plain: Tax breaks steered toward the top lower the net support that taxes and benefits give households below the median.
LE12.sign_meaning: When policy favors insiders more, net support from taxes and benefits for households below the median tends to fall.
LE12.qualification: CBO estimated that the 2025 law (Public Law 119-21) lowers resources for the bottom tenth of households by about $1,200 a year and raises the top tenth's by about $13,600 (2026 to 2034 averages, static estimates without behavioral responses).
LE12.mechanism: Insider-tilted tax law steers tax expenditures to the top, which lowers net support for households below the median. The 2025 law cuts resources for the bottom decile by about $1,200 a year and raises the top decile's by about $13,600.
LE12.citation: CBO tax expenditures (W064); CBO on P.L. 119-21 (W065)
LE12.counterevidence: Static distribution tables; behavioral responses are not modeled.

LE13.name: Net support raises households' spendable income
LE13.plain: Benefits add to what a household can spend and taxes subtract from it, so more net support raises income after taxes and transfers.
LE13.sign_meaning: When net support toward a group of households rises, that group's income after taxes and transfers tends to rise.
LE13.qualification: Read the arrow for the households receiving net support. CBO found the top 1%'s share of income falls from 18% to 14% after taxes and transfers (2022), so the same system lowers income shares at the top.
LE13.mechanism: Taxes and transfers change what a household can spend. CBO finds the top 1% share falls from 18% to 14% after taxes and transfers.

LE14.name: Public benefits lift households out of poverty
LE14.plain: Transfers such as Social Security and refundable tax credits lift people above the poverty line and give them room to absorb a shock.
LE14.sign_meaning: When net support from taxes and benefits rises, household financial security tends to rise.
LE14.qualification: Census reported that Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty in 2025; the effect depends on which benefit grows and on who pays the taxes that fund it.
LE14.mechanism: Transfers lift people above the poverty line. Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of SPM poverty in 2025; the 2021 child credit cut child poverty to 5.2%.

LE15.name: Higher income strengthens household security
LE15.plain: More income leaves more room to cover bills and to save a cushion for an unexpected expense.
LE15.sign_meaning: When household income rises, financial security tends to rise.
LE15.citation: Fed SHED (W074): 63% could cover a $400 expense with cash

LE16.name: Essential costs reduce household security
LE16.plain: Rent, child care, health premiums and insurance take income before anything can be saved.
LE16.sign_meaning: When essential costs rise, household financial security tends to fall.
LE16.qualification: The child care price ($13,184 on average in 2025) comes from Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group compiling state data.
LE16.mechanism: Rent, care, health premiums and insurance take income before anything is saved.
LE16.citation: JCHS (W013); Child Care Aware (W015, advocacy compilation); KFF (W014); SHED (W074)

LE17.name: Housing scarcity raises rents and prices
LE17.plain: When homes are scarce, renters and buyers compete for the same units, which pushes rents and prices up.
LE17.sign_meaning: When housing scarcity rises, essential costs tend to rise.
LE17.mechanism: Scarce housing raises rents and prices.
LE17.citation: JCHS (W013); register records under loop R8

LE18.name: Tariffs raise prices U.S. buyers pay
LE18.plain: Importers pay tariffs when goods enter the country and pass most of the cost on to U.S. businesses and consumers.
LE18.sign_meaning: When tariff costs rise, essential costs tend to rise.
LE18.qualification: New York Fed researchers found U.S. importers bore 94% of the burden from January to August 2025 and 86% by November, so the split shifts as contracts are repriced; tariffs reach essentials only through goods households buy.
LE18.mechanism: Tariffs are paid mostly by U.S. buyers and show up in prices.
LE18.citation: Amiti et al. (W070); Clausing and Obstfeld (W071); Yale Budget Lab (W069)
LE18.counterevidence: Incidence shifts over time as contracts reprice.

LE19.name: The executive sets tariff rates
LE19.plain: The president sets most tariff rates under trade laws Congress passed, and courts review whether each law allows the action taken.
LE19.sign_meaning: This line shows who has the power to decide. It does not say which way they will decide.
LE19.qualification: The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in February 2026 (Learning Resources v. Trump) that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs; most of those tariffs were replaced under Sections 122, 232 and 301.
LE19.mechanism: Tariff rates are set by executive action under delegated statutes. The Supreme Court struck the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026; most were replaced under Sections 122, 232 and 301.
LE19.citation: Learning Resources v. Trump (W029); Yale Budget Lab (W069)

LE20.name: Climate hazard raises insurance costs
LE20.plain: Insurers charge more, or decline to renew policies, where climate damage is more likely, which adds to housing costs.
LE20.sign_meaning: When climate hazard rises, essential costs tend to rise.
LE20.qualification: Treasury's Federal Insurance Office found the highest-risk fifth of ZIP codes paid 82% more for homeowners insurance than the lowest-risk fifth (2018 to 2022 data); the insurance industry disputed the data.
LE20.mechanism: Higher hazard raises insurance premiums and nonrenewals.

LE21.name: Disasters raise measured hazard and losses
LE21.plain: Each large disaster adds to recorded losses and changes how insurers and lenders price risk in exposed places.
LE21.sign_meaning: When major shocks occur, climate hazard and insurance costs tend to rise.
LE21.qualification: Counts of billion-dollar disasters (23 in 2025, compiled by Climate Central after NOAA retired its database in May 2025) mix rising hazard with more property in harm's way.
LE21.mechanism: Disasters raise measured hazard and losses.
LE21.counterevidence: Billion-dollar counts mix rising hazard with more exposed property.

LE22.name: Emissions add to long-run climate hazard
LE22.plain: Greenhouse gases build up in the atmosphere and raise the risk of extreme weather, and U.S. emissions are one part of that global total.
LE22.sign_meaning: When emissions rise, climate hazard tends to rise over decades, through the global stock of greenhouse gases.
LE22.qualification: This link follows emissions only. More electricity use raises hazard only to the extent its sources emit greenhouse gases, and U.S. emissions affect U.S. hazard only through the global stock.
LE22.mechanism: Emissions add to the global stock of greenhouse gases that raises hazard; any one country's share is a fraction of the global total.
LE22.counterevidence: U.S. emissions move U.S. hazard only through the global stock.

LE23.name: Climate risk weighs on home equity
LE23.plain: In high-hazard places, rising insurance costs and fewer available policies lower what buyers will pay, which cuts owners' equity.
LE23.sign_meaning: When climate hazard and insurance costs rise, homeowners' equity in exposed places tends to fall.
LE23.qualification: The evidence is Treasury's 2025 insurance analysis; no direct estimate of the effect on home prices is cited, and the effect concentrates in exposed areas.
LE23.mechanism: In high-hazard places, insurance cost and availability weigh on home values and owner equity.

LE24.name: Income builds household savings and assets
LE24.plain: Households save from income, so higher income over time adds to assets or pays down debt.
LE24.sign_meaning: When household income rises, household balance sheets tend to strengthen.
LE24.qualification: Income is a flow per year and the balance sheet is a stock, so a year of higher income adds to wealth only by the part that is saved.
LE24.mechanism: Income is what households save from.

LE25.name: Home equity strengthens owners' balance sheets
LE25.plain: Home equity is most owners' largest asset, so when it grows, their net worth grows.
LE25.sign_meaning: When homeowners' equity rises, household balance sheets tend to strengthen for owners.
LE25.qualification: The 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances put median net worth at $396,200 for homeowners and $10,400 for renters; renters gain nothing through this link.
LE25.mechanism: Home equity is most owners' largest asset; owners' median net worth is about 38 times renters'.

LE26.name: Essential costs drain savings and add debt
LE26.plain: When essentials cost more, households draw down savings or borrow to keep up.
LE26.sign_meaning: When essential costs rise, household balance sheets tend to weaken.
LE26.qualification: The Federal Reserve's survey for 2025 found 23% of renters fell behind on rent and 26% of adults skipped medical care because of cost; these show strain, and the drain on savings is not measured directly.
LE26.mechanism: High essential costs drain savings and add debt.
LE26.citation: SHED (W074): 23% of renters fell behind; 26% skipped care due to cost; KFF medical debt (W075)

LE27.name: Savings make shocks survivable
LE27.plain: A household with savings and manageable debt can absorb a lost paycheck or a large bill without falling behind.
LE27.sign_meaning: When balance sheets strengthen, household financial security tends to rise.
LE27.mechanism: Savings and lower debt make a shock survivable.

LT01.name: Engagement-ranked feeds raise hostile-content exposure
LT01.plain: Compared with a time-ordered feed, ranking built to hold attention changes what people see, and in a 2020 Facebook and Instagram experiment it showed more uncivil content.
LT01.sign_meaning: When more of a feed is ranked for engagement, compared with a time-ordered feed, exposure to hostile content tends to rise.
LT01.qualification: The direction depends on the platform and the content: in the 2020 experiment the time-ordered feed showed more political and untrustworthy content and less uncivil content, and in 2023 X's algorithm raised the share of conservative political content its users saw.
LT01.mechanism: Ranking decides what people see. Switching feeds to chronological raised political and untrustworthy content and cut uncivil content; X's algorithm raised the share of conservative political content its users saw.
LT01.citation: Guess et al. 2023 (W090); Gauthier et al. 2026 (W095); Piccardi et al. 2025 (W096)

LT02.name: Platform concentration may entrench engagement ranking
LT02.plain: When a few firms own the main feeds, a few ranking rules govern most attention, and advertising revenue rewards ranking for engagement.
LT02.sign_meaning: The proposed direction: more concentration among platforms goes with more reliance on engagement ranking.
LT02.qualification: Hypothesis. No study isolates the effect of concentration on ranking design, and smaller competing platforms also rank for engagement.
LT02.mechanism: When a few firms own the feeds, a few ranking objectives govern most attention, and ad-funded objectives favor engagement.
LT02.counterevidence: No study isolates concentration's effect on ranking design; competing platforms also optimize for engagement.

LT03.name: Platforms drew ad revenue from local news
LT03.plain: Advertising that once paid for local reporting moved to large platforms, and newsrooms shrank as revenue fell.
LT03.sign_meaning: When platforms and digital advertising become more concentrated, local reporting tends to shrink.
LT03.qualification: Newspaper ad revenue fell from about $49.4 billion (2005) to about $9.8 billion (2022, Pew). The strongest causal evidence covers Craigslist and classified ads, which cut coverage of local House members about 30%; for search and social advertising the link is plausible.
LT03.mechanism: Platforms took the advertising that paid for local reporting. Newspaper ad revenue fell from about $49.4 billion (2005) to about $9.8 billion (2022); where Craigslist arrived, newsroom staff fell and coverage of local House members dropped about 30%.
LT03.counterevidence: The strongest causal design covers classifieds, not search or social ads; for those the link is plausible.

LT04.name: AI use at work raises productivity modestly
LT04.plain: AI tools let workers finish some tasks faster, which raises output per hour where those tasks are common.
LT04.sign_meaning: When AI use at work rises, labor productivity tends to rise.
LT04.qualification: Contested. Acemoglu (2024) estimates at most about 0.66% higher total factor productivity over ten years, and a Danish study found chatbots saved about 2.8% of work hours; private forecasts run several times higher.
LT04.mechanism: AI tools raise output per hour where tasks are exposed.
LT04.citation: Acemoglu (W114): at most about 0.66% higher TFP over ten years; Humlum and Vestergaard (W105): about 2.8% of work hours saved
LT04.counterevidence: Private forecasts run several times higher; early measured gains are small.

LT05.name: AI adoption may weaken entry-level workers' position
LT05.plain: Where AI can do tasks that new hires used to learn on, employers may hire fewer young workers in exposed jobs, which weakens their position.
LT05.sign_meaning: When AI use at work rises, the bargaining power of entry-level workers in exposed jobs tends to fall, by a contested amount.
LT05.qualification: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (2025) found a 13% relative employment decline for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most exposed occupations. A Danish study ruled out earnings effects above 1 to 2%, and company research by Anthropic, which makes AI tools, found a barely significant drop in job-finding for exposed 22- to 25-year-olds.
LT05.mechanism: AI adoption weakens the position of entry-level workers in exposed jobs.
LT05.citation: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (W104): 13% relative employment decline for workers 22-25 in the most exposed occupations
LT05.counterevidence: Humlum and Vestergaard (W105) rule out earnings effects above 1-2% in Denmark; Yale Budget Lab (W106) finds no clear unemployment trend by exposure; Anthropic (W107, the author's company makes AI tools) finds a barely significant drop in job-finding for exposed 22-25-year-olds.

LT06.name: New AI capability enables workplace adoption
LT06.plain: New capabilities make adoption possible, and cost, training and fit with existing work decide how fast employers take them up.
LT06.sign_meaning: When technical capability expands, AI use at work tends to rise.
LT06.mechanism: New capability makes adoption possible; cost and training decide how fast.

LT07.name: Frontier AI concentrates computing capital in few firms
LT07.plain: Building frontier models takes computing power that only a few firms can afford, so gains in capability concentrate capital among them.
LT07.sign_meaning: When technical capability expands, AI capital and computing power tend to become more concentrated.
LT07.qualification: Stanford's AI Index reports nearly 90% of notable 2024 models came from industry; the firm spending figures come from a secondary compilation whose definitions vary.
LT07.mechanism: Frontier models need compute that few firms can buy, so capability gains concentrate capital.

LT08.name: AI capital gains flow to concentrated stockholders
LT08.plain: Returns from AI investment go to the firms' shareholders, and the top tenth of households holds about 88% of household stocks and mutual funds.
LT08.sign_meaning: When AI capital becomes more concentrated, stock ownership tends to become more concentrated.
LT08.qualification: The link shows who gains when AI firms' shares rise. Whether ownership itself becomes more concentrated depends on who buys and sells the shares, including retirement funds.
LT08.mechanism: Gains to AI capital accrue to equity holders, and the top tenth holds about 88% of household equities.

LT09.name: AI computing build-outs raise data-center load
LT09.plain: The computing capacity built for AI sits in data centers that draw large amounts of power from the grid.
LT09.sign_meaning: When more computing capacity is built for AI, data centers' demand on the grid tends to rise.
LT09.qualification: Documented for the amount of computing built: data centers used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023, and projections rise with planned build-outs. Concentration among firms is a separate variable (TC4), which reaches demand only through how much gets built (LT19).
LT09.mechanism: Compute build-outs are data centers that draw power.

LT10.name: Data centers raise electricity demand
LT10.plain: Data centers run around the clock, so each new facility adds to total electricity use.
LT10.sign_meaning: When data-center load rises, energy demand tends to rise.
LT10.qualification: This link raises electricity demand. The emissions that follow depend on how the added power is generated, so the energy and emissions parts of the receiving variable can move apart.

LT11.name: Data-center load raises household electricity bills
LT11.plain: In some grids, data-center demand pushes up the price utilities pay for generating capacity, and part of that cost passes into household bills.
LT11.sign_meaning: When data-center load rises, essential costs tend to rise in affected grids.
LT11.qualification: Documented for PJM, the grid operator for all or parts of 13 states and DC: its market monitor attributes $23.1 billion across three capacity auctions to data-center load, and PJM projected bill increases of 1.5 to 5% for some customers. Other grids differ.
LT11.mechanism: Capacity prices driven by data-center load pass into household bills. In PJM, the market monitor attributes $23.1 billion across three auctions to that load; PJM projected bill increases of 1.5-5% for some customers.
LT11.counterevidence: Documented for PJM; other grids differ.

LT12.name: Shared-data pricing software can raise rents
LT12.plain: When landlords feed competitors' private data into the same pricing software, it can recommend higher rents than competition would produce.
LT12.sign_meaning: When more landlords use shared-data pricing software, essential costs tend to rise.
LT12.qualification: Contested. The RealPage final judgment, entered May 19, 2026, includes no admission of wrongdoing, and estimates of the rent effect vary.
LT12.mechanism: Pricing software fed by competitors' nonpublic data can raise rents.
LT12.citation: DOJ RealPage final judgment and response to comments (W127)
LT12.counterevidence: The settlement includes no admission; estimates of the rent effect vary.

LT13.name: Antitrust enforcers decide what pricing software may do
LT13.plain: Antitrust agencies and courts can bar software that pools competitors' private data for live pricing, as the RealPage final judgment does.
LT13.sign_meaning: This line shows who has the power to decide. It does not say which way they will decide.
LT13.qualification: The proposed decree requires training data at least 12 months old and an outside monitor; court entry was pending as of May 2026.
LT13.mechanism: Antitrust enforcement can bar shared nonpublic data in live pricing. The RealPage judgment requires training data at least 12 months old and a monitor.

LT14.name: States and cities set rules for pricing software
LT14.plain: State and local governments can ban algorithmic rent coordination or require sellers to disclose algorithmic pricing, as New York did in 2025.
LT14.sign_meaning: This line shows who has the power to decide. It does not say which way they will decide.
LT14.mechanism: States and cities can ban algorithmic rent coordination or require disclosure (New York, 2025).

LT15.name: In-house digital teams improve service delivery
LT15.plain: Agencies that can build and run their own software deliver benefits and refunds with fewer failures.
LT15.sign_meaning: When government's digital capacity rises, the quality of public services tends to rise.
LT15.qualification: The evidence is case studies (HealthCare.gov's 2013 launch, unemployment insurance payment errors, Direct File's use in 2024 and 2025) without a controlled comparison.
LT15.mechanism: Agencies that can build and run their own digital services deliver benefits and refunds with fewer failures.
LT15.citation: GAO on HealthCare.gov (W117); GAO on UI improper payments (W118); Direct File volumes (W120)
LT15.counterevidence: Case evidence, not a controlled comparison.

LT16.name: The executive opens and closes federal digital teams
LT16.plain: Digital service teams created by executive decision can be closed by a later one, as with 18F in March 2025 and Direct File for the 2026 filing season.
LT16.sign_meaning: This line shows who has the power to decide. It does not say which way they will decide.
LT16.mechanism: Digital service teams built by executive decision can be closed by the next one: 18F closed in March 2025 and Direct File was not offered for 2026.
LT16.citation: Federal News Network (W119); CPA Practice Advisor (W120)

LT17.name: Congress decides funding for government digital capacity
LT17.plain: Congress funds agency technology and can create digital teams in law, though most IT money now goes to maintaining old systems.
LT17.sign_meaning: This line shows who has the power to decide. It does not say which way they will decide.
LT17.qualification: GAO reported in 2025 that about 80% of federal IT spending goes to operating and maintaining existing systems, the most critical of which are 23 to 60 years old.
LT17.mechanism: Congress funds and can charter in-house digital capacity; most IT money goes to maintaining old systems.

LT18.name: Generative AI cheapens production of hostile content
LT18.plain: Generative tools let one operator produce large volumes of attacking political posts, images and video at low cost.
LT18.sign_meaning: When technical capability expands, exposure to hostile content tends to rise.
LT18.qualification: This connection makes the same claim as T07: Synthetic media cuts the cost of hostile content, with the same variables and mechanism, so the two count as one piece of evidence; producing more content raises exposure only if platforms distribute it.
LT18.mechanism: Synthetic media lowers the cost of producing hostile content.

LT19.name: Concentrated AI capital may speed computing build-outs
LT19.plain: Firms that hold most of the capital for AI can finance very large data-center projects, so concentration may add to how much computing gets built.
LT19.sign_meaning: When a few firms hold more of the capital used for AI, the amount of computing built for AI may rise.
LT19.qualification: Hypothesis. The largest firms account for most reported AI capital spending, which fits the link, and no study separates the effect of concentration from overall demand for AI computing. Competition among many firms could also drive building.
LT19.mechanism: Concentrated capital can fund large build-outs.

R1.title: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other
R1.summary: Households with concentrated wealth can spend more on campaigns, outside groups and lobbying. That spending can win rules, such as low tax rates on investment income, that add to wealth at the top. The added wealth pays for the next round of spending.
R1.how_to_read: Concentration of household wealth raises money spent to influence politics, which raises policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, which in turn raise the concentration of household wealth.
R1.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R1.evidence_summary: The first and last steps are well supported: L01: Concentrated wealth funds more political spending rests on donor records, and L03: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top on CBO's accounting of who receives tax benefits. The middle step, L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors, is plausible and the weakest. A 2016 field experiment found that donors get meetings, and since affluent and middle-income Americans want the same policy about 90% of the time, any tilt shows only where they disagree.
R1.qualification: The loop runs on issues where wealthy donors' preferences differ from those of middle-income voters; on most issues the two groups agree, so its reach depends on the issue.
R1.case: Ohio House Bill 6: about $60 million routed through a nonprofit that did not disclose its donors helped pass a ratepayer-funded bailout of power plants, and former Speaker Larry Householder, a Republican, was sentenced to 20 years in June 2023. In Illinois, former Speaker Michael Madigan, a Democrat, was convicted in the ComEd bribery case in February 2025 and sentenced to 7.5 years. Both ended in criminal convictions for trading money for policy; they do not show how often lawful spending changes policy.
R1.reference_mode: Top 1% wealth share 22.8% (1989) to 32.5% (2026Q2, a record)
R1.nonlinearity: FEC quorum is a binary enforcement switch (zero since May 2025); NRSC v. FEC raised the coordination ceiling
R1.adaptation: Money re-routes: 527s (2004), super PACs and 501(c)(4)s (2010), party-coordinated spending (2026)
R1.valence: Harmful in current direction; would be benign if wealth were dispersed
R1.fix: Disclosure with a private right of action; an FEC that can act (quorum first, structure later); channel-specific limits. Matching is a candidate-entry fix, not an R1 fix (Kilborn and Vishwanath 2022).

R1b.title: Political spending and court rulings reinforce each other
R1b.summary: Money spent on politics pays for confirmation campaigns and test cases that shape which judges sit and which questions they hear. Those judges set the legal limits on political spending. Wider limits let more money into the next round.
R1b.how_to_read: Money spent to influence politics raises court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, which raise the money spent to influence politics.
R1b.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R1b.evidence_summary: L05: Court rulings widen permitted political spending is documented in decisions from Buckley v. Valeo (1976) to NRSC v. FEC (2026). The weakest step is L04: Political money helps shape judicial confirmations, graded plausible: the cited work is a history of organized legal movements (Teles 2008), with no estimate of how much money changes confirmations.
R1b.qualification: The doctrine variable has no published scoring rule and is read through named decisions, and nothing in the evidence ties a donation to a particular ruling.
R1b.case: On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court struck the limits on party-coordinated spending in NRSC v. FEC, following Citizens United (2010) and McCutcheon (2014). The rulings document the second step, courts widening permitted spending. They do not establish that political money shaped the appointments behind them.
R1b.nonlinearity: Step changes at rulings; five-justice threshold
R1b.valence: Harmful to equal voice; the doctrine treats spending as speech
R1b.fix: Eighteen-year Court terms; a fixed appointment cadence

R2.title: Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise
R2.summary: When Congress cuts its own analysts, members and committees lean on analysis supplied by interested industries. Policy drafted that way can tilt toward those industries. Rules that favor them can weaken support for rebuilding public expertise.
R2.how_to_read: Congress's ability to write and check policy lowers policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, and those advantages lower Congress's ability to write and check policy; two negative steps make the loop reinforcing.
R2.evidence_summary: Both steps are hypotheses. L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence draws on studies of reliance on lobbyists (Drutman 2015) and on model bills in state legislatures (Hertel-Fernandez 2019). The return step, L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise, is the weakest, since it rests on a single event: the 1995 staff cuts.
R2.qualification: Staff losses and lobbying totals are documented, and neither step has been tested, so the loop is a proposed explanation for the pattern.
R2.case: The House cut committee staff from 2,147 in 1993 to 1,266 in 1995, about 41%, and closed the Office of Technology Assessment (143 staff, $21.3 million budget). Reported federal lobbying passed $5 billion in 2025. The figures document lost capacity and the scale of lobbying; they do not show that either caused the other.
R2.adaptation: Lobbyists supply drafting where staff is thin
R2.valence: Harmful; Congress depends on interested expertise
R2.fix: Restore committee and support-agency staff; publish who drafted what

R3.title: Political hostility and hostile content may reinforce each other
R3.summary: People who dislike the other party seek out and share posts that attack it, and outlets and platforms supply more of them. Exposure to those posts may then raise hostility slightly. The proposed loop asks whether the two feed each other over time.
R3.how_to_read: Hostility toward the other political party raises exposure to hostile political content, which raises hostility toward the other political party.
R3.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R3.evidence_summary: L46: Hostility increases demand for hostile content is plausible, and its supply side rests on internal messages released in Dominion v. Fox (2023). The return step, L47: Hostile content may raise partisan hostility slightly, is contested and the weakest. Randomized feed experiments in 2020 and 2023 changed exposure a great deal and found precisely estimated null effects on partisan hostility, while a 2024 reranking test moved out-party warmth about 2 points on a 0 to 100 scale.
R3.qualification: Measured effects of exposure on hostility are small. A 2026 study of X (Gauthier and coauthors) found the feed algorithm moved users' policy priorities about a tenth of a standard deviation toward conservative positions with no effect on partisan hostility; policy views are a separate outcome from hostility.
R3.case: In a 2024 test with 1,256 X users over 10 days (Piccardi and coauthors), reranking posts that expressed partisan animosity moved feelings toward the other party by about 2 points in either direction. Internal messages released in Dominion v. Fox (2023) showed coverage choices made to hold an audience. The cases show each step can occur over days; they do not show the loop sustaining itself over years.
R3.nonlinearity: Attention saturation; exposure concentrated in a small share of users
R3.adaptation: Feed changes alter exposure without altering attitudes; users re-follow the same accounts (Gauthier et al. 2026)
R3.valence: Harmful if it runs; the best experiments find small or null short-run effects
R3.fix: Feed choice by default; ad archives with sponsor labels

R4a.title: Majorities draw maps that help them keep control
R4a.summary: A legislative majority draws district maps that make many of its seats safe. With most seats safe, swings in the popular vote flip few seats, so the majority holds on. Holding on lets it draw the next map.
R4a.how_to_read: Officeholders' control over election rules raises the number of seats with little electoral competition, which raises entrenched control of rule-setting institutions, which raises officeholders' control over election rules.
R4a.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R4a.evidence_summary: Two steps are documented by the 2025 to 2026 mid-decade redraws: L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats and L56: Durable majorities control maps and voting rules. The weakest is L55: Safe seats keep majorities in power, graded plausible, because seat safety is documented while its effect on how long majorities last rests on seats-votes analysis without a single estimate.
R4a.qualification: Courts and voters can interrupt the loop, as in Missouri, where the 2025 map is set aside for 2026 pending a November 3 referendum. Voters' residential sorting also makes seats safe without any map.
R4a.case: Texas's Republican-led legislature redrew its congressional map in August 2025, aiming at five more Republican seats, and California voters answered in November 2025 by approving Proposition 50 (64%), a map drawn to favor Democrats. After Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026), four Southern states redrew maps that removed majority-Black districts. In September 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court ordered Missouri's 2022 map used for the 2026 election, and Missouri voters decide Proposition A on the 2025 map on November 3, 2026. These events document the map-drawing steps; they do not measure how much the new maps extend any majority's hold.
R4a.evidence: documented for C4 to C1 and D7 to C4; plausible for C1 to D7
R4a.reference_mode: Share of seats decided by over 10 points, 1992 to 2024
R4a.nonlinearity: Requires a trifecta; mid-decade redraws removed the ten-year delay
R4a.adaptation: Commissions bypassed by voter override (Prop 50) or court maps; Rucho and Callais remove federal constraints
R4a.valence: Harmful to competition; the loop is neutral to which party runs it
R4a.fix: Citizen commissions (a fairness fix, not a competition fix); multi-member districts (2 U.S.C. 2c is one statute)

R4b.title: Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable
R4b.summary: Officeholders who control election rules can make registering or voting harder. Turnout then falls most among the groups facing the highest costs, and the electorate becomes less equal. A narrower electorate is easier to hold power against.
R4b.how_to_read: Officeholders' control over election rules lowers the equality of voter turnout, and less equal turnout raises officeholders' control over election rules; two negative steps make the loop reinforcing.
R4b.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R4b.evidence_summary: L44: Restrictive access rules widen turnout gaps is well supported for registration barriers, though voter ID laws showed effects near zero (Cantoni and Pons 2021). The return step, L45: Broad turnout makes entrenchment harder, is plausible and the weaker of the two; it rests on comparisons across states (Grumbach 2022).
R4b.qualification: Effects differ by rule and by state, so the existence of a restriction does not establish its size or which party gains from it.
R4b.case: After Shelby County v. Holder (June 2013) ended federal preclearance, covered states began changing voting rules within hours. Louisiana v. Callais (April 29, 2026) read Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act to require a strong inference of intent, and four states redrew within weeks. The cases document rule changes and do not measure the turnout gaps that followed.
R4b.reference_mode: Turnout gap by income quintile, 1980 to 2024
R4b.nonlinearity: Turnout effects of ID laws near zero; registration barriers larger
R4b.adaptation: Rules shift from ID to registration purges, drop-box limits, and Section 2 litigation after Callais
R4b.fix: Automatic registration; a federal floor for access; a Callais response in statute

R5.title: Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions
R5.summary: Households under financial strain have less time and money to spare for voting and public meetings. With turnout unequal, officeholders respond more to those who vote, and rules tilt toward wealthier and organized interests. Rules of that kind, such as letting a benefit lapse, leave struggling households with even less room.
R5.how_to_read: Households' financial security raises the equality of voter turnout; more equal turnout lowers policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, and those advantages lower households' financial security.
R5.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R5.evidence_summary: L35: Financial security makes turnout more equal is well supported (Schlozman, Verba and Brady 2012), and so is L37: Insider-tilted benefit rules reduce household security, through Census poverty data on benefits that expired. The middle step, L36: More equal turnout reduces policy favoritism, is plausible and the weakest: its main evidence is Australia's adoption of compulsory voting in the early 20th century (Fowler 2013).
R5.qualification: Time, money and civic skills each affect turnout, and the evidence does not support treating lack of free time as the single cause.
R5.case: Census survey data show about 80% of citizens in households above $100,000 voted in 2020, against about half of those below $30,000. The figures document the turnout gap in the first step. They do not show that the gap changed any policy.
R5.nonlinearity: Benefit cliffs (I121) make A4 a step function of earnings
R5.adaptation: Administrative burden substitutes for benefit cuts (I062)
R5.valence: Harmful; insecurity silences the people policy ignores
R5.fix: Automatic, universal benefits; meetings when workers can attend; on-cycle local elections

R6.title: Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other
R6.summary: When workers have less bargaining power, more of the income from production goes to owners, and wealth concentrates. Concentrated wealth funds political spending that can tilt labor law and its enforcement. Weaker labor rules leave workers with even less bargaining power.
R6.how_to_read: Workers' bargaining power lowers the concentration of household wealth; that concentration raises money spent to influence politics, which raises policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, which lower workers' bargaining power.
R6.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R6.evidence_summary: L30: Worker bargaining power limits top wealth concentration and L01: Concentrated wealth funds more political spending are well supported. The political steps are plausible: L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors carries the limits described for loop R1, and L31: Insider-tilted labor rules weaken worker bargaining rests on legal events from the Taft-Hartley Act (1947) to the labor board's period without a quorum in 2025. The weakest is L02.
R6.qualification: The bargaining-to-wealth step comes from studies of income inequality, and wealth also moves with asset prices; the political steps that close the loop share the limits of loop R1.
R6.case: Union membership fell from 20.1% of U.S. wage and salary workers in 1983 to 10.0% in 2025 (BLS; the 2025 figure is an eleven-month average). Workers at Amazon's JFK8 warehouse voted to unionize in April 2022, the National Labor Relations Board ordered bargaining in April 2026, and no contract had been reached in the latest reports. The case shows how long a first contract can take; it does not measure any effect on wealth.
R6.evidence: well-supported for A2 to A1; plausible for the rest
R6.nonlinearity: NLRB quorum; right-to-work as a state step
R6.adaptation: Employers shift to misclassification and subcontracting (I102, I103)
R6.fix: Fast remedies for retaliation; first-contract arbitration; sector boards

R7.title: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other
R7.summary: When a public service works, the people who use it gain a reason to trust the agency. Trust supports compliance and tax revenue, which help keep the service working. Run in reverse, a failing service loses trust and with it the support it needs.
R7.how_to_read: The quality of public services raises trust earned through performance, which raises the quality of public services.
R7.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R7.evidence_summary: Both steps are graded plausible. In L20: Better public services build earned trust, survey trust also moves with which party holds office (Hetherington 2005). L21: Earned trust supports compliance and service funding works through compliance and revenue, which tax morale research supports; its funding channel is a hypothesis and the weakest part of the loop.
R7.qualification: No study has measured the complete loop, and the claim that a service failure makes the next budget cut easier is a hypothesis.
R7.case: The 43-day federal shutdown (October 1 to November 12, 2025) furloughed about 670,000 employees, left about 730,000 working unpaid, cut flights at 40 airports and stopped the October jobs survey. The shutdown establishes a service failure. It does not show that the failure lowered trust, or that lower trust reduced funding; those steps carry their own grades.
R7.evidence: hypothesis for the named direction; plausible for the compliance channel; the delivery leg is documented case by case in the Delivery Log, though no study measures the loop closing
R7.nonlinearity: Trust floor: Congress at 9% may not fall further; further D5 failures may register nothing
R7.adaptation: Blame shifts to the out-party rather than to the institution
R7.valence: Direction-neutral loop; currently running down. Two channels: political support for funding ( R7) and voluntary compliance and revenue ( R17). R9 is its participation channel, kept as a design target.
R7.fix: Visible delivery, then say who delivered it; automatic continuing resolutions (they reduce pressure to finish budgets); statutory civil-service protection; funded evaluation

R8.title: Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building
R8.summary: When homes are scarce, the homes that exist sell for more, and owners' equity grows. Owners with that equity at stake attend zoning hearings and oppose new construction. Less construction keeps homes scarce.
R8.how_to_read: Housing scarcity raises homeowners' equity, which raises housing scarcity.
R8.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R8.evidence_summary: Both steps are well supported. L38: Scarcity raises existing home values rests on house-price studies and the owner-renter wealth gap in the Survey of Consumer Finances (1989 to 2022). L39: Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing rests on homevoter research (Fischel 2001) and records of Massachusetts planning meetings (Einstein, Glick and Palmer 2019); it is the weaker step because equity is one motive among several for opposing construction.
R8.qualification: The loop follows owners' equity and the gap between owners and renters. Rising home equity tends to lower the top 1% share of wealth (T12: Rising home equity lowers the top wealth share), so this loop does not explain that share.
R8.case: Auckland, New Zealand, upzoned in 2016; within five years the upzoned areas had permits for thousands of additional homes, about 4% of the housing stock, compared with a control (Greenaway-McGrevy and Phillips 2023). A companion working paper estimates three-bedroom rents 22 to 35% below a synthetic control six years on. In Minneapolis, rents rose about 1% from 2017 to 2022 against 14% in the rest of Minnesota, and the Minneapolis Fed attributes much of that gap to a 2020 drop in demand. These cases test the remedy of building more homes; they do not test the owner-opposition step.
R8.evidence: well-supported for both links; the loop no longer depends on A1
R8.nonlinearity: Build cycles; interest-rate lock-in of owners after 2022
R8.adaptation: Design review, parking, historic designation, litigation after zoning preemption
R8.valence: Harmful to entrants; beneficial to incumbent owners, which is why it persists
R8.fix: Legal housing near jobs by statute above the zoning room (Auckland 2016; Montana 2023; MBTA Communities); a renter seat at the table by design (on-cycle local elections, hearings when renters can attend)

R10.title: Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates
R10.summary: In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it. With little threat in November, officeholders answer to that smaller electorate and face less pressure from the wider public. Officials who cannot easily be removed can then write election rules that keep seats safe.
R10.how_to_read: Seats with little electoral competition raise how often the primary decides the winner, which lowers the risk of losing office; lower risk raises officeholders' control over election rules, which raises the number of seats with little electoral competition.
R10.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R10.evidence_summary: L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive and L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats are documented, and L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure is well supported. The weakest step is L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves, graded plausible: its evidence is the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control and legal analysis. Whether primaries make legislators more extreme is a separate, contested question, and the strongest tests found no effect.
R10.qualification: Seat safety also comes from where voters live, and the claim that primary reform makes legislators more moderate is contested, so the loop concerns accountability more than ideology.
R10.case: Alaska's top-four primary with ranked-choice general elections survived a 2024 repeal measure by 743 votes out of 321,203 after a December 2024 recount. A second repeal is on the November 3, 2026 ballot, combined with repeal of the state's rule requiring disclosure of the true source of political donations. One election cycle is too short to show the design's long-run effect on accountability.
R10.evidence: documented for C1 to C2; well-supported for C2 to C3; plausible for C3 to C4 (the weakest link)
R10.reference_mode: Share of House seats settled in primaries, 2012 to 2024
R10.nonlinearity: A seat becomes 'safe' above about a 10-point margin; Unite America, using Cook ratings rather than a margin threshold, counts 87% of House seats as effectively decided in the 2024 primaries and 88% in 2026
R10.adaptation: Parties coordinate candidates under top-four (Alaska 2024); repeal campaigns; state preemption of local reform
R10.valence: Harmful to accountability; the polarization branch (L09) is contested and drawn with a dash-dot line
R10.fix: Widen the deciding electorate: top-four with ranked general (Alaska) or a single all-party primary (California, Washington); commissions for fairness; multi-member districts for competition. Drop the moderation claim.

R11.title: Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms
R11.summary: Voters who dislike the other party rarely punish their own side for breaking democratic norms. That lowers the electoral risk of acting without Congress. Unilateral action by one side then raises the other side's sense of threat and its hostility.
R11.how_to_read: Hostility toward the other political party lowers the risk of losing office; lower risk raises presidential action without new legislation, which raises hostility toward the other political party.
R11.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R11.evidence_summary: Survey experiments (Graham and Svolik 2020) give strong support to L50: Partisan loyalty shields incumbents from voter punishment, and studies of presidential power back L51: Electoral pressure restrains unilateral presidential action (Howell 2003; Christenson and Kriner 2020). The weakest step is L52: Unilateral action deepens partisan hostility, graded plausible, which rests on social identity research (Mason 2018) without a direct test.
R11.qualification: In realistic matchups only about 3.5% of respondents defected from a norm-breaking candidate of their own party, which can decide close races, so the loop bites hardest where seats are safe.
R11.case: In survey experiments with 1,691 U.S. respondents (Graham and Svolik, published 2020), about 3.5% of respondents defected from their own party's candidate in realistic matchups, and the average penalty across all matchups was 11.7 points. The study establishes the first step and leaves untested whether unilateral action raises hostility.
R11.evidence: well-supported for B4 to C3; plausible for the rest
R11.reference_mode: Bright Line Watch norm-violation tolerance 2017 to 2026
R11.nonlinearity: Partisan asymmetry: the penalty is smaller when the violator is on your side
R11.adaptation: Party leaders frame violations as responses to the other side's violations
R11.fix: Electoral rules that reward coalition-building; common-identity institutions

R12.title: Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules
R12.summary: A majority that holds rule-setting bodies for years, including the Senate, decides which judges are confirmed. The courts then rule on maps, voting access and political money, and some rulings widen incumbents' control of election rules. That control produces safe seats that keep the majority in place.
R12.how_to_read: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition raise officeholders' control over election rules, which raises the number of seats with little electoral competition, which raises entrenched control of rule-setting institutions, which raises court rulings favoring the appointing coalition.
R12.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R12.evidence_summary: L06: Court rulings expand incumbents' control of election rules and L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats are documented. L55: Safe seats keep majorities in power and L57: Durable Senate majorities shape court appointments are plausible, and L57 is the weakest: the pattern of favorable rulings is read across decisions without a scoring rule, and some 2025 to 2026 rulings went against the appointing coalition.
R12.qualification: Senate seats are not drawn by district maps, so the step from safe seats to Senate confirmations runs through long-run party control of states; each state's two Senate seats, regardless of population, are a fixed feature of that step.
R12.case: The model reads Citizens United (2010), Shelby County (2013), Rucho (2019), Loper Bright (2024), Trump v. United States (2024), Trump v. Slaughter (2026) and Louisiana v. Callais (2026) as one sequence of rulings favoring the appointing coalition. Rulings in the 2025 to 2026 term also went the other way, including Trump v. Cook, Trump v. Illinois, Learning Resources and Barbara. The sequence documents the rulings; it does not show that the appointing coalition's hold on power produced them.
R12.evidence: documented for D3 to C4; plausible for C1 to D7 and D7 to D3
R12.nonlinearity: Appointment cohorts; life tenure makes the delay decades
R12.valence: Harmful to neutrality of the referee; neutral as to which coalition
R12.fix: Eighteen-year terms and a fixed appointment cadence; enforceable ethics

R13.title: Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action
R13.summary: When Congress cannot pass laws, presidents act alone through orders, emergencies, tariffs and spending freezes. Each time the executive settles a question, members of Congress have less reason to build the capacity to legislate. A weaker Congress leaves more room for the next unilateral act.
R13.how_to_read: Congress's ability to write and check policy lowers presidential action without new legislation, and that action lowers Congress's ability to write and check policy; two negative steps make the loop reinforcing.
R13.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R13.evidence_summary: L11: A weaker Congress invites presidential action is well supported (Howell 2003). The return step, L12: Presidential action erodes Congress's will to legislate, is plausible and the weaker, resting on legal and historical analysis (Chafetz 2017).
R13.qualification: Court rulings can strengthen or limit the executive from outside the loop, as the February 2026 tariff ruling did, so the loop's pace depends on doctrine.
R13.case: The Supreme Court struck the tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act in Learning Resources v. Trump (February 2026), and most were replaced under Sections 122, 232 and 301. Inspectors general were removed in January 2025, and a September 26, 2025 stay allowed a pocket rescission because the Impoundment Control Act gives grant recipients no cause of action. These events document unilateral action and do not measure any change in Congress's capacity.
R13.evidence: well-supported for D1 to D2; plausible for D2 to D1
R13.reference_mode: National emergencies in force; substantive bills enacted per Congress
R13.nonlinearity: 60-vote cloture threshold makes D1's output a step function of seats
R13.adaptation: Executive substitutes statutory authorities when one is struck (IEEPA to Sections 122, 232, 301)
R13.valence: Harmful to legislative government; amplified by L13 (doctrine), which sits outside the loop
R13.fix: Sunset clauses on emergencies; an express cause of action under the ICA; filibuster reform with a first-use rule on neutral structural items

R15.title: Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other
R15.summary: Workers with bargaining power sustain unions and other organizations that bring people of different incomes and parties together. Those ties draw members to the polls, so turnout becomes more equal. Policy that answers to a broader electorate is less likely to weaken workers' ability to organize.
R15.how_to_read: Workers' bargaining power raises civic ties across social and political groups, which raise the equality of voter turnout; more equal turnout lowers policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests, which lower workers' bargaining power.
R15.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R15.evidence_summary: L34: Civic ties make turnout more equal is well supported (Rosenstone and Hansen 1993). The other three steps, L32: Strong unions build cross-group civic ties, L36: More equal turnout reduces policy favoritism and L31: Insider-tilted labor rules weaken worker bargaining, are plausible, and the weakest is L32 because unions' effect on ties beyond the workplace is not measured.
R15.qualification: The complete loop has not been measured, and its main support comes from books on civic decline that describe trends without isolating this chain.
R15.case: Putnam's Bowling Alone (2000) and The Upswing (2020) and Skocpol's Diminished Democracy (2003) document the decline of membership organizations in the 20th century. These are works of scholarship and no single dated case is on record for this loop; the books do not test the full chain.
R15.valence: Harmful to efficacy and cross-class contact
R15.fix: Funded local institutions; unions; service; on-cycle local elections

R16.title: Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other
R16.summary: Local reporting tells voters what officials do, which draws challengers and raises the risk incumbents face. A proposed return step says competitive local politics keeps up demand for that reporting. If it holds, losing a paper weakens pressure, and weaker pressure leaves less demand for the next paper.
R16.how_to_read: Availability of local reporting raises the risk of losing office, and that risk is proposed to raise the availability of local reporting.
R16.evidence_summary: L26: Local reporting raises pressure on incumbents is well supported by studies of mayoral elections (Rubado and Jennings 2020). The return step, T01: Competitive politics may sustain demand for local news, is a hypothesis with no cited study and the weakest step; it alone closes the loop. A separate connection, L27: Local reporting can temper partisan hostility, links local reporting to partisan hostility and sits outside this loop.
R16.qualification: Until the return step is tested, the loop is a proposal, and the evidence supports only the one-way effect of local reporting on electoral pressure.
R16.case: Medill's 2025 State of Local News report (October 20, 2025) counted 213 counties with no local news source and about 50 million people with limited or no access to local news. A study of municipal bonds by Gao, Lee and Murphy (Journal of Financial Economics, 2020) found that after a local newspaper closes, borrowing costs for the county's governments rise by 5 to 11 basis points.
R16.evidence: well-supported for the step from local reporting to the risk of losing office; hypothesis for the closing step
R16.reference_mode: Counties with no local news source 2004 to 2025
R16.nonlinearity: Most advertising revenue has already left local news, so further effects of A3: Market concentration on Variable B2: Availability of local reporting are small.
R16.adaptation: Ghost papers and pink-slime sites substitute for local reporting
R16.valence: Harmful; note the loop closes only through a hypothesized demand link (T01)
R16.fix: Independent local-news funds; state tax credits for local reporting; an evaluation, because the fix side has none

R18.title: Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action
R18.summary: A president can remove inspectors general, leave commissions without a quorum or cut investigative staff. With fewer independent watchdogs, the next action taken without Congress meets less resistance. Each removal makes the next one cheaper.
R18.how_to_read: Presidential action without new legislation lowers the ability to investigate and enforce the rules, and weaker enforcement raises presidential action without new legislation; two negative steps make the loop reinforcing.
R18.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R18.evidence_summary: L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies is documented by the January 2025 removals and the Federal Election Commission's loss of a quorum on May 1, 2025. The return step, L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action, is plausible and the weaker: GAO found several 2025 impoundments unlawful, and restraint depends on courts and Congress acting on such findings.
R18.qualification: Watchdogs restrain action only when they answer to the law and their findings can be enforced, so the loop's strength depends on remedies such as subpoena enforcement and standing to sue.
R18.case: Seventeen inspectors general were removed by email on January 24, 2025, without the 30 days' notice the law requires. On September 24, 2025, a federal court said the removals 'almost undoubtedly' violated the law and reinstated no one, because the President could remove them again with proper notice; no ruling on the merits had been issued as of October 15, 2026. The case documents the first step and does not show that later actions met less resistance.
R18.evidence: documented for D2 to D4; plausible for D4 to D2
R18.reference_mode: IG vacancies and agency quorum status 2024 to 2026
R18.nonlinearity: Quorum thresholds (FEC, NLRB); notice-without-remedy converts B to R
R18.adaptation: The 2021 removals of NLRB general counsel Peter Robb and SSA commissioner Andrew Saul, both later upheld under Collins v. Yellen, are the other party's instances; each administration widens the channel the last one opened.
R18.valence: Harmful; this is 's B1b with its true polarity. When the person inspected can remove the inspector, the breaker becomes a bypass.
R18.fix: Remedies that survive Slaughter: records, succession, budget, subpoena enforcement, standing; an FEC and NLRB that keep a quorum by design

B1a.title: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism
B1a.summary: When favoritism in policy becomes visible, auditors, inspectors and prosecutors open investigations. Watchdogs that can enforce their findings correct some of it. Less favoritism leaves less to find, which is what makes this loop balancing.
B1a.how_to_read: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests raise the ability to investigate and enforce the rules, which lowers policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests.
B1a.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
B1a.evidence_summary: L16: Watchdogs reduce favoritism and waste in policy is well supported by GAO's record of corrections. L17: Visible favoritism can prompt investigations is plausible and the weaker step: investigations follow only some scandals, and a response needs a watchdog with staff and legal power.
B1a.qualification: The loop corrects only when watchdogs answer to the law and keep their staff, quorum and remedies; GAO's dollar figures count waste and errors broadly, a wider category than favoritism.
B1a.case: GAO credits its High Risk List work with $84 billion in financial benefits since 2023 and reported about $63 billion for fiscal 2025 on a budget under $1 billion, by its own accounting. The figures establish that audits produce corrections. They do not show how much of the correction concerned favoritism toward organized interests.
B1a.evidence: plausible for E1 to D4; well-supported for D4 to E1
B1a.nonlinearity: Works only with independence and a remedy
B1a.adaptation: Targets of scrutiny remove or defund the scrutinizer (R18)
B1a.valence: Beneficial when the inspector answers to the law; disabled by R18 in 2025
B1a.fix: IGs with post-Slaughter remedies; funded GAO and CRS; open records

B4.title: Electoral consequences can improve public performance
B4.summary: Poor public performance raises the risk that incumbents lose. Where seats are competitive, that risk turns into defeats or forced retirements. Officials who remain, and those who replace them, have reason to perform better, which eases the pressure again.
B4.how_to_read: The quality of public services lowers the risk of losing office; that risk raises the number of incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement, which raises the quality of public services.
B4.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
B4.evidence_summary: All three steps are well supported: retrospective voting in L23: Poor service raises incumbents' risk of losing, defeats where seats are competitive in L24: Electoral pressure leads to actual defeats, and better performance after replacement or its threat in L54: Removing incumbents improves performance of those remaining. For U.S. services the weakest is L54, since its main study covers Brazilian mayors.
B4.qualification: The loop works only where seats are competitive. The threat of defeat and an actual defeat are separate steps, and testing the loop needs evidence on both over several election cycles.
B4.case: Unite America, a reform advocacy group, counted 88% of House seats (383 of 435) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, by 22.68 million voters or 9.4% of eligible voters; its 2024 count (87%, about 7% of voting-age Americans) used a different base. In Indiana's 3rd District, the 2024 Republican primary was won with 19,507 votes, about 3.3% of the district's adults.
B4.evidence: well-supported where seats are competitive; C5 to D5 well-supported
B4.nonlinearity: Gain near zero in safe seats; retrospective voting is myopic (last-year effects dominate)
B4.adaptation: Incumbents shift blame to the other branch or party
B4.valence: The main balancing loop in the model. Its strength depends on C1: Seats with little electoral competition, C2: How often the primary decides the winner, Variable B2: Availability of local reporting and Variable B4: Hostility toward the other political party. The pressure (C3) and the sanction (C5) are separate variables.
B4.fix: Competitive general elections: the whole of Gate 1

B5.title: State and local experiments can correct policy favoritism
B5.summary: When policy favors insiders in a visible way, states and cities try their own fixes, often by ballot initiative. Reforms that work spread to other states and sometimes into federal law. As favoritism shrinks, the push for new experiments eases.
B5.how_to_read: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests raise state and local testing of reforms, which lowers policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests.
B5.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
B5.evidence_summary: Both steps are plausible. L48: Visible policy problems prompt state experiments rests on policy diffusion research (Walker 1969; Boehmke and Skinner 2012). L49: Proven state reforms can reduce policy favoritism is the weaker: the spread of reforms is documented, and whether that spread reduces favoritism is not measured.
B5.qualification: Adoption elsewhere does not show a reform worked, and state preemption and bans on local choice cut the loop (T05: State control limits local reform experiments).
B5.case: Automatic voter registration spread from Oregon in 2016 to 24 states plus DC by 2026, and paid leave reached 14 states plus DC. Running the other way, 19 states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections (2026 count). The spread is documented; it does not show the reforms reduced favoritism.
B5.reference_mode: States with AVR 2016 to 2026; states banning RCV 2022 to 2026
B5.adaptation: States ban local adoption and raise initiative thresholds after voters use them
B5.fix: Protect state and local experimentation; the ballot-initiative route

B2.title: Automatic benefits cushion economic shocks
B2.summary: When a recession cuts earnings, benefits written into law, such as unemployment insurance, expand without a new vote. The added support offsets part of the hardship households face. As hardship eases, the automatic payments shrink again.
B2.how_to_read: Household hardship, the reverse of households' financial security, raises automatic support, and automatic support lowers household hardship; neither arrow is a numbered connection.
B2.evidence_summary: The model grades the mechanism well supported. Neither step is a numbered connection with its own citation, so the evidence cannot be inspected step by step, and that missing chain is the weakest point.
B2.qualification: Only benefits with triggers in law respond automatically. The 2021 expanded child tax credit was a one-year decision that expired on a set date, so it shows what a permanent design could do without being an instance of one.
B2.case: Unemployment insurance expanded in 2009 and 2020 as joblessness rose. SPM child poverty fell from 9.7% in 2020 to 5.2% in 2021 under the expanded child tax credit, then rose to 13.4% in 2024 after the credit lapsed (as first published; Census revised the 2019 to 2024 rates in 2026). The child-credit series measures a temporary benefit's effect and supports the case for an automatic design; the credit itself had no automatic trigger, so it falls outside this loop's record.
B2.adaptation: Legislatures let discretionary versions expire (2021 credit)
B2.valence: Beneficial; side panel on A4, not drawn on the master map because it has no political feedback of its own
B2.fix: Triggers written into law instead of waiting on Congress

B3.title: New competitors can limit market power
B3.summary: High profits in a market attract new sellers. A new rival gives customers a choice and pushes prices and profits down. Lower profits leave less reason for further entry.
B3.how_to_read: Excess profits raise entry by new firms, entry raises competitive pressure, and competitive pressure lowers excess profits; all three are concepts outside the numbered model.
B3.evidence_summary: The model grades the mechanism well supported where entry is possible. Its three variables sit outside the model's numbered variables and none of its steps is a numbered connection, so the weakest point is the missing chain.
B3.qualification: Entry needs access, financing and scale, and vertical integration or serial acquisitions can block it, so high profits in a concentrated market do not guarantee that a rival appears.
B3.case: The three largest pharmacy benefit managers handle about 80% of U.S. prescriptions and own pharmacies they steer patients to. An FTC interim staff report (January 2025) found their affiliated pharmacies took in $7.3 billion above acquisition cost on 51 specialty generic drugs from 2017 to 2022, a measure of revenue above cost that differs from profit. The case shows a market where entry has not restored competition, which illustrates the loop failing; the related FTC insulin case had no final order as of October 14, 2026.
B3.nonlinearity: Network effects and vertical integration set entry cost above any profit signal
B3.adaptation: Fees shift to affiliates (PBM GPOs); serial acquisitions below review thresholds
B3.fix: Merger review with teeth; structural separation where conduct rules fail

R9.title: Taking part in a successful repair may support the next one
R9.summary: People who help make a public decision, and then see it carried out, may gain confidence that working together succeeds. That confidence could raise trust earned through performance. Higher trust could make people more willing to take part in the next effort.
R9.how_to_read: Effective participation raises accountable delivery, which raises trust earned through performance, which raises effective participation; only trust is one of the model's variables, and no arrow is a numbered connection.
R9.evidence_summary: The complete loop is a design hypothesis. Studies of citizen panels and participatory budgeting measure effects on participants, and the weakest step is the return from trust to wider participation, which has not been measured across the population.
R9.qualification: Effects are measured on the people who took part; evidence of lasting change in the wider public's trust or participation is limited.
R9.case: Oregon's Citizens' Initiative Review, participatory budgeting in New York City and the America in One Room deliberation (Fishkin and coauthors, published 2021) are the examples. Each measured changes among participants; none shows a change in trust across the public.
R9.adaptation: Consultation without a duty to respond produces cynicism (OECD)
R9.valence: Beneficial if built; the participation channel of R7
R9.fix: Citizen panels with a duty to respond; participatory budgets

core.title: Power and accountability
core.question: Which political and economic mechanisms connect influence, elections and government performance?

regions.title: Economic structure
regions.text: Who holds wealth and market power, and how scarce essentials are.

regions.title: Political inputs
regions.text: Money, organized interests, local news and public attitudes that reach officials.

regions.title: Electoral competition
regions.text: Whether officials can lose their seats, and who controls the rules of elections.

regions.title: Governing institutions
regions.text: Congress, the presidency, courts, watchdogs and the public services they run.

regions.title: Legitimacy
regions.text: Whose interests policy favors, and whether public trust follows performance.

regions.title: Outside drivers
regions.text: Conditions the model treats as given, such as technology and geography.

economy.title: How the economy reaches a household
economy.question: How does production become pay, household resources and essential costs?

regions.title: Production and income
regions.text: What the economy makes and who gets paid for it.

regions.title: Household budgets and wealth
regions.text: What a household earns, owes, owns and must pay.

regions.title: Credit, trade and environment
