regions.text: Interest rates, tariffs, climate risk and energy.

technology.title: Technology and its effects
technology.question: Which parts of technology change this system, and what have studies measured?

regions.title: Technology mechanisms
regions.text: Feed ranking, platform power, data, computing, public digital capacity, automation and pricing software.

R-01.title: All-party primaries with ranked general elections
R-01.summary: Every voter, whatever their party, could vote in one first-round election, and two or more candidates would advance to a November ballot that all voters use. In seats that one party usually wins, the choice now made in a low-turnout party primary would move to the full electorate. In Massachusetts, unenrolled voters already pick one party's ballot. Under Question 3, every voter would see all candidates on one primary ballot from 2028. The Atlas takes no position on Question 3 or Ballot Measure 2.
R-01.what_it_changes: In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure). An all-party primary sends more than one candidate to November, which aims to lower C2: How often the primary decides the winner and raise C3: Risk of losing office. A top-two design advances two candidates; a top-four design advances four and can be paired with a ranked-choice general election. The reform sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates), loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance) and loop R11 (Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms).
R-01.who_decides: States set nomination rules for state and federal offices. Where a state allows citizen initiatives, voters can change those rules at the ballot box, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska's repeal measure are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Legislatures can act by statute, rated low because legislators elected under the current rules rarely change them. Home-rule cities can adopt the approach for municipal offices (medium) unless state law bans ranked ballots. Congress could act for federal races under the Elections Clause of the Constitution, which gets the lowest feasibility rating because most bills need 60 Senate votes while the filibuster stands (R-12).
R-01.legal_authority: States control primary rules within limits the Supreme Court has set. In Jones (2000) the Court barred blanket primaries that force parties to accept nominees chosen by all voters. In Washington State Grange (2008) it upheld a top-two primary that does not name party nominees. A ranked general election also requires a state with no ban on ranked ballots.
R-01.implementation: Supporters first draft a measure and qualify it for the ballot, or a legislature passes a bill. A campaign follows. Before the first election under the new rules, election offices teach voters how the ballot works. After two election cycles, results can be judged by turnout in the round that decides each seat and by the number of contested general elections.
R-01.resources: Funding needs are low: certifying the counting method and paying for voter education. If the general election is ranked, counties also need tabulation equipment that can count ranked ballots and officials trained to use it.
R-01.enforcement: Election officials administer the rules and courts hear challenges. Parties can sue to protect their right of association. The counting method must be certified before use, and post-election audits check the results.
R-01.costs: Implementation is a small one-time cost for state and county election offices. In Massachusetts, Question 3 would take effect January 1, 2028, leaving time to prepare. Party leaders and incumbents who are secure in their primaries lose influence, first as a threat and in practice at the next open seat.
R-01.failure_risks: Party organizations in both major parties and incumbents secure in their primaries are expected to resist. Parties can coordinate so that only one of their candidates competes; in Alaska in 2024 one candidate withdrew after the top-four primary, with party consultants citing the risk of splitting the vote. Voters or legislatures can reverse the rule, and nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections. The reform can also fall short if turnout stays low in the deciding round, or if voters misread the ballot and trust in results drops.

problem_evidence.text: Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026, as reported by Unite America, an advocacy organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. Unite America's own count puts 383 seats (88%) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, which drew about 22.7 million voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. Both counts rest on ratings, which are forecasts, and on the group's definition of a safe seat.

remedy_evidence.text: More contested general elections and more candidates entering races are plausible results. Whether legislators become more moderate is contested: a 2014 study of state legislators by McGhee and colleagues found that more open primaries had little consistent effect on ideology, and experimental work finds that primary effects depend on conditions. Main limitation: Alaska's top-four system has a short record, so there is no long-run U.S. test of a top-four primary paired with a ranked general election.

R-01.tradeoffs: Parties lose control over who carries their label, and some voters lose a party ballot line they value. Ranked tabulation takes longer to count. When two candidates from the same party advance, voters from the other party have no nominee of their own in November.
success_measures: Share of seats with a competitive general election
Turnout in the round that decides each seat
Share of incumbents facing a credible general-election challenger
Voter understanding of the ballot, measured in exit surveys
Legislators' voting ideology, reported as exploratory because the best existing tests found no effect
R-01.alternatives: Open partisan primaries let voters outside a party choose that party's ballot. Fusion voting (R-47) is another option, and proportional House districts (R-03) change the general election and leave the primary as it is. Two options are set aside as rejected. Blanket primaries are unconstitutional under Jones (2000). Turnout drives in closed-primary states raise participation and leave the rules on who may vote in a primary as they are.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, two measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot would change how primaries work. Alaska's Ballot Measure 2 (petition 24ESEG) would repeal the state's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election and return to party primaries. Massachusetts voters decide Question 3, which would replace party primaries for state and congressional offices with one primary listing every candidate, the top two advancing to November; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2028. Nineteen states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, by the National Conference of State Legislatures' count.

routes.note: Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election, are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
Legislators elected under the current rules rarely change them.
This route is closed to cities and counties in the 19 states that prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, as of October 15, 2026.

R-02.title: Ranked-choice voting for single-winner races
R-02.summary: Voters would rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins more than half of the first choices, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots count for each voter's next choice, round by round. Voters who back minor-party or independent candidates would gain at the first ranked election, because a first choice for a long shot would stop helping elect the candidate they like least.
R-02.what_it_changes: Under plurality voting, two similar candidates can split their supporters and let a third candidate win; this is called the spoiler problem. Ranking removes that penalty, so more candidates can run, and it rewards candidates who seek second-choice support from other camps. The reform is linked to C3: Risk of losing office and to variable B4: Hostility toward the other political party. It sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).
R-02.who_decides: States and home-rule cities decide. Cities can adopt it by ordinance or charter where state law allows, rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030, though state bans block this route in some states. Voters in initiative states can adopt it by ballot measure (medium). Legislatures can adopt it by statute, a route rated low.
R-02.legal_authority: State election law governs the voting method. As of March 2026, 19 states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, and a statewide ban overrides city choices.
R-02.implementation: A state or city first authorizes the method. Local pilots come next. Voters are taught how to fill out the ballot before the first ranked election. After each election, officials audit the count and publish the results of every round. A certified tabulation system and the absence of a state ban are prerequisites.
R-02.resources: Funding needs are low. Jurisdictions need tabulation software that counts ranked ballots, certified before its first use.
R-02.enforcement: Election officials run the count. Certification of the tabulation method and post-election audits are the checks.
R-02.costs: The cost is small and falls on election offices for software, certification and voter education. Candidates who win plurality races because the field is split lose that advantage at the first ranked election.
R-02.failure_risks: Parties and officials in states that ban the method are likely to oppose it, and a statewide ban preempts any city that wants it. Repeals and bans have spread since 2023. The reform can also fail through voter confusion, or when slow counts are used to cast doubt on results. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Spoiler effects and vote splitting under plurality voting are documented in U.S. elections.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence that ranking improves campaign civility and voter understanding is moderate. Evidence that it raises turnout or produces more moderate winners is weak. Main limitation: some ballots drop out of the count. A 2015 study of four local ranked elections found that 9.6% to 27.1% of ballots ranked no candidate still in the final round, so winners often lacked a majority of all ballots cast.

R-02.tradeoffs: Some ballots run out of rankings before the final round, which is called ballot exhaustion. Counts take longer, and audits are more complex than for single-choice ballots.
success_measures: Number of candidates per race
Ballot exhaustion rate: the share of ballots with no ranked candidate left in the final round
Voter understanding of how to fill out the ballot, from surveys
Measures of negative campaigning
R-02.alternatives: Runoff elections address vote splitting with a second election. Approval voting, where voters mark every candidate they accept, and Condorcet methods, which pick the candidate who would beat each rival head to head, are other options. Rejected option: keeping plurality voting unchanged, because it keeps the spoiler problem.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, Alaska and Maine use ranked-choice voting in statewide elections; Ballotpedia also counts Hawaii, which uses it in a narrower set of races. FairVote, an advocacy group for ranked-choice voting, counted 36 cities and 3 counties using it or set to use it as of March 2026, New York City (for primaries) among them. Nineteen states prohibit it in some or all elections (National Conference of State Legislatures, March 2026; Ballotpedia also counted 19 in September 2026). On November 3, 2026 voters in Irvine, California, Honolulu and Longmont, Colorado decide whether to adopt it for local elections.

routes.note: Blocked in states with bans.

R-03.title: Proportional elections in multi-seat House districts
R-03.summary: Larger House districts would each elect several members, with seats shared in proportion to votes. Voters who support the minority party in a one-party region could elect someone at the first election under the new map, and incumbents in safe seats would face more competition. Small states with one or two seats would see little change.
R-03.what_it_changes: Single-member districts let maps and the way voters cluster geographically produce safe seats (L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats). With several seats per district and a proportional count, most seats become contestable and the majority tracks the vote. The aim is to lower C1: Seats with little electoral competition and D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions, even where geography sorts voters. The reform acts on loop R4a (Majorities draw maps that help them keep control), loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates) and loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules).
R-03.who_decides: Congress decides for the U.S. House by repealing the federal requirement of single-member districts (2 U.S.C. 2c) and requiring a ranked count that elects several winners; it gets the lowest feasibility rating for 2026 to 2030. State legislatures can adopt it for their own chambers (low). City councils can adopt it for local councils (medium): Cambridge, Massachusetts has counted this way since 1941, and Portland, Oregon adopted it in 2022.
R-03.legal_authority: Congress can set House district rules by statute, and current federal law requires single-member districts. A federal change needs 60 Senate votes while the filibuster stands, or filibuster reform (R-12). Any new system must also comply with the Voting Rights Act.
R-03.implementation: Pilots in state legislative chambers or city councils come first, with evaluation. A federal statute follows. The new districts would then phase in at the next apportionment, when House seats are reassigned among the states after the census.
R-03.resources: The main need is a one-time redesign of ballots and tabulation, along with voter education. Electing several winners per district requires a ranked count (R-02).
R-03.enforcement: Ordinary election administration carries it out. No special enforcement body is needed.
R-03.costs: A moderate one-time cost for new ballots, counting systems and voter education, borne by state and local election offices. Incumbents in safe seats lose their advantage at the first election under the new map.
R-03.failure_risks: Incumbents of both parties in safe seats tend to oppose it, along with majority parties in lopsided states. Their likely adaptation is to draw districts with few seats each, which keeps seats safe; districts electing three or fewer members are a named failure point. Pairing the system with closed primaries can also undercut it, and a later Congress could repeal it. Once in force, reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: Safe seats are documented. The link LX2: Residential sorting creates safe seats is rated well supported: sorting produces safe seats even without intentional map-drawing.

remedy_evidence.text: Support comes from comparisons across countries and from simulations. Carey and Hix (2011) found in cross-national data that districts electing three to eight members improve proportionality without fragmenting governments. Main limitation: no U.S. congressional election has used the system, so there is no direct American test.

R-03.tradeoffs: Each member would represent a larger area, which weakens the tie to one place. In small states with one or two seats, little changes. Coalition-building can get harder when more parties win seats.
success_measures: Seats-votes responsiveness: how closely each party's share of seats follows its share of the vote
Share of competitive seats
Representation of minority-party voters within each state
R-03.alternatives: Independent redistricting commissions (R-04) reduce partisan bias in maps but leave geographic sorting in place. Expanding the House (R-46) is a related option. Rejected option: single-member ranked voting as the end goal for House elections, because sorted districts stay safe under it; ranked voting for single seats (R-02) remains a separate reform.

status.text: The Fair Representation Act would elect members of the U.S. House by ranked-choice voting in districts that each send several members. It has been introduced in past Congresses and has not become law.

routes.who: Repeal the single-member mandate (2 U.S.C. 2c) and require ranked multi-winner counting
State legislatures for their own chambers

routes.note: Cambridge, Massachusetts has counted this way since 1941; Portland, Oregon adopted it in 2022.

R-04.title: Independent citizen commissions draw election maps
R-04.summary: A commission independent of the legislative majority would draw district maps under explicit criteria, with public hearings. Voters who support a state's minority party would see fairer maps at the next redistricting, due in 2031 after the census, unless a mid-decade redraw comes first. The legislative majority would lose the power to draw its own districts.
R-04.what_it_changes: A durable majority can use its hold on the legislature to draw maps and set access rules (L56: Durable majorities control maps and voting rules), and those maps produce safe seats (L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats). A commission cuts the step from D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions to C4: Officeholders' control over election rules. It works through loop R4a (Majorities draw maps that help them keep control).
R-04.who_decides: States decide for their own maps; Congress could act for congressional maps only. Voters in initiative states can create a commission by ballot measure, rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Legislatures can create one by statute or by referring an amendment to voters (low). A federal statute gets the lowest feasibility rating. State courts enforcing fair-district clauses in state constitutions offer a separate path (medium).
R-04.legal_authority: In Arizona State Legislature v. Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission (2015), the Supreme Court upheld commissions created by voter initiative, 5 to 4. Rucho v. Common Cause (2019) closed federal courts to partisan gerrymandering claims, which leaves the question to state law and state courts. Louisiana v. Callais (2026) narrowed Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act by requiring evidence that supports a strong inference of intentional discrimination.
R-04.implementation: Voters pass an initiative, or the legislature refers a measure to them. The commission must be seated before the next census. It then draws maps with public hearings, and courts review the result. Writing the commission and explicit map-drawing criteria into the state constitution is the prerequisite for durability.
R-04.resources: Commission staff, including demographers and mapping specialists, plus money to defend the maps in court.
R-04.enforcement: State courts enforce the commission's rules and review its maps.
R-04.costs: The direct cost is small: commission staff and litigation defense, paid by the state. The legislative majority bears a political cost starting at the next redistricting.
R-04.failure_risks: Majority parties in states without commissions would likely push back. In 2025 and 2026, legislatures in other states redrew maps mid-decade, and California voters approved a measure suspending that state's commission. A state that adopts a commission alone can lose seats to states that do not, which invites retaliatory redraws. Legislatures or voters can also override or suspend a commission. Durability is high where the commission is in the state constitution, and reversal risk is medium overall.

problem_evidence.text: Mid-decade redraws in 2025 and 2026 are documented. Unified state governments in Texas, Missouri, North Carolina and Ohio passed new congressional maps between censuses, and California voters answered with their own change at the legislature's request.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence that commissions reduce partisan bias comes from one descriptive study of the 2021-22 maps: Warshaw, McGhee and Migurski found less partisan bias in commission-drawn and court-drawn maps than in legislature-drawn ones. Evidence that commissions create more competitive seats is weaker. Main limitation: that study covers one redistricting cycle and uses descriptive measures.

R-04.tradeoffs: Commissions correct bias more than they increase competition. A state that adopts one while its neighbors do not can lose seats, and that risk can drive retaliatory redraws elsewhere.
success_measures: Efficiency gap and other measures of partisan bias in each map
Mid-decade redraws attempted, and how many were blocked
Number of competitive seats
R-04.alternatives: A federal standard or an interstate agreement would keep any single state from giving up seats alone. Proportional districts (R-03) address geographic sorting, which commissions leave in place. Rejected option: court-drawn maps as the default, because they are slow and depend on the courts.

status.text: About ten states give an independent or bipartisan commission a role in drawing congressional districts. Missouri voters decide Proposition A on November 3, 2026, a referendum on the congressional map the legislature passed in 2025 (House Bill 1). On September 25, 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court ordered that Missouri's 2022 map be used for the 2026 congressional election and barred lower courts from requiring the 2025 map. Alabama uses its 2023 plan in 2026, because on June 2, 2026 the Supreme Court lifted the injunction that had blocked it.

R-05.title: Automatic voter registration
R-05.summary: Eligible people would be registered to vote when they deal with a state agency, such as the motor vehicle office or a benefits office, unless they opt out. Renters, people who move often and young adults would gain at the next election after the system starts, because a registration step that falls hardest on them would be handled for them.
R-05.what_it_changes: Registration rules can lower turnout among the people they burden (L44: Restrictive access rules widen turnout gaps). Automatic registration removes one such cost. It aims to raise B5: Equality of voter turnout, where a smaller turnout gap between income groups counts as an increase. It operates on loop R4b (Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable).
R-05.who_decides: States run voter registration, so state legislatures are the main route, rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Voters can adopt it by ballot measure where initiatives are allowed (medium). Congress could set a national floor by statute (low).
R-05.legal_authority: States run registration under their own election laws. Congress could set a minimum standard by statute.
R-05.implementation: A legislature passes a statute first. State agencies then connect their records to the voter rolls. Once the system runs, audits check its accuracy. Agency data systems that can verify eligibility are a prerequisite.
R-05.resources: Modest spending on agency information technology, mainly to match data between agencies.
R-05.enforcement: State election agencies run and oversee the system.
R-05.costs: The cost is modest and falls on state agencies. It can lower costs by cutting paper processing.
R-05.failure_risks: Few groups resist openly. Weak verification can be used to discredit the system, and citizenship-verification steps added in some states in 2026 slow processing. Agencies that are not funded to connect their records can stall it. The reform has proved durable, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: Research finds that registration barriers lower turnout. Link L44 records that registration barriers have larger effects on turnout than voter ID laws, whose measured effects are near zero.

remedy_evidence.text: Registration rises where the policy is adopted: a 2019 Brennan Center for Justice analysis of seven early-adopting states found registration gains of 9% to 94% after adjusting for trends. Effects on turnout are small but positive. Main limitation: that analysis measured registration, so the turnout finding comes from separate research.

R-05.tradeoffs: Errors can enter the voter rolls if verification is weak. Sharing records between agencies raises privacy concerns.
success_measures: Registration rate by age and by how recently people moved
Turnout among people registered through the new system
Error rates in automatic registrations
R-05.alternatives: Same-day registration, which lets eligible people register when they vote, is the main alternative.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, 24 states and the District of Columbia have enacted or put in place automatic voter registration, by the count of the National Conference of State Legislatures (updated August 19, 2026).

R-06.title: Hold local elections alongside November races
R-06.summary: City and county elections would move to the same November ballot as state and national races. Turnout in local contests would rise at the first combined election, and younger voters and renters would make up more of the electorate. Groups that do well when few people vote would lose some influence over local decisions on zoning, schools and contracts.
R-06.what_it_changes: Off-cycle local elections draw small electorates that are older and more often homeowners. Moving them to November changes who votes. The aim is to raise B5: Equality of voter turnout and to weaken L39: Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing, since homeowners tend to fill the zoning room. The reform touches loop R8 (Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building), loop R15 (Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other), loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).
R-06.who_decides: State legislatures can require on-cycle local elections by statute, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; California and Nevada have such mandates. Cities can move their own elections through charter amendments (high). Voters can also act by ballot measure (medium).
R-06.legal_authority: State law governs municipal elections, so a legislature can set election dates for its cities. Cities with charters can change their own dates where state law permits.
R-06.implementation: A state statute or a city charter amendment sets the new date. The first consolidated election follows. Afterward, turnout and policy outcomes before and after the change can be compared. Nothing else has to happen first.
R-06.resources: Holding elections together saves money. Ballots get longer, so election offices must design them with care.
R-06.enforcement: Election officials carry out the new schedule. No special enforcement design is needed.
R-06.costs: Consolidation lowers costs for local governments, which stop paying for separate elections.
R-06.failure_risks: Organized local interests that do well in low-turnout elections are expected to resist. They can adapt through where local races appear on the ballot and by relying on roll-off, the pattern of voters skipping races near the bottom of a long ballot. Roll-off is the main way the reform could fall short. Once adopted, on-cycle schedules tend to stay, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: Turnout in off-cycle local elections is often 15% to 30%.

remedy_evidence.text: Using California voter files, Hajnal, Kogan and Markarian (2022) found that on-cycle timing roughly doubles turnout and makes the local electorate more representative. A school-district study by Kogan, Lavertu and Peskowitz (2018) found that off-cycle timing shifted the electorate and raised teacher pay relative to on-cycle districts, which links timing to policy. Main limitation: effects on housing and other policy outcomes are plausible but less established than the turnout effect.

R-06.tradeoffs: Ballots get longer. Local races can be lost among national ones, and some voters skip them.
success_measures: Turnout in local races
Age and homeownership mix of local voters
Housing units approved
R-06.alternatives: Voting by mail in local elections is the main alternative.

status.text: California's SB 415 (2015), in effect since January 1, 2018, bars a city or other local body from holding elections off the statewide election calendar when that has produced turnout at least 25% below its average turnout in the previous four statewide general elections. Nevada has also moved local elections onto the statewide calendar.

routes.note: California and Nevada have mandates.

R-07.title: Public matching for small donations and vouchers
R-07.summary: Candidates who join a voluntary program would receive public money that multiplies small donations, or voters would receive vouchers to give to the candidates they choose. Candidates without wealthy networks would gain in the first election cycle, because small donors would become worth their time. Incumbents who rely on large-donor networks would lose ground over several cycles.
R-07.what_it_changes: Public matching or vouchers change who funds campaigns (B1: Money spent to influence politics) and widen who can afford to run, which works on C3: Risk of losing office through more challengers. It touches loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance). Its target is candidate entry. Evidence does not show that it weakens loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other).
R-07.who_decides: Cities, states and Congress can each create programs. City programs are rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030, and New York City and Seattle run them. State programs are rated medium; Connecticut, Maine and Arizona run them. Voters can create a program by ballot measure (medium). A federal program is rated low.
R-07.legal_authority: Voluntary public financing is constitutional under the Supreme Court's decision in Buckley v. Valeo.
R-07.implementation: Designers first set contribution caps and the rules candidates must meet to qualify. The program then runs for one full election cycle. An evaluation follows, looking at the range of donors and at whether more candidates entered. A federal program would first need an election commission able to act (R-11).
R-07.resources: A recurring appropriation sized to expected participation, an independent administrator, auditors, and controls against fraud.
R-07.enforcement: An independent administrator and auditors check qualification and spending. New York City's program, for example, pairs matching funds with spending limits, disclosure, audits and sanctions.
R-07.costs: Moderate, paid from public budgets each election cycle.
R-07.failure_risks: Large donors and incumbents are likely to oppose it. Outside spending continues regardless and can swamp the program. Low participation, a fraud case or defunding can end it; some programs have been defunded before. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Political donations are concentrated. Research by Bonica, McCarty, Poole and Rosenthal (2013) found that the top 0.01% of donors give about 40% of itemized contributions.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence concerns donor participation and candidate entry, where effects are plausible. Kilborn and Vishwanath (2022) found that public matching does not make elected officials more moderate. Main limitation: direct effects on the wealth-and-policy loop are unproven.

R-07.tradeoffs: Public money can go to candidates many voters dislike, and fraud cases can occur.
success_measures: Range of donors by income and neighborhood
Number of candidates per race
Money lost to fraud
R-07.alternatives: Block grants to political parties (R-47) are the main alternative. Rejected option: presenting matching as a way to moderate politics, because evidence shows it does not moderate.

status.text: Public financing of campaigns through small-donor matching or vouchers operates in New York City, Connecticut, Maine and Arizona, and Seattle's Democracy Voucher program is running on a limited basis in 2026: only residents of City Council District 5 receive vouchers this year.

routes.note: New York City and Seattle run programs.
Connecticut, Maine and Arizona run programs.

R-08.title: Disclose the original funders of political spending
R-08.summary: Groups that spend money to influence elections would have to report who paid, including money passed through other organizations. Voters and journalists would see that information from the first reporting deadline after the law takes effect. Groups that now spend without naming their funders would lose that option.
R-08.what_it_changes: Political spending can buy access and influence over policy (L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors, rated plausible). Disclosure lets voters and enforcers see who pays. That strengthens oversight's ability to catch favoritism (L16: Watchdogs reduce favoritism and waste in policy) and turns donor influence into a political cost. The reform acts on loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other), loop R3 (Political hostility and hostile content may reinforce each other) and loop B1a (Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism).
R-08.who_decides: Congress, state legislatures and voters can each require it. A federal statute is rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. State statutes and state ballot measures are rated medium. On November 3, 2026, Montana voters decide I-194, which would prohibit some corporate political spending; it is a spending ban and does not require disclosure.
R-08.legal_authority: Disclosure rules have survived most court challenges since Citizens United v. FEC (2010), which struck limits on independent spending by corporations and unions and left disclosure requirements in place. Litigation over donor privacy continues.
R-08.implementation: A statute comes first, with rules that trace money through intermediaries to its true source. An enforcement design comes next: an agency able to act, backed by a right of private parties to sue. A public database of the filings follows. A working enforcer is a prerequisite, either a federal election commission with a quorum (R-11) or a state agency.
R-08.resources: Costs are small. The main need is data systems that collect, check and publish filings.
R-08.enforcement: At the federal level the Federal Election Commission enforces election law, but it has lacked a quorum, the minimum number of members needed to act, since May 1, 2025. State agencies enforce state laws. A private right of action, which lets affected parties sue, serves as a backup.
R-08.costs: The public cost is small. Groups that spend without disclosing their funders lose that ability at the first reporting deadline.
R-08.failure_risks: Groups that spend without disclosing tend to oppose it, mainly by routing money through layers of nonprofit organizations. A law with no working enforcer goes unenforced.

problem_evidence.text: Spending by groups that do not disclose their funders is documented. OpenSecrets, compiling Federal Election Commission data, counted $4.5 billion in outside spending on the 2024 elections, including more than $1 billion given to super PACs from sources that do not disclose their donors.

remedy_evidence.text: Studies find no measurable chilling effect of disclosure on donors, and moderate evidence that knowing the funder changes how persuasive voters find a message. Main limitation: disclosure works only when an agency can enforce it, which is the gap at the federal level today.

R-08.tradeoffs: Disclosure reduces donor privacy and can expose small donors to harassment, so reporting thresholds and protections need to match those risks.
success_measures: Share of election spending with an identified original source
Enforcement actions for disclosure violations
R-08.alternatives: Contribution limits, where courts allow them, are the main alternative. Rejected option: disclosure without an enforcer, because it goes unenforced.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, Congress has not passed a federal law requiring groups that spend on elections to disclose their original donors. The Federal Election Commission, which enforces existing disclosure rules, has lacked the four-member quorum it needs to vote on enforcement, rules and advisory opinions since May 1, 2025. Alaska's true-source disclosure rule is part of Ballot Measure 2, the repeal measure on that state's November 3, 2026 ballot.

routes.note: Montana's I-194, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would bar corporations and other entities chartered by the state, including nonprofits, unions and trusts, from spending in state elections. It changes state law and leaves the state constitution untouched. Its campaign, the Montana Plan, led by former Commissioner of Political Practices Jeff Mangan, says it is designed to work around Citizens United; the Montana, Billings and Kalispell chambers of commerce oppose it.

R-09.title: Ban stock trading by members of Congress
R-09.summary: Members of Congress would be barred from trading individual stocks, which removes a conflict between their own investments and their votes. The change would apply once enacted. Members who trade would lose that option, and the expected gain in public confidence has not been measured.
R-09.what_it_changes: The reform removes one documented conflict between members' personal finances and their votes. The reform is linked to E1: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests and to E2: Trust earned through performance, and sits on loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other). Whether spouses and other family members are covered is a key design choice, since trading by family members is the expected workaround.
R-09.who_decides: Congress can pass a statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. The House passed H.R. 7008 by 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026. On September 30, 2026, a Senate cloture vote, the vote to end debate, failed 53 to 47, short of the 60 votes required. Each chamber can also adopt a rule for its own members (medium).
R-09.legal_authority: Congress has authority over its own members, by statute or through each chamber's rules.
R-09.implementation: Congress passes a statute first. It then sets up enforcement outside the members' own ethics committees. Audits of compliance follow.
R-09.resources: No new funding is needed beyond staff to review members' financial disclosures.
R-09.enforcement: Today the House and Senate ethics committees enforce trading rules, which means members judge members. The reform calls for an enforcer outside Congress's committees with fines large enough to matter.
R-09.costs: No public cost is identified. Members who trade bear the cost of moving their savings into permitted investments.
R-09.failure_risks: Members who trade would likely push back. Likely workarounds include trades by family members and unrelated provisions, called riders, attached to the bill; the House-passed bill also carried a voter-ID title. Weak enforcement is the other main risk. Once law, reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: The conflict is documented: a 2021 Business Insider investigation found that dozens of members had violated reporting rules under the STOCK Act, the federal law that requires members to report trades. Evidence that members profit from trading is mixed. A 2013 study by Eggers and Hainmueller found that members' stock portfolios underperformed the market.

remedy_evidence.text: No federal ban has been tested, so its effect on members' behavior is unknown. An effect on public trust is plausible. Main limitation: trust surveys capture many influences, so a change after enactment would be hard to attribute to this rule.

R-09.tradeoffs: A ban raises concerns about recruiting candidates with large investments. Blind trusts, a common compromise, are an imperfect fix.
success_measures: Violations found and penalized each year
Trades disclosed after the legal deadline
R-09.alternatives: Blind trusts, or rules limiting members to diversified funds, are the main alternatives. Rejected option: a ban enforced only by committee fines, which is the current approach.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, a ban on stock trading by members of Congress has passed the House and stalled in the Senate. The House passed H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026. On September 30, 2026 a Senate motion to end debate on taking up the bill failed 53 to 47; 60 votes were needed.

routes.note: The House passed H.R. 7008 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026. On September 30, 2026 the Senate failed to invoke cloture on the motion to take it up, 53 to 47, short of the 60 votes required.

R-10.title: Limits on lobbying and the revolving door
R-10.summary: Former officials would face waiting periods before lobbying the offices they left, and lobbying disclosure would cover more of the people who do influence work. Public-interest advocates would gain over several years as insider access loses value. Former officials who lobby would lose some of the value of their connections once the law takes effect.
R-10.what_it_changes: Lobbyists with personal ties to officials command a premium for access. Limits on the revolving door, the movement of people between public office and lobbying jobs, reduce what that access is worth. The reform is linked to L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors and to the proposed loop R2 (Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise), whose links L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence and L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise are rated hypotheses.
R-10.who_decides: Congress can act by statute, rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. The President can set rules for executive-branch staff through ethics pledges (medium), though the next order can reverse them. Each chamber can tighten its own rules (low).
R-10.legal_authority: Congress and the President have clear authority over these rules for their own branches.
R-10.implementation: A statute comes first, then enforcement, then a review of how people evade the rules. Building Congress's own staff capacity (R-13) helps first, so members rely less on lobbyists.
R-10.resources: Costs are small. Disclosure systems must track registered lobbyists and former officials.
R-10.enforcement: The Office of Government Ethics and the Justice Department enforce current rules, and enforcement has historically been weak. The reform calls for an outside enforcer.
R-10.costs: The public cost is small. Former officials who move into lobbying bear most of the cost.
R-10.failure_risks: Lobbying firms are expected to resist. Their main adaptation is to call staff unregistered advisers, outside the registration rules; LaPira and Thomas (2017) estimate that roughly half of active lobbyists are unregistered, an estimate that depends on their method. Durability is low for limits set by executive order and medium for limits in statute; overall reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Access has a market price. A 2012 study by Blanes i Vidal, Draca and Fons-Rosen found that a lobbyist's revenue falls 24% when the senator they once worked for leaves office.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence that cooling-off periods change behavior is weak. Main limitation: unregistered influence work is hard to observe, so studies can miss the activity the rules target.

R-10.tradeoffs: Strict limits can make it harder to recruit experienced people into government.
success_measures: Cooling-off violations found
Share of committee staff who came from the industries the committee oversees
R-10.alternatives: Building Congress's own expertise (R-13) addresses the same dependence from the other side. Legislative term limits (R-35) appear here only as a rejected option: they are rejected because evidence links them to greater reliance on lobbyists.

status.text: Congress has not passed new lobbying disclosure or revolving-door limits in the 2025 to 2026 session.

routes.note: Reversible by the next order.

R-11.title: A Federal Election Commission able to act
R-11.summary: The Federal Election Commission, which enforces federal campaign-finance law, would regain enough commissioners to make decisions and work through its backlog. Candidates harmed by violations would gain as soon as a quorum returns, and violators would lose the cover of an agency that cannot act. A later step would redesign the commission so its independence can survive recent court rulings.
R-11.what_it_changes: Without a quorum, no federal rule on election money is enforced. Restoring the referee raises D4: Ability to investigate and enforce the rules. The commission's quorum loss is one of the documented cases under L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies, and a working commission lets L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action operate again. The reform works through loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other) and loop R18 (Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action).
R-11.who_decides: The President nominates commissioners, the Senate confirms them, and Congress sets the commission's structure. Senate confirmation of pending nominees is rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; nominees Stow and Woodson were referred to the Senate Rules Committee, with no hearing found. Restructuring the commission by statute is rated low.
R-11.legal_authority: The commission needs four votes to act. After Trump v. Slaughter (2026), in which the Supreme Court held the Federal Trade Commission's protection against removal without cause unconstitutional, similar protection for election commissioners is doubtful. Lasting independence would have to come from the commission's structure.
R-11.implementation: The Senate first confirms enough commissioners to restore a quorum. The commission then clears its backlog of cases. A redesign that can survive the Slaughter decision comes after that. Senate floor time is the prerequisite.
R-11.resources: Costs are small. The commission carries a backlog of about 300 cases.
R-11.enforcement: The commission is itself the enforcer of federal campaign-finance law.
R-11.costs: The public cost is small. People who have violated campaign-finance law lose the protection a stalled commission gives them, starting when the quorum returns.
R-11.failure_risks: Anyone who benefits from having no referee has reason to resist, and delaying nominations is the main tool. Reversal risk is high, because a single departure can end a quorum. The effort can also stall if confirmations do not happen, or if courts extend Slaughter so that commissioners can be removed at will.

problem_evidence.text: The commission has had no quorum since May 1, 2025, and two commissioners are seated as of October 2026. The Congressional Research Service describes this as the fourth quorum loss in the commission's history.

remedy_evidence.text: The case for a working commission rests on design lessons drawn from state election commissions. Main limitation: no study measures how quickly enforcement recovers after a quorum returns, and each structural redesign carries its own risk of partisan control.

R-11.tradeoffs: An odd-numbered commission, one way to end tie votes, risks control by one party.
success_measures: Days each year the commission has a quorum
Age of open enforcement cases
Enforcement actions completed
R-11.alternatives: A private right of action would let affected parties sue directly, so enforcement would not depend on the commission alone. Rejected option: waiting for a structural redesign before restoring the quorum.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, the Federal Election Commission has two of its six commissioners, Shana Broussard and Dara Lindenbaum, both Democrats, and has lacked a quorum since May 1, 2025. The Commission needs four votes to open investigations, issue rules or approve advisory opinions. President Trump nominated two Republicans, Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson, on February 11, 2026; their nominations are pending before the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, which had held no hearing on them as of mid-September 2026.

routes.note: Stow and Woodson referred to Rules; no hearing found.

R-12.title: Senate filibuster reform
R-12.summary: A majority of the Senate could pass ordinary bills without first gathering 60 votes to end debate. Whichever party holds the majority would gain that power right away, and the minority would lose its ability to block. More laws could pass, and policy could swing further each time control changes.
R-12.what_it_changes: When Congress cannot pass laws, presidents fill the gap with executive action (L11: A weaker Congress invites presidential action), and that reliance can weaken Congress further (L12: Presidential action erodes Congress's will to legislate). Letting a majority pass statutes aims to raise D1: Congress's ability to write and check policy. It operates on loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).
R-12.who_decides: A majority of the Senate decides, by changing its rules or by setting a new precedent. This route is rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030.
R-12.legal_authority: The Constitution lets each chamber of Congress set its own rules.
R-12.implementation: The Senate changes the rule first. The new process would then be used on structural statutes both parties could accept. After that, the test is whether later majorities reverse course. A majority willing to begin with such neutral measures is the prerequisite.
R-12.resources: No new funding is needed. Floor time is the constraint.
R-12.enforcement: The presiding officer and Senate precedent enforce the rule.
R-12.costs: There is no fiscal cost. The minority party loses its blocking power immediately.
R-12.failure_risks: The minority party is expected to resist, along with senators who value the bargaining power the rule gives each of them. They can adapt by moving priorities through budget reconciliation and riders on spending bills. The biggest risk is a first use for partisan advantage, which invites retaliation. Reversal risk is high, since the next majority can restore the old rule or exploit the new one.

problem_evidence.text: The 60-vote threshold for ending debate, called cloture, blocks most statutes. Senate records show cloture motions rose from single digits per Congress before 1970 to between 200 and 300 in recent Congresses. On September 30, 2026, a cloture vote on a stock-trading bill failed 53 to 47, short of the three-fifths required.

remedy_evidence.text: Majority passage would raise the number of laws enacted. Main limitation: the net effect on democratic quality is uncertain, because faster lawmaking can also mean larger reversals when control changes.

R-12.tradeoffs: Policy can swing more between majorities, and the minority's voice shrinks.
success_measures: Statutes passed through regular order
Major policy reversals per decade
Emergency declarations and other executive actions taken without new law
R-12.alternatives: A talking filibuster, which requires opponents to hold the floor, and exemptions for election-law bills are the main alternatives. Rejected option: leaving the rule unchanged, because every rules statute among the reform profiles would still need 60 votes.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, the Senate still requires 60 votes to end debate on most legislation. The September 30, 2026 vote to begin debate on the House-passed stock-trading bill failed 53 to 47 under that three-fifths rule.

R-13.title: Rebuild Congress's own staff and experts
R-13.summary: Congress would hire and keep more of its own analysts, on committees and at support agencies such as the Congressional Research Service, the Congressional Budget Office and the Government Accountability Office. Committees and the public would gain within two to four years, as members depend less on lobbyists to draft and assess bills. Lobbyists who now draft legislation would lose part of that role.
R-13.what_it_changes: In-house experts let members judge proposals without relying on interested parties. Link L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence and its return link L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise are both rated hypotheses; together they form the proposed loop R2 (Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise). The reform also raises D1: Congress's ability to write and check policy.
R-13.who_decides: The House and Senate decide through legislative-branch appropriations, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Each chamber can also change its rules on staff pay and roles, which carries the same rating.
R-13.legal_authority: Congress has clear authority to fund and organize its own staff.
R-13.implementation: Congress first benchmarks staff pay against comparable jobs. Hiring of analytic staff follows, along with stronger budgets for the Congressional Research Service, the Congressional Budget Office and GAO. Staff tenure and the volume of committee analysis are then measured.
R-13.resources: The cost is small relative to the federal budget. Recruiting and keeping skilled staff is the main capacity challenge.
R-13.enforcement: No enforcement mechanism is needed, because the reform is a funding and staffing decision.
R-13.failure_risks: Few groups resist openly. The likely adaptation is for party leaders to control how new staff are used, and the main failure risk is staff hired to serve leadership priorities. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Committee staff were cut by about 41% from 1993 to 1995. In its 2024 update, the Brookings Institution's Vital Statistics on Congress shows committee staff down roughly a third since the 1980s. A 2019 survey of senior congressional staff by Hertel-Fernandez, Mildenberger and Stokes found that they misjudge constituent opinion and rely on interest-group contacts.

remedy_evidence.text: That more staff raise Congress's capacity is plausible. The full feedback loop, in which thin staffing leads to policy that favors insiders and then to further cuts, is a hypothesis. Main limitation: no study measures that loop from start to finish.

R-13.tradeoffs: Spending on Congress's own staff invites the charge that Congress is paying itself.
success_measures: Average tenure of committee and support-agency staff
Committee analytic output, such as hearings held and reports issued
Share of GAO recommendations implemented
R-13.alternatives: Relying on outside policy organizations for analysis is the main alternative. Legislative term limits (R-35) appear here only as a rejected option; they are rejected because evidence links them to lost experience and greater reliance on lobbyists and staff.

status.text: The House has adopted part of the recommendations of its Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress, which worked from 2019 to early 2023.

routes.who: Chamber rules on staff pay and roles

R-14.title: Automatic funding to prevent government shutdowns
R-14.summary: If Congress missed a budget deadline, funding would continue at the prior year's level until a new spending law passed, so government services would keep running. Federal workers, contractors and people who rely on federal services would gain at the next lapse that would otherwise have closed offices. The threat of a shutdown would stop working as a bargaining tool.
R-14.what_it_changes: A continuing resolution is a temporary law that keeps funding at prior levels. Making one automatic shields D5: Quality of public services from shutdowns. The reform sits on loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other). A shutdown documents a service failure; the later steps of that loop, from failure to lower trust to lower funding, need their own evidence.
R-14.who_decides: Congress decides by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030.
R-14.legal_authority: Congress has clear authority over appropriations.
R-14.implementation: Congress passes the statute. It then monitors whether regular appropriations bills still pass on time.
R-14.resources: No new staff or systems are needed, and the budget effect is neutral.
R-14.enforcement: Enforcement is automatic: funding continues by law whenever appropriations lapse, with no agency needed to trigger it.
R-14.costs: The direct budget effect is neutral, since funding continues at prior levels. The reform would avoid losses like those from the 2025 shutdown, which the Congressional Budget Office estimated in a scenario analysis would permanently cost the economy $7 billion to $14 billion.
R-14.failure_risks: Appropriators who use deadlines to force action are likely to oppose it, and Congress can keep passing short continuing resolutions anyway. Riders can be attached to the automatic mechanism, and it can reduce the urgency to finish budgets. Once law, reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: The lapse from October 1 to November 12, 2025 lasted 43 days, the longest shutdown on record. Department of Homeland Security funding lapsed again from February 14 to April 30, 2026.

remedy_evidence.text: Support comes from design analysis. Main limitation: the federal government has never run under an automatic continuing resolution, so there is no U.S. test.

R-14.tradeoffs: Congress faces less pressure to pass full-year spending bills, and prior-year priorities stay locked in until it does.
success_measures: Days of funding lapse per year
Regular appropriations bills passed on time
R-14.alternatives: Rules that only guarantee pay for federal workers during shutdowns are the main alternative.

status.text: Fiscal year 2027 began on October 1, 2026 without a shutdown. H.R. 6500, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027, signed September 2, 2026, funds federal agencies through December 11, 2026.

R-15.title: Inspectors general with remedies that work
R-15.summary: Inspectors general, the internal watchdogs in federal agencies, would gain remedies that work when an administration obstructs them: reinstatement after unlawful removal, access to records, protected budgets and timely enforcement of subpoenas. Taxpayers and the public would gain over years as investigations continue under pressure. Officials under investigation would lose the ability to stall them, starting immediately.
R-15.what_it_changes: When the executive removes watchdogs or cuts their resources, detection weakens (L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies). Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action (L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action) and find and correct favoritism and waste (L16: Watchdogs reduce favoritism and waste in policy). The reform aims to keep D4: Ability to investigate and enforce the rules working. It touches loop B1a (Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism) and loop R18 (Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action).
R-15.who_decides: Congress decides, by amending the Inspector General Act and through appropriations; this route is rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Courts shape the outcome through litigation over removals (low), and in Storch v. Hegseth no ruling on the merits has been found.
R-15.legal_authority: Current law requires the President to give Congress written reasons 30 days before removing an inspector general, a notice requirement with no remedy attached. Trump v. Slaughter (2026) narrowed removal protection for principal officers, and whether its reasoning reaches inspectors general is untested.
R-15.implementation: Congress first passes a statute with protections designed for the law after Slaughter (see R-48). Funding for inspector general offices and GAO follows. The protections would then be tested in court.
R-15.resources: Budgets for inspector general offices and GAO, and the investigative staff they pay for.
R-15.enforcement: Courts and Congress enforce the protections, with courts deciding disputes over removals and subpoenas.
R-15.costs: The cost is small. GAO, Congress's audit agency, reports that its work returns many times its cost; it reported $62.7 billion in financial benefits for fiscal year 2025.
R-15.failure_risks: Administrations of either party under scrutiny tend to oppose it, using acting appointments and budget cuts. The main legal risk is that courts extend Slaughter to inspectors general. Since that decision, durability is low and reversal risk is high.

problem_evidence.text: On January 24, 2025, 17 inspectors general were removed. A federal district court found on September 24, 2025 that the removals violated the notice requirement, and it declined to order reinstatement.

remedy_evidence.text: The value of oversight is documented. Main limitation: new protections may not last, because their reach after the Slaughter decision is legally uncertain.

R-15.tradeoffs: Insulating watchdogs reduces elected officials' control over part of the executive branch.
success_measures: Inspector general posts that are vacant or held by acting officials
Inspector general recommendations implemented
Time for watchdogs to obtain requested records
R-15.alternatives: Oversight by congressional committees is the main alternative. Rejected option: notice requirements without remedies, which failed to prevent the 2025 removals.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, no ruling on the merits has been reported in Storch v. Hegseth, the suit by eight inspectors general removed on January 24, 2025. The federal district court in Washington, D.C. denied reinstatement on September 24, 2025 and paused the case until the Supreme Court decided Trump v. Slaughter, which it did on June 29, 2026. In July 2026 the court set a process for summary-judgment motions, with a conference planned for the week of August 24, 2026. Congress has not passed a new law strengthening protections against removing inspectors general.

routes.note: Storch v. Hegseth: no merits ruling found.

R-16.title: Supreme Court 18-year terms and enforceable ethics
R-16.summary: Supreme Court justices would serve regular 18-year terms, giving each presidential term two appointments, and the Court's ethics code would gain a process for enforcing it. Over decades, the Court's makeup would follow elections at a steady pace, and the timing of deaths and retirements would matter less. Whichever coalition the Court now favors would lose that edge gradually.
R-16.what_it_changes: Appointments now depend on when vacancies occur, and a durable Senate majority with the presidency decides who is confirmed (L57: Durable Senate majorities shape court appointments). Regular terms aim to steady D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, a proposed pattern assessed decision by decision. The reform acts on loop R1b (Political spending and court rulings reinforce each other) and loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules). Fixed terms for justices differ from legislative term limits (R-35), a rejected option.
R-16.who_decides: Congress could act by statute, with justices rotating to senior status after 18 years, though the statute's constitutionality is contested; it gets the lowest feasibility rating for 2026 to 2030. A constitutional amendment under Article V gets the same rating. Senate rules on the timing of confirmations are rated low.
R-16.legal_authority: Whether Congress can set terms by statute is contested under Article III of the Constitution, which provides that judges hold office during good behavior. A 2021 presidential commission on the Supreme Court noted this uncertainty. An amendment would settle it.
R-16.implementation: A statute or amendment comes first. The new terms would then phase in over 18 years as seats turn over. A statute would need 60 Senate votes or filibuster reform (R-12).
R-16.resources: No new funding or staff are needed.
R-16.enforcement: The Court itself would review any statute setting its terms. An enforceable ethics code would need a body to hear and decide complaints.
R-16.costs: There is no fiscal cost. The coalition that the current Court favors would lose ground over decades.
R-16.failure_risks: Coalitions with a favorable Court would likely push back, and justices can respond by timing their retirements. The main risk for a statute is that the Court strikes it down. Reversal risk is low if the change comes by amendment.

problem_evidence.text: Appointment timing is uneven, because seats open only when a justice dies or retires, so the number of appointments varies from one presidential term to the next. The Court adopted a code of conduct in November 2023, and independent handling and enforcement of complaints remain unresolved.

remedy_evidence.text: Support comes from simulations of how regular terms would change the Court's makeup. Main limitation: no such system has been tried, so there is no test.

R-16.tradeoffs: The transition would bring political conflict over which seats rotate first. Justices would also be less insulated from electoral politics.
success_measures: Appointments per presidential term
Ethics complaints filed and resolved
R-16.alternatives: An enforceable ethics code alone is the main alternative. Rejected option: expanding the Court, because expansion invites retaliation.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, Congress has not enacted 18-year terms for Supreme Court justices or an enforceable ethics code for the Court.

routes.note: Constitutionality contested.

R-17.title: Protect the career civil service
R-17.summary: Federal agencies would hire on merit and protect career employees from being fired for political reasons, keeping experienced staff in place. People who rely on agency services, such as tax help and Social Security, would gain within two to five years as staffing and expertise recover. Political leadership would lose some control over who serves in policy roles, starting immediately.
R-17.what_it_changes: Experienced career staff raise D5: Quality of public services. Better services can build trust (L20: Better public services build earned trust), and trust supports the compliance and funding that services need (L21: Earned trust supports compliance and service funding). The reform works through loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other) and loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).
R-17.who_decides: Congress can write protections into statute and reverse the Schedule Policy/Career rule, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. The executive branch can rescind the Office of Personnel Management rule (medium), but a later administration can restore it. Litigation over the rule is a third path (low).
R-17.legal_authority: Congress can set civil-service law by statute. Protections that exist only in executive rules can be changed by the next administration.
R-17.implementation: Congress passes a statute first, because only a statute gives durable protection. Agencies then hire to fill vacancies. Service measures, such as answer rates and wait times, track the results.
R-17.resources: Funding comes from agency budgets. Agencies would be rebuilding after about 378,000 separations in 2025, according to GAO.
R-17.enforcement: The Merit Systems Protection Board hears appeals from federal employees; its quorum was restored on October 28, 2025. Courts review its decisions.
R-17.costs: The fiscal cost is small. Political leadership gives up some control over staffing.
R-17.failure_risks: Administrations seeking more control are expected to resist, mainly by reclassifying positions into categories with fewer protections. If no statute passes, rule-based protections can be undone again. Reversal risk is high for protections set by rule.

problem_evidence.text: The Office of Personnel Management's Schedule Policy/Career rule, which creates a job category for policy-related positions with fewer protections against removal, took effect March 9, 2026; a June 3, 2026 executive order moved about 8,000 positions into it. GAO reports a net decline of about 256,000 employees, over 11%, at 24 major agencies from December 2024 to January 2026.

remedy_evidence.text: Aneja and Xu (2024) found that civil-service reform under the 1883 Pendleton Act cut postal delivery errors by about 20% in U.S. cities, mainly by reducing staff turnover after elections. Rauch and Evans (2000), studying 35 developing countries, found merit-based recruitment to be the feature of bureaucracies most associated with better performance ratings. Main limitation: both studies are historical or cross-national, and protections need performance management alongside them.

R-17.tradeoffs: Strong protections make it harder to remove poor performers.
success_measures: Vacancy rates in federal agencies
Share of IRS phone calls answered
Social Security Administration wait times
R-17.alternatives: Reforming performance management within existing protections is the main alternative. Rejected option: at-will employment for policy roles.

status.text: The Office of Personnel Management's Schedule Policy/Career rule took effect March 9, 2026. An executive order of June 3, 2026 moved about 8,000 positions, nearly all at grade GS-15 or above, into the new schedule, where employees serve at will and lose the usual adverse-action procedures and appeals. At least two lawsuits challenge the rule and the order behind it: one by the National Treasury Employees Union in federal court in Washington, D.C., and one by Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility and four unions in federal court in Maryland. A Congressional Research Service review dated March 26, 2026 reported no ruling in either case.

routes.who: Codify protections and reverse Schedule Policy/Career

routes.note: Reversible.

R-18.title: Expiring emergency powers and enforced spending law
R-18.summary: National emergencies declared by a president would end after a set period unless Congress voted to renew them, and the law against withholding money Congress has appropriated would be enforced on time. Congress would regain authority by default once the law took effect. Presidents would lose some room to act alone, and responses to a real emergency could be slower.
R-18.what_it_changes: Emergencies expand presidential power and rarely retract fully (LX5: Emergencies expand presidential power), and a weaker Congress leaves room for presidential action (L11: A weaker Congress invites presidential action). Tariffs show how this works: presidents set them under statutes that delegate power (LE19: The executive sets tariff rates). Sunsets return delegated power to Congress unless it acts again, which aims to limit D2: Presidential action without new legislation. Enforcing the law against impoundment, the withholding of appropriated funds, protects Congress's spending decisions. The reform operates on loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).
R-18.who_decides: Congress can pass an emergency sunset statute, modeled on the ARTICLE ONE Act, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Courts shape the result through impoundment and statutory-authority cases (medium): in Learning Resources v. Trump (February 20, 2026), the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs.
R-18.legal_authority: Congress can attach conditions, including expiration dates, to the powers it delegates. GAO issues findings on whether withholding funds violates the Impoundment Control Act. A statute would need 60 Senate votes or a majority large enough to override a veto.
R-18.implementation: Congress passes a statute first. A regular review cycle follows, in which Congress votes to renew or end each emergency. Litigation enforces the rules where needed.
R-18.resources: No new funding is needed. Congress must set aside time to review emergencies.
R-18.enforcement: Courts and GAO enforce the rules.
R-18.costs: There is no fiscal cost. The executive loses discretion as soon as the law takes effect.
R-18.failure_risks: Any administration is expected to resist. The main adaptation is statutory substitution: after the Supreme Court struck tariffs imposed under one law, most were replaced under Sections 122, 232 and 301 of other trade laws. A veto or broad exemptions can also defeat the reform.

problem_evidence.text: More than 40 national emergencies are active. The Brennan Center for Justice counts 150 statutory emergency powers, with some emergencies in effect for decades.

remedy_evidence.text: Cross-national evidence on emergency powers supports time limits. Main limitation: substitution under other statutes can blunt any single limit, as the 2026 tariff case showed.

R-18.tradeoffs: Responses to a real emergency could be slower.
success_measures: Number of active national emergencies
GAO findings of unlawful impoundment
Tariffs imposed without a vote of Congress
R-18.alternatives: Riders on appropriations bills can restrict specific uses of emergency power. Rejected option: relying on courts alone, because the executive can switch to another statute, as it did when tariffs moved from the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to Sections 122, 232 and 301.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, Congress has not amended the National Emergencies Act or the Impoundment Control Act. The Government Accountability Office keeps ruling on withheld funds: on October 7, 2026 it found Impoundment Control Act violations involving EPA's Community Change Grants and grants from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.

routes.who: Emergency sunset statute (ARTICLE ONE Act model)

routes.note: Learning Resources struck the IEEPA tariffs.

R-19.title: Rules for drug-pricing middlemen (PBMs)
R-19.summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), the companies that manage drug benefits for insurers and employers, would face rules that cut conflicts in how they earn money, such as rebates tied to list prices and steering patients to pharmacies they own. Patients with high out-of-pocket drug costs would gain from 2028, when key federal provisions take effect. PBMs that share owners with insurers and pharmacies would lose some revenue.
R-19.what_it_changes: Concentration among a few middlemen (A3: Market concentration) can raise what patients and plans pay for drugs, part of EC9: Cost of essentials. Breaking the conflicts aims to let savings reach patients and plans. The reform touches loop B3 (New competitors can limit market power).
R-19.who_decides: Congress has already acted: P.L. 119-75, enacted in February 2026, puts key PBM provisions into effect in 2028, a route rated high. The Federal Trade Commission can settle cases through consent orders, court-approved settlements that bind a company for a set term (medium). States can pass their own PBM laws (high). State attorneys general and the Justice Department also enforce.
R-19.legal_authority: Existing antitrust and consumer-protection law supports enforcement, and the new federal statute adds specific rules. The Supreme Court's decision in Rutledge v. PCMA (2020) allows states to regulate the rates PBMs pay pharmacies.
R-19.implementation: The FTC first finalizes its pending consent orders. The federal statute's provisions take effect in 2028. Audits then check whether savings pass through to patients and plans.
R-19.resources: Enforcement budgets and audit staff at the FTC and state agencies.
R-19.enforcement: The FTC and the states enforce through orders and audits. The FTC's ability to act has been affected by quorum problems after removals of commissioners.
R-19.costs: The public cost is small. PBMs that share owners with insurers and pharmacies lose revenue from 2028 onward.
R-19.failure_risks: PBMs and their affiliated insurers are likely to oppose it, and new fee structures are the expected adaptation. Fees reappearing in new forms is the main failure risk. Reversal risk for the statute is low, though the FTC's consent orders expire when their terms end.

problem_evidence.text: An FTC staff report released in January 2025 found that pharmacies affiliated with the three largest PBMs took in $7.3 billion above estimated acquisition costs on 51 specialty generic drugs from 2017 to 2022. The figure counts revenue above acquisition cost, which differs from profit, and it comes from an agency investigation without a court finding.

remedy_evidence.text: Separating PBM pay from list prices has not been tested at scale. Main limitation: if rebates fall, insurance premiums could shift, so savings to patients need monitoring.

R-19.tradeoffs: Premiums could rise for some plans if rebates fall, and the rules invite litigation.
success_measures: Net price patients pay at the pharmacy
Spread pricing: the gap between what a PBM charges a plan and what it pays the pharmacy
Closures of independent pharmacies
R-19.alternatives: Structural separation, which would bar PBMs from sharing owners with insurers and pharmacies, is the main alternative. Rejected option: disclosure alone.

status.text: Partly in place as of October 15, 2026. A federal law signed February 3, 2026 (Public Law 119-75) sets new rules for pharmacy benefit managers, the companies that run drug benefits for insurers and employers. Its main Medicare provisions start January 1, 2028, and later provisions run into 2029. In the Federal Trade Commission's insulin case, proposed consent orders with Express Scripts (February 4, 2026) and Caremark (July 14, 2026) still await a final Commission vote. The case against Optum Rx was withdrawn from trial on June 12, 2026 so the Commission could consider a settlement; no proposed Optum Rx order had been published by October 15.

routes.note: Express Scripts (proposed Feb 4) and Caremark (proposed July 14) not final as of Oct 14; Optum Rx withdrawn from adjudication June 12.

Enacted February 3, 2026 in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-75). Medicare drug-plan rules on benefit-manager fees and full rebate pass-through start January 1, 2028. Medicare pharmacy contract standards start January 1, 2029. Rebate pass-through and reporting for employer plans apply to plan years beginning 30 months after enactment, that is, on or after August 3, 2028.
Rutledge v. PCMA (2020) allows state rate regulation.

R-20.title: Merger enforcement for consumers and workers
R-20.summary: Antitrust agencies would block or unwind mergers that raise prices for buyers or lower wages for workers, keeping a second bidder in each market. Consumers and workers in affected markets would gain over years. Companies seeking such deals would lose them at review.
R-20.what_it_changes: When a few firms control a market, they can raise prices and, as employers, hold down pay (L29: Employer concentration lowers workers' bargaining power). Concentration may also lower workers' share of income (LE06: Market concentration lowers workers' income share, rated contested).
