Merger enforcement aims to keep A3: Market concentration in check, and it acts on loop B3 (New competitors can limit market power).
R-20.who_decides: The Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general bring merger challenges, rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. The agencies' merger guidelines can change by executive action (medium) and can be reversed the same way. Congress could write standards into statute (low).
R-20.legal_authority: The Clayton Act is the legal basis for challenging mergers. The 2023 Merger Guidelines describe how the agencies apply it; they are nonbinding.
R-20.implementation: Agencies review proposed deals and challenge harmful ones in court. Later, retrospective studies of completed mergers show what happened to prices and wages.
R-20.resources: Agency budgets for economists and trial lawyers.
R-20.enforcement: Courts decide merger challenges, and the agencies lost several cases in 2025.
R-20.costs: The public cost is small. Merging firms bear their costs at review.
R-20.failure_risks: Merging firms tend to oppose it. Their main adaptation is a series of small acquisitions below the size that triggers review; a 2019 study found that raising the reporting threshold in 2001 sharply increased unreported mergers between competitors. Court losses can also stall enforcement. Guidelines can be reversed by a later administration, and enforcement proceeds case by case.

problem_evidence.text: Retrospective studies of completed mergers find price increases in most cases studied (Kwoka, 2015), though the sample leans toward industries with usable price data. Hospital mergers that raised local concentration slowed wage growth for nurses and other staff (Prager and Schmitt, 2021).

remedy_evidence.text: Blocking harmful mergers plausibly protects prices and wages, while evidence on productivity effects is weak. Main limitation: winning a case differs from changing a market, so outcomes need follow-up study.

R-20.tradeoffs: Some mergers create efficiencies that blocking them would give up.
success_measures: Prices after completed mergers
Concentration in local labor markets
R-20.alternatives: Sector-specific regulation is the main alternative.

status.text: In the case brought by the Justice Department and states against Live Nation and Ticketmaster, a jury found for the states on April 15, 2026. Judge Arun Subramanian heard the companies' motions to overturn the verdict or order a new trial in late July and had not ruled as of early October 2026. On June 3 he paused discovery on remedies until those motions are decided; in May he had said a remedies hearing would come no earlier than February 2027. The Justice Department settled separately during trial and filed its proposed final judgment on June 12, 2026. A judge must still find that settlement in the public interest under the Tunney Act before entering it.

routes.note: Reversible.

R-21.title: Faster labor-law remedies and first-contract arbitration
R-21.summary: Workers fired illegally for organizing would get faster and stronger remedies. When a new union and an employer cannot agree on a first contract, a neutral arbitrator would set the terms. Workers trying to organize would gain over several years, and employers that resist organizing would face higher costs.
R-21.what_it_changes: Weak labor law and slow enforcement reduce what workers can win at the bargaining table (L31: Insider-tilted labor rules weaken worker bargaining). Penalties that deter illegal firings, and arbitration that produces a first contract, aim to raise A2: Workers' bargaining power. Where workers can bargain, more of each dollar of output goes to wages (LE05: Bargaining power raises workers' share). The reform works through loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other) and loop R15 (Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other).
R-21.who_decides: Congress can change federal labor-law remedies by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) can act through its cases (medium), and it has had a quorum since January 7, 2026. States can change bargaining law for their public employees (medium).
R-21.legal_authority: The National Labor Relations Act preempts most state law for private-sector workers, so private-sector remedies need federal action. Under current law the NLRB can order reinstatement and back pay, and the statute provides no civil penalties.
R-21.implementation: Congress passes a statute first. Faster remedies follow. The time newly organized workplaces take to reach a first contract is then measured. A Board with a working quorum is a prerequisite.
R-21.resources: The NLRB's budget, and staff to work through its backlog of cases.
R-21.enforcement: The NLRB and federal courts enforce labor law, and the process is slow.
R-21.costs: The public cost is small. Employers pay more for violations and may face higher labor costs once contracts are reached, with a short-run risk to employment.
R-21.failure_risks: Employers would likely push back, mainly through litigation that delays outcomes. Remedies that remain too slow to matter are the main failure risk. Board doctrine swings with each new Board majority, so durable change needs a statute. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Union membership was 10.0% in 2025, down from 20.1% in 1983, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics; the 2025 figure excludes October and is not strictly comparable with other years. The Economic Policy Institute reports that employers were charged with unfair labor practices in 41.5% of union election campaigns in 2016 and 2017, and with illegal firings in about 20%; those counts are charges filed with the Board. Using NLRB data from 1999 to 2004, Ferguson (2008) found that only a minority of organizing drives reach a first contract.

remedy_evidence.text: In Canadian provinces with first-contract arbitration, Johnson (2010) found fewer work stoppages over first contracts and more settlements, with variation across provinces. Main limitation: the evidence comes from Canada, so U.S. effects and implementation still need assessment.

R-21.tradeoffs: Employers face higher costs, and there is a short-run risk to employment.
success_measures: Days from union certification to a first contract
Time to resolve unfair labor practice charges
Union density: the share of workers who belong to a union
R-21.alternatives: Sector-wide standards (R-22) are the main alternative. Rejected option: relying only on changes in Board doctrine, which flip with each Board majority.

status.text: No federal statute as of October 15, 2026. The House passed the Faster Labor Contracts Act (H.R. 5408) on June 9, 2026 by 230 to 193. It would set deadlines for bargaining a first union contract and send unresolved disputes to mediation and then binding arbitration. The bill was received in the Senate on June 10 and has had no Senate vote. The National Labor Relations Board has had a quorum since January 7, 2026, with four of five seats filled since August 2026.

routes.note: The National Labor Relations Board has had a quorum since January 7, 2026. In the Amazon JFK8 case on Staten Island, the Board ordered Amazon on April 1, 2026 to recognize and bargain with the Amazon Labor Union (374 NLRB No. 82). Amazon's challenge is pending in a federal court of appeals, where the Board's General Counsel filed an answering brief on October 9, 2026. No first contract had been reported as of October 15, 2026.

R-21.effects_confidence: high (FCA stoppages); medium (first contracts, density link); low (density response)

R-22.title: Industry-wide wage boards and sector bargaining
R-22.summary: Boards with worker and employer representatives would set wage and safety floors for a whole industry, such as fast food or nursing homes, so standards would not depend on organizing one workplace at a time. Covered workers would gain when the first standard takes effect. Employers in the sector would see narrower margins, and evidence on job and price effects is disputed.
R-22.what_it_changes: Bargaining one workplace at a time covers few U.S. workers. Sector boards set floors across an industry, so competitors cannot undercut a covered workplace. The aim is to raise A2: Workers' bargaining power and EC3: Workers' share of income. The reform operates on loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other).
R-22.who_decides: States can create sector councils by statute, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; California has one for fast food, and Minnesota has one for nursing homes. Cities can create local boards (medium). Federal legislation gets the lowest feasibility rating.
R-22.legal_authority: The National Labor Relations Act limits what states and cities can do in private-sector bargaining, so boards must be designed around federal preemption.
R-22.implementation: A statute creates the board. Members are seated, and the board sets standards. Effects on employment and prices are then evaluated.
R-22.resources: Board staff, plus data on wages in each sector.
R-22.enforcement: State labor agencies enforce the standards.
R-22.costs: The public cost is small. Employers in covered sectors pay higher wages and lose some margin once the first standard takes effect.
R-22.failure_risks: Franchise employers are expected to resist, through litigation and ballot referendums. The main failure risk is job losses if floors are set too high. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Collective bargaining covers a small share of U.S. workers. Cross-country evidence compiled by the OECD in 2019 associates sector-level coordinated bargaining with higher coverage and lower wage dispersion; that association does not establish cause.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence is contested. Two studies of California's $20 fast-food minimum wage, set under the state's 2023 Fast Food Council law (AB 1228), disagree on its effects on jobs and prices; an early evaluation by Reich at UC Berkeley reported no detectable job loss. Main limitation: these are early studies of one state and one sector.

R-22.tradeoffs: Effects on employment and prices are disputed in the California case.
success_measures: Wages in covered sectors
Employment in covered sectors
Prices in covered sectors
R-22.alternatives: A higher minimum wage (R-23) is the main alternative.

status.text: Minnesota's Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board is operating: it meets monthly in 2026, and its industry minimum wages took effect September 10, 2026 after federal approval, including $19.00 an hour for general nursing home workers and $22.50 for certified nursing assistants. California's Fast Food Council, created by a 2023 state law, oversees the $20 fast-food minimum wage that took effect in April 2024.

routes.note: California fast food; Minnesota nursing homes.

R-23.title: Minimum wage that rises with an index
R-23.summary: The minimum wage would rise each year with a published measure of prices or wages, so the lowest-paid workers would keep pace between legislative votes. Low-wage workers would gain as the new floor phases in. Low-margin employers would bear higher labor costs over the same period.
R-23.what_it_changes: An indexed floor raises pay at the bottom without a new legislative vote every few years. It aims to raise EC7: Household income and A4: Households' financial security, and it touches loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other).
R-23.who_decides: State legislatures can act, rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030, and so can voters by ballot measure (high). Cities can set their own floors where state law does not preempt them (medium). Congress can raise the federal floor, a route rated low.
R-23.legal_authority: Federal, state and local governments have clear authority to set minimum wages, though states can preempt their cities.
R-23.implementation: The new floor phases in first. Indexing then adjusts it each year, and employment is monitored throughout.
R-23.resources: No public funding is needed. State labor departments carry out enforcement.
R-23.enforcement: Labor agencies enforce the floor, mainly through wage-theft investigations.
R-23.costs: There is no direct public cost. Employers with low margins pay higher wages during the phase-in.
R-23.failure_risks: Low-wage employers are likely to oppose it, and they can adapt by cutting hours. The chief risk is a floor set above what the local labor market can bear. Once indexed, the floor is durable and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 2009, according to the Department of Labor.

remedy_evidence.text: Within studied ranges, evidence finds little job loss. Cengiz, Dube, Lindner and Zipperer (2019), studying state increases through 2016, found no detectable job loss, a result other methods dispute. The evidence is strongest up to about 60% of the local median wage. Main limitation: higher floors fall outside the studied range; the Congressional Budget Office's 2019 median estimate for a $15 federal floor by 2025 was 1.3 million jobs lost and 1.3 million people lifted from poverty, with wide uncertainty.

R-23.tradeoffs: Employment effects become a concern when the floor rises above about 60% of the local median wage.
success_measures: Wages at the 10th percentile of earners
Employment rate
R-23.alternatives: The Earned Income Tax Credit, which adds to low earnings through the tax system, is the main alternative. Rejected option: floors without indexing.

status.text: As of the Labor Department's state table updated July 1, 2026, 30 states and the District of Columbia set a minimum wage above the federal $7.25 an hour.

routes.note: Where not preempted.

R-23.effects_confidence: high to 60% of median; low above

R-24.title: Paid family and medical leave insurance
R-24.summary: Workers would receive part of their pay while they take time off for their own illness, a new child or a sick family member, paid for by payroll contributions. Workers with new children or sick relatives would gain once benefits begin, a year after contributions start. Employers would pay contributions from the start.
R-24.what_it_changes: Caring for family takes time and money (EC9: Cost of essentials), and losing a job to provide care weakens A4: Households' financial security. Paid leave insurance pays for time to give care without losing the job. It acts on loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions).
R-24.who_decides: State legislatures can create programs, rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Voters can do so by ballot measure (medium). A federal program is rated low.
R-24.legal_authority: States and Congress have clear authority to create social insurance programs of this kind.
R-24.implementation: A statute passes first. Payroll contributions begin next. Benefits start a year after contributions.
R-24.resources: Payroll contributions fund the program, and the state needs a claims system to process applications.
R-24.enforcement: A state insurance agency runs the program and collects contributions.
R-24.costs: Payroll contributions finance the program, with employers paying from the start. Small firms face some disruption when staff take leave.
R-24.failure_risks: Some employers tend to oppose it, and they can adapt by offering private plans that opt out of the state program. The likeliest way it falls short is low use of the benefit among low-wage workers. Programs are durable, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: About one in four private-industry workers had access to paid family leave in March 2025, with access lowest among low-wage workers, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Care is costly: Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group, puts the national average childcare price at $13,184 in 2025. Federal time-use data for 2025 show women spending 2.38 hours a day on household activities and men 1.58.

remedy_evidence.text: Leave-taking rises under these programs: an early study of California's program found more leave and later more work hours among mothers. Long-run employment effects are contested; a later California study found lower employment and earnings for first-time mothers. Main limitation: most evidence comes from one state's program.

R-24.tradeoffs: Payroll costs rise, and small firms face disruption when staff take leave.
success_measures: Leave-taking by income level
Employment of mothers after a birth
R-24.alternatives: Requiring employers to provide paid leave directly is the main alternative. Rejected option: unpaid leave alone.

status.text: As of October 2026, 14 states and the District of Columbia have enacted paid family and medical leave insurance. Twelve of those states and the District were paying benefits; Maryland's and Virginia's programs have not started paying benefits.

R-25.title: Full child tax credit for low-earning families
R-25.summary: Families would receive the full child tax credit even if they earn little or nothing, because the credit would be fully refundable, paid out even when it exceeds the tax a family owes. Low-income families with children would gain from the first payment. Federal taxpayers would bear the cost each year, about $100 billion at the 2021 design.
R-25.what_it_changes: Benefits paid through the tax system lift households above the poverty line (LE14: Public benefits lift households out of poverty). A credit paid in full to families with little or no earnings raises EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits, where a higher value means more net support for the households discussed, and A4: Households' financial security. The reform works through loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions) and loop B2 (Automatic benefits cushion economic shocks).
R-25.who_decides: Congress decides. Budget reconciliation, which can pass the Senate with 51 votes, is the federal route, rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. States can create their own child credits, a route rated high.
R-25.legal_authority: Congress has clear authority over federal tax credits, and reconciliation can carry tax and spending changes with a simple Senate majority.
R-25.implementation: Congress enacts the credit permanently. Payments go out monthly. Child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts taxes and benefits, tracks the results. A funding decision is the prerequisite.
R-25.resources: Large: about $100 billion a year at the 2021 design. The IRS needs outreach to families who do not file tax returns.
R-25.costs: The cost is large, about $100 billion a year at the 2021 design, paid from the federal budget on an ongoing basis.
R-25.failure_risks: Members of Congress focused on limiting spending, and advocates of work requirements, would likely push back. Their main adaptation is to phase the credit in with earnings, which shrinks it for families with the lowest earnings. The biggest risk is a temporary design that lapses again, as the 2021 expansion did on its expiration date. Reversal risk is high if the credit is temporary.

problem_evidence.text: Child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure fell to 5.2% in 2021, when the expanded credit and other pandemic programs were in place, and was 13.4% in 2024 as first published. Census revised the 2019 to 2024 rates in 2026 after a correction to poverty thresholds. Several programs contributed to the 2021 drop, so it does not isolate the credit.

remedy_evidence.text: The poverty effect of the credit is large and well supported, and a 2019 National Academies review found that income support improves child outcomes. The effect on parents' employment is contested. Main limitation: the 2021 expansion lasted one year, so direct evidence on a permanent program is limited to that short period.

R-25.tradeoffs: The fiscal cost is large, and effects on parents' work are debated.
success_measures: Child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure
Share of families with children reporting they lacked enough food
Employment of parents
R-25.alternatives: A larger Earned Income Tax Credit or state child credits are the main alternatives. Rejected option: temporary expansions with expiration dates.

status.text: Under the July 2025 tax law (Public Law 119-21), the child tax credit is worth up to $2,200 per child. At most $1,700 of it is refundable, meaning paid to families whose credit exceeds the income tax they owe, and the refundable part requires at least $2,500 in earnings. Families with low or no earnings therefore receive part of the credit or none of it.

R-26.title: Recession aid that starts automatically
R-26.summary: Benefits such as unemployment insurance would expand automatically when published measures, such as rising unemployment, show a downturn, so help would arrive without waiting for Congress to agree on a new bill. Workers who lose jobs or hours in the next recession would gain. In good years the cost would be zero.
R-26.what_it_changes: Benefits written into law that grow as conditions worsen help households absorb a shock while Congress considers more (loop B2: Automatic benefits cushion economic shocks). Building triggers into law aims to raise EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits during downturns and to protect A4: Households' financial security.
R-26.who_decides: Congress decides by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030.
R-26.legal_authority: Congress has clear authority to set benefit rules and triggers in law.
R-26.implementation: Congress writes the triggers into law. The delivery systems are then tested before a downturn arrives. Modern state unemployment insurance systems are a prerequisite.
R-26.resources: Spending rises and falls with the economy. Capacity depends on state unemployment insurance systems, where outdated technology has caused problems (see R-39).
R-26.enforcement: Benefits start automatically when the trigger is met.
R-26.costs: The cost is zero in good years and rises in downturns.
R-26.failure_risks: Members of Congress focused on deficits are expected to resist, mainly by pressing for narrow triggers. Delivery is the likeliest way it falls short: GAO found improper payment rates in pandemic unemployment programs rose from 9.2% in fiscal 2020 to 18.9% in fiscal 2021, with outdated state systems a factor. Reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: Help was delayed in the 2008 and 2020 recessions. Unemployment insurance reaches roughly a quarter to a third of unemployed people, according to Labor Department data.

remedy_evidence.text: The stabilizing effect of benefits that expand in downturns is well supported. Main limitation: trigger design and delivery systems decide whether help arrives on time and reaches the right people.

R-26.tradeoffs: Triggers that fire at the wrong time could add to inflation.
success_measures: Days from a trigger being met to the first payment
Speed of employment recovery after a downturn
R-26.alternatives: Discretionary stimulus, passed by Congress in each downturn, is the main alternative.

status.text: Not enacted in federal law as of June 2026.

R-27.title: IRS enforcement of taxes already owed
R-27.summary: The IRS would get steady, multi-year funding to hire and train auditors for complex, high-income returns, with taxpayer rights protected. Taxpayers who already comply would gain over years as more of the tax owed is collected. High-income people who underpay would face a higher chance of audit.
R-27.what_it_changes: Tax law already steers many benefits to the top (LE12: Insider-tilted tax law reduces net household support), and weak enforcement widens the gap between the rules as written and what is paid. Auditing high-income returns collects tax owed and acts on E1: Policy advantages for wealthy and organized interests. A better-staffed IRS also improves D5: Quality of public services, such as phone service. The reform operates on loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other).
R-27.who_decides: Congress funds the IRS; multi-year appropriations are rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. The IRS sets its enforcement priorities by executive action (medium).
R-27.legal_authority: Congress has clear authority to fund tax enforcement.
R-27.implementation: Congress provides multi-year funding first. The IRS then hires and trains staff. Audits of high-income returns follow.
R-27.resources: Recurring, multi-year funding. Staff are the constraint: the IRS lost about a quarter of its staff in 2025.
R-27.enforcement: The IRS itself is the enforcement agency.
R-27.costs: The program pays for itself. The Congressional Budget Office's February 2024 benchmark is about $6.40 in added revenue, collected over several years, for each $1 of added enforcement spending, with returns falling as spending grows.
R-27.failure_risks: High-income filers and paid preparers are likely to oppose it, with new avoidance structures as the expected adaptation. Rescinded funding and staff who are never rebuilt are the main failure risks; funding has been rescinded before. Reversal risk is high.

problem_evidence.text: The IRS projects a net tax gap of $606 billion for tax year 2022: tax owed and never paid, even after enforcement. GAO found that audit rates for incomes over $5 million fell from 16% to about 2% between 2010 and 2019.

remedy_evidence.text: Using IRS data, Boning, Hendren, Sprung-Keyser and Stuart estimate that an added $1 spent auditing taxpayers above the 90th income percentile returns more than $12 in revenue, against about $5 for taxpayers below the median. Main limitation: returns fall as enforcement spending grows, and lasting gains depend on durable funding and fair treatment of taxpayers.

R-27.tradeoffs: More audits raise privacy and fairness concerns.
success_measures: Audit rate for incomes over $1 million
Net tax gap
Share of IRS phone calls answered
R-27.alternatives: A simpler tax code is the main alternative.

status.text: The IRS workforce fell from about 102,100 employees in January 2025 to about 74,500 on December 18, 2025, a drop of 27%, as reported by the National Taxpayer Advocate, an independent office within the IRS. The Small Business/Self-Employed division, which examines many business and individual returns, lost 38% of its staff over the same period.

R-28.title: Taxing inherited gains and capital income
R-28.summary: Gains on stocks, businesses and other assets would be taxed when their owner dies, and income from capital would be taxed more like wages. Future taxpayers would gain over decades as revenue rises and the largest fortunes grow more slowly. Large estates would pay more at the owner's death.
R-28.what_it_changes: Tax preferences for capital income help large fortunes grow (L03: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top). Under a rule called step-up in basis, gains on assets held until death escape income tax when heirs inherit them. Ending step-up and taxing capital income more like wages aims to slow the growth of A1: Concentration of household wealth and EC4: Concentration of stock ownership. The reform touches loop R1 (Wealth and political influence reinforce each other).
R-28.who_decides: Congress decides, through budget reconciliation; this route is rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030.
R-28.legal_authority: Congress has clear authority over federal tax law. Current law sets a top rate of 20% on long-term capital gains and dividends, against 37% on ordinary income.
R-28.implementation: Congress ends step-up first. Valuation rules for hard-to-price assets follow. Avoidance is then monitored. A capable IRS (R-27) is a prerequisite.
R-28.resources: IRS staff who can value assets such as private businesses.
R-28.enforcement: The IRS enforces the tax, relying on its ability to value assets.
R-28.costs: The reform raises revenue, estimated at $30 billion to $50 billion a year. Large estates pay at the owner's death.
R-28.failure_risks: Households holding large unrealized gains tend to oppose it, through trusts and lobbying. Avoidance and repeal are the main failure risks. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: The top 1% of households held 32.5% of household net worth in the second quarter of 2026, the highest since the series began in 1989, according to Federal Reserve data. The Congressional Budget Office found that 75% of the benefit of lower rates on capital gains and dividends went to the top 1% in 2019.

remedy_evidence.text: Calibrated economic models support the direction. Natural experiments with wealth taxes in Denmark and Switzerland found that taxing wealth reduces its measured accumulation at the top, partly through avoidance. Main limitation: that evidence concerns wealth taxes in other countries, and illiquid family businesses need explicit rules.

R-28.tradeoffs: Family businesses can lack the cash to pay the tax, and some owners will seek ways to avoid it.
success_measures: Top 1% share of household wealth
Capital gains realized each year
Revenue raised
R-28.alternatives: A wealth tax is the main alternative.

status.text: The July 2025 tax law (Public Law 119-21) set the federal estate-tax exemption at $15 million per person for deaths in 2026, up from $13.99 million in 2025. Two preferences for investment income remain in place under current law: lower tax rates on dividends and long-term capital gains, which Congress's Joint Committee on Taxation estimates will cost about $252 billion in fiscal 2026, and the exclusion of unrealized gains on assets held at death, estimated at about $73 billion.

R-29.title: Baby bonds: publicly funded child accounts
R-29.summary: Children would receive a publicly funded savings account early in life, with larger deposits for children from families with little wealth. Children born into families without wealth would gain at 18, when they can use the money. The main benefit arrives 18 years after the program starts.
R-29.what_it_changes: Family wealth shapes what young adults own and owe (EC8: Household assets and debts). Accounts seeded early give children without family wealth an asset at adulthood. The reform acts on loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions).
R-29.who_decides: States can create baby bond programs, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; Connecticut has one. Congress can act (low), and a 2025 federal law created $1,000 accounts for children.
R-29.legal_authority: States and Congress have clear authority to create such accounts.
R-29.implementation: The government seeds each account. The money grows over time, and outcomes are measured when account holders turn 18.
R-29.resources: Funding is large at national scale and small at a $1,000 deposit. Treasury offices must administer the accounts.
R-29.enforcement: The U.S. Treasury or state treasurers hold and manage the accounts.
R-29.costs: Large at national scale and small at a $1,000 deposit per child, paid from public budgets.
R-29.failure_risks: Few groups resist openly; underfunding is the likely response. Deposits too small to matter are the main failure risk. Once funded, programs are durable, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: The median net worth of families headed by someone under 35 was $39,000 in 2022, according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances.

remedy_evidence.text: The arithmetic is strong: money deposited early grows by adulthood. An Oklahoma randomized experiment with universal child accounts (SEED OK) found modest gains in young children's social and emotional development. Main limitation: how families use and add to accounts at national scale is untested, and long-run outcomes are unknown.

R-29.tradeoffs: Benefits arrive 18 years after the program starts.
success_measures: Account balances at age 18, by family wealth
R-29.alternatives: A fully refundable child credit (R-25), which pays families now, is the main alternative.

status.text: The July 2025 tax law created Trump accounts, savings accounts for children. The Treasury deposits $1,000 for each U.S. citizen child born from January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2028, and no money could go into the accounts before July 4, 2026. Connecticut runs a state-funded baby bonds program, which reported more than 33,000 eligible children in July 2025.

routes.note: Connecticut.

The July 2025 tax law (Public Law 119-21) created Trump accounts with a one-time $1,000 Treasury deposit for U.S. citizen children born from 2025 through 2028; accounts could first receive money on July 4, 2026.

R-30.title: More homes allowed by right near jobs
R-30.summary: Homes that meet clear, published rules could be built near jobs and transit without a separate discretionary approval, such as a hearing where neighbors can block each project. Renters and young households would gain within three to ten years as more homes are built and rents ease. Owners in high-demand places would give up some price growth and some control over their neighborhoods.
R-30.what_it_changes: Scarcity raises the value of existing homes (L38: Scarcity raises existing home values), and owners with equity at stake organize to block new supply (L39: Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing). Allowing homes by right moves the decision out of meetings dominated by those owners. The aim is to reduce A5: Housing scarcity and, through it, rents and prices (LE17: Housing scarcity raises rents and prices). The reform works through loop R8 (Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building).
R-30.who_decides: States can preempt local zoning by statute, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; under Massachusetts's MBTA Communities law, 157 municipalities were in compliance as of August 27, 2026. Voters can act by ballot measure (medium). Massachusetts Question 7, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would allow single-family homes on residential lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of frontage and public water and sewer. Cities can change their own plans (medium).
R-30.legal_authority: States can preempt local zoning, which lets them override town rules that block housing.
R-30.implementation: A state law comes first. Local governments then bring their zoning into compliance. Permits follow, then completed homes, and rents respond last. On-cycle local elections (R-06) help by widening who votes on local housing decisions.
R-30.resources: Infrastructure for the added homes, permitting staff in local governments, and builders able to take on the work.
R-30.enforcement: State agencies enforce compliance, and the attorney general can sue towns that do not comply, with courts deciding those cases.
R-30.costs: The direct public cost is small, though infrastructure for new homes carries a real cost. Owners in high-demand places give up some appreciation.
R-30.failure_risks: Incumbent owners and some local officials would likely push back. Their adaptations include drawing new zones where nothing can be built and filing lawsuits. The reform can also fail through compliance on paper only, or when construction costs and infrastructure limits prevent building. Reversal risk is medium, since local resistance continues.

problem_evidence.text: A record 22.7 million renter households, 49% of renters, were cost-burdened in 2024, meaning they spent more than 30% of income on housing, according to Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies.

remedy_evidence.text: Where zoning limits bind, allowing more homes raises building and lowers rents over time. Auckland, New Zealand's 2016 upzoning roughly doubled permits in upzoned areas, and six years later three-bedroom rents were 22% to 35% below a modeled comparison. Minneapolis is also cited, though a 2025 Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis analysis attributes much of that city's slower rent growth to a drop in demand in 2020. Main limitation: results depend on whether zoning was the binding limit, and infrastructure and construction costs can still block delivery.

R-30.tradeoffs: Owners in high-demand places give up some price growth and control, and neighborhoods change.
success_measures: Housing permits per 1,000 residents
Rents for new and existing units
Who moves into new homes, by income and age
R-30.alternatives: Rejected option: subsidies that help buyers or renters pay without adding supply, because on their own they raise prices.

status.text: Massachusetts: 157 cities and towns had zoning found compliant with the MBTA Communities Act as of August 27, 2026. That state law requires communities served by the Boston-area transit system to zone for multifamily housing by right. Question 7 on the November 3, 2026 state ballot, a law proposed by initiative petition, would allow single-family homes on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of frontage and public water and sewer; local rules on height, setbacks, open space and parking would still apply.

routes.note: Massachusetts MBTA Communities: 157 compliant.
Massachusetts Question 7 on single-family homes.

R-30.effects_confidence: high where binding; medium for US statutes

R-31.title: Childcare supply and pay for care workers
R-31.summary: Public money would fund childcare slots and the wages needed to recruit and keep staff, which lowers what families pay and keeps centers open. Parents of young children would gain within two to five years as supply grows. The cost is large and recurring, paid from public budgets.
R-31.what_it_changes: Childcare is a major cost for families with young children (EC9: Cost of essentials), and it weighs on A4: Households' financial security. Funding supply together with workforce pay aims to lower prices and keep centers open. It operates on loop R5 (Financial strain narrows who takes part in policy decisions).
R-31.who_decides: States can fund programs, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030, and cities can as well (medium). Congress can fund programs nationally, a route rated low.
R-31.legal_authority: States, cities and Congress have clear authority to fund childcare.
R-31.implementation: Governments first fund slots and wages. Supply then expands, and price and quality are measured as it grows. A pipeline of trained workers is a prerequisite.
R-31.resources: Large, recurring funding. Workforce shortages limit how fast supply can grow.
R-31.enforcement: State licensing sets and enforces standards for providers.
R-31.costs: The cost is large and recurring, paid from public budgets.
R-31.failure_risks: Officials who object to the cost are expected to resist, mainly by underfunding programs. Workforce shortages are the main failure risk. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Child Care Aware of America, an advocacy group compiling state data, puts the national average childcare price at $13,184 in 2025 and reports that center care for two children costs more than median rent in every state with data. A 2021 Treasury report found median childcare worker pay near the bottom of the wage distribution.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence that affordable childcare raises mothers' employment is strong: a 2017 research review found that a 10% drop in cost raises maternal employment by between 0.25% and 11%, a wide range. Evidence on outcomes for children is moderate. Main limitation: quality can suffer when programs grow fast; Quebec's universal program raised maternal employment and was linked to some negative effects on child behavior, a contested finding.

R-31.tradeoffs: Fast expansion risks lower quality, as research on Quebec's program suggests.
success_measures: Childcare price as a share of family income
Licensed slots per child
Employment of mothers with young children
R-31.alternatives: A fully refundable child credit (R-25) is the main alternative. Rejected option: vouchers that do not add supply.

status.text: State programs vary widely. New Mexico offers free child care to all families regardless of income, paying providers directly with no family copays, and its 2026 legislature wrote the program into state law.

R-32.title: Public and philanthropic funding for local news
R-32.summary: Public agencies and foundations would fund reporting on local government, with firewalls that keep funders out of editorial decisions. Residents of counties with little or no local news would gain over years as more reporters cover city halls and school boards. Whether these funds improve accountability has not yet been evaluated.
R-32.what_it_changes: Platforms took much of the advertising that once paid for local reporting (LT03: Platforms drew ad revenue from local news), and local coverage raises the risk officials face of losing office (L26: Local reporting raises pressure on incumbents). Funding with editorial firewalls aims to restore variable B2: Availability of local reporting, which rises with more reporters and falls as more counties lose their local source. It touches loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other) and loop B1a (Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism).
R-32.who_decides: Philanthropy can act now, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; Press Forward is one example. States can create funds and tax credits (medium), as New Jersey did with its Civic Information Consortium. A federal tax credit is rated low.
R-32.legal_authority: Governments have clear authority to fund journalism. Editorial independence has to be written into each program's design.
R-32.implementation: Funders provide money first. Coverage of local government is then measured. Firewalls between funders and newsrooms are a prerequisite.
R-32.resources: Recurring funding, and local newsrooms able to use it.
R-32.enforcement: Grant terms enforce the firewalls and the commitment to cover local government.
R-32.costs: The cost is small, paid by state budgets or foundations.
R-32.failure_risks: Critics of public money for the press would likely try to defund programs. Funds that go to outlets that do not cover government are the main failure risk. Programs that depend on annual appropriations are fragile, and reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Northwestern University's Medill Local News Initiative counted 213 U.S. counties with no local news source in 2025, with about 50 million people having limited or no access to local news. Gao, Lee and Murphy (2020) found that local government borrowing costs rise after newspapers close. Newspaper advertising revenue fell from about $49.4 billion in 2005 to about $9.8 billion in 2022, according to Pew Research Center.

remedy_evidence.text: Funding models exist. Main limitation: no evaluation has yet shown that these funds improve coverage or accountability, so their effect remains a hypothesis.

R-32.tradeoffs: Government funding of the press raises concerns about its independence.
success_measures: Reporters per county
Local government meetings covered by a reporter
Counties with no local news source
R-32.alternatives: Requiring platforms to pay publishers is the main alternative, and it is contested. Rejected option: funding tied to content.

status.text: New Jersey's state-created Civic Information Consortium reports more than $14.8 million invested in local news and information projects. Press Forward, a national coalition of philanthropic funders, reports more than $400 million invested in local news and 48 local chapters. Both figures come from the organizations' own websites as of October 2026.

routes.note: New Jersey Civic Information Consortium.
Press Forward.

R-33.title: Citizen assemblies that officials must answer
R-33.summary: A group of residents chosen by lottery to match the makeup of the community would study a hard public question and make recommendations, and officials would have to respond in public. The residents selected would gain a direct role right away. Officials would keep the final decision and would have to explain it.
R-33.what_it_changes: Randomly selected residents deliberate, and officials must answer them publicly. The reform is linked to E2: Trust earned through performance and to variable B3: Civic ties across social and political groups. It sits on loop R9 (Taking part in a successful repair may support the next one), a conceptual loop that remains a hypothesis.
R-33.who_decides: City councils can create assemblies, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. States can do so by statute (medium); Oregon's Citizens' Initiative Review is one state example.
R-33.legal_authority: Cities and states have clear authority to convene assemblies and require a response. A duty to respond leaves the final decision with elected officials.
R-33.implementation: Residents are selected first. They deliberate, officials respond, and the process is evaluated.
R-33.resources: Modest funding, mainly for trained moderators who run the sessions.
R-33.enforcement: A duty to respond publicly is the enforcement mechanism.
R-33.costs: Modest, paid by the city or state that convenes the assembly.
R-33.failure_risks: Officials and groups with established access to decisions tend to oppose it, and the likely adaptation is consultation held for show. Recommendations that are ignored are the main failure risk. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Trust in public institutions is low. An AP-NORC and USAFacts survey published in September 2026 found that 44% of U.S. adults trust information from federal agencies at least moderately. Surveys ask about different institutions, so each figure describes trust in one of them.

remedy_evidence.text: Effects on the residents who take part are strong. An OECD review published in 2020 catalogued close to 300 cases of representative deliberation and set out design principles and limits. Main limitation: evidence that assemblies change trust or participation across the wider population is weak.

R-33.tradeoffs: Panels are unelected, which raises questions about their standing.
success_measures: How closely assembly members match the population
Quality of officials' public responses
Follow-up on recommendations
R-33.alternatives: Public hearings are the main alternative. Rejected option: binding panels, whose decisions officials would have to adopt.

status.text: The OECD's 2020 study catalogued close to 300 representative deliberative processes, such as citizens' assemblies and juries, in its member countries.

routes.note: Oregon Citizens' Initiative Review.

R-34.title: Participatory budgeting: residents decide spending
R-34.summary: Residents would decide how to spend part of a city's budget, proposing projects and voting on them. Neighborhoods with low turnout would gain in the first cycle, and people who take part become more likely to vote in later elections. Council members would give up some discretion over that money.
R-34.what_it_changes: Residents decide part of a budget, which raises later voting among participants. The aim is to raise B5: Equality of voter turnout, where a smaller turnout gap between groups counts as an increase. It sits on loop R9 (Taking part in a successful repair may support the next one), a conceptual loop that remains a hypothesis.
R-34.who_decides: City councils decide through their budgets, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030.
R-34.legal_authority: Cities have clear authority over their own budgets.
R-34.implementation: The city sets aside an amount first. Residents propose projects and vote. The city builds the winning projects, and the process is evaluated.
R-34.resources: A share of the budget, plus outreach to bring residents into the process.
R-34.enforcement: The city carries out the residents' decisions.
R-34.costs: Small. The money comes from the existing budget.
R-34.failure_risks: Council members who lose discretion would likely push back, typically by setting aside small amounts. Budgets too small to matter are the main failure risk. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Turnout differs across income groups and neighborhoods.

remedy_evidence.text: In New York City, Johnson, Carlson and Reynolds (2023) found that taking part in participatory budgeting raised participants' later probability of voting by 8.4 percentage points compared with similar voters, with larger effects for young, lower-income and Black voters. Main limitation: the effect is measured among participants, and low participation or a small budget can limit the effect on the wider public.

R-34.tradeoffs: Low participation can skew which projects win.
success_measures: Later voting among participants
How funds are distributed across neighborhoods
R-34.alternatives: Citizen assemblies (R-33) are the main alternative.

status.text: New York City runs a citywide participatory budgeting process called The People's Money. Its fifth cycle took ideas from October 14 to November 18, 2026, with a public vote planned for spring 2027 and projects carried out from fall 2027 to fall 2028.

R-35.title: Rejected option: term limits for legislators
R-35.summary: Term limits force experienced legislators out after a set number of terms, and studies of state legislatures find that this weakens how legislatures work. Lobbyists are expected to gain influence once the first legislators reach their limits, an inferred step the studies did not measure.
R-35.what_it_changes: Term limits remove experienced legislators. The inferred result is that legislatures lean more on lobbyists and staff and produce less. The option sits on the proposed loop R2 (Congress becomes dependent on outside expertise), through L18: Congressional expertise may reduce insider influence and L19: Insider-tilted policy may weaken congressional expertise, and term limits push that loop in the harmful direction.
R-35.who_decides: No route is recommended for this option. For reference, voters in initiative states can impose limits on state legislators by ballot measure, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; a feasibility rating describes how likely adoption is and carries no endorsement. The idea is popular: a Pew Research Center survey in July 2023 found that 87% of U.S. adults favor term limits for members of Congress. Limits on Congress would require a constitutional amendment under Article V, which gets the lowest feasibility rating.
R-35.legal_authority: In U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton (1995), the Supreme Court held that states cannot impose term limits on members of Congress. States can limit terms for their own legislators.
R-35.implementation: No implementation steps are set out, because the evidence argues against adoption. Once adopted, limits operate automatically as legislators reach the maximum number of terms.
R-35.resources: Term limits need no funding. Their effect on capacity runs the other way: legislatures lose experienced members and what they know.
R-35.enforcement: Limits enforce themselves: a legislator who reaches the limit cannot run again.
R-35.costs: There is no direct fiscal cost. The cost is lost legislative experience; the cited studies measured polarization and legislative effort, and greater reliance on lobbyists is an inferred mechanism.
R-35.failure_risks: How adoption could fail is not assessed for a rejected option. Once adopted, term limits are durable and reversal risk is low, so the harms the evidence describes tend to persist.

problem_evidence.text: The condition that term limits target exists: many legislators serve long tenures. Evidence about harm comes from the studies of term limits below.

remedy_evidence.text: Here the grade measures confidence in a finding of harm: strong evidence that term limits weaken legislatures. That finding is the reason the option is rejected, and a strong grade on this page is a warning against adoption. Olson and Rogowski (2020), using state legislative roll-call votes from 1993 to 2016, found that term limits increased polarization, with larger effects in more professional legislatures. Fouirnaies and Hall (2022), studying about 6,000 legislators in states with term limits, found that members who can no longer run again sponsor fewer bills, do less committee work and miss more floor votes. Main limitation: these two studies measure polarization and legislative effort; greater reliance on lobbyists and staff is an inferred mechanism these studies did not measure directly.

R-35.tradeoffs: Term limits remove experienced members and push legislatures toward depending on outside expertise (loop R2).
success_measures: Reliance on lobbyists in legislatures with term limits, compared with legislatures without them
Bills passed in legislatures with term limits, compared with legislatures without them
R-35.alternatives: Building the legislature's own staff and expertise (R-13) is the alternative.

status.text: Research on state legislatures links term limits to weaker legislative capacity.

routes.note: 87% of adults favored congressional term limits (Pew, July 2023).

R-36.title: Lasting public investment in research and infrastructure
R-36.summary: Congress would fund research and infrastructure over several years and protect appropriated money from being canceled or left unspent, so projects reach completion. Future workers and the regions that host research would gain over 10 to 30 years. Current taxpayers would pay now for benefits that arrive later.
R-36.what_it_changes: Public research and infrastructure raise private productivity with long lags (LE01: Public research investment raises productivity). Congress appropriates the money (LE02: Congress decides public investment levels), and the executive can withhold, cancel or redirect it (LE03: The executive administers appropriated public investment). Gains depend on money arriving and staying, so delivery and durability matter as much as the size of the budget. The reform sits on no feedback loop.
R-36.who_decides: Congress can pass multi-year appropriations with protection against cancellation, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Agencies can build delivery capacity by executive action (medium), which a later administration can reverse. States can create infrastructure banks and research funds (medium). Courts enforcing impoundment law offer another path (medium).
R-36.legal_authority: Congress appropriates and the executive carries out spending. Enforcing the law against impoundment, the withholding of appropriated money (R-18), keeps funds from being held back.
R-36.implementation: Congress provides multi-year funding first. Agencies then staff up to deliver. Spending is tracked as it goes out, and returns are measured over a decade. Impoundment enforcement (R-18) and delivery staff protected by civil-service rules (R-17) are prerequisites.
R-36.resources: Multi-year funding, agency staff to deliver projects, and permitting capacity.
R-36.enforcement: GAO and the courts enforce spending law.
R-36.costs: The cost is moderate and paid by current taxpayers. Estimated returns on nondefense government research run 140% to 210%.
R-36.failure_risks: Members of Congress focused on deficits, and those backing competing priorities, are expected to resist, mainly through cancellation and slow spending. The main failure risk is money appropriated and never spent, or canceled by the next administration: GAO reported that $7.8 billion of $11 billion in CHIPS Act research awards was canceled. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Federally funded research and development fell from 1.86% of GDP in 1964 to 0.63% in 2022, according to the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. Money also flows out slowly: of Department of Transportation funds under the 2021 infrastructure law, 75.7% had been committed and 46.6% paid out as of July 31, 2026.

remedy_evidence.text: Two studies with different designs find high long-run returns. Fieldhouse and Mertens, in a 2024 working paper, estimate returns of 140% to 210% on nondefense government research, and Gross and Sampat (2023) found that World War II research spending seeded lasting regional clusters of innovation. Main limitation: each study rests on one identification strategy with wide uncertainty, a wartime shock may not generalize, and evidence on delivery is thin.

R-36.tradeoffs: Deficits rise, government may pick winners, and the payoff arrives slowly, after the officials who voted for it have left office.
success_measures: Share of appropriations spent on schedule
Research awards canceled
Patenting and productivity in regions that receive funding
R-36.alternatives: Tax credits for private research are the main alternative. Rejected option: one-time grants without the capacity to deliver.

status.text: Spending under the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act continues: of the $545.7 billion the Transportation Department administers, 75.7% had been obligated and 46.6% paid out as of July 31, 2026. For the CHIPS Act's chip-manufacturing incentives, the Commerce Department had funded 49 projects worth $31.5 billion and paid out $13.1 billion, by the Government Accountability Office's August 2026 count. Commerce also canceled $7.8 billion of the $11 billion appropriated for advanced microelectronics research awards.

routes.who: Multi-year appropriations with protection against cancellation

routes.note: Reversible.

routes.who: State infrastructure banks and research funds

R-37.title: Feed choice and data access for researchers
R-37.summary: Social media users could choose how their feeds are ranked, and independent researchers could study platform data under privacy safeguards. Users and researchers would gain once the rules take effect, and platforms would lose some control over their data. Experiments show that ranking changes move what people see, with small measured effects on how they feel about the other party.
R-37.what_it_changes: Ranking decides what people see (LT01: Engagement-ranked feeds raise hostile-content exposure). The direction of the effect depends on the platform and the ranking rule compared: switching to chronological feeds has raised some kinds of content and lowered others. Concentrated ownership may also entrench engagement ranking (LT02: Platform concentration may entrench engagement ranking, a hypothesis). The reform is a transparency and choice measure acting on loop R3 (Political hostility and hostile content may reinforce each other), whose key link is contested.
R-37.who_decides: Congress can pass a platform transparency and researcher-access statute, rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. State laws are also rated low because of First Amendment limits; in Moody v. NetChoice (2024), the Supreme Court recognized platforms' editorial rights. Platforms can act on their own (medium), and some have offered chronological feeds voluntarily.
R-37.legal_authority: Authority is narrow. Rules on how content is ranked raise First Amendment problems, while rules on data access and user choice stand on firmer ground.
R-37.implementation: Researcher access comes first. User choice of ranking follows, and public reporting comes after that. Privacy safeguards for data access are a prerequisite.
R-37.resources: A small public cost, plus infrastructure for researchers and privacy safeguards.
R-37.enforcement: The Federal Trade Commission or another designated agency would enforce.
R-37.costs: The public cost is small. Platforms bear compliance costs and lose some control of their data.
R-37.failure_risks: Platforms are likely to oppose it, mainly by keeping data access narrow. Two risks stand out: most users keep the default feed, and access may be too narrow to study effects. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Ranking changes what people see. In a 2020 experiment with Facebook and Instagram users, chronological feeds raised political and untrustworthy content and lowered uncivil content (Guess and colleagues, 2023). In a July to September 2023 experiment with 4,965 U.S. users of X, the platform's ranking algorithm shifted users' policy priorities in a conservative direction by about 0.11 to 0.12 standard deviations (Gauthier and colleagues, 2026).

remedy_evidence.text: Giving users choices shifts what they see, while large experiments found small or no effects on hostility toward the other party. The 2023 X experiment found precisely estimated null effects on partisan hostility, and a 2024 test that reranked hostile posts for 1,256 users of X over ten days moved feelings toward the other party by about 2 points on a 0 to 100 scale. Main limitation: most users keep default settings, so choice alone may change little.

R-37.tradeoffs: Data access carries privacy risk, and most users keep the default feed.
success_measures: Share of users choosing a feed other than the default
Studies published using platform data
Exposure to hostile political content
R-37.alternatives: Media literacy is the main alternative, including prebunking, which warns people about manipulation techniques in advance, and lateral reading, which checks what other sources say about a site. Rejected option: government mandates on what content to rank up or down.

status.text: No federal statute requiring feed-ranking choice or independent researcher access to platform data had been enacted as of June 2026.

routes.who: Platform transparency and researcher access statute

routes.note: State laws face First Amendment limits. In Moody v. NetChoice (July 1, 2024), the Supreme Court held that a platform's choices about what content to show and how to arrange it in feeds are expressive activity the First Amendment protects, and it sent the challenges to Florida's and Texas's platform laws back to the lower courts.
Platforms have offered chronological options voluntarily.

R-38.title: Limits on pricing software using rivals' data
R-38.summary: Software that recommends rents or prices would be barred from using competitors' private data to set live prices. Renters in large buildings would gain within one to three years if the practice has raised rents. Landlords that rely on shared data would lose that advantage.
R-38.what_it_changes: Pricing tools fed by competitors' nonpublic data may raise rents (LT12: Shared-data pricing software can raise rents, rated contested). Barring that input removes one channel for coordinated increases through TC7: Use of pricing algorithms. The reform acts on loop R8 (Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building).
R-38.who_decides: The Justice Department and state attorneys general can act through antitrust settlements, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; the RealPage final judgment, entered May 19, 2026, is the main example. States can ban such software or require disclosure (medium), and New York has done both. Cities can pass ordinances (medium).
R-38.legal_authority: The Sherman Act, the main federal antitrust law, and state consumer-protection and antitrust laws supply the authority.
R-38.implementation: A court decree or statute comes first. A monitor then checks compliance, and rents are measured afterward.
R-38.resources: Small funding, mainly for technical monitors who can audit software.
R-38.enforcement: Monitors and audits enforce the rules. The RealPage final judgment requires training data at least 12 months old and appoints a monitor.
R-38.costs: The public cost is small. Landlords give up some pricing efficiency.
R-38.failure_risks: Software vendors and large landlords tend to oppose it, and they can adapt by using older or aggregated data. The chief risk is coordination moving to channels a decree does not cover. Court decrees expire after a set period, so lasting limits depend on statutes. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: The harm is alleged and contested. The Justice Department's final judgment with RealPage contains no admission of wrongdoing, and estimates of the effect on rents vary.

remedy_evidence.text: The case for the limits rests on design logic. Main limitation: no evaluation of these limits exists yet.

success_measures: Rent growth in buildings that used the software
Vacancy rates
R-38.alternatives: Disclosure requirements alone are the main alternative. Rejected option: banning pricing software outright.

status.text: In force. The federal court in North Carolina entered the final judgment in the Justice Department's case against RealPage on May 19, 2026. It bars RealPage from using competitors' nonpublic data in live rent pricing, limits model training to data at least 12 months old, and appoints a monitor; it carries no money payment and no admission of wrongdoing. On September 30, 2026 the court allowed the states' own claims against RealPage and several landlords to proceed, ruling that the federal judgment does not resolve them.

routes.note: RealPage final judgment, entered May 19, 2026.

New York's algorithmic rent law (Senate bill S7882), signed October 16, 2025 and effective 60 days later, makes it unlawful to help arrange agreements among residential landlords not to compete, including through software that coordinates rents, and bars landlords from setting rents based on such tools' recommendations. A separate New York law (General Business Law section 349-a) requires a business that sets a price with an algorithm using a consumer's personal data to say so next to the price.

R-39.title: Government teams that build digital services
R-39.summary: Government would keep its own teams of technologists to build and run the software people use to claim benefits, get tax refunds and apply for permits. People who use those services would gain within one to three years through faster processing and fewer errors. Large contractors would lose some work.
R-39.what_it_changes: Agencies that can build and run their own digital services deliver with fewer failures (LT15: In-house digital teams improve service delivery). Congress funds and can charter that capacity (LT17: Congress decides funding for government digital capacity), while teams created by executive decision can be closed by the next one (LT16: The executive opens and closes federal digital teams). The reform raises TC5: Government's ability to build and run digital services, which feeds D5: Quality of public services. It works through loop R7 (Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other).
R-39.who_decides: Congress can charter a digital service and protect its funding by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Agencies can build teams by executive action (medium), though the next administration can close them; 18F closed in March 2025. States can create their own digital service teams (medium).
R-39.legal_authority: Congress and agencies have clear authority to build in-house capacity.
R-39.implementation: A charter comes first. Hiring follows, then replacement of old systems, then measurement of service. Civil-service hiring rules that let agencies recruit technologists (R-17) are a prerequisite.
R-39.resources: The cost is small compared with the more than $100 billion the federal government spends on information technology each year, about 80% of it on operating and maintaining existing systems.
R-39.costs: The public cost is small. Incumbent contractors lose some business.
R-39.failure_risks: Large contractors would likely push back, along with tax-preparation firms that oppose free government filing and lobby against it. The likeliest way it falls short is teams closed by the next administration. Durability is low for teams that exist by executive order and higher for those chartered by statute; reversal risk by order is high.

problem_evidence.text: GAO found that the federal government's 11 most critical legacy systems are 23 to 60 years old. According to GAO, HealthCare.gov launched before its performance was checked, after weak planning and oversight. During the pandemic, GAO found improper payment rates in unemployment programs rose from 9.2% in fiscal 2020 to 18.9% in fiscal 2021, with outdated state systems a factor.

remedy_evidence.text: Case evidence supports the approach. IRS Direct File, the agency's free online filing tool, accepted 140,803 returns in 2024 and 296,531 in 2025. Main limitation: these are individual cases without a controlled comparison, and teams have not survived changes of administration.

R-39.tradeoffs: Government builds software it could buy instead.
success_measures: Time to process benefit claims
Error rates in benefit payments
Legacy systems retired
Use of free government tax filing
R-39.alternatives: Better procurement of contracted software is the main alternative. Rejected option: one-off contracts for each crisis.

status.text: The General Services Administration closed its 18F digital services team in March 2025, affecting about 85 staff. The IRS did not offer its free Direct File service in the 2026 filing season and in November 2025 said no future launch date had been set. The Department of Government Efficiency lost its central leadership in 2025: in November 2025 the director of the Office of Personnel Management said it 'doesn't exist' as a central body. The executive order that created DOGE renamed the U.S. Digital Service as the U.S. DOGE Service, which still had about 50 employees in November 2025, and set DOGE's temporary organization to end on July 4, 2026.

routes.who: Statutory charter and protected funding for a digital service

routes.note: Executive action is easy to reverse. The General Services Administration closed its 18F digital services office in March 2025, after an email to staff identified it as non-critical in a reduction in force.

R-40.title: Notice and a voice for workers on AI
R-40.summary: Employers would have to tell workers when AI is used to hire, schedule or evaluate them, explain decisions and offer human review, and negotiate how tools are used where workers have a union. Workers in jobs exposed to AI would gain once the rules are enforced. Employers would bear compliance costs.
R-40.what_it_changes: AI adoption may weaken the position of entry-level workers in exposed jobs (LT05: AI adoption may weaken entry-level workers' position, rated contested). Notice, a way to contest decisions and a say through bargaining aim to protect A2: Workers' bargaining power. The reform operates on loop R6 (Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other).
R-40.who_decides: Unions and employers can bargain over AI, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; the Writers Guild's 2023 contract is an example. States can pass notice and review laws (medium), and Colorado's SB 26-189 takes effect January 1, 2027. City audit laws are rated low, since enforcement of New York City's Local Law 144 has been weak.
R-40.legal_authority: Authority to require notice is clear. Bargaining over how tools are deployed requires a union.
R-40.implementation: Notice comes first. Explanations of decisions and human review follow. Audits come next, and complaints are tracked. Enforcement capacity is a prerequisite.
R-40.enforcement: State agencies enforce, and enforcement has been weak so far. The New York State Comptroller found that New York City had received two complaints under Local Law 144 and found one instance of non-compliance among 32 companies, while auditors identified at least 17 potential instances.
R-40.costs: The public cost is small. Employers bear compliance costs once enforcement begins.
R-40.failure_risks: Employers and AI vendors are expected to resist, mainly by writing narrow definitions of covered tools. The biggest risk is no enforcement. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Whether AI is hurting entry-level workers is disputed. Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen (2025) found a 13% relative employment decline for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, a pattern consistent with an AI effect that does not prove one. A study of Denmark ruled out earnings effects above 1% to 2%, and the Yale Budget Lab found no clear unemployment trend by exposure. Research by Anthropic, a company that makes AI tools, found job-finding for 22- to 25-year-olds entering exposed occupations about 14% lower than in 2022, a barely significant result.

remedy_evidence.text: The remedy is a hypothesis. Main limitation: enforcement has been weak where these rules have been tried, as in New York City, so there is little evidence on what working rules would achieve.

R-40.tradeoffs: Compliance costs rise, and the rules may slow useful adoption of AI.
success_measures: Complaints filed and resolved
Union contracts with clauses on AI
R-40.alternatives: Funding for worker retraining is the main alternative. Rejected option: bans on AI use.

status.text: Colorado SB 26-189, signed May 14, 2026 according to a law-firm summary, takes effect January 1, 2027. When automated decision tools are used in consequential decisions, including employment decisions, it requires notice, a plain-language explanation within 30 days of an adverse outcome, and rights to correct data, request human review and appeal. It replaces Colorado's 2024 AI Act, which never took effect.

routes.note: Writers Guild 2023 contract.
Colorado SB 26-189 from Jan 1, 2027.

New York City Local Law 144 requires employers that use automated hiring tools to commission and post bias audits. A December 2025 audit by the New York State Comptroller found that the city's consumer protection agency received two complaints from July 2023 to June 2025 and found one violation among 32 companies it reviewed, while the auditors found at least 17 potential violations at the same companies.

R-41.title: Large power users pay their grid costs
R-41.summary: Large new electricity users, such as data centers, would pay for the grid capacity and upgrades their demand requires, through rates set by state utility commissions. Households in fast-growing grids would gain at the next rate case, the proceeding in which regulators set a utility's prices. Data-center operators would pay more.
R-41.what_it_changes: Data-center load raises electricity demand and, through capacity prices, household bills (LT11: Data-center load raises household electricity bills, rated plausible). Charging large loads for the costs they cause aims to keep those costs out of EC9: Cost of essentials, and it acts on TC6: Data centers' demand on the electricity grid. The reform sits on no feedback loop.
R-41.who_decides: For an investor-owned utility, the state public utility commission sets retail rates; tariffs set by commissions under state law are rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. For public power or a cooperative, a city council or co-op board decides. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), which oversees wholesale markets, can change market rules (low), and in the PJM region the grid operator's capacity auction also feeds into bills.
R-41.legal_authority: State commissions set retail electricity rates, and FERC oversees wholesale markets.
R-41.implementation: Regulators first design the tariff. Large loads then take on minimum demand charges or long-term contracts, which keep them paying for capacity even if their usage drops. Bill impacts are measured afterward.
R-41.resources: Large loads pay the added costs. Regulators need the capacity to forecast how much power new loads will draw.
R-41.costs: No public cost is identified. Data-center operators pay more starting with the next rate case.
R-41.failure_risks: Data-center developers are likely to oppose it, and they can adapt by locating in states with more permissive terms. Loads moving to states that spread these costs across all customers is the chief risk. Reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: In the PJM region, the independent market monitor attributes about $23.1 billion in capacity costs across three auctions to data-center load (January 2026 analysis). PJM estimated bill increases of 1.5% to 5% for some customers after its 2026/2027 auction. The pass-through to household bills is documented for PJM; other grids differ.

remedy_evidence.text: The case rests on design logic. Main limitation: no evaluation of these tariffs has been found, and loads may move to places offering different terms.

success_measures: Change in residential bills attributable to large new loads
Capacity prices in grid auctions
R-41.alternatives: Rules requiring large users to bring their own generating capacity are the main alternative. Rejected option: spreading these costs across all customers.

status.text: States set retail electricity rates, so tariffs that make data centers and other customers with the largest power demands pay for the grid costs they cause come from state utility commissions, and a growing number of utilities have adopted data-center-specific terms (Congressional Research Service, May 2026). Transmission rules are federal: on June 18, 2026 the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ordered all six regional grid operators it oversees to file, within 60 days, rules on how large loads connect to the grid, including measures against shifting transmission costs onto other customers, or to show that their current rules are adequate.

routes.note: Large-load tariffs are proposed or pending before several state commissions.

R-42.title: Congress votes on lasting tariffs
R-42.summary: Tariffs, which are taxes on imports, could stay in place beyond a short period only if Congress voted to approve them. Households and importers would gain when existing tariffs come up for review. Producers protected by tariffs would lose that protection unless Congress chose to keep it.
R-42.what_it_changes: Presidents now set tariff rates under statutes that delegate the power (LE19: The executive sets tariff rates), and U.S. buyers pay most of the cost (LE18: Tariffs raise prices U.S. buyers pay). Requiring a vote returns a tax power to Congress, the branch the Constitution assigns it to. The reform touches loop R13 (Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action).
R-42.who_decides: Congress decides by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; bills have been introduced in earlier sessions. Courts police individual statutes through suits over statutory authority (medium), as in Learning Resources v. Trump (February 20, 2026), where the Supreme Court held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs.
R-42.legal_authority: Article I of the Constitution gives Congress the power to impose tariffs. A statute requiring approval would need a President willing to sign it or a majority large enough to override a veto.
R-42.implementation: Congress passes the statute. Existing tariffs are then reviewed and put to a vote.
R-42.resources: No new funding or capacity is needed.
R-42.costs: Federal revenue changes as tariffs end or continue. Producers that benefit from protection lose it when tariffs lapse without a vote.
R-42.failure_risks: Any administration is expected to resist, along with protected industries. The main adaptation is shifting to other statutes: after the 2026 ruling, most tariffs imposed under the emergency-powers law were replaced under Sections 122, 232 and 301. A veto poses the biggest risk. Once enacted, a statute would be durable.

problem_evidence.text: Tariffs cost about $1,100 per household per year as of August 2026, according to the Yale Budget Lab. Researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that U.S. importers bore 94% of tariff costs from January to August 2025 and 86% by November.
