remedy_evidence.text: The approach is plausible. Learning Resources shows that courts police one statute at a time. Main limitation: no U.S. experience shows how a general vote requirement would work in practice.

R-42.tradeoffs: Responses in trade disputes would be slower.
success_measures: Tariffs in force without a vote of Congress
Tariff cost per household
R-42.alternatives: Narrowing each statute that delegates tariff power is the main alternative. Rejected option: relying on courts alone, because the executive can shift to other statutes.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, no law requiring congressional approval of tariffs has been enacted. On February 20, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize tariffs. The administration then imposed a 10% global tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, effective February 24, 2026; that section limits such tariffs to 150 days unless Congress extends them. On May 7, 2026 the Court of International Trade ruled 2 to 1, for the plaintiffs in one case, that those tariffs were not justified under Section 122, and the Federal Circuit put that ruling on hold in June 2026.

routes.note: Bills have been introduced in earlier sessions of Congress.
Learning Resources.

R-43.title: Building codes and mitigation against disaster losses
R-43.summary: States and cities would adopt and enforce stronger building codes and fund retrofits that reduce damage when storms and other hazards strike. Owners and renters in hazard areas would gain at the next disaster, and insurance would stay more available. Builders would face higher construction costs now.
R-43.what_it_changes: Higher hazard raises insurance premiums and nonrenewals (LE20: Climate hazard raises insurance costs), and in high-hazard places insurance costs weigh on home values (LE23: Climate risk weighs on home equity). Stronger codes and mitigation cut losses when hazards hit, which aims to lower EC11: Climate hazards and insurance costs. The reform sits on no feedback loop.
R-43.who_decides: States can adopt statewide codes, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Local governments adopt and enforce codes (medium). Congress funds mitigation grants (low), and FEMA administers federal mitigation money.
R-43.legal_authority: States and local governments have the authority to adopt building codes.
R-43.implementation: Governments adopt modern codes first. Enforcement follows, then funding for retrofits of existing buildings, then measurement of insurance claims after events. Inspection capacity is a prerequisite.
R-43.resources: Mitigation grants and building inspectors. New construction costs more.
R-43.enforcement: Local building departments enforce codes through inspections.
R-43.costs: Construction costs rise for builders, and the price of new homes goes up. Mitigation grants come from public budgets.
R-43.failure_risks: Some builders tend to oppose it, and local opt-outs are the likely adaptation. Codes that are adopted but not enforced are the main failure risk. Codes are durable, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: The Treasury Department's Federal Insurance Office found that from 2018 to 2022, homeowners in the riskiest fifth of ZIP codes paid 82% more for insurance ($2,321 on average) than those in the least risky fifth, and saw about 80% more nonrenewals. Insurance industry groups disputed the figures.

remedy_evidence.text: The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, a research group supported by property insurers, studied closed claims from Hurricane Charley (2004) in Charlotte County, Florida. Homes built after stricter codes took effect there in 1996 had 40% lower damage frequency and 60% lower damage severity. Main limitation: that study covers one storm in one county, and higher upfront costs and weak enforcement can limit the benefit.

R-43.tradeoffs: Codes raise the cost of new homes, which works against adding housing supply (R-30) at the margin.
success_measures: Insurance claims after hazard events
Insurance premiums in high-risk ZIP codes
R-43.alternatives: Relying on insurance pricing alone to signal risk is the main alternative. Rejected option: rebuilding to old codes after disasters.

status.text: Building codes are adopted state by state, and in many states each city or county decides which code to adopt and enforce.

routes.note: Federal mitigation grants depend on annual appropriations.

R-44.title: Competition remedies for search and ad markets
R-44.summary: Courts and agencies would impose remedies that open search and online advertising markets to rivals, such as bans on exclusive deals and requirements to share data. Publishers and advertisers would gain over years if the share of ad money captured by a few platforms falls. The dominant platforms would lose some control over these markets.
R-44.what_it_changes: Platforms took the advertising that paid for local reporting (LT03: Platforms drew ad revenue from local news), and concentrated ownership may entrench the goals that govern feeds (LT02: Platform concentration may entrench engagement ranking, a hypothesis). Remedies that open these markets aim to lower TC2: Concentration of platforms and digital advertising. The reform acts on loop R16 (Local news loss and weak electoral pressure may reinforce each other).
R-44.who_decides: The Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission and states enforce through litigation, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; the Google search and ad-tech remedies are the main cases. Congress could legislate (low).
R-44.legal_authority: The Sherman Act, the main federal antitrust law, supplies the authority.
R-44.implementation: A court orders a remedy first. A monitor then oversees compliance. Ad market shares and the share of ad revenue reaching publishers are measured afterward.
R-44.resources: Agency budgets, and technical staff able to oversee complex systems.
R-44.enforcement: Court-appointed monitors oversee compliance, and courts enforce the decrees.
R-44.costs: The public cost is small. Dominant platforms lose some revenue and control.
R-44.failure_risks: Platforms would likely push back through appeals and by launching new products outside a decree's reach. Remedies too weak to change market shares are the main failure risk. Decrees last only for their terms, and appeals can overturn them.

problem_evidence.text: Newspaper advertising revenue fell from about $49.4 billion in 2005 to about $9.8 billion in 2022, according to Pew Research Center. Where Craigslist arrived, newsroom staff fell 6% and coverage of local House members dropped about 30% (Djourelova, Durante and Martin, 2021). That study covers classified ads; for search and social advertising the link is plausible.

remedy_evidence.text: Conduct remedies, which regulate a company's behavior without breaking it up, are untested at this scale. Courts found Google liable in search (August 2024) and ad tech (April 2025) and ordered conduct remedies without divestiture, and the FTC lost its case against Meta in November 2025. Main limitation: the market effect depends on the remedy, and some cases remain unresolved.

R-44.tradeoffs: Benefits from integrated services may be lost.
success_measures: Shares of the digital advertising market
Share of advertising revenue that reaches publishers
R-44.alternatives: Interoperability mandates, which require platforms to work with rivals' products, are the main alternative.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, both federal antitrust cases against Google are past the liability stage. In the search case, Judge Amit Mehta's remedies of September 2, 2025 barred exclusive default-search contracts and required Google to share some search-index and user-interaction data with qualified competitors, and they did not require a sale of Chrome or Android; Google and the Justice Department each appealed parts of the judgment in early 2026, according to news reports. In the ad-tech case, Judge Leonie Brinkema issued remedies in early September 2026: a six-year order with interoperability and nondiscrimination requirements and a court-appointed monitor, without a forced sale of Google's ad exchange.

routes.note: Search case: remedies ordered September 2, 2025, with appeals filed by Google and the Justice Department in early 2026. Ad-tech case: a six-year behavioral order with a court-appointed monitor, issued in early September 2026.

R-45.title: Verifiable elections with paper records and audits
R-45.summary: Every vote would leave a paper record, results would be audited, officials would face firm deadlines to certify, and election workers would be protected from threats. Every voter would gain at every election, because results could be checked and accepted. Officials who refuse to certify lawful results would face court orders.
R-45.what_it_changes: Paper records, audits and certification on a schedule make results provable, so that C5: Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement can happen and be accepted. Every reform that works through elections rests on this floor. The reform is linked to B5: Equality of voter turnout and to E2: Trust earned through performance, and to loop R4b (Voting rules shape who can hold rule-makers accountable) and loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance).
R-45.who_decides: States can pass certification and audit statutes, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; 39 states and the District of Columbia have laws protecting election officials. Counties run elections and can strengthen administration directly (high). Congress can fund recurring grants (low).
R-45.legal_authority: States run elections. The Electoral Count Reform Act of 2022 governs the federal count of presidential electoral votes; it clarified certification duties and raised the threshold for objections in Congress.
R-45.implementation: Paper records and audits come first. Certification duties with deadlines follow. A system for responding to threats against officials comes next.
R-45.resources: Recurring federal money for election administration has been absent since 2020. Turnover among election staff strains capacity.
R-45.enforcement: State courts can compel officials to certify results.
R-45.costs: The cost is small, paid mainly by state and county election offices.
R-45.failure_risks: Officials who refuse to certify are expected to resist, mainly through litigation. Underfunded staff and refusals to certify are the main failure risks. Durability is high, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: An AP-NORC and USAFacts survey published in September 2026 found that 34% of U.S. adults trust the certification of the 2026 midterm results a great deal or quite a bit. In a 2025 Brennan Center survey of 858 local election officials, 38% reported threats, harassment or abuse.

remedy_evidence.text: Evidence is strong that paper records and audits catch errors. A risk-limiting audit, one common design, checks a statistical sample of paper ballots against the reported outcome. Main limitation: audits help only when trained staff run them and officials complete certification lawfully.

R-45.tradeoffs: Audits take time, which can delay final results.
success_measures: Risk-limiting audits completed
Certifications completed on time
Threats against election officials investigated and resolved
R-45.alternatives: No alternative to this floor is listed. It rejects replacing voting machines with hand counts, which raise error rates.

status.text: Nearly all U.S. voters now cast ballots on paper or on machines that produce a paper record that can be audited.

routes.note: Since 2020 many states have passed laws protecting election officials from threats, harassment or publication of their home addresses.

R-46.title: Expand the House of Representatives
R-46.summary: Congress would add seats to the House, so each member would represent fewer people, with a plan for apportionment and staffing. Residents of large states would gain at the next apportionment after the change. A larger chamber could also give party leaders more control.
R-46.what_it_changes: More seats mean smaller districts and more representatives per person, and pairing expansion with multi-member districts (R-03) multiplies the effect. The reform is linked to C1: Seats with little electoral competition and B5: Equality of voter turnout, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).
R-46.who_decides: Congress decides by statute, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030.
R-46.legal_authority: Congress fixed the House at 435 seats by statute in 1929, so it can change the number by statute. A bill would need 60 Senate votes or filibuster reform (R-12).
R-46.implementation: Congress passes a statute. The new size applies at the next apportionment, when House seats are divided among the states after the census.
R-46.resources: Facilities and staff for the added members, including room in the House chamber.
R-46.enforcement: No enforcement mechanism is needed; the new size takes effect through apportionment.
R-46.costs: The cost is small: offices, staff and space for the added members.
R-46.failure_risks: Incumbents are likely to oppose it. The main failure risk is that a larger chamber concentrates power in party leadership. Once enacted, the change is durable, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: After the 2020 census, the average House district had 761,169 residents, according to the Census Bureau.

remedy_evidence.text: Frederick (2010), in observational research, found that larger districts reduce members' contact with constituents and constituents' approval of the member, with modest effects. Main limitation: the effect of expansion on electoral competition is untested.

R-46.tradeoffs: A larger chamber can concentrate power in its leadership.
success_measures: Residents per House member
R-46.alternatives: Proportional multi-seat districts (R-03) are the main alternative.

status.text: The number of House seats has been fixed at 435 by federal law since the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929. Enlarging the House would take a new federal statute, and none has been enacted.

R-47.title: Fusion voting and public funding for parties
R-47.summary: More than one party could nominate the same candidate, so a voter could back a candidate on a smaller party's ballot line without splitting the vote. Public funding could also go to parties as well as candidates. Minor parties and their voters would gain in the first election cycle, and major parties would have reason to absorb the smaller lines.
R-47.what_it_changes: Fusion voting lets two parties nominate the same candidate, and party-centered funding helps organized coalitions form without spoiling races. The reform is linked to C2: How often the primary decides the winner and C3: Risk of losing office, and to loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates).
R-47.who_decides: States can legalize fusion by statute, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; it is legal in New York and Connecticut. Party-centered public funding at the federal level is rated low.
R-47.legal_authority: In Timmons (1997), the Supreme Court held that states may ban fusion, so each state decides whether to allow it.
R-47.implementation: A statute comes first. It runs for two election cycles, and then it is evaluated.
R-47.resources: Public funds for parties, and party organizations able to use them.
R-47.enforcement: Election agencies administer ballot lines and funding.
R-47.failure_risks: Major parties tend to oppose it, mainly through ballot-access rules that make it harder for small parties to qualify. The chief risk is major parties absorbing the smaller lines. Reversal risk is medium.

problem_evidence.text: Party organizations are weak, and getting on the ballot is harder for minor parties than for major ones, as state-by-state signature and fee requirements compiled by Ballotpedia show.

remedy_evidence.text: Experience in New York, where fusion is legal, informs the proposal. Main limitation: evidence comes from few states, and stronger party leaders and absorption of smaller lines are known risks.

success_measures: Votes cast on minor-party ballot lines
How long coalitions between parties last
R-47.alternatives: All-party primaries (R-01) are the main alternative.

status.text: Fusion voting lets one candidate appear on the ballot lines of more than one party. It is legal and in regular use in New York and Connecticut. Minor parties in Kansas and New Jersey have gone to court to overturn their states' bans. Massachusetts Question 3, on the November 3, 2026 ballot, would let a party endorse a candidate in a single all-candidate primary and show that endorsement on the ballot. Party-centered public funding remains a proposal.

routes.note: Legal in New York and Connecticut.

R-48.title: Agency independence after the Slaughter ruling
R-48.summary: After the Supreme Court's June 2026 decision in Trump v. Slaughter, Congress would protect independent agencies through other tools: public reasons and records for removals, protected budgets, agency structures the ruling leaves intact, and a written exception for the Federal Reserve. People affected by federal regulation would gain over years if those designs hold. The designs are untested, and their durability depends on how courts apply the decision.
R-48.what_it_changes: When officials can be removed at will, watchdogs and regulators weaken (L14: Presidential removals weaken watchdog agencies), and fewer independent enforcers are left to restrain unilateral action (L15: Independent watchdogs restrain unilateral action). After Slaughter, independence has to come from structure, such as records, stated reasons for removal, budget protection and the design of lower-level offices, because tenure protection no longer works for many officials. The reform works through loop R18 (Weakening watchdogs lowers the cost of further unilateral action).
R-48.who_decides: Congress can legislate, a route rated low in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. Litigation can test the designs (low); in Trump v. Cook, the Supreme Court denied a stay, and the case continues on the merits.
R-48.legal_authority: In Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026), the Supreme Court held 6 to 3 that the Federal Trade Commission's protection against removal without cause violates the separation of powers, and it overruled what remained of Humphrey's Executor, the earlier precedent that had allowed such protection. The Court reserved the question of the Federal Reserve.
R-48.implementation: Congress first maps which agencies the ruling exposes. It then passes a statute with new protections, which are tested in litigation.
R-48.enforcement: Courts decide whether the new designs hold.
R-48.costs: There is no fiscal cost. Presidents would face more process before removing officials.
R-48.failure_risks: Administrations would likely push back, mainly by removing officials anyway. The likeliest way it falls short is that the Court extends Slaughter to these designs. Durability depends on court doctrine.

problem_evidence.text: The Supreme Court decided Trump v. Slaughter 6 to 3 on June 29, 2026, striking down the FTC's protection against removal without cause.

remedy_evidence.text: The proposed designs are untested. Main limitation: their durability depends on how courts apply Slaughter, and no court has yet ruled on designs like these.

R-48.tradeoffs: Agencies would have less insulation from presidential control than they had before the ruling.
success_measures: Removals of agency officials accompanied by stated reasons
Days each year that multi-member agencies have a quorum
R-48.alternatives: Congressional oversight is the main alternative. Rejected option: re-enacting the tenure protections that Slaughter struck down.

status.text: On June 29, 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in Trump v. Slaughter that the President may remove Federal Trade Commission members at will, and it overruled Humphrey's Executor (1935). The same day, in Trump v. Cook, the Court voted 5 to 4 to deny the government's request to let the President remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook while her case continues. Cook is an interim order: she stays in office for now, and the Court has not decided whether the Fed's for-cause protection is valid.

routes.note: Cook stay denied; merits continue.

R-49.title: Civic work that crosses party lines
R-49.summary: Membership groups and service programs would bring people of different parties together for shared work, such as serving as poll workers, again and again over time. Members and their communities would gain on an ongoing basis. Measured drops in hostility tend to fade quickly, so lasting effects across the population are uncertain.
R-49.what_it_changes: Ties formed through shared work across party lines can reduce hostility (L33: Cross-group ties reduce partisan hostility, rated plausible) and make turnout more equal (L34: Civic ties make turnout more equal, rated well-supported). The reform builds variable B3: Civic ties across social and political groups and operates on loop R15 (Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other).
R-49.who_decides: Membership organizations can act now, a route rated high in feasibility for 2026 to 2030. States and election offices can run poll-worker programs (high); more than 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers from 2022 to 2024.
R-49.legal_authority: Civil-society programs need no government authority.
R-49.implementation: Organizations recruit members across party lines. Members work together on shared projects, and effects are measured over time.
R-49.failure_risks: Few groups resist. The biggest risk is that effects fade. Durability depends on keeping members engaged, and reversal risk is low.

problem_evidence.text: Hostility toward the other party is high.

remedy_evidence.text: A 2024 megastudy of 32,059 participants tested 25 interventions: 23 reduced partisan animosity, and the effects faded within about two weeks. A randomized evaluation of Braver Angels workshops at four universities found reduced polarization, with implicit and behavioral effects still present at the study's end (Baron and colleagues, 2025). Main limitation: most effects decay, and lasting change across the population is unmeasured.

success_measures: Membership drawn from more than one party
Animosity toward the other party among members
R-49.alternatives: Dialogue programs are the main alternative. Rejected option: one-off dialogue events.

status.text: Cross-partisan membership groups and national-service programs continue to operate; this reform has no single bill or rule whose status can be tracked.

routes.note: Over 163,000 veterans and military family members served as poll workers 2022-24.

R-50.title: Popular-vote compact and constitutional amendment options
R-50.summary: R-50 covers long-term options for how senators and presidents are chosen: constitutional amendments on Senate apportionment and the Electoral College, and the National Popular Vote compact, which needs no amendment. Under the compact, member states would award their electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner once states holding 270 electoral votes have joined. Voters in states that are not competitive in presidential races would gain if it takes effect.
R-50.what_it_changes: A durable Senate majority shapes the courts over decades, and Senate malapportionment, the unequal populations of states that each have two senators, is a fixed feature of that link (L57: Durable Senate majorities shape court appointments). These options act on D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions and D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, and on loop R12 (Entrenched majorities shape courts that rule on election rules).
R-50.who_decides: A constitutional amendment requires two-thirds of each house of Congress and three-quarters of the states, or a convention; it gets the lowest feasibility rating for 2026 to 2030. The National Popular Vote compact is an interstate compact, a set of matching state laws that take effect at a threshold, rated low; it needs states with 270 electoral votes and has 222.
R-50.legal_authority: Article V of the Constitution sets the amendment process. Whether the compact needs congressional consent under the Constitution's Compact Clause is an open question that courts would decide.
R-50.implementation: The compact takes effect once member states reach 270 electoral votes. Litigation is expected to follow.
R-50.resources: No new funding or capacity is needed.
R-50.failure_risks: Small states and the parties advantaged under current rules are expected to resist. Litigation and states withdrawing from the compact are the main risks. An amendment, once ratified, would be durable.

problem_evidence.text: Senate malapportionment is documented: every state has two senators regardless of population, so senators from small states represent far fewer people.

remedy_evidence.text: The compact is untested, and no court has ruled on it. Main limitation: it has not taken effect, so neither its legal standing nor its effects on campaigns are known.

R-50.tradeoffs: Member states could withdraw from the compact.
success_measures: Electoral votes held by states in the compact
R-50.alternatives: No alternative is listed and no option is rejected here.

status.text: As of October 15, 2026, 18 states and the District of Columbia, holding 222 electoral votes, have enacted the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. It takes effect only when its members hold at least 270 electoral votes, so it is 48 short. Virginia joined in April 2026.

routes.note: 18 states plus DC, 222 electoral votes of 270 needed.

routes.intro: A reform can travel through eleven routes, from a city council to a constitutional amendment. Each route names who acts there and what a change depends on. The routes do not have to follow a fixed order: a state can move its local elections onto the statewide calendar without Congress, a child credit can pass through budget reconciliation with a simple Senate majority, and a stock-trading ban needs 60 Senate votes. Each profile lists which routes are open, who acts on each, how feasible the change is from 2026 to 2030, and what it depends on.

feasibility_scale.high: The route is open, and the reform has been adopted somewhere through it since 2020.
feasibility_scale.medium: The route is open in some places, and a credible campaign could carry the reform through it by 2030.
feasibility_scale.low: The route exists, but it needs a coalition that does not exist now.
feasibility_scale.very low: It needs a supermajority, a constitutional change or a reversal of court doctrine.

dependencies.authority: Who has the legal power to adopt the change, and what courts have said about that power.
dependencies.funding: What it costs, who pays, and whether the money recurs each year.
dependencies.enforcement: Who makes it stick, with what remedy, and whether that enforcer can act.
dependencies.capacity: Whether the people and systems exist to run it.
dependencies.durability: How easily the next legislature, administration, court or ballot measure can undo it.

items.name: Local
items.instrument: Ordinance, charter amendment or local practice
items.who: City councils, county boards, charter commissions, voters in home-rule places
items.depends: State home-rule law and preemption, a higher government limiting what a lower one may do. In Dillon's Rule states, where cities hold only the powers the state grants, the legislature can override local choices at will; 19 states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections.

items.name: State statute
items.instrument: A bill passed by the legislature and signed, or a rule issued by a state agency or utility commission under a statute
items.depends: A majority in both chambers and the governor's signature or a veto override. Where D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions is high, the legislature that would pass a reform of election rules is the one that benefits from the current rules.

items.name: State ballot
items.instrument: Citizen initiative, referendum or legislative referral
items.who: Voters, petition campaigns, courts that review ballot language
items.depends: Available only in states that allow it. Signature thresholds, single-subject rules, legislatures that can override statutes passed by initiative, and repeal campaigns all apply.

items.name: Federal statute
items.instrument: Act of Congress, including appropriations and reconciliation
items.depends: Sixty Senate votes for most bills while the legislative filibuster stands (R-12: Reform the Senate filibuster); a simple majority for budget reconciliation, which can carry taxes and spending and excludes most rule changes.

items.name: Chamber rule or confirmation
items.instrument: House or Senate rule; Senate confirmation of nominees
items.depends: A majority willing to bind itself, and the next majority's willingness to keep the rule.

items.name: Federal executive action
items.instrument: Executive order, agency rule, guidance, staffing and budget execution
items.depends: Authority granted by statute, and the next administration. This is the least durable route: what one order does, another can undo.

items.name: Enforcement and litigation
items.instrument: Cases and settlements under existing law
items.who: The Justice Department, the Federal Trade Commission, the National Labor Relations Board, state attorneys general and private plaintiffs
items.depends: An agency with a quorum, staff and budget, and the courts. Consent decrees bind for a set term; verdicts can be appealed for years.

items.name: Court doctrine
items.instrument: Rulings that change what other routes may do
items.depends: No one controls this route directly. It moves through appointments, as D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions shapes D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition, and through litigation strategy over decades.

items.name: Article V
items.who: Two-thirds of each house of Congress and three-quarters of the states, or a convention
items.depends: Supermajorities across parties and regions. Treated as a long-horizon option.

items.name: Interstate compact
items.instrument: Matching statutes in several states that take effect at a threshold
items.depends: Enough states joining to reach the threshold, and courts accepting the compact without the consent of Congress where that question is disputed.

items.name: Civil society
items.instrument: Organizing, philanthropy, newsrooms, unions, membership groups, private contracts
items.depends: Money and members. No government action is needed, which makes it the fastest route and the easiest to underfund.

repairLog.intro: The repair log records 64 dated changes to the rules that decide who officials answer to: statutes, court rulings, ballot measures, executive actions and local laws from 1965 to the November 3, 2026 ballot. Each row gives the jurisdiction, what the rule did, the vote or margin, the instrument used, the feedback loop it acts on and anything that later reversed or limited it. Changes run in both directions and come from both parties. One row rests on a source that was not checked, and the row is labelled.
repairLog.coding_note: Each row is coded by one of five labels. 'Toward voters' means the change widens who can register, vote or have a ballot counted, makes each vote weigh more equally, opens the contest that decides the seat, makes political money more limited or more visible, strengthens an independent check on officials, or adds to household security through automatic benefits. 'Away from voters' means the change does the reverse. 'Voters kept existing rules' means a ballot measure failed and the rules in force stayed, coded the same whichever way the measure would have moved power. 'Pending' means voters or courts have not yet decided. 'Mixed' means the change moved in both directions at once or left the rules in practice unchanged; the row's own note says which. Three rules apply across parties. A partisan redraw of district maps in the middle of a decade is coded away from voters whichever party draws it and whether or not voters approved it; a court order that blocks one is coded toward voters, and one that lets it take effect is coded away. A change that widens who takes part in the deciding round (open or all-party primaries) or lets voters rank candidates is coded toward voters, and a law or amendment that bans those options is coded away; readers may weigh these entries differently, and the reform profiles R-01 and R-02 rate confidence in their effect on moderation as low. A row's direction describes the rule's effect on who officials answer to and carries no judgment of the people or parties involved.
