deliveryLog.intro: The delivery log records 24 times American government did something hard at scale and a number shows the result. Each entry names who enacted it, what was measured and how, and the qualification that travels with the result: the cost, the disputed finding, the critic or the reversal. An entry needs a measured result, a credible comparison with what would have happened otherwise, and a stated downside. Authorship runs across both parties. The 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments and the rules that removed lead from gasoline, the two largest measured environmental results here, were issued under Republican presidents. The 2021 expanded child tax credit and the Vaccines for Children program passed without Republican votes. Six entries (DL06, DL08, DL12, DL13, DL17 and DL24) rest on models, and each says so in its qualification. The evidence grade on each entry rates the measured result; the qualification says how far it can be carried.

rows.what_was_done: The federal government lent money at low interest to farmer-owned cooperatives to string power lines down roads that private utilities had judged would never pay for themselves.
rows.outcome: About 10 percent of American farms had central-station electricity in the early 1930s; by the mid-1950s farm households had nearly caught up with cities. Counties that received REA loans saw significantly higher crop output, crop productivity and farm land values than comparable counties that did not, and default rates on the loans stayed under 1 percent.
rows.measure: Share of US farms with central-station electric service, 1930s to 1950s (USDA and Federal Reserve historical series); county-level difference-in-differences on farm land values, crop output and productivity, 1930 to 1940 (Kitchens and Fishback).
rows.authorship: Democratic. Executive Order 7037 (Franklin Roosevelt, May 11, 1935), made permanent by the Rural Electrification Act of 1936.
rows.qualification: Kitchens and Fishback find the gains were concentrated in agriculture and that the Rural Electrification Administration had 'much smaller effects on nonagricultural parts of the economy': it did not produce a general rural boom, and the up-front subsidy was large even though the loans were repaid. The program also required the government to overrule a private market judgment about what was worth building, which is the objection its critics raise. The cooperative sector it created later became a politically protected industry that has resisted rate and environmental reform.
rows.source_title: Kitchens and Fishback, 'Flip the Switch: The Impact of the Rural Electrification Administration 1935-1940', NBER Working Paper 19743 (later Journal of Economic History)
rows.loop: Loop R7: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other (running in the improving direction)

rows.what_was_done: The GI Bill paid tuition and a living stipend for any returning veteran who enrolled in school, with no means test and no requirement to prove ability in advance.
rows.outcome: Bound and Turner estimate that World War II service plus the GI Bill raised college completion by roughly 5 to 6 percentage points and added about 0.3 years of education for the affected cohorts of white men, against a counterfactual built from cohorts just too old or too young to serve. Roughly 2.2 million veterans used the education benefit.
rows.measure: Cohort-based instrumental-variables comparison of educational attainment by birth year and state, US Census microdata, men born 1921 to 1933 (Bound and Turner 2002, Journal of Labor Economics).
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, passed unanimously in both chambers, sponsored in the House by Edith Nourse Rogers (R-MA) and signed by Franklin Roosevelt (D).
rows.qualification: The benefit was administered through existing colleges, and Southern institutions excluded Black veterans; Turner and Bound's companion work finds the GI Bill widened the Black-white education gap among Southern-born veterans while narrowing it outside the South. The estimated effect is also smaller than the popular account suggests, a few percentage points of college completion for the affected cohorts, and part of it comes from the war's disruption of schooling separate from the benefit. Later NBER work using linked census records (Kuka, Shenhav and others, 2024) finds that who chose to serve complicates the older estimates.
rows.source_title: Bound and Turner, 'Going to War and Going to College: Did World War II and the G.I. Bill Increase Educational Attainment for Returning Veterans?', Journal of Labor Economics 20(4)

rows.jurisdiction: Grand Rapids, Michigan, then most US municipalities
rows.what_was_done: A city commission voted to add a trace of fluoride to the municipal water supply, and the US Public Health Service measured the children's teeth before and after.
rows.outcome: Grand Rapids was the first fluoridated city in the world; after 15 years the cavity rate among children born after fluoridation began had fallen by roughly 60 percent. CDC's current estimate is that community water fluoridation reduces tooth decay by about 25 percent in children and adults, and that in communities of 1,000 or more people it saves an average of about 20 dollars per dollar spent. In 2022, 209 million people, or 72.3 percent of the US population on public water systems, received fluoridated water.
rows.measure: Caries rates in Grand Rapids schoolchildren, 1945 to 1960 (USPHS/NIDR trial); modern effect size and cost-benefit from CDC's 2024 Scientific Statement on Community Water Fluoridation, population coverage from CDC's 2022 Water Fluoridation Statistics.
rows.authorship: Municipal and nonpartisan. A Grand Rapids city commission decision, with the US Public Health Service running the study; adoption spread city by city through local votes under both parties.
rows.qualification: The modern effect of about 25 percent is much smaller than the 60 percent found in 1945, because fluoride toothpaste now delivers much of the same benefit; the added value of fluoridating water has fallen as the background changed. The documented harm is dental fluorosis, which in its common form is cosmetic. The 2024 National Toxicology Program monograph reported an association between fluoride exposures above 1.5 mg/L and lower childhood IQ, and a 2024 federal court ruling in Food & Water Watch v. EPA ordered EPA to respond under the Toxic Substances Control Act; CDC's statement predates that record and does not address it. Several states and cities have since ended fluoridation. The evidence for the modern effect size also rests largely on studies from before 1975, a weakness the Cochrane reviewers flag.
rows.source_title: CDC, Scientific Statement on Community Water Fluoridation (2024)

rows.what_was_done: Congress created a dedicated gas-tax trust fund and built 41,000 miles of limited-access highway to a single national standard.
rows.outcome: Fernald finds the interstate system delivered a large one-time productivity boost in the 1950s and 1960s, concentrated in vehicle-intensive industries, and that the productivity slowdown after 1973 is partly explained by the fact that the system was finished. Interstates now carry about a quarter of US vehicle miles at roughly half the fatality rate per mile of other roads.
rows.measure: Industry-level productivity growth regressed on road stock, weighted by each industry's vehicle intensity, US 1953 to 1989 (Fernald 1999, American Economic Review); vehicle miles and fatality rates by road class from FHWA and NHTSA.
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, proposed and signed by Dwight Eisenhower (R) and passed by a Democratic Congress.
rows.qualification: Fernald's central finding cuts both ways: 'the interstate system was highly productive, but a second one would not be.' At the margin, road investment is not unusually productive, so the case does not support more highway spending in general. The system also destroyed neighborhoods: federal and congressional estimates put displacement in the hundreds of thousands of households, concentrated in Black urban neighborhoods, and the Department of Transportation has since acknowledged this. Induced demand, the new driving that added road capacity attracts, absorbed much of the capacity added in cities.
rows.source_title: Fernald, 'Roads to Prosperity? Assessing the Link between Public Capital and Productivity', American Economic Review 89(3)
rows.loop: Loop R7: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other (running in the improving direction)

rows.what_was_done: Congress enrolled every American over 65 in a single hospital insurance program and stood it up in under a year, before computers were common in government.
rows.outcome: Roughly 73 percent of people over 65 had no meaningful hospital insurance before Medicare; the program raised coverage by about 75 percentage points in one year, the single largest change in health insurance coverage in US history. Out-of-pocket medical spending fell about 40 percent for the top quartile of elderly spenders and nearly 50 percent for the top decile.
rows.measure: Insurance coverage and the distribution of out-of-pocket medical spending among the elderly, before and after 1965, with non-elderly adults as a comparison group (Finkelstein and McKnight 2008, Journal of Public Economics).
rows.authorship: Democratic. Social Security Amendments of 1965 (Lyndon Johnson), House 313-115 and Senate 68-21, with minority Republican support.
rows.qualification: Finkelstein and McKnight cannot reject the possibility that Medicare had no effect on elderly mortality in its first ten years; their confidence interval runs from zero to a 3.9 percent annual reduction. The measured benefit is protection against catastrophic bills, and a gain in survival was not detected. The authors estimate that this reduction in financial risk alone justifies about two-fifths of Medicare's social cost. Medicare also drove hospital construction and spending growth for decades, and its fee-for-service improper payment rate has repeatedly exceeded 7 percent.
rows.source_title: Finkelstein and McKnight, 'What Did Medicare Do? The Initial Impact of Medicare on Mortality and Out of Pocket Medical Spending', Journal of Public Economics 92(7)

rows.what_was_done: A new federal agency was given power to write binding minimum safety standards for every car sold in America, starting with seat belts and energy-absorbing steering columns.
rows.outcome: NHTSA estimates 613,501 lives saved by vehicle safety technologies and their associated Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards from 1960 through 2012, including 27,621 in 2012 alone; seat belts account for 329,715 of the total. The death rate per 100 million vehicle miles fell from 3.35 in 1975, the first year of comparable federal crash data, to 1.26 in 2023.
rows.measure: Counterfactual removal of each safety technology from FARS crash records using NHTSA's published per-technology effectiveness estimates, 1960 to 2012 (DOT HS 812 069); fatality rate per 100 million VMT from NHTSA's 2023 overview.
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966, passed unanimously in both chambers and signed by Lyndon Johnson (D), after hearings led by Abraham Ribicoff (D) and sustained across every administration since.
rows.qualification: NHTSA calls its own number 'a hypothetical estimate' that assumes effectiveness rates held constant over five decades and that all other factors stayed the same; its crash database (FARS) begins in 1975, so the years 1960 to 1974 are extrapolated. Technologies introduced after 2005 are excluded. The standards also raised vehicle prices, and part of the measured decline belongs to state seat-belt laws, drunk-driving enforcement, trauma care and road design. U.S. fatality rates remain roughly double those of comparable rich countries, so the record shows a large improvement from a high starting point that still trails peer countries.
rows.source_title: NHTSA, 'Lives Saved by Vehicle Safety Technologies and Associated Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards, 1960 to 2012', DOT HS 812 069
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: A payroll tax funds a monthly check that arrives automatically at 62 or 65, indexed to inflation since 1972, with no application review of need.
rows.outcome: Social Security moved 27.6 million people above the Supplemental Poverty Measure threshold in 2023, and 28.8 million in 2025, more than any other program. The official poverty rate for Americans 65 and older fell from 35.2 percent in 1959 to roughly 10 percent today. Administrative costs run about 0.5 percent of benefits paid.
rows.measure: Census Bureau Supplemental Poverty Measure, counterfactual removal of program income, 2023 (Poverty in the United States: 2023, P60-283); Census historical poverty tables for people 65 and older, 1959 to present.
rows.authorship: Bipartisan over time. Social Security Act of 1935 (Franklin Roosevelt, D); automatic cost-of-living indexing and Supplemental Security Income enacted in 1972 and signed by Richard Nixon (R); the 1983 solvency package signed by Ronald Reagan (R) came from a bipartisan commission.
rows.qualification: The Supplemental Poverty Measure comparison is mechanical: it removes the benefit and holds everything else constant, so it does not model how people would have saved or worked without it, and it almost certainly overstates the program's own effect. The low administrative ratio comes partly from the simplicity of mailing checks on a fixed formula with little verification. Other parts of the agency perform worse: the backlog of disability determinations has run into the hundreds of thousands of cases. The trust funds are projected to run out in the mid-2030s, after which scheduled benefits cannot be paid in full without new legislation.
rows.source_title: US Census Bureau, Poverty in the United States: 2023 (P60-283)

rows.what_was_done: Congress set national health-based air quality standards and required EPA to enforce them against states and industry regardless of cost.
rows.outcome: EPA's peer-reviewed second prospective study estimates the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments produced 2.0 trillion dollars in benefits in the year 2020 against 65 billion dollars in costs, a ratio above 30 to 1, and avoided 230,000 adult premature deaths in 2020 alone, along with 17 million lost work days, 2.4 million asthma attacks and 200,000 heart attacks.
rows.measure: Modeled comparison of actual 1990-2020 emissions and air quality against a no-further-controls scenario frozen at 1990 levels, monetized using concentration-response functions and value-of-statistical-life estimates; reviewed by EPA's Science Advisory Board Council.
rows.authorship: Bipartisan, and Republican-signed at both key moments. Clean Air Act of 1970 signed by Richard Nixon (R) after passing the Senate 73-0 and the House 374-1; the 1990 Amendments were proposed and signed by George H. W. Bush (R) and passed 89-10 in the Senate and 401-21 in the House.
rows.qualification: These are modeled benefits; no deaths were counted directly. Nearly all of the monetized benefit comes from one pathway, fewer deaths from fine particles, and it rests on the value of a statistical life (the dollar amount regulators assign to a small reduction in the risk of death), a number economists contest. It also rests on cohort studies whose estimates at low exposures remain debated. EPA's own uncertainty range runs from 3 to 1 to 90 to 1. The costs fall unevenly on coal regions and energy-intensive manufacturing, and the Act's permitting rules are now a leading obstacle to building clean-energy infrastructure quickly.
rows.source_title: EPA, The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act from 1990 to 2020, Second Prospective Study (Final Report, 2011)
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: EPA ordered refiners to take lead out of gasoline on a fixed schedule, over sustained industry objection, and finished the job in 1996.
rows.outcome: The share of American children aged 1 to 5 with blood lead above 10 micrograms per deciliter fell from 88.2 percent in 1976 to 1980 to 8.9 percent in 1988 to 1991; within about a decade, high exposure was removed for nearly a whole generation of children. The geometric mean has kept falling, from 2.23 micrograms per deciliter in 1999 to 2000 to 0.670 in 2017 to 2018.
rows.measure: Measured blood lead in a nationally representative sample of children aged 1 to 5, NHANES II (1976-1980) through NHANES 2017-2018, compiled in EPA's Report on the Environment.
rows.authorship: Bipartisan and Republican-executed. Begun by EPA regulation in 1973 under Richard Nixon (R), sharply accelerated by EPA's 1985 phasedown rule under Ronald Reagan (R), completed by the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments under George H. W. Bush (R).
rows.qualification: This measures lead in children's blood, an exposure. The widely repeated effects on IQ and crime come from separate observational and quasi-experimental studies whose magnitudes are disputed, and the 'lead-crime hypothesis' in particular remains contested. Some of the decline also comes from removing lead from paint, solder and food cans. The work continues: lead service lines still serve millions of households, and Flint showed that government can fail badly on the same metal.
rows.source_title: EPA Report on the Environment, Blood Lead indicator
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: The tax code pays a refundable credit that rises with earnings, so low-wage workers can receive money back even when they owe no income tax, delivered through the return they already file.
rows.outcome: Refundable tax credits, principally the EITC and the refundable portion of the Child Tax Credit, lifted 3.4 million children above the Supplemental Poverty Measure threshold in 2023. In 2018 the two credits together moved 10.6 million people out of poverty. Quasi-experimental work finds EITC expansions raised employment among single mothers.
rows.measure: Census Bureau Supplemental Poverty Measure, counterfactual removal of the credits, 2018 and 2023; employment effects from difference-in-differences on expansion timing and family size (Hoynes and Patel; Eissa and Liebman).
rows.authorship: Bipartisan across four administrations. Created by the Tax Reduction Act of 1975 under Gerald Ford (R), made permanent and greatly expanded by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 under Ronald Reagan (R), expanded again in 1990 under George H. W. Bush (R) and in 1993 under Bill Clinton (D).
rows.qualification: The EITC has the highest improper payment rate of any large federal program: Treasury has estimated 22 to 26 percent of payments improper, and IRS studies have found 28.5 to 39.1 percent of dollars claimed were over-claimed. Most of it comes from errors about where a child lives, a rule the IRS cannot verify, and the sums are large. Rothstein and others argue employers capture part of the credit through lower wages, so firms keep some of the benefit. The credit also does almost nothing for adults without children, and it pays once a year while rent is due every month.
rows.source_title: US Census Bureau, Poverty in the United States: 2023 (P60-283) and Supplemental Poverty Measure releases; Tax Policy Center briefing book on refundable-credit error rates

rows.what_was_done: Congress capped total sulfur dioxide from power plants, handed out tradable allowances, and required continuous emissions monitors on every smokestack so the count could not be disputed.
rows.outcome: Annual sulfur dioxide emissions from covered power plants fell by more than 95 percent and nitrogen oxides by more than 89 percent from their 1990 and 1995 baselines. Wet sulfate deposition dropped more than 70 percent between 1989-1991 and 2020-2022, and monitored surface waters showed an 81 percent improvement in critical load exceedances. Compliance cost came in far below both industry and EPA pre-enactment projections.
rows.measure: Continuous emission monitoring system data reported from every covered unit, 1990 to 2022, with deposition measured by the National Atmospheric Deposition Program (EPA Acid Rain Program Results).
rows.authorship: Republican-authored. Title IV of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, proposed by George H. W. Bush (R) and designed around a market mechanism the administration chose deliberately over command-and-control; passed with large bipartisan majorities.
rows.qualification: Later emission cuts are not all due to the Acid Rain Program: EPA says the totals come from the program 'working together with' the Cross-State Air Pollution Rule and other regulations, and cheap natural gas displaced coal for reasons unrelated to the cap. Acidified lakes and forest soils have recovered more slowly than the deposition numbers suggest, because the soils lost minerals that buffer acid. The program's success is also often over-generalized: sulfur dioxide from a few hundred large smokestacks is a far easier trading problem than carbon from the whole economy.
rows.source_title: EPA, Acid Rain Program Results
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: The federal government buys childhood vaccines in bulk and gives them free to any provider treating an uninsured or Medicaid-eligible child, so a family's insurance status stops determining whether the child is vaccinated.
rows.outcome: CDC estimates that routine childhood immunization among the roughly 117 million children born in 1994 to 2023 prevented 508 million lifetime cases of illness, 32 million hospitalizations and 1,129,000 deaths, saving 540 billion dollars in direct costs and 2.7 trillion dollars in costs to society. The benefit-cost ratio is 3.3 to 1 from the payer's view and 10.9 to 1 from society's.
rows.measure: Disease-specific models comparing observed vaccination coverage with pre-vaccine incidence for each of the routinely recommended childhood vaccines, birth cohorts 1994-2023 (Zhou et al., MMWR 2024;73:682-685).
rows.authorship: Democratic. The Vaccines for Children program was created in the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1993 (Bill Clinton), which passed without a single Republican vote, after the 1989-1991 measles epidemic killed more than 100 children.
rows.qualification: These are modeled comparisons against disease rates before vaccines, without a controlled comparison group. They credit the whole effect of routine childhood immunization to the period and do not isolate the program's own contribution; private insurance and school mandates would have delivered much of it. Coverage gains have stalled and reversed since 2020: kindergarten vaccination coverage has fallen for several years in a row, exemptions are at record highs, and the United States recorded its largest measles outbreaks in decades in 2025 and 2026, putting its measles elimination status at risk. The program is an entitlement whose funding and advisory structure have both come under direct political pressure.
rows.source_title: Zhou F, Jatlaoui TC, Leidner AJ, et al., 'Health and Economic Benefits of Routine Childhood Immunizations in the Era of the Vaccines for Children Program - United States, 1994-2023', MMWR 2024;73:682-685
rows.loop: Loop R7: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other (running in the improving direction)

rows.what_was_done: The Defense Department built a satellite navigation system. A Republican president opened it to civilian use, and a Democratic president switched off the deliberate degradation of the civilian signal, giving the whole economy a free and precise location service.
rows.outcome: A study for the Commerce Department estimates GPS generated roughly 1.4 trillion dollars in economic benefit to the US private sector from 1984 through 2017, with about 90 percent of it accruing after 2010, measured against a counterfactual in which a Loran-based ground network would have been built instead.
rows.measure: Sector-by-sector benefit estimation across telecommunications, agriculture, surveying, location-based services, electricity, oil and gas, mining, maritime and finance, based on industry interviews and a stated Loran-C counterfactual (RTI International for NIST, June 2019).
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. Built by the Department of Defense; opened to civilian use by Ronald Reagan (R) in 1983 after the KAL 007 shootdown; Selective Availability, which deliberately degraded civilian accuracy, was ended by Bill Clinton (D) on May 1, 2000.
rows.qualification: The authors say the figure should be read as 'a rough order of magnitude' and give a range of 903 billion to 1.8 trillion dollars, a factor of two. It is a contractor study built on industry self-reports, without a peer-reviewed design for isolating cause. The comparison case is a judgment call: assuming a Loran network would have been built lowers the estimate, and no one can verify what would have happened. It is the best-documented version of the 'space program spinoff' claim. The widely quoted figures of 7 or 14 dollars returned per dollar of NASA spending lack a stated comparison and are left out of this log. GPS is also a single point of failure the country now depends on, with no funded civilian backup.
rows.source_title: RTI International for the National Institute of Standards and Technology, 'Economic Benefits of the Global Positioning System (GPS)', June 2019

rows.what_was_done: The Veterans Health Administration was rebuilt around primary care, a universal electronic health record and public performance measurement, at a time when almost no private hospital had any of the three.
rows.outcome: A RAND assessment covering all 135 VA hospitals against matched non-VA hospitals found VA performed the same or significantly better on all 6 patient-safety measures, all 3 mortality measures and 12 effectiveness measures, and worse on 3 readmission measures and 2 effectiveness measures. In outpatient care, VA outperformed commercial and Medicaid HMOs on all 16 effectiveness measures and Medicare HMOs on 14 of 16.
rows.measure: Nationally recognized inpatient and outpatient quality measures, VA facilities versus matched non-VA comparators, 2013-2014 data (Price et al., Journal of General Internal Medicine, 2018), consistent with three earlier systematic reviews.
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. The reorganization was led by Under Secretary Kenneth Kizer under Bill Clinton (D) and enabled by the Veterans' Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996, passed by a Republican Congress; every administration since has sustained the electronic record and the measurement regime.
rows.qualification: The study did not examine access or timeliness, where the VA has failed most visibly. In 2014 the Phoenix VA was found to have kept unofficial wait lists, and the VA and GAO have documented manipulated scheduling data at multiple facilities; the quality of care once a veteran is seen is a separate measure from getting care when it is needed. The VA also treats a selected population, and matching on measured characteristics does not fully control for that. The comparison uses 2013 to 2014 data, and the shift of care to community providers under the MISSION Act has since moved a growing share of veterans' care outside the system these measures cover.
rows.source_title: Price RA, Sloss EM, Cefalu M, et al., 'Comparing Quality of Care in Veterans Affairs and Non-Veterans Affairs Settings', Journal of General Internal Medicine 33(10)
rows.loop: Loop R7: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other (running in the improving direction)

rows.what_was_done: The city raised its cigarette excise tax from 8 cents to 1.50 dollars a pack, banned smoking in every indoor workplace including bars, and ran a graphic television campaign.
rows.outcome: Adult smoking prevalence in New York City fell from 21.5 percent in 2002 to 17.5 percent in 2006, a 19 percent relative decline and about 240,000 fewer smokers, while the national rate was close to flat. The decline continued afterward, to roughly 14 percent by 2010.
rows.measure: NYC Community Health Survey, annual random-digit-dial survey of adults, 2002 to 2006, reported in CDC MMWR 2007;56(24):604-608.
rows.authorship: Bipartisan at the city level. Mayor Michael Bloomberg, elected as a Republican, with Health Commissioner Thomas Frieden; the Smoke-Free Air Act of 2002 was passed by a Democratic City Council.
rows.qualification: CDC's own limitations section says the data are self-reported and open to social-desirability bias, that the survey excludes households without landlines, and that the study cannot separate the media campaign's effect from the tax, the smoke-free law or longer trends. This design cannot assign the result to any one measure. The tax also falls hardest on lower-income smokers and fed a large illegal cigarette market, and bar owners, who bore the disruption, strongly opposed the indoor smoking ban.
rows.source_title: CDC, 'Decline in Smoking Prevalence - New York City, 2002-2006', MMWR 2007;56(24)

rows.what_was_done: After Hurricane Andrew destroyed 63,000 homes, Florida tightened its building codes and then replaced a patchwork of local codes with one statewide code with real inspection behind it.
rows.outcome: After Hurricane Charley in 2004, an insurance-industry analysis of actual claims found homes built after the strengthened codes took effect had 40 percent lower claim frequency and 60 percent lower claim severity than older homes in the same storm. Later IBHS and CoreLogic work found modern-code homes had roughly half the post-hurricane mortgage delinquency rate.
rows.measure: Insurance claim frequency and severity by year of construction for homes exposed to Hurricane Charley, 2004 (Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety post-hurricane investigation).
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. Post-Andrew code strengthening and the 1998 statute creating a statewide Florida Building Code were enacted under Governor Lawton Chiles (D) with a Republican-led legislature; the statewide code took effect in March 2002 under Governor Jeb Bush (R), who defended it against rollback.
rows.qualification: The comparison is between newer and older houses, which differ in more than code compliance: construction quality, siting, materials and owner wealth all vary with the year a house was built, so the estimate is not cleanly causal. The Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety is funded by insurers, who have an interest in stronger codes. Codes raise construction costs and therefore housing prices, a real burden in a state with high housing costs, and Florida's legislature has repeatedly weakened code provisions since 2017. Better codes have not prevented Florida's property insurance market from becoming one of the most expensive and unstable in the country.
rows.source_title: Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety, Hurricane Charley building performance report; '10 Years After Hurricane Charley: A Lesson in Strong Building Codes', Insurance Journal

rows.what_was_done: The United States bought and delivered antiretroviral drugs at scale to countries where HIV treatment had been considered logistically impossible.
rows.outcome: PEPFAR reports an estimated 26 million lives saved since 2003, 20.1 million people supported on antiretroviral treatment, 5.5 million babies born HIV-free to mothers living with HIV, and 340,000 health workers trained, for total appropriations of just over 130 billion dollars.
rows.measure: Program monitoring data on patients on treatment and modeled mortality averted against a no-treatment counterfactual, reported annually by the State Department and corroborated by UNAIDS epidemiological estimates.
rows.authorship: Republican-initiated and bipartisan. Announced by George W. Bush (R) in the 2003 State of the Union and authorized by the United States Leadership Against HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria Act of 2003, which passed the House 375-41 and the Senate by voice vote; reauthorized repeatedly under both parties.
rows.qualification: The lives-saved figure is modeled. PEPFAR's own results page reports people on treatment and babies born HIV-free and gives no lives-saved number; the 26 million comes from program estimates that share credit with the Global Fund, national health ministries and generic drug makers whose price cuts made treatment affordable. The original earmark for abstinence and faithfulness programs took a third of prevention funding, and Lo, Lowe and Bendavid (Health Affairs, 2016) found no measurable effect on sexual behavior from it. In 2025 the program was restricted to a narrow waiver for 'life-saving services', USAID was dissolved, and new treatment enrollments, testing and PrEP starts all fell measurably; that drop is itself evidence the program was delivering care.
rows.source_title: Kaiser Family Foundation, 'The U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)'; US Department of State, PEPFAR Results and Impact
rows.loop: Loop R7: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other (running in the improving direction)

rows.what_was_done: During the worst federal disaster failure in modern memory, one agency positioned its aircraft and crews outside the storm track in advance and started flying rescues before the water stopped rising.
rows.outcome: GAO reports the Coast Guard rescued or evacuated more than 33,500 people during Hurricane Katrina, out of an estimated 60,000 who needed rescue, with no aircraft accidents. GAO attributed the performance to up-to-date and regularly exercised hurricane plans, standardized operations that let crews from anywhere in the country plug in, geographically dispersed assets, and explicit authority for on-scene initiative.
rows.measure: Rescue and evacuation counts and operational assessment, Hurricane Katrina response, August-September 2005 (GAO-06-903).
rows.authorship: Nonpartisan agency performance under a Republican administration. The capability was built over decades of statutory search-and-rescue authority and sustained funding under both parties; no new law produced it.
rows.qualification: This is a success inside a catastrophe. FEMA and the state and city governments failed so badly that roughly 1,400 people died, and the Coast Guard's own work was hampered by the failures GAO names: communications collapsed, food, water and fuel ran short, rescue swimmers faced threats to their safety from desperate evacuees, and 'different organizations involved in search and rescue did not always coordinate with each other.' The rescue counts are the agency's own reports. The case supports a narrow lesson: advance positioning, standard procedures and delegated authority made the difference for this agency. It says little about how government responds to disasters in general.
rows.source_title: GAO, 'Coast Guard: Observations on the Preparation, Response, and Recovery Missions Related to Hurricane Katrina', GAO-06-903
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: A Republican governor and a Democratic legislature required everyone to carry health insurance, subsidized it for people who could not afford it, and got the uninsured rate to the lowest in the country.
rows.outcome: All-cause mortality among non-elderly adults fell 2.9 percent in Massachusetts relative to matched control counties, and mortality from causes treatable by medical care fell 4.5 percent: an absolute decrease of 8.2 deaths per 100,000 adults. The authors estimate one death prevented per year for roughly every 830 adults who gained coverage. The uninsured rate fell 6.8 percentage points, a 57 percent relative decline.
rows.measure: County-level difference-in-differences comparing Massachusetts counties with demographically matched counties in other states, 2001-2005 versus 2007-2010 (Sommers, Long and Baicker, Annals of Internal Medicine 160(9)).
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. Chapter 58 of the Acts of 2006, signed by Governor Mitt Romney (R) and passed by a Democratic legislature 37-0 in the Senate and 154-2 in the House, building on a framework developed with Senator Edward Kennedy (D).
rows.qualification: The authors state that the design is 'nonrandomized' and 'subject to unmeasured confounders', so it cannot establish causation, and that Massachusetts, which is richer, healthier and has more doctors than average, may not generalize. A 2015 reanalysis by Kaestner using randomization inference found the mortality result was not statistically distinguishable from chance. The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment, a randomized trial, found clear financial and mental-health benefits from Medicaid coverage and no statistically significant effect on physical health measures over two years. The mandate was also coercive and unpopular in its first years, and Massachusetts health costs remained among the nation's highest.
rows.source_title: Sommers BD, Long SK, Baicker K, 'Changes in Mortality After Massachusetts Health Care Reform: A Quasi-experimental Study', Annals of Internal Medicine 2014;160(9):585-593

rows.what_was_done: California's workplace safety agency chose firms for inspection by lottery, which let researchers measure what an inspection does.
rows.outcome: Randomly inspected firms had 9.4 percent fewer injuries than control firms in the four years after inspection and 26 percent lower workers' compensation costs, an average saving of about 355,000 dollars per inspected firm, with no detectable effect on employment, sales, credit rating or firm survival.
rows.measure: Randomized comparison of 409 inspected California firms against 409 matched uninspected firms drawn from the same lottery pool, injury and workers' compensation outcomes tracked four years post-inspection (Levine, Toffel and Johnson, Science 2012;336:907-911).
rows.authorship: Nonpartisan agency operation. Cal/OSHA operates under a state plan approved by federal OSHA, created by the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, which was signed by Richard Nixon (R); the inspection lotteries ran under both Republican and Democratic governors.
rows.qualification: This covers one state, one agency and one population, high-hazard California firms eligible for the lottery, so the effect size should not be assumed to hold for OSHA nationally, for low-hazard industries or for today's inspection practice. The finding of no job loss is the paper's most disputed claim and has been challenged for lack of statistical power: the confidence intervals do not rule out modest employment effects. The result says nothing about whether OSHA's standards are well chosen, only that enforcing the existing ones paid. Federal OSHA inspects a small share of workplaces each year, so the study describes a tool that is rarely used at national scale.
rows.source_title: Levine DI, Toffel MW, Johnson MS, 'Randomized Government Safety Inspections Reduce Worker Injuries with No Detectable Job Loss', Science 2012;336(6083):907-911
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: NOAA ran public supercomputers, satellites and hurricane hunter aircraft, and published its own forecast errors every year so anyone could check whether the forecasts were getting better.
rows.outcome: National Hurricane Center Atlantic track forecast errors at 24 to 72 hours have fallen by about 75 percent over the past few decades. In 2024 the center set accuracy records at every forecast time: mean track errors of 28.0 nautical miles at 24 hours, 45.4 at 48 hours, 66.9 at 72 hours and 115.3 at 120 hours, improvements of 23 to 39 percent over the prior five-year means. A 3-day forecast today is more accurate than a 1-day forecast was in 1990.
rows.measure: NHC's annual forecast verification against best-track positions, Atlantic basin, 1990 to 2024 (NHC Forecast Verification Report 2024).
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. NOAA's forecast improvement programs were funded across administrations; the Hurricane Forecast Improvement Program grew out of post-Katrina appropriations under George W. Bush (R), and the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act of 2017 passed both chambers with broad bipartisan support and was signed by Donald Trump (R).
rows.qualification: Better track forecasts do not save lives on their own: evacuation decisions, building codes, storm-surge modeling and public compliance all sit between the forecast and the outcome. Intensity forecasting has improved far more slowly than track forecasting, which is why rapid intensification still produces surprises. Some of the gain comes from global models funded by other countries and from commercial satellite data. The verification is also reported by the agency being measured, though the best-track record is reconstructed independently. Staffing reductions at the National Weather Service in 2025 raised documented concerns about sustaining the observation network these forecasts depend on.
rows.source_title: National Hurricane Center Forecast Verification Report, 2024 Hurricane Season
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: For six months the Child Tax Credit was made fully refundable, raised, and paid out monthly, so families got the money whether or not they earned enough to owe tax.
rows.outcome: Child poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure fell from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021 as first published, a 46 percent decline and the lowest on record at the time. The Child Tax Credit alone lifted 5.3 million people out of poverty, including 2.9 million children. When the expansion lapsed, child poverty rose to 12.4 percent in 2022 as first published, putting 5.2 million more children below the line in a single year.
rows.measure: Census Bureau Supplemental Poverty Measure, 2020, 2021 and 2022, with counterfactual removal of the credit (Census, 'Expansions to Child Tax Credit Contributed to 46% Decline in Child Poverty Since 2020').
rows.authorship: Democratic, without a single Republican vote. American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (P.L. 117-2), signed by Joe Biden; the expansion was written to expire at the end of 2021 and was not renewed.
rows.qualification: Corinth, Meyer, Stadnicki and Wu argued that full refundability would reduce employment among single parents enough to offset a meaningful share of the poverty reduction. Later empirical work using 2021 data (Ananat and coauthors; Schild and coauthors at the Census Bureau and IRS) found no detectable employment decline, but the debate is open, and one year of data cannot settle long-run effects on work. The poverty comparison is mechanical and does not model changes in behavior. The expansion cost roughly 100 billion dollars for one year and was written to be temporary. It shows how fast the rate can move; keeping it there would take a law that stays in force. When the policy stopped, the same measure recorded a record one-year rise. Census revised its Supplemental Poverty Measure estimates for 2019 to 2024 in August 2026 after a correction to the poverty thresholds, so the figures here are the rates as first published.
rows.source_title: US Census Bureau, 'Expansions to Child Tax Credit Contributed to 46% Decline in Child Poverty Since 2020'

rows.what_was_done: Congress funds auditors who are independent of the agencies they audit, and they publish what they find whether or not the agency wants it published.
rows.outcome: GAO reported 67.5 billion dollars in financial benefits in fiscal 2024, about 76 dollars returned for every dollar spent on GAO, plus 1,232 other measurable benefits. The 74 federal Inspectors General reported roughly 71.1 billion dollars in combined potential savings, questioned costs and investigative recoveries against an aggregate 3.9 billion dollar budget, an approximate 18-to-1 return, along with 3,917 indictments and 3,675 successful criminal prosecutions.
rows.measure: Self-reported financial benefits attributable to audit recommendations implemented, fiscal year 2024 (GAO Performance and Accountability Report; CIGIE Annual Report to the President and Congress FY2024).
rows.authorship: Bipartisan. GAO was created by the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 under Warren Harding (R); the Inspector General Act of 1978 was signed by Jimmy Carter (D) and has been strengthened under both parties.
rows.qualification: Both figures are reported by the organizations claiming credit, using their own rules for attribution, and neither is independently audited. 'Potential savings' and 'funds put to better use' estimate what would happen if recommendations were carried out, and many never are; GAO's own priority recommendations often stay open for years. Questioned costs are not recoveries. The comparison case is also weak: agencies, courts or the press would have found some of the savings anyway. The independence that gives the work its value is fragile: at least 17 inspectors general were removed in January 2025 without the 30-day notice and case-specific reasons the statute requires.
rows.source_title: GAO, 'GAO's Work Led to $67.5 Billion in Financial Benefits'; CIGIE, Annual Report to the President and Congress, Fiscal Year 2024
rows.loop: Loop B1a: Independent oversight can limit policy favoritism

rows.what_was_done: The Congressional Budget Office estimated how federal revenue changes when the IRS hires more enforcement staff, so the return on an enforcement dollar became a number Congress could score.
rows.outcome: CBO uses a benchmark return on investment of 6.4, meaning about 6.40 dollars of revenue for each dollar of IRS enforcement spending over several years, including the indirect effect that audited taxpayers voluntarily pay about 20 percent more in later years and some unaudited taxpayers modestly increase payments as well.
rows.measure: CBO's revenue model for IRS enforcement appropriations, with diminishing returns applied above a roughly 10 billion dollar base, 2024-2034 window (CBO, 'How Changes in Funding for the IRS Affect Revenues', February 2024).
rows.authorship: Nonpartisan analysis of a contested policy. CBO is a bipartisan congressional agency; the funding it scored: 80 billion dollars in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022: passed with no Republican votes, and subsequent rescissions were Republican-led.
rows.qualification: The return falls as spending rises. CBO applies explicit diminishing returns: the return drops 10 percent for every 10 percent increase in enforcement spending above the base, and it decays 3 percent a year after 2026 as taxpayers adapt, so the return on a large new amount is far below 6.4. CBO scored an additional 80 billion dollars at roughly 2.5 to 1 net. The estimate comes from a model and holds voluntary compliance by corporations constant. Critics, including the Ways and Means Committee majority and EPIC for America, argue that collected revenue has lagged projections. Enforcement also imposes compliance burdens on taxpayers who did nothing wrong, and audit rates have historically fallen hardest on EITC claimants, the poorest filers, because those audits are cheap, so the return-per-dollar logic can point audits at the people least able to bear them.
rows.source_title: Congressional Budget Office, 'How Changes in Funding for the IRS Affect Revenues' (February 2024)
rows.loop: Loop R7: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other (running in the improving direction)

outcomes.question: If the reforms in this Atlas were carried out, what would they likely change, and what else would be needed?

answer.text: Most likely to improve, and soonest. Protection for the career civil service, IRS enforcement, remedies for inspectors general, congressional staff, automatic continuing resolutions and in-house digital service teams have the best-identified evidence and work through administration within two to five years. They also reverse fastest: a change made by executive order can last as little as one administration, and one made by statute as little as one Congress.

Transfers change poverty in the year they pay, as the 2021 child tax credit showed. Stock prices drive the top 1% share of wealth, which reached a record 32.5% in the second quarter of 2026; taxes on capital act over decades, and avoidance is large. More housing supply narrows the wealth gap between owners and renters, which is a different gap from the top 1% share.

The reforms mostly change structure: who draws maps, who decides nominations, whether political money is visible, how often justices are appointed, and whether a referee such as the Federal Election Commission can act. Evidence that any of them lowers affective polarization, the hostility partisans feel toward the other party, is weak.

Economic performance would change least in the near term. Public research pays high returns over the long run, and competition remedies lower prices one sector at a time. No promise of faster overall growth follows from these reforms.

outcomes.why_not_one_number: The four outcome families use different units. A reform can improve one while imposing a cost on another, and the evidence behind each estimate differs in quality. Keeping the families separate lets readers see those tradeoffs; adding them into one score would hide them.
outcomes.weakest_joints: Enforcement and durability are where reforms most often break down. Disclosure rules need a Federal Election Commission able to act, a stock-trading ban enforced by members of Congress themselves needs an outside check, and protection for inspectors general must now work within Trump v. Slaughter. Administrative changes can be reversed by the next administration. The order of steps differs by route. On the state track, a ballot initiative can change nomination rules first. On the federal track, the Senate's decision about the filibuster comes before any statute changing election or governing rules. Tax and transfer items can pass by budget reconciliation without waiting for either.
changes_required: Give every reform an enforcer and a plan for lasting past the next election before counting it as done.
Build delivery capacity first or alongside the equality measures it delivers: R-17: Protect a professional career civil service and R-39: Build public teams that can deliver digital services.
Evaluate the Alaska and Massachusetts nomination systems, and a pilot of proportional representation in one state legislative chamber, before claiming effects.
Consider options that strengthen parties next to primary reform: R-47: Allow fusion voting and consider public support for parties.
Keep term limits visible as a rejected option, with the evidence against them: R-35: Legislative term limits: rejected option.

Treat the technology reforms as narrow tools that change exposure, pricing data or notice, with no claim that they cure polarization: R-37: Give users feed choices and researchers usable data; R-38: Limit competitors' use of shared private data to set prices; R-40: Give workers notice and a voice when employers use AI; R-44: Open digital platform markets to effective competition.

outcomes.indicator_note: Each indicator gives its latest reading and two thresholds for 2036. The success threshold marks a clear improvement the reforms would aim for. The hold threshold marks the line below which conditions would be getting worse. Both are teaching benchmarks for judging results, and neither is a forecast.
outcomes.effect_codes_note: Reform profiles use these codes to show the expected direction and rough size of an effect on each outcome family. The codes are conditional on the reform working as described, and codes for different families are never added together.

scenarios.intro: Each scenario states a set of assumptions and gives the direction each outcome family would take if those assumptions hold. These are conditional directions. They make no forecast of what will happen and give no odds that any assumption comes true. The four outcome families are read separately and never added together. A scenario shows a number only when it names the method and the inputs behind it.

items.name: Baseline: no reform beyond current law
assumptions: Current law, including the 2025 budget law (P.L. 119-21) and P.L. 119-75, runs as written
The Senate keeps the legislative filibuster
Recent trends in executive action and court rulings continue

DQ.why: Mid-decade redraws and the narrower Section 2 standard after Louisiana v. Callais raise C4: Officeholders' control over election rules. The Federal Election Commission stays without a quorum.

GE.why: Workforce losses, funding lapses and closed digital service teams weigh on D5: Quality of public services.

EP.why: Productivity grows near its recent trend; tariffs add costs.

EQ.why: Stock prices push the top 1% share to records, and the 2025 law shifts resources toward higher-income households.

watch: Top 1% share of wealth each quarter

items.name: State and local track by 2030
assumptions: Initiatives and statutes pass in some states: nomination rules, local elections moved onto the statewide calendar, housing allowed by right, wage floors and child credits
Federal administrative capacity is restored only if the administration that takes office in 2029 chooses to restore it

DQ.why: C2: How often the primary decides the winner falls where nomination rules change, and local turnout rises when local elections share the ballot with statewide contests.

GE.why: State capacity rises where it is funded; federal capacity follows the administration.

EP.dir: slightly up in metro areas that reform housing rules
EP.why: New housing supply takes three to ten years to arrive.

EQ.dir: up for renters and low-income families in reform states
EQ.why: Wage floors, credits and housing supply help; top shares barely move.

items.interactions: More housing supply (R-30: Allow more homes under clear rules near jobs and transit) helps renters while slowing some owners' gains in home value. Moving local elections onto the statewide calendar (R-06: Hold local elections alongside major November elections) makes new supply politically easier, because a broader electorate votes.

items.name: A coherent federal package
assumptions: A Senate majority changes the filibuster and uses the change first on rules for elections and government
Statutes pass on the civil service, inspectors general, emergency powers, tariffs and public research
A permanent refundable child credit passes through budget reconciliation

DQ.dir: up on structure; uncertain on behavior
DQ.why: Maps, the visibility of political money and the schedule of court appointments change; evidence that any of it lowers affective polarization is weak.

GE.why: Capacity measures have the best-identified evidence and work through administration in two to five years.

EQ.dir: up quickly on income; slowly on wealth

Appropriations bills passed through regular order

overlays.name: Race and ethnicity
overlays.intro: The same rule on housing, savings or voting reaches households differently by race because of differences in what they own and in how voting rules apply to them.

through: L38: connection from A5 (Housing scarcity) to A6 (Homeowners' equity)
mechanisms.how: Home equity is the main asset of middle-class households, and ownership rates differ: 74.5% of non-Hispanic white householders own their homes, 45.4% of Black householders and 48.1% of Hispanic householders (second quarter 2026). The same rise in house prices therefore moves each group's wealth differently.

through: LE09: connection from EC4 (Concentration of stock ownership) to A1 (Concentration of household wealth)
mechanisms.how: Stock ownership is concentrated, and white households hold most corporate equity, so wealth growth led by stock prices widens racial gaps.

through: C4: Officeholders' control over election rules
L44: connection from C4 (Officeholders' control over election rules) to B5 (Equality of voter turnout)
mechanisms.how: Rules on voting access and districting reach groups differently after Shelby County v. Holder (2013) and Louisiana v. Callais (2026). Callais requires evidence supporting a strong inference of intentional discrimination before Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is violated.

comparisons.text: Median net worth in 2022: white households $285,000, Black households $44,900, Hispanic households $61,600
White households held 92.4% of household wealth in 2019 while making up 73% of households

overlays.counterevidence: Studies of how Shelby County changed turnout disagree. Voter-file estimates from the Brennan Center, an advocacy research group, using race estimated from names and addresses, find the white-Black turnout gap grew about 5 points by 2022. Komisarchik and White find no significant widening through 2020 when areas are weighted by Black population. Billings and coauthors, using another design, find 1 to 2 points.
overlays.limits: Race in voter files is often estimated from names and addresses. Asian American and American Indian samples are small in most of the surveys used here.

overlays.name: Historical exclusion
overlays.intro: Rules written decades ago still shape who owns homes and wealth today, because those rules set the starting amounts that later gains build on.

mechanisms.how: A federal housing program in the 1930s graded neighborhoods for lending risk, with race part of the grading. Places just inside the lowest grade had house values about 27% lower by 1980, a gap that faded to about 2.6% by 2010.

through: EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits
mechanisms.how: The 1935 Social Security Act excluded agricultural and domestic workers. That covered about 65% of employed Black workers and 27% of employed white workers, though 74% of the excluded workers were white.

GI Bill benefits raised education and homeownership for white men and for Black men born outside the South far more than for Black men born in the South. The home loans raised ownership for both Black and white veterans and widened the gap between them.

overlays.counterevidence: The Federal Housing Administration restricted lending before the 1930s neighborhood maps were drawn, and the agency that drew them lent widely in Black neighborhoods; the maps had little effect on where that agency lent. Whether the 1935 exclusion was racially motivated or a matter of administrative feasibility is disputed; one study argues administrative feasibility.
overlays.limits: Past rules can still affect accumulated wealth and the places people live. A6: Homeowners' equity and EC8: Household assets and debts carry those inherited starting levels. The map does not draw the historical rules as feedback loops operating today.

overlays.name: Disability
overlays.intro: People with disabilities meet the same labor market, benefit rules and polling places on different terms, and some benefit rules limit how much they may save.

mechanisms.how: In 2025, 22.8% of people with a disability were employed, compared with 65.2% of people without one.

through: EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits
mechanisms.how: Supplemental Security Income counts savings above $2,000 ($3,000 for a couple) against eligibility, a limit unchanged since 1989. Adjusted for inflation since 1972, it would be about $9,929. The rule caps the savings of people who rely on the program.
In 2022, 14.0% of voters with a disability reported difficulty voting, compared with 4.1% of voters without one.

overlays.limits: Disability is self-reported, and surveys define it differently.

overlays.name: Gender
overlays.intro: Rules on pay, care and representation reach women and men differently, partly because unpaid care work falls unevenly.

mechanisms.how: Women working full time, year-round earned 83.9% of men's median earnings in 2025. By a separate measure of weekly earnings, women earned 82.0% of men's in the second quarter of 2026.

Averaged over everyone 15 and older, women spent 2.38 hours a day on household activities in 2025 and men 1.58 hours. Mothers of children under 6 spent 2.8 hours a day on primary child care and fathers 1.7 hours. Care costs and care time land unevenly.
Women hold 150 seats in Congress in 2026, 28% of the total.

overlays.limits: The annual and weekly earnings ratios cover different populations. The American Time Use Survey lost data from September 30 to November 11, 2025 during the shutdown.

overlays.name: Geography
overlays.intro: Where a person grows up and lives shapes which services are within reach and how much their vote can change a result.

mechanisms.how: Children's adult outcomes move toward those typical of the place where they grow up, by about 4% for each year they live there.

through: TC5: Government's ability to build and run digital services
mechanisms.how: 197 rural hospitals have closed or converted to other uses since 2005. Broadband at 100 megabits per second download and 20 upload is missing for 28% of rural residents and 23% of people on tribal lands. In 2023, 54% of households earning under $25,000 had both home and mobile internet, compared with 80% of households earning $100,000 or more. Plans under the federal Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment program have been approved for 54 of 56 states and territories, covering about 4 million locations.

through: C1: Seats with little electoral competition
D7: Entrenched control of rule-setting institutions
D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition
mechanisms.how: Every state has two senators whatever its population, and people who vote alike tend to live near each other (X2: Population patterns and residential sorting). Together these make seats safe and majorities durable without anyone drawing a district line.

overlays.limits: County and commuting-zone averages hide wide variation within places.

overlays.name: Immigration status
overlays.intro: Immigration status changes which benefits a person can receive and what protection a worker has, while census counts include residents who cannot vote.

through: EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits
mechanisms.how: The 2025 budget law narrowed SNAP food-aid eligibility for many lawfully present noncitizens and narrowed Medicaid and CHIP eligibility effective October 1, 2026.
Foreign-born workers were 19.1% of the civilian labor force in 2025. Workers without legal status have weaker legal remedies against retaliation by employers.
The census count used to divide House seats includes all residents, while only citizens vote, so noncitizen residents affect how many seats a state has, while citizens alone decide who wins them.

overlays.limits: Estimates of the unauthorized population come from statistical models. The Atlas records no one's status and never asks readers for it.

overlays.name: Tribal sovereignty
overlays.intro: Tribes are governments, so this overlay asks whose government has authority as well as how outcomes differ.

through: EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits
mechanisms.how: In 2017 the Indian Health Service spent $4,078 per person, compared with $8,109 per person in Medicaid, though the two programs differ in scope.

through: D3: Court rulings favoring the appointing coalition
mechanisms.how: McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) held that the Creek reservation was never disestablished. Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022) gave states authority alongside the federal government over crimes by non-Indians against Indians in Indian country. Court doctrine decides whose government acts.

through: C4: Officeholders' control over election rules
mechanisms.how: Field hearings documented barriers to voting on reservations from distance, missing street addresses and ID rules; this is testimony, without a representative survey.

through: TC5: Government's ability to build and run digital services
mechanisms.how: In 2021, 71% of American Indian and Alaska Native households on tribal land had broadband, compared with 90% nationally, which limits online access to services.

overlays.limits: Tribal sovereignty concerns the authority of governments. This overlay therefore examines governing power as well as differences in outcomes.

overlays.name: Age and generation
overlays.intro: Rules on housing and benefits move resources between age groups, because older households own more homes and receive the largest income-support program.

mechanisms.how: Homeownership for householders under 35 was 35.2% in the second quarter of 2026, and median net worth for families headed by someone under 35 was $39,000 in 2022. Housing scarcity (A5: Housing scarcity) moves wealth from young renters to older owners.

through: EC6: Net support from taxes and public benefits
mechanisms.how: Social Security moved 28.8 million people out of poverty under the Supplemental Poverty Measure in 2025. Child poverty depends on credits that expire.

overlays.limits: Effects of age and of the year a person was born are hard to separate in data collected at one point in time.

overlays.name: Voting-rights restoration
overlays.intro: State rules on voting after a felony conviction decide whether millions of adults living in their communities can vote.

mechanisms.how: About 4.05 million people, 1.7% of the voting-age population, could not vote in 2024 because of a felony conviction; 72% of them were living in the community. The rate for Black Americans was 4.5%.

overlays.limits: The estimate comes from the Sentencing Project, an advocacy research group, using state data. State rules change often.

omissions.would_add: A sourced mechanism, for example in benefits, employment law or ballot access, with current data.
